sections.title: Basics first
sections.norm: basics first. feudal modern power = nature of power to centralize itself nation is country = territory state = military state police state kingdom empire company state nation state family pvt company ngo political party common man motive primary purpose of any constitution modern state structure vertically centralised horizontal separation of powers sovereignty = a small kingdom in central asia french revolution 1789 constitution of india 1950. 1 feudal is something which is old in time & regressive while modern is something new in time & progressive. hence, old can be gold like lata mangeshkar. father of modern india, raja ram mohun roy wanted us to go back to pure past of vedantic traditions. hence what is old is not always feudal or backward. 2. power = economic + political (decision making) + military + social (influence over people or awe in heart of people) + intellectual/technological + spiritual. increase/decrease in one power leads to increase/decrease in other powers. e.g. social media influencer's popularity leads to his/her economic power increase while a scandal can hurt political power of a politician. 3 it is in nature of power to centralize itself in strong personality (human/institution). however if personality weakens then power leaves either vertically downwards (decentralization) or via horizontal replacement. 4 nation is summation of people who are one (fraternity), equal (equality) & supreme (liberty). (definition given by french revolution/fr1789) 5 country = territory. 6 state = organization that rules/governs a country & its people. 1 military state = setup & sustained by military power; 2 police state = sustained by overuse of police; 3 kingdom = state where head of state decided by bloodline. empire = sum of kingdoms. 4 company state = a state setup by a company e.g. company state (1765–1858) in india by east india company (eic); 5 nation state = a state setup by the people/nation. 7 family = organization with motive of welfare of its members. 8 pvt company = organization with motive of profit for shareholders. 9 ngo = organization with social motive. 10 political party = organization with motive of power over state (1886 inc rule that inc to take up only political issues and not social issues i.e. they are political party not ngo). 11 common man motive = common man does not want to be mp/ml/minister, she wants security — physical, economic, socio-cultural, spiritual. 12. state = organization with territory motive & ideally should also have peoples' welfare motive (e.g. nation state). 13 primary purpose of any constitution (coi) is to create state structure. 14 modern state structure would have separation of power and a well defined internal organizational structure with clear goal & functions with clear mechanisms to ensure stability of the whole structure from top to bottom. on other hand, non-modern state structure has absence of institutional separation of power and susceptible to instabilities. [*💡 student confusion resolved: ncert says modern state has "centralised power exercised over a clearly defined territory." in class we say modern state has separation of power. both are correct and not contradictory. a state can be vertically centralised — strong union government having authority over provinces — and at the same time have horizontal separation of powers at union level i.e. parliament makes laws, prime minister implements, supreme court resolves disputes. it is like our parents centralise power over home but at that level powers are divided between mother and father.] 15 sovereignty = symbolic sovereignty (i.e. who is the head of the state), power to make laws, implement them and adjudicate disputes which arise during law making and their implementation i.e. legislative, executive & judicial power over external sovereign functions & domestic sovereign functions. external sovereign functions are defence, communications & foreign affairs i.e. war and diplomacy (including trade) while domestic sovereign functions are the rest e.g. home, finance, agriculture, industry, infrastructure, health, education, transport etc. sovereign functions are also called subjects or affairs. the 7th schedule of our coi1950 divides domestic affairs/subjects/sovereign functions between centre & provinces (better word than states else causes confusion). the word rule or govern is always related to exercising legislative, executive, judicial powers on domestic affairs. the state rules its country & its people while it talks or trade or fights with outside world. to understand how the mughal state came to dominate the subcontinent, we need to start not in india, but in a small kingdom in central asia.

sections.title: The Mughal Monarchs: a quick reference
sections.norm: the mughal monarchs: a quick reference. coding convention two reign periods list ends in 1857 alamgir ii shah alam ii akbar ii babur humayun akbar jahangir shahjahan aurangzeb shah farukhsiyar muhammad shah bahadur zafar bahadur shah zafar. keep this list as a reference. the dates embedded in each name follow a coding convention to help you remember reign years. # monarch reign 1 babur26-30 1526–1530 2 humayun30-40 1530–1540 & 1555–1556 3 akbar56-05 1556–1605 4 jahangir05-27 1605–1627 5 shahjahan27-58 1627–1658 6 aurangzeb58-07 (also known as alamgir) 1658–1707 7 bahadur shah07-12 (also known as shah alam i) 1707–1712 8 jahandar shah12-13 1712–1713 9 farukhsiyar13-19 1713–1719 10 muhammad shah19-48 (also known as rangila) 1719–1748 11 ahmad shah bahadur48-54 1748–1754 12 alamgir ii54-59 1754–1759 13 shah alam ii60-06 1760–1806 14 akbar ii06-37 1806–1837 15 bahadur shah zafar37-57 1837–1857 two observations. first, humayun30-40 is the only mughal ruler with two reign periods — overthrown by sher shah40-45 in 1540, in exile for years, back on the throne in 1555, dead the following year. second, the list ends in 1857 — the year of the great uprising against british rule. the last powerful mughal emperor, aurangzeb58-07 (alamgir), had died in 1707; his successors from bahadur shah07-12 to bahadur shah zafar37-57 (bahadur shah ii) are known as the later mughals & ruled in increasingly diminished authority until 1857, when zafar37-57 was deposed & exiled by the british. the mughal state, which had begun with a cannon blast at panipat in 1526, ended with cannon blasts in delhi.

sections.title: Mughal Take Over from Lodis
sections.norm: mughal take over from lodis. babur26-30 fergana timurid empire mughal mongol turko-mongol dynasty genghis khan (1206–27) timur (tamerlane) (1370–1405) timur had captured delhi in 1398 timurids could not hold fergana india — wealthy but politically fragile map of the fergana valley — central asia (uzbekistan / kyrgyzstan / tajikistan) small bronze cannons proved decisive the mughal kingdom was born still a kingdom — not yet an empire first battle of panipat, 1526 — mughal miniature of babur26-30 vs ibrahim lodi 1526, 1556, 1761 geography chose panipat — commanders merely followed. babur akbar aurangzeb. babur26-30 (1526–30) was born in 1483 to umar shaikh mirza, ruler of fergana — a semi-autonomous state in present-day uzbekistan, roughly half the size of modern haryana. fergana belonged to the timurid empire, & babur26-30 was himself a descendant of timur (tamerlane). mughal is a persian corruption of the word mongol. the mughals were a turko-mongol dynasty with ancestry connecting them to both central asia & east asia: maternal side — descendants of genghis khan (1206–27), founder of the mongol empire [1206–1368]. paternal side — direct descendants of timur (tamerlane) (1370–1405), the turkic conqueror who founded the timurid empire [1370–1507]. they took greater pride in their paternal ancestor — timur had captured delhi in 1398 — & consequently referred to themselves as timurids, not mughals. babur26-30 came to power young but could not hold fergana; by 1512 his central asian ambitions had collapsed. he did hold kabul (captured 1504), but kabul was economically poor. india — wealthy but politically fragile under the lodi dynasty — was the obvious opportunity. with artillery support from the ottoman empire (expert gunners), babur26-30 began attacking the delhi sultanate from 1519, culminating in the battle that changed indian history. 📷 map of the fergana valley — central asia (uzbekistan / kyrgyzstan / tajikistan) babur26-30 entered india through the khyber pass & met ibrahim lodi — the last ruler of the lodi dynasty (1451–1526) — on the plains of panipat. though his army was smaller (~12,000 men), his small bronze cannons proved decisive — a technology the lodis could not match. lodi was killed, the delhi sultanate (1206–1526) ended, & the mughal kingdom was born. this, however, was still a kingdom — not yet an empire. it would become an empire only under akbar56-05 (1556–1605) & reach its greatest territorial extent under aurangzeb58-07 (1658–1707). 📷 first battle of panipat, 1526 — mughal miniature of babur26-30 vs ibrahim lodi [kala amb memorial in haryana commemorates the 1761 third battle, not this one.] three of the most consequential battles in indian history — 1526, 1556, 1761 — were all fought at panipat. this was no coincidence. three geographical factors converged: first, panipat lay close to the khyber pass, the primary invasion route from central asia into the indo-gangetic plain; second, it sat in the narrow corridor between the thar desert (south) & the himalayan foothills (north), forming a natural bottleneck; third, the yamuna to the east acted as a defensive choke-point, ruling out flanking manoeuvres. geography chose panipat — commanders merely followed.

sections.title: Humayun30-40 & Sher Shah Suri40-45 (1540-45)
sections.norm: humayun30-40 & sher shah suri40-45 (1540-45). sher shah suri40-45 no foreign invader three reforms defined his legacy: 4.1) revenue. land measurement and revenue assessment zabti system 4.2) currency. rupiya 4.3) infrastructure. grand trunk road roots in sher shah's innovations safavid dynasty of iran significant political price battle of sirhind (punjab, 1555) fell from the stairs of his library hemchandra vikramaditya (hemu) samrat suri babur humayun shah akbar. babur26-30 died in 1530 & was succeeded by his son humayun30-40 (1530–40). sher shah suri40-45, an afghan-pathan born farid khan in bihar c. 1486, was no foreign invader — his ancestors had migrated to india under the lodis & settled as jagirdars in bihar. he won the title sher khan by killing a tiger single-handed while serving bahar khan lohani (governor of bihar under the lodis till 1526, then independent sultan md lohani who refused mughal sovereignty). suri40-45 defeated humayun30-40 at chausa (1539) & kanauj (1540). he then established the suri dynasty (1540–55) & pushed the mughals out of india entirely. though the suri dynasty lasted only fifteen years (1540–55), sher shah40-45's administrative innovations outlasted his reign. three reforms defined his legacy: 4.1) revenue. he introduced a standardised system of land measurement and revenue assessment — the precursor to akbar56-05's zabti system. each peasant received a patta specifying his revenue obligation, & the state took a qabuliyat — a written agreement — from the peasant. this two-document system gave both the state & the cultivator an enforceable record. (*patta is document given by state to ryot. it has land details, ryot name, lr to be paid while qabuliyat= proof that ryot agreed to pay lr. it is given by ryot to the state. suri40-45 was 1st to introduce this bilateral/mutual agreement system. in ancient times the system existed but not two sided. the state used to give patta (tamra patra- copper inscription)). 4.2) currency. he introduced the silver rupiya, a coin of standardised weight & purity — the ancestor of the modern indian rupee. 4.3) infrastructure. he upgraded the grand trunk road from peshawar to sonargaon in bengal, transforming communication & trade across the subcontinent. suri40-45 died in 1545; the suri dynasty held delhi until 1555, when humayun30-40 recaptured the throne. much of what akbar56-05 later systematised had its roots in sher shah's innovations. to retake his throne, humayun30-40 turned to the safavid dynasty of iran. the safavids agreed — at a significant political price. humayun30-40 had to adopt shia practices & outward observances, cede control of kandahar to iran, & promote persian culture in india. whether this amounted to genuine conversion remains debated; what is clear is that humayun30-40 publicly assumed shia forms as the price of the alliance. the lasting consequences — persian language and art became deeply embedded in mughal court culture, & a distinct irani group of mansabdars later emerged within the mughal administration. with 14,000 iranian troops at his back, humayun30-40 defeated the suris at the battle of sirhind (punjab, 1555). but fate intervened — in january 1556, humayun30-40 fell from the stairs of his library, struck his head, & died. into this vacuum stepped hemchandra vikramaditya (hemu) — from rewari in present-day haryana — who had served as chief commander & minister of the suris. he seized delhi & declared himself samrat.

sections.title: How was the Mughal Kingdom re-established (Panipat 1556)?
sections.norm: how was the mughal kingdom re-established (panipat 1556)?. bairam khan second battle of panipat (1556) akbar. on one side stood hemu controlling delhi. on the other, the mughal army under bairam khan — general, strategist, & guardian to the thirteen-year-old akbar56-05. hemu was defeated. the second battle of panipat (1556) was not just a military victory — it secured the mughal state in india for the next 150 years. diagram 1 — mughal kingdom re-established at panipat 1556

sections.title: How did Akbar56-05 build the Mughal State — the Mansabdari System
sections.norm: how did akbar56-05 build the mughal state — the mansabdari system. akbar56-05 machinery of the mughal state mansabdari system 6.1) what is a mansabdar? dual function 6.2) how was rank determined? zat + sawar. 6.3) who could become a mansabdar? lineage, not merit. 6.4) how were mansabdars paid? jagir, khalisa, inam. cash a) jagir land b) khalisa land c) inam land mashrut jagir: over 8,000 mansabdars four-fifths of all lr came from jagirs 6.5) what rules governed tankha jagirs? a) transferable. b) capped extraction. c) confiscation on death. 6.6) what was a watan jagir? rajput chieftains and autonomous rulers alert: milkiyat watan jagir inam vs watan: inam confiscated after death like tankha jagir watan 6.7) what held the system together — and what was its fatal weakness? patron-client relationship personal, not institutional the loyalty dissolved political instability impersonal loyalty to institution & law hollowed-out armies on paper babur humayun akbar. babur26-30 founded the mughal kingdom. humayun30-40 nearly lost it. but it was akbar56-05, ruling for fifty years (1556–1605), who built the actual machinery of the mughal state. that machinery was called the mansabdari system — a military-bureaucracy that defined how the state was administered, how its army was maintained, & how the king kept control over a vast & diverse territory. 6.1) what is a mansabdar? mansab means a post or rank; a mansabdar is the holder of that post. every mansabdar had a dual function — military & civil administrative. the same man who commanded troops also governed territory. this is precisely why the system is called a military-bureaucracy. 6.2) how was rank determined? zat + sawar. each mansabdar carried two ranks: zat (personal rank, governing seniority & status) & sawar (the number of horsemen he must maintain & provide to the king). net rank = zat + sawar. a mansabdar with zat 2,000 & sawar 3,000 held a net rank of 5,000. 6.3) who could become a mansabdar? lineage, not merit. if your ancestors had been mansabdars, you had the opportunity to become one. talent alone was not enough — not unlike pre-revolutionary france, where only the sons of nobles could enter the nobility. this rigidity would eventually become a source of serious weakness. 6.4) how were mansabdars paid? jagir, khalisa, inam. a mansabdar could be paid either in cash (a naqdi mansabdar) or in the form of a jagir — a specific piece of land whose land revenue they pocketed directly; this revenue paid the mansabdar's salary & covered the cost of maintaining his army. a jagir given in lieu of salary was called a tankha jagir, & its holder a jagirdar. ⚠ alert : iqtadar of delhi sultanate is like (jagirdar) mansabdar of mughal (*iqta=jagir (persian)) mughal land was therefore broadly divided into the following categories: a) jagir land — revenue to mansabdars. b) khalisa land — royal land; revenue went directly to the king & paid naqdi mansabdars plus other state expenses. c) inam land — gifted land; revenue went to a chosen beneficiary (e.g. a man of exceptional talent) to sustain himself. d) mashrut jagir: lr from this is like a temporary "top-up"/additional allowance given to an official to cover the extra costs of a specific, difficult assignment; it is automatically revoked the moment that assignment ends. (* like "base salary" vs. "the bonus") by the early 18th century, there were over 8,000 mansabdars, & four-fifths of all lr came from jagirs, only one-fifth from khalisa land. 6.5) what rules governed tankha jagirs? three: a) transferable. the king could rotate jagirs among mansabdars, or convert a jagirdar into a naqdi mansabdar at will. b) capped extraction. a jagirdar could collect only the pre-determined lr — not a rupee more. royal supervision existed specifically to prevent oppression of peasants & zamindars. c) confiscation on death. on the death of a tankha jagirdar, both the jagir & all accumulated wealth were confiscated. the predictable consequence — mansabdars spent lavishly during their lifetimes, since saving made little sense. 6.6) what was a watan jagir? watan means hereditary and permanent. unlike tankha jagirs, a watan jagir could be passed down & was not subject to rotation or confiscation. watan jagirs were given primarily to rajput chieftains and autonomous rulers who had submitted to the emperor — allowing them to collect revenue in their ancestral domains in exchange for military service & loyalty. however, the holder had to pay 10% of lr to the king — a tribute called peshkash, which acknowledged the king's ultimate authority & compensated him for giving up his right to reclaim the jagir. ⚠ alert: do not confuse an ordinary zamindar's milkiyat (hereditary personal property within his zamindari tract) with a watan jagir (a political grant to a chieftain, carrying sovereign-like privileges). inam vs watan: inam is a pure gift. it is confiscated after death like tankha jagir. watan is hereditary — given to a mansabdar doing duty for the king. it passes to heirs. 6.7) what held the system together — and what was its fatal weakness? the mansabdari system ran on a patron-client relationship between king & mansabdar. the king gave mansab & jagir; the mansabdar pledged personal loyalty & maintained the army. this co-opted politically powerful individuals who might otherwise have challenged royal authority. but the loyalty was personal, not institutional. a mansabdar's loyalty was to the king as a person — not to the state as an institution or to any law. it was transactional and conditional— give-and-take relationship. if the king could not deliver mansab & jagir (due to land shortage, financial pressure, or weak authority), the loyalty dissolved — & dissolved loyalty meant political instability. this is fundamentally different from a modern state, where bureaucrats & military officers owe their position to merit and service rules — impersonal loyalty to institution & law. in the mughal system, that impersonal foundation simply did not exist. & since the entire military strength of the mughal state depended on mansabdars actually maintaining the armies their sawar rank required, weakened royal supervision meant hollowed-out armies on paper, far fewer men in reality — a silent erosion of state power from within. diagram 2 — mansabdari system: jagir / khalisa / inam land + tankha vs watan jagir

sections.title: Mughal Land Revenue (LR) system
sections.norm: mughal land revenue (lr) system. rights in land belong to four stakeholders: of the owner of the tenant/ryot of the collector of tax of the state financial backbone of the state 7.1) who collected revenue — and how was it supervised? zamindars patwari qanungo amil amalguzar patta qabuliyat muqaddams zabti system scientifically measured the land nankar malikana khalisa lands jagir 7.2) who were the ryots — and were they equally protected? a) khudkashts customary occupancy rights b) pahikashts no occupancy rights and no legal protections 7.3) revenue farming/muqatai/ijaradari/farming system auctioned to the highest bidder ijaradar revenue farmer profit motive 3 to 5 years extract as much as possible within this short window stood outside the traditional rural economy the zamindar's extraction was capped by law; the ijaradar's was capped only by the peasant's capacity to endure. muqatai system maps almost perfectly onto the rise and decline of mughal state authority delhi sultanate (1206–1526) akbar56-05 (1556–1605) jahangir05-27 (1605–27) re-emerged marginally shahjahan27-58 (1627–58) aurangzeb58-07 (1658–1707) jahandar shah12-13 (1712–13) punjab and bengal farukhsiyar13-19 (1713–19) royal khalisa lands awadh under sadat khan22-39 (1722–39) hyderabad under nizam-ul-mulk24-48 (1724–48) warren hastings73-85 farming system in 1772 standard operating procedure the ryot at the bottom of the chain paid the price at every stage. akbar jahan aurangzeb babur jahangir shahjahan shah farukhsiyar khan mulk nizam hastings warren hastings. usually people think all rights in property are with the owner of property. that is not correct. rights in land belong to four stakeholders: of the owner — in mughal system, ultimately the king. today, right to sell, lease out, rent out property & right to get money from these transactions. right to fair tax. of the tenant/ryot — right to occupy/cultivate, right to fair rent. of the collector of tax — right to collect tax, right to be paid for service provided. of the state — right to assess/fix tax, right to enforce tax demand, right to receive tax. lr was the financial backbone of the state — it paid the mansabdars, maintained the army, kept the king's treasury alive. 7.1) who collected revenue — and how was it supervised? the state did not collect directly. it relied on zamindars (non-state actors) in zamindari tracts, who also held police duties. [✦ rule of thumb: state actors get salaries. non-state actors get a commission or profit for service performed for the state.] the revenue hierarchy ran through record-keeping → assessment → settlement → collection → oversight: a1) record keeping: village level — patwari maintained ledgers (bahi /bahi khata or khasra) of individual peasant holdings & crops. patwari was a non-state actor (*or accountant) paid by the village community. (*patwari was village accountant like kulkarni of maharashtra. difference was that unlike kulkarni, the patwari did not have watan/vatan right (*hereditary) to be village accountant. it was a customary right but not customary vatan right.) a2) record keeping: pargana level — qanungo consolidated patwari data; he was a state official & hereditary custodian of historical tax rates i.e. had vatan right. b1) assessment: pargana level — amil, the state's executive revenue officer at the pargana level, assessed the official demand & audited accounts. b2) assessment: sarkar level — amalguzar was supervisor of amil at the sarkar (district) level, assessed the official demand & audited accounts. c) settlement was done with ryot/peasant: patta (the title deed) was the official paper given to the individual peasant by the government. the government used the patwari's ledger/khasra to create a patta for each peasant. the patta told the peasant exactly how much land he officially held and exactly how much lr he was required to pay i.e. also served as a check against over-extraction. qabuliyat (the acceptance deed): it was the document signed by the peasant and given back to the government, promising that they agreed to pay the lr written on the patta. d) physical collection — muqaddams (village headmen) collected from cultivators. in zamindari tracts they deposited to zamindars (who extracted via their own amlas); in areas without intermediaries, muqaddams paid directly to the state. in later periods, contractual revenue farmers — ijaradars — also collected (*covered later). e) under akbar56-05's zabti system, the state did not trust zamindars with autonomous authority — state officials (amil at pargana level, working under amalguzar at district/sarkar level) scientifically measured the land & fixed the exact demand. the land records so created were archived/stored by qanungo at pargana level. lr was calculated as % of gross produce (*more lr from more fertile areas). mughal lr demand was % of gross produce & not net produce. the idea of subtracting cost of cultivation before taxing was a british reform that came much later — and only after the gross produce method had already caused widespread agrarian ruin. emperor lr as % of produce (*tells story of decline) akbar56-05 (1556-1605) 1/3rd shah jahan27-58 (1627-58), aurangzeb58-07 (1658-1707) high extraction -> 1/3rd to 1/2. later mughals (1707+) extreme extraction -> 1/3rd to 2/3rd. the zamindar acted as an obedient collection agent under strict supervision, ensuring surplus went to the central treasury, not his pocket. his legally fixed commission — around 10% — was called nankar or malikana. the zamindar's own personal lands were called milkiyat — & on these he paid lr like any other landholder. abwabs — customary tributes — were additional demands passed from state to zamindar to peasant. intermediary zamindars were big zamindars who received lr from primary zamindars and themselves collected lr where no primary zamindar was available in their assigned land. f) intermediary zamindars passed on lr from khalisa lands → to imperial treasury & lr from jagir →to jagirdars. at times primary zamindars directly sent lr to imperial treasury or to jagirdar as the case be. 7.2) who were the ryots — and were they equally protected? two categories: a) khudkashts cultivated the same land year after year. because of this continuity they acquired customary occupancy rights — i.e. they could not be removed. they functioned as small landowner-cultivators, held a patta. khudkasht = occupancy rights of cultivation, not ownership. the king owned all land. khudkasht could not be arbitrarily removed, but could not sell or mortgage the land either. b) pahikashts cultivated different lands across different seasons, often as share-croppers. because they had no fixed attachment to land, they had no occupancy rights and no legal protections — landless & rightless. sometimes called vagrant or banjara peasants because of this rootlessness. 7.3) revenue farming/muqatai/ijaradari/farming system — the logic was straightforward. instead of collecting through the zamindar network under state supervision, the right to collect all revenues from an area — land, traders, shopkeepers — was auctioned to the highest bidder, called an ijaradar or revenue farmer. the term revenue farmer deserves explanation. a farmer, in the economic sense, works with a profit motive; a peasant works for food security. the ijaradar was not a cultivator but a merchant or moneylender who bid for the right to collect revenue purely for profit. he was farming revenue, not land. the ijaradar paid the bid amount — fully or partially in advance — to the jagirdar (on jagir land) or to the state (on khalisa land), then collected his investment plus profit from the peasants & traders. contracts were typically 3 to 5 years. his incentive was to extract as much as possible within this short window — with zero interest in irrigation, peasant welfare, or long-term agricultural growth. ryots were squeezed hard. if the ijaradar failed to deliver, the contract was simply re-auctioned. because ijaradars were urban bankers & merchants with no roots in the countryside, they stood outside the traditional rural economy — no long-term stake in the land, no relationship with the peasants, no reason to preserve the balance even a corrupt zamindar might maintain out of self-interest. zamindar vs. ijaradar — why the difference mattered for the peasant. a zamindar's right was tied to his bloodline — he & his descendants had to live with the peasants forever, so he rarely squeezed them to starvation. his commission was a state-mandated ~10% (nankar/malikana). an ijaradar promised the state a fixed lump sum (say 1 lakh); if he extracted 3 lakh through torture & extortion, he kept the entire 2 lakh profit. the zamindar's extraction was capped by law; the ijaradar's was capped only by the peasant's capacity to endure. auctioning the right to collect taxes to a private bidder is ancient, but it was formally institutionalised in the subcontinent during the delhi sultanate (1206–1526) as the muqatai system. the practice persisted until akbar56-05 practically abolished it, replacing it with direct state collection through the zabti system. (babur26-30 had no time for revenue reforms in his four-year reign; the decisive break came under akbar56-05.). the trajectory of the ijaradari system maps almost perfectly onto the rise and decline of mughal state authority — abolished when the state was strong, revived when it was weak. delhi sultanate (1206–1526) — originated as the muqatai system — the first formal institutionalisation of revenue farming in india. akbar56-05 (1556–1605) — practically abolished it; replaced comprehensively with the zabti system. under a strong, centralised administration, there was no need for revenue farming. jahangir05-27 (1605–27) — re-emerged marginally as control over jagirdar-mansabdars loosened post akbar56-05's. shahjahan27-58 (1627–58) — reintroduced properly, but strictly for ruined or devastated lands where direct collection was impractical. however, aurangzeb58-07 (1658–1707) expanded it significantly — the costs of his endless deccan campaigns made the quick cash of revenue farming irresistible. jahandar shah12-13 (1712–13) — institutionalised it in the richest provinces — punjab and bengal — previously too valuable & too well-administered to hand over to revenue farmers. ijaradari was no longer a measure for infertile lands but a tool for maximum extraction from the empire's best territory. farukhsiyar13-19 (1713–19) — extended it fatally into royal khalisa lands. that the state was now auctioning off even its own directly-administered lands was a sign not just of fiscal desperation but of the collapse of the emperor's social contract with his people — it hurt the social power & moral authority of the emperor among the population. when the mughal successor states emerged — awadh under sadat khan22-39 (1722–39) & hyderabad under nizam-ul-mulk24-48 (1724–48) — they continued the ijaradari system. when the english east india company (eic) took administrative control of bengal, warren hastings73-85 (*governor of bengal presidency from 1772 & governor general of bengal presidency from 1773-75 (the regulating act of 1773 made him gg but hastings73-85 formally assumed office as gg in 1774)) — formalised it as the farming system in 1772, embedding this extractive mechanism directly into early british colonial administration. what had originated as the muqatai system under the delhi sultanate, been abolished by akbar56-05, & revived under weaker successors, had by the time of warren hastings73-85 become the standard operating procedure of revenue collection across large parts of the subcontinent. the ryot at the bottom of the chain paid the price at every stage. parameter zabti system ijaradari system how lr is fixed detailed survey auction settlement with (*i.e. lr to be paid agreed upon by state with?) (this person would also have responsibility to deposit lr to the state) ryot revenue farmer (ijaradar) collection by zamindar ijaradar motive of collector state-mandated commission profit motive peasant protection patta gives legal right no protection diagram 3 — mughal land revenue (lr) collection hierarchy + ryot categories diagram 4 — ijaradari system rise + decline arc (delhi sultanate → hastings73-85 1772)

sections.title: What was Akbar56-05's religious vision — Sulh-i-Kul, Ibadat Khana, Mahzar, Din-i-Ilahi?
sections.norm: what was akbar56-05's religious vision — sulh-i-kul, ibadat khana, mahzar, din-i-ilahi?. clear sequence 8.1) ibadat khana (1575). house of worship at fatehpur sikri 8.2) mahzar — the infallibility decree (1579). emperor, not the clergy 8.3) din-i-ilahi (1582). religio-political experiment 8.4) sulh-i-kul — universal peace. ideological foundation of mughal governance akbar. akbar56-05's approach to religion shaped the political character of mughal rule for generations. he moved in a clear sequence: 8.1) ibadat khana (1575). akbar56-05 established a house of worship at fatehpur sikri, where scholars from different faiths were invited to debate. the discussions exposed him to the diversity of religious thought — & to the bitter rivalries among the ulama. 8.2) mahzar — the infallibility decree (1579). akbar56-05 issued the mahzar, which gave him the authority to adjudicate religious disputes — effectively making the emperor, not the clergy, the final word on matters of faith. 8.3) din-i-ilahi (1582). akbar56-05 formulated the din-i-ilahi, a syncretic spiritual order borrowing from islam, hinduism, zoroastrianism, & christianity. din-i-ilahi is best understood as a religio-political experiment — not a movement. it could not become a movement because not many joined but its real significance lay in the principle it expressed. 8.4) sulh-i-kul — universal peace. the underlying idea: the state must treat all religions with equal respect, & no single faith should dominate policy. sulh-i-kul became the ideological foundation of mughal governance under akbar56-05 & continued to influence mughal politics long after his death.

sections.title: Who actually introduced Jizya in India?
sections.norm: who actually introduced jizya in india?. predates the sultanate by several centuries muhammad bin qasim. the jizya — a tax on non-muslims — is often associated with the delhi sultanate, but it predates the sultanate by several centuries. muhammad bin qasim first imposed jizya in sindh during the arab conquest of the 8th century. however, it was qutb-ud-din aibak & his successors who institutionalised it as a formal instrument of revenue & policy across the delhi sultanate from the early 13th century. the distinction matters — jizya arrived in india with the arabs, but became a pan-subcontinental administrative practice only under the sultanate.

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: Framework — how to analyse the decline
sections.norm: framework — how to analyse the decline. power = political + economic + military + social + technological. two analytical tools to apply in every decline question: vertical power shift = decentralisation. downward horizontal power shift = replacement. ww2 aurangzeb. the mughal state reached its greatest extent under aurangzeb58-07 — & began collapsing thereafter. within four decades it was reduced to a small area around delhi–agra and under maratha protection. think of state power as a five-component equation: power = political + economic + military + social + technological. the mughal decline is a simultaneous weakening across all five. [*💡 two analytical tools to apply in every decline question: vertical power shift = decentralisation. when emperor weakens, power moves downward. after 1707 emperors were weak personalities — so mansabdars under them became real centre of power. horizontal power shift = replacement. one entity replaces another at the same level. delhi sultanate replaced by mughal at panipat 1526. british super power replaced by us-ussr by end of ww2 in 1945. apply both lenses to every exam question on decline.]

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: Why did Aurangzeb58-07's wars sow the seeds of decline?
sections.norm: why did aurangzeb58-07's wars sow the seeds of decline?. dara shikoh and a period of peace follows the conquest bijapur (1686; adil shahi dynasty 1489–1686) golconda (1687; qutb shahi dynasty 1518–1687) bahmani sultanate (1347–1527) three-way fight marathas by 1705 marathas were winning gol gumbaz, bijapur — mausoleum (*burial building like taj mahal) of muhammad adil shah (1627 to 1656) of adil shahi dynasty (1489–1686) golconda fort, hyderabad — seat of the qutb shahi dynasty (1518–1687) aurangzeb akbar. aurangzeb58-07 came to power in 1658 after a brutal succession war (killing his elder brother dara shikoh) & governed as an empire-builder on a mission — determined to conquer all of india, particularly the deccan. war helps the state only if roi (return on investment) is positive and a period of peace follows the conquest — if wars never stop & territory won is eventually lost, it becomes an economic disaster. in the deccan aurangzeb58-07 annexed bijapur (1686; adil shahi dynasty 1489–1686) & golconda (1687; qutb shahi dynasty 1518–1687) — both successor kingdoms of the bahmani sultanate (1347–1527). in bijapur(1489-86), it was a three-way fight — mughals, the bijapur, & the marathas, who never accepted mughal authority. by 1705 marathas were winning; by the 1750s they had reversed most of aurangzeb58-07’s gains and some of akbar56-05 as well. 40 years of warfare drained the treasury (*govt’s bank account), broke the mansabdars financially (*as they had to maintain army), & translated directly into later military corruption (*i.e. mansabdars not maintaining army as per sawar). 📷 gol gumbaz, bijapur — mausoleum (*burial building like taj mahal) of muhammad adil shah (1627 to 1656) of adil shahi dynasty (1489–1686) 📷 golconda fort, hyderabad — seat of the qutb shahi dynasty (1518–1687)

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: How did Aurangzeb58-07’s religious policies erode the social foundations of the Mughal State?
sections.norm: how did aurangzeb58-07’s religious policies erode the social foundations of the mughal state?. state power needs social support orthodox interpretation of islam alienating non-muslim subjects re-introduction of jizya in 1679 (*abolished in 1564 muhammad bin qasim 712 ce qutb-ud-din aibak06-10 (1206–10) delhi sultanate(1206-1526), babur26-30 and humayun30-40 akbar56-05 abolished 1564 zulfiqar khan 1712 farukhsiyar13-19 re-introduced jizya in 1717 1720 abolished md shah19-48 kashi vishwanath temple at varanasi, demolished 1669 gyanvapi mosque maasir-i-alamgiri ahilyabai holkar of indore rebuilt it in 1780 kashi vishwanath temple & gyanvapi mosque, varanasi: guru tegh bahadur, the 9th sikh guru chhatrapati sambhaji, elder son of shivaji74-80 (1674–80) created martyrs aurangzeb aibak babur humayun akbar shah farukhsiyar muhammad shah shivaji chhatrapati shivaji. state power needs social support. aurangzeb58-07 followed an orthodox interpretation of islam in both personal life & governance, systematically alienating non-muslim subjects. 3.1 the re-introduction of jizya (1679) — & the history behind it the most damaging measure was the re-introduction of jizya in 1679 (*abolished in 1564) — an additional tax on non-muslim adult males. beyond the economic burden, the manner of collection made people feel religiously discriminated against, & resentment ran deep. jizya was first introduced by muhammad bin qasim in 712 ce after conquering sindh. by paying jizya, the non-muslim population was granted the status of zimmis (or dhimmis), meaning "protected people," allowing them to practice their religion and exempting them from military service (*this is a gain or a loss of employment opportunity for masses?). however, in an institutionalised manner, jizya was first introduced by qutb-ud-din aibak06-10 (1206–10) — first sultan of delhi sultanate(1206-1526), founder of the mamluk dynasty (1206-1290; mamluk means military slave). babur26-30 and humayun30-40 continued it; akbar56-05 abolished it in 1564 as part of his sulh-i-kul (universal peace) policy. aurangzeb58-07 reintroduced in 1679. zulfiqar khan (irani group; wazir of jahandar shah12-13) abolished it again in 1712 to get support of hindu nobles e.g. rajputs; farukhsiyar13-19 as new emperor reissued decree abolishing jizya in 1713 but then re-introduced jizya in 1717. in 1720, jizya was abolished for good by md shah19-48. overall one could argue that as the empire weakened, jizya faded with it. 3.2 temple policy —kashi vishwanath demolished (1669) aurangzeb58-07 refused temple repairs & reduced their land grants. more significantly, he demolished important temples. best-known case: the kashi vishwanath temple at varanasi, demolished 1669, replaced on the same site by the gyanvapi mosque. aurangzeb58-07's own court record, the maasir-i-alamgiri, documents his order. the temple's troubled history: razed earlier by qutb-ud-din aibak (1194, then slave-general of md. ghori before becoming first sultan of delhi in 1206) & sikandar lodi (1490). ahilyabai holkar of indore rebuilt it in 1780 near the original site. 📷 kashi vishwanath temple & gyanvapi mosque, varanasi: 3.3 why did executions backfire — guru tegh bahadur (1675), chhatrapati sambhaji (1689) aurangzeb58-07 executed prominent political rivals. in 1675, guru tegh bahadur, the 9th sikh guru. in 1689, chhatrapati sambhaji, elder son of shivaji74-80 (1674–80), after weeks of torture. both were offered convert-or-die; both refused. the executions did not suppress resistance — they created martyrs, hardening anti-mughal sentiment among sikhs & marathas. diagram 1 — jizya in india

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: Why did the Mansabdari system — the empire's own backbone — turn against it?
sections.norm: why did the mansabdari system — the empire's own backbone — turn against it?. personal loyalty to the emperor as an individual, not loyalty to the empire as an institution later mughals. the mansabdari system ran on personal loyalty to the emperor as an individual, not loyalty to the empire as an institution. a give-and-take: emperor grant mansabs & jagirs; nobles gave military service & loyalty. the strong emperors made this work; the weak emperors could not. after 1707 the later mughals could not control powerful mansabdars. when emperor could not grant desired mansabs & jagirs, the mansabdars became disloyal and acted upon this disloyalty (*earlier either fear or belief in fairness of a strong emperor they stayed in line) e.g. engaged in court politics for best mansabs and jagirs or tried replacing present emperor with their favourite from royal family. court politics crippled governance; those who should have led reforms- economic, administrative & military- were consumed by factional rivalry.

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: Why did the Mughal military weakened?
sections.norm: why did the mughal military weakened?. no technological or organisational reform: file firing grapeshot artillery bayonet haider ali61-82 (mysore) weak war commanders: military corruption: far fewer cavalry than their sawar rank required ali aurangzeb. three interconnected problems drove the decline. no technological or organisational reform: european powers succeeded with smaller numbers due to better command, tighter discipline, & tactical innovations — file firing (rotating lines for continuous fire), grapeshot artillery (multiple bullets in one shot; lethal at close range), & the bayonet (*knife) on the brown bess musket (*so a rifle became sword in close range). haider ali61-82 (mysore) reorganised military on the european model & remained formidable; the mughals, paralysed by factionalism, reformed nothing. weak war commanders: under the later mughals (1707-1858), court politics — not merit — determined military appointments. military corruption: under weak supervision mansabdars maintained far fewer cavalry than their sawar rank required, pocketing the difference. aurangzeb58-07's war drain & the jagirdari crisis compounded this. by the early 18th c the army was corrupt, under-equipped, poorly led, & technologically frozen.

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: What was factionalism, & how did it operate in the Mughal court?
sections.norm: what was factionalism, & how did it operate in the mughal court?. royal vs royal + royal vs noble + noble vs noble irani turani hindustani hindu deccani the absence of any clear succession rule successor states. think of factionalism as royal vs royal + royal vs noble + noble vs noble. the main competing groups: irani (shia persian, e.g. zulfiqar khan); turani (sunni turkish-uzbek — like mughal, e.g. nizam-ul-mulk); hindustani (converted indian muslims, e.g. the sayyid brothers); hindu (rajputs & jats, e.g. sawai jai singh); & deccani (nobles absorbed from bijapur 1686 & golconda 1687). after 1707, weak emperors could not control these groups. mansabdars competed to dominate the sitting emperor or install their preferred candidate — whoever controlled the emperor controlled mansabs & jagirs. worsened by the absence of any clear succession rule: every emperor's death was potentially a new power struggle. some mansabdars who could have stabilised the centre chose not to, instead using the chaos to carve out their own principalities (the successor states).

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: What was the Jagirdari crisis, & why did it hit so hard?
sections.norm: what was the jagirdari crisis, & why did it hit so hard?. jagirdari crisis khalisa more claimants for jagirs, but land under mughal control was shrinking 5% of mansabdars controlled 61% of jagir revenue transfer jagirs frequently extract maximum revenue in minimum time ijaradari system zamindars effect on peasantry jat kingdom aurangzeb. the jagirdari crisis was a structural mismatch: supply of jagirs & demand for them fell dangerously out of balance. it began with aurangzeb58-07's own decisions. after annexing bijapur (1686) & golconda (1687), their nobles were absorbed as mansabdars — but he declared most of their lands khalisa to fund the maratha war. mansabdars rose, jagir pool did not. the later mughals (1707-1858) kept appointing more mansabdars to buy loyalty — more claimants for jagirs, but land under mughal control was shrinking. distribution was deeply unequal: 5% of mansabdars controlled 61% of jagir revenue. luxury-goods inflation (driven partly by eic exports of indian goods) ensured that many could not maintain elite standard of living. consequences were multi-dimensional. the emperor had to transfer jagirs frequently to satisfy disgruntled naqdi mansabdars, but this created tenure insecurity. jagirdars had every incentive to extract maximum revenue in minimum time, none to invest in long-term productivity of land. extraction became more ruthless through the ijaradari system (revenue-farming), which stripped collection rights from zamindars, alienating the traditional stabilising force of the countryside (*zamindars were traditional leaders of rural society). effect on peasantry: over-extraction, stagnation, revolts led by alienated zamindars. a direct example: the jat kingdom, emerged from a 1695 peasant revolt under churaman jat, a zamindar. meanwhile the mansabdars did not maintain army as per sawar to maximize their earnings as no one knew when emperor would transfer jagir (*kal ho na ho jagir).

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: Proof of decline — what did factionalism look like in practice?
sections.norm: proof of decline — what did factionalism look like in practice?. jahandar shah12-13 (1712–13) zulfiqar khan of the irani group (1713–19) wazir (prime minister) sayyid brothers ( abdullah hussain ali of hindustani group) farukhsiyar13-19 peshwa balaji vishwanath13-20 (1713–20; maratha took over delhi 1719) md. shah19-48 (1719–48) nizam-ul-mulk24-48 (governor of hyderabad suba 1724-48) of the turani group with the irani defeated them governor of hyderabad suba in 1724. shah aurangzeb farukhsiyar vishwanath muhammad shah mulk nizam. 8.1 royal vs royal — how jahandar shah12-13 rose & fell when aurangzeb58-07 died in 1707, the empire had no stable succession mechanism. jahandar shah12-13 (1712–13) came to power backed by zulfiqar khan of the irani group — but only after executing the father of farukhsiyar13-19 (1713–19). zulfiqar khan's reward: the prestigious post of wazir (prime minister). factionalism's basic logic — back the right claimant, extract the reward. farukhsiyar13-19 did not forget. with support of the sayyid brothers (sayyid abdullah khan & sayyid hussain ali khan of hindustani group), farukhsiyar13-19 removed & executed jahandar shah12-13. abdullah became the new wazir & hussain ali became mir bakshi (chief military paymaster/commander) (*i.e. defence minister + defence finance authority) 8.2 royal vs noble — when an emperor refused to be a puppet farukhsiyar13-19 soon discovered the price of sayyid support — he was expected to govern as their puppet. he refused, & began building rival alliances. the sayyid brothers responded by reaching outside the court entirely, allying with the marathas under peshwa balaji vishwanath13-20 (1713–20; 15000 maratha cavalry temporarily took over delhi in 1719). then sayyid brothers killed farukhsiyar13-19 & installed md. shah19-48 (1719–48) as puppet emperor. 8.3 noble vs noble — how the turani group checked the sayyids the sayyids' dominance did not last. nizam-ul-mulk24-48 (governor of hyderabad suba 1724-48) of the turani group allied with the irani group & defeated them. nizam24-48 served as wazir from 1722–24 — but, recognising the imperial centre was beyond saving, he extracted mansab of governor of hyderabad suba in 1724. in 1740, he left delhi permanently. his departure from delhi was itself a signal of how far imperial authority had collapsed (*delhi to gayo, at least save my hyderabad) diagram 2 — factionalism + succession turmoil (1707–1724): jahandar shah12-13 → farukhsiyar13-19 → muhammad shah19-48 + nizam24-48 exits to hyderabad permanently in 1740.

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: Proof of decline — how the Marathas exposed the military collapse
sections.norm: proof of decline — how the marathas exposed the military collapse. recovered aurangzeb58-07's deccan gains akbar56-05 1737 peshwa bajirao20-40 (1720–40) delhi plundered 1738 large mughal army treaty of bhopal (1738) chambal and narmada subah of malwa aurangzeb akbar nizam bajirao shah muhammad shah. the military decline is best measured by what the marathas achieved. from 1705 they systematically defeated mughal forces. by the mid-18th century they had not only recovered aurangzeb58-07's deccan gains but taken lands annexed under akbar56-05, including gujarat. of major deccan territories, only hyderabad (formerly golconda) stayed outside maratha control — held by nizam24-48 as a successor state. in 1737, peshwa bajirao20-40 (1720–40) marched to delhi, plundered the capital, & briefly held md. shah19-48 as prisoner. in 1738 the marathas defeated a large mughal army commanded by nizam24-48. the aftermath was formalised in the treaty of bhopal (1738) — marathas received legal recognition of control over all lands between the chambal and narmada & the subah of malwa. imagine the mughal emperor became a hostage in his own capital.

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: What did Nadir Shah's invasion (1738-40) reveal — the five-pillar blow
sections.norm: what did nadir shah's invasion (1738-40) reveal — the five-pillar blow. battle of karnal (1739) sadat khan, nawab of awadh (1722–39; sadat22-39 of nizam24-48 as mir bakshi sadat22-39 convinced nadir shah to attack delhi for bigger plunder. nadir shah ruled as emperor of delhi for 60 days nadir shah’s invasion 1739 — five pillars of state power i) political. ii) social. two lakh civilians of delhi iii) military. first afghan invasion of 1748 iv) economic. ~100 crore rupees of the time (×250–300 for present value) peacock throne kohinoor diamond v) technological. the peacock throne — taken by nadir shah in 1739, along with the kohinoor diamond student doubt — if marathas had just plundered delhi in 1737 and defeated nizam in 1738, why were they not fighting nadir shah in 1739? marathas had returned south to their hq sadat nizam shah muhammad shah. nadir shah ruled a persian empire stretching into afghanistan — mughal-claimed territory — & desired india's wealth. his victory was made easier by weakening mughal empire plus factionalism. the battle of karnal (1739) was decisive — mughal army routed. sadat khan, nawab of awadh (1722–39; sadat22-39 of irani group), was taken prisoner and existing mir bakshi died fighting. now nizam24-48 as mir bakshi negotiated with nadir shah that he would take rs 50 lakh & not enter delhi. disgruntled that nizam24-48 was made mir bakshi instead of him, sadat22-39 switched sides and convinced nadir shah to attack delhi for bigger plunder. delhi fell, md. shah19-48 imprisoned, & nadir shah ruled as emperor of delhi for 60 days. sadat22-39 committed suicide when he was insulted by nadir shah after the victory instead of being rewarded. 📷 nadir shah’s invasion 1739 — the cost cut across all five pillars of state power. i) political. muhammad shah19-48 was publicly humiliated & did not stand up for his own dignity. for mansabdars watching, an emperor who could not stand for his dignity was not worth defending. ii) social. nadir shah's forces massacred roughly two lakh civilians of delhi. whatever social legitimacy remained evaporated in the streets of the capital. iii) military. a state that cannot defend its capital invites further challenges — the defeat directly encouraged the first afghan invasion of 1748 by ahmed shah abdali. iv) economic. nadir shah extracted wealth estimated at ~100 crore rupees of the time (×250–300 for present value) & took irreplaceable assets — most famously the peacock throne with the kohinoor diamond. mansabdars were forced to contribute from personal wealth. the empire, already in the jagirdari crisis, now lacked the economic means to rebuild a strong army. v) technological. resources that might have funded reform were gone — locking in the existing technology gap. 📷 the peacock throne — taken by nadir shah in 1739, along with the kohinoor diamond (*📌 student doubt — if marathas had just plundered delhi in 1737 and defeated nizam in 1738, why were they not fighting nadir shah in 1739? simple reason: marathas had returned south to their hq after the treaty of bhopal (1738). they had already extracted maximum concessions from the mughals through the treaty. allow the rival state to get weak — why should i interfere unless there is a deal like in 1752? that strategic patience is exactly what gave them the maratha protectorate of the mughal emperor in 1752.)

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: What did India look like by the mid-18th century?
sections.norm: what did india look like by the mid-18th century?. 1752, the mughal emperor came under maratha protection the protector had become the protected. 1754 the marathas installed alamgir ii54-59 (1754–59) ceased to exist the maratha state/empire stood at the top a small area around delhi and agra worth pinning (prelims 2003). shah alam ii60-06 away from delhi fear of his own wazir (imad-ul-mulk) alamgir ii shah alam ii aurangzeb. in 1752, the mughal emperor came under maratha protection — accepting maratha military guardianship against further afghan invasions. the protector had become the protected. in 1754 the marathas installed alamgir ii54-59 (1754–59) as their puppet emperor — a mughal ruler chosen by the very people the mughals had spent decades trying to suppress. by the mid-18th c, the mughal empire as a functional state had ceased to exist. what remained was not one state but many — a collection of regional powers, each with its own territory, army, & foreign policy. among these, the maratha state/empire stood at the top. the mughal emperor continued to sit in delhi, technically retaining symbolic sovereignty until 1858, but his actual authority extended little beyond a small area around delhi and agra — a ceremonial figurehead kept alive because his symbolic legitimacy was still useful to others. ◆ worth pinning (prelims 2003). shah alam ii60-06 spent the initial years of his reign away from delhi — the cause was fear of his own wazir (imad-ul-mulk), not fear of foreign invasion from the north-west frontier. diagram 3 — mughal decline arc (1707–1754): aurangzeb58-07 peak → jagirdari + factionalism + maratha victories + nadir shah → 1752 maratha protectorate → alamgir ii54-59 puppet 1754

sections.chapterTitle: The Decline of the Mughal State (1707 onwards)
sections.title: Exam Strategy — how to convert a PYQ into a FYQ
sections.norm: exam strategy — how to convert a pyq into a fyq. protagonist pyq (mains 2017) — fragmented polity 30% mughal decline (cause), 70% rise of regional powers (evidence) fyq (illustrative) — 70% mughal decline 30% regional powers same body of knowledge. two different protagonists. two very different answers.. the key skill is identifying the protagonist of a question — what it is actually centred on. once you identify the protagonist, you know where to place your emphasis. pyq (mains 2017) — "by mid-18th century, india was a spectre of fragmented polity. elaborate." protagonist = fragmented polity. weighting: 30% mughal decline (cause), 70% rise of regional powers (evidence). fyq (illustrative) — "in the first half of the 18th century, the mughal empire was reduced to a figment of imagination. elaborate." protagonist shifts to the mughal empire's own collapse. weighting flips: 70% mughal decline (maratha victories, nadir shah's invasion, karnal, bhopal, emperor-as-puppet); 30% regional powers (supporting evidence of mughal irrelevance). same body of knowledge. two different protagonists. two very different answers.

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Before we begin
