sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Framework — the three classes of mid-18th century regional state
sections.norm: framework — the three classes of mid-18th century regional state. successor states bengal, awadh, hyderabad rebel states marathas, sikhs, jats, afghans: farukhabad, rohilkhand already autonomous states rajputs, mysore, travancore this handout is on the successor states.. by the mid-18th century the mughal state had ceased to function as a single unified polity. what remained in its place was a patchwork of regional powers. we sort them into three classes. successor states — bengal, awadh, hyderabad — carved out by powerful mansabdars who extracted governing authority over a subah from the emperor. rebel states — marathas, sikhs, jats, afghans: farukhabad, rohilkhand — formed by those who openly rebelled. already autonomous states — rajputs, mysore, travancore — never under effective mughal control to begin with. this handout is on the successor states.

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Why were these rulers autonomous but never formally independent?
sections.norm: why were these rulers autonomous but never formally independent?. murshid quli khan (mqk17-27) in 1717 sadat khan22-39 in 1722 nizam-ul-mulk24-48 in 1724 (i) symbolic legitimacy (ii) ambitions at delhi wazir mir bakshi (iii) military assistance (iv) trade barriers khan mulk nizam. bengal was set up as a successor state by murshid quli khan (mqk17-27) in 1717; awadh by sadat khan22-39 in 1722; hyderabad by nizam-ul-mulk24-48 in 1724. each ruled de-facto as sovereign — none declared independence. four reasons: (i) symbolic legitimacy of a mughal subahdar's title commanded local nobles' obedience; (ii) ambitions at delhi kept open the prize mansabs — wazir (pm/imperial diwan) & mir bakshi (war paymaster) — nizam-ul-mulk served as wazir 1722–24 while simultaneously subahdar/governor of hyderabad; (iii) military assistance from other provinces in conflict; (iv) trade barriers — independence risked tariffs lethal for commercially active territories. (think eu members accepting partial sovereignty for open borders & seamless trade.)

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: A note on Mughal provincial titles
sections.norm: a note on mughal provincial titles. subahdar nazim nawab of the suba nizamat or naib nazim of bihar 3.1. geographical administration of the bengal subah the overarching structure: territory: capital: overall in-charge of nizamat nazim (subahdar) overall in-charge of diwani diwan parallel audit & intelligence officer of the bengal subah bakshi of the subah 3.2. chain of command bakhshi's four functions: ◆ function 1 — mansabdari records: ◆ function 2 — military payroll: ◆ function 3 — anti-corruption inspection: dagh chehra ◆ function 4 — intelligence (waqia-navis): ◆ bakshi had complete oversight of the empire's officer class as: who every noble was what they were paid whether they were honest what they were doing second-highest official in the empire 3.3. the regional breakdown within subah of bengal akbar khan mulk nizam. under akbar56-05's design, the subahdar (also nazim or nawab of the suba) was executive & military governor, responsible for the nizamat (defence, peace, criminal justice). mqk17-27 nazim of bengal, sadat khan22-39 subahdar of awadh, nizam-ul-mulk24-48 nawab of the hyderabad — same meaning i.e. same mansab. ⚠ alert: nawab ≠ subahdar always. a nawab could administer a sub-region within a suba — e.g. alivardi khan40-56 was nawab of patna (a region inside bengal subah) or naib nazim of bihar before becoming subahdar of the whole bengal subah in 1740. the naib nazim was deputy subahdar. the diwan was the chief financial & civil officer (land revenue + civil justice = diwani). crucially the diwan did not report to the subahdar — he reported directly to the imperial diwan at delhi. akbar56-05 deliberately made the two co-equal. this separation of the sword (nizamat) from the purse (diwani) is what kept the mughal empire stable for over a century. every successor state founder had to dismantle it. here is the integrated, fully-updated section with tables 3.1, 3.2, and 3.3 woven together with the bakshi explanation built in. 3.1. geographical administration of the bengal subah the overarching structure: territory: bengal subah (regions: west bengal, bihar, orissa, east bengal) capital: murshidabad (west bengal region) overall in-charge of nizamat [home minister i.e. law & order; criminal justice; defence i.e. war commander] = nazim (subahdar) — directly answerable to the emperor overall in-charge of diwani [revenue, civil admin, civil justice] = diwan — directly answerable to the emperor (under supervision of the imperial diwan i.e. wazir) parallel audit & intelligence officer of the bengal subah = bakshi of the subah — reports directly to mir bakshiat delhi, bypassing the nazim ◆ the nazim, the diwan, and the bakshi of the subah were mutually independent. none could overrule the others. all three reported only to their imperial counterparts at delhi, and ultimately to the emperor. 3.2. chain of command administrative branch primary function regional level (patna, cuttack, dacca) provincial level (murshidabad) imperial level (delhi) nizamat home minister (law & order, criminal justice) + defence (war commander) naib nazim nazim (subahdar) emperor (direct reporting; no intermediate minister) diwani revenue, civil administration, civil justice naib diwan diwan wazir-i-mumalik / imperial diwan (diwan-i-ala) → emperor bakshi (parallel audit & intelligence line) mansabdari records + military payroll + anti-corruption inspection (dagh & chehra) + intelligence (waqia-navis) subordinate bakhshis (attached to faujdars / contingents) bakshi of bengal subah mir bakshi(bakhshi-ul-mumalik) → emperor bakhshi's four functions: ◆ function 1 — mansabdari records: who holds what rank, who got promoted, who got demoted, who joined service, who died. the bakshi maintained these registers and updated them constantly. ◆ function 2 — military payroll: calculating each mansabdar's entitlement, assigning him a jagir of the right value, transferring jagirs every 2-3 years to prevent local roots — all of this paperwork was the bakhshi's job. during wartime he was in charge of expenditure in war. ◆ function 3 — anti-corruption inspection: to prevent military corruption by a mansabdar (under-recruiting troops), akbar56-05 gave the bakshi two inspection mechanisms: dagh —"branding." every horse maintained by a mansabdar was branded with an imperial mark on its flank. at inspection time, the bakshi counted only branded horses. chehra — literally "face" every soldier had his physical description (face, height, complexion, distinguishing marks) recorded in a register. ◆ function 4 — intelligence (waqia-navis): a network of information collectors (waqia-navis) was posted in every province, district, and significant town across the empire. their job was to send daily reports to delhi on everything happening locally — court intrigues, market prices, harvest conditions, military movements, suspicious behaviour by the nazim or diwan, rebellions brewing, foreign travellers arriving. these reports flowed up through the bakshi system, with the mir bakshi as the chief recipient. ◆ bakshi had complete oversight of the empire's officer class as: the bakshi knew who every noble was (mansabdari records) the bakshi knew what they were paid (payroll) the bakshi knew whether they were honest (dagh-chehra audit) the bakshi knew what they were doing (intelligence) that is what made him the second-highest official in the empire. 3.3. the regional breakdown within subah of bengal region within suba headquarters nizamat head (law & order, criminal justice, defence) diwani head (revenue, civil admin, civil justice) administrative status west bengal murshidabad nazim diwan direct rule bihar patna naib nazim naib diwan delegated rule (reports to murshidabad) orissa cuttack naib nazim naib diwan delegated rule (reports to murshidabad) east bengal dacca naib nazim naib diwan delegated rule (reports to murshidabad) ◆ the bakshi line operated as a parallel vertical reporting only to delhi.

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: The four-step process — how all three Successor States were built
sections.norm: the four-step process — how all three successor states were built. step 1. step 2. step 3. step 4. tankha jagirs (temporary, transferable) into vatan jagirs (hereditary) local loyalty of provincial mansabdars to the regional ruler step 5 — co-opting commercially powerful non-military groups given mansabs lineage-based result diffused autonomous polity akbar. the rise of these nobles followed a deliberate sequence. step 1. extract the mansab of subahdar. step 2. end akbar56-05's checks & balances — fill diwan, naib nazim & war commander with personal loyalists. step 3. build strong revenue administration — finance is crucial for everything else. step 4. convert tankha jagirs (temporary, transferable) into vatan jagirs (hereditary). vatan means hereditary; the emperor's historic tool of control — shifting jagirs at will — was traded away for local loyalty of provincial mansabdars to the regional ruler. step 5 — co-opting commercially powerful non-military groups (intermediary zamindars, revenue farmers, merchants, moneylenders, bankers). they were promised security of property, their taxes reasonable — &, most unprecedentedly, they were given mansabs. the mansabdari system was traditionally lineage-based (military / noble bloodlines only). appointing merchants & bankers to mansabs was a structural transformation — administrative rank & commercial wealth, historically kept apart, now merged. result: a diffused autonomous polity — nawab at the top, multiple influential actors beneath. all 5 steps were taken while accepting symbolic sovereignty of mughal emperor diagram 1 — six-step successor state formation: extract subahdar mansab → end checks & balances → strong revenue admin → tankha → vatan jagirs → co-opt merchants/bankers/ijaradars → keep mughal symbolic link → diffused autonomous polity common to bengal/awadh/hyderabad

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Bengal — how Murshid Quli Khan (MQK17-27) built the first Successor State
sections.norm: bengal — how murshid quli khan (mqk17-27) built the first successor state. bengal, orissa and bihar mqk17-27 murshidabad hooghly farukhsiyar13-19 already was diwan bengal neighbourhood (1750) — intermediary zamindars just fifteen were collecting 50% of bengal suba's land revenue farukhsiyar akbar. the bengal subah covered bengal, orissa and bihar — vast & commercially rich. mqk17-27 was the last bengal governor appointed as per wish of the emperor. capital: murshidabad on the hooghly — then the major port (british later developed calcutta as alternative). mqk17-27's path: diwan from 1700, then under farukhsiyar13-19 he also became deputy governor of bengal suba + governor of orissa. in 1717, when he was elevated to mansab of nazim of bengal subah he already was diwan (*combining finance + executive in one man= ending akbar56-05's checks & balances). mqk17-27 still sent tribute to delhi but emperor approval for appointments in bengal suba was now paper formality. 📷 bengal neighbourhood (1750) — 📷 nawab of murshidabad's boats on the ganga -by sita ram he was a brilliant revenue administrator. he collected land revenue via intermediary zamindars and got done detailed field surveys for fair assessment. the intermediaries grew powerful: by 1727 just fifteen were collecting 50% of bengal suba's land revenue. mansabdars who resisted him, had their tankha jagirs bengal taken & were given jagirs in orissa; resisting zamindars were dealt with punished by reducing land from which they collected land revenue.

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: The Jagat Seths — & why Bengal's power was diffused, not centralised
sections.norm: the jagat seths — & why bengal's power was diffused, not centralised. manikchand under mqk17-27 mehtab rai and swarup chand under alivardi khan40-56 richest banking house in the world hundi treasurer of bengal and daroga of the royal mint diffused coup of 1740 overthrew and killed the sitting nawab sarfaraz khan39-40 md shah19-48 khan shah muhammad shah. "jagat seth" was a hereditary title (not a personal name) held by successive heads of a banking family — manikchand under mqk17-27, mehtab rai and swarup chand under alivardi khan40-56. already powerful before 1717, under the successor state they rose to what dutch records called the richest banking house in the world. they loaned to zamindars (so revenue reached the state on time), loaned to merchants, & ran hundi services (pre-modern wire transfer). under shuja-ud-din md khan (1727–39), a jagat seth was appointed treasurer of bengal and daroga of the royal mint — central bank plus personal banker of the nawab in one family. power was diffused, not centralised — a network of nawab + intermediary zamindars + merchants + bankers, the nawab on top but dependent on cooperation. proof: the coup of 1740. alivardi khan40-56 (nawab of patna) overthrew and killed the sitting nawab sarfaraz khan39-40 with jagat seth’s backing. he secured it by promising emperor md shah19-48 one crore rupees plus sarfaraz's personal wealth for formal approval — which was duly given. the emperor had been reduced to a transactional figure.

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Bengal's virtual break — the Maratha raids & Alivardi Khan40-56
sections.norm: bengal's virtual break — the maratha raids & alivardi khan40-56. raghuji bhonsle of nagpur chauth orissa the virtual break was complete siraj-ud-daula56-57 mir jafar mir qasim60-63 khan alivardi daula qasim. under mqk17-27 bengal was autonomous, but tribute still was sent to delhi. under alivardi khan40-56 the break deepened — triggered by external shock. from 1745 to 1751, raghuji bhonsle of nagpur raided bengal repeatedly; alivardi40-56 could not defeat him. in 1751 a settlement gave bhonsle annual chauth (one-fourth revenues) of bengal & bihar, plus direct control of orissa. with part revenues now flowing to nagpur, alivardi40-56 stopped sending revenue to delhi entirely & stopped seeking emperor approval for provincial mansabdars appointments. the virtual break was complete — though formal independence was never declared. after alivardi40-56 his grandson from daughter, siraj-ud-daula56-57 →siraj’s war commander mir jafar (1757–60, eic-installed him as their puppet post-battle of plassey1757) → jafar’s son-in-law mir qasim60-63 → mir jafar restored (1763–65). from 1765 bengal's diwani (=revenue & civil administration) passed to the eic. diagram 2 — bengal successor state succession chain

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Awadh — from Sadat Khan22-39 to the virtual break of 1753
sections.norm: awadh — from sadat khan22-39 to the virtual break of 1753. sadat ali khan22-39 safdar jung39-54 new loyal class of local elites safdar jung39-54 was ahmad shah bahadur48-54 farukhabad no more revenue to delhi, no imperial authority inside awadh shuja-ud-daula54-75 shah alam ii60-06 ahmad shah abdali at the third battle of panipat 1761 battle of buxar (1764) nawab wajid ali shah shah alam ii khan jung nizam bahadur daula shuja. awadh was founded by sadat ali khan22-39, appointed subahdar in 1722 as reward for suppressing local revolts. he installed his nephew + son-in-law safdar jung39-54 as deputy governor & his own loyalist as diwan; tribute to delhi was reduced. revenue of awadh grew from efficient land assessment & taxes on trade. he created a new loyal class of local elites (indian muslims, afghans, hindus) by giving them mansabs & jagirs. unlike mqk17-27, sadat khan22-39 kept centre ambitions — he wanted a senior mansab at delhi (*central government). he convinced nadir shah to invade delhi in 1739 because the mir bakshi mansab/post had gone to chin qulich khan (another name of nizam24-48) instead of him. nadir shah ill-treated him post-victory; he committed suicide. safdar jung39-54 was appointed wazir by ahmad shah bahadur48-54 in 1748, he misused the office to annex farukhabad into awadh. other mansabdars opposed this and in 1753 he was forced to resign. the resignation was awadh's virtual break — no more revenue to delhi, no imperial authority inside awadh — though legally still part of the empire. his son shuja-ud-daula54-75 was appointed wazir by shah alam ii60-06; shuja54-75 fought alongside ahmad shah abdali at the third battle of panipat 1761 & was later defeated by the eic at the battle of buxar (1764). awadh survived nominally until eic annexation in 1856 from nawab wajid ali shah.

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Hyderabad — Nizam-ul-Mulk's path from Delhi to Deccan
sections.norm: hyderabad — nizam-ul-mulk's path from delhi to deccan. chin qulich khan — aka nizam-ul-mulk, aka asaf jah i — nizam24-48 turani sayyid brothers chauth sardeshmukhi succession after nizam24-48's death : charminar, hyderabad — the civic symbol of nizam24-48's autonomous successor state nizam aurangzeb shah muhammad shah jung. hyderabad was set up within the empire in 1724 by chin qulich khan — aka nizam-ul-mulk, aka asaf jah i — nizam24-48 — after defeating mubariz khan, the sitting nazim of the deccan. he was leader of the turani group of mansabdars. in aurangzeb58-07's deccan wars he & his father built strong roots in the region. in 1720 turani & irani group removed the sayyid brothers — kingmakers who controlled md shah19-48 — & formally restored imperial authority. but the structural problem remained: md shah19-48 was uninterested in governance. remember, around 5% of mansabdars controlled 61% of all jagir land revenue — the jagirdari crisis. as wazir from 1722–24, nizam tried to redistribute jagirs from big mansabdars to the smaller ones to diffuse the crisis but bigger mansabdars did not agree. he was defeated by marathas in 1728 & 1738 — forced to pay chauth & sardeshmukhi (10% hereditary maratha claim in the deccan). he served as mir bakshi (1739–40) during nadir shah's invasion. by 1740 he gave up on reforming the centre & moved to hyderabad permanently. succession after nizam24-48's death : nazir jung (1748–50) → muzaffar jung (1750–51, 3 months) → salabat jung51-62 (1751–62, french dominated under bussy) → nizam-ali-khan (1762–1803). 📷 charminar, hyderabad — the civic symbol of nizam24-48's autonomous successor state

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: How Nizam24-48 established Hyderabad as successor state
sections.norm: how nizam24-48 established hyderabad as successor state. khutba tolerance vatan/watan jagirs to gain loyalty of powerful mansabdars merchants and moneylenders ijaradars most pronounced transformation of mansabdari system result. by 1748 the emperor's sovereignty over hyderabad was purely symbolic — name on coins & in the friday khutba, zero influence over war, peace, treaties, or provincial mansabdar’s appointments. the hindu majority of hyderabad was economically powerful; nizam showed tolerance & punished opponents regardless of community. he converted tankha jagirs to vatan/watan jagirs to gain loyalty of powerful mansabdars; merchants and moneylenders got property security & were made mansabdars (*called upstarts) who in return gave financial support; ijaradars were also made mansabdars. of the three states, hyderabad saw the most pronounced transformation of mansabdari system— men of finance became mansabdars on a significant scale, tankha → vatan conversion was most aggressive. result: same diffused polity — nawab at top, influential sections under him.

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Carnatic — a State within a State (Carnatic within Hyderabad)
sections.norm: carnatic — a state within a state (carnatic within hyderabad). called the carnatic its own ruler vijayanagar empire was the strongest power in south india nayaks palayams poligar deccan sultanates destroyed the vijayanagar army ruled autonomously conquered & divided the carnatic conquered bijapur in 1686 and golconda in 1687 under mughal rule captured gingee fort rajaram89-00 zulfiqar khan siege lasted eight years captured gingee in 1698 into the hyderabad subah, with two parts north of the krishna river ruled directly south of the krishna river gingee as capital own nawab state within a state became independent in practice saadatullah khan last nawab directly chosen capital from gingee to arcot nawab post hereditary dost ali khan killed in 1740 by the marathas anwaruddin khan ending the dynastic rule hampi / vijayanagar ruins — the capital whose 1565 sack ended the empire as a major power aurangzeb shivaji chhatrapati shivaji sambhaji rajaram. hyderabad had a smaller state inside its borders called the carnatic. by law, it was part of the hyderabad province. but it had its own ruler — the nawab — and ran its own government. 11.1 backstory — the vijayanagar empire (1336–1646) for three hundred years, the vijayanagar empire was the strongest power in south india, and the carnatic was part of it. internal structure provinces were ruled by nayaks — telugu hindu governors from warrior families. nayaks divided their provinces into smaller parts called palayams. each palayam was run by a local chief called a poligar (or palayakkarar), who had his own private army and fort. 11.2 the long decline (1565–1698) a. defeat of vijayanagar at talikota (1565) a four-state alliance of the deccan sultanates — bijapur, ahmadnagar, golconda, and bidar — destroyed the vijayanagar army. the empire officially continued until 1646, but this defeat was the real end of its power. b. nayaks independent, then defeated by the sultanates after 1565, the southern nayaks of madurai, tanjore, and gingee ruled autonomously. distance protected them for a while. but by 1646, bijapur and golconda conquered & divided the carnatic between themselves. c. sultanates defeated by the mughals aurangzeb58-07 conquered bijapur in 1686 and golconda in 1687. the whole carnatic now came under mughal rule. d. gingee under marathas, then lost to the mughals chhatrapati shivaji74-80 (1674-80) had captured gingee fort from bijapur in 1677. after the mughals executed chhatrapati sambhaji80-89 (1680-89) in 1689, the next chhatrapati, rajaram89-00 (1689-1700), made gingee his base against the mughals. in 1690, zulfiqar khan (nawab of carnatic) surrounded the fort. the siege lasted eight years (longest by mughal). the mughals finally captured gingee in 1698. (zulfiqar khan later became wazir under emperor jahandar shah, 1712 until his execution in february 1713.) 11.3 dividing the region ⚠ alert: prelims 2021 trap — the carnatic and hyderabad relation. the mughals organized the southern lands into the hyderabad subah, with two parts: a. hyderabad lands north of the krishna river, ruled directly by the mughal governor (nizam). b. hyderabad-karnatic (the "carnatic") the twelve districts south of the krishna river, with gingee as capital. (this covered the old nayak kingdoms of gingee, tanjore, and madurai.) in eighteenth-century maps, it is simply the "carnatic." the carnatic had its own nawab, but he reported to the nizam — making it a "state within a state." 11.4 moving towards autonomy under nawab saadatullah khan (1710–1732) as the mughal empire weakened, the carnatic slowly became independent in practice. saadatullah khan was the last nawab directly chosen by the mughal emperor (in 1710). two big steps towards autonomy he moved the capital from gingee to arcot. he also made the nawab post hereditary in his family — without asking the mughal emperor for approval. (saadatullah was childless. he adopted his brother ghulam ali's son, dost ali, as his heir.) in name, the carnatic was still under the nizam of hyderabad. 11.5 after saadatullah his adopted nephew dost ali khan ruled next (1732–1740). dost ali was killed in 1740 by the marathas under raghuji bhonsle in the chittoor district of andhra pradesh — close to the tamil nadu border. the nizam chose anwaruddin khan as the new nawab in 1744 — ending the dynastic rule of saadatullah khan's family. 📷 hampi / vijayanagar ruins — the capital whose 1565 sack ended the empire as a major power

sections.chapterTitle: Regional States: the Successor States of Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad
sections.title: Synthesis — the common pattern & what it made possible
sections.norm: synthesis — the common pattern & what it made possible. structural pattern is identical extracts the subahdari horizontal vertical legitimacy and real power had come apart. across bengal, awadh & hyderabad — & carnatic inside hyderabad — the structural pattern is identical: powerful mansabdar extracts the subahdari, dismantles checks & balances, builds revenue strength, converts tankha → vatan jagirs, co-opts merchants/bankers/revenue farmers into the mansabdari system. none declared independence — the mughal umbrella served their interests. each state developed its own diplomacy, army, & fisc. carnatic adds a key point. fragmentation was not only horizontal (subahs breaking from the empire) but also vertical — sub-regions within a successor state developing their own semi-autonomous identity. what remained of emperor authority resembled a constitutional monarch with no executive power — a ceremonial head of state whose legitimacy was still useful to others. this is the india into which the eic was stepping: competing partially-autonomous states each with its own elite coalition, each with its own fiscal & military interests — & critically, a world where legitimacy and real power had come apart. that gap between formal authority & actual power is exactly what made the subcontinent vulnerable to outside penetration.

sections.chapterTitle: The Marathas: Rise, Administration & the Road to Panipat 1761
sections.title: Chhatrapati Shivaji74-80 (1674-80)— Background, Bijapur, Mughals, Svarajya
sections.norm: chhatrapati shivaji74-80 (1674-80)— background, bijapur, mughals, svarajya. 1.1 who he was — birth, family, training shivaji bhonsle 19 february 1630 jagirdar of poona dadaji kondadev mother jijabai captured his first fort at the age of 16 in 1646 maval region of maharashtra sahyadri range 1.2 why he rose against bijapur 1657 onwards systematic attacks on the kingdom of bijapur economically oppressive & religiously discriminatory policies aurangzeb58-07 1659 ali adil shah ii, sultan of bijapur afzal khan under the pretext of negotiations bagh nakh (tiger claws) bichhwa (dagger) 1.3 why he rose against the mughals — treaty of purandhar 1665 defeated the mughal general shaista khan in 1663 sacked the wealthy port of surat jai singh encirclement strategy 1665, jai singh laid siege to fort purandhar fort purandhar — where jai singh's 1665 siege forced shivaji74-80 to terms treaty of purandhar 1665 a tactical pause, not a permanent defeat surrendered 23 of his 35 forts accepted aurangzeb58-07 as emperor declined a personal mansab for himself sambhaji mughal mansabdar with a rank of 5,000 agreed to support the mughals in their war against bijapur 1666 mughal court at agra their escape became legendary sadhus mathura 1681 prince akbar defected to chhatrapati sambhaj (1680-89) 1.4 his dream of svarajya — the 1674 coronation at raigarh 1674 coronated at raigarh as chhatrapati independent from the mughals svarajya marathi-speaking region raigarh fort, maharashtra — site of shivaji74-80's 1674 coronation second half of the 17th century both bijapur & aurangzeb58-07 shivaji chhatrapati shivaji aurangzeb. 1.1 who he was — birth, family, training shivaji bhonsle was born on 19 february 1630 to shahji bhonsle & jijabai. his father was a jagirdar of poona & served as a general & mansabdar in bijapur [1489–1686], ruled by the adil shahi dynasty. this dynasty, along with the qutub shahi [1518–1687], had replaced the bahmani sultanate [1347–1527] in the deccan. his early training came from his guardian dadaji kondadev, who shaped him as a soldier and administrator. the deeper inspiration came from his mother jijabai and his own fierce ambition. he captured his first fort at the age of 16 in 1646. working from the maval region of maharashtra — a hilly, forested terrain in today's pune district, running through the sahyadri range — he gathered an army of local warriors & peasants. 1.2 why he rose against bijapur from 1657 onwards, shivaji74-80 launched systematic attacks on the kingdom of bijapur[1489–1686], which followed economically oppressive & religiously discriminatory policies. this was also the period when aurangzeb58-07 became mughal emperor. in 1659, ali adil shah ii, sultan of bijapur, sent his general afzal khan to kill shivaji under the pretext of negotiations. instead, shivaji killed the seven-feet-tall afzal khan using his concealed bagh nakh (tiger claws) & a bichhwa (dagger). 1.3 why he rose against the mughals — treaty of purandhar 1665 when aurangzeb58-07 launched his campaign for the conquest of the deccan, shivaji defeated the mughal general shaista khan in 1663. he further sacked the wealthy port of surat, which enraged aurangzeb58-07. in response, aurangzeb58-07 sent his general jai singh, who used an encirclement strategy to cut off supplies to maratha territories. in 1665, jai singh laid siege to fort purandhar(40–50 km southeast of pune). 📷 fort purandhar — where jai singh's 1665 siege forced shivaji74-80 to terms to prevent the massacre of his soldiers & people, shivaji negotiated treaty of purandhar 1665 — a tactical pause, not a permanent defeat. under its terms: 1. he surrendered 23 of his 35 forts to the mughals. 2. he accepted aurangzeb58-07 as emperor but declined a personal mansab for himself. 3. his son sambhaji was made a mughal mansabdar with a rank of 5,000. 4. he agreed to support the mughals in their war against bijapur. in 1666, shivaji74-80 & son sambhaji visited the mughal court at agra. they were insulted & imprisoned. their escape became legendary — disguised as sadhus with bodies smeared in ash they went to mathura. shivaji left sambhaji there with a brahmin family & took a long route back to his capital. aurangzeb58-07 marched to the deccan in 1681, when his own son prince akbar defected to chhatrapati sambhaj (1680-89) 1.4 his dream of svarajya — the 1674 coronation at raigarh in 1674, shivaji was coronated at raigarh as chhatrapati — legally declaring himself independent from the mughals. his kingdom, called svarajya ("own rule"), covered the marathi-speaking region. 📷 raigarh fort, maharashtra — site of shivaji74-80's 1674 coronation ) the maratha kingdom had thus been founded in the second half of the 17th century, built through wars against both bijapur & aurangzeb58-07. shivaji74-80 (1674–80) died of natural causes in 1680.

sections.title: Military Tactics — Army, Navy, Forts

jaladurg doctrine sea forts built on rocky islands or peninsulas along the coastline cannons positioned in these forts & along the coast kept enemy ships at a distance sindhudurg, vijaydurg, & suvarnadurg bombay their main base for trade bombay presidency in 1687 in 1736 removed the portuguese & ethiopian muslims from the konkan coast by 1739 effectively controlled salsette & bassein sindhudurg fort — island sea-fort on the konkan coast built by shivaji74-80 under the jaladurg doctrine 2.6 after shivaji — admiral kanhoji angre admiral kanhoji angre "shivaji of the seas" dominated the arabian sea for 30 years 1729 british, portuguese, dutch, the sawants siddis or habshis 1714 to 1724 eic in bombay guerrilla warfare at sea bigger, heavier british ships could not pursue the small, lightweight, fast-moving maratha vessels in shallow waters british defeated the maratha navy in 1756 one year before shivaji chhatrapati shivaji shibaji shahu. 2.1 the army — light cavalry & guerrilla warfare shivaji74-80 built a well-organised army of around 30,000 to 40,000 cavalry. he used the mountainous terrain & dense forests of the region to master guerrilla warfare. over the course of his campaigns, he captured 240 forts, many of them in the konkan region. the marathas developed a highly effective military strategy built on surprise — shock & awe — combined with guerrilla warfare tactics. their major fighting force was a horse-mounted army, with a focus on light cavalry for faster movement. this stood in sharp contrast to the mughals, who relied on heavy cavalry (*elephants, carrying support system like food etc). 2.2 the saranjami system — military land grants unlike the mughals, maratha civil officials did not hold military roles. chhatrapati shibaji74-80 never gave jagirs and paid officials in cash leading to a centralized polity. later chhatrapati shahu19-49 (1719-49) gave tankha jagirs to military commanders called saranjams (but never vatan jagirs- this prevented military loyalty getting tied hereditary land grants. thus more control to ruler.) the saranjami system was one of the key structural features of the maratha polity. under this system, revenue assignments on jagirs were given to the maratha sardars (*discussed later), the peshwa (prime minister of chhatrapati), & various military commanders — each drawing income from designated territories/jagirs to maintain their troops & administration. this led to fragmented polity as revenue & military power were dispersed rather than centralized. the two land-grant types must be distinguished. saranjam = a tankha jagir held by military commanders — temporary, tied to service, not heritable. vatan/watan = a hereditary right held by civil officials like patils (village head) & deshmukhs (revenue collectors like zamindars) — passed within the family. 2.3 the navy — father of the modern indian navy shivaji74-80 established a naval force of 20 ships in 1657, and full navy of 200 ships by 1664. the peak maratha navy reached 700 ships. his naval doctrine was not about matching the british or portuguese in deep-ocean warfare. it was a specialised, asymmetric coastal defence strategy — designed to: 1. protect maratha merchant ships. 2. secure the konkan coastline from the siddis of janjira. 3. prevent european powers from dominating konkan trade routes. he built forts in coastal areas, established naval bases in the arabian sea, & focused on intelligence gathering at sea. in 1668, shivaji allowed the french to establish a trading factory at rajapur. in return, he secured high-quality military supplies — european cannons, lead, & saltpetre for gunpowder. shivaji is called the father of the modern indian navy because he relied entirely on indigenous human resources, indigenous engineering, & indigenous strategy — never on european naval architects or shipbuilders. he recruited from local coastal communities — the kolis & bhandaris — who were master seafarers with deep knowledge of the tides, hidden rocks, & shallow creeks of the konkan coast. he appointed brilliant local commanders like mayanak bhandari & daulat khan. 2.4 the fleet — tactical ship design a key insight that shaped his navy was tactical ship design. shivaji recognised that copying the massive deep-water ("blue water") ships of the europeans would be a strategic disaster in the shallow estuaries of the konkan coast. instead, he built a lighter, faster fleet designed for coastal defence & hit-and-run tactics: 1. ghurabs — gunboats carrying heavy artillery. 2. galbats — fast, highly manoeuvrable rowboats with light sails that could tow the ghurabs into position during dead winds or chase fleeing enemy ships. 3. shibars & pals — larger vessels for transport & heavier engagements. to ensure self-reliance, shivaji established shipbuilding yards, sourcing timber from the teak forests of the sahyadri mountains. 2.5 the forts — the jaladurg doctrine his greatest strategic innovation was the jaladurg doctrine — sea forts built on rocky islands or peninsulas along the coastline. these forts provided security to docked vessels. cannons positioned in these forts & along the coast kept enemy ships at a distance. forts like sindhudurg, vijaydurg, & suvarnadurg were key examples. in gujarat, the eic so feared the marathas that they made bombay their main base for trade, leading to the establishment of the bombay presidency in 1687. the marathas actively captured ports from the portuguese — in 1736, they removed the portuguese & ethiopian muslims from the konkan coast, & by 1739 effectively controlled salsette & bassein. 📷 sindhudurg fort — island sea-fort on the konkan coast built by shivaji74-80 under the jaladurg doctrine 2.6 after shivaji — admiral kanhoji angre after shivaji74-80, the dominant naval figure was admiral kanhoji angre (called the "shivaji of the seas"), who dominated the arabian sea for 30 years in the early 1700s until his death in 1729. kanhoji fought against the british, portuguese, dutch, the sawants (a small kingdom since 1627), & the siddis or habshis (people of african ancestry, now found in gujarat, karnataka, andhra, & parts of sindh & baluchistan in pakistan). from 1714 to 1724, he frequently attacked the eic in bombay, using guerrilla warfare at sea. the bigger, heavier british ships could not pursue the small, lightweight, fast-moving maratha vessels in shallow waters. the result was a stalemate, & kanhoji eventually offered peace to the british. the british defeated the maratha navy in 1756 — one year before the eic defeated the bengal suba in the battle of plassey in 1757.

sections.title: Maratha Ashtapradhan — who the Peshwa was
sections.norm: maratha ashtapradhan — who the peshwa was. 4.1 the chhatrapati was not an absolute ruler not an absolute ruler working alone council of eight ministers called the ashtapradhan similar in concept british monarch & his privy council mughal emperor & his darbar separation of powers separate legislature, executive, & judiciary modern concept simply a council of ministers serving the chhatrapati 4.2 the eight ministers eight members of the ashtapradhan 1. peshwa 2. amatya 3. sachiv 4. sumanta 5. senapati 6. panditrao 7. nyayadhish 8. waqenavis 4.3 the peshwa's own council — darakhdars & the barbhai mandal peshwa too had his own council of senior civil servants darakhdars 1774 nana fadnavis council of twelve ministers — the barbhai mandal hazur daftar 200 people all records important for governance were maintained at the hazur daftar, including financial records. 4.4 provincial & village administration sarkars governor the office of governor of a province was auctioned not without checks hereditary officers who had dual reporting lines both the governor & directly to the peshwa tallied & verified against independently by the deshmukhi directly to the peshwa this cross-checking prevented governors from manipulating revenue figures. lowest level were the villages self-contained units patil financial, executive, & judicial revenue collection the patil reported directly to the peshwa kulkarnis patils deshmukhi heritable vatan rights passed down within their families 4.5 the judicial system final judicial decision rested with the peshwa respective maratha sardar panch at the village level peshwa at the top respected the decisions of the panchs ancient religious texts — the dharma shastras policing system was as efficient as the london police of that era very good network of information collection there existed a rule of law — even the highest authorities could be & were imprisoned for violations 4.6 sources of revenue multiple sources land revenue was the primary source the quality of soil, irrigation facilities available, & the crop being sown beyond land revenue 1. customs duty & octroi 2. judicial proceeds nazrana winning party jurmana losing party 3. fees from permits & licences cutting woods, manufacturing drugs, & private minting of government coins dams & canals were constructed loans were provided at low interest rates deshmukhi & patils not oppress the peasantry. 4.1 the chhatrapati was not an absolute ruler the chhatrapati was not an absolute ruler working alone. he governed with a council of eight ministers called the ashtapradhan. this was similar in concept to the british monarch & his privy council, or the mughal emperor & his darbar. it is important to note that the separation of powers — meaning a separate legislature, executive, & judiciary — is a modern concept. the ashtapradhan was simply a council of ministers serving the chhatrapati. 4.2 the eight ministers the eight members of the ashtapradhan were: 1. peshwa — prime minister. 2. amatya — finance. 3. sachiv — correspondence. 4. sumanta — foreign affairs. 5. senapati — military commander. 6. panditrao — religious affairs. 7. nyayadhish — justice. 8. waqenavis — intelligence. 4.3 the peshwa's own council — darakhdars & the barbhai mandal just as the british prime minister had his own council of ministers beneath the monarch, the peshwa too had his own council of senior civil servants, known as darakhdars. in 1774, twelve of these powerful men came together under nana fadnavis to form the council of twelve ministers — the barbhai mandal. the peshwa's secretariat at poona was called the hazur daftar. around 200 people worked there. all records important for governance were maintained at the hazur daftar, including financial records. 4.4 provincial & village administration within svarajya, the territory was divided into sarkars (provinces), each under a governor. notably, the office of governor of a province was auctioned. this was not without checks. the bureaucracy contained many hereditary officers who had dual reporting lines — they reported to both the governor & directly to the peshwa. the accounts submitted to the peshwa by a governor were tallied & verified against those submitted independently by the deshmukhi directly to the peshwa. this cross-checking prevented governors from manipulating revenue figures. at the lowest level were the villages, which functioned as self-contained units. each village was under a patil, who held all powers — financial, executive, & judicial — including revenue collection. the patil reported directly to the peshwa. village account keeping was handled by kulkarnis. both patils (village heads) & deshmukhi (revenue collectors) held heritable vatan rights — meaning their offices & associated rights passed down within their families. 4.5 the judicial system in svarajya, the final judicial decision rested with the peshwa. in samrajya, it rested with the respective maratha sardar. there was a proper hierarchy of courts, beginning with a panch at the village level & leading up to the peshwa at the top. the peshwa, as far as possible, respected the decisions of the panchs. the law used for justice delivery was drawn from ancient religious texts — the dharma shastras. the policing system was as efficient as the london police of that era, with a very good network of information collection. crucially, there existed a rule of law — even the highest authorities could be & were imprisoned for violations. 4.6 sources of revenue the maratha state drew revenue from multiple sources. land revenue was the primary source, fixed on the basis of the quality of soil, irrigation facilities available, & the crop being sown. beyond land revenue, the state collected: 1. customs duty & octroi on the trade of goods. 2. judicial proceeds — nazrana paid by the winning party in a dispute & jurmana paid by the losing party. 3. fees from permits & licences for activities like cutting woods, manufacturing drugs, & private minting of government coins. to support peasants, dams & canals were constructed & loans were provided at low interest rates. revenue officials — deshmukhi & patils — were kept under check specifically so they would not oppress the peasantry.

sections.title: Shahu19-49's Release — was Mughal "Pacifist Policy" really pacifist?
sections.norm: shahu19-49's release — was mughal "pacifist policy" really pacifist?. 5.1 the release in 1707 death of aurangzeb58-07 pacifist policy sikhs & marathas shahu19-49 was released from mughal imprisonment in 1707 5.2 but was it really pacifism? characterising post-1707 mughal policy as purely pacifist would be a flawed interpretation. pragmatic real-politik combination of reconciliation, opportunism, & divide-and-rule tactics weakened & therefore relied more on diplomacy than outright war included conspiracies & manipulation alongside genuine reconciliation nominal pacifism with plausible deniability for hostile actions carried out by mughal governors 5.3 two examples that show the pattern first — the sikh case (1707–08) 1707, bahadur shah07-12 granted guru gobind singh76-08 a high mansab & promised him anandpur mughal faujdar of sirhind, wazir khan, had guru gobind singh assassinated in 1708 in nanded, maharashtra no action was taken against wazir khan, & anandpur was never handed over to the sikhs. sirhind was a sarkar — a district — within the lahore suba faujdar held military, judicial, & land revenue functions over a district not a governor wielded considerably greater influence than a typical faujdar second — the maratha case (1707 onwards) gesture of reconciliation mughals did not stop their attacks on the marathas shahu's release triggered a civil war between him & tarabai exploited this situation shrewdly encouraging divided loyalties among maratha sardars & deshmukhs shahu, tarabai, & the mughals this was shrewd diplomacy, not pacifism. aurangzeb shahu shah singh. 5.1 the release in 1707 after the death of aurangzeb58-07, it is often said that the mughals adopted a pacifist policy towards their adversaries — including the sikhs & marathas. this was the policy under which shahu19-49 was released from mughal imprisonment in 1707, after his father sambhaji's assassination & decades of captivity. 5.2 but was it really pacifism? characterising post-1707 mughal policy as purely pacifist would be a flawed interpretation. what actually emerged was a pragmatic real-politik — a combination of reconciliation, opportunism, & divide-and-rule tactics. the mughals were weakened & therefore relied more on diplomacy than outright war, but that diplomacy included conspiracies & manipulation alongside genuine reconciliation. it was nominal pacifism with plausible deniability for hostile actions carried out by mughal governors. 5.3 two examples that show the pattern first — the sikh case (1707–08). in 1707, bahadur shah07-12 granted guru gobind singh76-08 a high mansab & promised him anandpur. yet very soon after, the mughal faujdar of sirhind, wazir khan, had guru gobind singh assassinated in 1708 in nanded, maharashtra, where the guru had accompanied bahadur shah07-12. no action was taken against wazir khan, & anandpur was never handed over to the sikhs. it must be noted here that sirhind was a sarkar — a district — within the lahore suba, & a faujdar held military, judicial, & land revenue functions over a district. he was not a governor, as some books incorrectly describe him, though wazir khan wielded considerably greater influence than a typical faujdar. second — the maratha case (1707 onwards). when shahu19-49 was released from mughal imprisonment in 1707 as a gesture of reconciliation, the mughals did not stop their attacks on the marathas. at the same time, shahu's release triggered a civil war between him & tarabai, who had been ruling in the name of her infant son shivaji ii since the death of rajaram in 1700. the mughals exploited this situation shrewdly — encouraging divided loyalties among maratha sardars & deshmukhs, who kept switching sides between shahu, tarabai, & the mughals. this was shrewd diplomacy, not pacifism.

infant son shivaji ii. this arrangement held the maratha state together for seven years. in 1707, the mughals released shahu19-49 — the elder son of sambhaji, who had been held in mughal imprisonment. shahu's release triggered a civil war between shahu19-49 & tarabai that lasted until 1719. during this civil war, maratha sardars & deshmukhs kept switching sides between shahu, tarabai, & the mughals — a state of affairs the mughals deliberately encouraged. 6.2 treaty of warna 1731 — the family settlement the family dispute was finally settled by the treaty of warna 1731. under this treaty, shahu19-49 gave kolhapur to sambhaji ii, who was the son of rajaram from his second wife rajasbai & had taken control from shivaji ii around 1714. from this point onwards, there were two separate chhatrapati dynasties: 1. shahu19-49's line — headquartered at satara. 2. sambhaji ii's line — ruling from kolhapur. 6.3 after shahu — the chhatrapati becomes ceremonial after shahu19-49, his adopted son ramraja, also known as rajaram ii, took over from 1749 to 1777. from this point onwards, the chhatrapatis became largely ceremonial — much like a powerless president. real power had moved elsewhere — to the peshwa, as we will see in sec.8 the last chhatrapati of the satara line was shahaji, who ruled from 1839 until 1848, when the british east india company (eic) annexed satara. the kolhapur kingdom survived much longer, continuing as a princely state from 1858 until its merger into india in 1947.

sections.title: Why Shahu19-49 Won — and Who Were the Maratha Sardars?
sections.norm: why shahu19-49 won — and who were the maratha sardars?. 7.1 why shahu19-49 prevailed a critical reason was the role of the sixth peshwa, balaji vishwanath13-20 highly able leader 1. the support of powerful brahmin banking families 2. the support of the new independent maratha sardars peshwa balaji vishwanath13-20 convinced admiral kanhoji angre to switch sides from tarabai to shahu19-49 in 1714 7.2 who were the maratha sardars? maratha sardars were local chiefs mini-kings held their own armies, forts, & dominated smaller territories post-1719 expanded dramatically to rise to a king-like status kingmakers of the confederacy 1. gaikwad of baroda 2. holkar of indore 3. scindia (shinde) of gwalior 4. bhonsle of nagpur 7.3 ⚠ alert — prelims 1995 (sardar–capital pairings) alert: prelims 1995 — map detail. 1. gaikwad → baroda 2. holkar → indore 3. scindia (shinde) → gwalior 4. bhonsle → nagpur maratha empire can therefore be visualised as five provinces peshwa + four sardars as rulers chhatrapati as head of state by 1750 it was effectively a confederation — weak centre, strong provinces. shahu vishwanath. 7.1 why shahu19-49 prevailed shahu19-49 ultimately prevailed in the civil war. a critical reason was the role of the sixth peshwa, balaji vishwanath13-20, a highly able leader who helped shahu19-49 secure: 1. the support of powerful brahmin banking families. 2. the support of the new independent maratha sardars (who emerged precisely during this period). a telling example of balaji vishwanath13-20's diplomacy: during the civil war, peshwa balaji vishwanath13-20 convinced admiral kanhoji angre to switch sides from tarabai to shahu19-49 in 1714. without kanhoji's coastal & naval power on his side, shahu's victory would have been far harder. 7.2 who were the maratha sardars? the maratha sardars were local chiefs — essentially mini-kings — who held their own armies, forts, & dominated smaller territories. post-1719, some of them expanded dramatically to rise to a king-like status. these four became the kingmakers of the confederacy: 1. gaikwad of baroda. 2. holkar of indore. 3. scindia (shinde) of gwalior. 4. bhonsle of nagpur. 7.3 ⚠ alert — prelims 1995 (sardar–capital pairings) ⚠ alert: prelims 1995 — map detail. pin the four sardar–capital pairings: 1. gaikwad → baroda 2. holkar → indore 3. scindia (shinde) → gwalior 4. bhonsle → nagpur the maratha empire can therefore be visualised as five provinces — peshwa + four sardars as rulers, with the chhatrapati as head of state. by 1750 it was effectively a confederation — weak centre, strong provinces.

sections.title: Svarajya & Samrajya · Chauth & Sardeshmukhi · the Peshwa Becomes Real Authority
sections.norm: svarajya & samrajya · chauth & sardeshmukhi · the peshwa becomes real authority. 8.1 svarajya vs samrajya sum of two parts: svarajya & samrajya svarajya original maratha kingdom established by shivaji74-80 capital at raigarh 1647-1689 az58-07 jinji from 1689-1698 satara by rajaram 1689-1700 peshwa's headquarters at poona territory within maharashtra direct rule culturally homogeneous samrajya territory outside maharashtra confederate chiefs — the maratha sardars administration here varied from one sardar to another. gujarat, khandesh, & malwa primary concern was not governance but the collection of chauth & sardeshmukhi 1719 onwards not directly by the chhatrapati but by the maratha sardars 8.2 chauth — one-fourth, externally collected chauth & sardeshmukhi tribute systems that existed even before the marathas tool of empire-building. 8.3 sardeshmukhi — additional 10%, internal & external symbol of their recognition of the chhatrapati's authority. sardeshmukhi symbol of maratha authority being recognised by that state. important distinction: 8.4 how chauth was divided when maratha sardars extracted chauth from a state outside the empire retained two-thirds of it & sent the remaining one-third to svarajya 8.5 how the peshwa office became hereditary originally not hereditary balaji vishwanath13-20 (1713-20) baji rao20-40 (1720-40) balaji bajirao40-61 /nana saheb40-61(1740-61) across three generations hereditary in effect 8.6 treaty of sangola 1750 — the chhatrapati becomes ceremonial shahu19-49 was an effective ruler, power shifted downward from the chhatrapati to the peshwa factionalism increased 8.7 the series of peshwas baji rao20-40 chimaji appa, sadasiv rao bhau nana saheb40-61 died within weeks of the defeat vishwas rao peshwa lineage: 1. balaji vishwanath13-20 2. baji rao20-40 3. balaji bajirao / nana saheb40-61 4. madhav rao61-72 "young" not just to his age but also to his inexperience died of natural causes in 1772 5. narayan rao72-73 murdered in 1773 in a conspiracy hatched by his own uncle, raghunath rao73-74 6. raghunath rao73-74 the baarbhai conspiracy nana fadnavis modern chanakya. 7. madhav rao ii74-95 nana fadnavis ruled as regent drove madhav rao ii74-95 to suicide in 1795 8. baji rao ii96-18 last peshwa third anglo-maratha war of 1817–19, svarajya was annexed by the eic. 8.8 the three broad phases of maratha polity after shivaji74-80 three broad phases 1. 1680–1719 — turmoil. from 1707 to 1719, civil war among the marathas themselves 2. 1719–1761 — growth & expansion. 3. 1761 onwards — decline. temporary revival in the 1770s first anglo-maratha war of 1775–82 madhav rao ii baji rao ii shivaji chhatrapati shivaji vishwanath rao bajirao saheb shahu. 8.1 svarajya vs samrajya the maratha empire can be understood as the sum of two parts: svarajya & samrajya. svarajya was the original maratha kingdom established by shivaji74-80, with its capital at raigarh (from 1647-1689 then conquered by az58-07 so capital = jinji from 1689-1698; capital = satara by rajaram (r. 1689-1700)) & the peshwa's headquarters at poona. it was the territory within maharashtra, under direct rule, & was culturally homogeneous. samrajya was the territory outside maharashtra, ruled by the confederate chiefs — the maratha sardars. administration here varied from one sardar to another. effective administrative structures were established only in parts of samrajya — notably in gujarat, khandesh, & malwa. elsewhere, the primary concern was not governance but the collection of chauth & sardeshmukhi. from 1719 onwards, the territories added beyond the original svarajya were called samrajya. these were governed not directly by the chhatrapati but by the maratha sardars — regional chiefs who held power in their own right. 8.2 chauth — one-fourth, externally collected both chauth & sardeshmukhi were tribute systems that existed even before the marathas. chauth was one-fourth (25%) of the revenue paid by a protected state to the marathas in exchange for military protection. but it was also a deliberate tool of foreign policy. the annual payment of chauth weakened the protected state economically & militarily over time. when it could no longer pay, the marathas annexed it. chauth thus functioned as a tool of empire-building. 8.3 sardeshmukhi — additional 10%, internal & external sardeshmukhi was an additional levy of 10% of land revenue, collected over & above the regular land revenue. deshmukhs collected sardeshmukhi from the ryots & deposited it to the chhatrapati. shivaji74-80 declared himself sardeshmukh — the head of all deshmukhs. the payment of sardeshmukhi by deshmukhs was therefore a symbol of their recognition of the chhatrapati's authority. when extracted from states outside the maratha empire, sardeshmukhi served as a symbol of maratha authority being recognised by that state. important distinction: chauth was collected only externally — from states outside the maratha empire — while sardeshmukhi could be collected both internally & externally. 8.4 how chauth was divided revenue from chauth & sardeshmukhi collected outside the maratha empire helped reduce the tax burden on the people within the empire itself. when chauth was extracted by chhatrapati/peshwa then all of it was retained by svarajya. when maratha sardars extracted chauth from a state outside the empire, they retained two-thirds of it & sent the remaining one-third to svarajya: division % purpose / beneficiary mokasa 66% (~2/3rd) kept by the maratha sardars for maintenance of their troops & cavalry contingents. babti 25% (1/4th) sent directly to the chhatrapati for personal use & the royal treasury. sahotra 6% allocated to the pant sachiv — the head of the royal secretariat, a member of the ashtapradhan. nadgaunda 3% at the chhatrapati's discretion — charitable grants, royal gifts, or minor officials. 8.5 how the peshwa office became hereditary the office of peshwa was originally not hereditary. balaji vishwanath13-20 (1713-20), who served as the sixth peshwa, changed this in practice. his son baji rao20-40 (1720-40) became the next peshwa, & then his son balaji bajirao40-61 /nana saheb40-61(1740-61) followed. once this custom/tradition was established across three generations, the office became hereditary in effect. 8.6 treaty of sangola 1750 — the chhatrapati becomes ceremonial shahu19-49 was an effective ruler, but he progressively delegated more & more power to the peshwa. after his death, a political crisis emerged when tarabai claimed that shahu's adopted son ramraja was not her grandson as had been stated at the time of adoption. to prevent the maratha state from being left without a chhatrapati, peshwa nana saheb40-61 backed ramraja — but also made him sign the treaty of sangola in february 1750. this treaty transferred all real power from chhatrapati ramraja to the peshwa. as power shifted downward from the chhatrapati to the peshwa, the maratha sardars felt even less constrained. they began acting more independently, & factionalism increased. 8.7 the series of peshwas baji rao20-40 had a brother named chimaji appa, whose son sadasiv rao bhau commanded the maratha army at the third battle of panipat in 1761 & died fighting. nana saheb40-61 did not fight in the battle but died within weeks of the defeat. his elder son vishwas rao also died fighting at panipat. the full peshwa lineage: 1. balaji vishwanath13-20 (1713–20) — the sixth peshwa, made the office hereditary in practice. 2. baji rao20-40 — son of balaji vishwanath. 3. balaji bajirao / nana saheb40-61 (1740–61) — son of baji rao; died weeks after panipat 1761. 4. madhav rao61-72 — younger son of nana saheb (his elder son vishwas rao having died at panipat). the word "young" here refers not just to his age but also to his inexperience. he died of natural causes in 1772. 5. narayan rao72-73 — brother of madhav rao; murdered in 1773 in a conspiracy hatched by his own uncle, raghunath rao73-74, who then became peshwa. 6. raghunath rao73-74 — uncle, the conspirator. the twelve ministers of narayan rao72-73 responded with their own conspiracy, the baarbhai conspiracy, removing raghunath rao73-74 from the peshwaship in revenge for narayan rao's murder. the man who led this conspiracy was nana fadnavis, a prominent minister of the peshwa. nana fadnavis had fought in the third battle of panipat 1761 & is regarded as a modern chanakya. crucially, he was the first to recognise that the eic had territorial ambitions in india & was not merely a commercial enterprise with trade motive. 7. madhav rao ii74-95 — infant peshwa, son of the murdered narayan rao72-73; nana fadnavis ruled as regent. the overbearing control of nana fadnavis drove madhav rao ii74-95 to suicide in 1795. 8. baji rao ii96-18 (1796–1818) — the last peshwa, son of raghunath rao73-74; his claim rested on bloodline. his rule ended with the third anglo-maratha war of 1817–19, after which the svarajya was annexed by the eic. diagram — peshwa hereditary chain: balaji vishwanath13-20 (6th peshwa, backs shahu, makes post hereditary) → baji rao20-40 (son; delhi plunder 1737, treaty of bhopal 1738) → balaji bajirao / nana saheb40-61 (panipat era; dies weeks after 1761 defeat) → madhav rao61-72 (young + able; temporary revival; natural death 1772) → narayan rao72-73 (murdered 1773 in palace conspiracy by raghunath) → raghunath rao73-74 (usurper uncle; briefly peshwa) → barbhai mandal 1774 (nana fadnavis, 12 ministers) removes raghunath; madhav rao ii74-95 (infant; suicide 1795) → baji rao ii96-18 (last peshwa; 3rd anglo-maratha war 1817-19 → svarajya annexed by eic) 8.8 the three broad phases of maratha polity the history of the maratha polity after shivaji74-80 can be divided into three broad phases: 1. 1680–1719 — turmoil. continuous mughal warfare following shivaji's death, & from 1707 to 1719, civil war among the marathas themselves. 2. 1719–1761 — growth & expansion. 3. 1761 onwards — decline. though with a temporary revival in the 1770s, most notably when the marathas defeated the eic in the first anglo-maratha war of 1775–82.

sections.chapterTitle: The Marathas: Rise, Administration & the Road to Panipat 1761
sections.title: Wars, Treaties & Territories — through to the 3rd Battle of Panipat 1761 & beyond
sections.norm: wars, treaties & territories — through to the 3rd battle of panipat 1761 & beyond. 9.1 the 1719 turning point — alliance with the sayyid brothers 1719 was a turning point. three major
