modern borders of the afghan state in 1747 before 1747, trusted commander of nadir shah governor of afghanistan invasion of 1756 culminated in the third battle of panipat in 1761 battle was fought between 1. the marathas 50,000 soldiers 2. an alliance of abdali47-72 (≈ 60,000) abdali47-72 najib-ud-daula57-70 ahmad khan50-82 shuja-ud-daula54-75 maratha military protection marathas effectively controlled delhi abdali's forces frequently raided north india son timur shah as governor of punjab & kashmir 1758, peshwa nana saheb40-61 sent his brother raghunath rao, who removed timur from lahore peak of maratha power — the maximum territory ever under maratha domination vishwas rao the emperor of hindustan 9.5 why abdali47-72 won — six factors 1. strength of his alliance awadh shuja54-75 rohilkhand & farrukhabad sikhs, rajputs, & jats all stayed neutral 60,000 soldiers against the marathas' 50,000 2. logistics. cut off the supply routes famine-like conditions developed 3. terrain. 4. firepower. horse-mounted swivel guns could pierce maratha armour 5. military leadership. abdali & najib-ud-daula of rohilkh alamgir ii madhav rao ii baji rao ii vishwanath farrukhsiyar shah muhammad shah nizam rao khan saheb jung abdali daula shuja ali shivaji chhatrapati shivaji shahu. 9.1 the 1719 turning point — alliance with the sayyid brothers the year 1719 was a turning point. peshwa balaji vishwanath13-20 engineered a decisive political alliance with the sayyid brothers, who were the kingmakers of the mughal court. together they removed the farrukhsiyar13-19 & placed muhammad shah19-48 on the throne as a puppet ruler. in return, the marathas secured three major concessions: 1. the mughals formally recognised maratha autonomous status in maharashtra. 2. the marathas received the chauth of malwa & gujarat. 3. they gained the right to collect chauth & sardeshmukhi from six mughal provinces of the deccan — khandesh, hyderabad, aurangabad, berar, bidar, & bijapur. since bijapur was later merged into golconda, some sources refer to golconda as the sixth province instead. the nizam's hyderabad state was later constituted from precisely these six erstwhile mughal provinces. this arrangement did not last long. in 1720, nizam24-48, the governor of hyderabad suba, defeated the sayyid brothers, ending their hold over the mughal court. muhammad shah19-48 was no longer purely their puppet — he became a joint puppet of the irani & turani factions of mansabdars. when nizam24-48 formally established hyderabad suba as an independent successor state in 1724, he refused to pay chauth & sardeshmukhi to the marathas. 9.2 the maratha decade of expansion (1727–39) the marathas responded with a decade of relentless military expansion: 1. 1727–28 — defeated the mughals in gujarat & extracted 60% of revenue as annual tribute. 2. 1728 — defeated hyderabad & regained the chauth & sardeshmukhi of the deccan. 3. 1729 — captured malwa & pushed reach into rajasthan. 4. 1731 — defeated a joint attack by nizam24-48 & local gujarat chiefs. 5. 1736 — defeated the portuguese & ethiopian muslims on the konkan coast. 6. 1737 — peshwa baji rao20-40 carried out a bold strike — he plundered delhi itself & held muhammad shah19-48 prisoner temporarily. 7. 1738 — defeated a large mughal army commanded by nizam24-48 and signed the treaty of bhopal (1738). under this treaty the marathas received the suba of malwa — formalising legally what they had already controlled de facto since 1729 — & sovereignty over all lands between the rivers chambal & narmada. 8. 1739 — treaty of bassein with the portuguese led to the annexation of bassein, also known as vasai. 9.3 expansion continues on multiple fronts (1745–54) 1. 1745–51 — raghuji bhonsle of nagpur regularly attacked the bengal suba & forced alivardi khan40-56 to give up control of odisha & pay chauth of bengal & bihar. chauth was paid until the battle of plassey in 1757. 2. 1751 — peshwa nana saheb40-61 attacked hyderabad & forced salabat jung51-62 to cede khandesh via the treaty of bhalke. 3. 1752 — the marathas took over ahmedabad, completing their annexation of gujarat. the peshwa appointed damaji gaikwad as the maratha chief & governor of gujarat, with his headquarters at baroda. 4. from 1751 onwards — the marathas regularly attacked the rajputs, extracting annual tributes & interfering in succession disputes. however, they were never able to fully conquer rajputana. they also failed to dominate the sikhs. 5. 1752 — the weakened mughal empire came under maratha protection — driven by fear of afghan invasions. 6. ahmad shah abdali launched at least seven invasions into india between 1748 & 1767, repeatedly destabilising the north. the first invasion, in 1748, was checked at the battle of manupur, where the mughal army fought the pitched battle against abdali's forces while the sikh misls harassed his supply lines. 7. 1754 — the marathas interfered in mughal succession & installed alamgir ii54-59 as their own puppet on the delhi throne. by the mid-18th century, the maratha state had emerged as the top power in india. 9.4 the third battle of panipat (1761) — sides & background ahmad shah abdali47-72 (1747-72), also known as durrani, founded the modern borders of the afghan state in 1747. he declared himself independent king following the death of nadir shah, who had been the emperor of iran & afghanistan. before 1747, abdali had served as a trusted commander of nadir shah & as governor of afghanistan, including participating in nadir shah's invasion of india in 1738–40. his invasion of 1756 culminated in the third battle of panipat in 1761. this battle was fought between: 1. the marathas on one side (≈ 50,000 soldiers). 2. an alliance of abdali47-72 (≈ 60,000) on the other, comprising: • abdali47-72 himself. • the rohillas under najib-ud-daula57-70 of rohilkhand. • the bangash pathans under ahmad khan50-82 of farrukhabad. • awadh under nawab shuja-ud-daula54-75. by 1752, the weakened mughal emperor had come under maratha military protection & the marathas effectively controlled delhi. from 1756 onwards, abdali's forces frequently raided north india. abdali had successfully installed his eleven-year-old son timur shah as governor of punjab & kashmir. in 1758, peshwa nana saheb40-61 sent his brother raghunath rao, who removed timur from lahore. this was the peak of maratha power — the maximum territory ever under maratha domination. nana saheb40-61 even contemplated making his son vishwas rao the emperor of hindustan. then the third battle of panipat changed everything. 9.5 why abdali47-72 won — six factors 1. strength of his alliance. awadh joined abdali because it felt strategically encircled by the marathas — they were already collecting chauth from bihar & bengal since 1751 in the east, controlling delhi in the west since 1752, & the maratha samrajya lay to the south. when the marathas sought an alliance with shuja54-75, he chose instead to join the islamic alliance. the indian afghan kingdoms of rohilkhand & farrukhabad backed abdali hoping for greater influence under an afghan emperor. the sikhs, rajputs, & jats all stayed neutral — a direct consequence of years of maratha plundering & tribute extraction. abdali's alliance fielded around 60,000 soldiers against the marathas' 50,000. 2. logistics. abdali successfully cut off the supply routes between the maratha camp at panipat & delhi. famine-like conditions developed — no food for the men, no fodder for the horses. 3. terrain. panipat's vast open plains gave no advantage to maratha guerrilla tactics, which depended on hills, forests, & narrow passes. 4. firepower. abdali's horse-mounted swivel guns could pierce maratha armour. 5. military leadership. both abdali & najib-ud-daula of rohilkhand provided strong, coordinated command. 6. maratha factionalism. raghuji bhonsle of nagpur refused to fight. he was opposed to nana saheb40-61 as peshwa. in 1765, the peshwa even went so far as to plunder nagpur in retaliation. he also did not participate in the first anglo-maratha war of 1775–82. 9.6 impact of the defeat the military losses were severe. key maratha leaders — sadasiv rao bhau & vishwas rao — died fighting. nana saheb40-61 had not fought in the battle himself, as someone was needed to guard other frontiers in the south. he arrived with reinforcements but by then the battle was already lost. he died within weeks of the defeat. the marathas lost 50,000 men in total, including both combatants & non-combatants. the defeat deepened factionalism within the maratha confederacy. young, inexperienced peshwas now came to power in succession — the young but brilliant madhav rao61-72, then incompetent narayan rao72-73, then the infant madhav rao ii74-95. internal disputes consumed energy that should have been directed outward. abdali too paid a heavy price. his army suffered serious losses & faced an anti-abdali revolt among his own generals back in afghanistan. he returned home with his loot but was unable to consolidate any lasting presence in india. the deeper consequence was a power vacuum at the centre of indian politics. the third battle of panipat did not decide who would rule india. what it decided was that neither the marathas nor abdali would rule india. that vacuum was eventually filled by the british eic, which went on to defeat the regional indian states one by one. 9.7 after panipat — decline with moments of strength the third battle of panipat halted the maratha rise & began their decline. but the decline of a large power takes time. the marathas continued to wield considerable influence in indian politics for decades afterwards. 1. 1765 — marathas defeated mysore & extracted tribute. 2. 1766 — treaty of hyderabad. hyderabad gave the northern sarkars to the eic in return for an annual payment of seven lakh rupees & protection against both the marathas & mysore. the northern sarkars (also called northern circars) were initially four districts — chicacole (srikakulam), rajmandri (rajahmundry), ellore (eluru), & mustafanagar (kondapalli) — with murtuzanagar (guntur) added later as a fifth. guntur was not transferred to the eic in 1766. 3. 1771 — mahadji scindia recaptured delhi from the rohilla afghans, who had taken it in 1761. 4. 1775–82 — first anglo-maratha war. the marathas defeated the eic — the only war in this period the eic lost. 5. 1782 — treaty of salbai. a maratha–eic military alliance that held until 1795. 6. 1784 — mahadji shinde (also known as scindia) hired benoît de boigne, a french military adventurer. de boigne raised & trained the fauj-i-hind, also called the campoo system (each campoo was an integrated force having own infantry, own cavalry, own artillery, thus self-sufficient units), that transformed the army from a traditional light cavalry force into a modern, disciplined european-style infantry -cavalry- artillery machine (*similar to haider ali61-82’s army which was also modernized with help of french; today also that cooperation continues). other maratha sardars followed this example — holkar, for instance, hired the frenchman dudrenec to train his own battalions. 7. 1795 — battle of kharda. a maratha victory over hyderabad. the eic stayed neutral as the marathas were still their ally under the treaty of salbai 1782. this was the last battle fought between hyderabad & the marathas (*reason below) 8. 1798 — hyderabad became the first indian state to sign a treaty of subsidiary alliance (also called subordinate alliance) with the eic, securing guaranteed eic protection & effectively ending its vulnerability to maratha pressure. 9. 1803 — eic captured delhi in the second anglo-maratha war. 10. 1817–19 — third anglo-maratha war. svarajya was annexed by the eic, ending the last peshwa baji rao ii96-18's rule. 9.8 why couldn't the marathas establish all-india rule? the marathas came closer than any other power in eighteenth-century india to establishing an all-india empire. yet they never crossed that threshold. the reasons are structural. 1. tribute, not annexation. in many cases, after a military victory, the marathas limited themselves to extracting chauth & sardeshmukhi rather than annexing the defeated territory & establishing direct rule. extracting tribute is not the same as ruling. ruling means making & implementing policies through your own administration on the ground. it begins after conquest, & for one central authority to rule effectively, power must be properly centralised — one country, one ruler, one law, & rule of law. 2. weak centre, strong sardars. the maratha centre was never strong enough for centralised rule, & it was weakened further by factionalism. power could never be properly centralised because the maratha sardars had always been autonomous. shivaji74-80 never gave jagirs to his officers, & shahu19-49 never gave vatan jagirs to military commanders. as a result, ambitious sardars who wanted their own principalities ventured out on their own initiative to build the samrajya. in territories brought under maratha control through the sardars' own efforts, the authority of the chhatrapati would naturally be weak. 3. the treaty of sangola 1750. as power shifted downward from the chhatrapati to the peshwa under sangola, the sardars felt even less constrained. factionalism grew. after 1761, a succession of weak peshwas accelerated this process further. 4. power was not properly centralized even in svarajya. within svarajya, local assemblies of vatan right holders — the deshmukhs & the patils — asserted themselves & exerted pressure on the peshwa. 5. in samrajya, effective centralised rule did not exist at all in many areas i.e. certain areas militarlity under a maratha sardar but no effective government machinery present on ground. establishing the rule of one central authority over the whole of india was therefore a distant goal, & after the third battle of panipat in 1761, it became an impossible one. 9.9 ⚠ alert: mains 2014 : why have so many empire-shaking battles been fought near panipat? the battles were never really fought for the city of panipat itself. they were fought because this region is the gateway to delhi. any power advancing from central asia or afghanistan towards delhi had to come through the khyber pass, & the natural staging ground before the final push to delhi runs through the region containing panipat, karnal, kurukshetra, & thanesar. for any ruler sitting in delhi, the strategically sound move was always to stop the enemy at these gates rather than let them reach the capital. several practical factors reinforced this: 1. the vast open fields of the region suited large armies manoeuvring for set-piece battles. 2. the weather supported prolonged campaigns. 3. the presence of many warrior communities in the area made military recruitment easier. 4. the region's agricultural productivity, combined with its proximity to delhi, made supplying a large army far more manageable than in more remote locations. the historical record speaks for itself: 1. mahmud of ghazni fought at thanesar in 1014 & had built an empire stretching from iran to today's pakistan by 1030. 2. muhammad ghori fought at thanesar in 1191. 3. the first battle of panipat in 1526 shook the delhi sultanate. 4. the second battle of panipat in 1556 ended the rule of hemu. 5. the battle of karnal in 1739 shook the mughals. 6. the third battle of panipat in 1761 shook the marathas.

sections.chapterTitle: The Jat Kingdom & the Afghan Kingdoms
sections.title: Framework — two more Rebel States alongside the Marathas
sections.norm: framework — two more rebel states alongside the marathas. farrukhabad rohilkhand. apart from the marathas, there were three more rebel states in 18th c : the jat kingdom of bharatpur in east rajasthan & the two afghan kingdoms- farrukhabad (est. 1714) & rohilkhand (crystallised 1737–40). all three used opportunity created by the weakening mughal empire to convert local military power into territorial rule but all three could not establish a large sustainable empire.

sections.chapterTitle: The Jat Kingdom & the Afghan Kingdoms
sections.title: The Jat Kingdom (1695-1763)
sections.norm: the jat kingdom (1695-1763). 2.1 who were the jats and why did they resist the mughals? agrarian community of north india cultivation as their traditional occupation deep-rooted jahangir05-27 harsh land revenue policies & the mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy zamindars traditional leaders of rural society organised resistance 2.2 how did jat resistance develop over time? first organised jat revolt came in 1669 zamindar gokla rajaram → churaman95-21 (1695-1721)→ badan singh → surajmal56-63 (1756-63) guerrilla warfare fast, decentralised, & difficult for a large mughal army to counter effectively jat kingdom of bharatpur east rajasthan south of delhi mathura & agra districts formally established by churaman jat (1695–1721) turned peasant discontent over high land revenue into political & military power lohagarh fort, bharatpur — the "iron fort" (because it was never conquered, even by the british) of the jat kingdom, built by maharaja surajmal56-63 2.3 what made surajmal56-63's reign the peak of jat power? maharaja surajmal56-63 (1756–63) reached its peak strong, centralised state forced the mughal emperor to formally recognise him as an autonomous ruler (*within mughal empire) forward-looking recruited european soldiers mughal-style revenue system removed relatives from court from delhi to agra & from the chambal river to the ganga present-day delhi, haryana, uttar pradesh, & rajasthan offered help to the marathas alliance could not be established 2.4 was the jat kingdom a better deal for the peasant than mughal rule? no peasant utopia real power rested with zamindars jahangir churaman surajmal. 2.1 who were the jats and why did they resist the mughals? the jats were primarily an agrarian community of north india, with cultivation as their traditional occupation. their hostility toward the mughal state was deep-rooted, stretching back to the reign of jahangir05-27, when harsh land revenue policies & the mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed zamindars — the traditional leaders of rural society — toward organised resistance. 2.2 how did jat resistance develop over time? the first organised jat revolt came in 1669, led by zamindar gokla. after him, the torch passed through a line of leaders — rajaram → churaman95-21 (1695-1721)→ badan singh → surajmal56-63 (1756-63) — each pushing jat resistance further. their preferred method was guerrilla warfare: fast, decentralised, & difficult for a large mughal army to counter effectively. the jat kingdom of bharatpur — located in east rajasthan, south of delhi, bordering the mathura & agra districts — was formally established by churaman jat (1695–1721). like many rebel-state founders of this era (*e.g. marathas, sikh), zamindar churaman turned peasant discontent over high land revenue into political & military power. 📷 lohagarh fort, bharatpur — the "iron fort" (because it was never conquered, even by the british) of the jat kingdom, built by maharaja surajmal56-63 2.3 what made surajmal56-63's reign the peak of jat power? under maharaja surajmal56-63 (1756–63), the jat state reached its peak. he built a strong, centralised state & forced the mughal emperor to formally recognise him as an autonomous ruler (*within mughal empire). his reforms were forward-looking: 1. he recruited european soldiers to modernise his military. 2. he introduced a mughal-style revenue system for administrative efficiency. 3. & — significantly — he removed relatives from court positions to reduce factionalism. (*compare this with factionalism in form of royal family infighting in mughal state) at its peak, the jat state stretched from delhi to agra & from the chambal river to the ganga, covering territories across present-day delhi, haryana, uttar pradesh, & rajasthan. after surajmal56-63's death in 1763, the jat state collapsed. surajmal56-63's offered help to the marathas before the 3rd battle of panipat 1761 but ultimately the alliance could not be established due to differences over war strategy & tactics. surajmal56-63 wanted to deploy guerrilla warfare strategy rather than traditional warfare while maratha commander sadashivrao bhau disagreed. jats sent essential supplies to marathas during the war. 2.4 was the jat kingdom a better deal for the peasant than mughal rule? though the kingdom was result of peasant revolts, it was no peasant utopia. land revenue remained high, & real power rested with zamindars — not with the ryots. the jat state replicated the same extractive structure it had risen against. diagram 1 — jat kingdom: gokla 1669 → rajaram → churaman (bharatpur 1695-1721) → badan singh → maharaja surajmal56-63 (1756-63 peak; reforms; delhi-agra/chambal-ganga territory) → 1763 collapse

sections.title: The Afghan Kingdoms
sections.norm: the afghan kingdoms. 3.1 who were the afghans and what brought them to north india? afghans had been migrating into north india military labour markets 3.2 was there ever a moment when afghans actually ruled delhi? sher shah suri40-45 story of all these afghan migrants compressed into one life suris, a clan of the pashtun tribe migrated from the sur region of afghanistan to india during the lodi sultanate period in the late 15th c small jagir in sasaram (present-day bihar) lodi sultans sher shah suri40-45 — born farid khan around 1486 in sasaram not in afghanistan but in bihar second-generation indian afghan north indian military labour market served under various masters, rising through ability rather than birth administrator under the afghan governor of bihar mughals after babur26-30 defeated the lodis in 1526 closely studied mughal administrative methods — a knowledge he would later turn against them power base in bihar & bengal military skill & administrative ability 1540 had defeated humayun30-40 (1530–40, first reign) at the battle of kanauj driving him into exile to persia & seizing the throne of delhi bangash pathans of farrukhabad very different ceiling on what they could achieve political window available to them was much narrower 3.3 what did sher shah suri40-45 actually achieve in just five years? reign of just five years reorganised the empire into a clean hierarchy careful land surveys fixed a fair land revenue demand directly with the peasant, cutting out the middleman zamindar first ruler to seriously attempt what we today call "administrative reform" streamlining the state machinery to make it both efficient & fair had only five years to do it death in 1545 competing warlord groups circulating through north india's military labor markets 1540 to 1555 – — marks this brief afghan interruption of mughal rule humayun30-40 recaptured delhi in 1555 after battle of sirhind death in 1556 sher shah suri's tomb, sasaram(bihar) — the red-sandstone mausoleum of the five-year afghan ruler of delhi 18th c brought a new surge of afghan migration progressive weakening of the mughal state two afghan kingdoms emerged from this window — farrukhabad (*today a district in uttar pradesh; bangash pathans) & rohilkhand (*also called rampur with capital bareilly; rohilla afghans) suri babur humayun akbar. 3.1 who were the afghans and what brought them to north india? afghans had been migrating into north india since the 15th c, driven by poor economic conditions & political instability back home. in the military labour markets of north india, they functioned largely as wandering warlords — skilled fighters available to whoever could pay. 3.2 was there ever a moment when afghans actually ruled delhi? the story of sher shah suri40-45 is in many ways the story of all these afghan migrants compressed into one life. his family — the suris, a clan of the pashtun tribe — had migrated from the sur region of afghanistan to india during the lodi sultanate period in the late 15th c. his grandfather had received a small jagir in sasaram (present-day bihar) in service of the lodi sultans. sher shah suri40-45 — born farid khan around 1486 in sasaram — thus grew up not in afghanistan but in bihar, as a second-generation indian afghan. he was very much a product of the north indian military labour market: he served under various masters, rising through ability rather than birth. he served as an administrator under the afghan governor of bihar, then briefly under the mughals after babur26-30 defeated the lodis in 1526. it was during this mughal service that he closely studied mughal administrative methods — a knowledge he would later turn against them. he built his own power base in bihar & bengal through a combination of military skill & administrative ability, & by 1540 had defeated humayun30-40 (1530–40, first reign) at the battle of kanauj, driving him into exile to persia & seizing the throne of delhi. (*compare story of suri40-45 with the bangash pathans of farrukhabad we will read about shortly — same afghan migrant background, same military labour market entry, but a very different ceiling on what they could achieve, partly because the political window available to them was much narrower.) 3.3 what did sher shah suri40-45 actually achieve in just five years? his reign of just five years punches far above its weight in indian history. on the administrative side, he reorganised the empire into a clean hierarchy — centre → province (suba) → district (sarkar) → sub-district (pargana) — a structure akbar56-05 would later adopt almost wholesale. he upgraded the grand trunk road connecting bengal to the north-west frontier, set up a reliable postal relay system (dak chowki), & introduced a standardised (by weight & value) silver coin — the rupiya — which became the basis of indian currency for c. on revenue, he commissioned careful land surveys & fixed a fair land revenue demand directly with the peasant, cutting out the middleman zamindar. (*in a sense, suri40-45 was the first ruler to seriously attempt what we today call "administrative reform" — streamlining the state machinery to make it both efficient & fair. unfortunately he had only five years to do it. his successors could not hold together what he built.) after his death in 1545, the afghans fragmented again into competing warlord groups circulating through north india's military labor markets. the period from 1540 to 1555 – called suri interregnum 1540-55 — marks this brief afghan interruption of mughal rule, ending only when humayun30-40 recaptured delhi in 1555 after battle of sirhind & briefly restored mughal authority before his death in 1556. diagram 2 — sher shah suri40-45: 15th-c sur clan migration → sasaram jagir → farid khan → 1540 battle of kanauj defeats humayun30-40 → suba/sarkar/pargana hierarchy (akbar56-05 inherits) → grand trunk road / dak chowki / rupiya / peasant-direct revenue → 1545 dies → suri interregnum 1540-55 → 1555 humayun30-40 returns 📷 sher shah suri's tomb, sasaram(bihar) — the red-sandstone mausoleum of the five-year afghan ruler of delhi the 18th c brought a new surge of afghan migration as political instability in their homeland intensified. the progressive weakening of the mughal state created exactly the kind of opportunity these groups had been waiting for. two afghan kingdoms emerged from this window — farrukhabad (*today a district in uttar pradesh; bangash pathans) & rohilkhand (*also called rampur with capital bareilly; rohilla afghans).

sections.chapterTitle: The Jat Kingdom & the Afghan Kingdoms
sections.title: Farrukhabad (est. 1714)
sections.norm: farrukhabad (est. 1714). 4.1 how did a bangash pathan warlord end up founding a kingdom near agra? farrukhabad how factional mughal court politics created vacuums that outsiders could exploit structurally weak from the start powerful neighbours, principally awadh, who preyed on it whenever the opportunity arose sequence of events across three rulers 4.2 md khan bangash14-43— the founder(1714–43) 1712–13 jahandar shah12-13 (1712–13) seized power by killing the father of farukhsiyar13-19 (1713–19) avenged this by removing jahandar shah12-13 md khan bangash14-43 pathan warlord supported farukhsiyar13-19 with 12,000 troops rewarded with the rank of nawab & revenue assignments in the farrukhabad region 1714 mohammadabad annoyed farukhsiyar13-19 diplomatic correction classic pattern: 1743 son qaim khan. 4.3 qaim khan — and the 1749 annexation by awadh 1749 safdar jung39-54 (1739–54) farrukhabad was formally annexed to awadh & plundered wazir's loyalty being to his own state rather than the emperor he nominally served 4.4 ahmad khan bangash50-82 — 1750–1802 1750. 1751-52 marathas jats drove out ahmad khan50-82 out of farrukhabad. 1751 treaty in 1752 resume rule but half of farrukhabad to holkar & scindia 1761 fought alongside 3rd battle of panipat recovered his full dominions including the half ceded in 1752 abdali left india in 1761, farrukhabad weakened. 1802 eic annexed farrukhabad "ceded provinces" 1857 revolt ultimately defeated bangash shah farukhsiyar jung rao surajmal khan. 4.1 how did a bangash pathan warlord end up founding a kingdom near agra? the founding of farrukhabad illustrates how factional mughal court politics created vacuums that outsiders could exploit. farrukhabad was structurally weak from the start — sitting between powerful neighbours, principally awadh, who preyed on it whenever the opportunity arose. its history is best understood as a sequence of events across three rulers. 4.2 md khan bangash14-43— the founder(1714–43) in 1712–13, jahandar shah12-13 (1712–13) had seized power by killing the father of farukhsiyar13-19 (1713–19). farukhsiyar13-19 avenged this by removing jahandar shah12-13. md khan bangash14-43, a pathan warlord, supported farukhsiyar13-19 with 12,000 troops & was rewarded with the rank of nawab & revenue assignments in the farrukhabad region — present-day farrukhabad district in central uttar pradesh, on the banks of the ganga. in 1714 he founded the city of farrukhabad, naming it after the emperor as a gesture of loyalty. (*he had first founded a town called mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed farukhsiyar13-19. farrukhabad — "the city of farrukh" — was the diplomatic correction. classic pattern: a rebel state acknowledging mughal sovereignty in name while building real autonomy on the ground.) in 1743, md khan bangash14-43 dies. succeeded by his son qaim khan. 4.3 qaim khan — and the 1749 annexation by awadh in 1749, safdar jung39-54 (1739–54) — simultaneously nawab of awadh & wazir of the mughal emperor — used his imperial position to engineer qaim khan's death in battle. farrukhabad was formally annexed to awadh & plundered. (*textbook example of the wazir's loyalty being to his own state rather than the emperor he nominally served — the highest mughal mansab had become a tool for personal & regional ambition.) 4.4 ahmad khan bangash50-82 — 1750–1802 ahmad khan 50-82 fought back and retook farrukhabad in 1750. in 1751-52, the marathas — specifically malhar rao holkar & jayappaji rao scindia, sent by peshwa balaji baji rao40-61, along with jats under surajmal56-63 — drove out ahmad khan50-82 out of farrukhabad. (note: awadh had requested marathas & jats in 1751.). as afghan invasion of ahmed shah abdali progressed, marathas signed a treaty in 1752 that allowed him to return & resume rule, but the price was handing over half of farrukhabad to holkar & scindia. in 1761, ahmad khan50-82 fought alongside ahmad shah abdali at the 3rd battle of panipat. with the marathas now defeated, he recovered his full dominions including the half ceded in 1752. but once abdali left india in 1761, farrukhabad weakened. in 1802, the eic annexed farrukhabad. (*the "ceded provinces" refers to the territories awadh was forced to hand over under the subsidiary alliance of 1801. farrukhabad was merged into the ceded provinces post annexation.) the bangash pathans participated in the 1857 revolt but were ultimately defeated.

sections.title: Rohilkhand (est. 1737–40)
sections.norm: rohilkhand (est. 1737–40). 5.1 how did afghan mercenaries turn into rulers of their own kingdom? rohilkhand afghan mercenaries slowly filling a power vacuum originally called katehr 17th & early 18th c local zamindars & regional governors in katehr began hiring afghan mercenaries to settle local disputes & enforce their authority afghan fighters — who came to be called rohillas rohilkhand was formed by these settled afghan mercenaries long before abdali word "rohilla" 5.2 1721 — the starting point: daud khan ali md khan21-48(1721-48) daud khan died in 1721 adopted son ali md khan21-48 took over starting point not yet an independent state, after 1721 ali md khan slowly absorbing lands uniting the scattered afghan mercenary groups 5.3 what finally pushed ali md khan21-48 to declare independence? mercenary strongman to independent ruler nadir shah's devastating invasion of delhi in 1739 compare this with farrukhabad: 5.4 how did the mughals respond — and why could they do nothing about it? mughal state, too weak standard strategy: co-opt what you cannot defeat 1740, granted ali md khan21-48 the title of subadar katehr was officially renamed rohilkhand co-option strategy 5.5 how did rohilkhand end? same arc as farrukhabad 1761 najib-ud-daula57-70 abdali at the 3rd battle of panipat 1761–71 delhi was effectively under rohilla influence 1771 mahadji scindia68-94 recaptured delhi rohilkhand was annexed by awadh with eic help in 1774 treaty of allahabad (1765) state of rampur with capital bareilly but under awadh legally from 1801 under eic legally alert: prelims 2010. immediate reason for the 3rd battle of panipat 1761 timur shah march 1758 raghunath rao73-74 sabaji scindia attock and peshawar conquest of punjab immediate trigger khan shah muhammad shah daula najib scindia rao bangash farukhsiyar jung. 5.1 how did afghan mercenaries turn into rulers of their own kingdom? rohilkhand did not emerge overnight. it was a gradual process — afghan mercenaries slowly filling a power vacuum left by a collapsing mughal state. to understand it properly, we need to go back a little. the region that became rohilkhand was originally called katehr — present-day western uttar pradesh, centred around bareilly & moradabad. during the 17th & early 18th c, as mughal central authority weakened, local zamindars & regional governors in katehr began hiring afghan mercenaries to settle local disputes & enforce their authority. these afghan fighters — who came to be called rohillas — gradually became a dominant armed presence in the region. (*note: rohilkhand was formed by these settled afghan mercenaries/rohilla afghans consolidating power from within the region — and were already entrenched in katehr long before abdali ever entered india.) (*the word "rohilla" itself comes from "roh" — the afghan homeland. so rohilkhand literally means "the land of the rohillas.") 5.2 1721 — the starting point: daud khan and ali md khan21-48(1721-48) when daud khan, the afghan commander who had consolidated these mercenary groups in katehr, died in 1721, his adopted son & protégé ali md khan21-48 took over leadership of the afghan troops. this is the starting point — not yet an independent state, but the moment one man gained control of a significant armed force in the region. after 1721, ali md khan moved methodically. rather than declaring independence immediately, he spent the next two decades consolidating — slowly absorbing lands from the very zamindars his men had been hired to protect, & uniting the scattered afghan mercenary groups under his sole command. 5.3 what finally pushed ali md khan21-48 to declare independence? the actual shift from mercenary strongman to independent ruler came with nadir shah's devastating invasion of delhi in 1739. with the mughal state completely paralysed, ali md khan stopped paying taxes to delhi & began ruling katehr as an independent power — capturing & consolidating key districts including bareilly & moradabad. (*compare this with farrukhabad: both afghan kingdoms used the same window — mughal paralysis — to convert military presence into territorial control. the difference is that md khan bangash14-43had done it earlier & more formally through mughal court politics, while ali md khan did it through slow ground-level consolidation followed by outright defiance during the 1739 crisis.) 5.4 how did the mughals respond — and why could they do nothing about it? the mughal state, too weak to crush ali md khan21-48 militarily, fell back on its standard strategy: co-opt what you cannot defeat. in 1740, emperor md shah19-48 (1719–48) formally granted ali md khan21-48 the title of subadar. from 1740, katehr was officially renamed rohilkhand — the land of the rohillas — & functioned as an autonomous state under nominal mughal sovereignty. (* ali md khan21-48 took control in 1721 but was officially recognized as nawab of rohilkhand by mughal in 1740. this co-option strategy was used repeatedly by the weakening mughal state. the title gave the rebel legitimacy; it gave the mughals the illusion of control. both sides understood the fiction). 5.5 how did rohilkhand end? the subsequent history of rohilkhand follows the same arc as farrukhabad — rise on the back of afghan military power, peak during the abdali alliance, & collapse once that external prop was removed. in 1761, under najib-ud-daula57-70, rohilkhand actively supported abdali at the 3rd battle of panipat. from 1761–71, delhi was effectively under rohilla influence (*mughal emperor was in awadh). with death of najib57-70 in 1770 and no abdali to support since 1761, rohilkhand weakened. in 1771, mahadji scindia68-94 recaptured delhi and allowed mughal emperor shah alam ii 60-06 (1760-1806) to return home (*red fort). most of rohilkhand was annexed by awadh with eic help in 1774. eic had helped due to treaty of allahabad (1765) that led to a military alliance. rest small part of rohilkhand became the autonomous state of rampur with capital bareilly but under awadh legally and from 1801 under eic legally when awadh gave half of awadh in subsidiary alliance. ⚠ alert: prelims 2010. abdali's immediate reason for the 3rd battle of panipat 1761 was to avenge the expulsion by the marathas of his son timur shah from lahore. in march 1758, raghunath rao73-74 crossed into punjab & drove away timur shah (abdali's son & governor of punjab & kashmir); the marathas then appointed adina beg khan as governor of punjab for an annual tribute of ₹75 lakh, & on his death sabaji scindia took charge. sabaji scindia was the general who commanded the maratha garrisons at attock and peshawar (on the afghan border) and fiercely defended them against abdali's forces. the maratha conquest of punjab from the afghans was a direct challenge abdali could not ignore — that was the immediate trigger. diagram 3 — farrukhabad + rohilkhand combined: md khan bangash14-43(1714 founding via farukhsiyar13-19) / ali md khan (katehr consolidation 1721) / 1739 nadir shah trigger (md shah19-48 grants nawab title) / 1749 safdar jung39-54 annexes farrukhabad / 1752 marathas restore ahmad khan / 1761 panipat alliance / 1771 mahadji scindia 68-64 retakes delhi / 1774 awadh+eic (treaty of allahabad 1765) annex rohilkhand → rampur / 1802 eic annexes farrukhabad

sections.chapterTitle: The Jat Kingdom & the Afghan Kingdoms
sections.title: Synthesis — Three Rebel States, Same pattern
sections.norm: synthesis — three rebel states, same pattern. jats farrukhabad rohilkhand each needed external support each collapsed when that support was removed. farukhsiyar surajmal. the jats built their state from an agrarian base upward — zamindar-led revolt → territory → reforming ruler. farrukhabad built from mughal court politics downward — 12,000 troops for farukhsiyar13-19 → nawab title → city → dynasty. rohilkhand built from the ground up over two decades — hired mercenaries → consolidation → independence under the 1739 delhi paralysis. each needed external support to peak — abdali for the afghan kingdoms; the marathas (tactical support, not full alliance) backing surajmal56-63. each collapsed when that support was removed.

sections.title: How did Sikhism begin, and what were its core beliefs?
sections.norm: how did sikhism begin, and what were its core beliefs?. guru nanak dev (1469–1539) babur26-30 1500 udasis 30 years 30,000 kilometres kartarpur langar babur. guru nanak dev (1469–1539) was a contemporary of babur26-30. sikhism rose from 1500 onwards, built on four core principles: 1. one supreme & formless god. 2. direct access to god without rituals or priests. 3. rejection of the caste system. 4. emphasis on honest living & selfless service. guru nanak dev ji undertook four major spiritual journeys — udasis — over 30 years, covering approximately 30,000 kilometres across india, south asia, tibet, & arabia. he finally settled in kartarpur, in present-day pakistan, where he established the institution of langar — the free communal kitchen designed to promote equality.

sections.title: When did conflict begin between the Sikhs and the Mughal State?
sections.norm: when did conflict begin between the sikhs and the mughal state?. anandpur shivalik hill chiefs 1606 arjan dev jahangir05-27 1675 teg bahadur aurangzeb58-07 jahangir aurangzeb. initially, there was no conflict between the sikh community & the mughal state. but as the sikh population grew & sikhs began demanding a sikh state in & around anandpur — west of shimla & south of chamba, an area under the shivalik hill chiefs who were mughal allies — religious & political tensions began to build. the first major flashpoint came in 1606, when the 5th guru arjan dev, was executed by jahangir05-27. this was a turning point. what had been a peaceful spiritual movement began its transformation into a martial community. the second major flashpoint came in 1675, when the 9th guru teg bahadur, was executed in delhi by aurangzeb58-07.

sections.title: What was the Khalsa, and why was it created?
sections.norm: what was the khalsa, and why was it created?. 1699 gobind singh76-08 khalsa december 1704 battle of chamkaur wazir khan 1707 bahadur shah07-12 mansab october 7, 1708 abchal nagar sahib gurdwara singh shah. in 1699, in anandpur, the 10th guru gobind singh76-08, established the khalsa — a sikh military organisation created to defend the sikh panth & struggle for a sikh state. (think of the khalsa as something like a nsg/stf — its creation marked the formal militarisation of the sikh community's political ambitions.) in december 1704, guru gobind singh76-08's two elder sons — sahibzada ajit singh (aged 18) & sahibzada jujhar singh (aged 14) — died in the battle of chamkaur. the same month, his two younger sons — sahibzada zorawar singh (aged 9) & sahibzada fateh singh (aged 6) — were buried alive in a wall on the orders of wazir khan, the mughal faujdar of sirhind. (faujdar: district military commander — comparable in local authority to a superintendent of police today. since 2022, 26th december is observed as veer bal divas in memory younger sahibzadas.) in 1707, the new emperor bahadur shah07-12, following pacifist policy (*using diplomacy more than war), granted guru gobind singh76-08 a high mansab & promised him a sikh state in & around anandpur. but the promise was never fulfilled. then, on october 7, 1708, wazir khan arranged for assassins to attack guru gobind singh76-08 at abchal nagar sahib gurdwara in nanded, maharashtra, where the guru had accompanied bahadur shah07-12. guru gobind singh ji76-08 killed the assassins himself but later succumbed to his injuries. he died at the age of 42. no action was taken against wazir khan. anandpur was never given to the sikhs.

sections.title: Why did Guru Gobind Singh76-08 declare the Guru Granth Sahib Ji as the final Guru?
sections.norm: why did guru gobind singh76-08 declare the guru granth sahib ji as the final guru?. guru granth sahib ji decision was deliberate prevent community tensions 📷 harmandir sahib (golden temple) and akal takht, amritsar — spiritual & temporal seats of the sikh community ( akal takht nirankaris & namdharis singh. few days before his death, guru gobind singh ji76-08 declared at abchal nagar sahib that he would be the last living guru, & that all spiritual authority would henceforth be vested in the guru granth sahib ji — the holy book he had compiled. this decision was deliberate. it was made to prevent community tensions between the jat community, which dominated the khalsa, & the khatri community of traders, to which all ten gurus had belonged. by vesting authority in the holy book rather than a human successor, the question of community dominance was permanently closed. 📷 harmandir sahib (golden temple) and akal takht, amritsar — spiritual & temporal seats of the sikh community (it was from the akal takht that the gurus issued hukumnamas — formal orders — & where sikh warriors took blessings before going into battle against the mughals) guru granth sahib ji was installed at the akal takht in the golden temple complex in amritsar. the 19th-century sects of nirankaris & namdharis, believe in a living guru and this has historically led to serious conflicts within the community. diagram 1 — sikh guruship lineage and the transition to the eternal guru: from guru nanak dev ji (1469–1539) through the ten human gurus to guru granth sahib ji as the final guru, declared by gobind singh ji76-08 at abchal nagar sahib in october 1708

sections.title: How did Banda Bahadur08-15 establish the first Sikh State — and why did it collapse?
sections.norm: how did banda bahadur08-15 establish the first sikh state — and why did it collapse?. 1708 banda bahadur08-15 battle of chappar chiri may 10, 1710 river ravi river jamuna farukhsiyar13-19 abdus samad khan 1715 jahandar shah12-13 ijaradari mansabs churaman jat95-21 (1695-1721) 1716 bahadur farukhsiyar shah jat. from 1708, the rebellion was carried forward by banda bahadur08-15. he defeated and killed wazir khan at the battle of chappar chiri on may 10, 1710, which also led to the conquest of sirhind. banda bahadur08-15 established a sikh state over territories between the river ravi & the river jamuna — with his own coins, his own officials, & his own seal for issuing administrative orders. farukhsiyar13-19 appointed abdus samad khan as governor of lahore specifically to suppress this sikh state. by 1715, banda bahadur08-15 was defeated. his downfall came due to following reasons: 1. khatri traders turned against him. constant warfare hurt trade, & the commercial class needs decisive victors & political stability to function. 2. the mughals used a deliberate policy of divide & rule. jahandar shah12-13 introduced ijaradari — the revenue farming system — in punjab specifically to co-opt khatri traders with business opportunities. both jahandar shah12-13 & farukhsiyar13-19 offered mansabs to khatri traders, who then switched sides. (note: this further increased the number of mansabdars, adding to the jagirdari crisis discussed earlier.) 3. hindu jat zamindars switched sides. churaman jat95-21 (1695-1721), for instance, went over to the mughals after they recognised his jat kingdom — granting him conditional dynastic autonomy in exchange for loyalty. with his economic & military support base eroded, banda bahadur08-15 was captured & executed in delhi in 1716 by farukhsiyar13-19. diagram 2 — banda bahadur08-15's first sikh state (1708–15): battle of chappar chiri 1710 → conquest of sirhind → sikh state between ravi & jamuna with own coins/officials/seal → farukhsiyar13-19 appoints abdus samad khan as governor of lahore → 1715 defeat → 1716 execution in delhi

sections.title: What kept the Sikh State alive after Banda Bahadur08-15's defeat?
sections.norm: what kept the sikh state alive after banda bahadur08-15's defeat?. misl chiefs misls 1770 12 major misls dal khalsa takeaway: maratha confederacy under the peshwas bahadur. the defeat of banda bahadur08-15 did not end the sikh state. the mughals were too weak to fully reassert control over punjab, & power became decentralised among misl chiefs. misls are kinship-based clans. they united during wars — particularly against afghan invasions — but otherwise operated independently. whenever a misl conquered a territory, the lands were distributed among its members in proportion to their military & monetary contribution. even the lowest-ranking soldier received a share of land. by 1770, there were 12 major misls in punjab, with the dal khalsa at the centre under a leader chosen by the misl chiefs — a confederacy structure with a weak centre & strong constituent units. ◆ takeaway: this confederacy structure mirrors patterns seen elsewhere in indian history — compare it to the maratha confederacy under the peshwas, where a nominal centre held together largely autonomous regional chiefs. decentralisation was both a source of resilience &, ultimately, a vulnerability.

sections.title: How did Ranjit Singh01-39 unify the Misls and build a powerful Sikh State?
sections.norm: how did ranjit singh01-39 unify the misls and build a powerful sikh state?. ranjit singh01-39 sukerchakia misl bhangi misl 1799 maharaja 1801 territorial expansion was rapid and systematic 1808 1809 treaty of amritsar multan (1818) kashmir (1819) peshawar (1834) singh. ranjit singh01-39 of the sukerchakia misl gained prominence during zaman shah's afghan invasions of punjab (1796–1799). following zaman shah's retreat, ranjit singh captured lahore from the bhangi misl in 1799, giving him the platform to establish dominance over the other misls. he was formally coronated as maharaja of the sikh state in 1801. the other misl chiefs were systematically reduced to tribute-paying vassals — retaining conditional control of their lands in return for loyalty and tribute to the crown. his territorial expansion was rapid and systematic: 1799 — conquered lahore 1808 — conquered jammu from the dogra rajputs. (jammu was later granted as a jagir to kishore singh in 1820, and formally made kishore singh's son, gulab singh, the raja of jammu in 1822). 1809 — signed the treaty of amritsar with the british, which restricted his expansion south of the sutlej river but secured his eastern frontier, allowing him to eventually launch major campaigns into multan (1818), kashmir (1819), and peshawar (1834).

sections.title: What were the terms of the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC?
sections.norm: what were the terms of the 1809 treaty of amritsar with the eic?. 1809 treaty of amritsar eic charles metcalfe sutlej river singh. in 1809, ranjit singh01-39 signed the treaty of amritsar with the eic, represented by charles metcalfe — the british eic's resident in the delhi court. (recall that the scindias had been removed from delhi in 1803 & the eic had established indirect rule there through a british resident.) the treaty had four key outcomes: 1. the eic recognised ranjit singh01-39 as the sovereign ruler of punjab. 2. it led to a military alliance (*later link to the eic's policy of ring fence). 3. the sutlej river was fixed as the border between the sikh state & company state. 4. ranjit singh01-39 was free to expand his state on his side of the sutlej without british interference.

sections.title: How far did Ranjit Singh01-39 expand the Sikh State after 1809?
sections.norm: how far did ranjit singh01-39 expand the sikh state after 1809?. 1818 1819 1834 hari singh nalwa 1838 tripartite treaty singh. with his eastern border secured by treaty, ranjit singh01-39 turned west & north: 1. 1818 — removed the afghans from multan. 2. 1819 — conquered kashmir. (*recall that ahmad shah abdali had captured punjab & kashmir during his invasions — punjab was taken back by the marathas in 1758 but not kashmir. ranjit singh01-39 now completed what the marathas had left unfinished.) 3. 1834 — conquered peshawar. (present-day khyber pakhtunkhwa of pakistan, bordering afghanistan along the durand line.) peshawar was conquered by hari singh nalwa, whose military reputation was so fearsome that, as historical accounts record, afghan mothers used his name to frighten unruly children — "if you don't stop crying, haria ragle will turn up." in 1838, ranjit singh01-39 signed the tripartite treaty between the sikh state, the eic, & shah shuja of afghanistan. the treaty was designed to establish british indirect rule in afghanistan through shah shuja as a puppet ruler — the aim being to create a buffer of afghanistan & punjab against the feared russian invasion of british india from the northwest. diagram 3 — ranjit singh01-39's territorial expansion 1801–38: 1801 lahore + 1808 jammu + 1809 whole of punjab + treaty of amritsar 1809 (sutlej as border with eic) → westward expansion 1818 multan + 1819 kashmir + 1834 peshawar (by hari singh nalwa) → 1838 tripartite treaty (sikh state + eic + shah shuja, against feared russian invasion)

sections.title: What kind of State did Ranjit Singh01-39 build — and what made it hold together?
sections.norm: what kind of state did ranjit singh01-39 build — and what made it hold together?. skilful combination of coercion, diplomacy maintenance of balance 40% jagirdari kardars stopped at the village level local chiefs & clans was respected fakir azizuddin dewan dina nath sahajdhari sikhs singh. ranjit singh01-39 built his power through a skilful combination of coercion, diplomacy, & the careful maintenance of balance between the misl chiefs, the khalsa army, khatri traders, & non-sikh nobles such as the dogras (*similar to the successor states we discussed earlier). the sikh state under him was both militarily strong & economically prosperous. revenue policy was fair for the masses & trade flourished — a strong state delivered the law & order stability that commerce requires. only 40% of land was under the jagirdari system. from the remaining land, revenue went directly to the king, giving him considerable monetary power. land revenue was the main income source & was collected by kardars whor was the chief administrative officer at the taluqa (district) level. he acted as the revenue collector, the local magistrate (judge), the police chief, and the customs officer. ranjit singh01-39 heavily relied on the ijaradari system. instead of being paid a fixed cash salary, a kardar would often act as an ijaradar but it was ensured that ryot is not oppressed by very high lr. the authority of the state stopped at the village level. the power of local chiefs & clans was respected. (*this will connect directly to the mahalwari settlement in punjab, where even the british respected this tradition of village-level autonomy — a continuity worth noting when we reach that chapter.) his administration was secular. key positions were held by men from different religious backgrounds — fakir azizuddin, a muslim, served as his foreign minister, while dewan dina nath, a hindu, handled the finances as finance minister. culturally, ranjit singh01-39 was magnanimous. the sikh identity under him expanded to include non-khalsa sikhs — the sahajdhari sikhs, who do not maintain the five ks of khalsa identity (kesh, kangha, kada, kirpan, kachhera). he thus built a state that was politically inclusive — respecting village & local autonomy — & culturally broad, respecting diversity both within the sikh community & beyond it. (the story of the sikh state after ranjit singh01-39 — including the anglo-sikh wars & eventual annexation by the eic — continues in a later chapter.)

sections.chapterTitle: Already Autonomous States: Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore
sections.title: Akbar56-05 and the Rajputs
sections.norm: akbar56-05 and the rajputs. 20 major rajput clans akbar56-05 mansabdars vatan jagirs akbar. around the 16th century, rajputana had no single central power. there were roughly 20 major rajput clans, each controlling its own territory. (in the language of modern international relations, this is what we call a multi-polar world — many power centres, no single dominant one.) akbar56-05 changed this. rather than trying to defeat all of them — which would have been expensive & uncertain — he co-opted the more powerful rajput chiefs. the chosen rajput chiefs were brought into the mughal system as mansabdars — ranked nobles who held military & administrative responsibilities. their home territories were recognised as vatan jagirs, meaning the land remained theirs but within the mughal framework. they accepted the mughal emperor as their sovereign, paid tributes, & contributed troops. as a group, they formed the hindu bloc within the mansabdari system. in return akbar56-05 helped them subdue the smaller rajput chiefs. the result was a partial consolidation of power. (rajputs made up roughly 15% of all mansabdars.)

sections.chapterTitle: Already Autonomous States: Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore
sections.title: Rajputs vs Aurangzeb58-07 and Marathas?
sections.norm: rajputs vs aurangzeb58-07 and marathas?. raj singh 1680 marwar 1707 sawai jai singh99-43 1751 second anglo-maratha war (1803–05) eic subordinate alliances protectorate suzeranity a note on sawai jai singh99-43 (1699-1743) of amber "sawai" aurangzeb58-07 mughal mansabdar, regional state-builder, astronomer & town planner 1. mansabdar & subedar. subedari of malwa agra 1734 conference of rajput rulers at hurda internal rajput rivalries 2. astronomy & the jantar mantars 2.1. five observatories/jantar mantars. delhi (1724), jaipur (1734), ujjain, mathura & varanasi unesco world heritage site (2010) samrat yantra local time to an accuracy of 2 seconds 2.2. astronomical tables zij-i-ulugh begi siddhantic zij-i-muhammad shahi (1733; scientific delegation to portugal (1730). 2.3. stone instruments over brass 3. founding of jaipur 1727 vidyadhar bhattacharya vastu shastra grid-pattern layout 1876 first planned city of modern india ashvamedha & vajapeya yajnas conscious assertion of hindu chakravartin status aurangzeb singh shah muhammad shah. this arrangement held through most of the 17th century. trouble came under aurangzeb58-07. the kingdom of mewar, under raj singh, had been expanding aggressively against neighbouring rajput states. aurangzeb58-07 grew uneasy — he did not want one rajput power to dominate all of rajputana & become a rival to the mughal state. then, in 1680, the situation worsened. a child came to the throne in marwar — a kingdom sitting astride the important trade route connecting delhi & agra to ahmedabad. aurangzeb58-07 chose to interfere in the succession. this was the trigger. marwar & mewar both revolted. but the revolt failed. other rajput chiefs refused to join — they feared that if the revolt succeeded, mewar would dominate them. so each stood aside, & the rebellion collapsed. after aurangzeb58-07's death in 1707, the rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms. the most prominent figure of this period was sawai jai singh99-43 of amber, who ruled jaipur & remained a powerful mansabdar in delhi — but on his own conditions. from 1751 onwards, the marathas began making regular raids into rajputana, extracting tribute & interfering in succession disputes. but they could never fully conquer the region. after the second anglo-maratha war (1803–05), the eic replaced marathas as the regional power & signed subordinate alliances (also called subsidiary alliances) with the rajput states. (subordinate alliance is like world history’s term protectorate: the indian ruler kept his throne but surrendered control of foreign policy & defence to the eic, which stationed its own troops — paid for by the indian ruler. in suzeranity= loss of external sovereign functions + loss of symbolic sovereignty) a note on sawai jai singh99-43 (1699-1743) of amber the title "sawai" (i.e. 1.25 more able than any contemporary ruler) was conferred by aurangzeb58-07. he was simultaneously a mughal mansabdar, regional state-builder, astronomer & town planner. 1. mansabdar & subedar. held subedari of malwa (1729–37) & agra. in 1734 conference of rajput rulers at hurda to forge a united front against marathas. collapsed due to internal rajput rivalries. malwa was annexed by marathas in treaty of bhopal (1738). 2. astronomy & the jantar mantars 2.1. five observatories/jantar mantars. built at delhi (1724), jaipur (1734), ujjain, mathura & varanasi. jaipur's is the largest — unesco world heritage site (2010). samrat yantra (largest sundial in the world at jaipur) could measure local time to an accuracy of 2 seconds. 2.2. astronomical tables tell where a celestial body — sun, moon, planet, star — will be at any given date & time. existing tables — both zij-i-ulugh begi (islamic) & siddhantic (hindu) — had accumulated errors over centuries. the jantar mantars generated fresh observational data to correct them in form of zij-i-muhammad shahi (1733; dedicated to md shah19-48). sent a scientific delegation to portugal (1730). commissioned sanskrit astronomical works. 2.3. chose stone instruments over brass for greater accuracy — samrat yantra (sundial for time), jai prakash yantra (celestial mapper), ram yantra (altitude meter for sun’s position). 3. founding of jaipur 1727 designed by vidyadhar bhattacharya on vastu shastra principles — grid-pattern layout. sawai ram singh painted it pink in 1876 to welcome the prince of wales. jaipur is the first planned city of modern india. 4. attempted to curb dowry & excessive marriage expenditure among rajputs — limited success. was last indian ruler to perform ashvamedha & vajapeya yajnas— a conscious assertion of hindu chakravartin status as mughal authority collapsed. diagram 1

sections.chapterTitle: Already Autonomous States: Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore
sections.title: How did a small southern kingdom stay independent from both the Mughals and the Marathas?
sections.norm: how did a small southern kingdom stay independent from both the mughals and the marathas?. never part of the mughal empire never expanded far enough south 1740s marthanda varma29-58 battle of colachel (1741) dutch east india company. cochin 1663 1759 — battle of bedara (also called battle of chinsura): 1795 (ceylon/ sri lanka) takeaway: varma. travancore was never part of the mughal empire. the mughal state simply never expanded far enough south to include it. by the 1740s, marthanda varma29-58 had built a strong, centralised state by subjugating local chiefs across the region. he also built a european-style military — modern weapons, trained soldiers. a landmark in the history of kerala was the battle of colachel (1741), where marthanda varma29-58's army crushed the dutch east india company. while the dutch had maintained their malabar headquarters at cochin (central kerala) since capturing it from the portuguese in 1663, this defeat was terminal for their imperial dreams. it permanently ended dutch political & military ambitions in kerala, relegating them to the status of mere merchants in cochin. 1759 — battle of bedara (also called battle of chinsura): the british eic defeated the dutch in bengal, crushing their remaining ambitions in india and final expulsion from south asia by the british in 1795 (ceylon/ sri lanka). ◆ takeaway: travancore also established a state monopoly over the trade of the malabar coast. the revenues from this trade were reinvested into the military, irrigation works, & transport infrastructure — a classic example of a small state using trade income to build state capacity.

sections.chapterTitle: Already Autonomous States: Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore
sections.title: Travancore vs Mysore & EIC
sections.norm: travancore vs mysore & eic. rama varma58-98 1766 haider ali61-82 malabar & calicut 1798 1805 subsidiary alliance (1805) velu thampi dalawa 1809 kundara proclamation (1809) varma ali. under rama varma58-98, travancore shifted in character. it became a centre of art & scholarship. but military strength declined. the consequences were quick. in 1766, haider ali61-82 of mysore annexed malabar & calicut. (malabar was the heart of the spice trade — pepper, cardamom, ginger. whoever controlled malabar's ports controlled a significant share of indian ocean commerce. this is why both mysore & the british were so interested in it.) after 1798, travancore came steadily under british influence. in 1805, a mutiny broke out among the nair troops over non-payment of salaries (*sashi tharoor is from nair community ). travancore sought british help — & in return was made to sign a subsidiary alliance (1805), effectively ending its independence. the final act of travancore's resistance came under velu thampi dalawa, the prime minister (dalawa) of travancore. (dalawa meant prime minister & the chief of the armed forces, but books may use the word dewan for pm of a state subordinated by british — & as dewan he was head of all administration, including revenue, civil, police, & criminal justice, since military was with the british.) angered by the humiliating terms of the subsidiary alliance of 1805 — particularly the heavy financial burden & the interference in travancore's internal affairs — velu thampi organised a revolt in 1809 against the british resident. he rallied the nair troops & issued a public proclamation — the kundara proclamation (1809) — calling on the people to rise against british control. the revolt, however, was suppressed. the british moved swiftly, & velu thampi, seeing no escape, took his own life. (this was one of the earliest organised resistance movements by an indian ruler against the subsidiary alliance system — & a directly tested topic in upsc.) diagram 2 — travancore

sections.chapterTitle: Already Autonomous States: Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore
sections.title: How did Mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century India?
sections.norm: how did mysore go from being a minor kingdom to one of the most powerful states in 18th-century india?. vijayanagar empire (1336–1646) battle of talikota rakkasa-tangadi 1565 1646 wodeyar dynasty chikka devaraja wodeyar72-04 (1672-1704) 1761 nanjraj haider ali61-82 risalas poligars deshmukhs wodeyar ali. mysore's origins as a significant state go back to the vijayanagar empire (1336–1646), of which it was a part. the empire's effective power was shattered at the battle of talikota (also called rakkasa-tangadi) in 1565, when a coalition of deccan sultanates decisively defeated the vijayanagar forces. though the dynasty lingered on in diminished form until 1646, 1565 marks the operational end of vijayanagar as a major power. after vijayanagar's decline, mysore gradually became autonomous under the wodeyar dynasty. under chikka devaraja wodeyar72-04 (1672-1704), mysore became militarily powerful & centrally governed. but the dynasty's strength did not last. by 1761, the wodeyars had been reduced to figureheads by a powerful & corrupt prime minister, nanjraj. haider ali61-82 ended that. he had begun as a junior military officer, his early career made possible partly because the wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts. he was capable, ambitious, & strategic. in 1761, he overthrew nanjraj & seized effective power — while keeping the wodeyar as a nominal head of state. (pattern alert@ 18th c : king becomes a puppet as personality weakens. recall peshwa-chhatrapati relationship.) haider ali61-82 took french assistance for military training, technology transfer, & organisational reform. the army was now structured on a european model, organised into risalas (regiments). each risala had a commander directly appointed by the king, ensuring personal loyalty upward. each unit had a clear chain of command. each was self-sufficient (*recall campoo system of scindhia)— its own weapons, transport, & supplies. the result was a fast, efficient military having regiments capable of independent action. he then spent roughly twenty years subjugating the poligars (local chiefs & landlords who controlled land, wealth of temples, & had their own armed men — the real rulers of the countryside since the vijayanagar era (1336-1646)) & deshmukhs (revenue collectors who functioned like primary zamindars). non-state power was systematically dismantled.

sections.chapterTitle: Already Autonomous States: Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore
sections.title: How did Mysore fund this military machine?
sections.norm: how did mysore fund this military machine?. khalisa jagirdari state officials collected taxes directly detailed field surveys invested in the productive capacity of the peasantry canals cash crops sericulture larger tax base most prosperous in india military fiscalism tipu. the land revenue reforms of both rulers worked together as a single coherent system. khalisa land (land whose revenue went directly to the state treasury) was expanded, while jagirdari land (land whose revenue was assigned to nobles or commanders) was minimised. this maximised state income while reducing the independent economic power of nobles. deshmukhs were removed as intermediaries and state officials collected taxes directly & received salaries — a far smaller outflow than the commissions that intermediaries had previously taken. (think of it as replacing a commission-based agent with a salaried employee — the state kept far more of the revenue now.) detailed field surveys were conducted to assess land fairly — accounting for soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access, & past production trends. this prevented over-assessment, meaning farmers were not taxed beyond what their land could produce. to further increase state revenue, the rulers invested in the productive capacity of the peasantry: 1. old irrigation canals were repaired & new ones built. 2. cash crops were promoted. 3. sericulture (the cultivation of silk via silkworms) was introduced. more income for peasants meant a larger tax base. even tipu82-99's enemies acknowledged that the population of mysore was among the most prosperous in india. these policies as a whole are called military fiscalism — the systematic generation of state wealth as a foundation for military power.

sections.chapterTitle: Already Autonomous States: Rajputs, Travancore, Mysore
sections.title: What made Tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?
sections.norm: what made tipu82-99 a different kind of ruler — and why did he still lose?. tipu82-99 30 trading centres factory a trading settlement haider ali 61-82 and tipu82-99 iron-cased rocket artillery 1785: tipu82-99 formally declared independence khalifa sanad 1790s 1789 1798 tree of liberty jacobin club alert: prelims 2001. who established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? answer: tipu sultan. france, turkey, & egypt mauludi lunisolar calendar why mysore lost? vijayanagar 2.0 neighbouring indian powers & the eic 1766 first anglo-mysore war (1767–69) fourth anglo-mysore war (1799) tipu ali wodeyar. tipu82-99 pushed mysore's ambitions further. he built a modern navy & established a government-owned trading company modelled on the eic — conducting oceanic trade in sandalwood, sulphur, rice, pepper, silk, & cardamom. the company set up 30 trading centres inside & outside india, including in muscat, oman. (in this historical period, a "factory" did not mean a manufacturing unit. it was a trading post — warehouses for storing goods, offices for conducting trade, homes for company employees, & often a fort for protection. the word comes from "factor," meaning a merchant agent — a factory was the place where factors worked. a trading settlement meant warehouses, homes, offices, & sometimes a fort.) haider ali 61-82 and tipu82-99 developed iron-cased rocket artillery (100% indigenous; range of 2 km; iron cylinder casings did not burst & could take high pressure compared to rockets (fireworks) with cardboard casings which existed since centuries in india and china)— a significant military innovation of the period. these war rockets were later studied closely by the british. william congreve's rockets, which the british military deployed in the early 19th century, drew directly from tipu82-99's designs. 1785: tipu82-99 formally declared independence — both from the wodeyars & from the mughal emperor. he sent a request to the khalifa (the religious head of the muslim world) for a sanad, an official order recognising him as a ruler independent of mughal authority. in the 1790s, tipu82-99 sent an ambassador to france seeking both military technology & a formal alliance against the british. this was not a random diplomatic move. since 1789, the french revolution had set france on a collision course with the monarchies of europe, including britain (*23 years war 1792-1815). in 1798, napoleon attacked egypt & the middle east — partly to disrupt british trade in the arabian sea. tipu82-99 exchanged communications with napoleon &, as a symbolic gesture of friendship, planted a tree of liberty in mysore (the tree of liberty was a symbol of the french revolution — planted across france & later across europe). he also became a member of the jacobin club — the radical political organisation at the heart of the french revolution. the british were alarmed — & his alignment with revolutionary france became one of the reasons for the fourth anglo-mysore war of 1799. ⚠ alert: prelims 2001. who established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? answer: tipu sultan. tipu82-99 set up modern embassies in france, turkey, & egypt — alongside other administrative innovations such as a new coinage & the mauludi lunisolar calendar. the jacobin membership & tree of liberty alarmed the british — a factor in the run-up to the fourth anglo-mysore war of 1799. why mysore lost? mysore's long-term ambition was to dominate all of south india & control its international trade (dream = vijayanagar 2.0). but constant warfare — against neighbouring indian powers & the eic — drained the state's resources faster than military fiscalism could replenish them. the ambition was real. the capacity, ultimately, was not enough. in 1766, haider ali61-82 invaded & annexed malabar & calicut (he could not successfully invade travancore). this led to the first anglo-mysore war (1767–69), as the eic feared losing its coastal trade of the malabar coast. the wars continued through the century. the fourth anglo-mysore war (1799) ended with the death of tipu82-99 at seringapatam, & mysore's power was broken. (4 wars: 1767-69, 80-84, 90-92, 99) diagram 3 — mysore's rise + ambition-vs-capacity collapse: vijayanagar empire 1336-1646 origins + battle of talikota 1565 operational end + wodeyar dynasty + chikka devaraja wodeyar72-04 → 1761 nanjraj-figurehead status → haider ali61-82 1761-82 nanjraj-overthrow + french-assisted risalas + poligars/deshmukhs subjugation + military fiscalism → tipu82-99 1782-99 modern navy + government trading company + iron-cased rocket artillery (congreve copies) + independence-from-wodeyars-and-mughal-emperor + khalifa-sanad request + 1790s ambassador to france + tree of liberty + jacobin club + mauludi calendar → constant warfare drained state faster than military fiscalism could replenish; 1766 travancore-malabar-calicut → first anglo-mysore war 1767-69 → fourth anglo-mysore war 1799 ended with death of tipu82-99 at seringapatam; mysore power broken

sections.title: Asia- the Economic Power of the World
sections.norm: asia- the economic power of the world. trade between europe & asia most profitable businesses in the known world main attractions were three route to china route to india arab traders not a wealthy continent luxuries accessible only to the rich spices held a special place. vasco da gama 1498 demand patterns shifted indian cotton textiles. for centuries before a single european ship docked on indian soil, trade between europe & asia was already one of the most profitable businesses in the known world. this trade had a clear geography — both of commodities & of control. the main attractions were three: 1. indonesia (the islands of java & sumatra) for spices. 2. india for textiles (+ malabar for spices) 3. china for silk & tea. the route to china was primarily a land route — the famous silk route. the route to india & indonesia was a mix of land & sea, passing through the middle east & the arabian sea. arab traders dominated the arabian sea leg of this journey, bringing goods from india & beyond to the ports of the middle east. from there, italian merchants — primarily from genoa & venice — took over, carrying goods across the mediterranean sea into european markets. both groups earned enormous profits at each handoff. but here is an important nuance about early modern europe: it was not a wealthy continent. the eastern goods flowing westward were luxuries accessible only to the rich. a common european could not afford indian cotton or chinese silk. what drove the scramble for this trade was the enormous profit it generated for whoever could supply these goods to europe's wealthy classes — the italian merchants of genoa & venice understood this & guarded their position zealously. among these goods, spices held a special place. until the 1600s, european food was as heavily spiced as indian food. spices were essential for preserving & making palatable the meat that europeans stored through winter — the industrial refrigerator did not exist; the clove & the pepper did. the trade with asia was so lucrative that the numbers almost defy belief. when vasco da gama arrived on indian shores in 1498, the goods he carried back sold in europe at 800% profit. by the 1600s, one kilogram of clove in europe cost the equivalent of one kilogram of gold. (*had the present been the 1650s, most of us would have been "spitting gold" as children — those cloves our mothers tucked into rice to add flavour, that we quietly picked out & pushed to the side of the plate.) as european incomes rose through the 17th & 18th centuries & spices became more widely available, demand patterns shifted — indian cotton textiles eventually became the most sought-after commodity from the east. but in the beginning, it was spice that started everything.

sections.title: Ottoman Blockade and Age of Discovery
sections.norm: ottoman blockade and age of discovery. interrupted in 1453 ottoman empire captured constantinople blockaded the traditional land trade routes age of discovery of the 16th century portugal & spain this era gave: astrolabe latitudes & longitudes modern world map geography caravel sail at an angle against the wind. this profitable system was violently interrupted in 1453, when the ottoman empire captured constantinople — today's istanbul — & blockaded the traditional land trade routes connecting europe to asia. european traders could no longer rely on the old routes. they needed a new way east. this necessity became the engine of one of history's great turning points: the age of discovery of the 16th century. european powers — led initially by portugal & spain — sent ships into the atlantic ocean, searching for a direct sea route to the east. what followed reshaped the world permanently. this era gave: 1. better use of the astrolabe for determining location & the magnetic compass for direction. 2. the system of latitudes & longitudes and the modern world map. 3. geography as a formal discipline. 4. the invention of the caravel — a ship with ability to sail at an angle against the wind

sections.title: Portuguese-Spain rivalry resolved by Treaty of Tordesillas 1494
