sections.norm: portuguese-spain rivalry resolved by treaty of tordesillas 1494. treaty of tordesillas in 1494 cape verde islands. portugal & spain led the charge — & almost immediately began competing over who owned the new sea routes & lands being discovered. to resolve this rivalry, pope alexander vi mediated the treaty of tordesillas in 1494. the treaty drew an imaginary line in the atlantic ocean — approximately 1,185 miles west of the cape verde islands — & divided the newly discovered world between the two powers. lands to the east of this line went to portugal; lands to the west went to spain. (this is why brazil, whose eastern tip fell on the portuguese side of this line, became the only portuguese colony in the americas — while the rest of the continent became spanish.) diagram 1 — treaty of tordesillas 1494: pope alexander vi mediation + line drawn ~1,185 miles west of cape verde islands + lands east → portugal, lands west → spain + brazil's eastern tip on portuguese side became the only portuguese colony in the americas

sections.title: the Portuguese in India
sections.norm: the portuguese in india. treaty of tordesillas (1494) vasco da gama arrived at calicut vasco da gama zamorin of calicut arab traders why south india was vulnerable: mughal empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist in india photo: kappad beach(calicut), where vasco da gama first landed in india in 1498 the portuguese approach to trade in india had a distinct character — part commerce, part conquest, & part coercion. estado da índia factory i) cabral's factories at calicut and then cochin (1500): first portuguese factory first permanent portuguese factory ii) vasco da gama's second voyage (1502): three primary objectives brutal massacre of innocent fishermen iii) fort manuel — first european fort in india (1503): cochin served as the first capital of portuguese india shifted to goa in 1530. almeida05-09 was the first governor (viceroy in common usage) of the portuguese estado da índia. blue water policy objective monopolistic trading regime without extensive territorial expansion cartaz system armed trade battle of diu (1509; almeida05-09 vs gujarat, calicut, foreign powers ) sultanate of gujarat mamluk sultanate of egypt ottoman empire republic of venice returned to india in 1508 i) arrest by almeida05-09: ii) release in 1509: iii) territorial transformation: annexed goa (1510) exception to the blue water policy luso-indian policy of albuquerque09-15 v) administrative and religious measures: headquarters cochin to goa in 1530. acquired bassein (1534) & diu (1535) from bahadur shah of gujarat slave trade forced conversions goa inquisition (1560–1812), st. francis xavier photo: breast ripper- used on women who refused to convert. alert: prelims trap — st. francis xavier. tobacco, red chillies, papaya, pineapple, & guava cocoa & rubber columbian exchange dominance proved short-lived the causes of decline were multiple: political factors: rise of the marathas religious backlash: goa inquisition (1560–1812) economic and administrative decay: piracy illicit trade/corruption by employees external competition: english & the dutch imperial overextension: takeaway: albuquerque almeida cunha. armed with this treaty of tordesillas (1494) & backed by the portuguese crown, vasco da gama arrived at calicut (today's kozhikode in kerala) in 1498, having sailed around the cape of good hope — the southernmost point of africa. (*the cape had been named "cape of good hope" by portugal's king john ii, as it represented hope of finally finding a sea route to india.) vasco da gama received permission to trade from the zamorin of calicut but faced heavy opposition from arab traders who dominated the existing trade. he traded & left — he did not establish a factory or a permanent settlement on this voyage. why south india was vulnerable: when the portuguese arrived, the mughal empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist in india. south india at the time was divided between the vijayanagara empire (1336-1646) & the deccan sultanates, without a unified central naval power. this political fragmentation is what allowed portuguese to establish their domination over trade and some territory of india in 16th century. photo: kappad beach(calicut), where vasco da gama first landed in india in 1498 the portuguese approach to trade in india had a distinct character — part commerce, part conquest, & part coercion. 4.1 structure of trade — a state enterprise unlike the private joint-stock companies that the british & dutch would later set up, portuguese trade was operated as a state enterprise called estado da índia— directly controlled by the portuguese crown through its official administration. thus, the portuguese government was the trader. 4.2 early factories, first fort, and the portuguese aggression (1498–1503) in this historical period, a "factory" did not mean a manufacturing unit. it was a trading post — warehouses for storing goods, offices for conducting trade, homes for company employees, & often a fort for protection. (the word comes from "factor," meaning a merchant agent. a factory was the place where factors worked.) feature trading depot (warehouse) factory (commercial hub) trading settlement (colonial enclave) primary function purely functional storage for goods awaiting ship arrival. administrative & commercial hq for merchant agents. broader territorial colony with civil & town administration. core components basic godowns & storage rooms. offices, warehouses, & homes for "factors" (agents). factory complex plus surrounding towns & annexed lands. permanent staff no. yes — merchant agents known as factors. yes — factors, soldiers, & administrative personnel. legal status minimal; simple permission to store goods. established via formal imperial or local farmans. zamindari (revenue) or sovereign territorial rights. territorial jurisdiction no. no. yes — over a defined zone or town. tax/customs authority no. no. yes. security level unfortified; low-level guards. often fortified with walls & cannons (e.g., fort manuel). heavily fortified military zones with stationed troops. historical example portuguese storage before factory at calicut (1500). english permanent factory at surat (1613). goa (post-1510) for portuguese pondicherry (post-1674) for french & calcutta (post-1690) for british i) cabral's factories at calicut and then cochin (1500): the first portuguese factory in india was established at calicut in 1500 by pedro cabral, who took permission for it from the samoothiri (called zamorin by the portuguese) — the hindu nair monarchs who ruled the kingdom of calicut (kozhikode) on the malabar coast of kerala. however, the calicut factory was short-lived — it was destroyed by arab merchants, in which approximately 50 portuguese were killed. cabral retaliated by bombarding calicut & then sailed south to cochin. the first permanent portuguese factory in india was established at cochin (1500), which survived under the protection of the raja of cochin. ii) vasco da gama's second voyage (1502): da gama returned to india on his second voyage with three primary objectives — to avenge the massacre of cabral's men, to force the zamorin of calicut into submission, & to violently expel arab trading competitors from the malabar coast. when the zamorin refused to expel muslim merchants, da gama bombarded calicut & engaged in a brutal massacre of innocent fishermen. this second voyage was significant as it marked the disruption of the traditional arab-venetian trade network & the forcible integration of indian ocean trade into the european mercantilist framework. iii) fort manuel — first european fort in india (1503): afonso de albuquerque09-15 arrived in india in 1503 as a naval commander. he successfully defended the raja of cochin against the zamorin of calicut & constructed fort manuel before sailing back to portugal in 1504. cochin served as the first capital of portuguese india until the headquarters shifted to goa in 1530. 4.3 blue water policy and the cartaz system — francisco de almeida05-09 (1505–1509) almeida05-09 was the first governor (viceroy in common usage) of the portuguese estado da índia. he introduced the blue water policy — an emphasis on naval supremacy rather than territorial conquest on land. since india had powerful land-based states, the portuguese under almeida05-09 chose not to seek a large territorial empire. instead, they focused on dominating the oceans & maritime trade routes since primary purpose for europeans to come to india was trade. the objective was to establish a monopolistic trading regime without extensive territorial expansion. central to the blue water policy was the cartaz system — a naval licensing system under which all non-portuguese ships were forced to purchase a pass (called a cartaz) & pay a licence fee to sail safely in the indian ocean. pay & get a pass; refuse & face attack. the primary target of this armed trade was the arab traders who had controlled the arabian sea trade for generations. the portuguese regularly raided & brutally attacked arab merchants, dismantling arab dominance over this trade. they used their naval threat to force local indian rulers &, later, mughal ships to pay for the cartaz & grant trade concessions. (*cartaz system is part of blue water policy) the battle of diu (1509; almeida05-09 vs gujarat, calicut, foreign powers ) was the culmination of almeida05-09's naval strategy. almeida05-09 decisively defeated a massive joint muslim naval coalition comprising the sultanate of gujarat, the mamluk sultanate of egypt, & the zamorin of calicut — backed further by the ottoman empire (which supplied troops & galleys) & the republic of venice (*whose lucrative european spice trade was being destroyed by portuguese dominance of the indian ocean). the scale of this coalition tells us how seriously the established trading powers of the old world viewed the portuguese threat. almeida05-09's victory at diu consolidated portuguese naval supremacy for the next century. 4.4 2nd governor afonso de albuquerque09-15 (1509–1515) albuquerque09-15 returned to india in 1508. i) arrest by almeida05-09: albuquerque09-15 came with royal orders from the portuguese king to take over leadership. however, almeida05-09 did not trust albuquerque09-15 and arrested him. ii) release in 1509: after almeida05-09 had won the decisive battle of diu (1509), a new portuguese fleet arrived which confirmed the king's orders. albuquerque09-15 was finally released to take office as the second governor (viceroy in common usage) of the portuguese india. (textbooks often call him "viceroy", but his legal title was governador — the formal administrative office which ruled portuguese territory in india. the same applies to almeida05-09.) iii) territorial transformation: albuquerque09-15 transformed the portuguese presence from a purely trading enterprise into a territorial colonial state. he annexed goa (1510) from the sultan of bijapur, gaining better control over in the arabian sea. (goa in 1510 was a notable exception to the blue water policy — a rare instance of portuguese territorial conquest on land.) iv) luso-indian policy of albuquerque09-15 (mixed portuguese and indian ancestry): via intermarriage between portuguese settlers & indian women. (*a substantial share of the women were war widows or captured women, often forced into these marriages without consent.) v) administrative and religious measures: albuquerque09-15 integrated local elites into the portuguese administration, attempted to regulate practices such as sati, & promoted christianity as a tool of political control. 4.5 peak under nuno da cunha29-38 (governor 1529–1538) nuno da cunha29-38 officially shifted the portuguese headquarters from cochin to goa in 1530. from here, the portuguese dominated the international trade of the indian ocean for nearly a century. under his governorship, the portuguese acquired bassein (1534) & diu (1535) from bahadur shah of gujarat, consolidating portuguese dominance along the western coast & control over strategic ports & maritime trade routes. 4.6 religious intolerance the portuguese were among the most religiously aggressive of all european powers in india. the activities of jesuit missionaries generated widespread resistance among local populations. their administration was marked by the slave trade (including in hughli settlement in bengal) and forced conversions — most notoriously the goa inquisition (1560–1812), an era of brutal persecution that caused deep socio-religious backlash. st. francis xavier (in india from 1542, died in 1552) spearheaded mass catholic conversions in coastal india while laying the ideological groundwork for the goa inquisition (1560–1812), —a brutal colonial church court established to investigate and punish heresy (beliefs contradicting church doctrine) and violently enforce portuguese cultural and religious orthodoxy. photo: breast ripper- used on women who refused to convert. ⚠ alert: prelims trap — st. francis xavier. the famous jesuit missionary st. francis xavier is closely associated with goa & the early portuguese missions in india. his remains are preserved in the basilica of bom jesus in old goa. however, st. francis xavier did not die in goa — he died on shangchuan island (off the coast of china) in 1552, while attempting to enter mainland china for missionary work. his body was later brought to goa. upsc prelims 2021 tested this distinction — the question expected candidates to know the location of his death, not his burial. do not confuse the two. 4.7 portuguese contribution — new world crops beyond conquest & trade, the portuguese also introduced several crops from the new world (the americas) to india that permanently transformed indian agriculture & cuisine. these include tobacco, red chillies, papaya, pineapple, & guava. (note: cocoa & rubber are also new world plants, but unlike the crops above they reached india only in the british period — not through the portuguese.) european exploration of the americas in the 15th and 16th centuries brought the so-called old and new worlds into contact with each other. in what is called the columbian exchange, numerous plants, animals, and microbes from europe, asia, and africa were introduced to the americas, and numerous others were transferred from the americas to europe, asia, and africa. 4.8 why did the portuguese decline? the portuguese were the first european power to establish a colonial presence in india & the first to introduce naval warfare & maritime trade control strategies to the indian ocean. yet their dominance proved short-lived. the causes of decline were multiple: i) political factors: the emergence of strong regional powers in persia, egypt, & north india challenged portuguese positions. especially, the rise of the marathas directly threatened portuguese. ii) religious backlash: the activities of jesuit missionaries & the brutality of the goa inquisition (1560–1812) generated deep resistance from local populations. iii) economic and administrative decay: corruption, inefficiency, decline in administrative discipline, & engagement in piracy & illicit trade/corruption by employees eroded the institutional foundations of portuguese power. iv) external competition: the entry of the english & the dutch — with superior naval technology, joint-stock financial systems, & more disciplined commercial organisation — steadily displaced the portuguese from their dominant position. v) imperial overextension: the diversion of portuguese imperial focus towards brazil (their far more lucrative colony in the americas), combined with general overextension & lack of institutional support from lisbon, meant that the estado da índia was increasingly starved of resources & attention. ◆ takeaway: the portuguese set the stage for all subsequent european expansion in india. their model of colonial administration centred in goa, their introduction of armed maritime trade, & their use of religious conversion as a tool of political control became patterns that later european powers — particularly the british — would study, adapt, & eventually supersede. summary table t1 — portuguese factories, forts, and key permissions year event / settlement permission / source significance 1498 vasco da gama at calicut trade permission from zamorin of calicut first direct sea route europe–india; no factory 1500 first factory at calicut (pedro cabral) permission from samoothiri/zamorin destroyed by arab merchant riots 1500 first permanent factory at cochin protection of raja of cochin first lasting portuguese factory in india 1502 vasco da gama's 2nd voyage — bombardment of calicut; arab-venetian trade disrupted 1503 fort manuel, cochin (albuquerque09-15; he was not governor then) — first european fort in india 1505–09 almeida05-09 as first governor (viceroy) portuguese crown blue water policy; cartaz system; battle of diu (1509) 1509–15 albuquerque09-15 as second governor portuguese crown captures goa (1510); luso-indian policy; territorial state 1530 capital shifted to goa (nuno da cunha29-38) — goa replaces cochin as capital 1534–35 bassein (1534), diu (1535) from bahadur shah of gujarat western coast dominance 1559 daman acquired — further western coast consolidation 1560–1812 goa inquisition — institutionalised religious persecution; centuries of forced conversion & brutality 1783 dadra & nagar haveli from marathas (treaty of 1779) compensation for a destroyed portuguese warship (santana). the 1779 treaty assigned revenue rights, but physical possession of the territory was only finalised in 1783. 1961 goa, daman and diu merged into india — end of portuguese presence

sections.title: How Did the Dutch and English Break the Portuguese-Spanish Monopoly?
sections.norm: how did the dutch and english break the portuguese-spanish monopoly?. two new naval powers breaking the strict monopoly held by spain & portugal freedom of navigation 1588, british navy defeated the spanish armada severely weakened spanish-portuguese naval supremacy armada defeated cape of good hope first priority for both the british & the dutch was indonesia a trilateral trade network. by the second half of the 16th century, two new naval powers had emerged in europe: britain & the dutch republic (netherlands). (* the netherlands, holland, & "the dutch republic" all refer to the same country. "dutch" is the adjective; "holland" is technically a region within the netherlands but is often used as a general name for the whole country.) both shared an immediate goal — breaking the strict monopoly held by spain & portugal over european international trade & achieving freedom of navigation in the oceans. the decisive moment came in 1588, when the british navy defeated the spanish armada — spain's supposedly "invincible armada" — in the atlantic ocean. this severely weakened spanish-portuguese naval supremacy. (by 1580, portugal had entered into a political union with spain. defeating spain therefore also meant opening up trade routes that portugal had controlled.) with the armada defeated, british & dutch ships could now travel safely to asia via the cape of good hope. the first priority for both the british & the dutch was indonesia — i.e. dominating the spice trade of the east indies (east indies referred to all lands east of the cape of good hope). india came into the picture somewhat later, & for a specific commercial reason: the people of the spice islands in indonesia had little interest in english or dutch goods, but they readily accepted indian cotton textiles in trade. to buy spices in indonesia, you first needed cloth from india. (this is an early example of a trilateral trade network: england → india → indonesia → england. it is also the commercial logic that eventually shifted the eic's focus from indonesia to the indian subcontinent.)

sections.title: What Made the Dutch VOC Historically Unique?
sections.norm: what made the dutch voc historically unique?. in 1602, the dutch east india company takeaway: world's first multinational company world's first joint-stock company. the voc's charter dutch first expedition in 1595 not to india. first factory masulipatnam 1605 other settlements chinsura in bengal (1653), cochin — where they captured the portuguese fort in 1663. in 1669, the voc was the richest private company in the world 1799, the company went bankrupt dutch east indies independence in 1945 ww2 varma. in 1602, the dutch east india company — formally the voc or vereenigde oost-indische compagnie— was established by a charter issued by the dutch parliament. the voc was created by merging six smaller dutch companies that had previously been competing with each other for eastern trade. ◆ takeaway: the voc was the world's first multinational company. more importantly, it was the first company to issue publicly tradable stocks & shares on a formal exchange — making it the world's first joint-stock company. an ordinary person could now become a part-owner of a company by buying its shares, without having any say in how the company was managed. this is the direct ancestor of today's stock markets — the bse, nse, nyse — & the entire modern shareholder economy we live in. the voc's charter gave it sweeping powers: the right to wage war, sign treaties, acquire territory, build forts, & mint its own currency. these are powers that ordinarily belong to a state — and this tells us how european powers thought about trade and companies: as an extension of state power. the dutch first expedition in 1595 sailed to the east indies (indonesia) — not to india. their first factory in india was established at masulipatnam in the northern sarkars in 1605. other settlements followed at pulicat in the carnatic (1610), surat in gujarat (1616), bimilipatam in the northern sarkars of golconda (1641), karaikal near pondicherry (1645), chinsura in bengal (1653), & later at kasimbazar, baranagore, patna, balasore, nagapatnam, agra, & cochin — where they captured the portuguese fort in 1663. ⚠ alert: prelims 2022 — gajapati dynasty & the dutch. a common upsc trap involves the claim that the dutch received land grants from the gajapati dynasty of odisha. this is incorrect — the dutch did not get land from the gajapati dynasty. the gajapatis were a 15th-century dynasty centred in odisha whose power had declined well before the dutch arrived. do not confuse later local rulers of the odisha coast with the gajapati dynasty itself. (prelims 2022 tested this.) at its peak in 1669, the voc was the richest private company in the world — 150 merchant vessels, 40 warships, an army of 10,000 soldiers, & 50,000 employees. over its lifetime it made 5,000 voyages from the netherlands to the east indies. in 1799, the company went bankrupt & was dissolved. its territorial possessions were taken over by the dutch government & became the dutch east indies — what we today call indonesia, which remained a dutch colony until independence in 1945 after ww2 . summary table t2 — dutch factories and key events in india year event / settlement source / context 1602 voc established dutch parliament charter 1605 masulipatnam (northern sarkars) first dutch factory in india 1610 pulicat (carnatic) — 1616 surat (gujarat) — 1641 bimilipatam (northern sarkars, golconda) — 1645 karaikal (near pondicherry) — 1653 chinsura (bengal) — 1663 cochin captured from portuguese key base in south india 1669 voc at its peak richest private company in the world 1741 battle of colachel defeated by travancore (marthanda varma29-58) 1759 battle of bedara / chinsura defeated by british eic 1795 kew letters — dutch posts taken over cochin, chinsura, pulicat, tuticorin 1799 voc bankrupt & dissolved dutch government takes over possessions

sections.title: English EIC and the Royal Charter of 1600
sections.norm: english eic and the royal charter of 1600. royal charter issued by queen elizabeth i 58-03 takeaway: royal charter britain or england? england & scotland in 1707 kingdom of great britain. 1801 ireland united kingdom the eic goal of the eic's formation forex forex board or court of directors.. the english east india company was formed on 31st december 1600 — its founding document was a royal charter issued by queen elizabeth i 58-03 (1558-1603) ◆ takeaway: a royal charter is essentially a licence granted by the monarch. if it was not renewed, the company would legally cease to exist. this single fact shaped the eic's entire relationship with the british state for the next two & a half centuries — the company's survival depended on the goodwill of whoever held power in britain. (*britain or england? in 1600, it was england — not britain — that granted this charter. england & scotland united in 1707 to create the kingdom of great britain. in 1801, ireland was added, creating the united kingdom. when we use the word "british" for the eic before 1707, we technically mean english.) the eic was the 4th joint-stock company in england, formed by pooling money from 215 london merchants — referred to as "merchant adventurers" — who wanted to challenge dutch dominance in european trade with the east. the stated goal of the eic's formation was not empire-building or colonialism but trade with the east. what the royal charter of 1600 gave the eic: 1. a monopoly over england's trade with the east indies for 15 years. 2. the right to carry gold (foreign exchange) out of england to purchase eastern goods. (*for a state, forex is the currency that matters in international trade — domestic currency works only within a country's borders. think of it this way: within a household, parents may create their own internal reward system for children, but the moment that child steps outside the home, only the currency accepted by the outside world has value. forex is that outside currency. until 1971, gold was forex until dollar took over) 3. management by a body of private people i.e. a governor, a deputy governor, & 24 members — which later evolved into the board or court of directors.

sections.title: Charters until 1793 and evolution of EIC's Legal Character
sections.norm: charters until 1793 and evolution of eic's legal character. shareholders received substantial dividends. cromwell51-60 issued a new charter in 1657, most consequential transformed the eic from a commercial trading body into a quasi-state power. takeaway: naval power capital voc (1602) eic (1600) 1657 state backing akbar56-05 king charles ii elizabeth i james i charles ii cromwell akbar. the eic's legal existence depended on charter renewal — & the story of these charters is also the story of shifting power in britain from the monarch to parliament. 8.1 — 1600 founding charter (queen elizabeth i 58-03 [1558-1603]) (discussed above). 8.2 — 1601-03 first voyage (james lancaster) the fleet sailed not to india but to indonesia — consistent with the eic's original priority of the spice trade. they reached islands of java & sumatra, where they established the very first eic factory. on the way, lancaster's fleet looted a portuguese ship, the são tomé, in the strait of malacca — i.e. cargo of textiles & spices. historian william dalrymple & others have noted that the eic's first major profit came not from trade but from outright piracy. shareholders received substantial dividends. the fleet returned in 1603. 8.3 — 1609 charter of king james i 03-25 (1603-25) replaced the original 15-year monopoly with a perpetual (indefinite) monopoly over trade with the east indies. 8.4 — 1657 cromwell's charter (context: king charles i 25-49(1625-49) attempted to levy taxes without parliament's consent and this triggered the english civil war (1642–51). the parliamentarians — largely protestant — defeated the royalists. charles i 25-49 was beheaded in 1649. england became a republic under oliver cromwell. after cromwell's death in 1658, his son briefly took over, but the republican experiment proved autocratic & unpopular. in 1660, monarchy was restored with king charles ii 60-85(1660-85) on the throne.) cromwell51-60 issued a new charter in 1657, declaring the previous royal charter invalid. the most important legal transformation in this charter was that it reorganised the eic into a permanent joint-stock company. previously, the eic had raised money separately for each individual voyage — investors pooled funds, the voyage happened, profits were distributed, & the fund dissolved. from 1657 onwards, the eic operated on a continuous, unified capital fund — money stayed invested in the company permanently, not voyage by voyage. this gave the company a far more stable financial foundation. 8.5 — 1661 charter of king charles ii60-85 this charter, issued after the restoration of monarchy, was arguably the most consequential in legal terms. it transformed the eic from a commercial trading body into a quasi-state power. the 1661 charter gave the eic the right to build forts, command troops, make war & peace, & exercise civil & criminal jurisdiction over their settlements in india (*the right to mint its own money was given to eic in 1676) ◆ takeaway: compare this to the 1600 charter: the original eic was a merchant association with a trade monopoly. the 1661 eic had the legal powers of a state within its territories. this legal transformation is the institutional foundation from which british colonial rule in india grew. a trading company had, step by step through successive charters, accumulated the powers of a sovereign. 8.6 — from 1793 onwards parliament takes over the british parliament begins passing acts for the renewal of eic's charter. ◆ takeaway: this shift mirrors the broader democratisation of britain — the transfer of power from the crown to elected representatives. the same parliament that now controlled the eic's charter was the parliament that would, through the 19th century, debate & legislate the governance of india. indian constitutional history & british political history are inseparable threads. diagram 2 — eic charter evolution: 1600 founding charter (elizabeth i58-03 — 15-yr east indies monopoly) → 1609 james i03-25 (perpetual monopoly) → 1657 cromwell charter (permanent joint-stock company) → 1661 charles ii60-85 charter (quasi-state power: mint, forts, troops, war/peace, civil/criminal jurisdiction) → 1793 onwards (parliament begins renewing charter) 8.7 — why couldn’t indian merchants dominate the new trade routes? (i) naval power — indian merchants did not have armed ocean-going fleets to break domination of europeans over trade routes. (ii) capital — voc (1602) and eic (1600) by 1657 had moved to permanent joint-stock company structures; they could pool huge sums needed for bulk trade. (iii) state backing — the mughal state after akbar56-05 did not focus on navy & focused on territorial expansion by investing in territorial army.

sections.title: Danish East India Company – Rise and Fall
sections.norm: danish east india company – rise and fall. established in 1616 12-year monopoly danes were never in the same league. selling all its indian mainland settlements to the british eic by 1845. danish settlements in india 1620 tranquebar (tharangambadi), tamil nadu fort dansborg official administrative headquarters of danish india 1624 — pondicherry (brief): roland crappé 1625 masulipatnam (andhra pradesh) pipli & balasore (odisha) 1755 serampore (srirampur / frederiksnagore), hooghly district, bengal tranquebar serampore danish colonial powers in tranquebar, serampore, & the nicobar islands serampore mission press — immense contribution to early printing & education in bengal king christian iv khan. the danish east india company was established in 1616 — driven by envy of the profits being made by the dutch & english. its charter was issued by king christian iv88-48 (1588-1648) of denmark-norway, granting a 12-year monopoly over trade between denmark-norway & east indies. the danes were never in the same league. their financial base was weaker & their military capacity limited. the first danish company ended around 1650. a second danish eic was set up in 1670, but this too wound down gradually, eventually selling all its indian mainland settlements to the british eic by 1845. danish settlements in india: 1. 1620 — first factory at tranquebar (tharangambadi), tamil nadu. first fort: fort dansborg. tranquebar served as the official administrative headquarters of danish india from 1620 until the danes left in 1845. 2. 1624 — pondicherry (brief): under roland crappé, the danes established a short-lived factory at pondicherry, but quickly abandoned it due to lack of resources, long before the french arrived. 3. 1625 — masulipatnam (andhra pradesh); pipli & balasore (odisha). 4. 1755 — serampore (srirampur / frederiksnagore), hooghly district, bengal. the danes received a parwana from nawab alivardi khan40-56 to set up this factory (*farman (imperial decree by mughal emperor); nishan (princely decree by prince of the royal blood); parwana (provincial decree / order by provincial governor)). while tranquebar remained the administrative headquarters, serampore (bengal) grew into the most commercially successful & culturally significant danish trading post in india. the danish were colonial powers in tranquebar, serampore, & the nicobar islands (*nicobar islands were sold separately to the british in 1868; today india's andaman & nicobar islands ut). in 1799–1800, the danes established the serampore mission press — associated with baptist missionaries including william carey — which translated the bible into indian vernacular languages, ran schools, & made an immense contribution to early printing & education in bengal. their architectural legacy at tranquebar & serampore, & their missionary work (*not forced conversions), remain the most visible traces of danish presence in india. summary table t3 — danish factories and key permissions in india year event / settlement permission / source 1616 danish east india company established charter of king christian iv88-48, 12-year monopoly 1620 tranquebar (tharangambadi) + fort dansborg first factory; admin hq of danish india till 1845 1624 pondicherry (brief) under roland crappé; abandoned shortly after 1625 masulipatnam; pipli & balasore — 1650 first danish company ends — 1670 second danish eic established — 1755 serampore (frederiksnagore), bengal parwana from nawab alivardi khan40-56 1799–1800 serampore mission press with william carey & baptist missionaries 1845 all mainland settlements sold to british eic — 1868 nicobar islands sold to british —

sections.title: How EIC Broke Portuguese Dominance and Establish Itself in India?
sections.norm: how eic broke portuguese dominance and establish itself in india?. 1608 captain william hawkins battle of swally (also called battle of suvali) in 1612, captain thomas best royal farman in 1613 permanent factory at surat. jahangir. in 1608, the eic decided to establish a factory at surat — then the most important port on india's west coast & firmly within portuguese-dominated territory. the eic sent captain william hawkins to the court of jahangir05-27 (r. 1605–1627). jahangir05-27 initially gave hawkins a mansab (rank of 400) & a jagir (a revenue-generating land grant), but hawkins was ultimately expelled from the mughal court due to persistent portuguese pressure. the lesson for the eic was clear: portugal had to be defeated militarily before the eic could establish itself on the west coast. this understanding led directly to the battle of swally (also called battle of suvali) in 1612, where captain thomas best led a small eic armed trading fleet to a decisive victory over the portuguese. the mughal state had its own reason to welcome this outcome — mughal ships regularly traded in the arabian sea but were perpetually vulnerable to portuguese piracy at sea, a source of ongoing humiliation for one of the world's most powerful land-based state of the time. impressed by the english military capability at sea, jahangir05-27 issued a royal farman in 1613 — the imperial decree that gave the eic the legal right to set up a permanent factory at surat. (*1612 is the year of the battle of swally & the local mughal governor's temporary permission/parwana. the legally permanent establishment came only in early 1613 when jahangir05-27 officially ratified the local agreement with an imperial farman. 1612 = military victory & local permission; 1613 = legal imperial farman.)

sections.title: Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)
sections.norm: royal farman of 1618 and thomas roe (1615-19). liberal trading rights thomas roe roe extracted series of privileges for eic and a royal farman (1618) during 1616–1619: agra, ahmedabad, & broach (bharuch) surat presidency (1618) eic's first administrative presidency in india later shift to bombay ( in 1687). shahjahan27-58 defeat the portuguese jahangir shahjahan. england wanted more than a single factory. it wanted liberal trading rights across the entire mughal empire. king james i 03-25 (1603-25) therefore sent thomas roe as his formal ambassador to jahangir05-27's court. roe arrived at surat in 1615 & stayed until 1619. (roe's account of these years — the embassy of sir thomas roe to the court of the great mogul — remains one of the most important primary sources we have on the mughal empire of this period, documenting court administration, wealth, politics, & daily life in close detail.) jahangir05-27 refused to sign a formal treaty between equals — the mughal emperor saw no reason to treat a trading company as a sovereign equal. but through sustained diplomacy & personal rapport roe extracted series of privileges for eic and a royal farman (1618) giving the eic the right to establish factories throughout the mughal empire & liberal trading rights — lower customs duties & ease of doing business. eic rapidly expanded its factory network during 1616–1619: new factories were established at agra, ahmedabad, & broach (bharuch) — all within the mughal empire. these factories, along with surat, operated under the newly constituted surat presidency (1618) — the eic's first administrative presidency in india, which coordinated all english trade on the west coast before the later shift to bombay ( in 1687). this enraged the portuguese, & naval conflicts continued to weaken their position. then in 1631–32, emperor shahjahan27-58 ordered his bengal governor qasim khan to take direct action — to defeat the portuguese & eject them from hugli, because the portuguese had been misusing their trade privileges: engaging in piracy & the slave trade from their bengal base.

sections.title: Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661- Dowry Diplomacy
sections.norm: anglo-portuguese treaty of 1661- dowry diplomacy. anglo-portuguese treaty of 1661, marriage as part of the settlement: dowry 500,000 pounds bombay & tangier trade & military cooperation this treaty guaranteed continued portuguese presence in goa, daman, & diu under english protection 1668 bombay to the eic annual rent of 10 pounds king charles ii. the relationship between portugal & england was finally formalised through the anglo-portuguese treaty of 1661, signed at whitehall in london. the occasion was a marriage: king charles ii60-85 of england married princess catherine of braganza of portugal. as part of the settlement: 1. portugal paid a dowry of 500,000 pounds in cash. 2. england received bombay & tangier (in morocco). 3. the two countries agreed on trade & military cooperation, with england agreeing to protect portugal's remaining possessions. this treaty guaranteed continued portuguese presence in goa, daman, & diu under english protection — a presence that lasted, remarkably, until 1961, when independent india militarily, after a people’s movement, took over these territories. in 1668, the british crown transferred bombay to the eic at an annual rent of 10 pounds — beginning bombay's long journey from a portuguese dowry to the commercial capital of british india.

sections.title: How Did the Dutch Rise, Dominate — and Then Fall in Asia?
sections.norm: how did the dutch rise, dominate — and then fall in asia?. by 1623, removed both the english & the portuguese from the indonesia. by 1658, ceylon anglo-dutch rivalry wars from 1654 to 1667, treaty of breda in 1667: indonesia india minor presences captured cochin from the portuguese in 1663 hq of dutch malabar dutch locations & hq roles first factory in india (1605) masulipatnam first fort in india (1610) fort geldria at pulicat main dutch hq in india pulicat (fort geldria) other dutch regional hqs cochin (fort kochi) chinsura two decisive military defeats 1. 1741 — battle of colachel: 1759 — bedara ( chinsura): in bengal, varma. by 1623, after the amboyna massacre (in which the dutch killed english traders in the spice islands — a brutal episode that ended english ambitions in indonesia), the dutch had effectively removed both the english & the portuguese from the indonesia. by 1658, the dutch also removed the portuguese from ceylon (today's sri lanka). the anglo-dutch rivalry then played out in a series of wars from 1654 to 1667, settling eventually into a practical geographical compromise formalised in the treaty of breda in 1667: 1. the british agreed to leave indonesia to the dutch. 2. the dutch agreed to leave the english alone in india. 3. both maintained minor presences in each other's primary domains. the dutch had captured cochin from the portuguese in 1663 & held it as the hq of dutch malabar (not their overall main hq — overall main hq was pulicat 1610–1690, then nagapattinam 1690–1795). dutch locations & hq roles — a careful disambiguation: first factory in india (1605): masulipatnam (andhra pradesh) — the earliest dutch factory in india, on a farman from the sultan of golconda. first fort in india (1610): fort geldria at pulicat — the first major dutch fortification in india. built on the ruins of an earlier portuguese structure, with permission from the local ruler of the vijayanagara empire. main dutch hq in india: pulicat (fort geldria) from 1610 to 1690 — the primary seat of the dutch governor in india during this period. in 1690, the main hq shifted from pulicat to nagapattinam (negapatam), where it remained until 1795. other dutch regional hqs (not overall hq): cochin (fort kochi) was hq of dutch malabar only (1663–1795). chinsura was hq of dutch bengal (fort gustavus, 1655–1795). exam trap: students confuse cochin as the overall dutch hq — it was only the dutch malabar regional hq. timeline location role / status 1605 masulipatnam first dutch factory in india. 1610 – 1690 pulicat (fort geldria) first dutch fort + main hq (coromandel coast). built on ruins of an earlier portuguese structure with vijayanagara permission. 1690 – 1795 nagapattinam (negapatam) main hq (shifted from pulicat). 1663 – 1795 cochin (fort kochi) hq of dutch malabar only — not overall hq. 1655 – 1795 chinsura hq of dutch bengal (fort gustavus). dutch influence in india then declined through two decisive military defeats: 1. 1741 — battle of colachel: the powerful travancore king marthanda varma29-58 (r. 1729–1758) decisively defeated the dutch, ending their political power in kerala. 2. 1759 — battle of bedara (also called battle of chinsura): the british eic defeated the dutch in bengal, crushing their remaining ambitions in india.

sections.title: Napoleon’s link with the Dutch Being Removed from South Asia?
sections.norm: napoleon’s link with the dutch being removed from south asia?. 1795 french army invaded the netherlands. "kew letters" by 1795, cochin on the kerala coast, chinsura in bengal, pulicat & tuticorin on the coromandel coast, & the coastal regions of ceylon prince william v. the final chapter of dutch presence in south asia was written not in india but in europe. in 1795, during the french revolutionary wars (1792-1804) — which led directly into the napoleonic wars (1804-1815)— the french army invaded the netherlands. they overthrew the dutch government & set up a puppet state called the batavian republic, entirely controlled by france. because the netherlands was now effectively allied with france — britain's primary adversary — britain declared all dutch overseas colonies enemy territory. the exiled dutch leader, prince william v51-95, had fled to london. from there, he issued legal orders known as the "kew letters" — instructing all dutch colonial governors to hand over their territories to the british for "safekeeping", so that france could not seize them. the british used this as their legal basis to take over the remaining dutch posts. by 1795, the british had occupied the dutch settlements that still remained in south asia — cochin on the kerala coast, chinsura in bengal, pulicat & tuticorin on the coromandel coast, & the coastal regions of ceylon (specifically the ports of trincomalee & colombo).

sections.title: Why Did Ceylon Not Become Part of British India — and What Was a Crown Colony?
sections.norm: why did ceylon not become part of british india — and what was a crown colony?. ceylon in 1795–96, managed through the madras presidency. this changed with the treaty of amiens in 1802 dutch formally & permanently ceded the coastal regions of ceylon to britain. significant legal & administrative decision declared ceylon a british crown colony takeaway:. when the british military first captured the dutch areas of ceylon in 1795–96, they handed administration to the eic — specifically managed through the madras presidency. this changed with the treaty of amiens in 1802 — a peace treaty signed in europe between britain & france, along with its dutch ally the batavian republic. in this treaty, the dutch formally & permanently ceded the coastal regions of ceylon to britain. what followed was a significant legal & administrative decision. the british government concluded that ceylon was too strategically important to be run by a trading company. they removed the eic's administration entirely & declared ceylon a british crown colony — ruled directly by the british state through an appointed british governor, completely separate from the eic's indian empire. ◆ takeaway: india was a colony ruled by the eic - a commercial entity with state-like powers; ceylon was a crown colony where the british state itself governed directly.

sections.title: What Were English/British EIC Presidencies — and How Did They Become Provinces?
sections.norm: what were english/british eic presidencies — and how did they become provinces?. regional headquarters of eic trade presidency status. a presidency was a regional headquarters of eic trade. the eic gave a settlement presidency status when it had grown large enough — with significant warehouses, offices, residential buildings, & a fort. initially these were small coastal towns. over time, as the eic annexed surrounding territories, these towns grew into cities, & the presidencies expanded into provinces of british india — that part of india governed directly by the british. the presidencies were named after the major forts built within them.

sections.title: How Did Each of the Three Presidencies Come to Be?
sections.norm: how did each of the three presidencies come to be?. eic's first factory masulipatnam in 1611. in 1639 madraspatanam hindu nayakas fort st george between 1639 & 1644 first fort built by the eic purchased a fort at cuddalore fort saint david madras presidency presidency of fort st george in 1652 actually implemented in india in 1653. from 1613 to 1687, surat was the eic's main trade centre 1661 portuguese marriage dowry eic in 1668 at rent of 10 pounds per annum. bombay presidency was established in 1687 bombay castle (also known as casa da orta) factory at hugli in 1651 — 1690 the calcutta establishment. presidency of fort william calcutta port calcutta eventually accounted for 60% of all eic trade from india 1800, fort william college calcutta port act, 1870 king charles ii charles ii rajaram shivaji chhatrapati shivaji shahjahan wellesley aurangzeb farrukhsiyar. 17.1 madras presidency (from 1652/1653) the eic's first factory in india was a temporary one — at masulipatnam (machilipatnam) in the northern sarkars (today's andhra pradesh), in 1611. (northern sarkars was the name for the northern coastal districts of andhra pradesh, outside mughal direct control.) in 1639, the eic — led by francis day — purchased land at the village of madraspatanam from hindu nayakas (provincial governors of the vijayanagara empire, 1336–1646) & built fort st george between 1639 & 1644 — the first fort built by the eic in india & the anchor of the first permanent settlement. in 1690, the eic purchased a fort at cuddalore, south of madras, from maratha chhatrapati rajaram89-00 & named it fort saint david. this fort had a layered history: partially built by the dutch from 1608, construction was halted due to portuguese pressure on the vijayanagara empire; a hindu merchant eventually completed it. in 1677, shivaji74-80 (chhatrapati shivaji) conquered the nearby jinji fort & the surrounding region including cuddalore, bringing it under maratha control before it later passed to the eic. the madras presidency was formally established as the presidency of fort st george in 1652 under orders of the court of directors of eic in london. due to the time required for the order to travel by ship, the decision was actually implemented in india in 1653. (both dates appear in different sources — the distinction is between the london order & the on-ground implementation.) 17.2 bombay presidency (1687) from 1613 to 1687, surat was the eic's main trade centre on the west coast. the shift happened due to the growing power of the marathas in gujarat, which made surat increasingly risky for the eic. bombay — a cluster of seven islands — offered a more defensible location. king charles ii60-85 received bombay in 1661 as part of the portuguese marriage dowry & transferred it to the eic in 1668 at rent of 10 pounds per annum. the bombay presidency was established in 1687, replacing surat as the eic's western headquarters. the bombay castle (also known as casa da orta) was originally built by the portuguese & expanded by the eic through the 18th century. 17.3 calcutta presidency (from 1699/1700) the eic's bengal presence began with a factory at hugli in 1651 — permitted by a nishan (a decree issued by a prince) from shah shuja, the mughal governor of bengal & son of shahjahan27-58. in 1690, eic founded a settlement at the village of sutanuti — the calcutta establishment. the calcutta presidency was formally established in 1699/1700 as the presidency of fort william with its own governor. through the 18th century, the eic developed the calcutta port aggressively. calcutta eventually accounted for 60% of all eic trade from india. in 1800, fort william college was established by wellesley98-05 for training eic civil servants. in 1870, the calcutta port act, 1870 created the calcutta port commissioners & the calcutta port trust — the first formal legal authority to govern & administer the port. (*child’s war, 1690 pardon & 1691 farman, and 1717 farman covered later as background of eic in chapter on battle of plassey) diagram 3 — three eic presidencies: madras 1652/1653 (fort st george) + bombay 1687 (1661 anglo-portuguese dowry under charles ii60-85; crown to eic 1668 at £10/annum) + calcutta 1699/1700 (presidency of fort william; aurangzeb58-07's 1690 pardon + ibrahim khan's 1691 farman + farrukhsiyar13-19's 1717 imperial farman 'magna carta of the company'); 60% of all eic trade by late 18th century

sections.title: The French in India — and the Story of Pondicherry
sections.norm: the french in india — and the story of pondicherry. french also established a significant presence in india french east india company founded in 1664 louis xiv43-15 later nationalised public sector undertaking or psu 1668 surat 1667 1669 masulipatnam golconda (1518–1687) 1673 chandarnagar shaista khan64-88 chandernagore 1674 pondicherry sikandar adil shah72-86 françois martin01-06 1701–1706 françois martin01-06 is the real founder of french power in india. pondicherry the capital in 1701 fort louis 1723 yanam hyderabad's nizam-ul-mulk24-48 asaf jah i 1724 mahe 1739 karaikal pratap singh39-63 venkoji 8. 1721 mauritius 1735 mahé de la bourdonnais35-46 union territory of pondicherry (formed 1962) alert: pondicherry's occupation history (*mnemonic pda-fdu-bfbf->india). portuguese danes french dutch british king louis xiv aurangzeb khan shah martin mulk nizam singh bourdonnais dupleix. before the eic's dominance became total, the french also established a significant presence in india. the french east india company (compagnie des indes orientales) was founded in 1664 by jean-baptiste colbert under king louis xiv43-15 (1643-1715; great-grandfather of louis xvi, who was overthrown in the french revolution of 1789.) it started as a private company but was later nationalised — making it, in today's terms, a public sector undertaking or psu. it expanded steadily: 1. 1668 — first factory at surat, on a farman given by aurangzeb58-07 in 1667. 2. 1669 — factory at masulipatnam, on a farman from the sultan of golconda (1518–1687). 3. 1673 — permission to set up a township in chandarnagar, from shaista khan64-88, the mughal governor of bengal. but due to financial crunch, it was only in 1690-92 that french established a settlement in chandernagore. 4 1674 — acquired pondicherry from the sultan of bijapur, sikandar adil shah72-86, & the sultan's local governor sher khan lodi. it was developed as a city by françois martin01-06, governor-general 1701–1706 (earlier governor). françois martin01-06 is the real founder of french power in india. he centralised french administration by making pondicherry the capital in 1701 & built fort louis to defend the new city. 5 1723 — acquired yanam, on permission from hyderabad's nizam-ul-mulk24-48 (also called asaf jah i). 6 1724 — acquired mahe on the malabar coast, from the local nair ruler vazhunnavar in 1721. built trade settlement in 1724-25 after overcoming rebellion by local ruler. named after mahé de la bourdonnais who came to help with a fleet from mauritius. 7 1739 — acquired karaikal (part of french pondicherry), granted by pratap singh39-63, the maratha ruler of tanjore (thanjavur), as a reward to the french for helping him in a succession dispute. (*thanjavur maratha dynasty was founded not by shivaji maharaj directly, but by his half-brother, venkoji (also known as ekoji) in 1674 by defeating nayaka rulers of madurai) 8. 1721 — mauritius established as a french colony, but proper control came only by 1735 under the brilliant naval officer & administrator mahé de la bourdonnais35-46, as governor. (he again arrived from mauritius with a naval fleet in 1746 & helped dupleix42-54 capture madras from the british in the 1st carnatic war (1746–48).) 9) referendum in 1949 in chandernagore merged it into india while the rest remained under french control until 1954. union territory of pondicherry (formed 1962): district coastline surrounded by (state) puducherry(capital) east coast (bay of bengal) tamil nadu karaikal east coast (bay of bengal) tamil nadu yanam east coast (bay of bengal) andhra pradesh mahe west coast (arabian sea) kerala ⚠ alert: pondicherry's occupation history (*mnemonic pda-fdu-bfbf->india). while pondicherry is synonymous with the french, they were not the first europeans to occupy it. the sequence of occupation is: portuguese (16th century) → danes (briefly in 1624) → french (1674) → dutch (captured briefly in 1693) → british. the english captured pondicherry in 1761 & restored it to the french via the treaty of paris in 1763; british captured it again during later conflicts (such as in 1793) before finally returning it to the french in 1814. pondicherry remained french until it was transferred to india in 1954.

sections.title: How Did a Trading Company Become a State?
sections.norm: how did a trading company become a state?. eic 1857 63% 78% 1661 charter gave the eic the wars fought to protect or expand trade second kind were wars fought for territory wars for territory two specific conditions: robert clive57-67 richard wellesley98-05 francis hastings13-23 dalhousie48-56 clive wellesley hastings dalhousie. companies exist to make profit for their shareholders. the eic was no different. but what the eic became in india was something far beyond a trading enterprise — it became a company state that, by 1857, controlled 63% of india's territory & 78% of its population. this chapter deals with empire building by eic. 1661 charter gave the eic the right to build forts, command troops, make war & peace, & exercise civil & criminal jurisdiction over their settlements in india (*the right to mint its own money was given to eic in 1676) types of wars fought by eic- for trade & for territory the wars the eic fought in india fall into two broad categories. the first kind were wars fought to protect or expand trade. the second kind were wars fought for territory — for empire building. these were different in nature & in motivation. wars for territory happened under two specific conditions: 1. when the governor or governor-general in india was personally ambitious — an empire builder by temperament. britain was far away. communication was slow. these men had enough operational freedom to pursue wars that london might not have formally approved. the major empire builders were robert clive57-67 (governor of bengal presidency, in two stints: 1757–60 & 1765–67), richard wellesley98-05 (1798–1805), francis hastings13-23 (1813–23), & dalhousie48-56 (1848–56). 2. at times, eic army put pressure for wars. any army has a structural interest in war — war brings bigger defence budget, prestige, promotions, & political relevance to the military. the eic army was no different. it routinely overhyped threats to borders, which created pressure for expansion. and expansion always created new borders, which created new threats (fictional or real) in form of new neighbours. it was a self-reinforcing cycle. (*think of how the pakistan army today has eaten pakistan from within by putting its vested interests above national interest, while the indian army has consistently done the opposite.)

sections.title: Wars for Trade
sections.norm: wars for trade. 2.1 in bengal and arabian sea: josiah child: london john child: constant warfare was disrupting eic trade disputes with the nawab of bengal heavy customs duties seized hugli crushed the eic in both bombay & bengal by 1690 the company had surrendered why did aurangzeb58-07 not simply abolish the company & expel the british? brought forex/gold into india eic's export business more valuable to the indian economy indian bankers earned interest indian merchants, artisans, & ryots farman right to duty-free trade in bengal in exchange for rs 3,000 per annum. aurangzeb. 2.1 anglo-mughal war of 1686–90 in bengal and arabian sea: the first significant military clash between the eic & an indian power. also called child's war (josiah child: chairman of the court of directors of eic in london + john child: governor of bombay and the "general" of all eic forces in india.). reasons were two-folds: aurangzeb58-07's constant warfare was disrupting eic trade (problems in sourcing goods from hinterland), ongoing disputes with the nawab of bengal over bribes & heavy customs duties levied on the eic. the eic seized hugli & escalated by attacking mughal ships in the arabian sea. aurangzeb58-07's military crushed the eic in both bombay & bengal. by 1690 the company had surrendered. in february 1690, aurangzeb58-07 pardoned the eic in return for rs 1.5 lakh compensation. why did aurangzeb58-07 not simply abolish the company & expel the british? because the eic was economically useful. its trade brought forex/gold into india & aurangzeb58-07 needed them for war. with aurangzeb58-07's own constant warfare disrupting domestic trade, the eic's export business was, ironically, even more valuable to the indian economy. indian bankers earned interest by lending money to the company for purchase of goods. indian merchants, artisans, & ryots all participated in & benefited from this trade ecosystem. 1691 farman (*technically called parwana as issued by the subahdar of bengal, not an imperial farman)— issued under aurangzeb58-07's approval, restored eic’s old privileges & gave it right to duty-free trade in bengal in exchange for rs 3,000 per annum. the company had been defeated militarily, yet it got this privilege due to benefits of european trade with india.

sections.title: Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63)
sections.norm: carnatic wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63). conquest by the eic began in bengal why the french were there joseph françois dupleix42-54 1740 eic-french contest two overlapping reasons european rivalry. war of the austrian succession (1740–48) seven years' global war (1756–63) succession disputes in carnatic & hyderabad dupleix. to understand why conquest by the eic began in bengal, one must first understand what was happening in south india — & why the french were there. joseph françois dupleix42-54 was the governor-general of the french eic from 1742-54. dupleix42-54 had personal ambitions of empire building & of dominating the international trade of south india. he would become the template for everything that followed. (*by 1740, french eic trade was roughly half the value of british eic trade.) 3.1 reasons for carnatic wars: the eic-french contest in india had two overlapping reasons: i) european rivalry. two global wars spilled into india — the war of the austrian succession (1740–48) led to 1st carnatic war (1746-48) & the seven years' global war (1756–63) led to the 3rd carnatic war (1756-63). as the two nations fought, their respective companies also entered into hostilities in india. ii) succession disputes in carnatic & hyderabad contributed to 2nd carnatic war (1749-54). the strategy was simple: put your chosen candidates in power to gain strategic influence.

sections.title: The 1st Carnatic War (1746–48) —the Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)?
sections.norm: the 1st carnatic war (1746–48) —the battle of adyar/st thome (1746)?. 1st carnatic war (1746–48) war of the austrian succession (1740–48) fort st george 10,000 cavalry battle of adyar/st thome (1746) 700 french-trained indian sepoys 300 french soldiers superior artillery tactical discipline regular cash salaries takeaway: treaty of aix-la-chapelle (1748) dupleix anwaruddin babar. 4.1 reason the 1st carnatic war (1746–48) was the indian chapter of the war of the austrian succession (1740–48), in which britain & france — along with their respective allies — fought each other across europe, america, & india, each wanting its preferred candidate on the austrian throne. 4.2 events during the war in india, dupleix42-54 captured the eic's fort st george in madras and eic was defeated. the nawab of carnatic, anwaruddin44-49, intervened — he expected the french to handover the fort to nawab as promised. dupleix42-54 refused. anwaruddin44-49 sent an army of 10,000 cavalry. what happened next changed the nature of power in india. at the battle of adyar/st thome (1746), fought on the north bank of the river adyar, a french force of roughly 700 french-trained indian sepoys & 300 french soldiers completely destroyed the nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. the french won due to three critical advantages that would define european military superiority in india across all the wars to come: 1. superior artillery — light, mobile european cannon that could be repositioned rapidly on the battlefield, against which massed cavalry had no answer (*link- like small bronze cannons of babar26-30) 2. tactical discipline — european-trained infantry fought in coordinated formations, including infantry squares that could hold ground against cavalry charges from any direction. 3. regular cash salaries — unlike indian armies where soldiers were often not paid regularly, european-trained sepoys received regular wages, which created a professional, reliable fighting force with no incentive to desert between campaigns. ◆ takeaway: this was not just a military victory. for the first time, it was proven conclusively that a small, disciplined, european-trained infantry with modern artillery could crush a vastly larger traditional indian army. the psychological impact was enormous — it gave europeans the confidence to start interfering directly in indian political disputes, which is exactly what dupleix42-54 proceeded to do. the indian royal elites also wanted to use military service of the europeans in their internal & external disputes. (* have you heard of the wagner group? it is a company which sells military service to russian state. in a way french were now wagner group of india.) 4.3 consequence — treaty of aix-la-chapelle (1748) however, in north america — more strategically important to france — britain had won. so in the treaty of aix-la-chapelle (1748) that ended the war of the austrian succession, both sides agreed to return each other's possessions in america & india. madras went back to the eic. for dupleix42-54, this was deeply frustrating — his victories in india were traded away at a negotiating table in europe. but he was not done. his next opportunity came almost immediately, in the form of succession disputes — one in hyderabad, one in carnatic.

sections.title: The 2nd Carnatic War (1749–54) — How Did Dupleix Invent the Blueprint for Empire in India?
sections.norm: the 2nd carnatic war (1749–54) — how did dupleix invent the blueprint for empire in india?. in carnatic : md ali wallajah (*md ali52-95) chanda sahib49-52 in hyderabad: nasir jung48-50 muzaffar jung50-51 dupleix42-54 muzaffar jung50-51 in hyderabad chanda sahib49-52 in carnatic battle of ambur (1749) battle of lakkireddipalli pass salabat jung51-62 the gains from phase 1: in hyderabad, northern sarkars 2,00,000 pounds in carnatic, rs 1 lakh per annum takeaway: this is exactly the model the british eic would refine & use trichinopoly 200 europeans & 300 sepoys 53 days 1754 godeheu treaty of pondicherry (1754) pratap singh39-63 anwaruddin ali sahib khan mulk nizam jung dupleix singh shivaji chhatrapati shivaji. 5.0 what were the succession disputes that triggered this war? in carnatic : anwaruddin44-49 had been appointed nawab of carnatic by the nizam of hyderabad in 1744. on his death, succession dispute began between his son md ali wallajah (*md ali52-95) & chanda sahib49-52 — son-in-law of the earlier nawab dost ali khan32-40 (1732-40). in hyderabad: nizam-ul-mulk24-48 died in 1748. his son nasir jung48-50 & grandson muzaffar jung50-51 were rivals for the throne. dupleix42-54 backed muzaffar jung50-51 in hyderabad (*mnemonic muzaffrance) & chanda sahib49-52 in carnatic (*mnemonic paris & moon/chanda are symbol of romance); an anxious eic backed the opposing sides. he wanted his chosen candidates in power for economic/trade & political influence. an anxious eic backed the opposing sides — nasir jung48-50 in hyderabad, md ali52-95 in carnatic. 5.1 phase 1 — french victory (1749–51) at the battle of ambur (1749), nawab anwaruddin44-49 was killed. chanda sahib49-52 was declared nawab of carnatic at the capital arcot. by december 1750, nasir jung48-50 was also killed & muzaffar jung50-51 was declared nizam. bussy was junior of dupleix42-54. accompanied by bussy's army, muzaffar jung50-51 began marching toward hyderabad — but was killed in february 1751 at the battle of lakkireddipalli pass by the afghan nawab of kurnool who felt cheated as was not given territory promised to him for his support. the nawab of kurnool was also killed. bussy now reached hyderabad & installed salabat jung51-62 as nizam — a son of nizam-ul-mulk24-48 & uncle of the recently killed muzaffar jung50-51. the gains from phase 1: in hyderabad, bussy was made the french resident & agent at the nizam's court, wielding real political influence. a french army was stationed for the nizam's protection — & hyderabad was to pay for it. the payment was the northern sarkars region (present day andhra pradesh): bussy administered it on behalf of the nizam & kept its revenues as payment for the french army. in northern sarkars, bussy's methods were brutal — terror & massacre of civilians for land revenue extraction. (*in andhra folklore, this terror is preserved in the word boochi — meaning ghost or the feared — derived from bussy's name.) he also extracted personal jagirs in masulipatnam & yanam, & obtained 2,00,000 pounds for the french eic from the nizam. in carnatic, dupleix42-54 declared himself nawab of all lands between the river krishna & cape comorin (= carnatic), with chanda sahib49-52 as his deputy nawab of arcot. he also extracted a personal jagir of rs 1 lakh per annum in villianallur near pondicherry. ◆ takeaway: dupleix42-54 had just invented the model of empire building in india: put your candidate in power, station your army at his expense, extract territory as payment, & sit in the court as the real power behind the throne. this is exactly the model the british eic would refine & use with devastating effect for the next century (*thanks dupleix42-54 would be thoughts of eic) 5.2 phase 2 —eic bounces back eic decided to fight back by supporting md ali52-95 (carnatic), who was holding out in trichinopoly. dupleix42-54 got obsessed with eliminating any future challenge to his power and hence made critical mistake of leaving the capital arcot unguarded and focusing on trichinopoly. robert clive, operating from madras with a small force of roughly 200 europeans & 300 sepoys took over arcot. he then defended it against a massive counter-siege for 53 days. the capital was now with british! (clive became a celebrated figure back in britain.) the french government in paris, anxious to honour the 1748 treaty & preserve its more lucrative american possessions, refused to help dupleix42-54. by 1754, the french had lost the 2nd carnatic war. 5.3 treaty of pondicherry (1754) dupleix42-54 was recalled to france, replaced by godeheu, on account of the high war expenditure. (he died in poverty in france in 1763, abandoned by the state he had served.) the treaty of pondicherry (1754) was a middle path: 1. french influence remained in hyderabad via bussy as agent, french army in hyderabad & northern sarkars with french. 2. french factories in pondicherry & carnatic were retained. 3. md ali52-95 became nawab of carnatic — hence now eic influence in carnatic. chanda sahib49-52, having escaped to tanjore (present-day thanjavur in tamil nadu), was beheaded by pratap singh39-63, the maratha raja of thanjavur — an old rival. (maratha rule in tanjore had begun in 1674 when venkoji — also known as ekoji, half-brother of chhatrapati shivaji74-80 — conquered the region.)

sections.title: The 3rd Carnatic War (1756–63)
sections.norm: the 3rd carnatic war (1756–63). 3rd carnatic war (1756–63) 7 years' global war (1756–63) count de lally eyre coote battle of wandiwash (1760) alert — prelims 1995: france lost, for four reasons tactical mistake 1759 poor leadership financial weakness superior british navy leadership: finances: tactical mistakes: treaty of paris (1763) pondicherry, mahe, karaikal, yanam & chandernagore in 1769, the french eic was abolished by france. takeaway: battle of plassey (1757) 6.5 later, treaty of hyderabad (1766) northern sarkars rs 7 lakh annually hyderabad subsidiary alliance 1798 mysore 1799 travancore 1805 carnatic annexed 1801 carnatic wars laid foundation of british domination of south india shah alam ii dalhousie dupleix. 6.1 reason the 3rd carnatic war (1756–63) was once again a european conflict brought to indian shores — the 7 years' global war (1756–63), fought across europe, the americas, africa, & india. count de lally (of french state not french eic) arrived from france with royal military and led the french alongside bussy of the french eic. eyre coote (of british state not eic) arrived from britain with royal military, and led the british alongside robert clive of the eic. 6.2 why did france lose 3rd carnatic war (1756-63)? the most decisive battle was the battle of wandiwash (1760) (*where french were washed way ). after that, the french lost everywhere — including pondicherry itself (*their headquarters officially since 1701 with fort louis) ⚠ alert — prelims 1995: upsc asked "match the battle to who fought it" by jumbling correct pairs [battle of buxar (1764) → eic vs mir qasim(with awadh & shah alam ii60-06); battle of chilianwala (1849) → eic under dalhousie48-56 vs the sikhs (2nd anglo-sikh war); battle of kharda (1795) → nizam of hyderabad vs the marathas; battle of wandiwash (1760) = french vs the east india company] france lost, for four reasons: 1. tactical mistake — bussy abandoned the northern sarkars to reinforce lally in carnatic. robert clive arrived from bengal and took over northern sarkars in 1759. 2. poor leadership — lally was despised by his own officers & sepoys for his rude conduct which demoralised the army. 3. financial weakness — french soldiers went unpaid for months. the french eic had spent heavily in the war of the austrian succession (1740–48) & the first two carnatic wars without commensurate gains. in contrast, britain had been profiting from eastern trade since 1600. british capitalism was mature; feudalism in france ended only after the french revolution of 1789 while the industrial revolution had begun in britain (1750-1850). 4. superior british navy — this gave britain decisive advantages in the coastal warfare of the northern sarkars & carnatic. britain's navy was able to dominate the coromandel coast. 6.3. why did the eic win carnatic wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63)? 1. france starved dupleix42-54 of reinforcements to preserve its gains from the 1748 treaty. 2. leadership: recall of dupleix42-54 after 2nd carnatic war hurt chances of french victory. lally displayed poor leadership in 3rd carnatic war. on other hand, robert clive and eyre coote displayed good leadership. 2. superior british navy 3. finances: the eic was a private joint-stock firm with deep capital; eic had accumulated wealth along with huge monetary gains after plassey1757. on the other hand the french eic was a state psu with weak finances. french economy was weak compared to britain which was world’s top economy of the time. past war expenditure without any formidable gains hurt french capabilities e.g. lally's troops went unpaid. 4. tactical mistakes: leaving arcot unguarded in 2nd carnatic war and leaving northern sarkars unguarded in 3rd carnatic war. 6.4 treaty of paris (1763) under the treaty of paris (1763), france lost all gains made in india since 1749 & was restricted to its pre-1749 position — france retained only five small trading posts — pondicherry, mahe, karaikal, yanam & chandernagore — & was barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases. in 1769, the french eic was abolished by france. (*this signifies that the french government had given up on ambitions of dominating international trade of india. also abolishment of french eic does not mean other french traders could not trade in india, just that the french state is not interested in running a government company for it.) after successfully countering the portuguese by 1612, the dutch by 1650s, & the french by 1763, the british eic now had monopoly over india’s international trade. ◆ takeaway: link with battle of plassey (1757). the 3rd carnatic war brought large numbers of british royal military troops to india, & it was this military strength — & clive shrewd diplomacy— that made plassey possible. without carnatic, there may not have been a plassey which led to empire building by eic. 6.5 later, in the treaty of hyderabad (1766), hyderabad formally ceded the northern sarkars to the eic in exchange for rs 7 lakh annually & protection against marathas & mysore. hyderabad became 1st indian state to sign subsidiary alliance with the eic in 1798, mysore signed in 1799, & travancore in 1805, while carnatic was annexed in 1801. thus carnatic wars, though fought for international trade of india, laid foundation of british domination of south india. diagram 1 — carnatic wars

sections.title: Plassey Marks the Beginning of Conquest
sections.norm: plassey marks the beginning of conquest. eic company state takeaway:. plassey marks the beginning of the transformation of the eic into a company state. conquest i.e. military domination and political supremacy — began here. but the eic did not legally take over sovereign functions in bengal after battle of plassey 1757. it focused on military control and on extracting wealth. ◆ takeaway: rule did not begin in 1757. conquest and the drain of wealth from india, however, did.
