sections.title: The Royal Farman of 1717: The Seed of Conflict
sections.norm: the royal farman of 1717: the seed of conflict. farmans: 1613 farman ( 1618 farman ( 1691 farman ( 1717 imperial/royal farman royal mint 38 villages nawab murshid quli khan (mqk17-27) allowed duty-free trade by the eic refused to let eic officials misuse dastaks refused use of the royal mint hurt sovereign authority allowed renting of villages but not purchase jahangir aurangzeb farrukhsiyar khan nizam. farmans: 1613 farman (by jahangir05-27) gave right to establish factory in surat after eic defeated portuguese in battle of suvali 1612; 1618 farman (by jahangir05-27) gave right to establish factories in whole of mughal empire and liberal trading rights- due to lobbying by thomas roe (british resident 1615-19); 1691 farman (by subahdar of bengal under aurangzeb58-07’s approval) gave right to duty free trade (dft) in bengal in exchange for 3000 rs per annum- eic trade economically beneficial & brought forex into india; 1717 imperial/royal farman was issued by farrukhsiyar13-19 ( & often called the "magna carta of the company") as a result of medical diplomacy. dr. william hamilton, an english surgeon with eic successfully treated farrukhsiyar13-19 for a serious illness; it gave eic- right to duty-free trade (dft) in deccan, gujarat and bengal (this time its royal farman reiterating pre-existing privilege granted under sign & seal of subahdar in 1691). right to use the royal mint — meaning the eic could mint indian coins and thus save the cost of converting gold into indian currency (sikkas) for purchasing indian goods. right to rent 38 villages around calcutta for expanding its trading settlement. the 1717 imperial/royal farman became a source of conflict between the eic & the nawab of bengal. bengal by 1717 was a successor state (*recall- successor means uttaradhikari who comes from within the family. here it is political family of mughal state (= mughal emperor & his mansabdars) hence certain powerful mansabdars established their rule in certain provinces and took away real powers of emperor making him symbolic authority. they were mqk17-27, sadat khan22-39, nizam24-48 in bengal, awadh & hyderabad respectively) nawab murshid quli khan (mqk17-27) allowed duty-free trade by the eic— but refused to let eic officials misuse dastaks for their own private trade. he refused use of the royal mint, since that hurt sovereign authority and government revenue (*government earned commission on conversion of gold to indian sikkas). he allowed renting of villages but not purchase.

sections.chapterTitle: Battle of Plassey 1757 & Battle of Buxar 1764
sections.title: The Dastak Problem
sections.norm: the dastak problem. what was misuse of dastaks? 1750, private trade by eic officials was worth 1,00,000 pounds per annum cornwallis86-93 misuse of dastaks led to tax/duty evasion loss of revenue for the bengal suba who was violating whose law ? interlopers free merchants dastak misuse cornwallis. what was misuse of dastaks? dastaks were permits issued by eic officials certifying that goods belonged to the eic, & hence exempt from export duty. in practice, eic officials also used these permits for their own private trade — claiming goods purchased in a personal capacity as company goods. they also sold dastaks to other exporters. by 1750, private trade by eic officials was worth 1,00,000 pounds per annum — roughly fifty times their annual salaries. the eic could not control this because even its own top officials in india engaged in private trade. (*note: cornwallis86-93 curbed private trade, an honest governor general of that era.) misuse of dastaks led to tax/duty evasion and loss of revenue for the bengal suba. who was violating whose law ? it is worth understanding exactly what was illegal & for whom. trade in the east indies by any british entity other than the eic violated the royal charter issued by the british crown — that was british law. interlopers — non-eic british merchants who traded with india & thus violated this charter, leading to court cases back in britain. free merchants — non-eic british merchants stationed in india who agreed to sell indian goods to the eic in india itself rather than exporting independently, making their trade artificially legal in the eyes of the british law. dastak misuse by eic officials — violated not british law but indian law; specifically, customs duty evasion.

sections.title: Siraj-ud-daula (Siraj56-57; 1756-57) & the Road to Plassey (1757)
sections.norm: siraj-ud-daula (siraj56-57; 1756-57) & the road to plassey (1757). why did nawab alivardi khan40-56 tolerate eic’s provocations, & why did his successor siraj not? alivardi khan40-56 siraj56-57 jagat seth krishna ballabh added new fortifications to calcutta captured calcutta. black hole tragedy j.z. holwell 146 were locked in & 123 died of suffocation 30–40 note khan adyar siraj curzon. why did nawab alivardi khan40-56 tolerate eic’s provocations, & why did his successor siraj not? afraid of french, the eic began adding fortifications in calcutta i.e. strengthening fort william (*thickening walls, filling gaps, raising the height) from 1755 without permission of alivardi khan1740-56. a fort is a military structure. building or expanding one on another sovereign’s territory without permission is a challenge to that sovereign’s authority. however, alivardi khan40-56 was pragmatic and followed path of diplomacy rather than military confrontation since eic’s trade was economically beneficial to bengal (*he must have also noticed battle of adyar1746 which proved military capabilities of european infantry). siraj56-57 was the precious grandson of alivardi khan40-56 through his daughter, as he had no sons & siraj56-57 was the only grandson. siraj56-57 was disliked in the bengal court. he had disrespected senior mansabdars & had at one point imprisoned jagat seth — the powerful banker — for extortion. he was young, impulsive, surrounded by enemies. when he came to power, he stopped all dastak misuse, hurting the private trade fortunes of eic officials. when the british gave asylum to krishna ballabh (for money) — a fugitive from siraj56-57’s court, charged with fraud — & then added new fortifications to calcutta. siraj56-57 first seized the eic factory at kasimbazar & then captured calcutta. during the capture of calcutta occurred the black hole tragedy: british prisoners were locked overnight in a small, airless guardroom in fort william. the colonial account — written by j.z. holwell, a survivor & briefly governor of bengal — claimed that 146 were locked in & 123 died of suffocation. modern historians suggest the actual number of dead was approximately 30–40. the incident became a powerful propaganda tool to justify the eic’s military response against siraj56-57 & to demonise indian rulers in the british public imagination. (*note: holwell built a monument in 1760 in memory of black hole tragedy. it fell into ruin & was demolished in 1821. viceroy curzon99-05 (1899-1905) built a marble replica in 1901 at the same spot. in 1940, netaji bose led a big agitation to remove it — calling it colonial propaganda to tarnish siraj56-57’s image — & used the campaign to build hindu-muslim unity. the monument was not demolished but shifted from the public square to the graveyard of st. john’s church, calcutta, where it stands today.)

sections.chapterTitle: Battle of Plassey 1757 & Battle of Buxar 1764
sections.title: Robert Clive, the Conspiracy & the Battle
sections.norm: robert clive, the conspiracy & the battle. was the battle of plassey (23rd june 1757) really a battle ? robert clive treaty of alinagar chandarnagar seven years’ global war (1756–63) what happened next was not war — it was conspiracy. battle of plassey (1757) mir jafar57-60 takeaway: buxar (1764, sec. 7) siraj jafar. was the battle of plassey (23rd june 1757) really a battle ? robert clive, arrived from madras with royal military forces, & recaptured calcutta. the treaty of alinagar (the name siraj56-57 had given to calcutta) restored all eic privileges. clive destroyed hugli port — being used by the french — & defeated the french at chandarnagar, since the anglo-french conflict was live as part of the seven years’ global war (1756–63). the french threat in bengal was neutralised. what happened next was not war — it was conspiracy. mir jafar was the commander of bengal’s army (*that’s what the books say but technically subahdar was commander of army. jafar was bakshi/bakhshi at province level i.e. war paymaster & head of military intelligence. since siraj56-57 was young & inexperienced, in practice jafar was the real commander). he approached clive and made a deal with eic to remove siraj56-57. at the battle of plassey (1757), mir jafar ensured that the bulk of the bengal army did not fight & turned back. siraj56-57 was easily defeated and he fled away— was later captured & beheaded on mir jafar’s son miran’s orders. mir jafar57-60 (was again subahdar from 1763–65) became subahdar but he was now eic’s puppet as eic did not withdraw from the military domination established after defeat of siraj56-57. political supremacy of the eic in india had begun. ◆ takeaway: plassey was no real battle. the eic’s victory in bengal came from court conspiracy. the first real military victory for eic comes seven years later at buxar (1764, sec. 7).

sections.chapterTitle: Battle of Plassey 1757 & Battle of Buxar 1764
sections.title: The Plassey Plunder (1757–65)
sections.norm: the plassey plunder (1757–65). what did the eic extract from bengal after plassey? behaving as a state immediate financial settlement after plassey 2,75,000 pounds royal british military 2,34,000 pounds 35,000 pounds per annum rs 2.25 crore 1757 & 1765 2.5 million pounds note 250 £70 million 3.5% of gdp. in 2026, the multiplier: x32,000) beyond the cash: how did plassey change bengal’s economy & polity, eic’s trade structure & eic army? misuse of dastaks gomastas drain of wealth own large standing army. robert clive laid foundation of real military strength of eic and of empire building by eic. mir qasim60-63 eic was the real political power in bengal after 1757. jafar qasim. what did the eic extract from bengal after plassey? remember that companies are organizations with profit motive and eic was a company even if it had started behaving as a state. the immediate financial settlement after plassey was staggering: 2,75,000 pounds to the royal british military for distribution to soldiers (*not eic army which was different). 2,34,000 pounds to clive personally, plus a personal jagir of 35,000 pounds per annum. rs 2.25 crore to the eic. between 1757 & 1765, a further 2.5 million pounds were extracted by the eic as political gifts from bengal. (*note: to understand the scale, multiply by 250 for inflation alone as per retail price index. alternatively, in 1760, gdp of britain was £70 million. £2.5 million is 3.5% of gdp. in 2026, uk gdp = £2.27 trillion. 3.5% of that equals £80 billion or 108.5 billion usd. the multiplier: approximately x32,000) beyond the cash: how did plassey change bengal’s economy & polity, eic’s trade structure & eic army? after plassey, there was rampant misuse of dastaks, & eic officials made large fortunes not just from private international trade but also from private domestic trade — now conducted through indian agents called gomastas who procured goods directly from peasants & artisans, cutting out indian merchants/traders. they also did not pay domestic taxes on this trade, hurting indian merchants competing against them further. the structure of the eic’s international trade also changed fundamentally. before plassey, gold had to be shipped from britain to buy indian goods. after plassey, bengal’s own diwani revenues funded the purchase of not just indian but also chinese goods — tea, silk, porcelain. further, gold from bengal treasury was also shipped to britain. thus, from gold inflow before 1757, now gold outflow from india. hence began the drain of wealth. the eic also used the plassey plunder to build its own large standing army. for a trading company, maintaining a large army made no economic sense (it hurt dividends to shareholders), but now it could be funded from bengal’s extracted wealth rather than from company profits. thus, robert clive laid foundation of real military strength of eic and of empire building by eic. when mir jafar57-60 could no longer meet the eic’s growing financial demands, the eic replaced him with his son-in-law, mir qasim60-63 — an efficient administrator. hence, eic was the real political power in bengal after 1757.

sections.chapterTitle: Battle of Plassey 1757 & Battle of Buxar 1764
sections.title: Battle of Buxar (1764): EIC Gets the Right to Rule
sections.norm: battle of buxar (1764): eic gets the right to rule. why did mir qasim60-63 rebel ? murshidabad to bihar punished zamindars who underreported abolished all internal duties level-playing field between indian merchants and eic officials shuja-ud-daula54-75 of awadh shah alam ii60-06 3 crore rupees, the territory of bihar & its treasury note imad-ul-mulk gaddar-ul-mulk ahmad shah bahadur in 1754 alamgir ii in 1759 battle of buxar (1764) hector munroe qasim60-63 escaped & died shuja54-75 was surprised to find himself not beheaded shah alam ii60-06 was treated with respect shah alam ii qasim daula shuja. why did mir qasim60-63 rebel ? qasim60-63 was an able man & he had no intention of remaining a puppet. to escape the eic’s constant supervision, he shifted his base from the capital murshidabad to bihar, where he could gather resources & build an army quietly. to gather money for army, he punished zamindars who underreported their land revenue, & for support of indian merchants he abolished all internal duties (*like gst today) on domestic trade to bring a level-playing field between indian merchants and eic officials doing untaxed domestic trade via their gomastas since 1757. this autonomous behaviour was intolerable to the eic. a battle was fought in bihar; qasim60-63 was defeated and eic brought back mir jafar as puppet nawab of bengal (1763-65). qasim60-63 escaped westward to awadh & forged an alliance with shuja-ud-daula54-75 of awadh & emperor shah alam ii60-06. shuja54-75 agreed on the promise of 3 crore rupees, the territory of bihar & its treasury — after victory. [note: shah alam ii60-06 had left delhi, frustrated with court factionalism & fearing for his life after the murders & brutalities inflicted on his predecessors by wazir imad-ul-mulk (also known as gaddar-ul-mulk). imad-ul-mulk had blinded emperor ahmad shah bahadur in 1754 & murdered emperor alamgir ii in 1759 — two successive mughal emperors destroyed by their own wazir. hence shah alam ii60-06 left delhi to establish his own kingdom in bengal (which had stopped paying tribute since 1751). he attacked bengal in 1761 but was defeated by eic. eic still respected him since he was emperor of hindustan. since then he was in awadh and had chosen shuja54-75 as his wazir.] battle of buxar (1764) was fought in bihar. all preparations had been made for a defensive strategy — laying siege to the fort where the eic army was stationed. but shuja54-75 lost patience. against the explicit advice of qasim60-63, he switched to an offensive strategy & ordered a direct attack on the fort — handing the advantage to the eic. the battle was closely fought & at one point the indian side appeared to be winning. then eic commander hector munroe launched a final charge & turned the tables. (*note: clive was in london at the time) qasim60-63 escaped & died somewhere later. shuja54-75 was surprised to find himself not beheaded. shah alam ii60-06 was treated with respect as in him resided the symbolic sovereignty of the mughal state. with him as an ally, the foreigner eic’s legal right as a political power in india would be stronger.

sections.title: Treaty of Allahabad (*ToA1765):
sections.norm: treaty of allahabad (*toa1765):. why is the treaty of allahabad of 1765 (*toa1765) so important — what exactly did it decide? treaty of allahabad (*toa 1765) toa1765 —can be understood by breaking it into three components: @ emperor, @ bengal, @ awadh. annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees militarily help him recapture delhi allahabad & kora mansabdar watan jagir diwani diwani of bengal suba i.e. bengal, orissa & bihar nizamat dual government (1765–72) md reza khan why did eic not annex bengal outright? companies work for profit, not for ruling chose not to 8.2.2 policy of indirect rule king or nawab british resident the resident all three were now in place appoint the deputy nawab by 1772, direct rule the reason was the great bengal famine of 1770 (gbf 1770) 50 lakh rupees benaras kora and allahabad duty-free trade policy of ring fence warren hastings73-85 mini subsidiary alliance subsidiary alliance wellesley98-05 note 1801 when any source says awadh was 1st to sign subsidiary alliance, its false as it was hyderabad in 1798. takeaway: policy of indirect rule, the policy of ring fence & the mini subsidiary alliance treaty of allahabad 1765 buxar shah alam ii shuja hastings warren hastings wellesley. why is the treaty of allahabad of 1765 (*toa1765) so important — what exactly did it decide? clive was sent back to india from london after the buxar victory to negotiate the settlement. the treaty of allahabad (*toa 1765) was signed by clive on behalf of the eic, & by shah alam ii60-06 & shuja54-75 on the indian side. it is one of the most consequential treaties in indian history, because it laid the legal & structural foundation of british empire/company state in india. (*note: clive did insider trading on eic shares. he asked his broker in london to buy eic shares before the terms of the toa1765 became public. this made clive one of the wealthiest men in europe.) toa1765 —can be understood by breaking it into three components: @ emperor, @ bengal, @ awadh. 8.1 — @ the emperor [ ▲ index ] the eic promised to pay shah alam ii60-06 an annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees, promised to militarily help him recapture delhi from the rohilla afghans (who had held it since 1761), & gave him allahabad & kora (taken from awadh) so emperor maintains his status. this was deliberate & clever. the eic was absorbing itself into the existing legal-political structure of the mughal state — positioning itself as a mansabdar (who maintains an army for the emperor & pays tribute) and bengal became, in legal terms, the eic’s watan jagir. (*recall this is exactly how rebel states got absorbed in the mughal empire instead of declaring independence) in practice, the eic paid neither the rs 26 lakh nor did it supply an army to recapture delhi. it was all legal formality. 8.2 — @ bengal: [ ▲ index ] 8.2.1 dual government (1765-72) diwani meant revenue administration, control of the revenue/treasury & civil administration & civil justice. the eic received the diwani of bengal suba i.e. bengal, orissa & bihar. this was the first time the eic formally received a sovereign function — e.g. the power to tax. before buxar, the eic had only trade income (since 31st december 1600). from 1765, it had two incomes: trade income & tax revenue from the richest province of india. the nizamat remained with the nawab legally (law & order, criminal justice; military- in practice was with eic). this arrangement was the dual government (1765–72). legally, the diwani was with the eic & the nizamat was with the nawab. in practice, the eic appointed a deputy nawab (naib nazim) — md reza khan — as its diwan. indian civil servants continued to run the administration, reporting to the eic on diwani matters & to the nawab on nizamat matters. the dual government meant, in effect, that sovereign functions had been split into two & two separate top authorities installed over each. why did eic not annex bengal outright? the eic was a company — & companies work for profit, not for ruling. when the opportunity existed to annex bengal outright, it chose not to, because annexation would bring administrative costs & responsibilities. military domination after plassey1757 meant the company was not threatened militarily. and after buxar1764 it only secured legal right over the finances of bengal— so now drain of bengal’s wealth was not illegal plunder but a legal right of eic. 8.2.2 policy of indirect rule —was now formally installed in bengal’s nizamat. the three elements of indirect rule are: king or nawab is a puppet. british resident is stationed in court. the resident controls the puppet & thus governs indirectly. all three were now in place. the eic also obtained the legal right to appoint the deputy nawab — meaning if the deputy subahdar refused to follow informal eic instructions in nizamat matters, then he could be removed by eic. by 1772, the british resident established complete indirect control over the nizamat. in that same year, the dual government was formally ended as nizamat taken over legally from nawab & replaced indian administrators with its own officers — establishing direct rule. thus the company state was properly established in bengal. the reason was the great bengal famine of 1770 (gbf 1770). the famine killed one crore people or an estimated one-third of bengal’s population. high land revenue demand and harsh tax collection methods continued even as crops failed & people starved. grain hoarding by speculators went unchecked because neither the eic nor the nawab took responsibility for famine relief — the eic claimed the famine relief was the nawab’s domain, & the nawab lacked the resources for it. due to famine, the land revenue collection and law & order collapsed forcing eic to establish its own direct rule. (*note: from 1772, the nawab of bengal became as powerless a figurehead as the chhatrapati of the marathas had become after treaty of sangola 1750.) 8.3 — @ awadh: [ ▲ index ] shuja54-75 was made to pay 50 lakh rupees to the eic as compensation. benaras was separated from awadh (the eic formally annexed it in 1775). kora and allahabad to emperor. the eic was granted duty-free trade in awadh — & dastak misuse began there too. the policy of ring fence was initiated with awadh. (*note: this policy is mainly associated with warren hastings73-85, but clive planted its seed here.) it meant creating a military buffer around the eic’s core territory by signing military alliances with neighbouring states. under this military alliance with awadh, if anyone attacked the eic in bengal, awadh was treaty-bound to help. (*think of it like the us using nato during cold war — a buffer of allied western europe protected the core i.e. usa from ussr.) a mini subsidiary alliance was signed: awadh was forced to partially outsource a core sovereign function — its own military— to the eic as size of awadh army was reduced and an eic army was permanently stationed in awadh & paid for by awadh via annual subsidy (*eic-“haha thank u dupleix4254 for 1751 idea@hyd”). thus eic now partially controlled military resources of awadh and combined with the military alliance it meant that these resources can be used directly by eic itself (under its command) for protecting bengal. the clauses relating to awadh are a prelude to the full subsidiary alliance that wellesley98-05 would formalise three decades later. [note: a formal & proper subsidiary alliance was signed with awadh in 1801, when awadh’s own army was disbanded & its foreign policy was also taken over by the eic — but the architecture was drawn here in 1765. when any source says awadh was 1st to sign subsidiary alliance, its false as it was hyderabad in 1798.] ◆ takeaway: clive was the father of the strategic policy toolkit that the eic used for empire building. the policy of indirect rule, the policy of ring fence & the mini subsidiary alliance — all were either invented or operationalised by clive in this single treaty. thus, foundations of empire was laid by clive in toa1765 and men like wellesley98-05 later built upon it.

sections.title: Chronology Box: 18th-Century Battles
sections.norm: chronology box: 18th-century battles. four empire-shaping battles alert: prelims 2005 — chronological order. ambur (1749) → plassey (1757) → wandiwash (1760) → buxar (1764). shah alam ii dupleix jafar qasim daula. the four empire-shaping battles fought in 18th-century india: # year battle combatants & outcome 1 1749 ambur dupleix42-54 (french) defeats anwaruddin; opens 2nd carnatic war. 2 1757 plassey eic (clive) + mir jafar57-60 conspiracy defeats siraj56-5756-57. 3 1760 wandiwash eic (eyre coote) crushes french (lally); ends 3rd carnatic war. 4 1764 buxar eic (hector munroe) defeats mir qasim60-63 + shuja-ud-daula54-75 + shah alam ii60-06. ⚠ alert: prelims 2005 — chronological order. ambur (1749) → plassey (1757) → wandiwash (1760) → buxar (1764). two french battles frame two english ones — french high at ambur, french out at wandiwash; eic political breakthrough at plassey, eic sovereign breakthrough at buxar.

sections.title: Who Were the Wellesleys?
sections.norm: who were the wellesleys?. richard wellesley98-05 wellesley98-05 fort william college 1800 henry wellesley arthur british royal army from 3rd carnatic war 1756-63 till 1858 two separate european military forces operated in india company’s army king’s army (royal military) legally & institutionally distinct 4th anglo-mysore war (1798–99) siege of seringapatam (1799) 2nd anglo-maratha war (1803–05) battle of assaye (1803) 1808 & 1815 wellesley. richard wellesley98-05 served as governor general of bengal from 1798-1805 & was joined in india by both his brothers- arthur and henry wellesley. wellesley98-05 was an empire builder. he understood that expanding the empire raised his profile among a nationalistic british public — useful for political ambitions back home. he established fort william college in calcutta in 1800 — to train british civil servants in indian languages, laws & customs before posting them to the districts. (⚠ alert: fort william college has been tested in upsc prelims three times — prelims 2018 on the institution-founder pair (alongside sanskrit college banaras & calcutta madarsa), and prelims 2020 + 2021 on the purpose of establishment.) henry wellesley handled administration & diplomacy of eic. arthur wellesley was a military commander — but arthur wellesley was not an eic officer. he was a commissioned officer in the british royal army, commanding the 33rd regiment of foot i.e. infantry. from 3rd carnatic war 1756-63 till 1858, two separate european military forces operated in india side by side: company’s army — eic’s own private military paid for by the eic [majorly indian sepoys but also had european sepoys + senior officers always european i.e. british] king’s army (royal military) — official british state’s regiments sent to india to support the eic. the eic had to reimburse the british state for the cost of royal troops deployed in india. both forces fought together — but they were legally & institutionally distinct. (note: the company state in india received direct military support from the british crown — hence the british state cannot escape responsibility for empire building in india.) arthur wellesley led his royal regiment alongside eic forces in the 4th anglo-mysore war (1798–99), including the siege of seringapatam (1799), & in the 2nd anglo-maratha war (1803–05), including the battle of assaye (1803). he also fought napoleon’s army between 1808 & 1815. [note: arthur wellesley on record stated that the marathas were the most formidable enemy he ever faced — & that the battle of assaye (1803) against them was the toughest fight of his entire military career. the marathas were harder to defeat militarily. had india not been a spectre of fragmented polity i.e. had there been one state ruling whole india then india wont have been colonised.]

sections.title: Pitt’s India Act 1784 Banned Conquest — How Wellesley98-05 re-initiated Conquest?
sections.norm: pitt’s india act 1784 banned conquest — how wellesley98-05 re-initiated conquest?. pitt’s india act of 1784 follow diplomacy rather than war napoleon–tipu82-99 alliance 1798 protecting india from european rivals primary goal of british foreign policy subsidiary alliance wellesley tipu hastings warren hastings. pitt’s india act of 1784 had banned conquest. the governor-general (gg) could not start an offensive war without the express command & authority of either the court of directors of the eic or of the board of control of the british state (*discussed in later chapter)— though gg had the right to enter war on grounds of defence. the reason was high war expenditure. the three carnatic wars (1746–63), battle of buxar (1764), two anglo-mysore wars (1767–69 & 1780–84), & the 1st anglo-maratha war (1775–82) had drained company finances. hence parliament mandated the eic to follow diplomacy rather than war (*recall pacifist policy of mughal after 1707- it was also for same reason) in form of policy of indirect rule & maintaining a balance of power among indian states instead of pursuing direct conquest. (note: wellesley98-05 could not legally start an offensive war without prior authorisation.) wellesley98-05 re-initiated conquest by overhyping the threat of a napoleon–tipu82-99 alliance. napoleon had attacked egypt in 1798 with the goal of controlling the middle east & hurting british trade, & he was in communication with tipu82-99 of mysore. a threat existed — but not a real one. britain’s navy was superior to france’s, & a french fleet heading for india through the arabian sea would have been destroyed before arriving. (note: the british had already burnt french ships in the mediterranean once napoleon landed in egypt, leaving his army stranded with no way home. ⚠ alert: prelims 2018 + 2021 — option (b) was true statement "napoleonic danger was a feature of sa". danger was not real i.e. less chance of napoleon attack on india but danger was there i.e. chance was there.) but the british state agreed anyway, because protecting india from european rivals was the primary goal of british foreign policy & it did not want to take any risks. wellesley98-05 also offered a middle path: the subsidiary alliance — political domination without the cost, administrative burden & symbolism of full annexation. [⚠ alert: prelims 1999 — q) "at a time when empires in europe were crumbling before the might of napoleon, which one of the following governors general kept the british flag flying high in india?" options: (a) warren hastings · (b) lord cornwallis · (c) lord wellesley ✓ · (d) lord hastings. two different governors general share the surname hastings — easy to confuse: warren hastings73-85 — pre-napoleon era. wrong. francis hastings13-23 (also called lord hastings) — post-napoleon era. wrong. the correct answer is (c) lord wellesley — i.e. wellesley98-05. his tenure (1798–1805) overlaps with napoleon's offensive phase (1796–1812). students sometimes pick (d) lord hastings because the name sounds napoleon-era — it is not. ]

sections.title: Two Roots of the SA: Dupleix42-54 + ToA1765
sections.norm: two roots of the sa: dupleix42-54 + toa1765. policy of subsidiary alliance two roots — one french & one british dupleix42-54 hyderabad in 1751 salabat jung51-62 bussy foreign adviser at court establish indirect rule treaty of allahabad (1765) formalised the relationship in a written treaty disbanded its army not a wellesley98-05 invention pre-meditated formalised plan of action treaty of allahabad 1765 dupleix jung wellesley clive. policy of subsidiary alliance did not appear from nowhere. it has two roots — one french & one british. 3.1 — french root (dupleix42-54 at hyderabad, 1751) [ ▲ index ] as governor general of french establishments in india (gg of french eic), dupleix42-54 installed the first mini or proto-form of the subsidiary alliance at hyderabad in 1751. when salabat jung51-62 became nizam-of-hyderabad with french backing, a french force under the bussy was permanently stationed, paid out in form of northern sarkars revenues (& control). dupleix42-54 had discovered the template: an external army at the indian state’s cost, with a foreign adviser at court who would not just advise but establish indirect rule. 3.2 — british root (clive’s toa1765 + wellesley98-05’s formalisation) [ ▲ index ] the mini subsidiary alliance that robert clive57-67 had planted at awadh via the treaty of allahabad (1765) — eic army in awadh paid by subsidy from awadh, reducing size of nawab’s controlled army and stationing of a british resident— was the british version, very close to the french template dupleix42-54 had pioneered. wellesley98-05 took the next step. he formalised the relationship in a written treaty, took over the indian state’s foreign policy explicitly, & disbanded its army. the subsidiary alliance was not a wellesley98-05 invention but policy of subsidiary alliance was initiated by him as policy means pre-meditated formalised plan of action with pre-decided intent which is reflected in form of series of events executed in line with that policy. wellesley formalised the sa into a policy, added takeover of foreign policy, disbanding of indian state’s army, & implemented this policy state by state across india.

sections.title: Model Treaty of Subsidiary Alliance + Legal Logic
sections.norm: model treaty of subsidiary alliance + legal logic. standard terms two groups british resident puppet poir military alliance army was disbanded eic-maintained army annual subsidy took over the indian state’s foreign policy eic protection against neighbours & domestic threats non-interference in internal affairs legal logic demanded foreign policy subsidy money taking foreign policy decision of war & peace loss of foreign policy. the standard terms of any subsidiary alliance fell into two groups, though actual terms varied a little from state to state depending on context. 4.1 — what the eic got [ ▲ index ] a british resident stationed permanently in the indian ruler’s court, with the ruler as a puppet (elements 1 & 2 of poir — but not yet element 3 i.e. british promised non-interference in internal affairs by british resident; though this promise was seldom kept & british breached the treaty in many cases). a formal military alliance between eic & the indian state. the indian state’s own army was disbanded & replaced by an eic-maintained army permanently stationed in the state. the indian state paid an annual subsidy to fund this eic army. so technically this army is owned by indian state. eic only maintains it but due to the 5th point, this ownership of indian state was lost. the eic took over the indian state’s foreign policy — decisions on war & peace, diplomacy, defence budget, & foreign trade. the gg’s consent was needed before any european could be stationed at the court, & the indian ruler had to consult him before negotiating with any other indian state or foreign power. the subsidy i.e. defence budget of indian state was decided by eic. (note: the annual subsidy money was not surplus income that could be used for anything by the eic — subsidy was to be spent only for maintaining the army.) 4.2 — what the indian ruler got [ ▲ index ] eic protection against neighbours & domestic threats. a formal promise of non-interference in internal affairs — succession, diwani, nizamat (minus military). 4.3 — why the eic took foreign policy: the legal logic [ ▲ index ] there is a legal logic to why the eic specifically demanded foreign policy. the eic maintained the army using the indian state’s own subsidy money. one could therefore argue that legal ownership & the right to deploy that army still belonged to the indian ruler. the eic closed this loophole by taking foreign policy — the decision of war & peace, & therefore the right to deploy the army, now legally rested with the eic. (note: hence the toa176 with awadh was a mini subsidiary alliance — as awadh’s own army was not disbanded & foreign policy was not taken over. the proper sa came only in 1801.) in short: posa = poir (informally) + porf + eic military replacing indian state’s military + annual subsidy + loss of foreign policy. 4.4 — ⚠ alert: prelims 2018 & prelims 2021 — upsc asked the same question in both years. [ ▲ index ] q) which statement does not apply to the subsidiary alliance? the four options tested features of sa. the false option was (c) "secure a fixed income for the company". sa's annual subsidy was earmarked for maintaining the eic army stationed in the host state — it was not surplus income for the eic. the other three options were true— maintain large standing army, defend against napoleonic danger, establish british paramountcy.

sections.title: Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States
sections.norm: vicious-chain consequences of subsidiary alliance for indian states. disbanded armies → mass unemployment. eic’s compounded military power at the host state’s expense. subsidy drain of wealth. tax hikes → unrest. maladministration accusations → annexation grounds. british resident wajid ali shah 1856 territory in lieu of cash. half of awadh hyderabad berar permanent loss of alliance-forming capacity. divide & rule takeaway every single sa signatory dupleix. disbanded armies → mass unemployment. disbanding indian state armies caused mass unemployment for military men — mansabdars lost their positions, sepoys lost their livelihoods. (note: the eic also recruited sepoys from outside the host state to reduce any chance of loyalty to the nawab in case he revolted — a classic divide & rule strategy.) eic’s compounded military power at the host state’s expense. since the eic maintained & commanded army in the indian state, operational control was entirely with the eic. also since it had taken over foreign policy, it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere. hence, the eic could now maintain a large army at the expense of indian states. (note: eic armies = army of the indian state maintained by eic using the indian state’s subsidy + eic’s own army maintained from its own money. both were available to the eic for its own wars.) subsidy payments were high to begin with & the eic gradually increased its demands. the same money could have been used by the indian ruler for his own state’s development. instead there was drain of wealth. tax hikes → unrest. to pay the ever-rising subsidy, indian rulers had to raise taxes. high taxes made rulers unpopular, fuelled peasant resentment, & created conditions for unrest. maladministration accusations → annexation grounds. the eic then accused indian rulers of maladministration. in reality the ruler had no real power left — the british resident had in many cases established indirect rule illegally, in direct breach of the treaty’s own promise of non-interference. the ruler had no power, but all the responsibility. the most stark example was nawab wajid ali shah of awadh — accused of maladministration, his state annexed in 1856. territory in lieu of cash. when subsidy could not be paid in cash, the eic simply took territory as payment. in 1801, half of awadh was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. in 1853, hyderabad was made to give berar. (*eic can say- “thanks dupleix42-54” — he gave this idea when he took northen sarkars from hyderabad in 1751.) permanent loss of alliance-forming capacity. by losing foreign policy & military control, indian states permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the eic. hence subsidiary alliance was, in effect, a sophisticated divide & rule instrument at the level of an entire subcontinent. ◆ takeaway eic via sa got all military and diplomatic powers with no responsibility of ruling and no burden of finances. the seven vicious-chain links explain why every single sa signatory ended up either annexed or permanently dependent.

sections.title: Which States Signed and Under What Circumstances
sections.norm: which states signed and under what circumstances. not forced on every signatory at sword-point indian ruler walked in willingly five arguments protection against internal revolts protection against external threats better than annexation preservation of royal dignity for winning succession disputes and for protection from neighbours- 1798 — hyderabad: 1799 — mysore (wodeyar dynasty): 4th anglo-mysore war (1798–99) battle of seringapatam (1799) 1801 — awadh: sadat ali khan ii rs 76 lakh wazir ali (1797-98) henry wellesley doab, gorakhpur & rohilkhand ceded districts the north-west provinces (nwp1836) june 1802 — gaikwad of baroda (treaty of cambay): december 1802 — peshwa bajirao ii96-18 (treaty of bassein/vasai): yashwantrao holkar treaty of bassein(1802) treaty of bassein (1739) 1803 — scindia of gwalior: 1803-05: jats, rajputs, bundelas 1805 — travancore: nair troops 1816 — bhonsle of nagpur (treaty of nagpur): 1816 appa sahib 1818 — holkar of indore (treaty of mandsaur): 3rd anglo-maratha war (1817–19) takeaway: 1798 → 1818 north-western provinces 1836 treaty of allahabad 1765 peshwa bajirao ii bajirao ii tipu shore wellesley hastings. 6.1 —why some rulers walked in willingly [ ▲ index ] the sa was not forced on every signatory at sword-point. in several cases the indian ruler walked in willingly, persuaded by five arguments: protection against internal revolts — a guaranteed eic army inside the palace walls was attractive insurance against rival claimants or mutinous nobles. protection against external threats — small states feared maratha chauth raids, mysorean expansion, or rohilla incursions far more than the distant british. better than annexation — the subsidy was, on paper, cheaper than annexation or a losing war against the eic. preservation of royal dignity — the ruler’s title, court & ceremonial status were formally preserved. the flag of sovereignty flew, even after its substance had been handed over. for winning succession disputes and for protection from neighbours- in many cases, rulers sought eic help for help in succession disputes and protection from other indian states. eic used this as an opportunity by making military help conditional upon indian ruler signing sa. 6.2 — the nine signatories (1798–1818) [ ▲ index ] 1798 — hyderabad: the nizam signed first to get eic protection against marathas & mysore. 1799 — mysore (wodeyar dynasty): forced to sign after defeat in the 4th anglo-mysore war (1798–99). tipu82-99 was killed at the battle of seringapatam (1799); the wodeyars were restored as a subsidiary throne. 1801 — awadh: in 1798, sadat ali khan ii had offered the eic rs 76 lakh as annual subsidy in exchange for john shore93-98 removing his nephew wazir ali (1797-98) from the nawabship. shore93-98 obliged. by 1801, sadat ali khan ii defaulted; wellesley98-05 sent his brother henry wellesley to impose a full subsidiary alliance. half of awadh — the doab, gorakhpur & rohilkhand — was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. (note: this was unfair — the revenue from this territory was twice the rs 76 lakh annual subsidy it was meant to cover. these territories became the ceded districts, & in 1836 were given full province status as the north-west provinces (nwp1836) of british india.) (*recall – most of rohilkhand was annexed by awadh with eic help in 1774. eic had helped due to toa1765 military alliance. rest small part of rohilkhand became the autonomous state of rampur but under awadh legally and from 1801 under eic legally. ) june 1802 — gaikwad of baroda (treaty of cambay): signed in exchange for eic help in a gaikwad succession dispute. december 1802 — peshwa bajirao ii96-18 (treaty of bassein/vasai): bajirao ii96-18 had been defeated by yashwantrao holkar (avenging his brother’s death). he fled, & signed the treaty of bassein(1802) to regain the peshwaship with eic support. (note: scindia & bhonsle read this as a peshwa selling the confederacy to the british — & the 2nd anglo-maratha war (1803–05) followed. the full treatment of bassein 1802 + the war that followed is in the anglo-maratha wars chapter + recall: marathas captured bassein from portuguese via the treaty of bassein (1739). brought it under peshwa control along with salsette). 1803 — scindia of gwalior: forced to sign during the 2nd anglo-maratha war (1803-05). 1803-05: during the war, the eic forced the jats, rajputs, bundelas to sign subsidiary alliances. they had earlier paid chauth & sardeshmukhi to the marathas; now they paid subsidy to the new regional power eic. 1805 — travancore: signed in exchange for eic help in crushing a mutiny by nair troops who had revolted due to non-payment of salary. the last sa signed under wellesley98-05 before his recall. 1816 — bhonsle of nagpur (treaty of nagpur): after defeat in the 2nd anglo-maratha war (1803-05), the bhonsles had resisted signing a full subsidiary alliance for over a decade. in 1816, appa sahib finally signed — using eic backing to win factionalism fight over who would be regent of bhonsle of nagpur. (note: the story belongs to the anglo-maratha wars chapter.) 1818 — holkar of indore (treaty of mandsaur): forced to sign after decisive defeat in the 3rd anglo-maratha war (1817–19). ◆ takeaway: the 9-sa in 20 years 1798 → 1818. the first seven were signed under wellesley98-05; the last two under francis hastings13-23.

sections.title: Direct Annexations + Wellesley98-05’s Recall
sections.norm: direct annexations + wellesley98-05’s recall. what territory did wellesley98-05 directly annex — & why was he eventually recalled? directly annexed territory 1799 — mysore territory. 4th anglo-mysore war 1799 early 1801 — half of awadh (ceded districts). nwp1836 1801 — carnatic. md ali52-95 (1752–1795) 2nd carnatic war 1749-54 1803–05 — 2nd anglo-maratha war. bhonsle of nagpur orissa scindia in gujarat all territory north of the river yamuna delhi recalled to london due to high war expenditure north-western provinces 1836 wellesley ali. what territory did wellesley98-05 directly annex — & why was he eventually recalled? beyond subsidiary alliances, wellesley98-05 also directly annexed territory: 1799 — mysore territory. significant territory taken from mysore after the 4th anglo-mysore war 1799. early 1801 — half of awadh (ceded districts). annexed as permanent subsidy payment (the nwp1836 territories — covered in sec. 6). 1801 — carnatic. annexed on grounds of maladministration, six years after the death of md ali52-95 (1752–1795), who had been the eic’s loyal ally since the 2nd carnatic war 1749-54. 1803–05 — 2nd anglo-maratha war. bhonsle of nagpur lost significant territory including orissa (which bhonsle had himself taken from bengal in 1751). scindia lost territory in gujarat & all territory north of the river yamuna — including delhi. wellesley98-05 was eventually recalled to london due to high war expenditure. empire building was profitable only if wars were short & cheap. his were neither.

sections.title: Why Was Mysore Such a Serious Threat?
sections.norm: why was mysore such a serious threat?. hyder ali61-82 tipu sultan82-99 two aspects of mysore's state policy threatening to the eic military fiscalism modern military & a navy state-owned trading company 1780s trade embargo pepper, cardamom & sandalwood malabar mauludi calendar delegations to france, turkey (ottoman empire) & egypt takeaway: military fiscalism + mercantilism ali sultan tipu. mysore under hyder ali61-82 & then tipu sultan82-99 was not just another indian state trying to survive. it was actively trying to dominate — the trade, the coastline, & the politics of south india. this made it a threat not just to the eic but to every neighbouring power. two aspects of mysore's state policy made it particularly threatening to the eic specifically. 1.1 — military fiscalism mysore followed a policy of military fiscalism — the primary goal of maximising state revenue was to fund an ever-stronger military. (* eic also had followed same model since 1765, to build a strong military.) under hyder ali61-82 & tipu82-99, mysore built a centralised state with a modern military & a navy, with french assistance — france provided arms & technical support in exchange for trade concessions to counter eic trade. this french connection made both the eic & neighbouring indian states even more anxious. 1.2 — mercantilist trading state tipu82-99 set up a state-owned trading company that entered international trade directly. (mysore was acting like a rival mercantilist state — exactly as the eic did. two mercantilist powers competing over the same trade routes & the same coastal markets cannot coexist easily.) tipu82-99 took this further — in the late 1780s he put a trade embargo on exports of pepper, cardamom & sandalwood from ports under mysore's control, & barred local merchants from dealing with british traders entirely. malabar was a critical source of pepper for the eic & under mysore's control since 1766. tipu82-99 also brought in his own mauludi calendar — a new lunisolar calendar based on the prophet's birth era, introduced to replace the islamic hijri calendar. tipu82-99 also sent delegations to france, turkey (ottoman empire) & egypt to seek anti-british alliances. ◆ takeaway: the rivalry between eic & mysore was not simply a military conflict. it was a clash between two entities following the same model — military fiscalism + mercantilism — in the same geography. only one could win. the eic's diplomatic advantage was that mysore's ambitions also threatened every other neighbouring state, making it easier to build coalitions against mysore.

sections.title: 1st Anglo-Mysore War (1767–69): EIC lost?
sections.norm: 1st anglo-mysore war (1767–69): eic lost?. modern arsenal (arms factory) at dindigul fort. in 1766 malabar same year northern sarkars marathas also saw mysore as rival eic crafted a triple alliance hyder ali61-82 broke the coalition 1767 paid the marathas 35 lakh rupees alliance with hyderabad 20 lakh rupees carnatic gates of madras eic navy from bombay mangalore treaty of madras (1769) defensive military alliance ali. 2.1 — reason even before hyder ali61-82 came to power he had started modernizing his military with help of french (present in mahe) e.g. in 1755 he established a modern arsenal (arms factory) at dindigul fort. this continued friendship threatened eic. in 1766, hyder ali61-82 annexed malabar (important for spice trade) and the same year eic promised to help hyderabad invade mysore so eic gets northern sarkars (important to connect bengal with madras). marathas also saw mysore as rival so they also joined and thus eic crafted a triple alliance of eic, hyderabad & marathas to invade mysore (*yes triple alliance was formed twice-2nd time in 1790). (*recall 1766: hyderabad gave eic northern sarkars in return for protection against mysore & marathas). 2.2 — events during the war hyder ali61-82 broke the coalition through skilled diplomacy. in 1767 he paid the marathas 35 lakh rupees to exit the war, then made an alliance with hyderabad by giving nizam 20 lakh rupees, promise to make nizam’s son nawab of carnatic and agreement to jointly attack carnatic in future (it was under md ali52-95-ally of eic). by 1768, however, hyderabad feared a counter-invasion of hyderabad itself by eic & exited by making peace with the eic. by 1769, hyder ali61-82 had outmanoeuvred eic forces & marched his army to the gates of madras. eic navy from bombay captured coastal areas of mysore e.g. mangalore. 2.3 — result: treaty of madras (1769) the eic, fearing the destruction of madras, was forced to sign the treaty of madras (1769). both sides returned conquered territories & agreed to a defensive military alliance — promising to help each other if attacked by a third party. (this was a porf arrangement only on paper — but a fake alliance in practice, as the very next war revealed.)

sections.title: 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780–84): How EIC broke Mysore-Marathas-Hyderabad Alliance?
sections.norm: 2nd anglo-mysore war (1780–84): how eic broke mysore-marathas-hyderabad alliance?. american war of independence (1776–83) mahe port of french in malabar in 1779 carnatic arcot battle of pollilur iron-cased rockets alert: battle of pollilur (september 1780) triple confederacy 1780–82) i.e. an alliance of marathas-mysore-hyderabad was established by nana fadnis guntur northern sarkars 1766 warren hastings73-85 broke this coalition december 1782 treaty of mangalore (1784) ali hastings warren hastings tipu. 3.1 — reason for war when marathas attacked mysore in 1771, the eic refused to honour its 1769 treaty obligation to come to mysore's defence. separately, france entered the american war of independence (1776–83) against britain in 1778 and the eic seized mahe port of french in malabar in 1779 (under mysore's military protection & through which hyder ali61-82 was importing french arms & ammunition)— this was the final trigger. 3.2 — events during the war hyder ali61-82 invaded carnatic, an eic ally, & captured arcot. then, hyder ali61-82 inflicted one of the worst defeats ever suffered by a european army in india at the battle of pollilur (sep 1780)— colonel baillie's disciplined infantry formations were annihilated as hyder ali61-82's troops using iron-cased rockets to devastating effect. pollilur was a shock to the eic. ⚠ alert: battle of pollilur (september 1780) has been tested in upsc prelims (rocket-warfare innovation by mysore). a triple confederacy (1780–82) i.e. an alliance of marathas-mysore-hyderabad against the eic was established by nana fadnis — the de-facto ruler & most important minister in the peshwa's council. (nana fadnis/fadnavis was the 1st indian statesmen to understand that eic was not in india just for trade but had ambitions of empire building.) hyderabad joined as the eic had illegally occupied guntur (one of the 5 districts of northern sarkars which was not handed over in 1766), & had stopped paying the annual 7 lakh rs agreed for ceding the northern sarkars. warren hastings73-85 broke this coalition through careful diplomacy. he returned guntur to hyderabad, removing their grievance. he then signed the treaty of salbai (may 1782) with the marathas — which ended the 1st anglo-maratha war (1775–82). the indian coalition was successfully dismantled; the marathas and hyderabad withdrew their support, leaving mysore isolated to fight the eic alone. nana fadnis ensured marathas don’t send army in favour of british (*chanakya neeti- let both rivals destroy each other) hyder ali61-82 died of cancer in december 1782. tipu82-99 took over & continued the war. 3.3 — result: treaty of mangalore (1784) the war ended in a stalemate. the treaty of mangalore (1784) saw both sides return each other's territories. status quo was maintained.

sections.title: 3rd Anglo-Mysore War (1790–92): When Did the Tide Finally Turn?
sections.norm: 3rd anglo-mysore war (1790–92): when did the tide finally turn?. travancore cornwallis86-93 three-front campaign treaty of seringapatam / srirangapatnam (1792) half its kingdom malabar, dindigul & baramahal war fine of 3 crore rupees two of his own sons as hostages tipu cornwallis. 4.1 — reason tipu82-99 attacked travancore, a formal ally of the eic. this gave cornwallis86-93 the justification to declare war. the eic formed triple alliance with marathas & hyderabad in 1790 (*in 1782-84 marathas did not fight mysore). 4.2 — events during the war the combined forces of eic, marathas & hyderabad put mysore under severe military pressure from multiple directions. tipu82-99 fought hard but could not hold against a coordinated three-front campaign. 4.3 — result: treaty of seringapatam (1792) tipu82-99 lost heavily. under the treaty of seringapatam / srirangapatnam (1792), mysore lost half its kingdom — including the rich territories of malabar, dindigul & baramahal. tipu82-99 also had to pay a war fine of 3 crore rupees, & was forced to surrender two of his own sons as hostages to guarantee compliance with treaty terms.

sections.title: 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1799): How Did Mysore Finally Fall?
sections.norm: 4th anglo-mysore war (1799): how did mysore finally fall?. napoleon wellesley98-05 the eic and hyderabad fought mysore arthur wellesley siege of srirangapatnam kanara, coimbatore & others wodeyar dynasty five-year-old krishnaraja iii subsidiary alliance (1799) tipu wellesley. 5.1 — reason tipu82-99's ongoing negotiations with napoleon gave wellesley98-05 his political pretext in london. britain was already at war with france. wellesley98-05, an empire builder by nature, used tipu82-99's secret letters to the french as proof of a threat — & got british approval for war. 5.2 — events during the war the eic and hyderabad fought mysore (*hyderabad had to due to sa of 1798). peshwa baji rao ii 96-18 did not send army on advice of nana fadnis, despite eic requests. arthur wellesley — commanding his royal regiment alongside eic forces — was among the key military commanders in the siege of srirangapatnam. tipu82-99 died defending his capital. 5.3 — result the best parts of mysore's remaining territory — kanara, coimbatore & others — were divided between the eic & hyderabad. the remaining central core of mysore was given back to the old wodeyar dynasty, with five-year-old krishnaraja iii placed on the throne under a subsidiary alliance (1799). the last major military threat to the eic in the south was over. some territory was offered to peshwa with condition of signing sa but marathas refused on advice of nana fadnis.

sections.title: Why Did Mysore Lose?
sections.norm: why did mysore lose?. four structural reasons no stable alliance. french naval gap. military fiscalism over-extension. seringapatam cornwallis86-93 wellesley98-05 cornwallis wellesley. four structural reasons explain the eventual defeat: 1. no stable alliance. mysore's aggressive expansion & the eic's diplomacy — prevented it from building stable alliances. 2. french naval gap. mysore was strategically dependent on french arms & ammunition. france entered the american war of independence (1776–83) & later the revolutionary wars (1792-1804) — but its navy was no match for britain's. a french fleet capable of resupplying mysore at scale never reached the indian coast. 3. military fiscalism over-extension. mysore's revenue-maximisation strategy funded a strong army but war fines (3 crore rupees after the 3rd war) drained out the treasury mysore needed to maintain a long campaign. eic was relatively rich. 4. seringapatam open to siege. once a three-way coalition (eic + marathas + hyderabad) could surround mysore from multiple directions — as in 1789–92 & 1799 — seringapatam's geography became a vulnerability rather than a stronghold. cornwallis86-93 & wellesley98-05 both concluded that mysore was too strong & too ambitious for indirect rule to work — it had to be defeated militarily & then subordinated. mysore fought well & modernised seriously. it lost because it fought largely alone.

sections.title: Dhondia Wagh
sections.norm: dhondia wagh. dhondia wagh mysore–maratha borderlands 1799–1800 "king of two worlds" colonel arthur wellesley 1800 1801 tipu. after seringapatam (1799), a former prisoner of tipu82-99 named dhondia wagh escaped & raised a mounted force from demobilised mysore soldiers (*sa disbanded army), raiding the mysore–maratha borderlands in 1799–1800. he styled himself "king of two worlds" & threatened eic supply lines. colonel arthur wellesley was sent and dhondia was killed in action in 1800 — with which the eic was formally supreme in southern india by 1801.

sections.title: A Note on Tipu82-99's Religious Policy
sections.norm: a note on tipu82-99's religious policy. syncretic yet contradictory sringeri sharada math shankaracharya forced conversions of nairs & christians malabar region coorg secularism was not a value for tipu82-99 but a tactic note: tipu cornwallis. tipu82-99's religious approach was syncretic yet contradictory — often a source of confusion. 8.1 — patronage in the mysore heartland he patronised the sringeri sharada math, wrote letters to its shankaracharya seeking blessings, got yajnas conducted before wars & made generous grants to several hindu temples in mysore. 8.2 — coercion in conquered malabar & coorg he also carried out forced conversions of nairs & christians in the malabar region & destroyed churches & temples during his military campaigns there. also he did the same brutalities in 1785 in coorg against kodavas people (*mountain warriors; still don’t need license to keep certain arms; earlier rule of hindu nayakas) who were resisting occupation by mysore. [*location (north to south) : mysore-coorg (in western ghats)-malabar; coorg connected capital (seringapatam) to the wealthy coastal ports of malabar] thus, it can be concluded that secularism was not a value for tipu82-99 but a tactic for domestic stability of his kingdom, as values as per discipline of psychology are hardest to change in one’s personality. [note: king of coorg signed alliance with eic in 1790 & helped cornwallis86-93’s army navigate the mountains in 3rd anglo-mysore war 1790-92.]

sections.title: Carnatic Annexed (1801)
sections.norm: carnatic annexed (1801). 2nd carnatic war (1749–54) md ali wallajah (1752–95) 1795 carnatic debts wellesley98-05 two justifications maladministration tipu82-99 nawab so financially compromised not worth preserving even as a puppet ali wellesley tipu. eic had influence over carnatic indirectly since the 2nd carnatic war (1749–54), keeping their ally md ali wallajah (1752–95) on the throne. eic’s grip tightened over carnatic after establishing domination over south india’s trade after 3rd carnatic war (1756-63). six years after death of md ali52-95 in 1795, the eic annexed carnatic in 1801. 9.1 — the carnatic debts: even before formal annexation, much of carnatic's wealth had already been quietly extracted through a mechanism called the carnatic debts. successive nawabs had borrowed massive sums from private eic officials at high interest rates, using the jagirs of carnatic as collateral. eic officials collected land revenue from these fertile lands directly as payment of interest. 9.2 — carnatic treaty (1801): annexation under wellesley98-05 wellesley98-05 used two justifications: 1. maladministration by the nawab. 2. the accusation that the nawab had been secretly communicating with tipu82-99. wellesley98-05 took the view that a nawab so financially compromised was not worth preserving even as a puppet.

sections.title: Travancore: What Happens When the SA Breaks Its Own Promises?
sections.norm: travancore: what happens when the sa breaks its own promises?. marthanda varma29-58 battle of colachel (1741) rama varma58-98 1798 "treaty of perpetual friendship" 1795 1800, a british resident 1805 travancore signed proper subsidiary alliance nair troops takeaway: clearest worked example velu thampi dalawa revolt & kundara proclamation (1809) treaty of allahabad 1765 varma tipu cornwallis wellesley. 10.1 — travancore before the sa: from marthanda varma29-58 to rama varma58-98 travancore's modern state had been built in the 18th century by marthanda varma29-58, who decisively defeated the dutch at the battle of colachel (1741) & reorganised the kingdom into a centralised revenue-based state. his successor rama varma58-98 maintained the eic alliance as a hedge against mysore — relevant during tipu82-99's late-1780s expansion & embargo on travancore's pepper exports (sec. 1). (rama varma58-98's eic alliance was the trigger for tipu82-99's attack on travancore in 1789, which cornwallis86-93 used as the pretext for the 3rd anglo-mysore war — see sec. 4.) after rama varma58-98's death in 1798, the kingdom entered fiscal & political strain. 10.2 — british resident stationed (1800), subsidiary alliance signed (1805) travancore signed a "treaty of perpetual friendship" with the eic in 1795 (during rama varma58-98's reign), where they agreed to pay for a british force to protect against tipu82-99. then in 1800, a british resident was stationed in travancore's court. (*can you see imprint of toa1765) in 1805, travancore signed proper subsidiary alliance with wellesley98-05 — the eic extracted this in exchange for helping the king crush a revolt by his own nair troops, who had mutinied over non-payment of salary. the state had now lost sovereignty on the standard sa template (see the sa-terms section of the chapter on wellesley's subsidiary alliance). ◆ takeaway: travancore is the chapter's clearest worked example of how the sa gets extracted: not at sword-point, but in exchange for internal-security help that the eic-resident has often had a hand in destabilising in the first place. the nair-troops mutiny over salary delays gave the travancore king an immediate problem; wellesley98-05 priced the help at full sovereign concession. within four years (sec. 10) the consequences would explode in the velu thampi dalawa revolt & kundara proclamation (1809).

sections.title: Velu Thampi Dalawa & the Kundara Proclamation (1809)
sections.norm: velu thampi dalawa & the kundara proclamation (1809). velu thampi dalawa heavy subsidy demands constant british interference in internal affairs january 1809 kundara kundara proclamation (1809) alert: kundara proclamation (january 1809) velu thampi died reduced to a subservient sa state. by 1809, the sa's consequences had become unbearable. velu thampi dalawa — prime minister of travancore, 1802–09 — led a major armed revolt against the eic, supported by soldiers & peasants angered by heavy subsidy demands & constant british interference in internal affairs — a direct breach of the sa treaty's own promise of non-interference. in january 1809, from the town of kundara, he issued the kundara proclamation (1809) — a public call to all travancoreans to rise against british paramountcy. ⚠ alert: the kundara proclamation (january 1809) is one of the most significant early revolts against the british in south india. the revolt was crushed within months. velu thampi died later the same year. travancore was reduced to a subservient sa state. (travancore is a small but telling case study. every consequence of the sa listed in the chapter on wellesley's subsidiary alliance — loss of military jobs, high taxes from subsidy pressure, poir creeping in illegally — played out here within just four years of signing.)

sections.title: Legacy: Southern Consolidation Completed
sections.norm: legacy: southern consolidation completed. four mysore wars carnatic annexation of 1801 travancore sa of 1805 sa of 1809 with cochin 1809 kundara suppressed from the krishna to kanyakumari 2nd & 3rd anglo-maratha wars (1803–05, 1817–19). the four mysore wars ended the last big southern rival to the eic. the carnatic annexation of 1801, the travancore sa of 1805, the sa of 1809 with cochin completed the southern consolidation. by 1809, with kundara suppressed, the eic was paramount from the krishna to kanyakumari — setting the stage for the 2nd & 3rd anglo-maratha wars (1803–05, 1817–19) in the north-west & deccan.

sections.title: Why Did the Deccan Matter So Much to the EIC?
sections.norm: why did the deccan matter so much to the eic?. deccan & konkan coast were commercially critical to the eic malabar coast maratha confederacy three anglo maratha wars & four anglo mysore wars. the deccan & konkan coast were commercially critical to the eic — large coastline, significant cotton trade from gujarat with china, & maratha control over parts of the malabar coast. the maratha confederacy along with mysore were the last major indian powers capable of checking eic expansion across the subcontinent. three anglo maratha wars & four anglo mysore wars (previous chapter) decided the outcome.

sections.title: 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82)
sections.norm: 1st anglo-maratha war (1775–82). factionalism within the maratha confederacy itself raghunath rao73-74 narayan rao72-73 baarbhai conspiracy (1774) nana fadnis treaty of surat (1775) salsette bassein (vasai, near mumbai) bharuch & surat warren hastings73-85 treaty of purandhar (1776) madhav rao ii74-95 salsette & bharuch not allow any french presence treaty of purandhar 1665 sheltering raghunath rao73-74 nana fadnis retaliated offering a port to the french 1779 battle of wadgaon 1782 2nd anglo-mysore war (1780–84) treaty of salbai (1782) gwalior military alliance between eic & marathas porf french settlements returned all maratha territory recognised madhav rao ii74-95 as peshwa pensioned off raghunath rao73-74. madhav rao ii rao hastings warren hastings ali. 2.1 — what triggered the 1st anglo-maratha war? the cause was factionalism within the maratha confederacy itself — a pattern that would repeat across all three wars. in 1773, raghunath rao73-74 became peshwa after the murder of nephew narayan rao72-73. then in the baarbhai conspiracy (1774), nana fadnis & eleven other ministers of the peshwa's council removed raghunath rao73-74 from power. raghunath rao73-74 then approached the eic's governor of bombay, william hornby, & signed the treaty of surat (1775) — under which the eic agreed to help him regain the peshwaship in return for salsette & bassein (vasai, near mumbai), along with some revenue from bharuch & surat. (notice the pattern — this is exactly what happened in carnatic & hyderabad during the carnatic wars. a succession dispute, a losing claimant, & the europeans offering military help in exchange for territory & influence. factionalism of indian states was europeans most reliable ally.) warren hastings73-85, the governor general in calcutta, overturned this treaty to avoid expensive war expenditure. he negotiated the treaty of purandhar (1776) with nana fadnis, under which: 1. the eic would recognise madhav rao ii74-95 as the legitimate peshwa, & raghunath rao73-74 would be pensioned off. 2. the eic would receive salsette & bharuch. 3. marathas would not allow any french presence in their domain. (notice warren hastings73-85 wanting to avoid war expenditure this was in with policy of relative isolation discussed in later; also recall treaty of purandhar 1665 from earlier chapter on rise of marathas as rebel state). however, the eic in bombay continued sheltering raghunath rao73-74. nana fadnis retaliated by offering a port to the french. talks collapsed & war resumed. 2.2 — events during the 1st anglo-maratha war? in 1779, at the battle of wadgaon (near pune), nana fadnis, mahadji scindhia & tukoji rao holkar defeated the eic & raghunath rao73-74. but the war continued inconclusively. by 1782, the eic was in a difficult position — but so were the marathas, who were also engaged in the 2nd anglo-mysore war (1780–84). the treaty of salbai (1782) — negotiated & signed at gwalior by mahadji scindhia on behalf of marathas— ended the war. its terms were: 1. military alliance between eic & marathas — the marathas broke their anti-british alliance (the triple confederacy) and agreed to fight on the side of eic if hyder ali61-82 did not restore the territories he had taken from the british and the nawab of arcot. (*porf established by eic with marathas.) 2. eic got salsette & bharuch. 3. no french settlements in maratha domain. 4. eic returned all maratha territory it had captured, recognised madhav rao ii74-95 as peshwa, & pensioned off raghunath rao73-74. (giving pensions was deliberate eic diplomatic practice —this way eic could use this person in future succession disputes.)

sections.title: Inter-War Period (1782–1803)
sections.norm: inter-war period (1782–1803). 21-year gap period of maratha decline mahadji scindhia madhav rao ii74-95 bajirao ii96-18 nana fadnis shaniwar wada wellesley98-05 madhav rao ii bajirao ii wellesley. the 21-year gap between treaty of salbai 1782 & treaty of bassein 1802 was not a period of maratha strength — it was a period of maratha decline. mahadji scindhia dominated maratha politics until his death in 1794. madhav rao ii74-95 committed suicide in 1795. bajirao ii96-18 then became peshwa (peshwa from 1796, formally tenured 1796–1818). with the death of nana fadnis in 1800 — the one man who had consistently held the maratha confederacy together for two decades — factionalism accelerated sharply. the maratha capital shaniwar wada at pune and the maratha confederacy was engulfed in factionalism. empire-builder wellesley98-05 was waiting for exactly this opportunity.

sections.title: 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) — Wellesley98-05's War
sections.norm: 2nd anglo-maratha war (1803–05) — wellesley98-05's war. vithoji rao holkar yashwantrao holkar daulat rao scindhia october 1802 treaty of bassein (dec 1802) scindhia, holkar & bhonsle gaikwad arthur wellesley battle of assaye (1803) war was lost by the marathas consequences were far-reaching bajirao ii96-18 regained the peshwaship scindhia lost all territory north of the river yamuna delhi & agra gujarat subsidiary alliance delhi policy of indirect rule shah alam ii60-06 bhonsle of nagpur lost orissa bhonsle was forced to sign a mini alliance jats, rajputs, bundelas 5. wellesley98-05 was recalled to london cornwallis86-93 policy of non-interference july 1805 october 1805 the vellore mutiny (1806): george barlow (acting gg, 1805–1807) cause: result: "prelude to 1857."] peshwa bajirao ii bajirao ii shah alam ii wellesley jung khan cornwallis. 4.1 — trigger: the treaty of bassein (december 1802) in 1801, vithoji rao holkar had been conducting plundering campaigns on peshwa's territories. he was captured & then brutally executed on the orders of peshwa bajirao ii96-18. to avenge the death of his stepbrother, yashwantrao holkar attacked & defeated both the peshwa & daulat rao scindhia (who had supported the peshwa) in october 1802. bajirao ii96-18 fled & signed the treaty of bassein (dec 1802) — agreeing to a subsidiary alliance with the eic in exchange for eic help to regain the peshwaship and hence the great army of svarajya was to be disbanded once eic put back its now puppet baji rao ii 96-18 as peshwa. the treaty of bassein (dec 1802) also triggered the 2nd anglo maratha war (1803-05). ironically, this caused scindhia, holkar & bhonsle — who had been rivals — to unite against the eic, despite their differences. gaikwad had already signed sa in june 1802 (treaty of cambay) to get help of eic in a succession dispute. 4.2 — battlefield: the battle of assaye (1803) the eic deployed significant military force. arthur wellesley, commanding his royal regiment alongside eic army, fought key engagements — including the battle of assaye (1803) against the marathas, which he later described as the toughest fight of his entire military career — harder, in his view, than anything he faced against napoleon in europe. 4.3 — consequences: the war was lost by the marathas. the consequences were far-reaching: 1. bajirao ii96-18 regained the peshwaship but now he was a puppet of eic. 2. scindhia lost all territory north of the river yamuna — including delhi & agra, & all his territory in gujarat. he was forced to sign a subsidiary alliance. in delhi, a british resident was stationed who established policy of indirect rule — the mughal emperor shah alam ii60-06 was now effectively under eic's indirect control. (*the way emperor was earlier puppet of zulfikar khan, then sayyid brothers, then irani & turani group, then safdar jung39-54, then marathas, now it was turn of eic.) 3. bhonsle of nagpur lost orissa — but stubbornly refused to accept the subsidiary alliance. (recall: bhonsle had raided bengal suba from 1745–51 & extracted chauth of bengal & bihar & control of orissa from alivardi khan40-56). bhonsle was forced to sign a mini alliance (similar in structure to the toa17765 with awadh) — ceding territory & accepting an eic army to be paid for by bhonsle, but not yet the full subsidiary alliance. 4. the jats, rajputs, bundelas —that had previously paid chauth & sardeshmukhi tributes to the marathas — were now forced to sign sa with the eic as the eic replaced the marathas as the dominant regional power of north & central india. 5. wellesley98-05 was recalled to london due to the high war expenditure in his tenure. cornwallis86-93 was despatched with clear orders to follow a policy of non-interference (*arrived in july 1805 and died in october 1805;) [note: the vellore mutiny (1806): during george barlow (acting gg, 1805–1807) this mutiny took place: cause: new dress codes that forbade sepoys from wearing religious marks (tilaks/turbans) and mandated leather cockades (ribbons shaped like christian cross on hat & made of cow/pig skin). result: an uprising in the vellore fort (north tamil nadu). it is often called the "prelude to 1857."]

sections.title: The Pindaris, Francis Hastings 13-23 (1813-23) & his Policy of Paramountcy (1813-58)
sections.norm: the pindaris, francis hastings 13-23 (1813-23) & his policy of paramountcy (1813-58). policy of non-intervention bhonsle holkar pindaris francis hastings13-23 policy of paramountcy (pop 1813–58) british resident began treating bajirao ii96-18 as a puppet appa sahib treaty of nagpur (1816) parsoji bhonsle arab & rohilla mercenaries 1817 bajirao ii96-18, appa sahib (regent of bhonsle of nagpur), & yashwantrao holkar united in revolt svarajya senapati (commander-in-chief) british residency sitabuldi hills battle of sitabuldi (november 1817) note: 1816 largest military force ever in india — about 1.2 lakh (troops battle of mahidpur (december 1817) battle of koregaon (1 january 1818) mahar soldiers peshwa bajirao ii96-18 surrendered in june 1818 bajirao ii peshwa bajirao ii wellesley hastings. after wellesley98-05, eic followed policy of non-intervention to prevent war expenditure. this gave bhonsle & holkar time to rebuild their military strength — & confidence. meanwhile, pindaris — disbanded soldiers of scindhia and holkar — began raiding eic territory in the northern sarkars and parts of the madras presidency. they were defeated by the next empire-builder gg francis hastings13-23, whose policy of paramountcy (pop 1813–58) re-initiated imperial expansion. under this policy, eic was to be paramount or supreme power in india and it would do anything, even annexation, if needed to protect its interests. thus, the british resident began treating bajirao ii96-18 as a puppet in a way that left him with no real authority. in nagpur, appa sahib had signed sa under the treaty of nagpur (1816) for eic help in a factionalism dispute over who would be regent of bhonsle of nagpur (maharaja, parsoji bhonsle suffered from paralysis, hence unable to rule.). however while the treaty required disbanding the official state army, rulers were allowed to keep retainers & police for internal security. appa sahib exploited this loophole by secretly recruiting fierce arab & rohilla mercenaries. once his power was secure — & having parsoji secretly murdered to become the actual maharaja — appa sahib now wanted rule independently and not as a puppet of british resident. sec. 6 3rd anglo-maratha war + pindari war (1817–19) 61— the battle of sitabuldi (november 1817) in late 1817, bajirao ii96-18, appa sahib (regent of bhonsle of nagpur), & yashwantrao holkar united in revolt — determined to end eic's political domination (*note: this is violation of sa treaties). this led to the 3rd anglo-maratha war (1817-19). bajirao ii96-18 had signed a subsidiary alliance under which the eic army had replaced the svarajya's own army — so technically he had no state army. he fought with men he personally recruited outside the eic's supervision. appa sahib acted as senapati (commander-in-chief). he used his arab mercenaries to launch a surprise, close-quarters attack directly on the british residency & the adjacent sitabuldi hills. despite heavily outnumbering the garrison, his forces were defeated at the battle of sitabuldi (november 1817).
