[note: battle of sitabuldi (november 1817) has been tested in upsc prelims. two things to note: (i) appa sahib signed the subsidiary alliance in 1816 but fought the british in 1817 — the sa did not prevent the war; its terms caused it. (ii) the "disbanded army" requirement was bypassed via arab + rohilla mercenaries hired as "internal security retainers" — the sa template's loophole exposed.] the eic deployed its largest military force ever in india — about 1.2 lakh (troops. 6.2 battle of mahidpur (december 1817) — holkar decisively defeated; 6.3. battle of koregaon (1 january 1818) — a small eic force of mahar soldiers held off a much larger peshwa army. later commemorated as the bhima-koregaon victory pillar. 6.4. peshwa bajirao ii96-18 surrendered in june 1818.

sections.title: Consequences of 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19)
sections.norm: consequences of 3rd anglo-maratha war (1817-19). the peshwaship was abolished. bithur, near kanpur svarajya annexed into bombay presidency. appa sahib deposed. holkar's subsidiary alliance via treaty of mandsaur (1818). satara + kolhapur not annexed. bajirao ii dalhousie. 1. the peshwaship was abolished. bajirao ii96-18 was pensioned off to bithur, near kanpur. (his adopted son was nana sahib —would later lead the kanpur revolt in 1857.) 2. svarajya annexed into bombay presidency. the original maratha homeland — became a province of the company state; the regional headquarters of eic trade evolved into a province of british india. 3. appa sahib deposed. replaced by a puppet. bhonsle lost huge territory. 4. holkar's subsidiary alliance via treaty of mandsaur (1818). holkar of indore was forced to sign after being decisively defeated at mahidpur. 5. satara + kolhapur not annexed. the eic maintained the chhatrapati's line as a symbolic gesture. (the chhatrapati had been a powerless figurehead since the 1750s anyway — keeping him alive cost nothing & avoided the optics of destroying a revered institution entirely. satara was annexed in 1848 under dalhousie48-56's doctrine of lapse)

sections.title: Why Did the Marathas Lose?
sections.norm: why did the marathas lose?. four structural reasons explain maratha defeat factionalism absence of unified command. eic's superior finances naval & logistics advantage. konkan coast. four structural reasons explain maratha defeat: 1. factionalism 2. absence of unified command. scindhia, holkar, bhonsle & gaikwad of baroda never coordinated effectively. 3. eic's superior finances. 4. naval & logistics advantage. the konkan coast could be blockaded by eic ships; the eic could move troops faster across india via sea and better road infrastructure than the marathas.

sections.title: Wars due to EIC Army overhyping threat to borders
sections.norm: wars due to eic army overhyping threat to borders. anglo-nepal war (1814–16) treaty of sugauli (1816) kumaon, garhwal & the terai 1st anglo-burmese war (1824–26) treaty of yandabo (1826) assam, nagaland, & parts of lower burma (arakan & tenasserim) cachar coorg war (1834) william bentinck28-35 vira raja 1st anglo-afghan war (1838–42) great game auckland36-42 forward policy shah shuja dost mohammed ellenborough42-44 annexation of sindh (1843) "char yaar" sir charles napier 1st + 2nd anglo-sikh wars (1845–46, 1848–49) hardinge44-48 dalhousie48-56 annexation of punjab in 1849 2nd anglo-burmese war (1852–53) pegu (lower burma) hastings amherst bentinck auckland ellenborough hardinge dalhousie. 1. anglo-nepal war (1814–16) — under francis hastings13-23. the treaty of sugauli (1816) made nepal a british protectorate; nepal lost kumaon, garhwal & the terai to british india. [note- protectorate is like subsidiary alliance: the state loses external sovereign functions but retains symbolic sovereignty and domestic sovereign functions.] 2. 1st anglo-burmese war (1824–26) — under amherst23-28. burma was doing territorial expansion. this gave opportunity to eic army overhype threat to borders. ahom kingdom of assam had supported the eic but in a stab in the back the treaty of yandabo (1826) annexed assam, nagaland, & parts of lower burma (arakan & tenasserim) to british india. cachar was annexed in 1830. 3. coorg war (1834) — under william bentinck28-35, on grounds of maladministration by vira raja. (massive coffee plantations were set up here after annexation.) 4. 1st anglo-afghan war (1838–42) — part of the great game between britain & russia. under auckland36-42's forward policy, the eic tried to install shah shuja in kabul against the actual ruler dost mohammed. disaster: 20,000 british & indian soldiers dead, expenditure of rs 1.5 crore, the famous retreat from kabul (only one european survivor reached british india). auckland36-42 was recalled. ellenborough42-44 ended the war; dost mohammed recaptured power but maintained good relations with stronger power i.e. british. 5. annexation of sindh (1843) — by ellenborough42-44 from the "char yaar" (four baloch chiefs of the talpur dynasty) without any justification. the military commander was sir charles napier. (napier sent a one-word latin dispatch to his superiors after conquering sindh: "peccavi" — meaning "i have sinned." the pun — "i have sindh" — captured the brazenness of the annexation perfectly.) 6. 1st + 2nd anglo-sikh wars (1845–46, 1848–49) — under hardinge44-48 & dalhousie48-56, leading to the annexation of punjab in 1849 (discussed in later chapter). 7. 2nd anglo-burmese war (1852–53) — under dalhousie48-56; pegu (lower burma) annexed. (discussed in later chapter).

sections.title: Dalhousie48-56: Peak of Expansion
sections.norm: dalhousie48-56: peak of expansion. controlled 63% of india no further annexations policy of paramountcy (pop1813-58) doctrine of lapse 2nd anglo-sikh war 1848 2nd anglo-burmese war 1852 annexation in lieu of subsidy berar 1853 maritime ring fence modernisation infrastructure five-policy framework policy of paramountcy 1813 dalhousie. by end of tenure of gg dalhousie48-56, the company state controlled 63% of india — home to 78% of its population. after dalhousie48-56, there were no further annexations. he used the policy of paramountcy (pop1813-58) in three ways: 1. doctrine of lapse — annexation by refusing to recognise adopted heirs. 2. wars — 2nd anglo-sikh war 1848–49 (punjab annexed) + 2nd anglo-burmese war 1852–53 (pegu annexed). 3. annexation in lieu of subsidy — berar 1853 from hyderabad. maritime ring fence + modernisation infrastructure + the five-policy framework.

sections.title: Doctrine of Lapse: Legal Principle vs Pretext
sections.norm: doctrine of lapse: legal principle vs pretext. court of directors of the eic in 1847 implemented systematically without a biological heir state was annexed dalhousie. the doctrine of lapse was formulated by the court of directors of the eic in 1847 but implemented systematically by dalhousie48-56. the doctrine was simple: if an indian ruler died without a biological heir, his rights lapsed — the state was annexed into british india. (under hindu law, adoption was a legitimate mechanism for succession — adopted sons inherited with full legitimacy. the doctrine of lapse refused to recognise this.)

sections.title: Annexations via Lapse: Chronology (1848–54)
sections.norm: annexations via lapse: chronology (1848–54). annexed seven states in seven years bhagat nag dalhousie. under the doctrine of lapse, dalhousie48-56 annexed seven states in seven years: # year state present-day region 1 1848 satara maharashtra 2 1849 sambalpur odisha 3 1849 jaitpur uttar pradesh, bundelkhand region 4 1850 baghat himachal pradesh — small hill state near solan 5 1852 udaipur chhattisgarh (formerly part of the central provinces) 6 1853–54 jhansi uttar pradesh 7 1854 nagpur maharashtra mnemonic: bhagat sambhal ja jhadio mein udta sa nag — baghat, sambalpur, jaitpur, jhansi, udaipur, satara, nagpur. ⚠ alert: the udaipur annexed in 1852 is not the famous rajput kingdom of udaipur/mewar in rajasthan but a smaller princely state in present-day chhattisgarh (then central provinces).

sections.title: The Inam Commission (1852)
sections.norm: the inam commission (1852). privileged landholdings inam commission insufficient-proof grants were confiscated 20,000 estates were seized dalhousie. dalhousie48-56 also targeted privileged landholdings. in 1852, the bombay presidency set up the inam commission to investigate tax-free grants (inams) made by earlier indian rulers to brahmins, temples & others. the commission demanded proof of title; insufficient-proof grants were confiscated. around 20,000 estates were seized in the bombay presidency alone. (the inam commission was the doctrine of lapse applied to land titles instead of thrones — if you cannot prove your claim to the company's satisfaction, the company takes it. the logic was identical)

sections.title: Doctrine of Lapse Applied to Pensions: Nana Sahib + 1857 Link
sections.norm: doctrine of lapse applied to pensions: nana sahib + 1857 link. doctrine of lapse to pensions refused to continue the state pension nana sahib nana sahib a key 1857 leader bithur peshwa bajirao ii bajirao ii dalhousie. dalhousie48-56 extended the doctrine of lapse to pensions. when peshwa bajirao ii96-18 died in 1851, dalhousie48-56 refused to continue the state pension of rs 8 lakh per annum to his adopted son nana sahib. the argument: adopted sons inherit private wealth, not political titles or state pensions. the pension refusal made nana sahib a key 1857 leader from bithur (where bajirao ii96-18 had been pensioned off in 1819 post-3rd anglo-maratha war).

sections.title: Annexation in Lieu of Subsidy: Berar (1853)
sections.norm: annexation in lieu of subsidy: berar (1853). annexation in lieu of subsidy 1798 hyderabad could not pay annexed berar dalhousie. dalhousie48-56's second instrument: annexation in lieu of subsidy. hyderabad had signed the first subsidiary alliance in 1798 and had been paying ever-rising subsidy ever since. by 1853, hyderabad could not pay. dalhousie48-56 annexed berar as permanent payment of the subsidy (*recall: 1801: half of awadh annexed as subsidy)

sections.title: Annexation of Awadh (1856)
sections.norm: annexation of awadh (1856). treaty of allahabad increased subsidy demands sadat ali khan ii rs 76 lakh full subsidiary alliance half of awadh ceded districts continued demanding more subsidy threat of peasant revolts annexed the rest of awadh maladministration wajid ali shah north-western provinces 1836 shore ali wellesley dalhousie. 1. 1765 — treaty of allahabad (by robert clive) established poir + porf + mini sa in awadh. 2. the eic gradually increased subsidy demands on awadh. 3. 1798 — john shore93-98 replaced wazir ali97-98 as nawab with uncle sadat ali khan ii in return for annual subsidy of rs 76 lakh & cession of allahabad fort. 4. 1801 — sadat ali khan ii defaulted. wellesley98-05 imposed full subsidiary alliance by sending henry wellesley. half of awadh — gorakhpur, rohilkhand & the doab — annexed as permanent payment of subsidy (called ceded districts; unjust as revenue was twice the subsidy). 5. the eic continued demanding more subsidy despite the permanent payment. the nawab had to raise taxes & by 1855, there was threat of peasant revolts. 6. 1856 — dalhousie48-56 annexed the rest of awadh on grounds of maladministration. by 1855, the british resident had established indirect rule & nawab wajid ali shah had no real power and hence no power but all responsibility. ⚠ alert: the 1856 awadh annexation was not under doctrine of lapse — wajid ali shah had heirs. (prelims 2008: which state was removed on misgovernance pretext? awadh.) year administrative status 1801 ceded districts formed from annexed half of awadh 1836 given full province status as north-western provinces (nwp1836) 1856 rest of awadh annexed 1877 both territories reorganised as "north-western provinces and oudh" 1902 renamed "united provinces of agra and oudh" 1937 renamed "united provinces" 1950 became uttar pradesh after independence 2000 uttarakhand carved out of it

sections.title: Sikh State Annexation: 1st + 2nd Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–49)
sections.norm: sikh state annexation: 1st + 2nd anglo-sikh wars (1845–49). policy of ring fence (porf) protective buffer directly annexed ideal buffer under maharaja ranjit singh01-39 factionalism tore the state apart royal family members dogra rajputs porf was now useless weakened from within military restraint khalsa army size was reduced territorial cession jalandhar doab the kashmir mechanism gulab singh maharaja of jammu & kashmir administrative oversight british resident (henry lawrence) kashmir question hindu monarchy over a muslim-majority population treaty of amritsar 1809 sutlej treaty of amritsar 1846 princely state of j&k multan (mulraj) haripur (chattar singh) revolted punjab was annexed maharaja duleep singh43-49 koh-i-noor surrendered to the british crown board of administration lawrence brothers last major independent state singh dalhousie. 8.1 — sikh state: from ideal buffer to annexation target as per the policy of ring fence (porf), the eic wanted stable, strong, friendly border states as a protective buffer around british india. if stability could not be achieved, the eic either established indirect rule (nepal 1814–16, afghanistan 1839, punjab 1845) or directly annexed (assam and parts of lower burma 1824–26, punjab 1849, burma 1852–53). the sikh state had been that ideal buffer under maharaja ranjit singh01-39. after his death in 1839, factionalism tore the state apart: 1. royal family members fought for succession. 2. the sindhanwaliyas — a jat clan or misl. 3. dogra rajputs who served as wazirs at different times. 4. the khalsa army itself. succession disputes & political murders followed; the porf was now useless as state weakened from within. (the khalsa army's democratic spirit — it wanted governance by panchayats, a form of collective military and civil self-governance— was harder for the eic to manage than a feudal-loyal army.) 8.2 — result of the 1st anglo-sikh war result — treaty of lahore (march 9, 1846). 1. military restraint: khalsa army size was reduced and an eic army was stationed. the khalsa was not fully disbanded out of respect for sikh religious sentiment. 2. territorial cession: the fertile jalandhar doab (land between beas and sutlej rivers) was annexed by the eic. 3. the kashmir mechanism: as the lahore darbar could not pay the full 1.5 crore war indemnity, they ceded the hills between the beas and indus (kashmir and hazara) to the eic. the eic then transferred (sold) these territories to gulab singh for 75 lakh nanakshahee rupees. gulab singh was recognized as maharaja of jammu & kashmir, subordinate to the british. * [note: this was formalized via the treaty of amritsar (march 16, 1846).] 4. administrative oversight: poir was initiated in punjab—a british resident (henry lawrence) was stationed as the effective regent. strategic note: kashmir—of enormous strategic importance—was sold to reward gulab singh’s neutrality. the “kashmir question” has its legal origin here, creating a hindu monarchy over a muslim-majority population. ⚠ alert: two treaties of amritsar must be distinguished: 1. treaty of amritsar 1809: between ranjit singh01-39 and the eic; established the sutlej as the sikh-eic boundary. 2. treaty of amritsar 1846: formalized the kashmir sale described above; the legal foundation of the princely state of j&k. 8.3 — 2nd anglo-sikh war (1848–49) reason. the sikh governors of multan (mulraj) and haripur (chattar singh) revolted—giving empire-builder dalhousie48-56 the opportunity he needed. result. 1. annexation: punjab was annexed from maharaja duleep singh43-49 (a child of 5 at accession). 2. the koh-i-noor: as part of the terms of surrender, the world-famous koh-i-noor diamond was taken from maharaja duleep singh and surrendered to the british crown. 3. administrative shift: punjab was initially governed by a “board of administration” (the lawrence brothers and charles mansel). conclusion. the last major independent state outside the company state was gone. the eic’s frontier now touched the natural boundaries of the afghan foothills.

sections.title: 2nd Anglo-Burmese War (1852–53): Lower Burma / Pegu
sections.norm: 2nd anglo-burmese war (1852–53): lower burma / pegu. porf logic securing the eastern frontier annexed lower burma / pegu british lake dalhousie ellenborough. fought on the porf logic of securing the eastern frontier from an expansionist burma. dalhousie48-56 annexed lower burma / pegu. combined with arakan & tenasserim (annexed 1824–26 under the 1st anglo-burmese war + treaty of yandabo 1826), this brought the eastern shore of the bay of bengal under british control — the bay was now effectively a british lake. (sindh was annexed in 1843 by charles napier under ellenborough42-44, not dalhousie48-56. dalhousie's annexations: lower burma 1852-53, berar 1853, punjab 1849, & the seven lapse states.)

sections.title: Britain's Maritime Ring Fence
sections.norm: britain's maritime ring fence. maritime empire every coastline that touched the indian ocean 1856 every sea approach to india had to be controlled. balochistan coast and gwadar. khan of kalat two treaties treaty of kalat (1854) major john jacob rs 50,000 treaty of jacobabad (1876) robert sandeman policy of subordinate union alert: gwadar — a unique 170-year omani enclave inside balochistan. 1783 gifted the port of gwadar to a prince of oman sultanate of oman over 170 years pakistan purchased gwadar from oman only in 1958 china-pakistan economic corridor (cpec) the persian gulf and iran (persia). temporary military force anglo-persian war treaty of paris (1857) formal diplomatic partition (1907). anglo-russian convention of 1907 british sphere economic control (1909). anglo-persian oil company (1909) dalhousie lytton. land empire is visible on a map. a maritime empire is harder to see — but just as deliberate. while the eic was annexing territories inland, it was simultaneously, piece by piece, bringing every coastline that touched the indian ocean under british control. by the time dalhousie48-56 left in 1856, the picture was complete. 10.1 — indian ocean coastline (bay of bengal + arabian sea, 1668–1853) 10.2 — sea approaches beyond india: balochistan + persian gulf porf logic did not stop at india's coastline. every sea approach to india had to be controlled. the british extended their reach further — not always through annexation, but through whichever instrument was cheapest and most effective. balochistan coast and gwadar. the makran coast — today's balochistan coastline — belonged to the state of makran, itself a vassal of the khan of kalat. the british brought this entire region under control through two treaties that fall on opposite sides of the most important dividing line in modern indian history: the revolt of 1857 and the government of india act 1858. 1. treaty of kalat (1854) — signed by the eic; negotiated by major john jacob under dalhousie48-56. the khan of kalat surrendered foreign policy & allowed eic military outposts inside kalat territory; in exchange the eic paid the khan an annual subsidy (rs 50,000) — a reverse-sa pattern, where the imperial power pays the local ruler in return for special rights to an external power. 2. treaty of jacobabad (1876) — signed by the british state; negotiated by robert sandeman under viceroy lytton76-80. by 1876, the government of india act 1858 had legally abolished the eic and transferred all power directly to the british crown. this treaty operated under the policy of subordinate union (1858–1947), not the eic's pop. it went significantly further than 1854 — the british state could now station troops permanently in kalat, construct railways and telegraphs through it, and act as supreme arbitrator in all disputes between the khan and his tribal chiefs (the sardars). (poir had fully arrived — the resident was not just in the court, he was now the court.) (the shift from 1854 to 1876 in kalat mirrors what happened to all 565 indian princely states overnight in 1858 — they went from being subordinates of a trading company to being legal subjects of the british crown. same geography, same subordination, but a completely different legal authority sitting above them. substantive treatment of this transition lives in the chapters on 1857 and the constitutional acts.) ⚠ alert: gwadar — a unique 170-year omani enclave inside balochistan. in 1783, the khan of kalat had gifted the port of gwadar to a prince of oman. gwadar thus became an overseas territory of the sultanate of oman — an omani enclave sitting inside the balochistan coast — for over 170 years. the british empire controlled everything around gwadar but never owned gwadar itself. pakistan purchased gwadar from oman only in 1958 — eleven years after independence. (today gwadar sits at the heart of the china-pakistan economic corridor (cpec) and is one of the most strategically debated ports in the world.) the persian gulf and iran (persia). persia remained a formally independent sovereign state — the british never annexed it. but formal independence does not mean freedom from foreign control. the british managed the persian coastline through three mechanisms: 1. temporary military force (1856–57). the anglo-persian war (1856–57) captured coastal cities including bushehr and kharg island. under the treaty of paris (1857), the british withdrew in exchange for iran giving up its claims to herat in afghanistan. (porf logic — protect the western land approach to india, not for iran's sake but for the ring fence around british india.) 2. formal diplomatic partition (1907). under the anglo-russian convention of 1907, britain and russia divided iran into spheres of influence. the southern coastal region along the persian gulf was officially recognised as the british sphere — naval dominance in the indian ocean secured without a single annexation. 3. economic control (1909). the anglo-persian oil company (1909) — later anglo-iranian oil company, today's bp — gave britain economic control of the iranian coastline. oil was extracted and shipped under british naval protection. (this is economic imperialism at its most efficient — control the resource, control the coast, without the cost of running a colony. the british had learnt by the 19th century that formal annexation was expensive. a sphere of influence and an oil company could achieve the same result far more cheaply.)

sections.title: Dalhousie48-56 as Moderniser
sections.norm: dalhousie48-56 as moderniser. most transformative gg utilitarianism 1. railways (1853). 2. telegraph (1853). 3. post office act (1854). 4. public works department (pwd). 5. wood's despatch (1854). 6. three universities (groundwork). 7. education (vernacular push). 8. female education & widow remarriage support. 9. universities — administrative architecture. dalhousie canning. ⚠ pyq — mains 2013 (10m, 200w): "in many ways, lord dalhousie was the founder of modern india." elaborate. (answer-guidance themes → companion, topic 41.) dalhousie48-56 was not just an annexationist — he was the most transformative gg in physical & institutional infrastructure. a follower of utilitarianism (james mill: reform-through-laws by a strong state), he built the skeleton of modern india's communication & administrative framework. 1. railways (1853). built primarily for army movement; secondarily for administration, raw-material extraction & market creation. first line — bombay to thane — opened 1853. by 1856, calcutta–raniganj (coal-rich region) & madras–arakkonam followed. 2. telegraph (1853). telegraph department established; ~4,000 miles laid across major cities. 3. post office act (1854). network with uniform half-anna (2 paise) rate — peshawar to calcutta. 4. public works department (pwd). removed from military control, made civilian. gt road (peshawar to calcutta) restored to functionality. canals & bridges built across india. 5. wood's despatch (1854). sometimes called the "magna carta of indian education" — blueprint for mass education: vernacular elementary schools, universities, structured education administration. dalhousie48-56 supported & implemented it. 6. three universities (groundwork). bombay, madras, calcutta — officially established 1857 under canning56-62 — groundwork was dalhousie48-56's. (dalhousie48-56 built the physical-institutional skeleton for colonial purposes — easier troop movement, cheaper administration, raw-material extraction, market creation. the infrastructure outlasted the purpose; india inherited it & built a nation on it.) 7. education (vernacular push). dalhousie48-56 favoured vernacular elementary schools for their utilitarian value — expanding them in bengal & bihar. supported wood's despatch (1854) push for mass vernacular education. also backed technical education — the goal being efficient labour, good consumers, & cheaper administration. 8. female education & widow remarriage support. j.e. drinkwater bethune (law member of dalhousie's council) opened a girls' school in calcutta in 1849 — the bethune school, india's first successful secular school for girls — which became the most well-known girls' school in india. (*savitribai & jyotirao phule's pune school (1 jan 1848) predates it as india's first girls' school overall; secular here means completely free from religious instruction.) ishwar chandra vidyasagar was closely associated with it. dalhousie48-56 actively supported vidyasagar's work on girls' education & the hindu widow remarriage act 1856. vidyasagar became principal of sanskrit college in 1851 & inspector of schools in 1856 — both under dalhousie's tenure. 9. universities — administrative architecture. dalhousie48-56 laid the groundwork via wood's despatch but left india in 1856. the three universities at bombay, madras, & calcutta were officially established in 1857 under canning56-62. also established — engineering college at roorkee. set up director of education at provincial level with inspector at district level — the administrative architecture for education governance.

sections.title: Five-Policy Arc (1600–1858)
sections.norm: five-policy arc (1600–1858). coherent sequence international trade selective warfare british resident in court controlling administration without formal annexation military alliance with frontier state buffer against external threats taking over foreign policy & military non-interference in internal affairs routinely broken through illegal poir treaty of bassein 1802 3rd anglo-maratha war (1817) francis hastings13-23 declared itself paramount diplomatic isolation sealed bubble eic was abolished british state took direct control defence, communications, foreign affairs domestic sovereign functions remained with the indian prince policy of subordinate union sovereignty formally with british crown the arc — 1600 to 1858 in five steps: trading company dominant power declaring all others subservient 565 indian princes why 1857 happened poir. bajirao ii when bajirao ii hastings warren hastings. the full arc of british policy towards indian states — from 1600 to 1858 — as a coherent sequence. 12.1 — policy of relative isolation (until 1813) the eic was militarily not confident in its early decades; primary interest was international trade. it stayed out of indian politics as far as possible — but not absolutely. it defended & expanded its trading interests through diplomacy & selective warfare, signed military alliances (treaty of allahabad 1765, treaty of salbai 1782) & interfered in succession disputes (treaty of surat 1775) to extract territories for trade expansion. (treaty of purandhar 1776 illustrates the isolation pull — hastings73-85 wanted to settle commercially & avoid full war.) 12.2 — policy of indirect rule (poir) + policy of ring fence (porf) poir — british resident in court controlling administration without formal annexation. examples: bengal by 1772, delhi 1803, travancore by 1809, satara by 1818, punjab 1846, awadh by 1855. porf — military alliance with frontier state to act as buffer against external threats. examples: awadh (toa 1765), hyderabad (treaty of masulipatnam 1766), mysore (treaty of madras 1769), marathas (treaty of salbai 1782), sikh (treaty of amritsar 1809). 12.3 — policy of subsidiary alliance / posa (1798–1858) eic subordinated indian rulers as junior alliance partners by taking over foreign policy & military — both funded by annual subsidy from the indian state — while formally promising non-interference in internal affairs. the promise was routinely broken through illegal poir. bajirao ii96-18 signed the sa via treaty of bassein 1802 to regain his throne; the treaty promised non-interference. but british resident mountstuart elphinstone soon bypassed the peshwa & began interfering directly — creeping poir through the back door. when bajirao ii96-18 launched the 3rd anglo-maratha war (1817), it was not aggression — it was a ruler trying to shake off interference the treaty had explicitly promised would never happen. (no powers, but all the blame — same pattern as awadh 1856, sec. 7.) 12.4 — policy of paramountcy / subordinate isolation (1813–58) initiated by francis hastings13-23. from 1813, the eic formally declared itself paramount — supreme power among all states in india. to protect british interests, the eic would interfere in internal affairs & annex if needed. (earlier this happened in practice; from 1813, the eic shed pretence. indian states were to have no rights if british interests demanded otherwise.) diplomatic isolation — cutting off an indian state's right to deal with other states independently — had existed since early sa treaties. after 1813, the eic dropped the fiction of equal-sovereign alliance: every indian state, large or small, was locked in a sealed bubble — no communication, negotiation, or alliance with any other state without the eic as absolute gatekeeper. conceptually: policy of paramountcy = policy of sa minus the rights of the indian state. 12.5 — policy of subordinate union (1858–1947) after 1857, the eic was abolished & the british state took direct control. indian rulers were now not just subordinate but legally part of the british empire — hence "union". paramountcy became the formal legal relationship between the british monarch & the indian prince. (note: prince — not king. indian rulers were now legally junior members of the british imperial family, not independent sovereigns.) sovereignty & all external sovereign functions — defence, communications, foreign affairs — were with the british crown. domestic sovereign functions remained with the indian prince. conceptually: policy of subordinate union = policy of paramountcy + sovereignty formally with british crown. the arc — 1600 to 1858 in five steps: 1. trading company that wanted to be left alone (1600) 2. military alliance partner (1765) 3. dominant power controlling neighbours' armies & foreign policies (1798) 4. state openly declaring all others subservient to its interests (1813) 5. crown that absorbed 565 indian princes as legal subordinates (1858) each stage built legally & institutionally on the previous. this logical unfolding is exactly why 1857 happened when it did.

sections.title: Critique + Post-Dalhousie
sections.norm: critique + post-dalhousie. consolidated the company state but destroyed its legitimacy 1857 revolt annexation-aggrieved rani lakshmibai of jhansi nana sahib bahadur shah zafar37-57 disbanded sikh soldiery dispossessed talukdars all joined or supported the revolt handed power to canning56-62 in 1856 government of india act 1858 abolished the company state queen victoria's proclamation of 1858 no further annexations followed — bajirao ii dalhousie zafar bahadur shah zafar canning lytton. 13.1 — consolidation at the cost of legitimacy dalhousie48-56 consolidated the company state but destroyed its legitimacy. almost every major leader of the 1857 revolt was annexation-aggrieved: 1. rani lakshmibai of jhansi — lapse 1854 (sec. 3). 2. nana sahib — bajirao ii96-18 pension refused 1851 (sec. 5). 3. bahadur shah zafar37-57 — the last mughal, whose titular dignity dalhousie48-56 sought to end. the court of awadh (sec. 7), the disbanded sikh soldiery (sec. 8), the dispossessed talukdars & the inam-holders stripped by the inam commission 1852 (sec. 4) — all joined or supported the revolt. (*recall: inam commission = lapse applied to land titles — same legitimacy-override logic.) 13.2 — post-dalhousie: canning56-62 inherits + queen victoria ends lapse dalhousie48-56 handed power to canning56-62 in 1856 — who inherited the empire dalhousie built & the revolt his annexations had sowed seeds of. after the suppression of 1857 revolt, the government of india act 1858 abolished the company state & transferred power to the british crown. queen victoria's proclamation of 1858 formally ended the doctrine of lapse & pledged that the treaties & rights of indian rulers would be respected — explicit reversal of dalhousie48-56's core policy. paramountcy → subordinate union (sec. 12.5). no further annexations followed — a line dalhousie's successors (including viceroy lytton76-80) did not cross, even where paramountcy-era instruments were tightened (e.g. treaty of jacobabad 1876 with kalat — sec. 10.2). the empire was complete; it only needed managing.

sections.title: Before we begin
sections.norm: before we begin. cornwallis lytton curzon. sec. 1 — why ideology comes before policy sec. 2 — foundation: white man's burden (wmb) 2.1 — roots of british civilizational confidence 2.2 — wmb as roof + counter-ideologies as reaction sec. 3 — orientalism (1765–1813): rule india, the india way 3.1 — orientalism defined 3.2 — eic's adoption of orientalism 3.3 — orientalism's political angle sec. 4 — authoritarianism: cornwallis86-93 + conservatism 4.1 — the cornwallis86-93 shift 4.2 — cornwallis86-93's aloof-elite doctrine 4.3 — conservatism: munro, malcolm, elphinstone, metcalfe sec. 5 — three new ideologies (post 1813): liberalism + utilitarianism + evangelicalism 5.1 — the post-1813 sharp turn 5.2 — liberalism 5.3 — utilitarianism 5.4 — evangelicalism 5.5 — common ground across the three ideologies sec. 6 — the liberalism shift 1828–35 sec. 7 — racism + authoritarianism (post 1857) 7.1 — six-front sharp shift after 1857 7.2 — post-1857 architects: lytton76-80 + curzon99-05 sec. 8 — law & order paternalism sec. 9 — forward policy in afghanistan: ellenborough → lytton sec. 10 — dufferin's upper burma (1886) sec. 11 — imperial preference sec. 12 — foreign ideologies motivating india's anti-colonial struggle 13.1 — pre-1900 political/ideological currents 13.2 — three 20th-century shocks that radicalised indian nationalism 13.3 — returning indian leaders brought these currents home sec. 13 — summary

sections.title: Why Ideology Comes Before Policy
sections.norm: why ideology comes before policy. ideas that shaped colonial policy not just profitable but also morally right genuine belief convenient narrative to make imperialism look ethical. british imperial ideologies — the ideas that shaped colonial policy. not a single fixed set; they changed over time, sometimes competed. but they shared one function — they gave the british a way to tell themselves & the world that what they were doing in india was not just profitable but also morally right. every ideology was both a genuine belief held by some englishmen & a convenient narrative to make imperialism look ethical — both layers operate simultaneously.

sections.title: Foundation: White Man's Burden (WMB)
sections.norm: foundation: white man's burden (wmb). western european civilisation was superior white man's burden (wmb) genuine reason to believe in their own superiority world's first modern democracy birthplace of the industrial revolution top global power defeated napoleon waterloo (1815) capitalism & science roof over everything else how exactly should we civilise india anti-colonial counter-ideologies worldwide american revolution french revolution (1789) irish home rule movement inspired colonised peoples indian nationalists. all other ideologies rested on one foundational belief — western european civilisation was superior, & the british therefore had a responsibility to civilise the rest of the world. this was the white man's burden (wmb). 2.1 — roots of british civilizational confidence several events gave the british genuine reason to believe in their own superiority: 1. world's first modern democracy — english civil war + glorious revolution (17th century). 2. birthplace of the industrial revolution (c. 1750–1850). 3. won the seven years' global war (1756–63) — top global power. 4. financially backed the coalition that defeated napoleon at leipzig (1813); led the allied armies to final victory alongside prussia at waterloo (1815). 5. capitalism & science transforming british society at unprecedented pace. (a nation that achieves all this within 150 years can convince itself it is destined to lead the world — every major imperial power has had its own version of wmb.) 2.2 — wmb as roof + counter-ideologies as reaction wmb was the roof over everything else. the specific ideologies below were different answers to the same wmb question: how exactly should we civilise india? wmb also generated its opposite — powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies worldwide: 1. american revolution — political movement from 1765, war of independence 1776–83. 2. french revolution (1789) — liberty, equality, fraternity. 3. european revolutions of 1830 & 1848. 4. irish home rule movement (1870–1914) + irish armed struggle for independence (1916–1921). these challenged imperial-superiority assumptions & inspired colonised peoples — including indian nationalists. (cross-link: sec. 12 develops these foreign ideologies motivating india's anti-colonial struggle — mains 2014.)

sections.title: Orientalism (1765–1813): Rule India, the India Way
sections.norm: orientalism (1765–1813): rule india, the india way. william jones studied sanskrit older & grammatically more sophisticated great ancient civilisation same family orientalism rule india, the india way. two practical reasons militarily not yet confident before 1813 ruling through indian customs not ready for british modernity hastings73-85 was orientalism's most prominent champion. four major orientalist institutions political manipulation aryan invasion theory argument of kinship rhetoric of love to disguise the reality of exploitation hastings warren hastings wellesley. 3.1 — orientalism defined in the 18th century, the british used language & literature as the measure of civilisation. when scholars like william jones studied sanskrit, they found it older & grammatically more sophisticated than ancient greek & latin. the conclusion was striking: india had been a great ancient civilisation, & european & indian languages belonged to the same family. (sanskrit, greek & latin were shown to be related — what we today call the indo-european language family. genuine scholarship, not propaganda.) this gave rise to orientalism — india's ancient past was glorious even if its present was degenerate, so the british should study indian tradition & rule india according to its own customs & laws. in short: rule india, the india way. 3.2 — eic's adoption of orientalism two practical reasons reinforced the ideology: 1. the eic was militarily not yet confident before 1813 — victory in the carnatic / mysore / maratha wars was never guaranteed, & one badly handled cultural insult could trigger mass resistance. ruling through indian customs reduced that risk. 2. some englishmen believed india was not ready for british modernity — imposing alien systems would cause more damage than good. hastings73-85 was orientalism's most prominent champion. he argued that the more the british understood indian traditions, the lighter the chains of colonialism would feel. under this philosophy, four major orientalist institutions were founded: # year institution founder + capacity 1 1781 calcutta madrasa warren hastings73-85, in his capacity as governor-general of bengal, primarily for the study of islamic law and customs. 2 1784 asiatic society of bengal sir william jones, serving as puisne judge of the supreme court at calcutta, to study asian history, antiquities, and culture. 3 1791 sanskrit college in banaras jonathan duncan, acting as the british resident at benares (banaras), for the study of hindu law and philosophy. 4 1800 fort william college, calcutta wellesley98-05, in his capacity as governor-general of bengal, to train newly recruited eic civil servants in indian languages and administration. (wellesley98-05 had an additional motive for fort william college: keeping french republican ideas away from his officers — the french revolution 1789 had overthrown the monarchy by 1792, & wellesley98-05 did not want anti-monarchy ideas infecting his men.) 3.3 — orientalism's political angle a subtle political manipulation was embedded in orientalism. the british supported the aryan invasion theory — ancient india's cultural greatness was actually brought by europeans who migrated to india in ancient times. even while praising india, the british claimed credit. the argument of kinship — that europeans & indians were separated kin connected through language — was used to reduce indian opposition to british rule: we are not foreigners, we are cousins who have come home. a rhetoric of love to disguise the reality of exploitation. ⚠ alert (prelims 2020 trap): wellesley98-05 established the fort william college at calcutta because: 1. board of directors asked — wrong (wellesley98-05's own initiative). 2. revive oriental learning — wrong (the asiatic society 1784 + sanskrit college 1791 served that purpose; fort william's purpose was civilian training). 3. provide employment to carey — wrong (william carey was an employee, not the founding purpose). 4. train british civilians ✓ correct: (d) train british civilians. memory hook: fort william college = train eic civilians in indian languages.

sections.title: Authoritarianism: Cornwallis86-93 + Conservatism
sections.norm: authoritarianism: cornwallis86-93 + conservatism. critics from the beginning past was glorious & its present was degenerate imposing the british system cornwallis86-93 ruled india, the english way. specifically all-british senior admin. rule of law via codification. permanent settlement (1793) in bengal aloof elite. american war of independence determined not to allow the same thing to happen in india keep the rulers separate from the ruled. never let india become home. wellesley98-05 thomas munro (governor of madras 1820–27) hybrid of orientalism & authoritarianism ryotwari settlement orientalist in form, authoritarian in substance. mountstuart elphinstone, john malcolm & charles metcalfe cornwallis wellesley. 4.1 — the cornwallis86-93 shift orientalism had its critics from the beginning. the study of ancient india had only confirmed that india's past was glorious & its present was degenerate — which made restoring the past pointless & called for imposing the british system instead. cornwallis86-93 was the first gg to implement this vision systematically. he ruled india, the english way. specifically: 1. all-british senior admin. replaced all indians in senior administrative positions with british officials. his argument: indian administrators were corrupt & incompetent; only british authority could deliver rule of law. (deeper argument: only by removing indians from power can the british civilise india — the corrupt-native-needing-the-honest-foreigner narrative used through 1947 to justify exclusion.) 2. rule of law via codification. the charter act 1793, influenced by cornwallis86-93, established civil law & protection of individual rights & private property. reintroduced separation of powers at the district level — the district collector would no longer also function as the district judge. 3. permanent settlement (1793) in bengal, converting zamindars into large landlords on the english model. (substantive treatment → land revenue systems chapter.) 4. aloof elite. eic officials actively discouraged from mixing with indians. indian wives discouraged. eurasians barred from eic service. eic officials having indian wives were barred from purchasing land in india. 4.2 — cornwallis86-93's aloof-elite doctrine cornwallis86-93 had personally commanded the british army's defeat in the american war of independence (1776–83). he had watched british settlers in the 13 american colonies develop deep roots — family, property, identity — & then fight for independence as their homeland. he was determined not to allow the same thing to happen in india. keep the rulers separate from the ruled. never let india become home. wellesley98-05 shared this authoritarian instinct. both administrations were control-oriented, centralised, & mistrustful of indian agency. 4.3 — conservatism: munro, malcolm, elphinstone, metcalfe thomas munro (governor of madras 1820–27) was a hybrid of orientalism & authoritarianism. india should be governed through its own traditions — but it would be the british who governed, with no leadership role for indians. total power centralised in eic hands, but power exercised through indian forms. reflected in his ryotwari settlement (1801–07, 1820+) in madras presidency — inspired by the ancient indian model of the state collecting revenue directly from the peasant without intermediaries. but all collection was done by eic officials, with no indians in senior roles. orientalist in form, authoritarian in substance. mountstuart elphinstone, john malcolm & charles metcalfe followed the same school. (elphinstone, a disciple of munro, later implemented the ryotwari settlement in bombay.)

sections.title: Three New Ideologies (Post 1813): Liberalism + Utilitarianism + Evangelicalism
sections.norm: three new ideologies (post 1813): liberalism + utilitarianism + evangelicalism. by 1813, the landscape had changed dramatically defeated all major indian powers holkar, bhonsle & the sikh state industrial revolution rule india the british way new economic motive market for british manufactured goods three ideologies liberalism, utilitarianism, evangelicalism. great bengal famine of 1770 modernised through the best ideas of the age liberate india from feudalism modern british institutions thomas macaulay, his three signature interventions: law commission (1834) minute on indian education (1835) charter act 1813 (liberal-influenced reform) sati abolition act 1829 utilitarianism — history of british india (1818) effective schoolmaster law commission in 1834 change the religion, change everything. protestant christianity rise of capitalism & modernity charles grant charter act 1813 lex loci act / removal of religious-caste disabilities act (1850) benevolent colonialism produced the revolt of 1857 bentinck. 5.1 — the post-1813 sharp turn by 1813, the landscape had changed dramatically: 1. the eic had defeated all major indian powers — only holkar, bhonsle & the sikh state remained as potential rivals. 2. the company's army had grown huge. 3. britain had defeated napoleon. 4. the industrial revolution was in full swing. the eic was now confident enough to rule india the british way — openly, aggressively, without apology. there was also a new economic motive: an india with western tastes & western education would become a market for british manufactured goods. three ideologies filled the space orientalism had occupied: liberalism, utilitarianism, evangelicalism. 5.2 — liberalism liberals argued that the eic had governed india badly under orientalism. the great bengal famine of 1770 — one crore indians perished while the eic doubled land revenue — was cited as proof. india needed to be modernised through the best ideas of the age — best meaning western. liberalism's goal was to liberate india from feudalism: feudal polity (no democracy), feudal economy (agrarian, closed, unequal), feudal society (birth-based discrimination, no women's rights) — & replace it with modern british institutions. thomas macaulay, legal member of the gg's council under the charter act 1833, was the most prominent liberal. his three signature interventions: 1. law commission (1834) — codified western-style laws for british india by 1837. 2. minute on indian education (1835) — proposed western education in english to create what he called brown sahibs — brown on the outside, british on the inside; a class of indians serving as cultural intermediaries between the british rulers & the indian masses. 3. charter act 1813 (liberal-influenced reform) — ended the eic's monopoly over indian trade & allowed non-eic british businesses to enter india freely. (economic liberalism for british businesses, not for indian ones.) social reforms followed too — bentinck28-35 brought the sati abolition act 1829 under liberal influence (substantive home → social reforms chapter). 5.3 — utilitarianism utilitarianism — associated with jeremy bentham & james mill — argued india needed not culture change but good policy & strong rule of law. the state's job was to design laws that maximised benefit for the largest number of people. james mill's history of british india (1818) declared india's great past a myth & argued india needed an effective schoolmaster — someone to impose good governance from above. mill joined the court of directors of the eic in london & pushed for the establishment of the law commission in 1834 under macaulay. (utilitarianism contains an inherent authoritarian streak.) 5.4 — evangelicalism evangelists argued india's fundamental problem was its religion — which promoted superstition, ignorance, idolatry & tyranny of priests, & blocked scientific thinking. religion shapes values; values shape society. change the religion, change everything. their model was protestant christianity in western europe — where protestant ethics had supported the rise of capitalism & modernity. charles grant, a member of the court of directors & later an mp, influenced the charter act 1813 to legalise the entry of christian missionaries into india. the lex loci act / removal of religious-caste disabilities act (1850) allowed a convert to retain inheritance rights in family property — removing one practical obstacle to conversion (substantive home → social reforms chapter). 5.5 — common ground across the three ideologies all three pushed for reform of the colonial state & together built the narrative of benevolent colonialism — we are here to help you. many englishmen who believed in these ideologies were sincere. and yet, all three together contributed to the conditions that produced the revolt of 1857 — cultural, economic & political resistance to a colonial project that had touched almost every aspect of indian life.

sections.title: The Liberalism Shift 1828–35
sections.norm: the liberalism shift 1828–35. charter act 1833 1835 minute high-water mark of liberal confidence sati abolition act 1829 thuggee suppression 1830s–40s macaulay's education minute 1835 cornwallis code progressively revised bentinck. the short window from bentinck28-35 through to the charter act 1833 & macaulay's 1835 minute is the high-water mark of liberal confidence in india. four headline interventions: 1. sati abolition act 1829 — criminalised widow-burning. (substantive home → social reforms chapter.) 2. thuggee suppression 1830s–40s — under captain william sleeman — restored police order on the grand trunk roads. (substantive treatment → sec. 8; prelims 1997 anchor.) 3. macaulay's education minute 1835 — made english the medium of higher instruction, displacing persian. 4. cornwallis code progressively revised into a uniform criminal procedure — the foundation macaulay's 1834 law commission would build on.

sections.title: Racism + Authoritarianism (Post 1857)
sections.norm: racism + authoritarianism (post 1857). revolt of 1857 sharp shift on multiple fronts reformist impulse retreated sharply. racial sciences shift. aryan invasion theory kept but twisted. "dogs and indians not allowed" authoritarianism increased. social reforms slowed sharply. lytton76-80 & curzon99-05 prestige, paramountcy & racial hierarchy lytton76-80 vernacular press act 1878 arms act 1878 curzon99-05 partition of bengal (1905) lytton curzon. the revolt of 1857 shook the british — not just militarily, but psychologically. the scale of indian violence against british rule — soldiers, civilians, women, children — broke the paternalistic narrative. the british had told themselves they were here as trustees & reformers. 1857 told them that a very large number of indians did not see it that way. 7.1 — six-front sharp shift after 1857 the response was a sharp shift on multiple fronts: 1. reformist impulse retreated sharply. liberalism, utilitarianism & evangelicalism reform impulses (sec. 5) collapsed. many british concluded that indians were simply beyond redemption through reform. 2. racial sciences shift. european racial classification in the second half of the 19th century shifted from language (the orientalist criterion) to physical features. indians were now classified as an inferior & fundamentally different race — not as separated kin (sec. 3 orientalism), but as a lower order of humanity. 3. aryan invasion theory kept but twisted. yes, europeans had founded the vedic civilisation — but because they had intermarried with indigenous indians over millennia, they had lost their racial superiority & degraded. (even india's ancient greatness now used as evidence of indian inferiority.) 4. "dogs and indians not allowed" — seen on signs at clubs & parks in colonial india — captures the spirit of post-1857 british attitudes. 5. authoritarianism increased. the british became distrustful of sharing power with indians in any meaningful way. 6. social reforms slowed sharply. queen victoria's proclamation of 1858 explicitly promised religious tolerance & non-interference in indian customs — direct acknowledgement that the religious interference of missionaries & reformers had been a major grievance of 1857. from here, social & political reforms came mainly in response to pressure from indian leaders, not british initiative. 7.2 — post-1857 architects: lytton76-80 + curzon99-05 the post-1857 architects of this harder imperialism were lytton76-80 & curzon99-05 — men for whom empire was a project of prestige, paramountcy & racial hierarchy. 1. lytton76-80 — the vernacular press act 1878 & arms act 1878 reinstated racial privilege (substantive home → print culture chapter for vpa). 2. curzon99-05 — the partition of bengal (1905) was the same mindset administratively applied (substantive home → swadeshi movement chapter).

sections.title: Law & Order Paternalism
sections.norm: law & order paternalism. law-and-order paternalism thuggee and dacoity suppression thuggee and dacoity department informant networks approver testimony swift judicial commissions 3,000 thugs were convicted 1831 & 1841 alert (prelims 1997 trap): general henry prendergast annexation of upper burma alexander burnes 1st anglo-afghan war 1841 captain robert pemberton correct: captain sleeman. bentinck. between orientalism & liberalism, the eic also ran a parallel track of law-and-order paternalism — reclaiming the roads, the courts & rural policing in the name of the peasant's physical safety. the flagship example is the thuggee and dacoity suppression campaign of the 1830s–40s, built around captain (later major-general sir) william sleeman, under bentinck28-35. sleeman's thuggee and dacoity department (set up 1835) combined three operational tools: 1. informant networks infiltrating thug bands. 2. approver testimony — captured thugs giving evidence against their associates in exchange for lighter sentences. 3. swift judicial commissions — dedicated tribunals delivering rapid trials. together these dismantled organised highway murder cults that had made long-distance trade on the grand trunk road a life-and-death gamble. over 3,000 thugs were convicted between 1831 & 1841. ⚠ alert (prelims 1997 trap): who was associated with suppression of thugs? distractors: 1. general henry prendergast — led the annexation of upper burma 1885–86 (sec. 10). 2. alexander burnes — afghan-frontier political agent killed in the 1st anglo-afghan war 1841 (sec. 9). 3. captain robert pemberton — assam/burma frontier officer. correct: captain sleeman. memory hook: sleeman = thugs; prendergast = burma; burnes = afghanistan.

sections.title: Forward Policy in Afghanistan: Ellenborough42-44  → Lytton76-80
sections.norm: forward policy in afghanistan: ellenborough42-44 → lytton76-80. forward policy classic pyq trap auckland36-42 1st anglo-afghan war 1839–42 ellenborough42-44 lytton76-80 2nd anglo-afghan war 1878–80 treaty of gandamak 1879 ripon80-84 alert (prelims 1999b trap): correct: (d) lytton. revision — russophobia & the great game: policy of ring fence anglo-russian convention of 1907 ellenborough lytton auckland ripon dufferin. the forward policy was the militarised face of post-1840s british imperialism on the northwest frontier — britain should actively push its effective frontier into afghanistan to pre-empt tsarist russian influence, rather than defend a fixed line at the indus. its arc ran through multiple ggs & is a classic pyq trap: 1. auckland36-42 launched the disastrous 1st anglo-afghan war 1839–42 to reinstall shah shuja against dost mohammad. the retreat from kabul (january 1842) wiped out almost an entire british-indian army. 2. ellenborough42-44 initiated what later came to be called the forward policy — a punitive return to kabul in 1842 to restore british prestige, followed by a doctrine of pushing the frontier outward. 3. lytton76-80 carried forward this forward policy & launched the 2nd anglo-afghan war 1878–80 — forcing the treaty of gandamak 1879 (a mini subsidiary alliance as british resident stationed + army stationed + foreign policy taken + khyber pass & some other lands to british + in return british to pay 6 lakh annually to amir) but war continued into its 2nd phase after the massacre of british resident louis cavagnari at kabul. 4. ripon80-84 reversed the forward policy & withdrew british forces from afghanistan — the pendulum swing liberal governments in london demanded. ⚠ alert (prelims 1999b trap): who followed a spirited forward policy towards afghanistan? options: 1. minto — minto ii (1905–10) was a viceroy of a different era (post-curzon). 2. dufferin — dufferin84-88 is famous for upper burma 1886 (sec. 10), not afghanistan. 3. elgin — either elgin i (1862–63) or elgin ii (1894–99) — different era; not forward policy. 4. lytton ✓ — lytton76-80 carried forward the forward policy via the 2nd anglo-afghan war 1878–80. correct: (d) lytton. memory hook: lytton = forward; ripon = retreat. ◆ revision — russophobia & the great game: russophobia was the british fear that czarist russia, expanding through central asia, would one day reach the north-west land approach to india. this anglo-russian rivalry over central asia is remembered as the great game — and it shaped british frontier & foreign policy far more than trade. the forward policy traced above was the offensive answer to that fear — pushing the effective frontier outward through the two anglo-afghan wars (1839–42 & 1878–80). its defensive twin was the policy of ring fence — keeping strong, friendly border states as a buffer around british india, with afghanistan & punjab as that buffer in the north-west. the 1838 tripartite treaty (sikh state, eic & shah shuja) was built on exactly this buffer logic (see ch 6, ch 14). on the persian flank the same logic produced the anglo-persian war 1856–57 and, finally, the anglo-russian convention of 1907, which split iran into three — a russian sphere in the north, a neutral buffer in the middle & a british sphere in the south (see ch 14).

sections.title: Dufferin's Upper Burma (1886)
sections.norm: dufferin's upper burma (1886). upper burma 3rd anglo-burmese war 1885–86 dufferin84-88 1852 1937 alert (prelims 2000 trap): correct: (a) dufferin84-88. dufferin dalhousie lytton curzon. the last major territorial extension of british india was in upper burma, annexed in january 1886 after the 3rd anglo-burmese war 1885–86. the viceroy was dufferin84-88. king thibaw was deposed & exiled to ratnagiri. the field commander was general henry prendergast — the same prendergast who appeared as a distractor for the prelims 1997 thuggee question (sec. 8). upper burma was merged with lower burma (british from 1852) & governed as a province of british india until the 1937 separation. ⚠ alert (prelims 2000 trap): last major extension of british indian territory? options: 1. dufferin ✓ — dufferin84-88 added upper burma in january 1886. 2. dalhousie — dalhousie48-56 was the big annexation gg (punjab 1849, awadh 1856, doctrine of lapse), but his last major extension was awadh 1856 — dufferin came later & added upper burma 1886. 3. lytton — lytton76-80 carried forward the forward policy (sec. 9), but did not make territorial extensions; he tightened paramountcy-era instruments (e.g. treaty of jacobabad 1876) without annexing. 4. curzon — curzon99-05 came later; his partition of bengal 1905 was administrative reorganisation, not territorial extension. correct: (a) dufferin84-88. memory hook: dufferin = 1886 = upper burma = last major extension.

sections.title: Imperial Preference
sections.norm: imperial preference. "imperial preference" ottawa conference of 1932 operational effect on india: alert (prelims 1999a trap): correct: (a) special privileges on british imports in india.. "imperial preference" was a commercial tariff arrangement — constituent units of the british empire (britain, the dominions & india) granted one another preferential (lower) tariff rates denied to non-empire competitors. formalised at the ottawa conference of 1932, locking india's trade into an empire-first structure that subordinated indian industrial interests to british manufacturing needs. (substantive treatment → drain theory chapter.) operational effect on india: british goods entered indian ports at lower tariff than german, japanese, or american competitors. india's tariff regime systematically advantaged the very british manufacturing economy that indian industries were trying to compete with. ⚠ alert (prelims 1999a trap): the term imperial preference applied to: 1. special privileges on british imports in india ✓ 2. racial discrimination by the britishers — wrong (a separate phenomenon, sec. 7). 3. subordination of indian interest to that of the british — too vague (general description of colonialism, not the specific definition). 4. preference given to british political agents over indian princes — wrong (political department protocol, not imperial preference). correct: (a) special privileges on british imports in india. memory hook: imperial preference = tariff = british imports get special treatment in india. # name notable work 1 alexander rea excavated at amaravati and bhattiprolu 2 a.h. longhurst excavated at nagarjunakonda and hampi 3 robert sewell wrote *a forgotten empire (vijayanagara)* 4 james burgess first director of the archaeological survey of western and southern india 5 walter elliot of the madras civil service; catalogued andhra buddhist sites and coins

sections.title: Foreign Ideologies Motivating India's Anti-Colonial Struggle
sections.norm: foreign ideologies motivating india's anti-colonial struggle. anti-colonial counter-ideologies returning students & political exiles american revolution (1765–83) french revolution of 1789 european revolutions of 1830 & 1848 irish home rule (1870–1914) irish armed struggle (1916–21) against britain challenged imperial superiority inspired colonised peoples worldwide industrial revolution's destructive impact on indian handloom russian revolution of 1917 post- ww1 principle of self-determination travelled through people gandhi from south africa nehru from cambridge alert (mains 2014): ww1 . wmb (sec. 2) produced its opposite — powerful anti-colonial counter-ideologies across the globe — that travelled back into india through newspapers, returning students & political exiles. 13.1 — pre-1900 political/ideological currents 1. american revolution (1765–83) — political movement from 1765, war of independence 1776–83. 2. french revolution of 1789 — liberty, equality, fraternity. 3. european revolutions of 1830 & 1848 — democratic uprisings across the continent. 4. irish home rule (1870–1914) + irish armed struggle (1916–21) against britain — direct anti-british inspiration. all challenged imperial superiority & inspired colonised peoples worldwide. 13.2 — three 20th-century shocks that radicalised indian nationalism 1. industrial revolution's destructive impact on indian handloom — deindustrialisation fed the drain theory of dadabhai naoroji & r.c. dutt. 2. russian revolution of 1917 — gave the indian left a peasant-worker mobilisation model & an anti-imperial vocabulary. 3. post- ww1 principle of self-determination (wilson's fourteen points, 1918) & rising anti-racism — made continued british rule increasingly indefensible in international forums. 13.3 — returning indian leaders brought these currents home the world-developments did not travel through ideas alone — they travelled through people: 1. gandhi from south africa — anti-colonial training from indian-diaspora struggles in south africa (1893–1915). 2. nehru from cambridge — western liberal-democratic political theory absorbed during cambridge studies, returned to apply in indian congress politics. ⚠ alert (mains 2014): "what were the major political, economic and social developments in the world which motivated the anti-colonial struggle in india?" (10m, 150w). a good mains-grade answer chains the 3-bucket framework: enlightenment + american + french + irish revolutions (political/ideological) → industrial revolution deindustrialisation (economic) → russian revolution 1917 + wilson's self-determination + anti-racism (social/ideological) → returning indian leaders (gandhi from south africa, nehru from cambridge) bringing these currents home. (companion appendix fyq_mains has the full 5-part theme treatment.)

sections.norm: summary. hastings warren hastings cornwallis wellesley bentinck lytton curzon dufferin. # ideology period champions flagship measure 1 white man's burden foundation (throughout) all englishmen civilising-mission rhetoric 2 orientalism 1765–1813 warren hastings73-85, william jones, colebrooke, wilson calcutta madrasa 1781; asiatic society 1784; sanskrit college 1791; fort william college 1800 3 authoritarianism 1786–1805 cornwallis86-93, wellesley98-05 cornwallis code 1793; permanent settlement 1793; aloof elite 4 conservatism 1801–27 munro, malcolm, elphinstone, metcalfe ryotwari settlement; political agencies 5 liberalism 1813–57 t.b. macaulay, bentinck28-35 sati abolition 1829; minute on education 1835; law commission 1834 6 utilitarianism 1813–57 bentham, james mill, js mill law commission 1834; codification; ipc 1860 7 evangelicalism 1813–57 charles grant, wilberforce, zachary macaulay charter act 1813 (missionaries); lex loci act 1850 8 racism / crown paramountcy post 1857 lytton76-80, curzon99-05, dufferin84-88 queen's proclamation 1858; vernacular press act 1878; upper burma 1886; imperial preference (ottawa 1932)

sections.title: The Mughal Blueprint for Land Revenue
sections.norm: the mughal blueprint for land revenue. khudkasht patta system abwabs primary zamindar intermediary zamindar jagirdar khalisa one critical point ijaradari system. under the mughal system, the actual cultivator was called the khudkasht. he held customary occupancy rights over his land — meaning he could not simply be thrown off. he paid land revenue as per the patta system, where a document called a patta recorded the amount he owed — a legal safeguard against arbitrary over-extraction. he also paid abwabs — informal tributes — to his primary zamindar. the primary zamindar kept his commission & passed the rest upward — either to an intermediary zamindar, or directly to the jagirdar (if the land was a jagir) or to the state (if it was khalisa land). intermediary zamindars did the same — collected, kept their cut, passed the rest up. government officers called amils & amalguzars supervised this chain, ensuring zamindars did not under-report collections. one critical point: the zamindar was not the owner of land. he was a revenue collector with a commission. the khudkasht had customary rights of occupancy. (the concept of private legal ownership of property was not a mughal idea — it was a british one, imported from english law. zamindars also held police duties alongside their revenue functions.) when the state needed money in a hurry, it introduced the ijaradari system — auctioning the right to collect land revenue to the highest bidder, a practice we will see the british replicate.

sections.title: Bengal — Three Experiments
sections.norm: bengal — three experiments. diwani treaty of allahabad (toa1765) frantic experimentation to squeeze more land revenue back-to-back droughts great bengal famine of 1770 regulating act of 1773 reza khan was made a scapegoat imprisoned without trial revenue farmer district collector (dc) revenue farmers extracted the maximum system self-defeating rights in land break into five layers: right to cultivate & occupy fair rents sell, lease, rent & mortgage land receive tax proceeds & revise tax rates assessment settlement rent taxes farming system of 1772 auction bengal, orissa, bihar, north madras, benaras cornwallis86-93 permanent settlement act of 1793 thomas munro permanent settlement (ps1793) four key pillars why cornwallis86-93 chose zamindars as landlords? three reasons: english-style landlordism agrarian capitalists agrarian capitalism loyalty of zamindars political stability not made landowners why permanent? why absolute? incentivise the zamindar state certainty of land revenue (lr) reduce administration trade-off set the initial demand very high double the 1765 level collection district collector diverged sharply short term: jotedars long term: but cornwallis86-93's core economic vision failed. absentee landlordism emerged. the ryot's situation became catastrophic. zamindars regained coercive powers in 1799. regulation vii of 1799 seize a tenant's property without a court order peasant revolts after 1793 alert (prelims 2001 + 2011 + 2024 trap cluster): prelims 2001 prelims 2011 prelims 2024 decades of peasant revolts compelled to act rent act of 1859 occupancy rights less than 12 years rents could not be increased patta system was revived lost the power to imprison tenants poorly implemented loophole evict the tenant just before he completed 12 years indigo revolt (1859–63) pabna agrarian leagues (1873) bengal tenancy act of 1885 clearly defined in law powers of zamindars significantly reduced occupancy rights strengthened closed the earlier loophole implemented the act sincerely treaty of allahabad 1765 permanent settlement 1793 hastings warren hastings cornwallis wellesley ripon dufferin. 2.1 — experiment 1: dual government (1765–72) in 1765, the eic received the diwani (right to collect land revenue) of bengal, orissa & bihar through the treaty of allahabad (toa1765). rather than administer it directly, the eic appointed deputy subadar muhammad reza khan as its diwan. the mughal system of revenue collection continued — the eic followed orientalism (indian traditions best administered on their own terms). ideology did not stop greed. in the five years that followed, frantic experimentation to squeeze more land revenue out of bengal: the patta system was ignored, rents extracted far beyond what pattas recorded. then back-to-back droughts hit. the result: the great bengal famine of 1770, killing between 50 lakh & 1 crore indians. the eic's response — doubled land revenue demand in 1770 & used brutality to collect. for the first time, some british men acted as whistleblowers — writing to london newspapers about the atrocities. the famine destroyed the agrarian economy. land revenue income collapsed. since from 1757 the eic had been using india's own land revenue to buy indian goods for trade — rather than bringing gold from england — the income shock cascaded. by 1772, the eic was on the verge of bankruptcy: rampant corruption by its officials (the "nabobs"), the 1770 famine, & heavy expenses of army + dual system. the eic approached the british government for an emergency bailout. parliament granted £1.4 million at 4% interest, but on strict condition the eic submit to parliamentary oversight — leading directly to the regulating act of 1773. in bengal, reza khan was made a scapegoat — imprisoned without trial on charges of corruption from 1772–74. 2.2 — experiment 2: the farming system of warren hastings73-85 (1772) hastings73-85, himself an orientalist, revived the mughal ijaradari system. the right to collect land revenue in each district was auctioned to the highest bidder — the revenue farmer (named so because, like a farmer, he aimed to extract profit from the land through a contract; not an agricultural farmer who tills the soil). the revenue farmer operated under the supervision of a european district collector (dc) (european = english, scottish or irish — not english alone). outcome was predictable: revenue farmers extracted the maximum possible from ryots to recover their auction bid & earn profits. in many cases the demand was so impossibly high that peasants simply chose to pay nothing — making the system self-defeating. land revenue income did not improve. rural population was ruined. 2.3 — primer: tax, property, and settlement rights in land break into five layers: a) the ryot's right to cultivate & occupy his plot. b) the right to fair rents (for a tenant ryot) or fair land revenue (for an owner). c) the landowner's right to sell, lease, rent & mortgage land — & to receive those proceeds. d) the right to collect taxes. e) the right to receive tax proceeds & revise tax rates. assessment = deciding how much tax is owed. done through detailed field survey (soil quality, irrigation, crop type, plot size, rainfall) — or summarily, just rough estimate. the demand can be a fixed absolute amount or a percentage of produce. permanent or revisable. settlement = with whom did the state negotiate the tax demand, & who is responsible for depositing it? crucial distinction. rent is always paid by a tenant to a property owner. taxes are always borne by the property owner. the state is always the ultimate recipient — but can choose to collect through its own officers or through non-state intermediaries. with this framework: in the farming system of 1772, assessment was done via auction & settlement was done with the revenue farmer. 2.4 — experiment 3: permanent settlement act, 1793 applied in bengal, orissa, bihar, north madras, benaras (mnemonic: bob migrated from north madras to benaras & settled permanently). cornwallis86-93 (gg of bengal 1786–1793) was sent to bengal with one primary assignment: fix the land revenue problem. after several experiments, he passed the permanent settlement act of 1793 (ps1793) passed by the gg(bengal)'s council. it was also extended to madras on his instructions. however, by 1801, thomas munro convinced the court of directors in london to replace it with ryotwari in madras — though it survived in north madras. hence, permanent settlement(1793) operated as land revenue system in bengal, orissa, bihar, benaras and north madras. the permanent settlement (ps1793) had four key pillars: pillar 1 — landownership went to the zamindar. zamindars were given full proprietary rights for the first time — making them legal owners of land. now, land became a commodity: saleable, purchasable, leasable, rentable, mortgageable. land continued to be hereditary i.e. transferable within the family. why cornwallis86-93 chose zamindars as landlords? three reasons: a) ideological belief in english-style landlordism — he wanted to convert zamindars into agrarian capitalists, like the landed gentry of england. legal ownership would give security of property which would make it more likely that the zamindar invests in land’s productivity. b) agrarian capitalism would improve food security, boost agricultural trade & grow eic's land revenue income. c) loyalty of zamindars — traditional leaders of rural society — would improve political stability. revenue farmers, despite being wealthy, were not made landowners — they were not part of the traditional agrarian economy & lacked agricultural expertise. pillar 2 — settlement was done with the zamindar. fewer, bigger counterparties made collection administratively simpler. the state negotiated/settled land revenue with zamindars; zamindar was responsible for depositing land revenue. pillar 3 — assessment was permanent. land revenue fixed at 10/11 of the zamindar's pre-existing revenue (what he had been collecting from ryots before deducting his commission), with 1789–90 as the base year. fixed forever — permanently — as an absolute annual amount, not a percentage. why permanent? why absolute? a) to incentivise the zamindar: since revenue demand would not increase no matter how profits grew, he had every reason to invest & produce more. b) to give the state certainty of land revenue (lr): even in a drought year, the state knew exactly what it would receive. c) to reduce administration: no repeat assessment surveys needed. d) trade-off: because the state was giving up its right to increase land revenue in future, it set the initial demand very high. estimates vary — some historians say double the 1765 level; others say 20% above 1757 levels. pillar 4 — the sunset clause. if a zamindar failed to pay land revenue by the evening of a pre-set deadline, his land would be auctioned to anyone who agreed to pay the required land revenue. (the new buyer only needed to agree to pay — not make immediate payment — given the large amounts involved.) collection was to be done by state officers — the district collector. 2.5 — impact of permanent settlement (ps1793) results diverged sharply from cornwallis86-93's intentions. 1. short term: land auctions were frequent — the demand was so high that many zamindars defaulted. two groups bought lands at auction: jotedars (rich farmers, but not as wealthy as zamindars) & the zamindar's own family members, who bid to keep land within the extended family. over time the system stabilised, & zamindars did become loyal to the british (this loyalty showed during 1857, when bengal's zamindars largely stayed on the british side). 2. long term: the british did get certainty & regularity of land revenue income. that objective was achieved. 3. but cornwallis86-93's core economic vision failed. zamindars did not invest in land productivity. the demand left them little surplus for investment — & whatever old family wealth they had, they did not risk it in an uncertain colonial environment. 4. absentee landlordism emerged. zamindars leased lands to intermediaries for a lease amount & moved to cities. the hands-on agrarian capitalist vision was abandoned. 5. the ryot's situation became catastrophic. ps gave legal rights to zamindars but did not recognise the ryot's customary rights at all. the ryot became a "tenant at will" — evicted without legal protection. patta system ignored. zamindars extracted high rents. abwabs, though now illegal since they had no legal basis, continued to be collected. 6. zamindars regained coercive powers in 1799. cornwallis86-93 had originally removed zamindars' police powers — his view was that a zamindar was a businessman, not
