law enforcement. but wellesley98-05 reversed this through regulation vii of 1799. the zamindar now got back: a) seize a tenant's property — crops, cattle — without a court order if rent was defaulted. b) imprison tenants. c) increase rents at will. 7. the result was a wave of peasant revolts after 1793. ⚠ alert (prelims 2001 + 2011 + 2024 trap cluster): 1. prelims 2001 — why did zamindars not issue pattas under ps1793? correct: (b) there was no official check upon the zamindar. under ps, zamindars only had to pay 10/11 of revenue to the state; everything below that was beyond state supervision. 2. prelims 2011 — why did litigation surge after cornwallis86-93's 1793 settlement? correct: (b) making the eic an overlord of zamindars (formal land-titles transferable to others on default). the sunset clause auctioned titles on default — legal petitions multiplied. 3. prelims 2024 — cornwallis86-93's revenue: which is correct? statement 1: ryotwari peasants exempted in bad harvest — wrong (ryotwari was munro's, not cornwallis86-93's; & ryotwari did not automatically exempt). statement 2: ps — zamindar removed if failed to pay — correct (sunset clause). correct option: (b) 2 only. memory hook: cornwallis86-93 = permanent only; sunset clause = zamindar lost land on default. 2.6 — the rent act of 1859 and the bengal tenancy act of 1885 after decades of peasant revolts, the british were finally compelled to act. the rent act of 1859 introduced protections for tenant ryots in bengal presidency: a) a tenant who had cultivated the same plot continuously for more than 12 years gained occupancy rights — could not be evicted without a court order, & rents could not be increased without the zamindar showing just cause. b) for tenants with less than 12 years on a plot, rents could not be increased frequently. c) patta system was revived — zamindars had to collect rents at recorded rates. d) zamindars lost the power to imprison tenants. looked good on paper. in practice, poorly implemented. zamindars found a loophole: evict the tenant just before he completed 12 years of continuous cultivation, thereby permanently denying occupancy rights. private armed men maintained through bribery. officials turned a blind eye. this drove the indigo revolt (1859–63) & the pabna agrarian leagues (1873), where ryots fought specifically for occupancy rights. the bengal tenancy act of 1885 (act iii of 1885) came after ripon80-84 set up the rent commission in 1880. (passed under dufferin84-88's tenure, with the bengal legislative council enacting it.) now: a) rights of all stakeholders — zamindars & ryots — clearly defined in law. b) powers of zamindars significantly reduced. c) occupancy rights strengthened: even tenants who had cultivated different plots in the same village for a total of more than 12 years would now get occupancy rights over the last plot cultivated. this closed the earlier loophole. d) the government implemented the act sincerely this time.

sections.title: Ryotwari Settlement
sections.norm: ryotwari settlement. sind, coorg, assam, madras & bombay poligars experiment failed thomas munro ryotwari in madras alexander read why did munro push for ryotwari five reasons scottish ideology: no big zamindars in madras: state finances: eliminating intermediaries: political stability: landowner. ryot settlement. assessment phase 1 — initial assessment (based on gross produce) alexander read & thomas munro 33% to 50% of estimated gross produce technically complex surveys often improper arbitrary severe over-assessment widespread poverty & land abandonment phase 2 — reformed assessment (based on rental value / net produce) ricardian theory of economic rent in bombay: wingate settlement of 1835 in madras: madras torture commission report (1855) madras rules (1855/1864) bombay exception (early on): patils deshmukhs corruption in madras: mirasidars alert (prelims 2012 + 2017 trap cluster): prelims 2012 prelims 2017 read & munro = ryotwari cornwallis86-93 = permanent cornwallis86-93 patils lost their historic status. massive indebtedness not solely due to ryotwari bombay deccan peasant riots of 1875 permanent settlement 1793 cornwallis wellesley. applied in: sind, coorg, assam, madras & bombay (mnemonic: scam-b — and indeed, it was a b-grade scam). 3.1 — ryotwari in madras (1801 onward, firmly from 1820) the starting attempt in madras was the same as bengal — extend ps. cornwallis86-93 & wellesley98-05 tried to create big zamindars in madras by recognising the poligars (landed magnates who had maintained their own private armies & enjoyed autonomy since the vijayanagar empire of 1336–1646) as landowners. but this experiment failed. thomas munro convinced the court of directors in london in 1801 to replace it with ryotwari in madras. he had first experimented with it in parts of madras as early as 1792 under alexander read. the system was diluted after he left for britain in 1807 but he firmly re-established it when he returned as governor of madras (1820–27). why did munro push for ryotwari instead of permanent settlement? five reasons: a) scottish ideology: munro was from scotland, where the hero of agrarian society was the yeoman farmer — a landowner who also cultivated his own land (think of a more prosperous khudkasht). he was also an orientalist & argued that in ancient india there were no intermediaries between the state & the actual cultivator. b) no big zamindars in madras: in bengal, murshid quli khan (1717–27) had deliberately created super-rich intermediary zamindars — by 1727, just 15 such zamindars collected 50% of bengal's land revenue. this wealth base made ps viable there. madras had no such class. c) state finances: madras was under severe financial stress due to low land productivity & the cost of past wars — the three carnatic wars (1746–63) & four anglo-mysore wars (1767–99). ps, by fixing land revenue forever, gave the state no room to increase income as productivity grew. d) eliminating intermediaries: the poligars' profits came at the state's expense. remove them, & their share could be redistributed — partly as higher state income, partly as lower burden on ryots. e) political stability: removing the poligars as a class of powerful non-state actors would reduce political resistance. loyalty of the masses would come from giving them land. 3.2 — under ryotwari landowner. the ryot held legal title to his land. settlement. done directly with the ryot. the state dealt with each cultivator individually. assessment (detailed field surveys; % or amount). evolved in two phases, shifting from gross output to net rental value after early failures. based on detailed field surveys (soil productivity, irrigation, acreage, crops, past trends), with room for revision & remission during bad harvests. a) phase 1 — initial assessment (based on gross produce) i) where/when: introduced in madras by alexander read & thomas munro (1792–1820). ii) demand: 33% to 50% of estimated gross produce (total agricultural output). iii) flaw: technically complex surveys often improper. method was arbitrary & ignored the cost of cultivation. iv) result: severe over-assessment led to widespread poverty & land abandonment. ryots faced a brutal cycle: crop failure → borrow from moneylenders at high interest → default → lose mortgaged land or lose it in government auctions. b) phase 2 — reformed assessment (based on rental value / net produce) i) concept: recognising the ruin of the agrarian economy, the criteria shifted to the ricardian theory of economic rent. demand based on net produce (gross crop value minus cost of cultivation: seeds, manure, bullocks, labour, implements). ii) in bombay: elphinstone brought ryotwari here. r.k. pringle (1830) first applied the economic rent theory but faulty calculations led to an excessive 55% demand. fixed by the wingate settlement of 1835 (bombay survey system by wingate & goldsmid, implemented across bombay deccan by 1847), which assessed land fairly & fixed a reasonable annual amount for 30 years. iii) in madras: following the madras torture commission report (1855), which exposed severe oppression, the madras rules (1855/1864) capped land revenue demand at a maximum of 50% of net produce / rental value for 30 years. (addressing these grievances kept madras relatively quiet during the 1857 revolt.) a) bombay exception (early on): after annexing the maratha svarajya (3rd anglo-maratha war, 1817–19), the eic initially used patils (village headmen) & deshmukhs to collect revenue — a nod to orientalism. b) corruption in madras: the lower bureaucracy relied on mirasidars (rich landowner-cultivators acting as village-level revenue officers). because the dc & his officers held concentrated judicial, police & revenue powers, mirasidars abused this authority to oppress ryots, force defaults & buy the best lands in auctions. the stated goal of eliminating big intermediaries failed — mirasidars became big landowners themselves. ⚠ alert (prelims 2012 + 2017 trap cluster): 1. prelims 2012 — ryotwari: which statements are correct? statement 1: rent paid directly by peasants to government — correct (settlement done directly with the ryot). statement 2: government gave pattas to ryots — correct (the patta system that ps1793 had killed in bengal was preserved here). statement 3: lands surveyed & assessed before being taxed — correct (detailed field surveys). correct option: (c) 1, 2 & 3. 2. prelims 2017 — architects of ryotwari? statement 1: cornwallis — wrong (cornwallis86-93 was the ps architect). statement 2: alexander read — correct (started 1792 in madras). statement 3: thomas munro — correct (extended, returned as governor of madras 1820–27 to re-establish). correct option: (c) 2 & 3 only. memory hook: read & munro = ryotwari (scottish/yeoman); cornwallis86-93 = permanent (english landlordism). memory hook: *read & munro = ryotwari (scottish/yeoman); cornwallis86-93 = permanent (english landlordism)*. 3.3 — impact in bombay a) patils lost their historic status. earlier, a patil held executive, judicial, revenue & police powers & earned a commission. now he was just an ordinary government officer collecting taxes for a salary. b) massive indebtedness to marwari & gujarati moneylenders swept through central deccan in the 1850s. c) not solely due to ryotwari — crop failures played a role, & so did the collapse of cotton prices after the end of the us civil war (1861–65), when us raw cotton flooded global markets again, destroying the premium indian cotton had earned during the war years. (indian cotton exports had boomed during 1861–65 because the union naval blockade cut off confederate cotton exports. when the war ended, the boom collapsed.) the combined result was the bombay deccan peasant riots of 1875.

sections.title: Mahalwari Settlement
sections.norm: mahalwari settlement. central provinces, united provinces, punjab taluqdars milkiyats amils/amalguzars tehsildars regulation vii of 1822 mahal mahalwari was a hybrid system ryot was made landowner lambardar taluqdar remained the landowner partly like ryotwari partly like ps collection was by state officers. r.m. bird revised mahalwari system assessment done at the mahal level decided by the community itself auction individual ryot lands 66% of the rental value (net assets) for 30 years dalhousie48-56 extended mahalwari to punjab & central india. improper field surveys debt to moneylenders summary settlement 1857 revolt in the north-western provinces & awadh dalhousie. applied in: central provinces, united provinces, punjab (mnemonic: mahal → taj mahal → tea → tea in a cup, hence mahalwari in cup — central provinces, united provinces, punjab). (note: up of 1937 = united provinces of agra & oudh created in 1902, which evolved into what we today call uttar pradesh.) 4.1 — the mahalwari settlement in the awadh region, before british arrival, taluqdars (intermediary zamindars) & primary zamindars dominated the agrarian economy. when half of awadh came under british administration in 1801 to form the nucleus of the north-western provinces, the period 1801–22 saw severe over-extraction of land revenue by the eic. taluqdars who resisted lost their milkiyats (landed estates) — an entire class of landed magnates was crushed. in mahalwari areas, revenue officers of the mughal era (amils/amalguzars at the district level & tehsildars at the sub-district level) grew powerful, buying up the best lands in auctions. (note: amlas are distinct from these; they were private employees of the zamindars, not state officers.) moneylenders, bankers & merchants also acquired milkiyat lands. holt mackenzie's recommendations were then implemented through regulation vii of 1822, creating the mahalwari settlement. mahal = a community of people at the village, estate or district level. 4.2 — the hybrid structure the mahalwari was a hybrid system — it did not make one uniform choice about who the landowner would be: a) in most areas, the ryot was made landowner & settlement was done with the mahal, & the lambardar (representative of mahal) acted as the interface between the state & the community, preserving traditional village autonomy. (the mahal decided how the total land revenue demand would be distributed internally among its members.) b) in some areas, the taluqdar remained the landowner & settlement was done with him. here the law did recognise the occupancy rights of ryots & mandated recording of rents — patta system had legal backing. hence "hybrid" — partly like ryotwari (ryot as landowner) & partly like ps (zamindar as landowner). collection was by state officers. 4.3 — the revised mahalwari system initially, land revenue was assessed at the level of individual fields/ryots, but improper surveys led to excessive demands. in 1833, r.m. bird introduced the revised mahalwari system in the north-western provinces: a) assessment done at the mahal level, not at individual plot level — respecting the community's collective character. b) individual contribution within the mahal decided by the community itself. c) if the mahal's collective land revenue fell short, the state could auction individual ryot lands. d) land revenue fixed at 66% of the rental value (net assets) for 30 years, subject to state revision. dalhousie48-56 extended mahalwari to punjab & central india. 4.4 — why mahalwari failed improper field surveys → unjust land revenue → ryots either lose land in state auctions or fall into debt to moneylenders & lose mortgaged land. when awadh was finally annexed in 1856, a summary settlement was done — land revenue decided without field surveys, simply because surveys take time. result: unjust demands for many ryots & consequent landlessness. all of this — crushing of taluqdars 1801–22, unjust revenue demands, summary settlement of 1856, landlessness of ryots — fed directly into the 1857 revolt in the north-western provinces & awadh, among the most intense theatres of that rebellion.

sections.title: Commercialization of Agriculture
sections.norm: commercialization of agriculture. cash crops like indigo, cotton, opium, jute & sugarcane pressure to grow cash crops structural transformation of indian agriculture famines of the late 19th century alert (prelims 2021 trap): correct: (c) commercialisation of indian agriculture.. under the mughal system, much of the revenue demand could be met in kind — grain for grain. the british, however, demanded revenue in cash. to generate cash, ryots were compelled — or induced by moneylenders & traders — to shift from food crops (which fed their families but fetched low market prices) to cash crops like indigo, cotton, opium, jute & sugarcane (which could be sold for money to meet the revenue demand). the higher the revenue demand, the greater the pressure to grow cash crops. result: a structural transformation of indian agriculture — land that had historically grown rice, wheat & millets was now given over to crops destined for british factories or global commodity markets. food security declined. when droughts or floods hit, there was less food grain in reserve — because the land had been planted with indigo or cotton instead. this link between high cash-revenue demands & the forced shift from food to cash crops is one of the most important long-term legacies of british land policy, & it fed directly into the famines of the late 19th century. ⚠ alert (prelims 2021 trap): economically, one of the results of british rule in india in the 19th century was: 1. increase in exports of indian handicrafts — wrong (handicrafts suffered under deindustrialisation). 2. growth in the number of indian-owned factories — wrong (no conclusive evidence). 3. commercialisation of indian agriculture ✓ — correct (the cash-revenue demand forced ryots from food crops into indigo/cotton/opium/jute/sugarcane). 4. rapid increase in urban population — wrong (no conclusive evidence). correct: (c) commercialisation of indian agriculture. memory hook: cash revenue demand → cash crops → food security collapse → late-19th-century famines.

sections.title: Reading the Three Systems Together
sections.norm: reading the three systems together. ideology, geography & fiscal pressure permanent settlement ryotwari ryots suffered high land revenue demands predatory moneylending alert (prelims 2000 trap — match list i-ii): jagirdari system zamindari system not the owner of land revenue collector with a commission ryotwari system mahalwari system (b) a-1, b-4, c-2, d-3 jagir zamindar ryot mahal permanent settlement 1793 cornwallis. why three different systems? ideology, geography & fiscal pressure all pulled in different directions. cornwallis86-93, an englishman who believed in landlordism, created permanent settlement. munro, a scotsman who believed in the yeoman farmer, created ryotwari. mahalwari was a practical compromise for regions where neither clean model fit. 6.1 — permanent settlement vs ryotwari vs mahalwari dimension permanent settlement (1793) ryotwari (1801, 1820+) mahalwari (1822, revised 1833) landowner zamindar ryot mostly ryot; sometimes taluqdar (hybrid) settlement with zamindar ryot directly mahal (via lambardar) or taluqdar assessment permanent — fixed forever (10/11 of pre-existing revenue) detailed field surveys; 50% net rental value (madras rules 1855/1864) for 30 years mahal-level; 66% rental value (net assets) for 30 years collection by district collector state officers state officers where applied bengal, orissa, bihar, benaras, north madras (bob+benaras+n. madras) sind, coorg, assam, madras, bombay (scam-b) central provinces, united provinces, punjab (cup) architect / driver cornwallis86-93 (english landlordism) alexander read + thomas munro (scottish yeoman) holt mackenzie + r.m. bird (hybrid practical) key failure absentee landlordism; ryot becomes "tenant at will"; patta collapses over-assessment; mirasidar abuse; bombay deccan riots 1875 improper surveys; summary settlement of 1856 → 1857 nw provinces/awadh epicentre 6.2 — common causes of ryot suffering across the three systems what united all three was a common outcome: ryots suffered. whether the landowner was a zamindar, the ryot himself, or a taluqdar — the combination of high land revenue demands, faulty surveys, legal vulnerability & predatory moneylending left the cultivating class worse off than they had been under the imperfect but customary protections of the mughal system. ⚠ alert (prelims 2000 trap — match list i-ii): match the description with the system: a. land allotted to big feudal landlords → jagirdari system (a jagir was assigned to a mughal mansabdar/noble — the big feudal lord of the imperial aristocracy; the zamindar passed the collected revenue upward to the jagirdar if the land was a jagir — sec. 1). b. land allotted to revenue farmers / rent collectors → zamindari system (sec. 1 is explicit — the zamindar was not the owner of land; he was a revenue collector with a commission, collecting from the cultivator & passing the rest upward. ps1793 later made him a proprietor (sec. 2.4 pillar 1), but his defining role in the chain is collection). c. land allotted to each peasant with the right to sublet, mortgage, transfer, gift or sell → ryotwari system (the ryot held legal title — sec. 3.2). d. revenue settlements made at village level → mahalwari system (mahal-level assessment after r.m. bird's 1833 revision — sec. 4.3). correct option: (b) a-1, b-4, c-2, d-3 — a=jagirdari, b=zamindari, c=ryotwari, d=mahalwari. memory hook: jagir = land allotted to the mughal feudal noble · zamindar = revenue collector with a commission · ryot = peasant with legal title & sale rights · mahal = village-level settlement.

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Drivers of British State Regulation of the EIC
sections.norm: drivers of british state regulation of the eic. the decline of eic's autonomy began nearly a century before 1857 1857 was the final nail, not the first wound. two lenses @gg company state in india governor general @br state eic and the british state / crown how much control london had over the company money: battle of plassey (1757) treaty of allahabad (toa1765) 1767 £400,000 per annum fear of another america: 1765 stamp act crisis 1783 the usa was created protecting the taxpayer: 1772 bankrupt £1.4 million loan white man's burden betrayed: great bengal famine of 1770 "nabobs" career ambitions of eic men: robert clive warren hastings73-85 select committee result: court / board of directors (cod) regulating act of 1773 treaty of allahabad 1765 hastings warren hastings. the 1857 revolt is often seen as the reason eic rule ended. but if one reads the laws parliament passed from 1773 onwards, the story is clear — the decline of eic's autonomy began nearly a century before 1857. each charter act and regulation act slowly stripped the eic of powers and transferred them to the british state. 1857 was the final nail, not the first wound. understand the two lenses through which every provision below is classified: - @gg — provisions that impacted the structure and functions of the company state in india — centralising power in the governor general and shaping india's internal administration. - @br state — provisions that shaped the relationship between eic and the british state / crown — essentially, how much control london had over the company. 1.1 — why the british state wanted to regulate the eic 1. money: after the battle of plassey (1757) and the treaty of allahabad (toa1765), the eic was receiving both plunder and bengal's land revenues. in 1767, the british state demanded £400,000 per annum from the eic arguing that state had helped eic in conquest. the state simply wanted its share. 2. fear of another america: the american revolution began in 1765 — with the stamp act crisis marking the start of the political revolution — and by 1783 the usa was created. (note: the political revolution began in 1765 with colonial resistance to british taxation; the armed war of independence began in 1775.) british settlers in 13 north american colonies had declared independence. the british state was anxious — what if eic officials, growing rich and powerful in india, did the same? 3. protecting the taxpayer: in 1772, the eic went bankrupt and was bailed out with a £1.4 million loan from the state. (think of it as a government bailing out a "too big to fail" private company today.) the state now wanted oversight to prevent reckless war expenditure. 4. white man's burden betrayed: the great bengal famine of 1770 and the spectacle of "nabobs" — corrupt eic officers returning to britain filthy rich — embarrassed the state and went against the narrative of a civilising mission in india. 5. career ambitions of eic men: senior eic officials like robert clive and warren hastings73-85 (warren hastings, governor general 1773–1785) also wanted a formal relationship with the state. association with the crown gave greater legitimacy and career advancement to such figures. 1.2 — select committee of parliament (1772) 1. parliament set up a select committee to study eic's affairs in india and to advise on what the relationship between the british state and eic should be with respect to eic's territorial possessions. (only political functions were examined — in capitalism, the state does not interfere in a company's business.) 2. result: eic retained its monopoly over trade with india. however, the court / board of directors (cod) in london were now made accountable for eic's political functions in india. this led directly to the regulating act of 1773.

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Regulating Act of 1773
sections.norm: regulating act of 1773. governor of bengal presidency was elevated to governor-general of bengal presidency (gg/bengal). general governors of bombay and madras were subordinated to gg(bengal) emergency circumstances suspended if they disobeyed bankruptcy of 1772 commercial affairs were untouched. supreme council of bengal four councillors (gg + 4) majority vote of the four councillors gg only had a casting vote legislative function matters of war and peace parliament's right to regulate eic's political affairs was legally recognised gg was to collect information court of directors (cod) cod was to submit information on political matters to the british state. supreme court was to be set up in calcutta one chief justice and three puisne judges chief justice of the calcutta supreme court sir elijah impey 1774 cases involving british-born subjects and their indian servants in bengal presidency british law corruption tenures: supreme court was set up in calcutta in 1774 conflict arose between the sc and gg's council huge distance no modern communication poor supervision by the british state centralisation of power in gg began central executive and central legislature governors of bombay and madras continued to act independently "emergency circumstances." treaty of surat (1775) governor of bombay without gg's approval 1st anglo-maratha war (1775–82). no veto over his council paralysis philip francis edmund burke impeachment trial against hastings73-85 ultimately acquitted amending act of 1781 calcutta's territory british subjects in bengal presidency eic property in fort william alert (prelims 2005 trap): consider the following statements warren hastings73-85 wrong a supreme court correct the indian penal code hastings73-85 1773 ipc 1860 hastings warren hastings cornwallis. 2.1 — @gg (provisions shaping company state structure in india) 1. governor of bengal presidency was elevated to governor-general of bengal presidency (gg/bengal). he remained governor of bengal but was now a higher authority — a general — over the governors of bombay and madras in specific matters. 2. governors of bombay and madras were subordinated to gg(bengal) in matters of war and peace, except in emergency circumstances. they could be suspended if they disobeyed. the logic was simple — high war expenditure had caused the bankruptcy of 1772, so gg was made accountable. and accountability without power is meaningless. (with great responsibility must come great power, else there is only failure.) 3. commercial affairs were untouched. in commerce, governors continued as independent regional managers. 4. a supreme council of bengal was created with four councillors (gg + 4). all decisions were by majority vote of the four councillors. gg only had a casting vote — a tiebreaker. (this was a check on any empire-building ambitions of the gg.) 5. legislative function was given to gg's council — it could make laws governing bengal and on matters of war and peace. 2.2 — @br state (provisions shaping eic–british state relationship) 1. for the first time, parliament's right to regulate eic's political affairs was legally recognised. its commercial affairs remained outside supervision. (since 1600, eic had commercial functions; since 1765 it also had political/public functions — civil, military and revenue — as it transformed into a company state.) 2. gg was to collect information on commercial and political matters and send it to the court of directors (cod) in london. cod was to submit information on political matters to the british state. 3. a supreme court was to be set up in calcutta with one chief justice and three puisne judges (pronounced "puny", i.e. junior judges) — all chosen by the crown. the first chief justice of the calcutta supreme court was sir elijah impey, appointed in 1774. (similar courts were later set up in madras in 1800 and bombay in 1823, where earlier cases involving british subjects were handled by mayor's courts.) this court was to hear cases involving british-born subjects and their indian servants in bengal presidency as per british law. 4. to curb corruption, eic officials were barred from accepting gifts from indians. 5. tenures: i. directors of eic — 4 years, not eligible for re-election immediately. ii. gg(bengal) — 5 years, re-appointable. iii. councillors — 4 years. iv. all first appointees were named directly in the act itself. future appointees were to be named by cod. 2.3 — impact of 1773 act 1. the supreme court was set up in calcutta in 1774. (note: the regulating act was passed in 1773; warren hastings73-85 formally assumed office as the first gg of bengal in 1774.) however, conflict arose between the sc and gg's council — gg wanted to handle cases arising from acts done by eic officials in their official capacity. 2. the huge distance between india and london, and no modern communication, meant poor supervision by the british state. 3. centralisation of power in gg began — the journey of what would become india's central executive and central legislature started here. 4. governors of bombay and madras continued to act independently due to the vague phrase "emergency circumstances." for example, the treaty of surat (1775) was signed by the governor of bombay without gg's approval, leading directly to the 1st anglo-maratha war (1775–82). 5. gg had no veto over his council. this lack of veto, combined with factional politics, led to paralysis. philip francis, a councillor who aspired to replace hastings73-85, constantly opposed gg's proposals and wrote complaint letters to london. this contributed to parliamentarian edmund burke leading an impeachment trial against hastings73-85 in the british parliament on corruption charges. hastings73-85 spent his life savings defending himself and was ultimately acquitted. (robert clive was similarly tried in parliament in 1773 and acquitted.) 6. the amending act of 1781 (also called bengal judicature act / declaratory act) resolved the jurisdictional conflict. the sc's jurisdiction was now: i. all cases within calcutta's territory. ii. all cases of british subjects in bengal presidency (excluding cases arising from official acts of eic officials, which went to gg's council). iii. all cases related to eic property in fort william. ⚠ alert (prelims 2005 trap): consider the following statements — 1. warren hastings73-85 was the first governor-general who established a regular police force in india on the british pattern — wrong (this provision was not part of the regulating act 1773 framework; the regular police force on british pattern was cornwallis86-93's reform under the cornwallis code 1793). 2. a supreme court was established at calcutta by the regulating act, 1773 — correct (see sec. 2.2 #3 above — supreme court at fort william, calcutta, with one chief justice + three puisne judges; sir elijah impey first cj, 1774). 3. the indian penal code came into effect in the year 1860 — correct (ipc was macaulay's draft from the 1834 law commission, enacted as the ipc 1860). correct option: (b) 2 and 3 only. memory hook: *hastings73-85 ≠ regular police force; sc at calcutta = 1773 act ✓; ipc 1860 ✓.*

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Pitt's India Act / East India Company Act (1784)
sections.norm: pitt's india act / east india company act (1784). 13 north american colonies in 1783 american war of independence (1776–83) it shifted from mere supervision to direct control of the eic. "british territorial possessions in india" double government of eic affairs (1784–1833): board of control (boc) on commercial affairs, boc's role: secret committee of three directors confidential orders directly to india all incoming and outgoing letters to india to the boc eic retained commerce and patronage the crown's prior approval was not required dual control over gg (1784–1858): indecision problem gg(bengal)'s council size 4 councillors to 3 cic became ex-officio ordinary member of gg's council gg was given both a regular vote and a casting vote. governors of bombay and madras were now subordinated to gg(bengal) more clearly defined "except in emergency circumstances" council of 3 governors of bombay and madras "conquest in india is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation." banned imperial expansion dual control of gg no effective control no veto over his council problem of indecision continued conflict arose between gg and c-i-c amending act of 1786 giving gg a veto over his council in extraordinary circumstances empowering eic to appoint the same person to both posts of gg and c-i-c cornwallis86-93 (gg 1786–1793) first person to hold both posts firsts at one place: warren hastings73-85 1st gg(bengal) william bentinck28-35 1st gg(india) charles canning56-62 louis mountbatten 1st gg of partitioned india c. rajagopalachari 1st indian gg rajendra prasad 1st president of the republic of india system of controlling eic's political affairs alert (prelims 2002 + 2004 trap cluster): 2. prelims 2004 — which pair is not correctly matched? correct option per upsc official key: (c) vernacular press act : curzon hastings73-85 ⇒ pitt's act 1784 ⇒ vernacular press act 1878 cornwallis hastings warren hastings bentinck canning dalhousie lytton. (named after british prime minister william pitt.) 1. britain lost its 13 north american colonies in 1783 after the american war of independence (1776–83), which created the usa. the anxious british state could not afford to lose india. it shifted from mere supervision to direct control of the eic. 3.1 — @br state (provisions shaping eic–british state relationship) 1. the act used the phrase "british territorial possessions in india" but still left ambiguous whether british india belonged to the british eic or the british state. 2. double government of eic affairs (1784–1833): eic's political affairs were now placed under supreme control of the british state via a newly created board of control (boc) in london — effectively a ministry for indian affairs. boc comprised six members: one of the secretaries of state who was to be the president of boc (secretary of state means a cabinet minister), the chancellor of the exchequer (i.e. british finance minister) and four members of the privy council. (the privy council was the advisory body of the crown comprising, but not limited to, the pm and cabinet — earlier it functioned like the mughal darbar or the chhatrapati's ashtapradhan.) on commercial affairs, the top authority remained the court of directors (cod of eic) while on political affairs, the top authority was now the boc of the british state. 3. boc's role: to superintend, direct and control all acts related to civil, military and revenue government of british territorial possessions in the east indies. the use of "east indies" was deliberate — it ensured territories annexed outside india (e.g. burma later) also fell under boc's authority. 4. the act also created a secret committee of three directors within the cod, through which the boc could send confidential orders directly to india — bypassing the full court of directors. this was designed for sensitive military and diplomatic matters where secrecy was paramount. 5. cod was now required to send all incoming and outgoing letters to india to the boc. (in 1773 it was information; now original letters — the anxiety of the british state about eic had clearly escalated after british settlers achieved independence by winning american war of independence 1776–83.) 6. eic retained commerce and patronage (in 1784) — the right to independently appoint eic officials including principal servants (gg, governors, c-in-c, councillors). the eic's court of directors retained the exclusive power to nominate and appoint these principal servants — the crown's prior approval was not required (a doubt on this under the 1784 act was settled by a declaratory/amending act of 1786). the crown's control instead ran through the board of control (policy) and the crown's unilateral power, since 1784, to recall/remove any servant of the eic. 7. dual control over gg (1784–1858): boc could pass binding orders both to the cod and directly to the gg, bypassing cod. therefore, gg now had two bosses in political/civil/military/revenue matters — cod and boc. in commerce, gg had only one boss — cod. 3.2 — @gg (provisions shaping company state structure in india) to resolve the indecision problem: 1. gg(bengal)'s council size was reduced from 4 councillors to 3. it was mandated that one of these 3 seats must be occupied by commander-in-chief of army as an ex-officio ordinary member (*ordinary means this was mandated in the pitts india act). hence, cic became ex-officio ordinary member of gg's council. 2. gg was given both a regular vote and a casting vote. so even with just one councillor's support, gg could create a tie and then break it in his favour. (earlier, gg needed at least two councillors to support him. here in a way one councillor is removed and his vote is given to gg.) 3. governors of bombay and madras were now subordinated to gg(bengal) in matters of war, peace and revenue. (earlier it was only war & peace; this is how the permanent settlement of 1793 could be extended to parts of madras.) 4. responsibilities of gg and governors were more clearly defined to remove the vagueness caused by the phrase "except in emergency circumstances" of regulating act 1773. 5. a council of 3 was created under each of the governors of bombay and madras. (this is where the journey of today's state assemblies and council of ministers began — though without any separation of powers.) 6. the act stipulated: "conquest in india is repugnant to the wish, policy and honour of this nation." it thus banned imperial expansion — a direct response to the heavy war expenditure of the 1st anglo-maratha war (1775–82) and 2nd anglo-mysore war (1780–84). (in reality, only one thing was repugnant and that was fiscal decline of superpower — link today's fear of de-dollarisation for us.) 3.3 — impact of 1784 act 1. dual control of gg in practice meant no effective control — gg could play his two masters (cod and boc) against each other, especially given the great distance and absence of modern communication. 2. gg still had no veto over his council and if all three councillors opposed him — the problem of indecision continued. 3. conflict arose between gg and c-i-c as the decision of war and peace rested with gg, but the right to actually use the army rested with c-i-c — creating friction. 4. the amending act of 1786 amended pitt's india act (1784) by: i. giving gg a veto over his council in extraordinary circumstances. ii. empowering eic to appoint the same person to both posts of gg and c-i-c to avoid rift. (the posts were not merged, and it was not compulsory — just permitted.) this was done due to insistence by cornwallis86-93 (gg 1786–1793) and he became the first person to hold both posts. (in british parliamentary and corporate law, a vote is granted to a physical, living person, not to a job title. therefore, even if a single man held five different commissions, he remained one "member present" and could only physically cast one ordinary vote.) 5. for record, let's have the firsts at one place: i. warren hastings73-85 = 1st gg(bengal) in 1773. ii. william bentinck28-35 = 1st gg(india) in 1833. iii. charles canning56-62 = 1st "viceroy & gg" in 1858. iv. louis mountbatten = 1st gg of partitioned india (now a symbolic head) from 15 aug 1947. v. c. rajagopalachari = 1st indian gg (june 1948 – 26 jan 1950). vi. rajendra prasad = 1st president of the republic of india. 6. the system of controlling eic's political affairs set up from 1773 to 1786 continued till 1858 with very little structural change — i.e., binding orders by boc to cod and also to gg; principal servants appointments only after crown approval(this one from 1793); original letters to boc; gg as main authority in india. ⚠ alert (prelims 2002 + 2004 trap cluster): 1. prelims 2002 — match acts to provisions: list i: a. charter act 1813 · b. regulating act 1773 · c. act of 1858 · d. pitt's india act list ii: 1. set up a board of control in britain to fully regulate the eic · 2. company's trade monopoly in india was ended · 3. power to govern transferred from eic to british crown · 4. company's directors asked to present to british government all correspondence and documents pertaining to administration correct mapping: a-2 (charter act 1813 ended eic's india trade monopoly except tea + china) · b-4 (regulating act 1773 — cod information to british state) · c-3 (goi act 1858 — crown takeover) · d-1 (pitt's india act 1784 — board of control). correct option: (a) a-2, b-4, c-3, d-1. 2. prelims 2004 — which pair is not correctly matched? (a) pitt's india act : warren hastings — wrong match (pitt's india act 1784 was british pm pitt's act; warren hastings73-85 was gg of bengal under regulating act 1773, not pitt's act). (b) doctrine of lapse : dalhousie48-56 — correctly matched. (c) vernacular press act : curzon — wrong match (vernacular press act 1878 was lytton76-80's, not curzon's). (d) ilbert bill : ripon — correctly matched. correct option per upsc official key: (c) vernacular press act : curzon is the answer marked as "not correctly matched". (note: pair (a) is also factually wrong — hastings was under regulating act 1773, not pitt's india act 1784 — but upsc chose the more flagrant lytton/curzon mismatch as the intended answer.) memory hook: *hastings73-85 ⇒ regulating act 1773 (not pitt's act); pitt's act 1784 ⇒ william pitt the younger; vernacular press act 1878 ⇒ lytton76-80 (not curzon).*

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Charter Act (1793)
sections.norm: charter act (1793). eic was now only a manager or agent of the british state sovereignty over british india was with the british state — not eic. size of boc was decreased. president of boc two junior members under him need not be from the privy council salary of boc members was now to be paid by the eic. eic's charter was renewed for 20 years first time by the parliament (not the monarch) principal servants of eic but only after approval of the crown eic retained commerce and patronage gg(bengal)'s power over his council and over governors of bombay and madras increased further. gg could supersede the authority of their governors cic’s appointed extraordinary member of gg’s council by cod (& he was) gg’s council = gg + cic + 3 ordinary members background — **could** hallmark — civil law: a code of all regulations governing bengal be framed cornwallis. 4.1 — @br state (provisions shaping eic–british state relationship) 1. the act stated: "subjects of the crown cannot acquire sovereign powers over territory on their own but only on behalf of the crown." therefore eic was now only a manager or agent of the british state. sovereignty over british india was with the british state — not eic. (however the sovereignty of mughal over whole of india was accepted until 1858.) 2. size of boc was decreased. the president of boc was retained with only two junior members under him, who need not be from the privy council. this concentrated more real authority in the president of boc and reduced factionalism. (imagine being a junior officer on a committee chaired by a very senior officer — you rarely contradict.) 3. salary of boc members was now to be paid by the eic. (this fact will later connect to the "home charges" under the drain of wealth theory of the moderates.) 4. eic's charter was renewed for 20 years — and first time by the parliament (not the monarch). (note: democracy in england was not a one-day but gradual affair.) 5. principal servants of eic (gg, governors, commander-in-chief or c-i-c of eic army, councillors) were to be appointed by the eic but only after approval of the crown. (the british state thus took hold of the head of the company state in india while its body remained under eic — making any declaration of independence from britain impossible.) 6. eic retained commerce and patronage — the right to independently appoint eic officials other than the principal servants. 4.2 — @gg (provisions shaping company state structure in india) 1. gg(bengal)'s power over his council and over governors of bombay and madras increased further. when present in madras or bombay, gg could supersede the authority of their governors. even during his absence from bengal, he could issue directives to presidencies without consulting his own council. 2. cic’s seat was given to a civilian. cic could be appointed extraordinary member of gg’s council by cod (& he was)— leading to gg’s council = gg + cic (extra-ordinary member) + 3 ordinary members. background — gg's council (1773) = gg + 4 councillors. pitt's india act 1784 mandated one seat for the commander-in-chief as ex-officio ordinary member + reduced size to gg + 3. gg's council (1784) = gg + 2 councillors + c-i-c. 1793:cic changed from ordinary member to extraordinary member of gg's council — his seat given to a civilian. under the charter act of 1793, the commander-in-chief **could** be appointed as an extraordinary (*i.e. special) member by the cod (he was appointed) gg's council (1793) = gg + cic (extra-ordinary member) + 3 councillors (ordinary members)] 3. hallmark — civil law: the act mandated that a code of all regulations governing bengal be framed. these regulations dealt with rights of persons and property. courts were now bound to follow these regulations when passing orders. all laws were to be printed in vernacular languages so people could know their rights and privileges. (notice the influence of cornwallis86-93 — his belief in rule of law and anti-corruption was evident in this provision; also these laws would be hindu and islamic laws and the permanent settlement act of 1793 for land revenue and property.)

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Charter Act (1813)
sections.norm: charter act (1813). hallmark: westernisation of india begins the narrative for ending monopoly: adam smith "wealth of nations" british national interest: industrial revolution (1750–1850) source of raw materials export market no longer in british national interest westernisation of indian society liberals, utilitarians and evangelists great ancient india was a myth "undoubted sovereignty of crown over indian territorial possessions." sovereignty was of british state — not eic. eic's monopoly over trade with india was ended. cultural colonialism began: christian missionaries push to education and social reforms the debate charter act of 1813 contributed to the 1857 revolt charter was renewed for 20 years. alert (prelims 2019 trap): consider the following statements about 'the charter act of 1813':. hallmark: westernisation of india begins 5.1 — context 1. the narrative for ending monopoly: earlier, adam smith in *"an inquiry into the nature and causes of the wealth of nations" (1776) or simply "wealth of nations" had argued for a free market economy (laissez faire) — freedom of enterprise with no state intervention. monopoly was therefore under intellectual attack since 1776 and now the liberals, utilitarians and evangelists argued that british manufacturers would industrialise india through technology transfer and fdi, which would fulfil the white man's burden (wmb). there was also heavy lobbying pressure from manufacturers and non-eic traders* to end eic's monopoly. 2. british national interest: the industrial revolution (1750–1850) was progressing in britain. british manufacturers now wanted india as a source of raw materials and as an export market. it was no longer in british national interest for a trading company (eic) to hold a monopoly over british business with india. 3. for push to westernisation of indian society, the liberals, utilitarians and evangelists argued that the idea of a great ancient india was a myth, and westernising india was the fulfilment of the white man's burden. 5.2 — @br state (provisions shaping eic–british state relationship) 1. the act re-clarified: "undoubted sovereignty of crown over indian territorial possessions." sovereignty was of british state — not eic. (note: at this stage the crown was not challenging mughal sovereignty over india as a whole.) 2. eic's monopoly over trade with india was ended. however, eic retained monopoly over tea, opium trade and trade with china. 3. cultural colonialism began: christian missionaries could now enter india for conversions with a licence either from cod or from the boc. a push to education and social reforms was mandated. eic was to spend ₹1 lakh per annum on education. the debate on western vs indian education and medium continued till 1835 when it was settled in favour of western education in english. 4. charter act of 1813 contributed to the 1857 revolt by enabling cultural colonialism and undermining indian institutions and social structures. 5. charter was renewed for 20 years. ⚠ alert (prelims 2019 trap): consider the following statements about 'the charter act of 1813': 1. it ended the trade monopoly of the east india company in india except for trade in tea and trade with china — correct (see sec. 5.2 #2 above — tea + opium + china retained as exceptions). 2. it asserted the sovereignty of the british crown over the indian territories held by the company — correct (see sec. 5.2 #1 above — "undoubted sovereignty of crown over indian territorial possessions"). 3. the revenues of india were now controlled by the british parliament — wrong (this provision actually came earlier under pitt's india act 1784, where the boc was empowered to superintend, direct and control all acts related to civil, military and revenue government of british territorial possessions in the east indies). correct option: (a) 1 and 2. memory hook: *charter 1813 = end eic india trade monopoly (tea + china + opium retained) + crown sovereignty re-clarified + missionaries + ₹1 lakh education p.a.; revenue control was pitt's act 1784.*

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Charter Act (1833) / St. Helena Act
sections.norm: charter act (1833) / st. helena act. st. helena: eic lost its monopoly commercial function was fully ended it now had only a political function, and even that only as an agent of the british state. boc's supervisory power minister for indian affairs in 1833. charter 1833 is a landmark in indian constitutional history: gg(bengal)-in-council was elevated to gg(india)-in-council. uniform laws and administration across all of british india gg(india) was made executive and legislative head of british india legislative powers of governors of bombay and madras were taken away. centralisation in gg peaked in 1833 decentralisation back to provinces began in 1861 and peaked in 1935. background — **could** now one council — two avatars (from 1833 onwards): law member (thomas macaulay) grain of separation of power between executive and legislative functions at the level of gg's council the journey of a separate legislature began here. executive meetings (1833): gg + cic + 3 ordinary members legislative meetings (1833): +1 law member (macaulay) 1834, a law commission under macaulay 1837 civil procedure code (1859), indian penal code (1860), criminal procedure code (1861) racial equality was promised: uncovenanted civil services (ucs ) and subordinate judicial positions below district judge opened to indians to reduce the cost of administration macaulay's act xi charter renewed for 20 years. alert (prelims 2003 + 2007 + 2023 trap cluster): 2. prelims 2007 — first gg of india? 2023 hastings warren hastings bentinck. - st. helena: the island of st. helena in the south atlantic — one of the remotest places on earth — was taken over from eic by the british state. it was a port of call for refueling and repair of ships. napoleon was sent here after his defeat in 1815 and died here in 1821. (the fact that it was remote enough to keep napoleon in permanent exile tells you how isolated it was — and the eic had been using it as a maritime asset.) 6.1 — @br state (provisions shaping eic–british state relationship) 1. eic lost its monopoly over tea trade, opium trade and trade with china. its commercial function was fully ended — eic would no longer conduct business. it now had only a political function, and even that only as an agent of the british state. (the "double government of eic affairs (1784–1833)" thus ended — no more dual identity of trader and ruler.) 2. boc's supervisory power was extended to all administrative affairs in india — not just policy and laws, but also supervision over implementation of laws, officers, their transfers and postings. (link to the 2023 supreme court case on delhi administrative affairs between centre and delhi's elected executive — the question of who controls bureaucracy in a territory is always politically charged.) 3. the president of boc was renamed minister for indian affairs in 1833. 6.2 — @gg (provisions shaping company state structure in india) 1. charter 1833 is a landmark in indian constitutional history: gg(bengal)-in-council was elevated to gg(india)-in-council. as eic's territory expanded and britishers entered india in larger numbers post-1813, the need for uniform laws and administration across all of british india became pressing. (one country, one law, one executive is a hallmark of good governance — think of gst today or the napoleonic code of 1804.) 2. gg(india) was made executive and legislative head of british india — empowered to make and administer laws for whole of british india, equally applicable to indians and britishers alike. 3. legislative powers of governors of bombay and madras were taken away. (they were restored via the indian councils act of 1861.) 4. therefore: centralisation in gg peaked in 1833. decentralisation back to provinces began in 1861 and peaked in 1935. (this is the journey of federalism and centre-state relations in pre-independence india.) 5. background — gg's council (1773) = gg + 4 councillors. pitt's india act 1784 mandated one seat for the commander-in-chief as ex-officio ordinary member + reduced size to gg + 3. gg's council (1784) = gg + 2 councillors + c-i-c. 1793:cic changed from ordinary member to extraordinary member of gg's council — his seat given to a civilian. under the charter act of 1793, the commander-in-chief **could** be appointed as an extraordinary (*i.e. special) member by the cod (he was appointed) gg's council (1793) = gg + cic (extra-ordinary member) + 3 councillors (ordinary members)] now one council — two avatars (from 1833 onwards): one law member (thomas macaulay) was added to gg(india)'s council to draft uniform laws. this introduced the grain of separation of power between executive and legislative functions at the level of gg's council (not at gg's level — he remained head of both). the journey of a separate legislature began here. i. executive meetings (1833): gg + cic + 3 ordinary members participated in day-to-day administration, collecting taxes, or fighting a war. ii. legislative meetings (1833): the above executive members were joined by +1 law member (macaulay) to draft new laws. 6. in 1834, a law commission was set up under macaulay for codification of laws. work completed by 1837 but deliberation and updates continued. full implementation post-1857 via — civil procedure code (1859), indian penal code (1860), criminal procedure code (1861). (in 2024, india replaced these with bharatiya nyaya sanhita / bns, bharatiya nagarik suraksha sanhita / bnss, and bharatiya sakshya adhiniyam.) 7. racial equality was promised: "no person to be deprived of chance to enter eic service on grounds of religion, race, birth or colour." uncovenanted civil services (ucs — roughly equivalent to today's group b) and subordinate judicial positions below district judge (e.g. munsifs) were opened to indians to reduce the cost of administration. further, in 1836 macaulay's act xi brought europeans under the civil jurisdiction of the company's courts (courts where indians were judges in lower courts; these were separate from british crown-run supreme courts in presidency towns). 8. charter renewed for 20 years. ⚠ alert (prelims 2003 + 2007 + 2023 trap cluster): 1. prelims 2003 — which provision was not made in the charter act of 1833? (a) the trading activities of the eic were to be abolished — correct (this was in 1833 — sec. 6.1 #1). (b) the designation of the supreme authority was to be changed as the governor-general of india in council — correct (this was in 1833 — sec. 6.2 #1). (c) all law-making powers to be conferred on governor-general in council — correct (this was in 1833 — sec. 6.2 #2 + #3, bombay/madras legislative powers taken away). (d) an indian was to be appointed as a law member in the governor-general's council — wrong (this was not in 1833 — the law member appointed was macaulay, an englishman; indian law member came much later). correct option: (d) is the provision not made in the 1833 act. 2. prelims 2007 — first gg of india? 1. robert clive was the first governor-general of bengal — wrong (warren hastings73-85 was the first gg of bengal under regulating act 1773). 2. *william bentinck28-35 was the first governor-general of india — correct* (under charter act 1833, the gg/bengal designation was changed to gg/india, and bentinck28-35 was the holder of that designation in 1833). correct option: (b) only 2. 3. prelims 2023 — by which act was the gg of bengal designated as the gg of india? (a) regulating act 1773 — wrong (this act created gg/bengal). (b) pitt's india act 1784 — wrong (this act created the boc + double government, did not redesignate). (c) charter act 1793 — wrong (this act increased gg's power but did not redesignate). (d) charter act 1833 — correct (this act elevated gg/bengal to gg/india — sec. 6.2 #1). correct option: (d) charter act 1833. memory hook: *charter 1833 = gg/bengal → gg/india + bentinck28-35 first gg/india + macaulay law member (englishman, not indian) + st. helena act + eic commercial function fully ended.*

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Charter Act (1853)
sections.norm: charter act (1853). charter was now valid only "till parliament specifies otherwise" no fixed renewal period eic lost patronage covenanted civil services (ccs) were opened to indians revenues of british india were placed under control of the british parliament the gg's council: background — **could** then in 1833 one law member was added legislative sittings macaulay in 1853, the one law member of 1833 was promoted to full executive (ordinary) member 6 new legal members were added executive meetings: gg + cic + 4 councillors (ordinary members) legislative meetings: +6 legal members full legislative council sat as [gg + cic + 4] + 6 = 12 persons 1833 only gg's council could make laws for all of british india province-specific laws gg was empowered to appoint a lieutenant governor (lg) for bengal 1854, dalhousie48-56 frederick james halliday as the 1st lg of bengal dalhousie. 7.1 — @br state (provisions shaping eic–british state relationship) 1. charter was now valid only "till parliament specifies otherwise" — no fixed renewal period. (a sword was now permanently hanging over eic's neck, as the charter was eic's founding document.) 2. eic lost patronage — the power to independently appoint its officials — as a civil services examination was introduced. the 1st exam was held in 1855 in london. from this point, eic hardly controlled policies in india. 3. covenanted civil services (ccs) were opened to indians (ucs had been opened in 1833). 4. revenues of british india (i.e. the budget) were placed under control of the british parliament. 7.2 — @gg (provisions shaping company state structure in india) 1. deeper separation of powers between executive and legislative functions was introduced within gg(india)'s council by adding 6 more legal members. 2. the gg's council: background — gg's council (1773) = gg + 4 councillors. pitt's india act 1784 mandated one seat for the commander-in-chief as ex-officio ordinary member + reduced size to gg + 3. gg's council (1784) = gg + 2 councillors + c-i-c. 1793:cic changed from ordinary member to extraordinary member of gg's council — his seat given to a civilian. under the charter act of 1793, the commander-in-chief **could** be appointed as an extraordinary (*i.e. special) member by the cod (he was appointed) gg's council (1793) = gg + cic (extra-ordinary member) + 3 councillors (ordinary members)] (don't include gg as a member for prelims; unless the question explicitly says "total strength of the council", the word "members" means just the councillors.) 3. then in 1833 one law member was added — but only for legislative sittings. the first person to hold this job was macaulay. 4. in 1853, the one law member of 1833 was promoted to full executive (ordinary) member and 6 new legal members were added (4 representing bengal, bombay, madras, northwest provinces + chief justice of calcutta sc + 1 regular judge of calcutta sc). thus in 1853: i. executive meetings: gg + cic + 4 councillors (ordinary members) (the promoted law member now being the 4th ordinary member) participated. ii. legislative meetings: the above executive members were joined by +6 legal members — hence the full legislative council sat as [gg + cic + 4] + 6 = 12 persons working together to draft laws. 5. since 1833, only gg's council could make laws for all of british india. but every country has issues that need province-specific laws. the four provincial representatives in council would draft such laws. (e.g. the rent act of 1859 for bengal would be drafted by the bengal member.) 6. gg was empowered to appoint a lieutenant governor (lg) for bengal to reduce his workload. (since 1833, gg was effectively pm of british india and also cm of bengal — an impossible dual burden.) in 1854, dalhousie48-56 (dalhousie, gg 1848–1856) appointed frederick james halliday as the 1st lg of bengal. 7.3 — governor vs lieutenant-governor (lg) feature governor lieutenant-governor (lg) jurisdiction presidencies (e.g. bengal, bombay, madras). the oldest, most prestigious centres of power. provinces (e.g. punjab, up, bihar). newer or subdivided territories. appointed by the british crown directly. the governor-general of india (with crown approval). background usually british aristocrats, peers, or high-profile politicians imported from london. usually veteran indian civil service (ics) officers; career bureaucrats. autonomy & reporting high. could correspond directly with the secretary of state in london. low. strictly subordinate; all communication went through the governor-general. executive council yes. ruled collectively as the "governor-in-council." no. ruled as a sole executive for the vast majority of the colonial period. 7.4 — evolution of the council (1833–1853) year executive meetings legislative meetings 1833 gg + cic + 3 (since 1793) +1 law member (macaulay) 1853 gg + cic + 4 (law member made executive member) +6 legal members added

sections.chapterTitle: Constitutional History of EIC's British India (1773–1858)
sections.title: Government of India Act (1858) / Act for Better Government of India
sections.norm: government of india act (1858) / act for better government of india. eic was blamed for mismanagement of indian affairs and for the 1857 revolt eic's monopoly on violence was broken ending eic rule absentee sovereignty with direct rule of the british state free traders (non-eic merchants) indian western educated middle class greater accountability and modernisation britain wanted stronger control over india after 1857. eic rule was replaced by direct rule of the british state in british india. policy of subordinate union towards indian rulers: mughal sovereignty over indian territory was legally ended. british crown was now sovereign over the whole of india: british india 63% of territory, 78% of population ruled directly by gg princely states ruled by indian princes under a legal relationship called paramountcy with the crown sovereignty, defence, communications and foreign affairs (sov, d, c, fa) domestic affairs remained with the prince zafar37-57 pensioned off to rangoon in burma secretary of state for india (sos) replaced the president of boc council of india (india council) board of control (boc 1784) sos with 15 members seven members of eic's cod were absorbed into the india council dual control over gg (1784–1858) ended: "viceroy & gg" only to the sos no change in the actual powers of gg(india) as "viceroy & gg." in 1858, canning56-62 became the 1st viceroy held only in london queen victoria's proclamation (1858) transfer of governance from the east india company to the british crown disclaimed any intention to annex indian states placed the indian administration under the british crown. religious non-interference fair treatment of all subjects opportunity in public service without discrimination of race or creed granted amnesty royal titles act (1876) empowered queen victoria to take the title of kaesar-i-hind / empress of india 1877, lytton76-80 imperial / delhi darbar victoria was coronated as kaesar-i-hind alert (prelims 2006 + 2014 trap cluster): 1. prelims 2006 — two-statement on charter 1833 + goi 1858: wrong under the goi act 1858, the british parliament abolished the east india company altogether and undertook the responsibility of ruling india directly correct option: (b) only 2. 2. prelims 2014 — objects of queen victoria's proclamation (1858): to disclaim any intention to annex indian states to place the indian administration under the british crown (a) 1 and 2. goi 1858 eic canning56-62 zafar bahadur shah zafar canning dalhousie lytton. 8.1 — background 1. the eic was blamed for mismanagement of indian affairs and for the 1857 revolt in which many british were killed and eic's monopoly on violence was broken. 2. the british public demanded ending eic rule — replacing absentee sovereignty with direct rule of the british state. (since charter act 1793, sovereignty was with british state but it was absent and ruled india through its agent, the eic.) 3. free traders (non-eic merchants) wanted direct british rule, claiming eic ignored their interests. 4. the indian western educated middle class wanted direct british rule for greater accountability and modernisation. (the industrial revolution and democracy in britain came under british state rule — not under a company. these educated indians had internalised this and wanted the same for india.) 5. britain wanted stronger control over india after 1857. 8.2 — @br state (provisions shaping eic–british state relationship) 1. eic rule was replaced by direct rule of the british state in british india. (a touch of irony — in 1856, eic had annexed awadh on grounds of maladministration; now eic was removed on the same grounds. in 1874, eic was formally dissolved.) 2. policy of subordinate union towards indian rulers: mughal sovereignty over indian territory was legally ended. (mughal state 1526–40, 1556–1858 — legally came to an end. note: mughal sovereignty was not over whole of india — e.g. travancore was never part of the mughal state and the sikh state was legally independent.) british crown was now sovereign over the whole of india: i. british india (approximately 63% of territory, 78% of population) was to be ruled directly by gg. ii. princely states were to be ruled by indian princes under a legal relationship called paramountcy with the crown — whereby sovereignty, defence, communications and foreign affairs (sov, d, c, fa) rested with crown while domestic affairs remained with the prince. (think of it as article 370 without democracy.) 3. zafar37-57 (bahadur shah zafar, last mughal emperor, 1837–1857) was pensioned off to rangoon in burma. 4. secretary of state for india (sos) replaced the president of boc / minister for indian affairs as the main authority and director of policy in india. 5. council of india (india council) replaced the board of control (boc 1784) in london — headed by sos with 15 members. seven members of eic's cod were absorbed into the india council for continuity and experience. 6. dual control over gg (1784–1858) ended: as "viceroy & gg" he now reported only to the sos. (as gg, he was ruler of british india. as viceroy, he was representative of the crown in india — like a vice-captain representing the captain when the captain is not on the field.) 7. no change in the actual powers of gg(india) as "viceroy & gg." 8. in 1858, canning56-62 (charles canning, gg 1856–1862) became the 1st viceroy. 9. the same civil services exam continued and continued to be held only in london. 8.3 — queen victoria's proclamation (1858) the queen victoria's proclamation (1858) announced the transfer of governance from the east india company to the british crown. the proclamation specifically: a) disclaimed any intention to annex indian states (directly walking back from dalhousie48-56's doctrine of lapse and the awadh annexation 1856). b) placed the indian administration under the british crown. c) promised religious non-interference, fair treatment of all subjects, and opportunity in public service without discrimination of race or creed (a re-affirmation of the charter act 1833 racial-equality clause). d) granted amnesty to those who had taken part in the 1857 revolt, with limited exceptions. 8.4 — royal titles act (1876) 1. the royal titles act (1876) by british parliament empowered queen victoria to take the title of kaesar-i-hind / empress of india. 2. in 1877, lytton76-80 (lytton, viceroy 1876–1880) organised the imperial / delhi darbar where victoria was coronated as kaesar-i-hind. (she had been unofficially using this title since 1858.) ⚠ alert (prelims 2006 + 2014 trap cluster): 1. prelims 2006 — two-statement on charter 1833 + goi 1858: 1. the charter act, 1833 abolished east india company monopoly of indian trade — wrong (charter 1833 ended eic's commercial function entirely — tea + opium + china monopoly all gone — but the eic's indian-trade monopoly itself had already been ended by charter act 1813. so the statement is technically wrong: 1833 ended all remaining commercial monopolies (tea + opium + china), not the indian-trade monopoly which was 1813's act.) 2. *under the goi act 1858, the british parliament abolished the east india company altogether and undertook the responsibility of ruling india directly — correct (see sec. 8.2 #1 above — eic rule replaced by direct rule of british state; eic formally dissolved 1874)*. correct option: (b) only 2. 2. prelims 2014 — objects of queen victoria's proclamation (1858): 1. *to disclaim any intention to annex indian states — correct (see sec. 8.3 (a) above — direct walk-back from dalhousie48-56's doctrine of lapse)*. 2. *to place the indian administration under the british crown — correct (see sec. 8.3 (b) above — the proclamation announced the transfer)*. 3. to regulate east india company's trade with india — wrong (by 1858 the eic's commercial function had already been ended (charter 1833) and the company itself was being dissolved; the proclamation had nothing to do with regulating eic trade). correct option: (a) 1 and 2. memory hook: *goi 1858 = crown takeover + eic abolished + sos for india + 15-member india council + canning56-62 = 1st viceroy + mughal sovereignty legally ended (zafar37-57 to rangoon); queen victoria's proclamation 1858 = "no annexation" walkback + crown takeover + religious non-interference + race/creed-blind public service + amnesty.*
