sections.title: Conquest in India: Policy vs Drift
sections.norm: conquest in india: policy vs drift. eic india act 1784 1775–82 1780–84 british state was responsible for conquest that charter state provided military aid at critical junctures: battle of plassey (1757) was won with the help of the royal british military 1857 revolt nearly overthrew company rule arrival of royal military in october 1857 state financed the company: trade monopoly over britain's east indies trade (1600–1813) king charles ii rented bombay dowry from the portuguese in 1661 £10 per annum in 1668 thomas roe jahangir05-27's court to lobby for eic interests bailed out eic with a £1.4 million loan in 1772 50,000 1698 00,000 1767 1558 1603 state controlled the empire builders: after 1784, principal servants (the sub-imperialists themselves) could be appointed only after crown approval. binding orders could be passed directly to gg. eic as foreign policy tool: dominated world trade via eic 1st afghan war (1838–42) fought by eic part of the great game between britain and russia in the 19th century alert (prelims 1996 trap — match gg/cic names to acts): governor of bengal presidency under regulating act 1773 warren hastings73-85 (1773–85) cornwallis86-93 (1786–93) cornwallis = code 3 governor general of india under charter act 1833 dalhousie48-56 (1848–56) dalhousie = code 2 viceroy & gg under act of 1858 canning56-62 minto = code 4 gg & crown representative under goi act 1935 wavell wavell = code 1 correct option: (a) a-3, b-2, c-4, d-1 reg act 1773 cornwallis86-93 1833 dalhousie48-56 1858 1905–10 goi 1935 1943–47 jahangir dalhousie cornwallis hastings warren hastings bentinck canning. 9.1 — no official policy of conquest on the surface, britain had no official policy of conquest. imperial expansion was largely driven by sub-imperialism — the policies, actions and personal ambitions of senior eic officials in india. many eic officials built political careers back home after their india tenures. in fact, pitt's india act (1784) explicitly banned conquest in india — a response to the heavy expenditure of the 1st anglo-maratha war (1775–82) and 2nd anglo-mysore war (1780–84). 9.2 — british state responsibility however, the british state was responsible for conquest, for the following reasons: a) tools of conquest were given by the state: eic's charter gave it the right to wage war, acquire and administer territory. that charter was issued initially by the crown and later by parliament. b) state provided military aid at critical junctures: the battle of plassey (1757) was won with the help of the royal british military. when the 1857 revolt nearly overthrew company rule, it was the arrival of royal military in october 1857 that turned the tide. (the state assisted both in the initiation and the survival of conquest.) c) state financed the company: the state granted eic a trade monopoly over britain's east indies trade (1600–1813). king charles ii rented bombay — received as dowry from the portuguese in 1661 — to eic for just £10 per annum in 1668. thomas roe was sent as a state representative to jahangir05-27's (emperor jahangir, r. 1605–1627) court to lobby for eic interests. the state bailed out eic with a £1.4 million loan in 1772. d) follow the money trail: over 1,50,000 pounds were given to the british monarch during the 17th century in return for charter renewals. in 1698, parliament gave monopoly to a "new company" because it offered a £2 million loan vs eic's £7,00,000. in 1767, eic was mandated to pay £4,00,000 per annum to the state. many parliamentarians and even queen elizabeth i (1558–1603) were shareholders of eic and received dividends. e) state controlled the empire builders: after 1784, principal servants (the sub-imperialists themselves) could be appointed only after crown approval. binding orders could be passed directly to gg. (those who did the empire-building were, in effect, favourites of the state.) f) eic as foreign policy tool: britain dominated world trade via eic, much as today large mncs serve as instruments of a state's foreign policy (think google or private banks as tools for sanctions against russia, or airtel's role in africa's telecom revolution). the 1st afghan war (1838–42) fought by eic was part of the great game between britain and russia in the 19th century. 9.3 — prelims 1996 — gg-to-act match ⚠ alert (prelims 1996 trap — match gg/cic names to acts): list i (office) — a. governor general of presidency of fort william in bengal (under regulating act 1773) · b. governor general of india (under charter act 1833) · c. governor general and viceroy of india (under indian councils act 1858) · d. governor general and crown representative (under government of india act 1935) list ii (personality) — 1. archibald percival wavell · 2. james andrew broun-ramsay (dalhousie48-56) · 3. charles cornwallis (cornwallis86-93) · 4. gilbert john elliot-murray-kynynmond (minto) · 5. louis mountbatten correct mapping per chapter logic + upsc official key: a. governor of bengal presidency under regulating act 1773 — held first by warren hastings73-85 (1773–85), then by cornwallis86-93 (1786–93) — upsc's cornwallis = code 3 is the answer. (note: upsc framed the question around cornwallis86-93's tenure in this office, not hastings73-85's, because cornwallis86-93 is the more famous holder.) b. governor general of india under charter act 1833 — bentinck28-35 was the first gg/india in 1833, but the chapter has noted dalhousie48-56 (1848–56) as the most famous gg/india of the era — dalhousie = code 2. c. viceroy & gg under act of 1858 — canning56-62 was 1st viceroy in 1858; upsc's question framed around the era's most famous viceroy — minto = code 4 (minto ii was viceroy 1905–10 under the post-1858 framework). d. gg & crown representative under goi act 1935 — wavell was gg & crown representative 1943–47 — wavell = code 1. correct option: (a) a-3, b-2, c-4, d-1 (cornwallis – dalhousie – minto – wavell). memory hook: *gg/bengal under reg act 1773 ⇒ cornwallis86-93 era; gg/india under charter 1833 ⇒ dalhousie48-56 era; viceroy & gg under 1858 framework ⇒ minto era (viceroy 1905–10); gg & crown representative under goi 1935 ⇒ wavell (1943–47).*

sections.chapterTitle: EIC Administration: Judiciary, Civil Services, Police
sections.title: Administration as the Machinery of the State
sections.norm: administration as the machinery of the state. machinery of the state build this machinery from scratch judiciary, civil services & police. note for mains: economic impact drain of wealth + economic critique de-industrialisation + destruction of indian handicrafts sepoy army composition + grievances administrative skeleton economic & military flesh. administration is the machinery of the state — how the state implements its policies, laws & schemes on the ground. when the eic transitioned from a trading company to a company state (charter act 1833 ended its commercial function), it had to build this machinery from scratch — or, more accurately, decide how much of the existing indian machinery to keep & how much to replace. this chapter covers three pillars: judiciary, civil services & police. ⚠ note for mains: upsc mains pyqs mapped to administration overwhelmingly ask about the economic impact of british rule — drain of wealth, de-industrialisation & the sepoy army as imperial tool. these cannot be answered from this chapter alone: - drain of wealth + economic critique → moderates / drain theory chapter. - de-industrialisation + destruction of indian handicrafts → british imperial ideology + land revenue systems chapters. - sepoy army composition + grievances → 1857 revolt chapter. this chapter provides the administrative skeleton; those chapters supply the economic & military flesh.

sections.title: Judiciary
sections.norm: judiciary. not walking into a blank slate established legal traditions which law should apply written down or left to judges' discretion lawyers be allowed to represent parties political, social & financial implications two separate hierarchies civil matters criminal matters civil matters sadar diwani adalat pandits judged hindu cases maulvis judged muslim cases criminal matters sadar nizamat adalat islamic law governed criminal proceedings kazis were the actual judges treaty of allahabad 1765 diwani nizamat dual government orientalism muhammad reza khan collecting land revenue great bengal famine of 1770 ended the dual government direct administration diwani (civil) courts nizamat (criminal) courts imprisoned without trial separation of revenue & judicial powers 18 mofussil courts regulating act of 1773 supreme court in calcutta in 1774 madras (1800) bombay (1823) 1775 gentoo code (1776) 1778 al-hidayah the hedaya (1791) code of 1781 cornwallis86-93 father of civil services permanent settlement of 1793 (ps1793) separation of powers diwani adalats provincial court of appeal shifted from murshidabad to calcutta charter act 1793 four provincial courts of circuit anglo-muhammadan law indian penal code 1860 example a: the "weapon" rule replaced by "intent" rule islamic law: the weapon used intent of the accused example b: the end of "blood money" (diyat) diyat a major crime is an offence against the state example c: the abolition of mutilation amputation of limbs british modification: outlawed mutilation hard labour removed indians from all senior positions european officials lawyers were now permitted to appear in courts increase in litigation separation of powers (key reason): abolition of court fees: creation of a legal profession: alert (prelims 2010 trap): correct: (c). separated judicial & revenue functions ryotwari areas separation of judicial & revenue powers was ended. concentration of power in one official ryotwari system elphinstone charter act of 1833 law member thomas macaulay law commission (1834) civil procedure code (cpc) — 1859 indian penal code (ipc) — 1860 criminal procedure code (crpc) — 1861 opened to indians bentinck28-35 provincial courts of appeal courts of circuit 1835 act xxix of 1837 sadar diwani & sadar nizamat adalats in the northwest provinces indian high courts act 1861 high courts in madras, bombay & calcutta in 1862 goi act 1935 federal court permanent settlement 1793 hastings warren hastings cornwallis bentinck akbar. 2.1 — why judicial reform was so complicated the eic was not walking into a blank slate. it was entering a society with established legal traditions, different religious communities & a functioning — though imperfect — court system. the questions it had to answer were not simple: - which law should apply — hindu, islamic, or british? - should laws be written down or left to judges' discretion? - what should be the hierarchy of courts? - should lawyers be allowed to represent parties? - should judges be indians or british? - in which language should courts function? each carried political, social & financial implications. the answers changed as british confidence, ambition & administrative needs evolved. 2.2 — the mughal judicial system in bengal (before 1772) the mughal system in bengal had two separate hierarchies — one for civil matters & one for criminal matters. civil matters — local level up to the sadar diwani adalat at the suba (provincial) level. in inter-personal matters (marriage, inheritance), personal laws of hindus & muslims were applied. pandits judged hindu cases; maulvis judged muslim cases. at the top, the diwan served as chief justice of the sadar diwani adalat (diwani = finance, land revenue & civil justice). around this time muhammad reza khan, the naib nazim, held the posts of chief justice of both sadar diwani adalat & sadar nizamat adalat. for land revenue & non-personal civil disputes, original jurisdiction lay with the zamindar at the local level (in his revenue court, the kachari). appeals went up: zamindar → amil (provincial revenue officer at district level; the chapter uses "amil" here only because it is a snapshot of the corrupted, mutated system of 18th-century bengal — the canonical mughal-administrative term is amalguzar) → sadar diwani adalat at the provincial capital (murshidabad), presided over by the diwan or naib diwan. criminal matters — nizamat adalats (commonly called faujdari adalats) at the district level, with the sadar nizamat adalat at the top. since the mughal state was an islamic state, islamic law governed criminal proceedings — applied uniformly regardless of religion. at the local village level, the zamindar held petty criminal jurisdiction alongside his police duties. for major crimes, cases bypassed the zamindar & went straight to the district faujdari adalat. strict division of labour: the kazis were the actual judges who pronounced verdicts (with muftis providing expert interpretation of islamic law), while the district faujdar (executive police chief) secured the accused & physically executed the sentence. the naib nazim headed the sadar nizamat adalat. (civil courts were religion-specific — your judge depended on your faith. criminal courts were state-uniform — the law of the ruling state applied to everyone.) 2.3 — the dual government period (1765–1772) after the treaty of allahabad 1765, the eic gained diwani rights over bengal — revenue administration, treasury & control of property / civil courts. (modern welfare duties like health/education were not included — those were traditionally handled by private/religious patronage, not the mughal government.) the nawab retained nizamat (law & order). this created the dual government. guided by orientalism, the eic did not rush to impose its own system. muhammad reza khan continued to head both diwani & nizamat on the eic's behalf. indian officials remained effective decision-makers on the ground. the eic was mainly concerned with collecting land revenue. this hands-off approach had a predictable outcome. revenue collection was poor. law & order deteriorated — made catastrophic by the great bengal famine of 1770, which killed roughly one-third of bengal's population. 2.4 — direct government (1772) and the judicial plan of warren hastings73-85 in 1772, hastings73-85 (governor from 1772, gg of bengal 1773–1785) ended the dual government & assumed direct administration of both diwani & nizamat. rationale: eic administration, based on rule of law & equality before law, would be fairer & more efficient — & would firmly establish british authority. (ideology shifts slightly from pure orientalism toward a hybrid: rule more directly, but still use indian legal frameworks.) new judicial structure: - in diwani (civil) courts, the british dc was made the judge, assisted by pandits & maulvis for hindu & muslim personal law. personal laws continued in marriage/inheritance. - in nizamat (criminal) courts, kazis & muftis continued as judges but were now supervised by the european dc. the british considered law & order too sensitive to fully replace. - the sadar diwani adalat & sadar nizamat adalat were now headed by the governor (from 1773, gg of bengal) & his council members. from 1772 to 1774, naib nazim muhammad reza khan was imprisoned without trial, accused of corruption & poor law-and-order maintenance. when conditions still failed to improve, he was released in 1774 & reinstated as head of the sadar nizamat adalat. 2.4.1 — changes of 1773 by warren hastings73-85 two further adjustments: 1. a proper attempt at separation of revenue & judicial powers — an officer who served as dc was not to also serve as a judge. in practice, overlap remained, but the principle was established. 2. to bring justice physically closer to people, diwani adalats at the district level were replaced by 18 mofussil courts, each headed by a european judge. (mofussil refers to rural areas & countryside districts below the district headquarters.) 2.4.2 — the supreme court (1774) the regulating act of 1773 led to the establishment of a supreme court in calcutta in 1774, specifically to hear cases involving british subjects in bengal, under british law. (of british people, by british judges, applying british law — a completely separate judicial track.) supreme courts followed in madras (1800) & bombay (1823). the supreme court was entirely separate from the indian court hierarchy. 2.4.3 — codification of laws in 1775, a committee of 11 pandits compiled hindu law into a single coherent legal code so courts could engage in uniform interpretation. the english translation was published as the gentoo code (1776). (the word "gentoo" came from the portuguese "gentios" — a derogatory term for hindus, used because hindus worshipped multiple gods unlike monotheistic christians.) in 1778, a similar effort was made for islamic law. due to mughal rule, islamic law was already well organised. the eic simply translated the most authoritative existing arabic legal manual — the al-hidayah — first into persian by indian scholars, then into english as the hedaya (1791). the code of 1781 made written orders compulsory & prescribed rules for court functioning. 2.5 — the cornwallis code of 1793 (judiciary) cornwallis86-93 (gg 1786–1793) introduced the most systematic judicial reform of the early period. he is rightly called the father of civil services — but his influence on the judiciary was equally significant. 2.5.1 — why did cornwallis86-93 reform the judiciary? he had just introduced the permanent settlement of 1793 (ps1793), creating a new class of large zamindars as private property owners. for this to work, zamindars needed secure property rights — courts they could trust, revenue officials who could not harass them. an officer who collected your tax should not also be the judge hearing your appeal against his own actions. so cornwallis86-93 properly implemented separation of powers at the level of the dc — the district collector was stripped of all judicial powers & confined to revenue collection & administration. 2.5.2 — in civil matters the 18 mofussil courts were replaced by diwani adalats at the district level & city courts for urban areas. bengal was divided into four divisions — patna, murshidabad, calcutta & dacca — & a provincial court of appeal was set up in each. these heard appeals from district diwani adalats & city courts. appeals from provincial courts went to the sadar diwani adalat, shifted from murshidabad to calcutta. personal laws of hindus & muslims continued in civil matters. ps1793 governed land revenue disputes. per charter act 1793, all regulations for governing bengal were codified, written orders made compulsory & laws printed in vernaculars so people could know their rights. 2.5.3 — in criminal matters faujdari / nizamat adalats at the district level were abolished. four provincial courts of circuit were set up in the four divisions. a court of circuit is a court that physically moves around its division, hearing cases in different areas in rotation. this eliminated the need for a district-level criminal court. appeals from the courts of circuit went to the sadar nizamat adalat. islamic law continued in criminal matters — but with british legal modifications. this hybrid became known as anglo-muhammadan law. for about 70 years — until the indian penal code 1860 — courts applied this hybrid legal code. 2.5.4 — anglo-muhammadan law in practice — three examples example a: the "weapon" rule replaced by "intent" rule - islamic law: under strict hanafi jurisprudence, whether a killing was capital murder depended on the weapon used. killing with a sharp iron instrument (sword) was murder. strangling, drowning or killing with a heavy stone was often treated as a lesser crime — the instrument was not "designed" to draw blood. - british modification: cornwallis86-93 abolished this loophole. the intent of the accused was declared the deciding factor, not the instrument. this aligned criminal liability with the modern legal principle of mens rea. example b: the end of "blood money" (diyat) - islamic law: murder was largely treated as a private dispute between families. heirs of the victim had the legal right to pardon the killer in exchange for financial compensation — blood money (diyat). - british modification: the british modified the law so relatives could no longer pardon a murderer. this established the modern principle that a major crime is an offence against the state, not just a private injury. example c: the abolition of mutilation - islamic law: the standard punishment for serious theft or dacoity was amputation of limbs — cutting off a hand or foot. - british modification: the eic completely outlawed mutilation. replaced with sentences of hard labour & rigorous imprisonment — typically 7 to 14 years. 2.5.5 — personnel and a new profession — lawyers cornwallis86-93 was authoritarian. he removed indians from all senior positions. all courts were headed by european officials. kazis & muftis were retained only as assistants, not judges. the office of naib nazim was abolished. one progressive change: lawyers were now permitted to appear in courts. this created a new professional class — the indian lawyer — & along with ps1793 (which made land a tradeable commodity), also a class of property dealers. 2.5.6 — why the new system increased litigation after the permanent settlement (1793) there was an increase in litigation due to changes made to the judicial system (which in practice made it inefficient) via the cornwallis code of 1793: 1. separation of powers (key reason): the district collector was stripped of all judicial and magisterial powers. previously, the collector could swiftly and informally resolve revenue disputes on the spot. after 1793, all of these disputes had to be formally filed in the diwani adalats (civil courts). 2. abolition of court fees: cornwallis initially abolished court fees to make justice "accessible." this instantly flooded the courts with both genuine and frivolous suits. the fees had to be reimposed just two years later in 1795. 3. creation of a legal profession: the formal recognition of lawyers (vakils) and a rigid hierarchy of appeals meant cases were deliberately prolonged and appealed. ⚠ alert (prelims 2010 trap): by a regulation in 1793, the dc was deprived of his judicial powers & made the collecting agent only. why? 1. (a) efficiency of revenue collection — partial truth, not the principal motivation. 2. (b) judicial power must be european-only, revenue can be indian — wrong (cornwallis86-93 in fact removed indians from all senior positions including revenue). 3. (c) absolute power in one person was undesirable ✓ — correct (sec. 2.5.1: separation of powers; the post-ps1793 zamindar class needed independent courts). 4. (d) judicial work demanded deep india knowledge — partial truth, not principal motivation. correct: (c). memory hook: dc stripped of judicial powers in 1793 = separation-of-powers principle; post-ps1793 zamindar class needed independent courts. 2.6 — judicial system in ryotwari areas the bengal model of separated judicial & revenue functions worked in a zamindari system. but in ryotwari areas — where the ryot was recognised as the direct landowner — conditions were very different. a very large number of small landowners meant a very large number of land-related disputes. district courts were physically distant for poor ryots in villages. in madras, the bengal system was therefore replaced in 1814 on munro's advice. separation of judicial & revenue powers was ended. the european dc & his subordinates were given judicial powers so disputes could be resolved at the ground level. (less paperwork, less travel, faster justice — at least in theory.) this led to greater indianisation at the lower judiciary, since dc's subordinates included indian officials. the downside was enormous concentration of power in one official. the dc now collected taxes, maintained order & judged disputes — including disputes arising from his own tax collection decisions. in bombay, the same ryotwari system was applied in 1819 by elphinstone, a follower of munro's philosophy. 2.7 — charter act 1833 (judicial impact) the charter act of 1833 made the gg of india the single central legislative authority for all of british india, & the laws passed were to apply equally to indians & britishers alike. (a major conceptual shift — one law for everyone, regardless of race.) one law member was added to the gg's council. thomas macaulay was appointed, & a law commission (1834) was set up under him to systematically codify all laws. codification was substantially complete by 1837, but full implementation came after 1857: - civil procedure code (cpc) — 1859 - indian penal code (ipc) — 1860 - criminal procedure code (crpc) — 1861 subordinate judicial positions below the rank of district judge were opened to indians. (overall impact on the common indian: justice had become psychologically distant — new laws were western, complex & unfamiliar. physically distant for rural areas. financially distant — legal fees few could afford. the system was more systematic; it served the educated & propertied far better than the poor.) 2.8 — reforms by william bentinck28-35 (gg 1828–33; gg of india 1833–35) bentinck28-35 abolished the divisional courts — both the provincial courts of appeal (civil) & the courts of circuit (criminal) that cornwallis86-93 had created. reason: these courts had become parking grounds for inefficient officers (punishment postings for non-performers), contributing to high pendency. high-ranking officers also meant high state expenditure. ended as a fiscal-prudence measure. judicial powers & pending cases transferred to district judges. in 1835, bentinck28-35 replaced persian in courts — with vernaculars in lower courts & english in higher courts. legal backing via act xxix of 1837. removal caused anxiety among muslim elites — persian education had been an important pathway to administrative careers. (context on persian: introduced under the delhi sultanate in the 13th century. major boost when humayun, to get persia's safavid dynasty military support to reclaim his throne from the suri dynasty (1540–55), accepted the condition of promoting persian. akbar56-05, with finance minister todar mal, made persian compulsory for all administrative records.) he also created sadar diwani & sadar nizamat adalats in the northwest provinces (the portion of awadh annexed in 1801, given full province status in 1836), so people from this region did not have to travel to bengal to file appeals. 2.9 — indian high courts act, 1861 the indian high courts act 1861 led to the establishment of high courts in madras, bombay & calcutta in 1862. the calcutta high court was created by merging three existing courts: the sadar diwani adalat, the sadar nizamat adalat & the supreme court at calcutta. (finally ended the dual-track system of separate courts for indians & british.) 2.10 — government of india act 1935 — federal court the goi act 1935, implemented from 1937, established a federal court — the direct ancestor of today's supreme court of india. it dealt with inter-governmental disputes (centre vs province, province vs province) & heard appeals from high courts. (today's supreme court, set up under the constitution of india 1950, continues this role with expanded jurisdiction.)

sections.chapterTitle: EIC Administration: Judiciary, Civil Services, Police
sections.title: Civil Services
sections.norm: civil services. service patronage-based system merit-based administrative cadre how many indians would be allowed in nomination 1800–1806: 1806–1858: 1858 onwards: cornwallis86-93 first proper structure to civil services covenanted civil service (ccs) uncovenanted civil service (ucs) charter act 1853 strict seniority for promotions founder of civil services in india alert (prelims 2010 trap): charter act of 1833 charter act of 1853 civil service examination civil services commission (1854) 1855 maximum age limit 23 years held only in london 1864 satyendranath tagore 1867 indianisation of civil services two core demands simultaneous examination in india response was hostile keep indians out of senior positions statutory civil services act 1878 sosforindia goi act 1858 1887 three tiers 1892 by executive order not a provision of ica 1892 inm context: 25% indians in senior positions goi act 1919 public service commission for india 33% indians all india services (ais) central civil services 1924 20% of senior positions filled by promotion from pcs. 40% indians 40% europeans 50:50 ratio public service commission ais central services provincial services october 1926 goi act 1935 federal public service commission provincial public service commissions 1947 26 january 1950 union public service commission (upsc) article 378 ww1 wellesley cornwallis hastings warren hastings lansdowne bentinck lytton ripon dufferin. 3.1 — what a "service" means in any organisation, officials may be simply employed, or organised into a service. a service means a pre-defined career path, fixed rules for pay, promotion & removal, & a clear structure of seniority & accountability — the difference between being an employee & being a member of a cadre. the history of civil services under the eic is a story of moving from chaotic patronage-based system toward a structured, merit-based administrative cadre — with the additional tension: how many indians would be allowed in? 3.2 — recruitment — from patronage to examination initially, eic officials were recruited by nomination — not merit. posts were either purchased or handed out through patronage. eic directors actively lobbied british parliamentarians with offers of jobs for their sons. this system bred corruption & incompetence. 3.3 — training until 1800, essentially on the job. then: - 1800–1806: fort william college, calcutta — set up by wellesley98-05 for training in indian laws, customs & languages. - 1806–1858: haileybury college, london (east india college). - 1858 onwards: british universities. 3.4 — cornwallis86-93 — founder of civil services cornwallis86-93 brought the first proper structure to civil services. he reorganised eic officers into two tiers: covenanted civil service (ccs) (like today's group a) — senior officers who signed a formal legal contract, called a "covenant," with the eic's court of directors in london before sailing to india. high defined pay, clear career path. under cornwallis86-93, reserved strictly for europeans. uncovenanted civil service (ucs) (like today's group b) — junior officers hired locally in india by the gg or provincial governors. lower pay, less formal. this became the space where indians were allowed to serve — initially in very low-level clerical roles, gradually expanding to deputy collectors & deputy magistrates by the 1830s–40s as the empire grew & required cheaper local administrators. one important clarification: cornwallis86-93 did not introduce merit-based selection for entry. entry remained patronage-based — nomination by the eic's court of directors in london — right until the charter act 1853. what he did introduce was strict seniority for promotions once an officer was already inside. eic bosses in london could no longer simply push their underqualified relatives into senior ranks over experienced officers. he also massively increased salaries to reduce corruption incentive, curbed private trade by eic officials, & introduced separation of powers — the dc was stripped of judicial powers in 1793. (this is why he is called the founder of civil services in india — he converted a corrupt, patronage-ridden set of employees into a structured, professionalised service.) ⚠ alert (prelims 2010 trap): who among the following ggs created the covenanted civil service of india which later came to be known as the indian civil service? 1. (a) hastings73-85 — wrong (1st gg of bengal under reg act 1773; introduced judicial plan but not the ccs structure). 2. (b) wellesley98-05 — wrong (set up fort william college 1800 for ccs training, but did not create the ccs service structure). 3. (c) cornwallis86-93 ✓ — correct (sec. 3.4: reorganised eic officers into ccs + ucs tiers; raised salaries massively; curbed private trade; introduced strict seniority for promotions; founder of civil services in india; ccs later renamed indian civil service (ics) in 1892 by executive order under lansdowne88-94 on aitchison commission 1887 recommendations (not by ica 1892 — admin order of the era)). 4. (d) bentinck28-35 — wrong (opened ucs to indians under charter 1833 + encouraged some senior indian recruitment, but did not create the ccs structure). correct: (c) cornwallis86-93. memory hook: cornwallis86-93 = founder of ccs (covenanted) + ucs (uncovenanted) two-tier structure 1793; ccs later renamed ics by executive order in 1892 (lansdowne88-94, per aitchison commission 1887 — not by ica 1892). 3.5 — charter act 1833 and bentinck28-35 (1828–35) the charter act of 1833 opened the uncovenanted civil services to indians — primarily to reduce administration cost by using cheaper indian labour in junior roles. bentinck28-35 went slightly further & encouraged recruitment of indians to some senior positions. 3.6 — charter act 1853 — exam opened to indians the charter act of 1853 was a landmark — it mandated a civil service examination for the ccs, & indians were eligible to appear. in 1854, a select committee of parliament under macaulay recommended replacing patronage-based recruitment with exam-based recruitment for a permanent civil service. this led to the establishment of the civil services commission (1854) in london, which held its first examination in 1855. but eligibility on paper did not mean access in practice. the maximum age limit ranged from 18 to 23 — kept deliberately low. in 1859, the crown reduced the maximum permissible entry age for the cs exam to 23 years. (it was subsequently reduced further to 22 in 1860, 21 in 1866, & 19 in 1876 — implemented in 1878 so as to not impact preparing aspirants.) the syllabus was dominated by english literature. (this was designed to produce what macaulay had called "brown sahibs": indians educated in english culture & values, culturally loyal to britain.) the exam was held only in london. for an indian candidate, this meant the cost of travel to england, inferior preparation compared to british candidates, & a syllabus that rewarded english cultural knowledge over indian. in 1864, satyendranath tagore (brother of rabindranath tagore) became the first indian to clear the ccs exam. in 1867, four more indians cleared it. 3.7 — the fight for indianisation (1860 onwards) from 1860 onwards, the western-educated indian middle class — the very product of british educational policy — began demanding indianisation of civil services. two core demands: - simultaneous examination in india (not just london). - a higher maximum age limit. the british response was hostile. post-1857, british administrators were insecure about indian assertion & determined to keep indians out of senior positions. 3.7.1 — statutory civil services act, 1878 (under lytton76-80) parliament had given directions for indianisation in 1870. instead of holding the exam in india or raising the age limit, lytton76-80 (viceroy 1876–1880) brought in lateral entry via nomination through the statutory civil services act 1878. under this, loyal elite indians could be nominated to posts previously reserved for ccs officers — but only carefully vetted, politically loyal individuals were selected. the statutory authority over the rules, regulations, syllabus, & age limits for the ccs was vested in the sosforindia after goi act 1858. (*note- books put responsibility on lytton76-80 for reducing age limit & credit ripon80-84 for increasing age limit, as sosforindia was greatly influenced by gg's input — but that's not the legal truth.*) 3.7.2 — aitchison commission (1887) dufferin84-88 appointed it in 1886; report came in 1887. it recommended dropping the terms “covenanted” & “uncovenanted” & dividing services into three tiers — imperial civil service (ics), provincial civil service (pcs) & subordinate civil service. implementation came in 1892 by executive order under lansdowne88-94 (not a provision of ica 1892 — classic 🚨 exam trap; per ch 28 sec. 9). ccs → ics, ucs → pcs, & the statutory civil services (created 1878) were abolished (partly through moderate nationalist pressure). provincial civil services were recruited through exams & selection held in india to ensure greater indian participation in administration. 3.8 — islington commission (1912) inm context: swadeshi movement (1905–11), delhi conspiracy case (1912), ghadar movement (1913–15), home rule leagues (1916–18), & british wartime claims of fighting for democracy during ww1 (1914–19). the commission was set up in 1912 but published its report only in 1917. it recommended 25% indians in senior positions — via exam & via promotion from pcs (*1st time reservation recommendation). however, it rejected the nationalist demand for simultaneous examination in india, arguing that educational standards in india were not uniform enough. (the real reason, unstated: the british feared an exam in india would produce more indian officers than they were comfortable with.) 3.9 — montagu-chelmsford reforms / goi act 1919 inm context: rowlatt satyagraha (1919). the goi act 1919 mandated: - simultaneous examination in india (first held in 1922). - setting up of a public service commission for india (established in 1926). - gradual increase to 33% indians in senior positions (*1st time reservation implementation). the ics was also restructured. since goi act 1919 divided subjects between centre & provinces (dyarchy), the ics was split into all india services (ais) & central civil services. (the structure of ais & central services we see today in india is essentially this 1919 structure, continued & modified by the constitution.) 3.10 — lee commission / royal commission on superior civil services (1923) inm context: khilafat movement (1920–24) & non-cooperation movement (1920–22). set up to examine demands for indianisation of ais & central services, with equal numbers of british & indian members. its report (1924) recommended: - 20% of senior positions filled by promotion from pcs. - 40% indians in senior positions via exam. - 40% europeans in senior positions via exam. - achieve 50:50 ratio between indians & europeans within 15 years via exam. - recommended that the public service commission, as originally mandated by goi act 1919, should be established. - services were to continue as: ais (ics, ips, indian forest service, etc.), central services (foreign affairs, customs, railways, etc.) & provincial services (health, education, etc.). the public service commission was finally set up in october 1926 with ross barker as the first chairman. 3.11 — goi act 1935 inm context: hindustan republican army (1924), cpi (1925), hsra (1928), anti-simon agitations (1928), lahore conspiracy case (1928), civil disobedience movement (1930–34), chittagong armoury raid (1930–33), martyrdom of bhagat singh, sukhdev, rajguru, bhagwati charan vohra & chandrashekhar azad (1931). the goi act 1935 made federal distribution of subjects between centre & provinces a formal constitutional structure. it mandated: - a federal public service commission (set up in 1937, replacing the 1926 psc — the direct predecessor of today's upsc). - provincial public service commissions for each province or group of provinces. by 1947, more than 50% of civil service positions had been indianised. with the inauguration of the constitution of india on 26 january 1950, the federal public service commission became the union public service commission (upsc) under article 378 of the constitution. (article 378 is a transition provision — it ensures membership of the british-era upsc & state pscs continued seamlessly into the post-1950 bodies. articles 315 & 316 govern the upsc & state pscs. article 312 governs all india services.)

sections.title: Police
sections.norm: police. law & order as extremely sensitive mughal system of policing was left untouched overall head: rural districts (sarkars): faujdars towns & urban areas: kotwals villages: english magistrates (dc/dm) very few dms oppress the masses freely new police structure ended the police powers of zamindars thanas daroga district magistrate (dm) district collector & district magistrate dc (revenue role) dm (law-and-order role) nexus quickly developed oppression of the rural poor 1799 1802 madras torture commission report of 1855 irish constabulary model road-tested it province by province sindh (annexed 1843) punjab (post-annexation, 1849). bombay (1853). madras (1859). 1st police commission (1860) 1861 police act a common upsc trap: charles napier (napier gave the blueprint; m.h. court's commission drew the national map using it.) police act, 1861 provincial police clear hierarchy of specialist posts inspector general (ig) superintendent of police (sp) sub-inspector (si) si → sp → ig sp to dc/dm ig to lg / governor organisational chart police raj indians were excluded from all senior positions formalisation into a structured cadre 1893 2nd police commission sir andrew fraser imperial police (ip) provincial police service (pps) deputy superintendent of police (dysp) criminal investigation department (cid) department of criminal intelligence (1903) not 1920 montagu-chelmsford reforms (goi act 1919) indianization by 1931 from 1939 1948 indian police service (ips) all india services act, 1951 1861 built the structure, 1902–03 built the service, 1948–51 built the ips. article 312 ww2 permanent settlement 1793 hastings warren hastings cornwallis wellesley canning curzon. 4.1 — the inherited system (pre-1781) the eic treated law & order as extremely sensitive. the mughal system of policing was left untouched for the longest time. under the mughal system in bengal: - overall head: naib nazim (deputy subadar). - rural districts (sarkars): under faujdars (sarkar here means sub-divisional unit, not government — different meanings in different regions). - towns & urban areas: under kotwals. - villages: zamindars held police duties & paid village watchmen from their own resources. 4.2 — warren hastings73-85's reforms of 1781 the great bengal famine of 1770 had led to a sharp increase in crime. hastings73-85 replaced faujdars with english magistrates (dc/dm) in rural districts. zamindars retained their police duties under the dm's supervision. the problem: very few dms, & supervision of zamindars was poor. zamindars, with little oversight, continued to oppress the masses freely. 4.3 — the daroga system of cornwallis86-93 (1793) cornwallis86-93 introduced a new police structure consistent with his overall vision: - ended the police powers of zamindars — under ps1793, zamindars were to be agrarian capitalists, not local police authorities. - divided each district into thanas of 30 square miles each. - each thana was under a new officer called daroga (indian), appointed & supervised by the dm. - the english district magistrate (dm) was made the absolute, supreme head of law & order within his district. rather than creating an intermediary like an english naib nazim or inspector general, cornwallis86-93 centralised ultimate oversight of criminal & police administration directly in the gg & his council. chain of command: darogas → dm → central government. 4.3.1 — dc and dm: two roles, usually one person in most of british india — & in india today — the district collector & district magistrate are the same person holding two roles simultaneously. cornwallis86-93 separated the judicial function from this officer (dc/dm lost power to be a judge), but revenue & law-and-order functions remained combined. the two hats: - dc (revenue role) — collection of land revenue, managing government land, maintaining land records & collecting various taxes. (direct british descendant of the mughal diwani / amalguzar function.) - dm (law-and-order role) — head of the district's criminal administration; coordinates with the sp to maintain peace, prevent riots & issue executive orders such as section 144 of crpc. (direct british descendant of the mughal nizamat / faujdari function.) 4.3.2 — result: the daroga–zamindar nexus a daroga–zamindar nexus quickly developed. zamindars bribed darogas. zamindars continued to maintain private armed men (lathiyals). this nexus became the primary instrument of oppression of the rural poor throughout the early 1800s. the british attributed this failure to "indian corruption" rather than to the structural weaknesses of the system. in 1799, wellesley98-05 restored police powers to zamindars — essentially acknowledging that the daroga system had not worked. in 1802, the daroga system was extended to madras but was later abolished there too due to its failures. the resulting atrocities of revenue officials were exposed by the madras torture commission report of 1855, which led to corrective measures. 4.4 — the police act, 1861 the daroga system (1793) had failed. the british now looked for a proven alternative & found it in the irish constabulary model — a centralised, hierarchical, quasi-military police force effective in ireland since 1787, designed as much for suppressing political agitation as for preventing ordinary crime. (the british were not primarily building a crime-prevention force — they were building a political control mechanism. the irish model, born out of colonial experience in ireland, was purpose-built for this.) 4.4.1 — province-by-province road-test (pre-1861) before applying it nationally, the british road-tested it province by province: - sindh (annexed 1843) — charles napier was the military general who conquered sindh in 1843 & set up the sindh police on the irish constabulary model immediately after conquest. - punjab (post-annexation, 1849). - bombay (1853). - madras (1859). the 1st police commission (1860) set up by canning56-62 under m.h. court simply formalised what had already proved effective on the ground. it borrowed heavily from this successful sindh model when drafting the 1861 police act. a common upsc trap: many guidebooks incorrectly state that charles napier headed this commission. he did not. (napier gave the blueprint; m.h. court's commission drew the national map using it.) 4.4.2 — the police act, 1861 the police act, 1861 was passed in march 1861 by the gg's council, as last restructured by charter act 1853. (the indian councils act 1861 came in august 1861 & created the imperial legislative council (ilc).) the police act (1861) created the provincial police structure across all provinces: - provincial police — each province of british india to have its own police organisation. - clear hierarchy of specialist posts from top to bottom: - inspector general (ig) — head of provincial police, reporting to the governor / lieutenant governor (lg). - superintendent of police (sp) — in charge of district police, reporting to the dc / dm. - sub-inspector (si) — in charge of the thana, reporting to sp (not to dc as earlier). operational accountability ran upward through the police chain: si → sp → ig. political accountability ran to civilian authority: sp to dc/dm, ig to lg / governor. this was the organisational chart — nothing more. in 1861, the british simply posted military officers or nominated european men into these senior posts. no formal cadre, no competitive exam, no unified service — just employees of provincial governments. the posts existed; the service did not yet. from 1857 onwards, a "police raj" was created — indians were excluded from all senior positions. the emphasis was on effective policing, intelligence collection & political surveillance. 4.4.3 — formalisation into a structured cadre the formalisation into a structured cadre happened in stages: - 1893 — first open competitive examination for senior police posts held in london. top candidates were appointed as probationary assistant superintendents of police, under the authority of the secretary of state for india. - 1902–03 — curzon99-05 (viceroy 1899–1905) set up the 2nd police commission under sir andrew fraser, which submitted its report in 1903. the fraser commission organised superior police officers into a single, unified, all-india cadre — officially the imperial police (ip) (informally indian police). its scheme was implemented from ~1905: - provincial police service (pps) created — a new rank, deputy superintendent of police (dysp), accommodated indians at the officer level, but always junior to the british ip. - criminal investigation department (cid) set up in every province, along with a central intelligence bureau — the department of criminal intelligence (1903), forerunner of today's ib. - but the imperial police (ip) itself was kept closed to indians — the fraser commission did not recommend the appointment of indians to the ip, preserving racial superiority at the top. - 1920 — direct entry into the elite ip was officially thrown open to indians (simultaneous exams in england & india from 1921). this was largely a result of the montagu-chelmsford reforms (goi act 1919), which mandated the gradual indianization of the superior civil & police services. - by 1931 — only 20% of sps were indians. the british were reluctant to hand over district-level police command to indians. - from 1939 — more indians were posted as sp due to non-availability of british candidates, most of whom were being recruited for ww2 (1939–45). - 1948 — the ip was administratively replaced by the indian police service (ips) via a home ministry resolution. formal statutory backing came via the all india services act, 1951. 1861 built the structure, 1902–03 built the service, 1948–51 built the ips. (today's ips is an all india service under article 312 of the constitution, with state police under state governments — directly inheriting this 1861 framework.)

sections.chapterTitle: EIC Administration: Judiciary, Civil Services, Police
sections.title: Three-Pillar Administrative Legacy
sections.norm: three-pillar administrative legacy. structural improvement followed political convenience, not principle triggered by a crisis concession wrested by the indian national movement never voluntarily indianised economically necessary politically unavoidable codified law organised civil service hierarchical police independent india would inherit hastings warren hastings cornwallis. the eic's administrative evolution across judiciary, civil services & police reveals a consistent pattern: structural improvement followed political convenience, not principle. each major reform was either triggered by a crisis (great bengal famine 1770, 1857 revolt) or was a concession wrested by the indian national movement after sustained pressure. the british never voluntarily indianised their administration beyond what was economically necessary (to reduce costs) or politically unavoidable (to manage nationalist pressure). what they did leave behind, however inadvertently, was a set of institutions — codified law, an organised civil service, a hierarchical police — that independent india would inherit, adapt & build upon. pillar inherited (mughal) foundational reform mid-19th c. consolidation modern legacy judiciary diwani adalats (civil, pandits/maulvis) + nizamat adalats (criminal, kazis/muftis/faujdars) hastings73-85's 1772 plan + 1774 calcutta sc; cornwallis code 1793 with anglo-muhammadan law charter 1833 (macaulay law commission 1834) → cpc 1859 + ipc 1860 + crpc 1861; indian high courts act 1861 (hcs at madras/bombay/calcutta 1862) goi 1935 federal court (1937) → supreme court of india 1950; cpc/ipc/crpc replaced 2024 by bns/bnss/bsa civil services mansabdari nobility under mughal patronage cornwallis86-93 (1793) = founder of ccs + ucs two-tier structure; salaries raised, seniority for promotions charter 1853 = exam mandated, indians eligible (london-only); ics renamed by exec order 1892 (lansdowne, per aitchison 1887 — not by ica 1892) lee commission 1923 → psc 1926 → goi 1935 federal psc (1937) → upsc 1950 (article 378); ais under article 312 police naib nazim → faujdars (rural) + kotwals (towns) + zamindars (villages) hastings73-85's 1781 reforms; cornwallis86-93's daroga system 1793 (failed via daroga–zamindar nexus) irish constabulary road-test (sindh 1843 napier → punjab 1849 → bombay 1853 → madras 1859); 1st police commission 1860 (m.h. court) → police act 1861 (march 1861) 2nd police commission 1902-03 (fraser) → imperial police (ip) cadre; 1948 home min. resolution → ips; ais act 1951 + article 312

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: The "Renaissance" Framing
sections.norm: the "renaissance" framing. renaissance 14th-century intellectual rebirth 19th-century bengal bore a striking resemblance socio-religious reform. the word "renaissance" originally named western europe's 14th-century intellectual rebirth — a conscious recovery of ancient learning, driven by reason & aimed at human welfare. 19th-century bengal bore a striking resemblance. the same problems existed: an oppressive priestly establishment misusing social power, absence of modern education, birth-based privilege & deep poverty. the response was similar too — reformers reached back into ancient indian scriptures to restore what was great, while applying reason & rationality to remove what was not. (note: the european renaissance triggered a cascading chain — reformation in religion, end of feudalism in society, growth of capitalism in economy, enlightenment in polity, & the scientific & industrial revolutions. the bengal renaissance had a similar cascading effect. it fed a modern western educated middle class, & from that class emerged the leaders of the indian national movement.) why call it socio-religious reform & not simply social reform? because in india, religion did not merely coexist with social practice — it determined it. sati, child marriage, caste hierarchy, widow remarriage, polygamy — all were justified by selective interpretations of religious texts. you could not touch the social practice without confronting the religious sanction behind it.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: The Social Issues
sections.norm: the social issues. major social ills reformers identified idol worship is not inherently a social ill ramakrishna paramhansa polytheism is inherently pluralistic. the major social ills reformers identified: education, idolatry, priestcraft, child marriage, widow remarriage, female infanticide, polygamy, polytheism & casteism. (mnemonic: educated female italian prime minister did pre poll campaign — education, female infanticide, idolatry, priestcraft, child marriage, widow remarriage, polygamy, polytheism, casteism.) idol worship is not inherently a social ill — it helps a worshipper concentrate spiritual energy, & not all priests are negative figures. ramakrishna paramhansa himself was a temple priest. polytheism is inherently pluralistic & thus secular in character. social ills arise when there is absence of genuine spirituality, when social power is misused & when society is fragmented by divisions. the problem was never the practice itself but its distortion.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Why Social Reform Began in the 19th Century
sections.norm: why social reform began in the 19th century. 3.1 — the role of the british liberals, utilitarians & evangelists 3.2 — cultural nationalism as a response cultural nationalism 3.3 — western education (1835 onwards) doctrine of reason. 3.1 — the role of the british after 1813, the british moved away from orientalism (which had treated indian culture & learning as worthy of respect & study) towards a new coalition of liberals, utilitarians & evangelists who actively supported western education & social reform. the evangelists also promoted conversion to christianity — which simultaneously created fear among indians about the survival of their religion, & created pressure to reform from within. 3.2 — cultural nationalism as a response as the british moved away from orientalism, they began arguing that the greatness of ancient india was a myth. indian social reformers pushed back. their response was rooted in cultural pride — we will prove you wrong by actually cleaning up what has gone wrong & recovering what was great. this is the spirit of cultural nationalism that ran through all 19th-century reform movements — mild before 1857, far stronger after. 3.3 — western education (1835 onwards) reformers educated in western thought were exposed to the doctrine of reason — no practice, however old or sacred-seeming, is beyond rational scrutiny. this became their primary intellectual tool for challenging irrational & inhumane social practices.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Who Led the Reforms — Over Time
sections.norm: who led the reforms — over time. 4.1 — first half of the 19th century white man's burden (wmb) 4.2 — second half of the 19th century post-1857, things changed sharply far less interested in social reform more overtly racist. 4.1 — first half of the 19th century early social reformers were western-educated men from upper castes. they were willing to seek the colonial government's help in passing reform legislation. the british, for their part, were willing to assist — it fitted the ideology of the white man's burden (wmb) — the colonial-era belief that it was the "civilised" englishman's duty to uplift "backward" peoples. 4.2 — second half of the 19th century post-1857, things changed sharply. the british became far less interested in social reform & far more overtly racist in their criticism of indian civilisation. (note: the 1857 revolt shook british confidence & bred contempt towards indian society.) the reform movement shifted to more culturally nationalistic leaders, some of whom did not have western education at all.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Classifying the Reformers
sections.norm: classifying the reformers. method beliefs goals 5.1 — by method did not attempt to build a mass movement tried to build mass movements purely on rationality both rationality & scripture 5.2 — by beliefs logic & rationality were the final authority vedas to be infallible 5.3 — by goals gradual reform radical & immediate reform. three useful axes — by their method, their beliefs & their goals. 5.1 — by method some reformers did not attempt to build a mass movement at all — ram mohan roy is the primary example. others went beyond the educated elite & deliberately tried to build mass movements: keshab chandra sen, swami dayanand saraswati & swami vivekananda. a third group relied purely on rationality — most notably derozio & his young bengal. they did not succeed in creating a mass movement because their target population was religious, & pure rationality without engagement with faith failed to move them. those who used both rationality & scripture were more successful — roy, ishwar chandra vidyasagar, swami dayanand saraswati & swami vivekananda. 5.2 — by beliefs some reformers held that logic & rationality were the final authority. if there was a conflict between rational argument & scriptural text, they chose rationality. this characterised the pre-1857 reformers — roy & his contemporaries — reflecting that era's milder cultural nationalism & greater comfort with western intellectual frameworks. others held the vedas to be infallible. for them, the answer to social ills lay not in importing western reason but in recovering the pure original teaching of the vedas, which they argued had been corrupted over centuries. swami dayanand saraswati, ramakrishna paramhansa & swami vivekananda belonged to this camp. this reflects the stronger cultural nationalism of the post-1857 era. 5.3 — by goals some believed in gradual reform — roy, debendranath tagore, the brahmo samaj & the prarthana samaj. they moved slowly, deliberately avoiding issues considered too sensitive to hindu society such as caste & marriage practices. their fear was alienation from the very masses they wanted to uplift. others pushed for radical & immediate reform. derozio's young bengal, keshab chandra sen, swami dayanand saraswati, swami vivekananda & ishwar chandra vidyasagar took up even the most sensitive issues without apology, & wanted change at a fast pace.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Child Sacrifice at Sagar Island (1803)
sections.norm: child sacrifice at sagar island (1803). sagar island wellesley. in 1803, wellesley98-05 banned the practice of child sacrifice at sagar island (sagar dwip, where the ganga meets the bay of bengal — a major hindu pilgrimage site) in bengal. an early sign that the colonial government was willing to use executive power against specific social practices.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Henry Vivian Derozio & Young Bengal (Late 1820s–1831)
sections.norm: henry vivian derozio & young bengal (late 1820s–1831). 7.1 — derozio hindu college, calcutta not question everything 7.2 — what the derozians did 1838 society for acquisition of general knowledge 7.3 — why they failed total faith in western rationality unbridgeable gap separation of powers freedom of press indianisation of the civil services trial by jury. 7.1 — derozio henry vivian derozio was a eurasian teacher at hindu college, calcutta. he died suddenly in december 1831. during his active years — late 1820s until his death — his followers were not called "young bengal." they were known as "derozians," "ultra-reformers," or simply "the radicals." the label young bengal came later. (note: the retrospective label "young bengal" echoes "young italy" — mazzini's movement of the same era. both were educated youth breaking from a tradition-bound older generation.) derozio's core method was simple — question everything. he pushed his students to challenge orthodoxy (the tendency to follow old practices blindly without rational examination) using reason, western sciences & in some cases outright atheism. 7.2 — what the derozians did in 1838, young bengal set up the society for acquisition of general knowledge under tarachand chakravarty as president & ramgopal ghosh as vice president. a forum for debating western sciences & social reforms. notice what is absent — no attempt to build a mass movement, no engagement with the religious sentiments of the population. 7.3 — why they failed young bengal's total faith in western rationality, combined with complete disregard for religion, created an unbridgeable gap between them & the masses — who were religious. you cannot move a population by appealing purely to reason when faith is the very air they breathe. (note: they ate beef & drank wine, causing considerable public scandal. radical ideas plus radical lifestyle made for great controversy but poor mass politics.) they did, however, share with roy a set of political demands ahead of their time — separation of powers, freedom of press, indianisation of the civil services & trial by jury (where guilt is decided by a group of citizens rather than a single judge — a more democratic mechanism).

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Raja Ram Mohan Roy & the Brahmo Samaj (1828)
sections.norm: raja ram mohan roy & the brahmo samaj (1828). 8.1 — raja ram mohan roy father of modern india a scholar challenged the british claim of christian superiority universalism calcutta unitarian committee (1821) 8.2 — roy's beliefs polytheism monotheistic translated the upanishads brahmoism doctrine of reason other-worldliness doctrine of karma doctrine of incarnation sati sati is murder as per every shastra 8.3 — roy on education for roy, rationality was supreme vedas were not infallible western education & western sciences sanskrit college in calcutta in 1824 benaras sanskrit college (1791) jonathan duncan sanskrit college, calcutta (1824) amherst23-28 ishwar chandra vidyasagar macaulay's minute on indian education (1835) english education act 1835 8.4 — roy's method — use the state roy bentinck28-35 macaulay 8.5 — roy's administrative demands separation of powers freedom of press indianisation of the civil services trial by jury amherst bentinck. 8.1 — raja ram mohan roy ram mohan roy is called the father of modern india — & the title is not unearned. he was the first major figure to grasp that social reform in india could not be separated from religious reform, because religion determined social practice. he was also the first to attempt a genuine intellectual synthesis between indian tradition & western modernity. roy was a scholar of extraordinary range — the vedas, sanskrit, persian literature, & christian scripture. he challenged the british claim of christian superiority not by dismissing christianity but by engaging it seriously. his own position was universalism — the belief that all religions lead to the same god. for hindus, the vedas were the supreme path. but he did not argue for conversion & did not treat hinduism as the only road. he believed in cultural synthesis — take the best of western modernity, combine it with the best of indian tradition. (note: rabindranath tagore would later hold the same position.) roy also founded the calcutta unitarian committee (1821) — a forum that reflected his universalist engagement with christian theological ideas alongside hindu reform. 8.2 — roy's beliefs roy's primary intellectual concern was polytheism. he argued — from the upanishads themselves — that authentic hinduism is monotheistic, that it points to one god. he translated the upanishads into bengali specifically to prove this. brahmoism, the religious movement he founded, is essentially defined by this commitment to monotheism. beyond polytheism, he condemned idolatry, priestcraft, child marriage, the poor condition of widows, infanticide, casteism, & polygamy. he also applied the doctrine of reason to challenge three specific religious ideas: • other-worldliness — belief in heaven & hell as literally real places. • doctrine of karma — the idea that present circumstances are determined by acts in a past life. • doctrine of incarnation — the idea of gods taking human birth. on sati, his position was categorical — through careful textual analysis, he argued that sati is murder as per every shastra. this was a crucial move — not just a moral argument but a scriptural one, because he knew that only a scriptural argument would carry weight with the british government & with orthodox hindus. 8.3 — roy on education for roy, rationality was supreme & the vedas were not infallible. (note: this is where roy differs from the post-1857 reformers like dayananda & vivekananda, for whom the vedas were beyond question.) he wanted the colonial government to spend public money on western education & western sciences — not on indian classical learning. when the government proposed setting up a sanskrit college in calcutta in 1824, roy actively opposed it. (note: two colleges sound similar; do not confuse them. benaras sanskrit college (1791) was set up by jonathan duncan during cornwallis's tenure specifically to train pandits for administering hindu law — a purely administrative need of the colonial state. sanskrit college, calcutta (1824) was set up much later under amherst23-28 on the recommendation of the orientalist faction within the general committee of public instruction. this is the college roy opposed. it later became famous when ishwar chandra vidyasagar became its principal in 1851, opened its doors to non-brahmin students, & introduced western sciences alongside sanskrit.) roy's advocacy for english-medium western education directly influenced macaulay's minute on indian education (1835) — roy died in 1833, two years before the policy was finalised — which became the foundational policy document for british education in india & led to the english education act 1835. 8.4 — roy's method — use the state roy was willing — strategically & deliberately — to use british legislative & executive power for social reform. he worked closely with bentinck28-35, thomas macaulay, & the philanthropist david hare. this cooperation was key to the most significant legislative victory of his life. 8.5 — roy's administrative demands beyond social reform, roy also demanded structural political changes — separation of powers, freedom of press, indianisation of the civil services, & trial by jury. (note: young bengal made exactly the same demands — this was the emerging consensus among the western educated middle class of the era.)

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Sati
sections.norm: sati. 9.1 — sati defined eran pillar inscription of bhanugupta no practice of sati rig veda post-vedic smritis 9.2 — why it persisted into the 19th century social pressure, greed, & patriarchy coerced suicide or outright murder inheritance greed & patriarchal control 9.3 — the scale of the problem johar sanskritisation 9.4 — how it was abolished opposed sati since 1813 campaign was led by roy bentinck28-35 radhakanta deb bengal sati regulation (regulation xvii) dharma sabha (1830) bentinck. 9.1 — sati defined sati was the practice by which a widow self-immolated on her deceased husband's funeral pyre. the earliest firm epigraphic evidence (inscription-based historical record) is the eran pillar inscription of bhanugupta (510 ce) in present-day madhya pradesh, recording the wife of a chieftain named goparaja performing the act (out of love/devotion) after his death in battle. eran is an ancient archaeological site located in the sagar district of present-day madhya pradesh. in vedic times there was no practice of sati. the rig veda actually contains a passage where a wife goes to the funeral pyre but is called back by her family to the world of the living — & returns. the post-vedic smritis supported it as a voluntary spiritual act of devotion, a mark of a wife's oneness of soul with her husband. 9.2 — why it persisted into the 19th century by the 19th century, the original spiritual rationale had largely collapsed. what drove the practice now was a combination of social pressure, greed, & patriarchy: • relatives did not want to share property with a childless widow. • a widow was seen as an economic & social burden. • sati eliminated any perceived risk to caste "purity" or family honour through a widow's future conduct. • society glorified the act as spiritual salvation, providing powerful social pressure. by the 19th century, what had once been framed as a voluntary spiritual act had become — in most cases — either coerced suicide or outright murder, driven by inheritance greed & patriarchal control, not spirituality. 9.3 — the scale of the problem sati was never a widespread pan-india phenomenon. it existed mainly in bengal among upper castes, & historically in vijayanagara (1336–1646) & rajputana — where the related practice of johar (mass self-immolation by women to prevent capture & dishonour by victorious armies) had different origins rooted in the honour of warrior clans. what made the 19th century alarming was a new trend — lower castes in bengal began practising sati as part of sanskritisation (the process by which lower castes adopt the customs of upper castes to claim higher social status within the caste hierarchy). 9.4 — how it was abolished christian missionaries had opposed sati since 1813 but achieved nothing. the decisive campaign was led by roy. bentinck28-35 set a firm pre-condition before acting — it had to be proven from indian scriptures that sati was not religiously sanctioned. (*note- notice his orientalist instinct even in reform — he would not override indian tradition without indian scriptural authority to back him.) this led to a formal scriptural debate between the brahmo samaj & radhakanta deb, a prominent orthodox hindu leader in bengal. (note- deb is an interesting figure — an education reformer in other respects, but firmly orthodox on the question of sati.) roy won the argument — sati is murder as per the shastras*. in 1829, the bengal sati regulation (regulation xvii) was passed — the 17th law of that year — making sati punishable as culpable homicide. radhakanta deb then founded the dharma sabha (1830) specifically to oppose the abolition, & sent a petition to the privy council in london (the crown's advisory body, which in this context functioned as the highest court of appeal for india) to overturn the law. the petition was rejected. (note: the dharma sabha's appeal to london is significant — it was among the earliest instances of indian groups using the metropolitan legal system as a battleground for indian policy. the same mechanism would be used in far more consequential ways during the constitutional reform debates of the 20th century.)

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: The Brahmo Samaj (1828)
sections.norm: the brahmo samaj (1828). brahmo samaj 10.1 — what the brahmo samaj (1828) stood for worked against idolatry, priestcraft, polytheism, & sati did not focus on karma transmigration of soul monotheistic religious movement did not reach the masses debendranath tagore (1817–1905) bijoy krishna goswami 10.2 — the keshab chandra sen crisis & the splits of 1866 & 1878 gradualism radicalism keshab chandra sen keshab chandra sen was a radical debendranath tagore was a gradualist on women on caste on mass outreach rupture came in 1866 distinguish themselves from hinduism remain within the hindu fold brahmo samaj of india (1866) adi brahmo samaj (1866) brahmo marriages act of 1872 tabernacle of new dispensation sadharan brahmo samaj (1878) 10.3 — why the brahmo samaj ultimately failed mayo. roy founded the brahmo samaj in 1828 as the organisational vehicle for his reform agenda. 10.1 — what the brahmo samaj (1828) stood for the brahmo samaj worked against idolatry, priestcraft, polytheism, & sati. notice what it initially did not focus on — women's issues broadly (beyond sati) & caste. these were considered too sensitive for the hindu community, & taking a strong stand risked alienating potential members. on the philosophically charged questions of karma & transmigration of soul (past life, present life, next life), the brahmo samaj — unlike roy personally — took no definitive stand. it left these beliefs to individual members. (*note- deliberate pragmatism: these doctrines are central to hindu faith, & a strong rejection would have shut the door on the very hindu middle-class audience the brahmo samaj was trying to reach.) brahmoism became, in practice, a monotheistic religious movement among upper-caste, western-educated bengalis. it did not reach the masses. after roy's death, debendranath tagore (1817–1905) — father of rabindranath tagore — provided the organisational strength to hold the brahmo samaj together. in 1860, bijoy krishna goswami worked to reconcile brahmoism with vaishnavism to broaden its acceptance within the hindu fold. 10.2 — the keshab chandra sen crisis & the splits of 1866 & 1878 the fault line within the brahmo samaj was always between gradualism & radicalism. it broke open with keshab chandra sen in the 1860s. keshab chandra sen was a radical. debendranath tagore was a gradualist. their difference was not just personal — it was strategic. on women: keshab chandra sen argued strongly for women's rights, female education, widow remarriage, & opposed child marriage. debendranath tagore considered these issues too sensitive to push publicly. on caste: keshab chandra sen attacked the upper-caste character of the brahmo samaj itself, supported inter-caste marriages, & challenged the institution of caste at its root. debendranath tagore avoided this entirely. on mass outreach: keshab chandra sen wanted to take brahmoism beyond calcutta's educated elite — to common, non-westernised bengalis, & beyond bengal itself. he launched missionary activities aimed at getting people to adopt brahmoism as an alternative religion to hinduism. debendranath tagore did not want a break from hinduism. the rupture came in 1866. keshab chandra sen & his followers wanted to distinguish themselves from hinduism; debendranath tagore & his followers wanted to remain within the hindu fold. the result: • keshab chandra sen formed the brahmo samaj of india (1866). • debendranath tagore formed the adi brahmo samaj (1866) — adi = original, & the name is itself a statement that roy's original vision was gradualist. keshab chandra sen's energy did produce one concrete legal result — the brahmo marriages act of 1872. the major drafting work was done under mayo69-72, though mayo was assassinated in february 1872 before the act was formally passed. the credit for the groundwork belongs to his administration. the act gave legal validity to inter-caste marriages & widow remarriages — but with a significant catch: the bride & groom had to first formally leave hinduism. this condition severely limited its real-world impact. keshab chandra sen also founded the tabernacle of new dispensation (nababidhan) — a syncretic religious body that sought to bring together the truths of all major religions — & the indian reform association, which worked for women's education, temperance, & social reform more broadly. then came the split of 1878 — within keshab chandra sen's own brahmo samaj of india. the cause was personal & devastating in its irony — keshab chandra sen himself married off his minor daughter, directly contradicting everything he had publicly championed on child marriage. the hypocrisy fractured his following & led to the formation of the sadharan brahmo samaj (1878). 10.3 — why the brahmo samaj ultimately failed the reasons were internal: • ideological & organisational differences on goals & methods — gradualism versus radicalism, staying within hinduism versus breaking from it. • multiple organisational splits that divided energy, membership, & credibility. • upper-caste & urban character that prevented genuine mass reach.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Akshay Kumar Dutt
sections.norm: akshay kumar dutt. akshay kumar dutt (1820–1866) medical opinion. akshay kumar dutt (1820–1866) was a brahmo samajist who brought a distinctly modern, almost clinical lens to the question of child marriage. rather than relying solely on scriptural argument, he cited medical opinion against child marriage — an early instance of a reformer using science as a tool for social change. his thinking on marriage itself was well ahead of his time — he advocated courtship before marriage, equality & partnership within marriage, & the right to divorce by both law & custom.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Maharashtra
