sections.norm: maharashtra. paramhansa mandali prarthana samaj atmaram pandurang m.g. ranade goals methods arya samaj kandukuri veeresalingam pantulu 12.3 — m.g. ranade (1842–1901) mahadev govind ranade was the central intellectual force behind organised social reform in maharashtra. a student of elphinstone college, bombay, he became a judge of the bombay high court & a member of the bombay legislative council. he edited indu prakash — an anglo-marathi weekly — with r.g. bhandarkar. he is remembered as the father of indian economics, a critic of british economic policies, & one of the first voices to argue that the colonial state should actively promote industrialisation & state welfare programmes. ranade's book — essays on indian economics (1898), was the first systematic analysis of the indian economy from an indian perspective. the british awarded him the companion of the order of the indian empire (for his work on a committee on fiscal stability). rise of maratha power maharashtra girls education society organisations he built: poona sarvajanik sabha indian national social conference lokhitavadi gopal hari deshmukh. 12.1 — paramhansa mandali (1849) maharashtra's first organised reform attempt was the paramhansa mandali, set up in 1849. it followed the same path as young bengal — relying primarily on rationality, rejecting religious authority — & it failed for the same reason. a religious society cannot be moved by reason alone. 12.2 — prarthana samaj (1867) the more significant & lasting effort came in 1867 with the prarthana samaj, set up by atmaram pandurang with the active help of keshab chandra sen, who wanted brahmoism to spread beyond bengal. (note: the prarthana samaj is essentially brahmoism transplanted to maharashtra — same ideological dna, different soil.) its membership was drawn largely from western-educated marathi brahmins, gujarati merchants, & the parsi community. (note- the same upper-caste, upper-class character that limited the brahmo samaj 1828 in bengal.) the most important figure associated with it was m.g. ranade, assisted by r.g. bhandarkar & k.t. telang*. goals: like keshab chandra sen's brahmo samaj of india 1866, the prarthana samaj 1867 focused on women's issues & caste — in addition to the standard positions of anti-idolatry, monotheism, & opposition to priestly domination. methods: here it diverged sharply. in method, the prarthana samaj 1867 followed debendranath tagore's gradualism — it did not want a break from hinduism & preferred slow, careful reform from within. this made it more acceptable to mainstream hindu society. the downside of that caution was gradual irrelevance. when swami dayanand saraswati's arya samaj arrived in 1875 — religious, radical, self-assertive, & charged with strong cultural nationalism — it drew away many who had found the prarthana samaj 1867's measured pace unsatisfying. the prarthana samaj 1867 did open branches outside maharashtra — in gujarat, karachi, & madras. in telugu-speaking areas of the madras presidency, kandukuri veeresalingam pantulu set up a society specifically for widow remarriage. overall, social reforms moved slowly in madras — western education had spread more unevenly there, & casteism ran deep. 12.3 — m.g. ranade (1842–1901) mahadev govind ranade was the central intellectual force behind organised social reform in maharashtra. a student of elphinstone college, bombay, he became a judge of the bombay high court & a member of the bombay legislative council. he edited indu prakash — an anglo-marathi weekly — with r.g. bhandarkar. he is remembered as the father of indian economics, a critic of british economic policies, & one of the first voices to argue that the colonial state should actively promote industrialisation & state welfare programmes. ranade's book — essays on indian economics (1898), was the first systematic analysis of the indian economy from an indian perspective. the british awarded him the companion of the order of the indian empire (for his work on a committee on fiscal stability). his intellectual commitments were equally wide. he wrote rise of maratha power, asserting a strong maratha cultural identity. he worked actively for female education, widow remarriage, & against child marriage, & co-founded the maharashtra girls education society with r.g. bhandarkar. organisations he built: the main force behind the prarthana samaj 1867, ranade also founded the poona sarvajanik sabha in 1870 — one of the earliest regional political organisations in india, focused on the rights of peasants in the bombay presidency. (note- it is a precursor organisation to the inc — a regional political body before a national one existed.) its prominent members included bal gangadhar tilak & gopal hari deshmukh*. he also founded the indian national social conference, whose first session was held alongside the inc's madras session in 1887. the conference had a deliberate focus — no scriptural debates. it argued for social reform purely on the basis of the doctrine of logic — reason, evidence, & human welfare — not religious authority. 12.4 — gopal hari deshmukh — lokhitavadi (1823–1892) gopal hari deshmukh, known by his pen name lokhitavadi (meaning one who speaks for the welfare of the people), held perhaps the most radical position of any maharashtra reformer on the question of religion & society. his argument was direct — social reform is the first priority, above religion. if the scriptures conflict with social reform, change the religion, because religion is made by man, not the other way around. (note: compare this with roy, who used scripture to argue for reform, & with dayananda, who held the vedas infallible. lokhitavadi stood at the other end — for him, human welfare trumped religious authority without qualification.)

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Jyotirao Phule (1827–1890)
sections.norm: jyotirao phule (1827–1890). jyotirao phule 13.1 — on education hunter education commission of 1882 india's first girls' school in pune savitribai phule 13.2 — on women infanticide prevention centre 13.3 — on dalit rights gulamgiri (slavery) american abolitionists satyashodhak samaj 1873 din bandhu (1877) 13.4 — on peasants cultivator's whipcord (1881) 13.5 — on workers night schools for labourers bombay millhands association (1890) narayan lokhande. if most reformers of the 19th century spoke about the oppressed, jyotirao phule spoke for them — & organised them. he is the first major reformer whose work comprehensively addressed not one or two social ills but the entire architecture of oppression — caste, gender, class, & economic exploitation, all at once. 13.1 — on education phule submitted detailed suggestions to the hunter education commission of 1882, arguing for a decisive shift towards universal, practical, primary education — funded & run by the state, with targeted access for lower-caste communities & girls, trained non-brahmin teachers, mother-tongue instruction, nominal fees or scholarships, & tighter inspection & governance. but his most famous act came decades earlier. in 1848, he opened india's first girls' school in pune, with his wife savitribai phule as the first female teacher. (*note- savitribai taught while stones & dung were thrown at her on her way to school each day.) 13.2 — on women beyond education, phule worked for widow remarriage & against child marriage. in 1863, he set up an infanticide prevention centre — a safe home that enabled anonymous deliveries for pregnant widows, sheltered survivors of sexual assault, & provided an orphanage for children who could not be kept. it addressed social stigma & the resulting infanticide with a practical, institutional solution at a time when most reformers were still debating in conference halls. 13.3 — on dalit rights in 1873, phule wrote gulamgiri (slavery) in marathi — a searing text that equated the condition of shudras & ati-shudras with that of african american slaves, & placed the blame squarely on the priestly class. he dedicated the book to the american abolitionists — activists, writers, & political leaders in the united states who fought through the first half of the 19th century to end slavery. [note: phule saw a direct parallel — both shudras/ati-shudras under caste & african americans under slavery were born into bondage with no exit, & in both cases the oppressor hid behind tradition & divine sanction.] in the same year he founded the satyashodhak samaj 1873 (truth-seekers' society), which systematically challenged orthodoxy & the caste system. he also started the newspaper din bandhu (1877) for the oppressed classes. 13.4 — on peasants in cultivator's whipcord (1881), phule showed how religion, bureaucracy, & economic exploitation — moneylenders, high land revenue, ritual expenses — combined to grind down shudra cultivators. festivals, life-cycle rituals, & everyday religious demands were not just cultural practices — they were instruments of economic extraction. he advocated economic self-reliance, land reforms, use of military labour for rural development, & ran night schools for peasants. 13.5 — on workers phule ran night schools for labourers. he also co-founded the bombay millhands association (1890) with narayan lokhande (main founder) — one of the earliest organised efforts to address the rights of industrial workers in india (*not a formal trade union as it had no membership fees, no formal rules, and no funds.)

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Child Marriage
sections.norm: child marriage. 14.1 — why child marriage was so hard to uproot garbhadhan ceremony 14.2 — the legislative attempts ishwar chandra vidyasagar indian penal code 1860 (ipc1860) canning56-62 akshay kumar dutt (1820–1866) 14.3 — the rakhmabai case (1884–1888) rakhmabai rakhmabai defence committee malabari she lost queen victoria alert (prelims 2020): restitution of conjugal rights 14.4 — the age of consent act 1891 11-year-old phulmoni lansdowne88-94 age of consent bill 1891 tilak r.g. bhandarkar act x (10) of 1891 reform failed at the ground level child marriage continued across all castes indian penal code 1860 canning lansdowne. 14.1 — why child marriage was so hard to uproot child marriage in india was not simply a social custom — it had explicit religious backing. the garbhadhan ceremony, rooted in hindu tradition, prescribed marriage before puberty & consummation of the marriage at puberty. this made child marriage reform far more contested than, say, sati — because here the reformers were not arguing against a distortion of scripture but against a practice that scripture actively sanctioned. orthodox opposition was therefore stronger, more principled in its own terms, & harder to defeat. 14.2 — the legislative attempts efforts by ishwar chandra vidyasagar contributed to the indian penal code 1860 (ipc1860) under canning56-62, which set the minimum age of consummation at 10 years (section 375 ipc1860 — definition of statutory rape). it was a beginning — but a modest one. akshay kumar dutt (1820–1866) added a medical dimension, citing health evidence against child marriage alongside the moral argument. 14.3 — the rakhmabai case (1884–1888) the human face of this debate was rakhmabai. married as an infant, she had lived separately from her husband for years. at 22, when her husband took her to court for denial of conjugal rights, she fought back — arguing the marriage was invalid. the rakhmabai defence committee, led by reformer malabari (whose 1884 note on child marriage & enforced widowhood had already caused a storm in maharashtra), stood on her side. orthodox hindus supported the husband. she lost. (post-1857, orthodox hindu opinion was strong enough to win in court.) then queen victoria herself overruled the decision & dissolved the marriage. ⚠ alert (prelims 2020): the rakhmabai case of 1884 is a recurring upsc stem. upsc tests it in the context of (a) age of consent debate & (b) the doctrine of restitution of conjugal rights — i.e. questions of marriage law & a woman's bodily autonomy. to answer right, the student should know that rakhmabai is not a women's-education case; the right answer involves age of consent + restitution of conjugal rights, not women's right to gain education. 14.4 — the age of consent act 1891 in 1890, the death of 11-year-old phulmoni due to sexual abuse by her husband brought the issue to a head. lansdowne88-94 introduced the age of consent bill 1891, raising the minimum age of consummation to 12 years. the controversy was fierce. tilak argued that the british had no right to interfere in indian custom & religion, & that reform must come from social movement — not colonial legislation. on the other side, r.g. bhandarkar of poona deccan college & the prarthana samaj 1867 produced research showing that the dharmashastras actually permit marriage after puberty. the bill was passed in march 1891 as act x (10) of 1891. despite all this, reform failed at the ground level. census data from the 1900s revealed that child marriage continued across all castes. (*note- the census was conducted every ten years from 1881 onwards — it gave reformers hard data, but data alone could not change behaviour rooted in religion, economics, & social pressure.)

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Female Infanticide
sections.norm: female infanticide. hypogamy mayo69-72 female infanticide act of 1870 sec. 15a — lex loci act 1850 lex loci act 1850 conversion to a different religion would no longer cause forfeiture mayo. female infanticide in north & west india continued largely unabated through this period. the reasons were structural — landowning high-caste men practised hypogamy (marrying multiple women, often from lower castes), which made finding suitable grooms for daughters of such marriages extremely difficult. high dowry demands compounded the problem. mayo69-72 passed the female infanticide act of 1870, but legislation alone could not reach the problem at its roots. census data continued to show high girl-child mortality rates — not from direct infanticide alone, but from nutritional neglect — girls were systematically fed less, cared for less, & allowed to die. this could not be legislated away. it required a transformation in how society valued women — & that transformation was still far off. sec. 15a — lex loci act 1850 the lex loci act 1850 (also called the removal of religious/caste disabilities act 1850) was a critical piece of legislation that protected the property & inheritance rights of converts but in doing so it promoted conversions to christianity and contributed to fear for religion under threat. before this act, hindus who converted to christianity (or any other religion) automatically forfeited their right to ancestral property under traditional hindu law — a powerful disincentive to conversion. the act overrode this rule. conversion to a different religion would no longer cause forfeiture of inheritance rights. the state now stood on the side of individual choice in law but on side of conversion in practice. (*note- the act has been called "the legal foundation of religious freedom in colonial india" by british — but the assessment is contested. orthodox hindus & western educated middle class saw it as a state-engineered tilt towards conversion, since it removed the strongest social-economic deterrent. christian missionaries saw it as a long-overdue protection of converts from predatory disinheritance. the act did materially weaken the orthodox community's hold on individual choice, & it did make conversion materially safer.)

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (1820–1891)
sections.norm: ishwar chandra vidyasagar (1820–1891). ishwar chandra vidyasagar ishwar chandra bandyopadhyay vidyasagar reason & rationalism are supreme i have no time to think about god 16.1 — the educator principal sanskrit college (calcutta; set up in 1824) inspector of schools director of education female education 25 schools for female education improve sanskrit literature make it accessible through bengali. rabindranath tagore vidyasagar's greatest contribution father of modern bengali prose 16.2 — widow remarriage 1,000 signatures hindu widow remarriage act of 26 july 1856 dalhousie48-56 7 december 1856 16.3 — polygamy 25,000 signatures alert (prelims 2005 + prelims 2021): bankim chandra chattopadhyay dalhousie. ishwar chandra vidyasagar — born ishwar chandra bandyopadhyay on 26 september 1820 in bengal — was a prodigy in every sense. he studied sanskrit literature for years, shifted to calcutta at a young age (where a widow became his caregiver — a detail that perhaps shaped his lifelong commitment to widows' welfare), passed the hindu law committee examination, & earned the title vidyasagar (ocean of knowledge) in 1839. he mastered english, sanskrit, & bengali, & used prize money from academic awards to set up a school & get rare sanskrit texts printed. his ideology was straightforward — reason & rationalism are supreme. he famously said, "i have no time to think about god" — his entire energy went into social reform. he rejected other-worldliness & focused on the world in front of him. 16.1 — the educator vidyasagar's contributions to education were institutional, not just intellectual. as additional secretary & later principal of sanskrit college (calcutta; set up in 1824), he implemented reforms with force — including threatening resignation if lower-caste students were not admitted and introduced western sciences alongside sanskrit. (*note- this is the same college roy had opposed in 1824. vidyasagar transformed it from within.) he wanted western education & culture delivered in the vernacular — not just in english — so that knowledge could reach beyond the elite. as inspector of schools in bengal— he set up 20 model schools & ended the practice of physical punishment in schools. (*note- inspector of schools operated at the district level; the top authority at the provincial level was called the director of education (like the sp & dgp in the police hierarchy).) he believed female education was the only true route to uplifting society. between november 1857 & may 1858 — even as the country was in the throes of the 1857 revolt — he opened 25 schools for female education, with 1,300 girls enrolled at any given time. attendance, books, & transport were all free. he worked to improve sanskrit literature & make it accessible through bengali. rabindranath tagore said that vidyasagar's greatest contribution was to the bengali language itself. he is remembered as the father of modern bengali prose. 16.2 — widow remarriage vidyasagar's most celebrated legislative battle was for widow remarriage. in 1855, he wrote a book on the miseries of widowhood & submitted a petition to the government with 1,000 signatures supporting a law to allow widow remarriage. the result was the hindu widow remarriage act of 26 july 1856 under dalhousie48-56. the first remarriage under the act took place on 7 december 1856. vidyasagar did not merely campaign — he married his own son to a widow, putting his principles into practice in his personal life. 16.3 — polygamy on polygamy, he was equally forceful. in 1855, he submitted a petition with 25,000 signatures to the lieutenant governor of bengal demanding a ban. he followed this with two books against polygamy in 1871 & 1873. ⚠ alert (prelims 2005 + prelims 2021): bethune school (later bethune female school) is associated with ishwar chandra vidyasagar as secretary — he was the key figure who built it as the foundation institution for female education in bengal. (bankim chandra chattopadhyay was the first graduate of calcutta university — that is a separate fact, often paired with bethune to confuse the student. don't conflate.)

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Widow Remarriage
sections.norm: widow remarriage. hindu widow remarriage act of 1856 organised orthodox resistance vishnu shastri pandit jyotirao phule veeresalingam pantulu pandita ramabai ultimate result was failure won the scripture-based debate women's reform-acts timeline. the hindu widow remarriage act of 1856 was a landmark — but it did not solve the problem. there was a structural catch — upon remarriage, a widow lost her right to the property of her deceased husband. this single condition was enough to keep the law largely ineffective in practice. the reform effort was scattered across regions & reformers but consistently ran into organised orthodox resistance: • in maharashtra, vishnu shastri pandit formed a society for widow remarriage in 1866 — but orthodox rivals immediately set up a counter-organisation. the debate continued well after the 1856 law. • jyotirao phule made efforts among lower castes in maharashtra for widow remarriage but failed. • in madras, veeresalingam pantulu set up a society for widow remarriage. • pandita ramabai of maharashtra was a rare, extraordinary exception. a brahmin woman who stayed unmarried for long, she eventually married a man from a lower caste. after her husband's death, she went to england to study medicine, converted to christianity (drawing criticism even from reformers), & went to the united states where she raised money for a widow home in bombay. she opposed the emerging new role model of the "educated but obedient wife." (*note- she was the kind of reformer who made even reformers uncomfortable.) the ultimate result was failure. post-1857, orthodox hindus had stronger social support & won the scripture-based debate — proving, to most people's satisfaction, that hinduism did not permit widow remarriage. the damage spread downwards — even lower castes, who had traditionally allowed widow remarriage, now stopped the practice in an effort to align with upper-caste norms. (*note- sanskritisation working in reverse — adopting upper-caste restrictions, not just upper-caste customs.) by 1900, only 38 widow remarriages* had taken place in maharashtra. the reform succeeded only in haryana, where widow remarriage had already been an accepted practice. women's reform-acts timeline (sati abolition 1829 → lex loci 1850 → religious disabilities 1850 → hindu widow remarriage 1856 → age of consent 1860 → female infanticide 1870 → native marriages 1872 → age of consent 1891 → sharda 1929) — synthesises the women + reform acts arc from sec. 9 through sec. 17.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Character & Failures of Early 19th-Century Reform
sections.norm: character & failures of early 19th-century reform. why did they largely fail 18.1 — what defined these movements western-educated upper castes women scriptures cultural nationalism 18.2 — why they failed no mass movement. top-down, not bottom-up. british involvement bred distrust. gradualism slowed everything down no women in leadership upper-caste leadership only silence on caste post-1857 shift in power rival orthodox organisations consistently out-mobilised reformers orthodox hindus won the scripture debate on widow remarriage post-1875 — the rise of hindu revivalism reformer organisations grid bentinck. what was the character of these early reform movements, & why did they largely fail? 18.1 — what defined these movements • they were led by western-educated upper castes — anti-priest in orientation but upper-caste in composition. • the primary focus was on women — partly because reformers cared, & partly because the british had begun using the status of women as the benchmark for judging the level of a civilisation. (a colonial-era frame, but one that reformers worked within.) • scriptures were central to every argument — reformers used them, orthodox hindus used them, & even the british insisted on scriptural justification before acting. (*note- recall bentinck28-35's pre-condition before abolishing sati.) • cultural nationalism was present throughout — reforms were a response to british civilisational criticism, & reformers looked for modernity within indian traditions rather than simply adopting british culture as superior. 18.2 — why they failed the failures were structural & ran deep: • no mass movement. western-educated reformers did not attempt to reach the masses. roy wrote in complex sanskritised bengali prose that the common person could not understand. the prarthana samaj 1867 had only 72 members. small organisations, elite language, no grassroots presence. • top-down, not bottom-up. reforms relied on british legislative & executive authority — passed from above rather than demanded from below. • british involvement bred distrust. using british authority triggered widespread fear among ordinary people that their religion was under threat. this pushed them towards orthodox leaders rather than reformers. • gradualism slowed everything down & allowed orthodox resistance to consolidate. • no women in leadership — despite all the reforms being women-centric, not a single major reform organisation was led by a woman. • upper-caste leadership only — lower castes did not associate with movements led entirely by those who benefited from the caste system. • silence on caste — reformers either belonged to upper castes themselves or feared alienating upper-caste hindus. the central structural issue of indian society was largely avoided. • post-1857 shift in power — when second-wave reformers did try to build mass movements, they found that the leadership of the masses had already been captured by orthodox sections. the early reformers had left a vacuum. • rival orthodox organisations consistently out-mobilised reformers — the dharma sabha against the brahmo samaj on sati, the counter-society against vishnu shastri pandit on widow remarriage, & so on. • orthodox hindus won the scripture debate on widow remarriage — & the damage was not limited to the upper castes. lower castes followed suit. • post-1875 — the rise of hindu revivalism — which had both a positive face (stronger assertion of indian traditions, radical reform from within) & a negative face (communal tensions, assertion of hindu supremacy over other religions). reformer organisations grid (brahmo samaj 1828, young bengal, paramhansa mandali 1849, satya shodhak samaj 1873, deoband 1867, prarthana samaj 1867, arya samaj 1875, theosophical society 1875, aligarh movement 1875, ramakrishna mission 1897, sndp 1903, ahmadiya 1889) — full map of 19th-century socio-religious reform organisations.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Arya Samaj (1875)
sections.norm: arya samaj (1875). 19.1 — swami dayanand saraswati mool shankar swami virajananda rishi dayanand maharishi 19.2 — his beliefs back to the vedas satyarth prakash doctrine of reason 19.3 — the arya samaj — founded 10 april 1875, bombay arya samaj 10 april 1875 ten tenets 19.4 — what the arya samaj did attacked social ills from within the vedic framework on caste varnashram system on women shuddhi movement gurukuls projected hinduism as a "religion of the book" shruti apaurusheya advocated swarajya 19.5 — successes and failures punjab & the north-west provinces dayanand anglo-vedic (dav) college trust & management society 1 june 1886 lala hans raj shaheed bhagat singh lala lajpat rai, v.d. savarkar, madam cama, ram prasad bismil, m.g. ranade, madan lal dhingra, & subhas chandra bose alert (prelims 2001): 1875 lala lajpat rai k. hedgewar. 19.1 — swami dayanand saraswati his original name was mool shankar, & he was from gujarat. he did not marry. he left home young & spent 20 years travelling across india in search of spiritual truth. his journey ended in mathura, where he met swami virajananda, who directed him to learn directly from the vedas. it was from the vedas that dayanand found his answers about human existence. virajananda gave him a task — spread vedic knowledge — & a new name: rishi dayanand. he would later be called maharishi. 19.2 — his beliefs maharishi dayanand's foundational conviction was simple — the vedas are the ultimate, infallible source of all true knowledge. everything that came after — the rituals, the idol worship, the caste hierarchy, the priestly domination — was corruption. the answer was not western modernity. the answer was to go back to the vedas. he wrote this argument out in full in satyarth prakash (the light of meaning of truth, 1875) — deliberately written in hindi, not sanskrit, so it could reach the masses rather than just the learned. the book is the foundational text of the arya samaj. it attacks idol worship, polytheism, animal sacrifice, untouchability, child marriage, & birth-based caste. it also critically examines the theological claims of christianity, islam, jainism, & buddhism — arguing that vedic hinduism is superior to all of them. he emphasised the doctrine of reason, but with a crucial claim — the vedas alone contain scientific truths, & therefore hinduism is not backward — it is ahead. 19.3 — the arya samaj — founded 10 april 1875, bombay the arya samaj (society of the nobles) was founded on 10 april 1875 in bombay. its motto: "krinvanto vishvam aryam" — make this world noble. its ten tenets covered god, vedas, dharma, truth, righteous conduct, promotion of physical & social good, love & justice, knowledge over ignorance, collective welfare, & individual freedom within social rules. 19.4 — what the arya samaj did • attacked social ills from within the vedic framework — denounced idolatry, polytheism, priestcraft, rituals, birth-based caste distinctions, & child marriage; supported widow remarriage, inter-caste marriage, & female education. • on caste — discarded the birth-based caste system & denounced untouchability. in its place, upheld the varnashram system — a four-fold organisation of society based on profession, not birth. brahmans were scholars, kshatriyas protectors, vaishyas traders, shudras in service — but these were changeable with change in profession, not hereditary, & not hierarchical. (*note- dayananda was not defending caste. he was proposing a meritocratic alternative rooted in vedic tradition.) • on women — argued that an educated man needs an educated wife. launched programmes to support widow remarriage in the 1880s. • shuddhi movement — a programme to bring back those who had been voluntarily or involuntarily converted to islam or christianity. (*note- "those who sought" their way back — purification was for those who came forward, not a forced re-conversion programme under dayananda himself.) • gurukuls — set up to teach vedic knowledge & train followers to spread it further. • projected hinduism as a "religion of the book" — like islam & christianity — asserting the vedas as shruti (that which is heard) & apaurusheya (not of human origin, representing eternal cosmic truths). • advocated swarajya — a country free of foreign influence. his was an aggressive, self-assertive response to british civilisational criticism. 19.5 — successes and failures the arya samaj failed in east & west india. it succeeded most powerfully in punjab & the north-west provinces — especially after dayananda's death in 1883, when it became both more popular & more aggressive. [note: why punjab? the punjab of the late 19th century was a region of intense religious competition — hinduism, sikhism, islam, & christian missionaries were all actively competing for followers. the arya samaj's assertive, organised, scriptural approach suited this environment perfectly.] after his death, his disciples established the dayanand anglo-vedic (dav) college trust & management society. the first dav high school opened at lahore on 1 june 1886, with lala hans raj as its headmaster. shaheed bhagat singh was educated at the dav school in lahore. though maharishi dayanand & the arya samaj were never directly involved in the independence struggle, his teachings influenced lala lajpat rai, v.d. savarkar, madam cama, ram prasad bismil, m.g. ranade, madan lal dhingra, & subhas chandra bose. ⚠ alert (prelims 2001): common upsc trap — pin three facts. (i) arya samaj was founded in 1875 (not 1835). (ii) lala lajpat rai was a follower of arya samaj, not its critic — he supported the vedas-based reform programme. (iii) under k. hedgewar, the rss (founded 1925) was inspired in part by arya samaj's organisational model — the student should be careful about the chain of influence.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Revivalism — Positive & Negative
sections.norm: revivalism — positive & negative. reform & revivalism began to diverge positive revivalism swami dayanand saraswati, ramakrishna paramhansa, & swami vivekananda negative revivalism shuddhi movement singh sabha movement. post-1857, reform & revivalism began to diverge into two distinct streams. positive revivalism meant a stronger, more confident assertion of indian traditions in response to british civilisational criticism. reformers like swami dayanand saraswati, ramakrishna paramhansa, & swami vivekananda represented this — attacking social ills from within the tradition rather than by importing western frameworks. negative revivalism — which intensified after dayananda's death in 1883 — was different in character. under leaders like pandit lekh ram & pandit guru dutt, the arya samaj shifted towards a more militant posture — preaching the vedas with missionary zeal, running an aggressive shuddhi movement to re-convert from islam, sikhism, & christianity. in response, the singh sabha movement among sikhs intensified, & muslims launched the tanzim & tabligh movements. the cow protection movement of the same era led directly to the cow killing riots of 1893.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Ramakrishna Paramhansa
sections.norm: ramakrishna paramhansa. ramakrishna paramhansa implicit rejection of western values chakri. ramakrishna paramhansa was a temple priest — not a western-educated reformer, not a writer, not a debater. he was a spiritual man who believed in meditation, renunciation, & monotheism. western ideas & western education left him entirely untouched. he did not directly criticise colonial rule. but his pure, uncompromising focus on hinduism was itself an implicit rejection of western values & culture. his popularity among educated bengalis is revealing. these were men who had taken up clerical jobs under british administration — what he called chakri (the grinding routine of office work) — & found them spiritually hollow. reformism, by the 1870s, had come to feel like an admission that indians were uncivilised. ramakrishna offered something different — not reform, not self-criticism, but the spiritual richness of their own tradition, undiluted. he argued that chakri left no time for the pursuit of spiritualism — & that this absence of spiritual purpose was the real source of the educated middle class's dissatisfaction.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Swami Vivekananda
sections.norm: swami vivekananda. swami vivekananda superiority of hindu philosophy universalism was genuine glory of hindu civilisation acknowledged degeneration daridra narayan ramakrishna mission in 1897 akhadas & gymnasiums accepted idol worship greater mass acceptance 1893 parliament of religions in chicago netaji bose revivalists selectively used his beliefs ramakrishna mission schools, dispensaries, hospitals, & relief work sister nivedita (margaret noble) — vivekananda's irish disciple.. swami vivekananda was ramakrishna's most famous disciple — & a different kind of figure: intellectual, activist, globally engaged. he believed in the superiority of hindu philosophy but was not a revivalist in the negative sense. his universalism was genuine — he argued that a christian could become a better christian by studying the philosophy of vedanta. no conversion. no aggression. spread the values, not the label. he had faith in the glory of hindu civilisation but acknowledged degeneration — not during mughal or british rule specifically, but in recent times, without assigning blame to a particular religion. his most original intellectual contribution was the equation — service of jiva is worship of shiva — meaning that social service is a spiritual act. he popularised the concept of daridra narayan (god residing in the poor) & argued that existing reform movements were too elitist. real work meant going to the masses through service — not just meditation, not just debate. to do this work, he founded the ramakrishna mission in 1897, named after his guru. its purpose was dual — spread the message of vedanta & undertake social service. he wanted to create an army of followers who would carry the message of vedanta, the upanishads, buddha, & jesus — a universalist mission in practice, not just in theory. he also started a movement for akhadas & gymnasiums, arguing that indian masculinity — grounded in both physical strength & mental spirituality — was superior to western conceptions of strength alone. indians were not "feminine" as british racial theory claimed. they were differently strong. he accepted idol worship & certain hindu rituals as legitimate aids to developing religious feeling — unlike dayananda, who rejected them entirely. this gave him far greater mass acceptance. in 1893, he represented hinduism at the parliament of religions in chicago, arguing that western materialism & indian spiritualism must come together for the welfare of mankind. his address made him internationally famous. he never gave a political message — his nationalism was purely cultural. netaji bose called him the spiritual father of the indian national movement in bengal. after his death in 1902, revivalists selectively used his beliefs — his faith in the supremacy of vedas, his acceptance of some hindu rituals, his confidence in the glory of hindu civilisation — & reframed his acknowledgement of recent degeneration as degeneration specifically under muslim & christian rule. today, the ramakrishna mission runs schools, dispensaries, hospitals, & relief work across india & the world. sister nivedita (margaret noble) — vivekananda's irish disciple. an irish disciple of swami vivekananda, she played a vital role in nurturing cultural nationalism. beyond her tireless work for the education of indian women (the nivedita school at calcutta, opened 1898), she viewed india's independence as a spiritual necessity. her irish revolutionary background led her to provide secret support & guidance to revolutionary groups in bengal — particularly the anushilan samiti — bridging the gap between spiritual revival & political militancy. she wrote the master as i saw him (1910), capturing vivekananda's teaching for a western audience, & lived in india until her death in 1911.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee (1838–1894)
sections.norm: bankim chandra chatterjee (1838–1894). bankim chandra chatterjee anandamath (1882) bharat mata bande mataram rabindranath tagore jana gana mana madanapalle alert (prelims 2021): tagore translating jana gana mana into english adyar (madras). bankim chandra chatterjee held that without religious revival, there could be no revival of india. but his was a hindu secular outlook — he used religion as a cultural & nationalist force, not a communal one. he portrayed krishna as a modern politician & nation-builder. he promoted rational hinduism, not orthodox hinduism. his novel anandamath (1882) gave india the concept of bharat mata (mother india as a goddess) & contained bande mataram, which became the anthem of the indian national movement. (*note- bankim chandra was the first graduate of calcutta university — established in 1857.) a related note on the national anthem: rabindranath tagore composed jana gana mana in bengali. he later translated it from bengali into english himself at madanapalle (in present-day andhra pradesh) in 1919, where it was also set to music. students often associate bande mataram & the national anthem together — but they have distinct origins. bande mataram came from bankim's anandamath (1882); jana gana mana was composed by tagore much later & received its english rendering at madanapalle. ⚠ alert (prelims 2021): madanapalle (andhra pradesh) is associated with tagore translating jana gana mana into english in 1919 — not with the theosophical society headquarters, which is at adyar (madras). upsc commonly traps students who confuse madanapalle with adyar. to answer right, the student should know: madanapalle = tagore + jana gana mana english translation; adyar (madras) = theosophical society headquarters from 1882.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–1898)
sections.norm: sir syed ahmed khan (1817–1898). sir syed ahmed khan quams hindu quam muslim quam muslim league (1906) partition in 1947 muhammadan anglo-oriental college at aligarh aligarh muslim university aligarh movement mohammadan educational congress jamia millia islamia (1920) non-cooperation movement (1920–22) abdul majid khwaja, maulana mehmud hasan, maulana md ali, hakim ajmal khan, & dr mukhtar ahmed ansari nehru report in august 1928. sir syed ahmed khan was the most significant muslim social reformer of the 19th century. on social questions, his positions were modern — he supported widow remarriage, opposed triple talaq, polygamy, purdah, & child marriage, & advocated western & female education — all without abandoning the core beliefs of islam. his was a programme of modernisation without surrender of faith. but his political theory was divisive. he argued that india was not a nation of one people but a summation of quams (nations or communities). the hindu quam & the muslim quam were separate — different in religion, different in identity. he believed in unity between quams, but insisted on their separateness. the muslim quam, he argued, deserved special status as the community that had ruled india before the british. to achieve that status in the new colonial order, western education was essential. (*note- this two-nation logic, planted here in the 1870s & 1880s, would grow through the muslim league (1906) to partition in 1947 — the intellectual genealogy is direct.) in 1875, he founded the muhammadan anglo-oriental college at aligarh (later aligarh muslim university) to build unity & educational strength within the muslim quam. this was the institutional heart of the aligarh movement. in 1886, he set up the mohammadan educational congress as a deliberate rival to the inc, which he viewed as a hindu organisation. [note: the contrast with the inc's position is sharp — the inc argued for a composite indian nationalism that crossed religious lines. sir syed argued for separate communal identities with separate political interests. these two visions would be in conflict for the next 70 years.] in contrast, jamia millia islamia (1920) was set up in aligarh in the united provinces by a breakaway faction at amu. when gandhi gave the call during the non-cooperation movement (1920–22) for students to leave british-supported institutions, amu stayed pro-british. the breakaway group left & founded jamia millia islamia — built on anti-colonial islamic activism, pro-independence, led by western-educated radical nationalists. its founding leaders included abdul majid khwaja, maulana mehmud hasan, maulana md ali, hakim ajmal khan, & dr mukhtar ahmed ansari (who later headed the all-party conference that produced the nehru report in august 1928).

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Narayana Guru (1856–1928)
sections.norm: narayana guru (1856–1928). narayana guru ezhava community one of the most casteist societies advaita vedanta one religion, one caste, one god for mankind 25.1 — narayana guru's work institutional consecration of temples aruvippuram in 1888 institutional work spread steadily across kerala shri narayana dharma paripalana yogam (sndp) 1903 25.2 — his relationship with gandhi sivagiri in 1925 gandhi 25.3 — narayana guru's significance. narayana guru was born in 1856 in travancore (present-day kerala) into the ezhava community — a lower-caste group that faced severe caste discrimination in kerala's rigidly hierarchical social order. ezhavas were: • denied entry into temples; • forbidden from using public roads near upper-caste homes; • barred from many forms of education & employment. the kerala of narayana guru's childhood was, by most accounts, one of the most casteist societies in india. he became a wandering ascetic in his youth, studied sanskrit, tamil, & malayalam, & immersed himself in advaita vedanta — the philosophical tradition that sees all of existence as one undivided consciousness. it was from this philosophical root that his social vision grew. if all beings are expressions of the same divine reality, then caste — the idea that some humans are inherently superior or inferior by birth — is not just socially unjust. it is philosophically incoherent. his famous slogan captured this with precision — "one religion, one caste, one god for mankind." 25.1 — narayana guru's work narayana guru's method was neither purely legislative nor purely philosophical. it was institutional — & in this sense he resembles phule more than he resembles roy or even vivekananda. his most significant act was the consecration of temples. in a society where lower castes were denied entry into hindu temples, he built & consecrated his own temples — open to all, regardless of caste. the first was at aruvippuram in 1888, where he consecrated a shiva idol. when upper-caste critics objected that a lower-caste man had no right to consecrate a temple, his reply was direct — "this is not a brahmin's shiva. this is an ezhava's shiva." (*note- all without leaving hinduism, without converting, without legislation.) his institutional work spread steadily across kerala: • established temples, schools, & ashrams — each open to all castes, functioning as spaces of social equality in a society that had none. • founded the shri narayana dharma paripalana yogam (sndp) in 1903 for the social, educational, & economic upliftment of the ezhava community & lower castes broadly. 25.2 — his relationship with gandhi narayana guru was a contemporary of gandhi. gandhi visited him at his ashram at sivagiri in 1925 & was moved — he later described narayana guru as one of the greatest men he had ever met. the two shared a commitment to ending untouchability, though their methods & philosophical frameworks were different: • gandhi worked within the congress framework, addressing caste as part of a broader national movement. • narayana guru worked from within the community itself, building institutions & demanding dignity on the ground, in kerala, where the problem was acutest. [note: three responses to the same caste failure — gandhi's assimilationist approach, narayana guru's reformist-institutionalist work within advaita vedanta, & ambedkar's exit through conversion to buddhism. narayana guru chose to fight caste from inside the hindu philosophical tradition where ambedkar chose to leave it.] 25.3 — narayana guru's significance three specific reasons: • he represents the reform movement reaching south india seriously — & doing so not through western-educated upper-caste leadership but through a lower-caste ascetic working from within his own community. • his method — building parallel institutions rather than petitioning the state or debating in conference halls — was new. he did not ask the british for a law. he did not debate orthodox hindus in print. he simply built temples & opened them to everyone, creating facts on the ground. • his grounding in advaita vedanta gave him an argument that orthodox hinduism could not easily dismiss. he was not rejecting hinduism. he was holding it to its own highest standard.

sections.chapterTitle: Social Reforms, Education Reforms & Print Culture
sections.title: Education Reforms
sections.norm: education reforms. 26.1 — why western education came so late orientalism edmund burke (1729–1797) pitt's india act of 1784 william jones warren hastings73-85 26.2 — key orientalists asiatic society of bengal in 1784 dwarkanath thakur/tagore calcutta madrasa in 1781 sanskrit college, calcutta (1824) fort william college, calcutta in 1800 26.3 — who pushed for western education three distinct groups pushed back against orientalism david hare calcutta school book society (1817) hindu college, calcutta (1817) sir edward hyde east raja ram mohan roy hare school (1818) died of cholera presidency college thousands of calcuttans joined his funeral procession alert (prelims 2009): alexander duff general assembly's institution, calcutta (1830) john malcolm thomas munro elphinstone charles metcalfe charles grant charter act 1813 rs 1 lakh p.a. on education 26.4 — macaulay's minute (1835) — decision and reasons macaulay's minute on indian education (1835) english education act 1835 wood's despatch of 1854 macaulay famously declared white man's burden reduce cost of administration create brown sahibs downward filtration theory: 26.5 — william adam's reports on vernacular education (1835-38) most critical documentary evidence 26.5.1 — context william adam 1835-38 26.5.2 — core findings massive scale 1,00,000 pathshalas caste inclusivity false extreme flexibility suspended during harvest curriculum 26.5.3 — historical impact no "education vacuum" wd1854's real innovation was grants-in-aid & inspectorate, not vernacular education itself. 26.6 — key features of the english education act 1835 goal: medium: cut-off: 26.7 — subsequent milestones 1844 1847 roorkee engineering college iit roorkee in 2001 1849 bethune school for women j.e. drinkwater bethune ishwar chandra vidyasagar secretary organised women's education movement in bengal. 1851: ishwar chandra vidyasagar principal of sanskrit college (1824) opening sanskrit education to non-brahmins integrated western subjects 1856: vidyasagar inspector of schools hindu widow remarriage act 1856 26.8 — wood's despatch (1854) "magna carta of english education in india") charles wood dalhousie48-56 education departments in provincial governments teacher training programmes universities in madras, bombay, & calcutta impact: 1857 canning56-62 panjab university, lahore (1882) allahabad university (1887) bankim chandra chatterjee joddu nath bose calcutta university in 1858 1870 vernacular implementation expanding elementary schools technical education alert (prelims 1996 + prelims 2002 + prelims 2018): chronological order 26.9 — universities & education governance architecture three presidency universities bombay, madras, & calcutta 1857 under canning56-62 engineering college at roorkee (1847) 26.10 — why the british pulled back from higher education after 1870 decreased funding for higher education the real reason curzon99-05 1882 ripon80-84 26.11 — hunter commission (1882–83) — key findings hunter / indian education commission municipalitie wood's despatch 1854 woods dispatch 1854 hastings warren hastings wellesley bentinck dalhousie canning curzon ripon chelmsford. 26.1 — why western education came so late western education reforms did not arrive until after 1813 — & the reason was orientalism. the dominant ideology among british administrators in the late 18th & early 19th century held that indians should be governed the indian way, which meant understanding & working within indian literature, languages, & laws. reform could wait. in england, edmund burke (1729–1797) — the politician whose critique of eic's conduct led to pitt's india act of 1784 — believed indians were not ready for western-style reforms or education. in india, the two leading orientalists were william jones & warren hastings73-85. 26.2 — key orientalists william jones (judge at the calcutta supreme court, 1783–94) was a scholar of ancient greek, roman, & persian literature who was mesmerised by sanskrit. he argued that sanskrit epics & poetry were of greater literary stature than anything in greek, roman, or english literature — a claim that stunned european intellectuals & did more to raise the prestige of indian civilisation abroad than almost any other single act of the era. his key contributions: • together with hastings73-85, initiated codification of hindu & islamic laws into english — in 1775 & 1778 respectively — so the british could administer india using its own legal traditions. • founded the asiatic society of bengal in 1784 for oriental research. (*note- dwarkanath thakur/tagore — grandfather of rabindranath tagore & father of debendranath tagore — was a member of the asiatic society. the tagore family's connection to the intellectual currents of 19th-century bengal ran deep.) warren hastings73-85 set up the calcutta madrasa in 1781 for the study of arabic, persian, & islamic law — to understand indian legal systems & train indians to assist eic in ruling india the indian way. the sanskrit college, calcutta (1824) followed later, for better understanding of hindu laws. (*note- the same college roy opposed in 1824 & vidyasagar later transformed from within.) wellesley98-05 also set up fort william college, calcutta in 1800 to train newly-arrived british civil servants in indian languages, laws, & customs before they took charge. (*note- william carey taught bengali & sanskrit here.) 26.3 — who pushed for western education three distinct groups pushed back against orientalism. david hare was a watchmaker from calcutta who became one of the most remarkable reformers of his era: • championed western education in english alongside roy & radhakanta deb. • co-founded calcutta school book society (1817) with radhakanta deb — set up elementary schools & printed textbooks in english & bengali. • co-founded hindu college, calcutta (1817) along with sir edward hyde east (chief justice, calcutta supreme court — convened the hindu society) & raja ram mohan roy (later presidency college — the same institution where derozio taught). • founded hare school (1818). • visited hindu college daily & was attached to his students. in 1842, he died of cholera in calcutta. christian missionaries refused him a burial site, considering him a non-believer. he was finally laid to rest within the grounds of presidency college itself. thousands of calcuttans joined his funeral procession. ⚠ alert (prelims 2009): hindu college, calcutta (1817) was co-founded by sir edward hyde east, david hare, & raja ram mohan roy (the three central figures, alongside members of calcutta's hindu society). the pyq stem groups david hare with alexander duff & asks for the third founder — the answer is raja ram mohan roy. note that alexander duff himself was actually associated with the general assembly's institution, calcutta (1830) — a separate institution that later became scottish church college — not with hindu college 1817 (duff arrived in india in 1830). often confused with henry vivian derozio (he was a teacher at hindu college, not a founder), vidyasagar (he was principal of sanskrit college, not hindu college), or keshab chandra sen (no founding role). john malcolm (governor of bombay, 1827–30) favoured radical social reforms, pushed for western education & sciences, driven by the doctrine of reason & humanism. he belonged to a remarkable cohort of liberal british administrators that included: • thomas munro (governor of madras, 1820–27). • elphinstone (governor of bombay, 1819–27 — twice refused appointment as gg because he wanted to finish his book on india). • charles metcalfe (gg, 1835–36 — whose liberation of the press led to conflict with the court of directors of eic & his consequent resignation in 1838). charles grant was an evangelist who simultaneously served as member of parliament & director in the court of directors of eic: • presided over charter act 1813 — legalised entry of christian missionaries & mandated rs 1 lakh p.a. on education. • wanted western education in english to empower indians with awareness of laws against eic official corruption. • believed spreading christianity would create political stability through a common religion. 26.4 — macaulay's minute (1835) — decision and reasons the debate between orientalists & their opponents was finally settled by macaulay's minute on indian education (1835), implemented through the english education act 1835. it decided in favour of western education in english & served as the main policy framework until wood's despatch of 1854. this was the product of roy's advocacy (he died in 1833, two years before the policy was finalised), bentinck28-35's support, & macaulay's drafting. macaulay famously declared that "a single shelf of a good european library was worth the whole native literature of india & arabia." (*note- so called liberal reformers holding colonial bias.) the official stated reasons: • fulfil white man's burden by giving western sciences & humanities to india. • empower indians against corruption of eic officials. the real reasons: • reduce cost of administration — macaulay's law commission (1834) was formulating western-style laws. they needed western-educated indians to implement them at the lower levels of the bureaucracy. • create brown sahibs — macaulay explicitly wanted indians who were "indian in blood & colour, but english in taste, in opinions, in morals, & intellect" — loyal to british interests, glorifying british culture, & creating a domestic market for british goods. why did elite indians support it? • access to government jobs, legal practice, medical practice, teaching, journalism. • genuine belief that western sciences could modernise & industrialise india. downward filtration theory: british would not build mass education infrastructure. they would educate only the urban elite, who would then transmit education downward to the masses — at no additional state cost. high fees blocked the urban poor. rural areas got nothing. 26.5 — william adam's reports on vernacular education (1835-38) adam's three reports = the most critical documentary evidence of indigenous education before macaulay's minute 1835 & wd1854 dismantled it. 26.5.1 — context i) bentinck28-35 appointed william adam (scottish missionary who co-founded the calcutta unitarian committee with roy, 1821) to survey indigenous education in bengal & bihar. ii) three reports submitted 1835-38 — same window macaulay's minute settled the anglicist-orientalist debate. (*adam's findings describe the system macaulay's policy then bypassed.) 26.5.2 — core findings i) massive scale: over 1,00,000 pathshalas in bengal & bihar alone — almost every village had one. (*note- flatly contradicts the colonial "india was illiterate before british arrival" narrative.) ii) caste inclusivity: children of all castes (except absolute lowest / untouchables) often sat together; flexibility let poor agrarian families participate. (*note- watch the exam trap: "adam concluded the indigenous system was rigid & excluded lower castes" is false.) iii) extreme flexibility (most frequently tested) — decentralised, adapted to rural agrarian life: no fixed fee (teachers paid in kind — rice, grain — or cash by parents' ability); no printed books or fixed syllabus (oral instruction, slate practice, local texts); no separate buildings (banyan trees, temples, mosques, teacher's home); no annual exams or timetables (continuous individualised assessment); suspended during harvest — synchronised with the agrarian calendar, not imposed against it. iv) curriculum: strictly functional — basic literacy, arithmetic, accounts for daily agrarian + commercial life. (*link- exactly what macaulay dismissed as "useless"; he wanted an anglicised elite, not the literate peasantry that already existed per adam.) 26.5.3 — historical impact adam's reports proved india had no "education vacuum" waiting to be filled. a functioning, mass-scale vernacular system existed — starved of funding & destroyed by the shift toward english-medium administrative education. (*recall- wd1854 will later propose "vernacular primary schools" as a state innovation — hollow when read against adam: tens of thousands already existed. wd1854's real innovation was grants-in-aid & inspectorate, not vernacular education itself.) 26.6 — key features of the english education act 1835 • goal: promote european literature & science among indians. • medium: all funds for education to be used for english education alone. • cut-off: no more government money for printing oriental works; no new stipends for students entering oriental institutions — though existing institutions like the calcutta madrasa & benaras sanskrit college were not abolished. 26.7 — subsequent milestones 1844: knowledge of english made compulsory for government jobs. this dealt a serious blow to vernacular languages. 1847: roorkee engineering college set up (became a university in 1949; iit roorkee in 2001). 1849: bethune school for women set up by j.e. drinkwater bethune (law member of dalhousie's council & president of the council of education), bringing female education under grants-in-aid (non-returnable state funding). ishwar chandra vidyasagar as secretary - actively supported the institution, helped expand its reach - making it a cornerstone of the organised women's education movement in bengal. 1851: ishwar chandra vidyasagar became principal of sanskrit college (1824), calcutta — under dalhousie48-56's tenure. from this post, he pushed for opening sanskrit education to non-brahmins & integrated western subjects (mathematics, english literature) into the curriculum. 1856: vidyasagar became inspector of schools (in bengal) — also under dalhousie's tenure. the same year, the hindu widow remarriage act 1856 was enacted with vidyasagar's advocacy & dalhousie's government backing. 26.8 — wood's despatch (1854) the wood's despatch of 1854 (labeled as "magna carta of english education in india") was a set of directions sent from london by charles wood, president of the board of control (1784), to dalhousie48-56. it was the most comprehensive education policy statement the british had issued & represented a significant shift away from macaulay's downward filtration theory. what did it direct? • western education for the masses in vernaculars at elementary level; vernaculars plus english at high school (class 9th & 10th); english at college level. (*note- in today's terms — elementary = class 1st to 8th; secondary/high school = class 9th–10th; senior secondary = class 11th–12th.) • set up education departments in provincial governments — closer to the field, better placed to assess infrastructure gaps. • set up teacher training programmes to build human resource for mass education. • continue supporting female education. • set up universities in madras, bombay, & calcutta with departments covering law, engineering, sanskrit, persian, & arabic. what were the real goals? • cheap supply of clerks to reduce cost of administration. • spread western culture among the masses to enlarge the market for british goods. • glorify british rule among the masses for political stability. • moral development & intellectual growth — colonial framing of european superiority over indian thought. impact: • dalhousie48-56 supported the despatch & laid the groundwork; the three universities in madras, bombay, & calcutta were officially established in 1857 under canning56-62 (dalhousie left india in 1856). • two more universities followed under wood’s despatch architecture — panjab university, lahore (1882) and allahabad university (1887) — taking the british-india total to five presidency-grade universities by the close of the 19th century. • bankim chandra chatterjee & joddu nath bose were the first two graduates of calcutta university in 1858. • overall result — failure. female education remained neglected, high fees blocked mass education, mass infrastructure was never built. 1870: subject of education transferred to provinces. dalhousie48-56's vernacular implementation. dalhousie supported the despatch & implemented its vernacular push by expanding elementary schools in bengal & bihar. he also backed technical education — the goal being efficient labour, good consumers, & cheaper administration. ⚠ alert (prelims 1996 + prelims 2002 + prelims 2018): wood's despatch 1854 has been tested multiple times. to answer right, the student should know — wood's despatch (1854) recommended (a) grants-in-aid system, (b) establishment of universities, (c) english as medium at college level + vernaculars at elementary level + both at high school. upsc also tests the chronological order: macaulay's minute (1835) → wood's despatch (1854) → hunter commission (1882) → sargent report (1944). 26.9 — universities & education governance architecture wood's despatch (1854) laid the groundwork for the three presidency universities — but dalhousie48-56 left india in 1856 before their formal opening. the universities at bombay, madras, & calcutta were officially established in 1857 under canning56-62 — on the foundation dalhousie had built. bankim chandra chatterjee & joddu nath bose were among the first graduates of calcutta university in 1858. in addition to the presidency universities, dalhousie's tenure also saw the engineering college at roorkee (1847) gain institutional standing — it later became thomason college, then a university in 1949, then iit roorkee in 2001. administrative architecture for education governance. wood's despatch also set up the institutional spine: a director of education at each provincial level + inspector of schools at the district level. this director-inspector hierarchy was the colonial-era administrative skeleton for education governance — a structure that survived into independent india's education bureaucracy. 26.10 — why the british pulled back from higher education after 1870 in 1870, the state decreased funding for higher education in bengal — officially in the name of increasing funding for mass vernacular education. the real reason: • educated indians were producing increasingly nationalist writing in the press. • the anglo-indian press had begun describing college-educated indians as seditious. [note: brown sahibness had begun waning within 35 years of the english education act. the doctrine of reason the british handed to indians was being turned against british rule itself. by 1904, curzon99-05 would call universities "factories of sedition." the white man's burden narrative was looking increasingly farcical.] 1882: under ripon80-84, education was made a free enterprise — private institutions could open schools & colleges with state financial assistance & reduced bureaucratic control. higher education grew rapidly, but only the richer sections benefitted. 26.11 — hunter commission (1882–83) — key findings set up under ripon80-84 to assess progress since wood's despatch, the hunter / indian education commission found primary & secondary education in serious trouble — worsened by the 1870 transfer of education to cash-strapped provinces. recommendations: • transfer education to municipalities in urban areas & district boards in rural areas (both recently empowered by ripon80-84's local self government resolution of 1882). • focus on mass education in vernaculars. • strengthen female education especially outside madras, bombay, & calcutta. • divide secondary education (class 9th & 10th) into literary & vocational streams for skill development. • create a special fund for mass education for backward communities (rejected). 26.12 — curzon's attack on the universities curzon99-05 famously declared "universities are factories of sedition." based on the raleigh commission report, he pushed through the indian universities act 1904: • universities brought under direct government control — government could veto or amend university senate regulations. • decreased number of fellows (phd holders) per university & reduced their tenure. • most fellows to be government nominees rather than elected by professors. • stricter affiliation conditions for private colleges (a direct attack on the growing network of nationalist & swadeshi educational institutions). • rs 5 lakh p.a. allocated for education promotion. he also established the indian agricultural research institute at pusa, bihar (1905) — funded by henry phipps, a family friend — recognising that for an agrarian economy, agricultural education mattered. 26.13 — sadler commission (1917–19) — key recommendations (named after dr. michael sadler) • college entry after class 12th instead of class 10th. • strengthen secondary education (class 9th & 10th). • universities must be residential, autonomous, & unitary — not a scattered collection of affiliated colleges. (*note- sadler can be credited with the concept of the modern university campus system in india.) under liberal chelmsford16-21, seven new universities were established, including osmania university in the princely state of hyderabad. the government of india act 1919 formally gave the subject of education to the provinces. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): assertion (a): the first-ever bill to make primary education compulsory in india was rejected in 1911. reason (r): discontent would have increased if every cultivator could read. the bill was moved by gopal krishna gokhale in the imperial legislative council. upsc official answer: (a) — both a and r are true, and r is the correct explanation of a. the colonial state's anxiety that mass literacy would breed political consciousness and discontent was a documented reason for rejecting compulsory primary education in this era; cost-burden concerns also played a role but were secondary to the political-control logic that upsc's key recognises as the principal explanation. 26.14 — hartog committee (1929) — key observations • rapid growth in schools & colleges had come at the cost of quality. • at end of class 8th, students should choose between vocational education & academic progression — only deserving students to proceed to class 9th. • strengthen primary education (class 1st to 8th) as the foundation. 26.15 — wardha scheme (1937) when the inc formed governments in several provinces in 1937, it proposed its own vision through the wardha scheme of national education — shaped by gandhian philosophy & developed by the zakir hussain committee: • learning by doing — activity-based learning through field work, creating direct school-community contact. • english only after class 8th. • handicraft skilling as part of the regular curriculum. • free & compulsory education in vernaculars until 7 years of age. [note: the contrast with macaulay's vision could not be sharper. macaulay wanted english-medium, elite-focused, top-down education to create brown sahibs. the wardha scheme wanted vernacular, activity-based, community-rooted education to create citizens. one was designed for colonial stability; the other for self-governance.] 26.16 — sargent plan (1944) — also called sargent report the last major educational despatch of the british era — officially titled the report of the central advisory board of education on post-war educational development in india. the most comprehensive but unimplemented educational blueprint in british india. 26.16.1 — core objective i) goal: reconstruct the indian education system to reach the educational standard of contemporary england. ii) timeline: phased plan of 40 years to achieve 100% literacy in india. (*note- the 40-year horizon became the central nationalist grievance — see 26.16.4.) 26.16.2 — structural blueprint john sargent (educational advisor to the goi) proposed an age-based structure: i) pre-primary: 3–6 years. ii) basic elementary (universal & free): 6–14 years — split into junior basic (6–11) & senior basic (11–14). (*link- heavily inspired by gandhi's wardha scheme of basic education (sec. 26.15) — colonial absorption of nationalist pedagogy.) iii) high school: 11–17 years, selected students only. two streams: a) academic — for university-bound students (arts / sciences). b) technical / vocational — for immediate employment in agriculture or industry. iv) university: undergraduate degree standardised to 3 years. 26.16.3 — additional recommendations i) adult literacy: complete liquidation of adult illiteracy within 20 years. ii) special needs: one of the first british reports to explicitly mandate provisions for education of the physically & mentally differently-abled. iii) teachers: massive expansion of teacher training, physical education, & compulsory medical inspection of students. 26.16.4 — nationalist criticism & financial reality i) indian leaders furiously rejected the 40-year timeline — waiting till 1984 to achieve basic literacy was an insult; a free india could do it much faster. ii) the british drafted this utopian plan without allocating the funds required to execute it. 26.17 — overall impact of western education by 1921 — 92% illiteracy, only 2% of women literate. failures: • no mass infrastructure for education ever built. • education remained costly, blocking mass access. • vernacular education suffered severely after english made compulsory for government jobs in 1844. • upper-caste & british officials nexus worked against education for backward communities. • female education consistently neglected outside the three presidency towns. unintended consequences — & they were significant: • western education's doctrine of reason led indians to assess their own cultural practices critically → drove the social reform movements we have been studying. • a culture of public debate developed through the press → created civil society. • a passion for western sciences rose among educated indians → roy & others believed western sciences were the only route to modernisation. • most consequentially — the western educated middle class produced by this system turned the tools of western political thought (liberty, rights, representation, nationalism) against british rule itself. education acts timeline (charter act 1813 → macaulay's minute 1835 → wood's despatch 1854 → hunter / indian education commission 1882 → indian universities act 1904 → raleigh commission → sadler 1917-19 → hartog 1929 → sargent report 1944) — full chronological arc of british education policy in india. 26.18 — archaeological survey of india (1861) + field antiquarians western scholarship in colonial india ran on two parallel tracks — language/textual study (orientalism, see chapter 15 sec. 3) and field archaeology (institutionalised as the asi). archaeological survey of india (asi) — founded by alexander cunningham in 1861 as director-general; reorganised as a permanent department in 1871. the asi documented, excavated, and preserved india's pre-islamic and indo-islamic built heritage. the asi's first generation were field antiquarians working across the madras presidency, the deccan & south india. five names — tested as a block by upsc — are: 1. alexander rea 2. a.h. longhurst 3. robert sewell 4. james burgess 5. walter elliot ⚠ alert (prelims 2023 trap): alexander rea, a.h. longhurst, robert sewell, james burgess & walter elliot were associated with: 1. archaeological excavations ✓ 2. english press — wrong (indian press / english press has separate substantive home). 3. churches in princely states — wrong (none of the five was a missionary). 4. railways — wrong (none was a railway engineer). correct: (a) archaeological excavations. memory hook: five british surnames + late-19th-century activity + you don't know any individually = asi archaeological work.
