brought by the portuguese to goa, operated by joão de bustamante initially for religious texts. it would be over two centuries before it became a tool for political & social debate. key early milestones: • 1780: bengal gazette (english) launched in calcutta by james augustus hicky — india's first newspaper. shut down in 1782 by warren hastings73-85 for criticising the british. the press & power were in conflict from the very beginning. • 1784: calcutta gazette founded by francis gladwin with east india company patronage — a semi-official organ, not a fully independent paper. • 1789: bombay herald founded by william ashburner — first newspaper in bombay; renamed bombay gazette in 1791. • 1790: bombay courier founded by luke ashburner (william's brother); later merged with the times of india. • 1799: censorship press act by wellesley98-05 — wartime pre-censorship during anglo-mysore wars. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998 a/r): wellesley98-05 did impose the press regulation act (also called censorship act) in 1799 — assertion is correct. reason given by upsc (that the government was alarmed about the press's role in indian renaissance / nationalism) is false: the 1799 regulation was a wartime censorship measure during the french revolutionary wars era (anxiety about french sympathisers and revolutionary ideas spreading through calcutta's anglo-indian press), not about anticipating indian renaissance or indian nationalism — which were not yet political phenomena in 1799 (brahmo samaj was 1828; inc was 1885). the pre-1857 colonial state was worried about european-language print, not indian-language nationalist print. correct answer: (c) a true but r false. 27.2 — growth of vernacular press & early regulations (1800–1857) roy understood the press as a tool for social reform before almost anyone else: • 1821: sambad kaumudi (bengali) — founded by roy to advocate social reforms. • 1822: mirat-ul-akhbar (persian) — founded by roy to promote liberal ideas. • 1823: licensing regulations by acting gg john adams — required licences for press operation; forced closure of roy's mirat-ul-akhbar. • 1826: udant martand — india's first hindi newspaper (weekly), founded by pandit jugal kishore shukla. • 1835: metcalfe act (press liberation act) by charles metcalfe (gg 1835–36) — revoked licensing laws, earning him the title "liberator of the indian press." • 1854: samachar sudha varshan — first daily hindi newspaper, founded by shyam sundar sen. the 1857 revolt changed the atmosphere. the british blamed the vernacular press for spreading dissent, & stricter regulations followed. 27.3 — repressive regulations & the nationalist press (1858–1900) 1878 was the pivotal year of both repression & nationalist press growth: • vernacular press act (gagging act) by lytton76-80 — targeted regional-language newspapers specifically. papers like som prakash, dacca prakash, & samachar were directly affected. repealed in 1882 by ripon80-84. • the hindu (english) founded in madras by g. subramania iyer & m. veeraraghavachariar — started as a weekly, became a daily in 1889. other key nationalist papers of the era: • 1862: bengalee (english) — founded by girish chandra ghosh. surendranath banerjee purchased it in 1879 & transformed it into a powerful nationalist voice. • 1861–62: indian mirror (english) — founded by manomohan ghosh with major financial backing from debendranath tagore; keshab chandra sen also played a major role in its early years. • 1868: amrita bazar patrika (bengali, & in english from 1878) — founded by sisir kumar ghosh; became a major nationalist publication. it famously converted overnight from bengali to english in 1878 specifically to escape the vernacular press act. • 1881: kesari (marathi) & mahratta (english) — founded by bal gangadhar tilak, promoting nationalism. • 1882: swadesamitran (tamil) — founded by g. subramania iyer, advocating self-reliance. • 1887: sudharak (marathi) — edited by gopal krishna gokhale. ⚠ alert (prelims 2005): who repealed the vernacular press act? answer — ripon80-84 in 1882. common distractors are dufferin, curzon, hardinge — none repealed the act. lytton76-80 is the one who imposed it (1878); ripon80-84 repealed it (1882). ⚠ alert (prelims 2007): som prakash newspaper was started by ishwar chandra vidyasagar (not by dayananda saraswati, ram mohan roy, or surendranath banerjee). som prakash was one of the vernacular newspapers directly affected by lytton's 1878 vernacular press act. 27.4 — 20th century: resistance & regulations (1900–1947) the nationalist press intensified — & so did the repression: • 1908: newspaper (incitement of offences) act under minto05-10 — allowed seizure of presses inciting violence. • 1910: indian press act under minto05-10 — mandated security deposits from newspapers; fines & confiscation of printing presses for publications criticising colonial policies. repealed in 1921 after tej bahadur sapru committee recommendations. • 1931: indian press (emergency powers) act under irwin26-31 — suppressed coverage of the civil disobedience movement (1930–34). • 1932: foreign relations act — barred criticism of foreign governments allied with britain. • 1942: press regulating act — wartime censorship during ww2 . cinema arrives — lumière brothers, 7 july 1896 (bombay): cinema arrived in india on the heels of its global invention. on 7 july 1896, the times of india carried the advertisement of the lumière brothers — "the marvel of the century, the wonder of the world living photographic pictures in life-sized reproductions" — for the first cinematograph screening at watson's hotel, bombay. india's first feature film, raja harishchandra, followed in 1913 under dadasaheb phalke. print sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Setting the Stage
sections.norm: setting the stage. wemc inm 1857. the western educated middle class — the wemc — responded to british rule largely through socio-religious reform movements. they believed in the benevolence of british rule, that the british would modernize india, and many of them directly benefited from the new economy & jobs that british rule created. but it was the peasants & the tribals — the people at the very bottom of the new colonial order — who responded first, and they responded not with petitions but with defiance, and often with violence. inm leaders later called these pre-1857 revolts the "pre-history of modern nationalism." it does not mean these revolts were failures. it means they were the first draft of a political resistance that would, over a century, become the indian national movement. the 1857 revolt was, in many ways, the culmination of a hundred years of such small & big rebellions. to understand 1857, you must first understand what drove the peasants & tribals to revolt — again & again — in the decades before it.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Drivers of the Peasant Revolt
sections.norm: drivers of the peasant revolt. 2.1) why did the ryot have so many grievances under british rule? several land revenue systems squeezed the peasant 1772 the permanent settlement of 1793 ps1793 the rent act of 1859 high land revenue demands put up for auction moneylender 1860 1918 2.2) what role did religion play in the pre-1857 revolts? dual role sati abolition act 1829 lex loci act 1850 hindu widow remarriages act 1856 no political parties no newspapers with mass reach no formal organisations permanent settlement 1793. 2.1) why did the ryot have so many grievances under british rule? the british introduced not one but several land revenue systems across india, and each one, in its own way, squeezed the peasant. under the farming system of 1772 in bengal, land revenue collection was auctioned off to the highest bidder — a revenue farmer. the revenue farmer extracted as much rent as he could from the peasant, with the support of british officials, since the collection happened under the district collector's supervision. the peasant had no protection. the permanent settlement of 1793 (ps1793) replaced the revenue farmer with the zamindar as the permanent owner of the land. this sounds like an improvement, but for the ryot it was not. the zamindar could charge high rents, impose illegal extra cesses called abwabs, and evict tenants at will. the ryot had no occupancy rights — no security of tenure. and when he went to court, he found british law firmly on the side of the zamindar, since all legal rights in land were formally vested in the zamindar. the rent act of 1859 was supposed to correct this by giving occupancy rights to ryots who had cultivated a piece of land continuously for more than twelve years (a ryot who cultivated the same plot continuously for over twelve years earned the right not to be arbitrarily evicted — this was called occupancy right), but its implementation in bengal was ineffective, and the exploitation continued. in areas under ryotwari & mahalwari settlements, the oppression came directly from the british government through high land revenue demands. when a ryot could not pay, his land was put up for auction. this drove him to the moneylender. high interest rates led to deepening indebtedness, and default meant losing the land to the moneylender. the peasant went from being a cultivator with land to a labourer on someone else's field. contract farming under the indigo system was a separate horror. in bengal until 1860, and later in bihar until 1918, european indigo planters forced ryots to cultivate indigo on a portion of their land. the ryot was made to take a loan from the planter at the outset, then sold the indigo back to the planter at a price far below market rate. he was perpetually in debt to the planter. worse, indigo exhausted the soil, reducing the productivity of the land he used for food crops. if he refused to cultivate indigo, the planter's indian agents, local british officials, and courts would come down on him. there was no escape. ◆ a useful way to understand this: the indigo system was not just economic exploitation — it was a debt trap by design. the loan at the beginning ensured that the ryot was always obligated to the planter. this is the same structural logic as modern-day bonded labour. 2.2) what role did religion play in the pre-1857 revolts? religion played a dual role — it was both a grievance & an organiser. as a grievance: many peasants & traders felt that british rule threatened their religion. christian missionaries were converting people. the british ended revenue-free & rent-free land tenures traditionally held by temples, mosques, and religious institutions. social reform laws — the sati abolition act 1829, the lex loci act 1850 (which gave the right of inheritance even after conversion to another religion), and the hindu widow remarriages act 1856 — were seen by many as direct interference in religious life. as an organiser: pre-1857 india had no political parties, no newspapers with mass reach, no formal organisations. (modern organisations like the indian national congress, the bjp, the rss — all absent before 1857 — do the work today that religion did for the pre-1857 revolts: providing leadership, coordination, and unity.) when a religious sect revolted, it already had a leader, a philosophy, a sense of community, and the habit of collective action. religion filled the organisational vacuum.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Drivers of the Tribal Revolt
sections.norm: drivers of the tribal revolt. 3.1) what was different about the tribal experience? tribal autonomy extraction of land revenue zamindars from the plains legal owners of tribal land cash payment of land revenue moneylenders followed loss of land banned jhum cultivation way of life law that completed the dispossession the indian forests act 1878 1876–80 2,000 reserved forests everything was prohibited protected forests everything was permitted village forests very few were actually created 1878 forest rights act 2006 forests act customary right abkari (excise) administration claimed a monopoly highest-bidding contractors religious rituals criminalising indigenous brewing ncm cdm 1813. 3.1) what was different about the tribal experience? tribals lived in forests & hills, away from the mainstream society of the plains. they had two things that gave their life its shape: tribal autonomy (in civil & criminal matters, they governed themselves by their own customary law) and their relationship with the forest — as home, as livelihood, as identity. british rule destroyed both. the primary concern of the british was extraction of land revenue. so into the tribal areas came zamindars from the plains — made legal owners of tribal land. or tribal lands were farmed out to revenue farmers. or in some cases, the tribal chief was recognised as a zamindar, with the same exploitative powers. in some other cases, tribal ryots were made individual landowners — breaking up the collective, community-based relationship that tribals had with their land. high land revenue demands & the british insistence on cash payment of land revenue — instead of payment in produce — meant that moneylenders followed. indebtedness followed. loss of land followed. (this cash-payment requirement was a masterstroke of dispossession: a subsistence farmer who grows grain but must pay in rupees has to sell in the market first, making him vulnerable to price fluctuations & middlemen at every step.) the british also banned jhum cultivation — slash-and-burn or shifting cultivation — because they wanted settled peasant communities paying land revenue regularly. for hill tribals, jhum was not just an agricultural technique; it was their way of life. the ban on jhum & on hunting effectively criminalised their way of existing. the chenchus of hyderabad, for instance, were pushed to the edge of extinction. then came the law that completed the dispossession. ◆ side box: the indian forests act 1878 — how the british stole the forest the indian forests act 1878, passed under viceroy lytton (1876–80), divided all forests into three categories. the british called this "scientific forestry." in practice, it was legal dispossession. why did they need it? the railway boom of the 1870s required an enormous supply of durable timber — teak, sal, deodar. each mile of railway track needed roughly 2,000 wooden sleepers. the state needed absolute control over the best forests to feed this demand without interruption. the three categories: 1. reserved forests — the most commercially valuable forests. everything was prohibited unless specifically permitted. the state legally extinguished all traditional rights of local communities — no grazing, no firewood collection, no jhum. sole purpose: unhindered commercial timber extraction by the government & its contractors. 2. protected forests — forests with commercial potential but with too much existing local usage to close immediately. everything was permitted unless specifically prohibited. the state allowed basic usage but retained the power to declare specific tree species as state property & to close off sections at any time. this was a transitional category — over time, many protected forests were quietly upgraded to reserved forests as the state consolidated control. 3. village forests — forests assigned to specific village communities. very few were actually created. and even where they existed, the colonial state dictated strict rules: how many cattle could graze, how much wood could be taken, which species were off-limits. if the village broke colonial rules, access could be revoked entirely. the british never surrendered ownership; they never left any forest truly in local hands. the legal masterstroke: before the british arrived, forests were common property resources, managed by the communities living in & around them. the 1878 act redefined this reality. it transformed customary rights — things that communities had exercised for generations — into privileges granted by the mercy of the colonial state. a privilege can be taxed, restricted, or revoked at any time. overnight, collecting firewood to cook dinner, grazing a cow, or clearing a small patch of forest for a subsistence crop made millions of forest dwellers into trespassers on their own ancestral land. (today, the forest rights act 2006 attempts to begin correcting what this act did.) beyond the forests act, land acquisition for railway & road construction & for commercial timber extraction displaced tribals from their homes. they were often forced into unpaid labour on the very projects that dispossessed them. ◆ side box: the abkari system — taxing the tribals' own drink before british rule, brewing local liquor from palm sap (toddy) or mahua flowers was a customary right — lightly regulated or untaxed. the british changed this through the abkari (excise) administration. the colonial state claimed a monopoly over the manufacture & sale of all intoxicating liquors & drugs. it then auctioned off the right to tap palm trees & sell liquor to the highest-bidding contractors. the contractors, having paid large sums to the government, raised prices steeply to recover their investment. traditional brewing without a government licence was criminalised. for tribal communities, drinks like toddy or mahua were not merely recreational — they were tied to religious rituals, festivals, and daily nutrition. by criminalising indigenous brewing, the british forced communities to buy back their own traditional drinks at inflated prices from government-licensed vendors. excise duties on liquor became one of the largest sources of provincial revenue — second only to land revenue in many areas. (*note- this grievance later fed the temperance / anti-liquor strand of the indian national movement — gandhi's call to picket liquor shops in the ncm & cdm.) the entry of christian missionaries after 1813 added a religious dimension to the already deep economic & cultural wound.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Two Kinds of Uprisings
sections.norm: two kinds of uprisings. 1857 4.2) peasant revolts — led by the peasants themselves.. there were two distinct kinds: 4.1) civil uprisings — led by the elite: a raja, a zamindar, a mansabdar. the peasants participated, but the leadership & the cause were primarily that of the dispossessed elite. (the 1857 revolt is the biggest example of this kind.) 4.2) peasant revolts — led by the peasants themselves.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Civil Uprisings
sections.norm: civil uprisings. raja chait singh of benaras treaty of faizabad 1775 1789 permanent settlement eic upsc 1799 1797–98 1799–1805 1857 1803–05 1809 1805 the paika rebellion traditional landed militia of odisha permanent settlement 1793. 5.1) 1778–81: raja chait singh of benaras — benaras had been annexed by the eic through the treaty of faizabad 1775. chait singh was essentially a big zamindar who enjoyed the title of raja & the loyalty of his people. he had his own military & fort. his estates were seized due to non-payment of land revenue, and he revolted. (ps1793 later formally brought benaras into the bengal-bob-north madras-benaras revenue settlement.) 5.2) 1789: bishnupur & birbhum revolts, bengal — local zamindars & their ryots in bishnupur & birbhum, squeezed by the revenue demands of the permanent settlement's precursors, rose in revolt against the eic's revenue machinery. these revolts are minor in scale but appear frequently as upsc distractors — worth recognising by name & date. 5.3) 1799: nawab wazir ali — the deposed nawab of awadh (who had ruled only from 1797–98 before being replaced) revolted with peasant support. 5.4) 1799–1805: poligar revolts — the poligars were traditionally autonomous local chiefs in south india. british rule of law & equality before law hurt their elevated social status. (this is the same grievance that taluqdars had in the 1857 revolt — the loss of privilege that had previously been backed by customary law.) the ryotwari settlement took away their lands. high land revenue demands on peasants brought popular participation. they revolted, and were crushed. 5.5) post-2nd anglo-maratha war (1803–05): the subordinate alliance (sa) imposed a british resident on maratha states. bundela chiefs, suffering under resident interference, revolted with peasant support. 5.6) 1809: dewan veluthampi of travancore — after the subsidiary alliance of 1805, the british resident began interfering in travancore's internal affairs. veluthampi, the dewan, revolted alongside nair troops & peasants. he was crushed. 5.7) 1817: the paika rebellion, khurda, odisha — the paikas were the traditional landed militia of odisha — a warrior class with deep roots in the region's feudal order. the rebellion was led by feudal aristocrats, chiefly bakshi jagabandhu (the military commander of the raja of khurda) and marginalised zamindars. their primary goal was to restore their lost hereditary privileges, authority, and rent-free estates. yet despite elite leadership, the rebellion drew massive grassroots support from ordinary peasants, salt makers, and the tribal kondhs of ghumusar — making it a true multi-class uprising. after conquering odisha (1803), the eic had stripped the paikas of their rent-free land tenures (jagirs), imposed extortionate short-term settlements demanding revenue strictly in silver (sicca) rather than traditional cowrie shells, banned local sea-salt production to create a monopoly that skyrocketed prices, and dethroned the revered raja of khurda — uniting both elite loyalists & the masses against the british. the rebels systematically destroyed british symbols of authority — police stations, courts, and salt monopoly offices. they briefly captured puri, forced eic forces to retreat, and proclaimed the raja of khurda as their sovereign. the british declared martial law & crushed the core uprising with overwhelming military force by 1818. bakshi jagabandhu led a jungle guerrilla war until surrendering under negotiated terms in 1825. the paika rebellion remains one of the most formidable pre-1857 armed uprisings. due to its scale & multi-class participation, it is heavily debated in modern historiography as a candidate for india's true "first war of independence."

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Peasant Revolts Led by Peasants
sections.norm: peasant revolts led by peasants. 6.1) the 1783 rangpur rebellion, north bengal 1772 1770 rangpur peasants targeted the grain stores debi singh & gobinda singh attacked prisons 6.2) mysore 1830–31 1799 eic. 6.1) the 1783 rangpur rebellion, north bengal grievance: the farming system of 1772 had unleashed revenue farmers on the peasantry. debi singh & gobinda singh were particularly oppressive, and british officials colluded with them. this came on top of the devastating great bengal famine of 1770, which had already broken the economic spine of the peasantry. action: the rangpur peasants targeted the grain stores of the revenue farmers debi singh & gobinda singh — they looted them. they attacked prisons & freed imprisoned ryots. they attacked local courts. this matters: the peasants were not blindly violent. they knew exactly what was oppressing them — the revenue farmer, his grain stores, the prison, the court. they hit each one. for a time, they ran their own government, funded by self-imposed taxes. result: crushed by the eic. 6.2) mysore 1830–31 grievance: the wodeyar dynasty had been restored to mysore in 1799 after tipu sultan's defeat in the fourth anglo-mysore war. but the subsidiary alliance of 1799 required the mysore state to pay a heavy annual subsidy to the british. to meet this, the wodeyar government imposed high land revenue demands. the peasants of mysore revolted against both the wodeyar administration & british agents. result: the eic crushed the revolt — as was its obligation under the sa 1799, which required the british to protect the ruler.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Religion-Led Revolts
sections.norm: religion-led revolts. 7.1) the sanyasi & fakir rebellion (1760–1850s), north bengal & bihar 1800 50,000 eic high land revenue monopoly over domestic trade in bengal 1882 7.2) pagal panthi revolt (1823–33), east bengal karim shah tipu shah high rents, illegal abwabs denial of occupancy rights promised lower rents political programme 7.3) titu mir of 24 parganas (1831) wahabi sect shah waliullah of delhi indigo planters, zamindars, and british officials set up their own government bamboo fort at narkelberia 7.4) the faraizi movement (1830s, then revived 1870s), bengal haji shariatullah dudu mian naya mian quran was the only true source purge islam of all un-islamic beliefs land belongs to god crushed by the british 7.5) moplah / mopilla revolts in malabar (1840, then 1870s, and 1921) moplahs were muslim ryots janmies big landlords 1789–92 1921 2006 upsc permanent settlement 1793. 7.1) the sanyasi & fakir rebellion (1760–1850s), north bengal & bihar this rebellion ran across nearly a century, peaking around 1800 when some 50,000 members were participating. it brought together two religious groups — the dasnami sanyasis (who included peasants & small traders) and the madari fakirs (peasants who had traditionally held revenue-free or rent-free land tenures, now ended by the eic). despite being hindu & muslim respectively, the two groups cooperated because their religious philosophies had common ground and, more importantly, their economic grievances were identical. grievances: high land revenue, high rents after ps1793, and the eic's monopoly over domestic trade in bengal. (recall that mir qasim of bengal (1760–63) had tried to end internal duties before the battle of buxar 1764, because eic agents were using their trading privileges to strangle local merchants — the same squeeze that now hurt the sanyasi traders.) result: finally crushed by the british. ◆ bankim chandra chattopadhyay's novel anandamath (1882) was inspired by the sanyasi rebellion. its song vande mataram became the anthem of the indian national movement. the roots of nationalist imagination, it turns out, lay partly in this very revolt. 7.2) pagal panthi revolt (1823–33), east bengal leaders: karim shah, and after him, tipu shah. grievance: against zamindars — for high rents, illegal abwabs, and denial of occupancy rights. action: tipu shah promised lower rents once the zamindars & british were defeated. this was essentially a political programme, delivered through religious leadership. result: crushed by the eic. 7.3) titu mir of 24 parganas (1831) titu mir belonged to the wahabi sect & taught the reformist philosophy of shah waliullah of delhi. his followers were poor peasants who also adopted a distinct physical identity — a unique beard & dress — which itself became a marker of resistance. grievance: a tax on beards levied by the local zamindar, oppression by indigo planters, zamindars, and british officials. action: titu mir's followers set up their own government with self-imposed taxes. they were organised enough to build a famous bamboo fort at narkelberia village. result: crushed by the eic army. 7.4) the faraizi movement (1830s, then revived 1870s), bengal leaders: father-son duo — haji shariatullah in the 1830s, dudu mian in the mid-century, and naya mian in the 1870s. the faraizis believed that the quran was the only true source of islamic law, and wanted to purge islam of all un-islamic beliefs & practices — a return to the faith in its original form. grievance: oppression by indigo planters, zamindars, and british officials. action: dudu mian gave the movement its most powerful slogan: land belongs to god, therefore any rent or tax on land is ungodly. (from a student's perspective, notice how effective this framing is: you are not just fighting an economic injustice, you are fighting a sin. that is a far more powerful mobilising argument.) they set up their own government, courts, and collected their own taxes. result: crushed by the british. (the british historian w.w. hunter, in his book the indian musalmans, argued that british neglect of muslims had contributed to the faraizi movement, and that the british should favour muslims for the sake of political stability. this argument — that a discontented community is a dangerous one — would later have long-term political consequences for british policy on hindu-muslim relations.) 7.5) moplah / mopilla revolts in malabar (1840, then 1870s, and 1921) context: the moplahs were muslim ryots of the malabar coast. the janmies were members of brahmin princely families who had historically been big landlords. there were also supervisors who collected land revenue on behalf of janmies. traditionally, the earnings from the land were shared among all three groups, giving each a customary right in the land. how british rule broke this: malabar was annexed by the eic after the third anglo-mysore war (1789–92). the british land revenue system recognised only the janmies as the legal owners of land. overnight, the moplahs lost all their customary rights & were reduced to exploited tenants, while the janmies were backed by british law. (british orientalists even provided ideological cover, arguing that according to tradition, lord parshuram had gifted all the land to the janmies — giving the moplahs' dispossession the appearance of ancient legitimacy.) character of the revolt: the moplahs revolted violently, and the revolt took on a communal colour — because the oppressor & the oppressed happened to have different religious identities. (this dynamic — economic oppression along religious lines hardening into communal conflict — recurs in malabar in 1921 during the non-cooperation movement. for the 1921 moplah rebellion in detail, see the chapter on the non-cooperation movement & its aftermath.) result: crushed by the eic army. ⚠ alert (prelims 2006): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following revolts was made famous by bankim chandra chatterjee in his novel 'anand math'? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) sanyasi rebellion. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — bhil uprising; (b) ✗ — rangpur and dinapur uprising; (c) ✗ — bishnupur and birbhum rebellion

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Tribal Uprisings — Pre-1857
sections.norm: tribal uprisings — pre-1857. 8.1) pahariya revolt (1778), rajmahal hills eic 8.2) bhil revolts (1818–31), western india 1818 1831 8.3) ramosi uprising (1822), western ghats 1822 8.4) kol uprising 1831–32, chhota nagpur & singhbhum tribal autonomy of the kols was destroyed outsiders called suds lost their customary land rights targeted the property of the suds, not their lives 8.5) kandh uprising 1837–56, odisha (ghumsar/kalahandi) banned human sacrifice ritual of meriah prolonged resistance, eventually crushed 8.6) khasi uprising 1829–1833 influx of outsiders loss of khasi land 8.7) santhal hool / rebellion 1855–56, rajmahal hills (jharkhand) 1857 1855 unholy trinity win back their fatherland from the dikus british authority in the region collapsed 50,000 2018 inm 1882. 8.1) pahariya revolt (1778), rajmahal hills the pahariyas were among the earliest tribals to resist british encroachment. when the eic extended revenue collection & administrative control into the rajmahal hills, the pahariyas — hill-dwelling hunter-gatherers & shifting cultivators — rose in revolt against the destruction of their autonomy & livelihood. the british responded with a combination of military force & a policy of containment, pushing the pahariyas further into the hills. 8.2) bhil revolts (1818–31), western india the bhils of the khandesh & rajputana hills revolted repeatedly between 1818 & 1831. british annexation of maratha territories after the third anglo-maratha war (1818) brought the bhil homelands under direct eic control. the imposition of new land revenue demands, the entry of plains-based moneylenders, and the curtailment of the bhils' traditional forest rights provoked a series of uprisings. the british suppressed them militarily but also deployed the bhil corps — a locally recruited force — as a pacification strategy. 8.3) ramosi uprising (1822), western ghats the ramosis were a hill tribe of the western ghats region near pune. traditionally employed as watchmen & guards under the maratha state, they lost their customary occupations & status after the british takeover of maratha territories. dispossessed & marginalised, the ramosis rose against british authority in 1822. the uprising was localised but violent, and was eventually put down by force. 8.4) kol uprising 1831–32, chhota nagpur & singhbhum grievance: the tribal autonomy of the kols was destroyed by british rule. worse, the raja of chhotanagpur had farmed out tribal lands to merchants & moneylenders — outsiders called suds. the kols lost their customary land rights. action: the kols targeted the property of the suds, not their lives. again: the tribals knew their oppressors. result: crushed by the army. 8.5) kandh uprising 1837–56, odisha (ghumsar/kalahandi) leader: chakra bisoi. grievance: the british banned human sacrifice — a practice tied to the kandhs' religious ritual of meriah. to the british it was a humanitarian intervention; to the kandhs, it was an attack on their religion & autonomy. result: a prolonged resistance, eventually crushed. 8.6) khasi uprising 1829–1833 leader: u tirot sing. grievance: the british construction of the brahmaputra valley–sylhet road brought an influx of outsiders — british businesses, their indian agents, and british officials — into khasi territory, causing loss of khasi land & disruption of their way of life. result: crushed. 8.7) santhal hool / rebellion 1855–56, rajmahal hills (jharkhand) the santhal rebellion is one of the most powerful pre-1857 uprisings. the santhals called their homeland damini-i-koh — the skirts of the hills. the british had opened it up for settlement, bringing in non-santhal zamindars & moneylenders — people the santhals called dikus (outsiders). railway & road construction further devoured santhal land. leaders: brothers sido murmu & kanhu murmu. action: 8.7.1) in 1855, the santhals gave the british a formal prior warning — a public declaration of revolt to come. this is political action, not mere violence. 8.7.2) they then rose with bows & arrows against what they called the unholy trinity — the british, the zamindars, and the moneylenders — to win back their fatherland from the dikus. 8.7.3) british authority in the region collapsed. 8.7.4) the british retaliated with organised military force, burning villages & killing approximately 50,000 santhals. result: the revolt was crushed with extreme ferocity. however, its political impact was real: a separate administrative unit — santhal parganas — was created, with formal protections for tribal culture & identity. the british imposed restrictions on the transfer of santhal land to non-tribals within the santhal parganas — an early form of protective land legislation that acknowledged the diku problem. (⚠ prelims 2018 asked about restrictions on transfer of tribal land — santhal parganas is the key example.) ◆ (in modern inm, bankim chandra's bharat mata concept in anandamath 1882 drew on this same emotional idea of a fatherland that must be reclaimed — the santhals had articulated it in their own idiom three decades earlier.)

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Understanding the Character of Pre-1857 Revolts
sections.norm: understanding the character of pre-1857 revolts. 9.1) were these revolts examples of modern nationalism? modern nationalism liberty, equality, fraternity united leadership clear ideology & goal mouthpiece pre-1857 revolts fell short not all-india movements no coordination only local leaders not democracy in any modern sense 9.2) then why call them "pre-history of modern nationalism"? unmistakably political ideology — they had it restore the moral order organisation — they had it set up their own governments programme — they had it political awareness — they had it sharply 1855 1899 1857 inm. 9.1) were these revolts examples of modern nationalism? no. modern nationalism rests on a specific idea of the nation & a specific idea of politics. think of the french revolution's famous formula: liberty, equality, fraternity. a modern nation is one where citizens feel united as one people (fraternity/unity), equal before the law (equality), and collectively supreme — meaning national interest, not the interest of any king, caste, or class, is paramount (liberty/sovereignty). modern politics, flowing from this, requires: a united leadership, a clear ideology & goal, a plan (long-term) and programme (short-term), a mouthpiece (newspaper, website) to articulate ideology & justify actions, and an organisational structure through which directions from leadership reach every follower on the ground. by these standards, the pre-1857 revolts fell short: 9.1.1) they were not all-india movements — no unity across regions. 9.1.2) they had no coordination with each other. 9.1.3) they had only local leaders — no one thought of india first & their region second. 9.1.4) they lacked proper planning. 9.1.5) their goal was not democracy in any modern sense. 9.2) then why call them "pre-history of modern nationalism"? because they were unmistakably political — not apolitical, not merely criminal, not merely religious. and political action, even in an older vocabulary, shares something essential with modern politics. ideology — they had it. they wanted to restore the moral order that british rule had disturbed. their vocabulary was not the modern one of rights, democracy, colonialism, or "no taxation without representation." but immoral rule implies oppression, implies denial of economic, cultural, and political rights. different language, same moral architecture. organisation — they had it. religion provided bonds of unity, leadership, and the habit of collective action, especially where a whole sect revolted. many of them set up their own governments, their own courts, and collected their own taxes. that is a functioning parallel state, however temporary. programme — they had it. meetings were held, plans were made. political awareness — they had it sharply. the peasants of rangpur did not randomly burn villages. they targeted the revenue farmer's grain stores, the prison, and the courts. the kols targeted property, not lives. the santhals declared: "we have always hunted game in these forests. now we hunt our oppressors." these people understood exactly what instrument was being used to oppress them. political symbolism — they had it. public marches & meetings (not secretive). the santhal warning of 1855. birsa munda's uprising timed for christmas 1899 (see post-1857 section below). the santhal idea of the fatherland that must be reclaimed. ◆ crimes are committed secretly. politics is done in public. these revolts were public — a distinction the inm leaders later recognised when they called them the pre-history of modern nationalism.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-1857 Peasant & Tribal Revolts and Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.title: Post-1857 Tribal Uprisings
sections.norm: post-1857 tribal uprisings. 10.1) munda ulugulan 1899–1900, chhota nagpur loss of lands to outsiders christian missionaries birsa had supernatural healing powers british bullets would turn to water 1899 10.2) rampa rebellion / fituri, rampa hills of andhra land acquisition for road construction loss of lands to moneylenders prohibition of podu cultivation restriction on use of forest resources tax on toddy muttadars local estate holders 1920 ncm 1922 1924 2018 upsc 2020 1857 1921 1859–60. 10.1) munda ulugulan 1899–1900, chhota nagpur leader: birsa munda grievances: loss of lands to outsiders; oppression by british officials; missionary activities of christian missionaries in tribal areas. the role of religion: the people came to believe that birsa had supernatural healing powers — and that british bullets would turn to water when fired at him. (this belief — that a leader has divine protection — is a recurring feature in popular uprisings where people face a vastly more powerful enemy. it is not superstition alone; it is the psychologically necessary act of making resistance feel possible.) religion gave courage where reason might have said surrender. political symbolism: birsa chose christmas of 1899 to launch the ulugulan. this was a deliberate act — rising against british power on the most sacred day of the religion that missionaries were using to erode munda identity. :) result: crushed by the british. 10.2) rampa rebellion / fituri, rampa hills of andhra grievances: 10.2.1) commercial exploitation of forests. 10.2.2) land acquisition for road construction. 10.2.3) loss of lands to moneylenders & merchants. 10.2.4) prohibition of podu cultivation (shifting cultivation, equivalent to jhum). 10.2.5) restriction on use of forest resources. 10.2.6) tax on toddy (the local drink — the abkari system at work, as described above). leadership: the muttadars — local estate holders, roughly equivalent to poligars or taluqdars in their region. (this follows the same pattern as civil uprisings: elite leaders with popular participation.) first phase: crushed by 1880. second phase — the gandhian & post-gandhian overlap: in 1920, the rampa tribals' movement merged into mahatma gandhi's non-cooperation movement (ncm). their form of civil disobedience was the violation of forest laws — specifically in andhra, under the leadership of alluri sitarama raju. after the withdrawal of the ncm in 1922, alluri sitarama raju concluded that india could be liberated only by force. he re-initiated the fituri — the violent rebellion. he was captured & executed in 1924. ◆ (the rampa rebellion sits at a fascinating intersection. it starts as a pure tribal economic revolt in the 1870s, merges with gandhi's mass movement in 1920, and then — after gandhi's withdrawal — produces a leader who draws the opposite lesson from gandhi. alluri sitarama raju becomes a revolutionary martyr in the andhra tradition, celebrated in popular memory to this day.) ⚠ alert (prelims 2018): upsc tested this. q) after the santhal rising subsided, what was/were the measure/measures taken by the colonial government? 1. the territories called 'santhal paraganas' were created. 2. it became illegal for a santhal... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) both 1 and 2. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — only 1; (b) ✗ — only 2; (d) ✗ — neither 1 nor 2 ⚠ alert (prelims 2020): upsc tested this. q) with reference to the history of india, 'ulgulan' or the great tumult is the description of which of the following events? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) birsa munda's revolt of 1899–1900. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — the revolt of 1857.; (b) ✗ — the mappila rebellion of 1921.; (c) ✗ — the indigo revolt of 1859–60.

sections.title: Defining the Revolt of 1857
sections.norm: defining the revolt of 1857. 1857 1998 upsc 2005. the revolt of 1857 was not simply a military mutiny. it was a sepoy mutiny combined with a civil rebellion — two streams that flowed together into one of the most significant events in the history of british rule in india. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) the educated middle class in india to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) opposed the revolt of 1857. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — supported the revolt of 1857; (c) ✗ — remained neutral to the revolt of 1857; (d) ✗ — fought against native rulers ⚠ alert (prelims 2005): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following territories was not affected by the revolt of 1857? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) chittor. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — jhansi; (c) ✗ — jagdishpur; (d) ✗ — lucknow

sections.title: The Opening Shots
sections.norm: the opening shots. mangal pandey 34th bengal native infantry fired at european officers 1857 1837–1857 1858 zafar. on 29 march 1857, mangal pandey, a sepoy of the 34th bengal native infantry (bni) at barrackpur near calcutta, fired at european officers. his fellow sepoys refused to arrest him. mangal pandey was hanged on 8 april 1857. jemadar ishwari prasad, who had refused to restrain pandey, was hanged on 22 april 1857. the 34th bni was disbanded as collective punishment. on 10 may 1857, sepoys at meerut mutinied. the next day they marched to delhi & proclaimed bahadur shah zafar3757 (1837–1857, last mughal emperor) as emperor of hindustan. by end of may, the revolt had spread across the north-west provinces & awadh, with the civil population joining in. british rule collapsed across a large swathe of north & central india — from 11 may to 20 september 1857 in delhi, and broadly until spring of 1858. the violence on both sides was enormous. for the first time in a century, the british monopoly over organised violence in india was broken.

sections.title: Why the Sepoys Mutinied
sections.norm: why the sepoys mutinied. 3.1) service-related grievances racism earned far less than european soldiers highest rank an indian could reach was subedar 1856 3.2) socio-religious grievances recruited from upper castes respected caste customs caste privileges were reduced forced to serve in burma, sindh, or afghanistan risking loss of caste charter act 1813 enfield rifle cartridges cow & pig fat bitten before loading 3.3) political grievance 3.4) agrarian grievances lands auctioned lost to moneylenders british courts backed moneylenders sepoy was a peasant in uniform greased cartridge was merely the trigger began in the bengal army ratio of british to indian soldiers was lowest. 3.1) service-related grievances i) racism: indian sepoys earned far less than european soldiers, received smaller pensions, and faced routine slurs — referred to as "suar" (pigs). the highest rank an indian could reach was subedar, worth only 60–70 rupees a month. ii) economic: to offset high war expenditure, the british cut sepoy salaries & abolished the allowance for serving outside one's home region in 1856. (this regional allowance mattered doubly — losing it was both an economic blow and, for many upper-caste men, a religious insult, since serving far from home or crossing water was seen as causing loss of caste.) 3.2) socio-religious grievances early on, the british had recruited from upper castes & respected caste customs — ruling the indian army the indian way. (this was the ideology of orientalism — to govern india, work within indian traditions, at least initially.) but as the empire expanded & the army became more heterogeneous, maintaining caste-specific customs became inconvenient. the british now wanted a uniform army culture where loyalty ran to the employer, not to caste or religion: i) caste privileges were reduced — food restrictions, religious symbols, and the right to refuse service in polluting regions were curtailed. ii) sepoys forced to serve in burma, sindh, or afghanistan — risking loss of caste — who refused were dismissed or punished. iii) presence of christian missionaries in cantonments since charter act 1813 created anxiety about forced conversion. iv) then came the rumours — cow & pig bone dust mixed into flour; grease on the new enfield rifle cartridges (which replaced the brown bess musket) made from cow & pig fat, requiring the cartridge to be bitten before loading. whether true or not, these rumours landed on already fertile ground: the fear that the british were engineering a loss of hindu & muslim identity to make conversion easier. 3.3) political grievance the single largest source of recruits for the bengal army was awadh. nearly every family there had a member in the british indian army. the annexation of awadh in 1856 felt like a personal betrayal. their loyalty had cost them their homeland. 3.4) agrarian grievances i) summary settlements in awadh fixed lr without proper field surveys → unreasonable demands. ii) peasants unable to pay → lands auctioned by government, or lost to moneylenders through debt. iii) new british courts backed moneylenders, completing the dispossession. iv) the sepoy was a peasant in uniform — these wounds were his family's wounds. the greased cartridge was merely the trigger. the revolt began in the bengal army because upper-caste identity had been most carefully preserved there, and the ratio of british to indian soldiers was lowest in that army.

sections.title: Why the Civil Population Rebelled
sections.norm: why the civil population rebelled. 4.1) feudal elites & dispossessed rulers doctrine of lapse stripped ruling families of power displaced elites ii9618 1796–1818 1858 maulvi ahmadullah shah rallied both hindu & muslim support awadh permanent settlement act 1793 1856–62 1856 1862 1859 2006 4.2) taluqdars & big landowners 1801 4.3) peasants 1857 4.4) religion — a fear shared across society religion was under threat 1813 socio-religious reforms escalated anxiety religious disabilities act 1850 lex loci act taxing revenue-free lands of mosques, temples pundits & maulvis gave this resentment a voice 2005 upsc baji rao ii. 4.1) feudal elites & dispossessed rulers annexations under the doctrine of lapse & other policies had stripped ruling families of power — and with each fallen ruler, the entire dependent court aristocracy fell too. these displaced elites now had both motive and, in many cases, remaining private resources to lead a rebellion. key leaders: i) nana sahib — kanpur; adopted son of baji rao ii9618 (1796–1818), denied pension after annexation ii) begum hazrat mahal — lucknow iii) khan bahadur khan rohilla — bareilly iv) rani lakshmi bai — jhansi. she fought fiercely & died in battle at gwalior on 17–18 june 1858, becoming one of the most celebrated symbols of the revolt. v) maulvi ahmadullah shah — a fiery religious leader from faizabad who rallied both hindu & muslim support & became one of the most formidable rebel commanders in awadh. vi) kunwar singh — a zamindar of jagdishpur, bihar; had lost his lands under the sunset clause of the permanent settlement act 1793 (which mandated forfeiture of zamindari rights on non-payment of lr by a fixed sunset deadline — a harsh, inflexible rule that destroyed many old landed families); his brother amar singh was also active in the revolt vii) bahadur shah zafar — delhi; canning5662 (viceroy 1856–62) had announced in 1856 that mughals would henceforth be called only "princes" and would vacate the red fort. after the fall of delhi, zafar was captured, tried, and exiled to rangoon (burma), where he died in 1862 — the last mughal emperor, ending his days as a prisoner far from the empire his ancestors had built. viii) tantia tope — nana sahib's most capable military commander, who became the revolt's greatest guerrilla fighter. after the fall of kanpur & jhansi, tantia tope refused to surrender. he waged a prolonged guerrilla campaign across central india — evading british columns, striking & retreating, keeping the revolt alive long after other centres had fallen. he was eventually betrayed by his associate man singh, captured by the british, and hanged in april 1859. (prelims 2006 asked about tantia tope — his guerrilla warfare & betrayal are standard exam facts.) 4.2) taluqdars & big landowners the mahalwari settlement in the north-west provinces (half of awadh had been under sa since 1801) and in awadh (annexed 1856) transferred land rights to actual cultivators in many cases, stripping taluqdars of their personal estates. the british also disbanded private forts & armies. then rule of law — equality before the law — finished the process by removing their social superiority. having lost economically, militarily, and socially, taluqdars threw their lot in with the peasants. 4.3) peasants high lr → debt to moneylenders → loss of land through government auctions & moneylender takeovers. traditional occupancy rights were gone. british courts sided with moneylenders. so peasant anger in 1857 was directed both at the british government & at moneylenders — both were seen as oppressors. 4.4) religion — a fear shared across society the whole rural society shared a fear that its religion was under threat. this fear was not invented: i) since 1813, christian missionaries had operated in india, at times under police protection. ii) socio-religious reforms, however well-intentioned, escalated anxiety: a) sati abolition act, 1829 b) hindu widows' remarriage act, 1856 c) removal of caste & religious disabilities act, 1850 (also called the lex loci act — latin for "law of the place"; here, a law that gave inheritance rights to those who converted to another religion, thereby incentivising conversion to christianity) iii) the british had also started taxing revenue-free lands of mosques, temples, and religious sects — hindus & muslims both felt the threat. iv) pundits & maulvis gave this resentment a voice & spread it among the people. there was a shared moral conviction across communities: that british rule had disrupted the right political, economic, social, and religious order. the goal of 1857 was to restore what had been lost. ⚠ alert (prelims 2005): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following places did kunwar singh, a prominent leader of the revolt of 1857 belong to? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) bihar. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — madhya pradesh; (c) ✗ — rajasthan; (d) ✗ — uttar pradesh ⚠ alert (prelims 2006): upsc tested this. q) with reference to the 'revolt of the year' 1857 which of the following was betrayed by 'friend' captured and put to death by the british? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) tantia tope. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — nana sahib; (b) ✗ — kunwar singh; (c) ✗ — khan bahadur khan

sections.title: Why the British Won
sections.norm: why the british won. 5.1) rebels had no financial resources. 5.2) peasant fighters lacked modern weapons & training. superior leadership centralised bureaucracy telegraph & communication network no effective central command no coordination concentrated on delhi symbolic heart of the revolt fell fragmented & localised one at a time whole indian army did not revolt punjabi & gurkha soldiers actively helped the british confined to north & central india. 5.1) rebels had no financial resources. 5.2) peasant fighters lacked modern weapons & training. 5.3) british had superior leadership, a centralised bureaucracy, a professional army, and a functioning telegraph & communication network. 5.4) no effective central command on the indian side — multiple regional leaders, no coordination. 5.5) a tactical error: rebel energy was concentrated on delhi. when delhi fell, the symbolic heart of the revolt fell with it. 5.6) the uprising was fragmented & localised — the british defeated rebel groups one at a time. 5.7) the whole indian army did not revolt. bombay & madras regiments stayed quiet; punjabi & gurkha soldiers actively helped the british. (the bengal army was the largest, so roughly half the indian army had mutinied — but the other half held, and that was enough.) 5.8) civil rebellion was confined to north & central india — minor participation elsewhere.

sections.title: War of Independence — The Debate
sections.norm: war of independence — the debate. most contested question about 1857 6.1) three positions colonial view sepoy mutiny 1909 mainstream historical view far more than a mutiny modern nationalism was absent 1857 6.2) arguments against it being a war of independence whole india did not participate ryotwari areas ryots had become landowners punjab benefited from canal construction bengal permanent settlement of 1793 benefited from british rule stayed out wemc 1858 taluqdars who had retained their land stayed out spontaneous — no planning, no manifesto not a modern republic or democracy restore the old order 6.3) arguments that it was much more than a mutiny modern nationalism was absent more than narrow self-interest eic out of all of hindustan regional leaders did communicate 18th-century decentralised setup real power at provincial level mughal emperor as a symbolic weak centre movement of the masses, not just elites elites were pushed into leadership bahadur shah zafar, nana sahib, and the rani of jhansi peasants & artisans continued fighting after their taluqdar leaders had surrendered initiative returned common people 2000 upsc 1917 1919-22 1942. this is the most contested question about 1857, and it has no simple answer. 6.1) three positions i) colonial view: primarily a sepoy mutiny. the civil rebellion was just lawless elements exploiting disorder. ii) v.d. savarkar (1909 book): the indian war of independence, fought for swadharma & swaraj. karl marx also saw it as a nationalist revolt. iii) mainstream historical view: far more than a mutiny — but modern nationalism was absent, so it cannot be called a proper war of independence in the modern sense. (modern nationalism requires: the nation as the sum of equal people who feel a common identity; power vested in the people — democracy & republic, not monarchy; liberty, equality, fraternity. by this standard, 1857 falls short.) 6.2) arguments against it being a war of independence i) whole india did not participate — only north & central india was mainly active. a) ryotwari areas (sindh, coorg, assam, madras, bombay — scam b): ryots had become landowners under british rule :) b) punjab: middle-class peasants benefited from canal construction c) bengal: zamindars had benefited from the permanent settlement of 1793 ii) those who benefited from british rule stayed out: a) wemc believed in british rule as a force for modernisation & had gained jobs & status under it b) princes whose territories were not annexed largely stayed loyal to the british & some actively aided them as well, e.g. rajput kings. however, rajputana did witness upheaval in the form of sepoy mutinies & mass revolt, the most famous being kota where leadership was provided by lala jaidayal & mehrab khan & rebels completely took over the city & effectively held their own king hostage in his palace for six months. they killed the british political agent major charles burton. the british army could only reconquer the city in 1858. iii) taluqdars who had retained their land stayed out. iv) the whole indian army did not revolt. v) the revolt was spontaneous — no planning, no manifesto, no coordination. (modern political movements require organised planning & coordination — which itself embodies the element of fraternity.) vi) the goal was not a modern republic or democracy. it was to restore the old order — the rule of monarchs & feudal lords. 6.3) arguments that it was much more than a mutiny modern nationalism was absent — yes. but something more than narrow self-interest was present: i) common enemy & common hatred — against annexations, high lr, loss of land, oppression by moneylenders & eic officials, destruction of indian industry. ii) the sepoys' own declarations went far beyond personal grievances — they cited high lr, increased chowkidari tax, rising unemployment of artisans & learned men, toll taxes on public roads, and the declining status of the indian ruling class. they were, in effect, speaking for all indians. iii) hindu-muslim unity — a shared belief that hindustan belonged to hindus & muslims alike. as aitchisonobserved: "in this instance we could not play off the mohammedans against the hindus." (this unity of purpose across religious lines was what made the revolt so dangerous for the british — and why divide-and-rule became central to post-1857 policy.) iv) the rebels did not just want the british out of their own area — they wanted them out of all of hindustan. (fighting only for your village is self-interest; fighting to free the whole country is fraternity — an embryonic national consciousness.) v) regional leaders did communicate with each other, however imperfectly. vi) the rebels did not seek a return to 17th-century centralised mughal rule. they envisioned something closer to the 18th-century decentralised setup — real power at provincial level, with the mughal emperor as a symbolic weak centre. (early instinct towards federalism. :)) most importantly, it was a movement of the masses, not just elites: vii) in many cases, elites were pushed into leadership. bahadur shah zafar, nana sahib, and the rani of jhansi took up roles partly because circumstances compelled them. viii) peasants & artisans in many regions continued fighting after their taluqdar leaders had surrendered. ix) the sepoy was a peasant in uniform — when he removed that uniform, the initiative returned to where it had always come from: the common people. ⚠ alert (prelims 2000): upsc tested this. q) "in this instance we could not play off the mohammedans against the hindus.'' to which one of the following events did this remark of aitchison relate? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) revolt of 1857. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — champaran satyagraha (1917); (c) ✗ — khilafat and non-cooperation movement (1919-22); (d) ✗ — august movement of 1942

sections.title: Why 1857 is a Watershed
sections.norm: why 1857 is a watershed. 7.1) political impact: end of the eic eic government of india act, 1858 ended eic rule queen victoria declared sovereign of india direct crown rule over british india paramountcy over indian princes secretary of state for india replaced the president of the board of control 1858 1857 wemc inm 7.3) administrative impact: policing 1st police commission (1860) police act, 1861 7.4) administrative impact: civil services charter act 1853 maximum age of eligibility deliberately set at 19 too old before they were ready 1870 1878 ccs 2006 upsc lytton. fallout 7.1) political impact: end of the eic the eic was blamed in britain for mismanaging indian affairs. public pressure mounted to end what had been a peculiar arrangement of absentee sovereignty — (real sovereign power was british, but britain was absent as the actual ruler; it governed india through an agent — the eic — creating a dangerous gap between real authority & day-to-day governance). the government of india act, 1858 (act for better government of india, 1858) ended eic rule: i) queen victoria declared sovereign of india — direct crown rule over british india, paramountcy over indian princes. (the formal title kaiser-i-hind — empress of india — came later, through the royal titles act, 1876, and was proclaimed at the delhi durbar of 1877. victoria had used the title informally since 1858, but it was the 1876 act that made it official.) ii) a secretary of state for india — a full cabinet member — replaced the president of the board of control as the top authority in britain on indian affairs. iii) on 1 november 1858, queen victoria issued a proclamation promising religious tolerance & governance in accordance with india's own traditions & customs. socio-religious reforms — and the promotion of christianity — were shelved. 7.2) ideological impact: racism, authoritarianism, and the unintended birth of modern nationalism post-1857, british attitudes hardened. indians were now seen as racially inferior — incapable of self-governance & beyond reform. the british became more autocratic, more unwilling to give indians any senior role in bureaucracy, police, or military. but this backfired. the western educated middle class (wemc) — educated in british institutions, believing in british liberalism — had wanted a share in governance. they were now shut out. that frustration became the seed of the modern nationalism-based inm that began developing in the second half of the 19th century. (the british, in trying to lock the door to indian participation, inadvertently created the very class that would eventually break it down.) 7.3) administrative impact: policing 1857 made clear how vulnerable the british were without effective policing & intelligence. the 1st police commission (1860), set up by canning5662 under m.h. court, led to the police act, 1861 — passed in march 1861. it created a proper provincial police structure with a clear chain of command — for the first time — running from the inspector general (reporting to the governor/lg) down through the superintendent of police at district level to the sub-inspector at the thana. from 1857 onward, a police raj was effectively created, with indians excluded from all positions of importance. 7.4) administrative impact: civil services i) exam introduced under charter act 1853, but now it would not be held simultaneously in india. ii) maximum age of eligibility deliberately set at 19–23 — low enough to ensure most indian candidates would be too old before they were ready. (indian students typically finished their education later than their british counterparts — the age cap was a quiet but effective barrier.) iii) statutory civil service (1870, implemented 1878 by lytton7680): indians could now be nominated to certain posts previously reserved for covenanted civil service (ccs) officers — but only loyal, hand-picked elites were chosen. co-option, not inclusion. ⚠ alert (prelims 2006): upsc tested this. q) who was the governor-general of india during the sepoy mutiny? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) lord canning. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — lord bentinck; (c) ✗ — lord hardings; (d) ✗ — lord lytton

sections.title: Changes in the Army — Peel Commission
sections.norm: changes in the army — peel commission. 1857 1858 1859 1858–59 coup-proof no future bengal army-style mutiny 1860 eic 8.2) fixed ratios of british to indian soldiers — implemented through executive war office directives: bengal army 1 british soldier for every 2 indian soldiers indian artillery monopoly broken barred from serving in artillery units 8.4) "divide & rule" regiments — regiments restructured internally to prevent solidarity: deliberate mix of castes, religions, and ethnicities no single group could dominate namak ka haq 8.7) large permanent standing army maintained to counter future revolts. 8.8) minimum or no indians in senior military positions. financial control of the army placed firmly under civilian authority inm. the british understood clearly that 1857 was, at its core, a military mutiny. preventing another one required a complete restructuring of the army — not just minor adjustments. for this, the crown appointed the royal commission on the reorganisation of the indian army in july 1858. it submitted its report in march 1859. it is popularly known as the peel commission, after its head — major-general jonathan peel, who also served as secretary of state for war(1858–59) in the british cabinet. (jonathan peel was the younger brother of sir robert peel — the british prime minister who created the modern london police force. the peel family had a hand in restructuring both indian policing & the indian army after 1857.) the commission's goal was to design a "coup-proof" colonial army — one in which no future bengal army-style mutiny would ever be possible. its recommendations were implemented not through a single act but through a combination of legislation & executive military orders over the following years. how the recommendations were implemented 8.1) the european forces (india) act, 1860 — the major legislative outcome. it abolished the eic's separate european army & formally merged those soldiers into the regular british crown army. (this triggered a brief "white mutiny" among eic european soldiers, who resisted the transfer without a financial bounty — an irony not lost on history. !!!!) 8.2) fixed ratios of british to indian soldiers — implemented through executive war office directives: i) bengal army (where the mutiny had been worst): 1 british soldier for every 2 indian soldiers (1:2) ii) madras & bombay armies: 1:3 8.3) indian artillery monopoly broken — through military policy, the british took complete & exclusive control of the artillery. indian soldiers were entirely barred from serving in artillery units or handling heavy weapons. (control of artillery = control of the most decisive firepower. no indian artillery meant no indian capacity to wage a conventional offensive war against the british. a structural check, not just a policy one.) 8.4) "divide & rule" regiments — regiments restructured internally to prevent solidarity: i) deliberate mix of castes, religions, and ethnicities within each regiment ii) no single group could dominate or form a cohesive bloc iii) inter-regional interaction between army units actively discouraged — pan-india unity among regiments had been the british nightmare in 1857; it was now structurally prevented 8.5) martial races — recruitment based on the idea of "martial races": jats, rajputs, sikhs, gurkhas & others described as naturally loyal, courageous, and good fighters — but in the british framing, also deemed incapable of independent leadership. (ideal soldiers, in other words, but never officers. a theory that was as much about control as about capability. :)) regions that had stayed loyal in 1857 were heavily favoured. 8.6) a culture of loyalty to "the salt" — namak ka haq — and to one's community's honour, actively promoted. 8.7) large permanent standing army maintained to counter future revolts. 8.8) minimum or no indians in senior military positions. 8.9) financial control of the army placed firmly under civilian authority — the military could not independently mobilise resources. 8.10) the army was actively deployed against inm activities & peasant revolts. sepoys kept in barracks to minimise political exposure to the growing inm. ◆ 1857 was the hinge. eic's improvised governance ended; the crown took direct charge with a restructured army, new police, & redesigned civil services — all built to prevent recurrence. the reforms were more efficient & more repressive — planting the wemc that would later demand independence.

sections.title: What Changed After 1857
sections.norm: what changed after 1857. 1857 greater awareness of british laws & institutions filed court cases wemc. the revolt of 1857 was a turning point not just in british policy but also in the character of indian resistance. the peasant revolts that came after 1857 were different from earlier uprisings in two important ways. first, peasants now had a greater awareness of british laws & institutions. they did not just pick up weapons — they filed court cases. they organised themselves. they used the legal system that colonial rule had imposed on them as a tool against that very rule. second, the western educated middle class — or wemc — began to take up peasant causes. lawyers, writers, journalists, and reformers who had received english education started speaking for the ryot in english newspapers, in courts, and in public associations. this was a new dynamic. the peasant was no longer alone.

sections.title: The Indigo Revolt (1859–63)
sections.norm: the indigo revolt (1859–63). 2.1) context: how did indigo cultivation begin? 1788 eic nij system planters bought land directly gave loans at low interest rates commercial arrangement it was a trap 2.2) what were the grievances of the ryots? indigo destroyed soil fertility not remunerative to pay back one loan, the ryot had to take another remove him from his occupied land international trigger indigo prices on global markets fell financial crisis on the stock exchange 1854 charter act of 1853 2.3) what did the ryots do? social boycott of indian agents no-rent campaign rent act of 1859 permanent settlement of 1793 rent act 2.4) the role of the western educated middle class (wemc) 1860 rs 1,000 hindu patriot somprakash strong editorials in favour of the ryots 1851 2.5) result 1863 1897 basf 2020 1917 champaran agrarian act of 1918 upsc. 2.1) context: how did indigo cultivation begin? in 1788, the east india company (eic) began promoting indigo cultivation in bengal by giving loans to ten european planters. (the eic could have given the same loans to local zamindars, but chose european planters — preferential treatment from day one.) from this beginning grew a system of exploitation that would eventually boil over into open revolt. two systems of indigo cultivation operated in bengal. the nij system — where planters bought land directly & cultivated indigo themselves — faced a practical problem. buying large tracts of land, organising labour, and arranging bullocks & ploughs was expensive & complicated. so planters shifted to the ryoti system. under this arrangement, the planter leased land from zamindars (after the permanent settlement of 1793, zamindars were large landowners & land had become a commodity that could be sold, rented, leased, or mortgaged), and then signed contracts with tenant ryots. the contract had three key conditions: i) the ryot had to grow indigo on at least 25% of the land he occupied. ii) the planter gave loans at low interest rates & also sold indigo seeds & seed drills to the ryot. iii) the planter then purchased the cultivated indigo from the ryot. on paper, this looked like a commercial arrangement. in practice, it was a trap. 2.2) what were the grievances of the ryots? the ryots had real & compounding grievances. indigo destroyed soil fertility. once a plot was used for indigo, its productivity for food crops fell sharply — hurting the ryot's overall income. the price the planter paid for indigo was not remunerative. low soil fertility plus low prices meant the ryot remained perpetually in debt, even though the loan rates were low. to pay back one loan, the ryot had to take another. and since he could not repay, the planter had grounds to remove him from his occupied land (during the lease period, the planter was effectively the de-facto zamindar for that ryot). the cycle of debt kept the ryot permanently tied to indigo cultivation — not by force of arms, but by force of finance. then came an international trigger. indigo prices on global markets fell, partly due to a financial crisis on the stock exchange (a crisis in financial markets caused a general slowdown in the british economy — as people lost money, their buying power fell & demand for goods including indigo dropped). now planters offered the ryots even less for their cultivated indigo. the squeeze became unbearable. the immediate administrative trigger was a sympathetic lieutenant governor of bengal who directed district collectors to take the side of ryots in disputes, on the ground that forced cultivation was against the spirit of capitalism & free market economics. (the post of lieutenant governor of bengal had been created in 1854 to reduce the workload of the governor-general of india, a change made possible by the charter act of 1853.) 2.3) what did the ryots do? the ryots responded with a sophisticated, multi-pronged campaign: i) they refused to accept new loans & refused to cultivate indigo. ii) they organised a social boycott of indian agents of the planters. (this was effectively non-cooperation — decades before mahatma gandhi.) iii) when planters went to court to enforce contracts, ryots began a no-rent campaign. (again, non-cooperation before gandhi's era.) iv) when planters attempted eviction, ryots went to court to enforce their occupancy rights under the rent act of 1859. (after the permanent settlement of 1793, the ryot was a tenant — and the rent act gave him certain legal protections.) 2.4) the role of the western educated middle class (wemc) (the spirit of fraternity at work here — a key element of modern nationalism. the educated class standing up for the oppressed peasant was a new phenomenon in indian public life.) the wemc played a decisive role in amplifying the ryots' cause: i) 1860 — neel darpan (blue mirror): playwright deenbandhu mitra wrote this powerful play depicting the oppression of ryots by indigo planters. it created enormous public awareness. ii) bengali poet michael madhusudhan datta translated neel darpan into english, and christian missionary james long published it — bringing the issue to the attention of audiences in england. the planters filed a case of libel (maan-haani) against long, and he was convicted, fined rs 1,000 (paid by kaliprasanna sinha), and sentenced to one month's imprisonment. iii) hindu patriot (english) and somprakash (bengali) published strong editorials in favour of the ryots. iv) even the british indian association (1851) — an organisation of educated zamindars — supported the ryots. their motivation was partly self-interest: they resented the dominance of european planters over the rural economy. 2.5) result the indigo commission (1860) was set up. it ruled that ryots must honour existing contracts but were free to refuse future ones. by 1863, indigo cultivation had largely shifted from bengal to bihar, where it operated as the tinkathia system — essentially the same as the ryoti system, but here the ryot was forced to grow indigo on 3/20th (three-twentieths) of the land he occupied. the long-term death blow to natural indigo, however, came not from peasant resistance but from chemistry. in 1897, the german company basf developed synthetic indigo, which was cheaper & more consistent than the natural product. as synthetic indigo flooded global markets, the demand for natural indigo collapsed — destroying whatever economic logic had remained in the plantation system. (⚠ prelims 2020 — the role of basf's synthetic indigo in the decline of natural indigo cultivation.) the bihar chapter of this story would close only in 1917, when mahatma gandhi (mg) launched the champaran satyagraha, leading to the champaran agrarian act of 1918, which brought the tinkathia system to its end. ⚠ alert (prelims 2020): upsc tested this. q) indigo cultivation in india declined by the beginning of the 20th century because of to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) its unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — peasant resistance to the oppressive conduct of planters.; (c) ✗ — national leaders' opposition to the cultivation of indigo.; (d) ✗ — government control over the planters.

sections.title: Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873), Bengal
