sections.norm: pabna agrarian leagues (1873), bengal. the rent act of 1859 1857 wemc snb 1911 3.1) result 1880–84 1880 bengal tenancy act of 1885 the act. the ryots of pabna district in bengal had a different grievance. the rent act of 1859 had granted them occupancy rights — the right not to be arbitrarily evicted. but zamindars were routinely violating these rights. on top of that, rents were being raised illegally, and illegal extra cesses called abwabs were being collected. the ryots organised themselves into agrarian leagues — a formal structure of collective action. they pooled money to fight their cases in court. a leader called ishan chandra roy then replicated the movement in neighbouring districts. (organisation & legal awareness — the two new features of post-1857 revolts, clearly on display here.) the wemc was divided on this issue. hindu patriot (english) and amrita bazar patrika (bengali & english) supported the zamindars. but bengalee (english), edited by surendra nath bannerjea (snb), supported the ryots. the anglo-indian press also sided with the ryots — because here it was an indian landlord under attack, not a peasant defying a european. ◆ terminology check (easy to confuse): before the 1911 census, "anglo-indian" referred to a european living in india, and "eurasian" meant someone of mixed british-indian descent. the 1911 census flipped this — "anglo-indian" now meant a person of mixed descent, and "eurasian" fell out of use entirely. 3.1) result governor-general ripon (1880–84) set up a rent commission in 1880, which led to the bengal tenancy act of 1885. this act gave occupancy rights to ryots who had cultivated different plots of land in the same village continuously for more than twelve years. the act was properly implemented & finally brought genuine relief to bengal's ryots.

sections.title: Maharashtra
sections.norm: maharashtra. 4.1) 1873–74: no tax campaign 1873–74 4.2) bombay deccan riots (1875) high land revenue under the ryotwari system oppression by moneylenders 1859 1870 17,000 refusing to extend any further loans did not attack moneylenders burned debt bonds the deccan agriculturists relief act of 1879 4.3) 1896–97: no tax campaign 1896–97. 4.1) 1873–74: no tax campaign in 1873–74, ryots in maharashtra launched a no-tax campaign against a hike in land revenue (lr). this was direct, organised resistance to colonial fiscal policy. 4.2) bombay deccan riots (1875) grievances: high land revenue under the ryotwari system, oppression by moneylenders, and loss of land. background: the limitation law of 1859 in bombay had ruled that interest on a loan could be applied only for three years, regardless of when the ryot repaid. moneylenders found a workaround — they made the ryot sign a fresh debt bond after three years, with the accumulated interest now added to the principal. the debt could never truly be paid down. action: the poona sarvajanik sabha (1870) — associated with m.g. ranade — collected 17,000 signatures on powers-of-attorney to represent ryots. it successfully convinced the government to declare that confiscation of land should be the last resort in recovering land revenue arrears. moneylenders retaliated by simply refusing to extend any further loans — leaving ryots unable to even pay their land revenue. this is when violence broke out. the ryots did not attack moneylenders' lives. they burned debt bonds. (an awareness of the instrument of oppression, not just its wielder.) result: the deccan agriculturists relief act of 1879 was passed. it gave protection against loss of land due to indebtedness & regulated interest rates. 4.3) 1896–97: no tax campaign in 1896–97, another no-tax campaign broke out because the government refused to grant any remission (a one-time reduction) in land revenue despite widespread crop failure.

sections.title: Punjab
sections.norm: punjab. 5.1) kuka revolt (1871–72) reformist sikh sect purify sikhism through social reform living guru 1872 5.2) punjab canal colony agitations (1907) control inheritance of land in the canal colonies increase water rates three organisations mobilised the peasantry 1877 1875 1873 1857. 5.1) kuka revolt (1871–72) leader: baba ram singh, head of the namdhari sect. the namdharis were a reformist sikh sect with a distinct identity. they sought to purify sikhism through social reform. they believed in a living guru & in the guru granth sahib as the holy book. they upheld strict equality of status for women. they rejected rituals, relying only on the chanting of mantras — hence the name "kuka" (reciter). they were anti-priestly & strongly pro-cow protection. the revolt began as violence against cow slaughterers & priests, and then turned against the british. baba ram singh was exiled to burma in 1872. 5.2) punjab canal colony agitations (1907) in west punjab, from 1885 to 1940, british built canals in semi-desert areas to convert them into fertile lands for land revenue income. these areas were called canal colonies and lands were allocated to farmers from other parts of punjab at no or nominal costs with condition that they would bring land under cultivation and pay water rates and land revenue. some lands were given as reward for civil & military service while some large plots were sold to the large investors. in 1907, the british government introduced a bill that would allow the government to: control inheritance of land in the canal colonies and increase water rates & fines for violations of canal colony regulations. three organisations mobilised the peasantry: the lahore indian association (1877), the arya samaj (1875), and the singh sabha (1873). a no-tax campaign began, which later escalated into riots. the british response was twofold — repression, and then quiet withdrawal of the bill as post-1857, the indian army was heavily recruited from punjab, particularly from the sikh community. disaffection among punjab's peasantry could spread to the army, the way it did in 1857 revolt.

sections.title: A Thread Running Through All These Revolts
sections.norm: a thread running through all these revolts. not reacting with blind rage forming leagues, pooling resources, filing cases not yet the indian national movement soil in which that movement would grow inm. look across bengal, maharashtra, and punjab & a pattern emerges. in each case, peasants were not reacting with blind rage. they were organising — forming leagues, pooling resources, filing cases. they were using the tools of the colonial legal system against colonial exploitation. and in each case, sections of the western educated middle class — journalists, lawyers, reformers — were lending their voice. this is not yet the indian national movement. but it is the soil in which that movement would grow. ◆ think of these revolts as the rehearsal. the inm would later perfect the methods — non-cooperation, no-tax, boycott, legal challenge — that peasants were discovering through trial & error in these decades.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: How the Indian National Movement Began
sections.norm: how the indian national movement began. inm wemc. who led the inm, and where did it begin? the indian national movement (inm) was, in its mature form, led by the western educated middle class (wemc). but the first organised political voice in modern india was not theirs. it belonged to a different group — the educated landed class — whose regional associations were the earliest formal platforms for articulating indian political demands.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: The First Associations (1851–52)
sections.norm: the first associations (1851–52). 1851 1838 1911 1852 charter act of 1853 2013 upsc the ilbert bill 2017 british indian association 1851. the first major voluntary organisation in india was the british indian association [bria1851], set up in calcutta in 1851. radhakanta deb was its first president. its membership drew from educated men of the landed class. it was also the first all-indian organisation in character — unlike dwarkanath tagore's landholders' society (1838), which had included many non-official anglo-indians. (note: before 1911, the term 'anglo-indian' referred to europeans settled in india, not to those of mixed parentage as it does today.) the same year saw the founding of the bombay association (1852) and the madras native association (1852) — both with similar profiles: educated, landed, conservative. the immediate reason all three were formed was the same — the british parliament was deliberating on the charter act of 1853, and indian elites wanted to present their demands before it. ⚠ alert (prelims 1996): upsc tested this. q) match list i with list ii and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: [list i (period)] a. 1883 b. 1906 c. 1927 d. 1932 [list ii (event)] 1. announcement of communal award... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) a-4 b-3 c-2 d-1. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — a-4 b-3 c-1 d-2; (b) ✗ — a-3 b-4 c-1 d-2; (d) ✗ — a-3 b-4 c-2 d-1 ⚠ alert (prelims 2013): upsc tested this. q) the ilbert bill controversy was related to the to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) removal of disqualifications imposed on the indian magistrates with regard to the trial of the europeans. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — imposition of certain restrictions to carry arms by the indians; (b) ✗ — imposition of restrictions on newspapers and magazines published in indian languages; (d) ✗ — removal of a duty on imported cotton cloth ⚠ alert (prelims 2017): upsc tested this. q) consider the following pairs: 1. radhakanta deb — first president of the british indian association. 2. gazulu lakshminarasu chetty — founder of the madras mahajana sabha. 3. surendranath banerjee — founder of the indian association. which of the pairs given above is/are correctly matched? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) 1 and 3 only. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — only 1; (c) ✗ — 2 and 3 only; (d) ✗ — 1, 2 and 3.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: Their Demands
sections.norm: their demands. three associations sent separate petitions not a joint one common grievances high taxes elite personal interests salt & opium monopolies did not oppose british rule itself un-british rule no demands were met too much to lose from destabilising british rule. these three associations sent separate petitions — not a joint one. (this tells us something: they were not yet thinking as a single national fraternity, but as three regional lobbies.) their grievances fell into two categories: 1. common grievances: high taxes, expensive & incompetent administration, neglect of education & public works. 2. elite personal interests: opposition to salt & opium monopolies. they did not oppose british rule itself. they opposed what they called un-british rule — the argument being that british governance was, by definition, just & fair, and that exploitation was simply a departure from that standard. (notice the 'brown sahib' thinking here. the phrase 'un-british' carries a hidden assumption — that british rule is, by default, good rule. they were not calling colonialism wrong; they were calling exploitation 'un-british'. this is a very different thing.) unsurprisingly, no demands were met. these conservatives had too much to lose from destabilising british rule. the colonial land revenue systems had directly benefited them, and their social standing depended on british patronage. they were not going to rock the boat. (a useful framework to carry forward: conservatives want very little change; moderates want gradual reform; extremists want faster change; revolutionaries want immediate & fundamental transformation. we will meet all four types as this story unfolds.)

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: The INM After 1857
sections.norm: the inm after 1857. inm 1857. was the inm a product of british colonial policies? if so, how? in a deep irony, the british built many of the very tools that would eventually be used against them. the growth of the inm after 1857 was, in large part, a consequence of colonial policies themselves. let us trace the key factors.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: Western Education
sections.norm: western education. 1857 wemc western education did not spread evenly downward filtration theory humayun30-40 aurangzeb58-07 1999 upsc humayun aurangzeb. the rapid expansion of western higher education after 1857 created a new social group — a politically conscious wemc. (it is specifically 'higher' education that matters here — it is in colleges & universities that people develop political ideology & a sense of public affairs. primary schooling alone does not produce political movements.) the british had intended this class to be loyal 'brown sahibs.' but as the wemc realised that the british had no genuine intention of sharing power, admiration turned to criticism — and criticism turned into a demand for indian rights. however, western education did not spread evenly across india, and this had a direct consequence: the inm itself grew unevenly. the downward filtration theory (1835) had focused education only on the elites of the presidency towns. mass education remained neglected — confirmed bluntly by the census of 1921, which showed only 8% overall literacy & a mere 2% female literacy, despite the wood's dispatch (1854) and the hunter commission (1882–83) both calling for broader expansion. as a result, early inm leadership was dominated by upper-caste (uc) marathis, tamilians, and bengalis of the presidency towns. muslims were comparatively underrepresented in early western-educated politics, partly due to a desire among educated muslims to preserve persian literary culture, and partly due to the conservative influence of the ulamas over their communities. ◆ why was persian so embedded in indian muslim culture? the mughal court used persian as its official language. humayun30-40 had taken help from the safavid dynasty of persia (shia) to reclaim power from the suri dynasty (1540–55). the nawabs of awadh were shia. the kingdoms of golconda & bijapur were ruled by shia dynasties until aurangzeb58-07 annexed them in 1686 & 1687 respectively. persian was therefore not just a language — it was a cultural identity, and for many educated muslims, abandoning it meant abandoning something precious. ⚠ alert (prelims 1999): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following indian leaders was dismissed by the british from the indian civil service? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) surendranath banerji. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — satyendranath tagore; (c) ✗ — r.c. dutt; (d) ✗ — s.c. bose

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: The Press
sections.norm: the press. 1875 wemc. by 1875, india had over 400 newspapers in english & vernacular languages, with a combined readership of more than 1.5 lakh. the press was the primary tool of the wemc. it built inter-regional awareness, spread nationalist ideas, and helped regional leaders grow into national ones. (when a regional leader begins writing & speaking on all-india issues — the budget, civil services, famine — he gradually becomes a national leader. the press was the engine of that transformation.)

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: Railways and Telegraphs
sections.norm: railways and telegraphs. railways & the electric telegraph connect distant parts of india. from the 1850s onwards, railways & the electric telegraph began to physically & communicatively connect distant parts of india. leaders from bombay, bengal, madras, and punjab could now meet, correspond, and coordinate. the infrastructure of empire became, unintentionally, the infrastructure of anti-colonial politics.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: British Racism and Authoritarianism
sections.norm: british racism and authoritarianism. western education was the slow fire british racism was the accelerant racial discrimination the 'black acts' (bethune's bills): mofussil supreme court in a presidency town sadr amins, munsifs criminal jurisdiction 'white rebellion' charter act of 1833 ilbert bill sec. 12 1850 lex loci act caste disabilities act income tax withdrawn under press pressure famines swept different parts of india 1870 wemc 1875. how did british racism & authoritarianism fuel the inm? if western education was the slow fire that built the inm, british racism was the accelerant. every act of racial discrimination — every policy that reminded indians of their subordinate status under their own sky — added recruits to the movement. (in films, the villain is necessary. he is what gives the hero a reason to rise. in the story of the inm, british racism & authoritarianism played that role — it is the biggest single contributor to the movement's growth.) the key incidents: 8.1) 1850 — the 'black acts' (bethune's bills): before 1850, a european charged with a crime in the mofussil (rural areas outside the presidency towns) had the legal privilege of being tried only by the supreme court in a presidency town (calcutta, bombay, or madras) — bypassing the local company courts where indian judges (sadr amins, munsifs) presided. this made justice for ordinary indians nearly impossible, since witnesses & complainants had to travel to a presidency town at great cost. the black acts ended this privilege & brought europeans in the mofussil under the criminal jurisdiction of the ordinary district courts where indians served as judges. europeans in india protested so vigorously in press that its called 'white rebellion' and the acts had to be suspended. (recall: the charter act of 1833 had promised racial equality. the black acts were an attempt to act on that promise. the same principle was later again brought via — see 1883's ilbert bill, sec. 12.) 8.2) 1850 — lex loci act (removal of religious/caste disabilities act): granted the right of inheritance to converts from any religion to any other. passed despite indian opposition; widely seen as a tool to promote conversion to christianity. 8.3) 1868 — income tax: first introduced in 1860, then withdrawn under press pressure, then re-introduced in 1868 — even as famines swept different parts of india through the 1860s & 70s. the wemc responded with a sharp slogan: no taxation without representation. (the worst famine of this period was the great madras famine of 1876–78, caused by two consecutive years of drought. approximately one crore indians died. :( ) 8.4) 1870 — education cuts in bengal: the anglo-indian press had been calling the wemc 'seditious.' the colonial response was not to engage with their criticism, but to cut higher education spending in bengal — while military expenditure & high taxes continued as before. 8.5) british racism also deepened cultural nationalism — and extremist leaders like lala lajpat rai, bal gangadhar tilak, bipin chandra pal (lal-bal-pal), and aurobindo later used that cultural nationalism to strengthen political nationalism. (recall the cultural nationalism of this period represented by arya samaj 1875, swami vivekananda, and bankim chandra chatterjee.)

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: The Lytton Years (1876–1880)
sections.norm: the lytton years (1876–1880). viceroy lytton76-80 charter act 1853 goi act 1919 1878 1877 wemc 1877–80 vernacular press act arms act 1878–80 1838–42 lytton. viceroy lytton76-80 managed to antagonise practically every section of educated indian opinion in just four years. 9.1) 1876 — ics age limit cut from 21 to 19: since the examination was held only in london, this change made it near-impossible for indians to compete. the demand for an examination centre in india was rejected outright. (the ics exam had been established by charter act 1853 & first held in 1855. a simultaneous exam in india would only be accepted under goi act 1919, with the first india-based exam held in 1922.) 9.2) 1878 — statutory civil services act: a new service category was created — but entry was by nomination, not examination. only loyalists were nominated. (think of this as colonial 'lateral entry' — designed to look inclusive while ensuring the loyalists got in. :( ) 9.3) 1877 — delhi durbar: an enormous & expensive imperial spectacle, held while the great madras famine was killing people across south india. queen victoria was crowned kaesar-i-hind (empress of hindustan). the wemc press was scathing. (there was also a three-year press campaign, 1877–80, by the wemc demanding indianisation of the civil services — the durbar only added fuel to it.) 9.4) 1878 — vernacular press act: targeted the vernacular press, which had grown sharply critical of british policy. printers & publishers were required to deposit a security bond that could be forfeited if they published anything 'objectionable' — in practice, anything anti-british. the british liberal mp gladstone publicly criticised the act from london. the most dramatic response came from the amrita bazar patrika, which converted itself overnight from a bengali newspaper to an english one, placing itself outside the act's reach. !!!! 9.5) 1878 — arms act: indians required a licence to own arms; europeans & eurasians were exempt. b.c. pal launched press campaigns against this openly discriminatory law. 9.6) 1878–80 — second afghan war: lytton waged a costly campaign in afghanistan, driven by fear of russian influence there — at a time when the indian treasury was already stretched by famine relief costs. the treaty that ended the war shaped the modern borders of afghanistan. (the first afghan war of 1838–42 had been fought for exactly the same reason — fear of russian expansion. it had been an expensive disaster. the british appear to have learned very little.)

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: Ripon's Interlude (1880–1884)
sections.norm: ripon's interlude (1880–1884). 1880 lord ripon80-84 bengal tenancy act of 1885 1873 rent act of 1859 1881 factories act 10.3) 1882 — vernacular press act repealed. 1882 arms act ics ripon. when gladstone's liberal party won the 1880 british elections, he sent a reformist viceroy to india: lord ripon80-84. the contrast with lytton was stark. 10.1) 1880 — rent commission: set up by ripon, it eventually led to the bengal tenancy act of 1885. (recall the pressure created by the pabna agrarian leagues of 1873 for fair implementation of the rent act of 1859 in bengal.) 10.2) 1881 — factories act: child labour banned for children under 7; working hours capped for children under 12; four monthly holidays mandated. (moderate indian leaders opposed this act — it would hurt indian capitalists who were already struggling against competition from cheaper british manufactured goods. a reminder that 'indian interests' were not always a single, unified position.) 10.3) 1882 — vernacular press act repealed. 10.4) 1882 — arms act amended: now everyone, including europeans, needed a licence to own arms. (a liberal gesture — but note that ripon amended the act, not repealed it. he was a reformer, but he was still a colonial ruler.) 10.5) 1882 — age limit for ics exam raised back to 21. ripon also pushed for a simultaneous exam in india. this was strongly opposed by europeans in india & the proposal failed.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: Local Self-Government (1882)
sections.norm: local self-government (1882). local self-government resolution/act of 1882 train indians in the practice of self-government elected district boards elected by land revenue payers & rent payers municipalities were strengthened two-thirds of members had to be elected local bodies were given charge autonomy in day-to-day functioning 1882–83. ripon's most significant reform was the local self-government resolution/act of 1882. the stated goal was to train indians in the practice of self-government. the key changes were: 11.1) in rural areas, elected district boards were set up across british india. members were to be elected by land revenue payers & rent payers — not nominated by officials. 11.2) in urban areas, municipalities were strengthened: a minimum of two-thirds of members had to be elected, and the chairperson had to be a non-official member. 11.3) local bodies were given charge of health, education, sanitation, roads, and communications — with autonomy in day-to-day functioning. the government retained the power to inspect & dissolve a local body. (note the distinction: regulation, not total control.) 11.4) the hunter education commission (1882–83) followed, recommending transfer of the education subject to local bodies & a focus on mass education in vernacular languages — especially female education. implementation remained poor. ◆ compare this with present-day india: local self-government is now a constitutional right under part ix (panchayati raj) and part ix-a (municipalities), inserted by the 73rd & 74th constitutional amendments of 1992. ripon's 1882 act was the colonial seedling; the 1992 amendments made it a constitutional tree.

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: The Ilbert Bill Controversy (1883–84)
sections.norm: the ilbert bill controversy (1883–84). wemc ilbert bill 1883–84 c.p. ilbert indian district judges to try cases involving britons arms act. the single episode that most sharply exposed british racial attitudes — and most decisively radicalised the wemc — was the ilbert bill controversy of 1883–84. the bill, drafted by law member c.p. ilbert, proposed to extend the jurisdiction of indian district judges to try cases involving britons in the mofussil (rural) areas. this would end an existing privilege by which a briton in rural india could not be tried before an indian judge. the reaction from the european community in india was immediate & furious. they organised, lobbied, and protested — and the bill had to be withdrawn & amended. the final version required a mixed jury in any case involving a briton. for the wemc, this episode settled any remaining doubt. the british were not going to treat indians as equals — not in courts, not in civil services, not in political life. the controversy triggered massive press campaigns across the country & is rightly considered a major milestone in the growth of indian political consciousness. ⚠ alert (prelims 2003): upsc tested this. q) with reference to colonial rule india, what was sought by the ilbert bill in 1883? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) to bring indians and europeans on par as far as the criminal jurisdiction of courts was concerned. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — to impose severe restrictions on the freedom of the native press as it was perceived to be hostile...; (c) ✗ — to encourage the native indians to appear for civil service examinations by conducting them in india; (d) ✗ — to allow native indians to possess arms by amending the arms act

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: The Rise of WEMC-Led Associations (Post-1870)
sections.norm: the rise of wemc-led associations (post-1870). 1870 wemc 1852 1876 1875 snb ics 1877 m. veeraraghavachariar g. subramania iyer the hindu p. anandacharlu organised inm under wemc leadership had begun 2002 upsc. how did the western educated middle class build their own political organisations? from 1870 onwards, a new kind of indian political organisation began to appear — one led not by conservative landlords, but by young, politically minded professionals of the wemc. these organisations challenged the older landed-class bodies & gradually replaced them as the principal voice of indian opinion. 13.1) bombay: the old bombay association of 1852 was briefly revived in 1876 when dadabhai naoroji & naoroji ferdunji returned from london. but the younger generation was not satisfied with its conservative outlook. the poona sarvajanik sabha (1870), set up by m.g. ranade, brought together leaders like k.t. telang, p.m. mehta, and later g.k. gokhale & bal gangadhar tilak. its stated aim was to represent the interests of all sections of society — a significant departure from the landlord focus of the earlier bodies. in 1875, the sabha sent a petition to the british house of commons demanding direct indian representation — one of the earliest such demands addressed to the imperial parliament itself. 13.2) bengal: surendranath banerjee (snb) founded the indian association (1876) in bengal with the explicit goal of 'representing the people.' (snb had actually passed the ics examination but was not selected due to an age dispute arising from differences between the english calendar & the hindu calendar. personal injustice, as is often the case, became political fuel.) 13.3) punjab: the lahore indian association (1877) was set up in punjab by sardar dyal singh majithia, when surendranath bannerjee toured punjab (not founders, but prominent leaders- lala lajpat rai & ajit singh). 13.4) madras: after the madras native association closed in 1862, political activity in madras went into a lull before being revived by the madras mahajan sabha (1884) by m. veeraraghavachariar, g. subramania iyer (the legendary nationalist journalist who also founded the hindu newspaper) & p. anandacharlu. by 1870, then, an organised inm under wemc leadership had begun. (pre-1870: wemc was politically active but without formal organisation. post-1870: wemc active & organised. the shift matters — organised movements are qualitatively different from individual opinion-making.) through the 1870s–90s, there was a phase of coexistence & gradual transition as wemc organisations steadily replaced the older conservative associations of the landed class. ⚠ alert (prelims 2002): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following submitted in 1875 a petition to the house of commons demanding india's direct representation in the british parliament? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) the poona sarvajanik sabha. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — the deccan association; (b) ✗ — the indian association; (c) ✗ — the madras mahajan sabha

sections.chapterTitle: Pre-INC Organisations and the Early Indian National Movement
sections.title: What These New Associations Did
sections.norm: what these new associations did. wemc associations not merely talking shops leadership of peasants indigo revolt bombay deccan riots famine relief poona sarvajanik sabha arbitration courts inland emigration act 1859 indian councils act of 1861 permanent settlement of 1793 ps1793 indian councils act of 1892 ica1892 wemc 1885 permanent settlement 1793 indian councils act 1892. these wemc associations were not merely talking shops. they took on concrete roles: 14.1) leadership of peasants — for example, during the indigo revolt (1859–63), the bombay deccan riots (1875), and the punjab canal colony agitations (1907). 14.2) famine relief — the poona sarvajanik sabha organised relief during the famines of the 1870s & held arbitration courts to provide cheaper dispute resolution, since the cost of fighting cases in colonial courts was prohibitive for ordinary people. 14.3) labour rights — they protested against the plantation labour & inland emigration act (1859), which gave planters the power to arrest workers who tried to leave their contracts — effectively creating conditions of serfdom. 14.4) political demands — representation in legislative councils (set up by the indian councils act of 1861); separation of powers between legislature, executive, and judiciary; reduction in home charges; extension of the permanent settlement of 1793 (ps1793) to other areas. later, these associations also began using british institutions — particularly the legislative councils, especially after the indian councils act of 1892 (ica1892) allowed more indians as members — as platforms for criticising british policies from within the system. this was the foundation. out of this soil — western education, a free press, racial provocation, organised wemc associations, railways & telegraphs — the indian national congress would emerge in 1885.

sections.title: The Foundation of the Indian National Congress (INC)
sections.norm: the foundation of the indian national congress (inc). ilbert bill 2015 upsc. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) which of the following pairs are correctly matched? list i: 1. theodore beck 2. ilbert bill 3. pherozeshah mehta 4. badruddin tyabji list ii: 1. mohammadan anglo oriental college, aligarh 2. lord... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. pair 4 (badruddin tyabji → muslim league) is wrong because tyabji was the 1st muslim inc president (madras 1887) and died aug 1906 — before the muslim league was founded (dec 1906 at dacca). wrong options (commonly picked): (a) ✗ — 1, 2, 3 and 4 (includes wrong pair 4); (b) ✗ — 2 and 4 (excludes correct pair 1 + 3); (c) ✗ — 1, 3 and 4 (includes wrong pair 4) ⚠ alert (prelims 2015): upsc tested this. q) consider the following statements : 1. the first woman president of the indian national congress was sarojini naidu. 2. the first muslim president of the indian national congress was badruddin... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) only 2. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — only 1; (c) ✗ — both 1 and 2; (d) ✗ — neither 1 nor 2

sections.title: The Birth of the INC
sections.norm: the birth of the inc. 1885 inc 1998 upsc 2008. the indian national congress was founded in bombay in december 1885. its first president was womesh chandra bonnerjee. the man credited with the most active role in bringing it together was allan octavian hume — a retired british civil servant who toured india in the early 1880s & persuaded political leaders in bombay, madras, and calcutta to gather for a common conference. but what exactly motivated hume? this is one of the more debated questions around the inc's founding. and it brings us to the famous — and famously wrong — "safety valve theory." ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) the congress is tottering to its fall and one of my great ambitions while in india, is to assist it to a peaceful demise. this statement is attributed to to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) lord curzon. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — lord dufferin; (c) ✗ — lord lytton; (d) ✗ — none of these ⚠ alert (prelims 2008): upsc tested this. q) where was the first session of the indian national congress held in december, 1885? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) bombay. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — ahmedabad; (c) ✗ — calcutta; (d) ✗ — delhi

sections.title: The INC as a British Safety Valve — The Debate
sections.norm: the inc as a british safety valve — the debate. 3.1) what does the safety valve theory say? inc viceroy dufferin84-88 3.2) why is the safety valve theory wrong? seven volumes of secret reports were never found close personal friend of hume dufferin84-88 2011 upsc 1893 dufferin. 3.1) what does the safety valve theory say? the theory says that hume founded the inc not out of any genuine sympathy for indians, but as a deliberate british strategy. the idea was to create a platform where the educated indian elite could air grievances peacefully — and thus prevent a violent mass uprising against british rule. the origin of this theory lies in a biography of hume written by william wedderburn in 1913. according to wedderburn, in 1878 hume came across seven volumes of secret reports compiled by religious gurus. these reports allegedly described a conspiracy by the lower classes to overthrow british rule. alarmed, hume met viceroy dufferin84-88 (lord dufferin, viceroy 1884–1888). together, dufferin & hume then brought educated indians together to form the inc — as a "safety valve" to vent grievances & prevent revolt. r.p. dutt, the noted historian, also supported this reading: that the inc was formed to prevent a mass uprising. 3.2) why is the safety valve theory wrong? the theory does not hold up. here is why: i) those seven volumes of secret reports were never found in any archive. they have no reference anywhere except in wedderburn's biography — a book written by a close personal friend of hume, nearly four decades after the supposed events. ii) dufferin84-88 did not take hume seriously. far from being a co-conspirator, dufferin actually hated the moderates. he did not see them as leaders of the indian masses at all. he called them a "microscopic minority of babus working for self-interest" — hardly the language of a man who thought they could prevent a mass revolt. iii) dufferin did not welcome the formation of the inc. he quietly asked the governor of bombay to be alert about it. he feared it would grow into something like the irish home rule league — a nationalist movement that had caused serious trouble for the british in ireland. (the irish home rule league, led by figures like charles parnell in the 1870s–80s, demanded irish self-governance within the british empire. it became a powerful political force that consistently embarrassed & pressured the british government. the comparison dufferin drew was not a compliment — it was a warning signal.) so the man the safety valve theory credits as co-designer of this plan actually viewed the inc with suspicion, not satisfaction. the entire theory rests on a single unverifiable source, written by a friend, about events he did not witness. ⚠ alert (prelims 2011): upsc tested this. q) what was the purpose which sir william wedderburn and ws caine had set-up the indian parliamentary committee in 1893? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) to agitate for indian political reforms in the house of commons. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — to campaign for the entry of indians into the imperial judiciary; (c) ✗ — to facilitate a discussion on india's independence in the british parliament; (d) ✗ — to agitate for the entry of eminent indians into the british parliament

sections.title: Would the INC Have Formed Even Without Hume — The Debate
sections.norm: would the inc have formed even without hume — the debate. 1885 4.1) what were these pre-1885 associations doing? 1878–80 vernacular press act 1878 right to join volunteer corps indian association (1876) surendranath banerjea editor of bengalee 4.2) were efforts for an all-india body already underway? 1851 1853 1877 national conference in calcutta in 1883 1884 inc 4.3) then why did wedderburn write what he wrote? portray hume as a patriot 4.4) so what was hume's real usefulness? acted as a mediator bridge differences among the various regional organisations 1913. yes. and this is the more important point. political activity among indians was rising steadily before 1885 — across all three presidencies & even beyond. the pre-1885 regional associations had been pushing on issue after issue. none of their demands had been met. the logical next step was an all-india organisation. 4.1) what were these pre-1885 associations doing? their protests & campaigns covered a wide range: i) protests against the lex loci act of 1850. ii) nationwide protests against the income tax of 1868. iii) a campaign in 1877 for indianisation of the civil services. iv) campaigns against the afghan war (1878–80) and the vernacular press act (1878). v) active support for the ilbert bill (1883–84). vi) a demand for the right to join volunteer corps — units that had been restricted to europeans only. vii) in 1885, an appeal to british voters in britain to vote for pro-indian candidates. the lead actor in many of these agitations was the indian association (1876) of surendranath banerjea — editor of bengalee & one of the most prominent political voices of the era. the indian association was a permanent organisational body, and banerjea used it to launch the indian national conference (1883) — a periodic gathering that brought delegates from across british india together. the conference met in 1883 & 1885, but then merged into the inc in 1886. however, the indian association itself continued to exist as a separate body. but banerjea was not alone; associations in other parts of india were equally active. 4.2) were efforts for an all-india body already underway? they were. well before hume made his move, indian organisations were already trying to build national structures: i) the british india association (1851) had attempted to open branches in bombay & madras, specifically to submit a joint petition to london during the charter renewal of 1853. ii) journalists invited to the 1877 imperial darbar formed the native press association — an all-india body. they elected surendranath banerjea as president & resolved to meet annually. iii) the indian association held a national conference in calcutta in 1883. another was scheduled for 1885. (these were parallel efforts — the indian national conference & the inc were running on nearly identical tracks by 1885, which is why the merger in 1886 was natural rather than forced.) iv) in 1884, delegates from across india gathered at the theosophical society's annual convention in madras — another instance of an all-india gathering finding its feet. v) by 1885, a national fund had been established specifically for political campaigns — both inside india & in london. the machinery was already being built. the 1885 conference that became the inc was not a sudden british invention. it was the natural culmination of decades of organised political work. 4.3) then why did wedderburn write what he wrote? wedderburn was hume's close friend. he wanted to portray hume — a briton working for indian political rights — as a patriot: a man who had sacrificed his career to save the british empire from its own folly. the safety valve narrative served that purpose. it made hume look prescient & heroic. but it was, at its core, a story written for a friend's legacy, not as history. 4.4) so what was hume's real usefulness? hume's actual contribution was more practical than mythological. he acted as a mediator — helping to bridge differences among the various regional organisations that were competing with each other for leadership of a future national body. getting bombay, calcutta, and madras to sit together was not a simple task. hume helped make it happen. more importantly, gokhale put it plainly in 1913: the british would never have allowed an all-india organisation to be formed under the leadership of an indian. having a british founder gave the inc a protective cover in its early years. :) so if the british thought they were using the inc as a safety valve, indians were using hume as a lightning conductor — to channel the energy of political organisation past the british reflex to shut it down.

sections.title: Key English Figures Behind the INC
sections.norm: key english figures behind the inc. 5.1) a.o. hume — the founder viceroy mayo69-72 viceroy lytton76-80 ripon80-84 government resolution of 1882 inc 1885 5.2) william wedderburn — the co-founder who became a biographer indian high courts act of 1861 5.3) justice john jardine — the liberal lawyer 1906–1918 5.4) george yule — the merchant president 1888 nbfc 1970 5.5) alfred webb — the irish friend 1894 2004 upsc mayo lytton ripon. 5.1) a.o. hume — the founder hume's motivations were reformist, even if the safety valve story distorts them. as secretary of the department of revenue, agriculture & commerce in 1871, he had worked under viceroy mayo69-72 (lord mayo, 1869–1872) to improve agricultural yields. he opposed viceroy lytton76-80's (lord lytton, 1876–1880) heavy expenditure on the afghan war (1878–80) — and was dismissed from his post for it. he supported ripon80-84's (lord ripon, 1880–1884) reforms, especially the local self-government resolution of 1882. he was a liberal in the british political tradition — someone who believed in representative governance. he wanted the inc to function like "his majesty's opposition" — a formal, legitimate channel of political dissent, the way an opposition party functions in a democracy. in 1885, he also published a direct appeal to british voters to elect pro-indian candidates to parliament. he served as the general secretary of the inc — not its president, but arguably its most active organiser in the early years. 5.2) william wedderburn — the co-founder who became a biographer william wedderburn, a retired civil servant who had served as ex-secretary to the bombay government, was a co-founder of the inc in 1885. he went on to become the 2nd non-indian president of the inc — serving in that role in 1889 & again in 1910. like hume, he had supported ripon's reforms. he favoured the establishment of cooperative banks to provide cheap loans to farmers. his pro-indian positions cost him — he was denied a judgeship at the bombay high court. (high courts had been established under the indian high courts act of 1861 & began functioning from 1862.) later, as a member of parliament in britain, he actively supported inc demands through the 1890s, working in close partnership with gopal krishna gokhale. 5.3) justice john jardine — the liberal lawyer john jardine was also a co-founder of the inc in 1885. he had served as chief secretary of bombay & as a judge of the bombay high court. he later became an mp (1906–1918) and was a liberal. 5.4) george yule — the merchant president george yule holds the distinction of being the 1st non-indian president of the inc, presiding over the allahabad session in 1888. he was a merchant & businessman — founder of the agency house "andrew yule & company" in calcutta. he also served as president of the indian chamber of commerce. ◆ an agency house was a type of british trading & financial firm that operated in colonial india — think of it as a cross between a private bank, an investment firm, and a business management company, all rolled into one. these firms were not banks in the formal sense, but they performed bank-like functions: they raised capital, extended credit, and financed trade. on top of that, they acted as agents for running actual business enterprises — tea plantations, jute mills, coal mines, shipping companies. in today's language, an agency house was something like a combination of an nbfc (non-banking financial company), a private equity firm, and a holding company. the managing agency system — where one firm controlled & managed multiple different businesses for a fee or a share of profits — became a dominant feature of the colonial indian economy. houses like andrew yule & company, jardine henderson, and bird & company controlled vast networks of industrial enterprises. this system was eventually abolished in independent india in 1970 because it concentrated enormous economic power in few — and mostly british — hands, and was seen as a vehicle of economic drain & monopoly. yule, therefore, was not merely a businessman. he sat at the top of one of these powerful colonial commercial structures. the fact that a man of his economic standing was willing to preside over the inc in 1888 was itself politically significant. he also had the distinction — if that is the right word — of having killed 400 tigers, which tells you something about the social world these colonial-era figures inhabited. 5.5) alfred webb — the irish friend alfred webb was an irish politician who served as an mp in the 1890s & holds the distinction of being the 3rd non-indian president of the inc, presiding over the madras session of 1894. he was invited personally by dadabhai naoroji, with whom he shared a close friendship. webb was strongly opposed to racism — he supported britain's first anti-racist journal. he was also opposed to the opium trade into china. (webb's irish background likely shaped his sympathy for people living under imperial rule — ireland had been under british control for centuries & was still fighting for home rule even as webb presided over the inc in 1894.) ⚠ alert (prelims 2000): upsc tested this. q) consider the following statements about the indian national congress 1. sarojini naidu was the first woman to be the president of the congress. 2. cr das was in prison when he functioned as the... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) 2 and 4. statement 2 (cr das presided from prison — gaya 1922) is true. statement 4 (alfred webb 1894) is true. statement 1 is false — annie besant was 1st woman inc president (calcutta 1917), not sarojini naidu (kanpur 1925, the 2nd woman). statement 3 is false — a.o. hume was founder/general secretary, never president; george yule was the 1st british/non-indian inc president at allahabad 1888 (per sec. 5.4). wrong options: (a) ✗ — 1 and 3 (both false); (c) ✗ — 2, 3 and 4 (includes wrong statement 3 about hume); (d) ✗ — 1, 2, 3 and 4 (includes statement 1+3 both false) ⚠ alert (prelims 2004): upsc tested this. q) consider the following statements 1. the first session of the indian national congress was held in calcutta. 2. the second session of the indian national congress was held under the presidentship of... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) 2 and 3. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — 1 and 2; (b) ✗ — only 2; (d) ✗ — only 3

sections.title: Core Philosophy
sections.norm: core philosophy. 1947 indian high courts act of 1861. the secretary of state for india, charles wood, put it plainly: the government of india must be a "despotism controlled from home." (despotism is simply a dictatorship. "home" meant britain. and the dictator at the top of the chain was the secretary of state for india himself, sitting in london.) this one line captures the fundamental feature of british indian governance — and it remained the operating principle right until 1947. the ica 1861 was, at its core, a comprehensive restructuring of the british indian state. the british were thinking comprehensively: the legislature & executive were to be restructured via ica 1861, and the judiciary was simultaneously reorganised under the indian high courts act of 1861. two laws, one year, complete state machinery overhauled.

sections.title: ICA 1861's Restructure of Legislature & Executive
sections.norm: ica 1861's restructure of legislature & executive. ica 1861 vec ilc 2.1) when meeting for day-to-day executive work → it was the vec 2.2) when meeting to make laws → it became the ilc (= vec + additional members) government of india act 1919 provincial legislative councils (plcs) governor's executive councils (gecs). out of the governor-general's council, the ica 1861 effectively created two bodies: the viceroy's executive council (vec) for day-to-day executive functions, and the imperial legislative council (ilc) for law-making. both operated under the authority of the viceroy/governor-general. however, it is important to be precise here. the ica 1861 did not create two separate, independent institutions. what it did was simpler, and more clever. the vec was expanded by adding "additional members" specifically for law-making sessions. these additional members — other british officials & a handful of nominated non-officials — formed an outer ring, brought in only when laws were being made. so the same council wore two hats: 2.1) when meeting for day-to-day executive work → it was the vec 2.2) when meeting to make laws → it became the ilc (= vec + additional members) every vec member was automatically part of the ilc. the design of ilc guaranteed the british executive a built-in official majority in every legislative vote. ◆ this arrangement — the expanded-council model — continued until 1919 (montagu-chelmsford reforms / government of india act 1919), although the outer ring gradually grew & gained marginal new powers under ica 1909 (morley-minto reforms). goi 1919 abolished this model entirely & replaced it with a fully bicameral central legislature — the council of state (cos) and the central legislative assembly (cla) — functioning as a body structurally distinct from the vec. at the province level, a parallel structure was created: provincial legislative councils (plcs) and governor's executive councils (gecs).

sections.title: Evolution of the Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC)
sections.norm: evolution of the viceroy's executive council (vec). vec ica 1861 1833 3.1) in 1833, executive meetings of gg's council = [gg + 3 + cic (extra-ordinary member appointed by cod)] 3.2) legislative meetings of gg's council = [vec + 1 legal member] 1853 cic 3.4) legislative meetings of gg's council = [vec + 6 legal members] legal recognition portfolio system the act 5 ordinary members home, revenue, finance, law, & military checks & balances military member field command 1874 public works canning. understanding the vec requires tracing it backward before we can understand what the ica 1861 changed. in 1833, the composition shifted from 1793 status i.e. [gg + 3c + cic (extra-ordinary member)] as a law member was added for law making. 3.1) in 1833, executive meetings of gg's council = [gg + 3 + cic (extra-ordinary member appointed by cod)] 3.2) legislative meetings of gg's council = [vec + 1 legal member] in 1853, the composition shifted further as the law member was elevated to ordinary executive member & 6 legal members were added for law making. 3.3) in 1853, executive meetings of gg's council = [gg + 3 + cic (extra-ordinary member appointed by cod) + 1 legal member (of 1833) elevated to executive member] 3.4) legislative meetings of gg's council = [vec + 6 legal members] the ica 1861 gave legal recognition to the portfolio system introduced by canning56-62 in 1859 — the practice of allocating specific departments (what we would today call ministries) to individual vec members, whose decisions on their portfolios would be final, subject to the viceroy's veto. this formalised cabinet-style administration at the centre. a 5th ordinary member was added constitutionally in 1861 to handle finance — effectively a finance minister. this was directly a consequence of the 1857 revolt, which left the british indian economy heavily in debt. the act formally expanded the executive council to 5 members, institutionalizing the role of finance member (a practice begun in 1859 with james wilson, who died in 1860 before the act was passed). the post was introduced in 1859 but constitutional backing came in 1861. the first to hold this post in 1859 was james wilson, who introduced income tax in 1860 (he died in 1860). later, income tax was withdrawn due to pressure by western educated middle class indians but was re-introduced in 1868. thus the vec was now structured as: gg + 5 ordinary/regular members + c-i-c (extraordinary member appointed by secretary of state for india) the act expanded the regular cabinet to 5 ordinary members — each running one portfolio: home, revenue, finance, law, & military. (note- the military member here was the ordinary administrative military member — not the cic.) why did the crown not make the cic an ordinary member or even an automatic ex-officio member? deliberate checks & balances over the armed forces: - administrative military member (ordinary member, sits in vec): handled paperwork — logistics, defence budget, administrative orders for the military department. - operational cic (extraordinary member): supreme field command over the actual army — the man giving battle orders. (think of it as: the military member ran the office, the cic ran the battlefield. the crown did not want one man wearing both hats — that would have concentrated too much power in one office.) by the 1870s, massive investment in railways, canals, and infrastructure required its own dedicated administrative portfolio. thus, a 6th ordinary member was added in 1874 to handle the portfolio of public works. (updated cabinet: 6 ordinary members — home, revenue, finance, law, military, & public works.)

sections.title: The Legislature (now called ILC)
sections.norm: the legislature (now called ilc). ilc vec 6 to 12 additional law members half must be non-officers cic permanent settlement of 1793 ica 1892 1851. whenever a question mentions the indian councils acts (1861, 1892, 1909), you must conceptually split the government into two distinct boxes in your mind: the legislative council (ilc): the executive council (vec) plus the "additional members" (who were a mix of officials & non-officials) under ica 1861, now 6 to 12 additional law members could be nominated by the viceroy for the ilc of which half must be non-officers. thus ilc = vec + 6 to 12 = (gg + 4 + 1 finance member added in 1861) + 6 to 12. earlier, all were officers. this introduced a grain — a tiny element — of popular & representative governance, since a non-officer lawmaker could be an indian. law-making is, after all, an integral part of governance. why? because the official majority was guaranteed. the vec alone (gg + 5 + cic (extraordinary member) = 7) already outnumbered or matched even the maximum possible non-officials (6 out of 12 additional members). the british could afford this gesture because the math was rigged. in 1862, 3 indians were nominated to the ilc: the raja of banaras, the maharaja of patiala, and dinkar rao of gwalior (knighted in 1877 as sir dinkar rao). all were elites, some from princely states. the british logic was simple: since the elite indians had stayed loyal during 1857, their cooperation should be rewarded & secured. by having cooperation of elite indians in lawmaking, they could do divide & rule (the same logic seen in the permanent settlement of 1793 & the 'brown sahib' policy of 1835 — co-opt the elites, exploit the masses.) however, until ica 1892, only 45 indians were nominated in total — mainly zamindars & moneylenders from the british indian association (bria, 1851), british businessmen, and some rulers of princely states. a deliberate selection of loyalists.

sections.title: Powers of the ILC
sections.norm: powers of the ilc. 5.1) discussion: only with the viceroy's prior approval. 5.2) ask questions to executive: not allowed. 5.3) bring & pass resolutions: not allowed. 5.4) introduce bills: only with the viceroy's prior approval. 5.5) budget discussion/vote: not allowed. 5.6) the viceroy held absolute veto power over all bills. ordinance power valid for 6 months ilc. (the powers of any legislature, in increasing order of significance: discussion → questions + discuss answers & ask supplementary questions → pass resolutions → passing bills → discussing & passing the budget (voting on individual items in budget & on budget as a whole) → creating the executive → dismissing the executive → amending & drafting the constitution.) the ilc's status was at the very bottom of this ladder: 5.1) discussion: only with the viceroy's prior approval. 5.2) ask questions to executive: not allowed. 5.3) bring & pass resolutions: not allowed. 5.4) introduce bills: only with the viceroy's prior approval. 5.5) budget discussion/vote: not allowed. 5.6) the viceroy held absolute veto power over all bills. 5.7) the viceroy also had ordinance power — the power to make law by executive order, valid for 6 months. (an ordinance is essentially law made by the executive, bypassing the legislature.) the ilc was therefore not a modern parliament in any meaningful sense. it had a small membership, entirely nominated (no elections), and no control whatsoever over the executive. it was a consultative add-on to the viceroy's own council — useful to the british because it looked like participation while delivering none.

sections.title: At the Province Level
sections.norm: at the province level. mirrored the arrangement at centre plc = governor (or lt governor) + executive council members + additional members relationship between the centre & the provinces 1833 ica 1861 nwp 1773 goi act 1935 6.1) bengal — 1862. 1897 1849. the provisions at the province level mirrored the arrangement at centre. plcs & gecs were created. structurally, ilc & plc were similar. under ica 1861, each plc = governor (or lt governor) + executive council members + additional members nominated for law-making (similar formula to ilc = vec + additional members). but there was something more significant happening here in terms of the relationship between the centre & the provinces. centralisation had peaked in 1833, when the legislative powers of bombay & madras were taken away & concentrated at the centre. ica 1861 began reversing that. it restored the legislative powers of bombay & madras, and proposed new provincial legislative councils (plcs) for bengal, punjab, and the north-western provinces (nwp). ◆ this marks the beginning of a long arc: centralisation began in 1773, peaked in 1833, and decentralisation began in 1861 — finally peaking with provincial autonomy under the goi act 1935. the new plcs were set up in: 6.1) bengal — 1862. 6.2) nwp — 1886. (nwp was that half of awadh which was annexed as permanent payment of subsidy in 1801 subsidiary alliance & where mahalwari was 1st applied in 1822; given province status in 1836 but without a legislature & under a lg.) why the delay? memories of 1857 were still raw, and the british were cautious about loosening executive grip. 6.3) punjab — 1897. (annexed in 1849.) why the delay? frontier province — the british preferred strong executive control there rather than the slower deliberation of a legislative body. (why a plc for bengal? bengal's provincial council had evolved into gg(india)'s council by 1833, became the viceroy's/gg's council in 1858, and then got rebranded as ilc & vec in 1861 — which is why bengal needed a fresh plc of its own.)

sections.title: True Federalism — Just a Small Beginning
sections.norm: true federalism — just a small beginning. plc ica 1892 ilc vec goi 1935 bill approval approval was needed before certain bills 1919 state reorganisation create new provinces & appoint lieutenant-governors indian councils act india act. even as some power was being decentralised, the executive control remained tightly centralised in centre. the viceroy's powers over provinces under ica 1861 included: 7.1) nomination of non-officers to plc: non-official members of each plc were nominated by the governor of that province — however, no such nomination was legally valid until it received the formal sanction of the viceroy. this is a textbook example of "giving with one hand & taking with the other." (by ica 1892, this requirement for viceroy's sanction on provincial nominations was ended, shifting more genuine power to the governors.) 7.2) rule-making: he framed the rules for the functioning of the ilc, plcs, vec, and gecs. (this power was ended only by goi 1935, which brought provincial autonomy.) 7.3) bill approval: his approval was needed before certain bills could even be introduced. (this has a parallel in article 304 of our constitution of india, 1950, which requires the president's recommendation for certain state bills.) (this was relaxed by goi 1919 & further by goi 1935, as subjects were divided between centre & provinces.) 7.4) one country, one budget: there was no separate provincial budget — only one budget for british india as a whole. (compare: our constitution's article 202 gives every state legislature its own state budget.) (this was ended by goi 1919, which separated the provincial budget from the central budget for the first time.) 7.5) state reorganisation: he could create new provinces & appoint lieutenant-governors. (compare: articles 3, 4, and 155 of our coi 1950.) (under goi 1935, this power shifted from the viceroy to the crown — i.e. effectively to the british pm.) ⚠ alert (prelims 2002): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following acts of british india strengthened the viceroy's authority over his executive council by substituting 'portfolio' or departmental system for corporate functioning? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) indian councils act, 1861. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — government of india act, 1858; (c) ✗ — indian councils act, 1892; (d) ✗ — indian councils act, 1909

sections.title: ICA 1861 Summary
sections.norm: ica 1861 summary. 8.1) philosophy: despotism controlled from home (charles wood) 8.2) executive (vec): gg + 5 ordinary members + cic (extraordinary) legislature (ilc) additional members portfolio system given legal recognition 1st indians raja of banaras, maharaja of patiala, dinkar rao provincial bodies bombay & madras legislative powers restored 8.7) new plcs created: bengal 1862, nwp 1886, punjab 1897 legislature powers no questions, no resolutions, no budget discussion viceroy powers absolute veto election method all members nominated federalism not federal decentralisation from 1833 peak nature of govt despotism canning. 8.1) philosophy: despotism controlled from home (charles wood) 8.2) executive (vec): gg + 5 ordinary members + cic (extraordinary) 8.3) legislature (ilc): vec + 6–12 additional members (half non-official) 8.4) portfolio system: given legal recognition (introduced by canning56-62 in 1859) 8.5) 1st indians: raja of banaras, maharaja of patiala, dinkar rao (1862) 8.6) provincial bodies: plcs & gecs created; bombay & madras legislative powers restored 8.7) new plcs created: bengal 1862, nwp 1886, punjab 1897 8.8) legislature powers: minimal — no questions, no resolutions, no budget discussion, no vote 8.9) viceroy powers: absolute veto, ordinance (6 months), prior approval for bills 8.10) election method: all members nominated — no elections 8.11) federalism: not federal — decentralisation from 1833 peak, centre made budget 8.12) nature of govt: despotism — no responsible government anywhere

sections.chapterTitle: Moderates in INC: Ideology, Demands, Negatives
sections.title: Moderates' Ideology
sections.norm: moderates' ideology. two western philosophical traditions utilitarianism & liberalism constitutionalism responsible government rule of law rti did the moderates oppose british rule? their ideology gets interesting british rule was exploitative inc secular in orientation capitalism & industrialisation on british lines. what was the intellectual foundation of the moderates? the moderates were shaped by two western philosophical traditions: utilitarianism & liberalism. utilitarianism holds that the right action is the one that produces the greatest good for the greatest number & believe in laws & good governance as mechanism for change. liberalism stresses individual rights, rule of law, and constitutional governance. together, these gave the moderates conviction: that gradual constitutional reform is the right way for reform. from this grew their belief in constitutionalism — the idea that a legitimate state should provide responsible government, protect the rights of citizens, and operate under rule of law. (think of constitutionalism as values reflected in our preamble, the basic structure doctrine & directive principles of state policy.) they believed in constitutional methods — meaning, they would use only the institutions & mechanisms that the state itself provided to redress grievances. (think of today's equivalents: fighting elections, using the legislature, approaching the judiciary, filing rti applications, using cpgrams, writing to citizen charters, sending petitions to government. all of these are constitutional methods.) did the moderates oppose british rule? this is where their ideology gets interesting — and, to later generations, frustrating. the moderates knew that british rule was exploitative. they were not naïve. but they believed in the providence of british rule: that if sufficiently pressurised, the british could be made to modernise india. their goal was therefore not independence but limited self-government — a greater indian share in governance within british rule. why so limited? because they believed that the indian masses, without widespread western education, were not yet ready for full self-rule. their ultimate long-term vision — though they rarely stated it loudly — was self-government like canada or australia, with full british citizenship. not removal of british rule, but removal of what surendranath banerjea famously called "un-british rule" — meaning the gap between britain's own stated liberal values & its actual conduct in india. the first president of the inc, w.c. bonnerjee, captured this perfectly when he declared that the inc was "loyal to the british & well-wishers of the british." they were secular in orientation & actively promoted national unity. they also believed in capitalism & industrialisation on british lines as the path to indian prosperity.

sections.chapterTitle: Moderates in INC: Ideology, Demands, Negatives
sections.title: Goals & Methods
sections.norm: goals & methods. goals self-government within british rule not the removal of british rule itself methods prayers & petitions no mass action the "strategy of mendicancy," defence of the moderates: gokhale 1913 inc. goals: their goal was limited — self-government within british rule. they wanted only the removal of the undesirable aspects of british rule, not the removal of british rule itself. as surendranath banerjea put it, they wanted to end "un-british rule." their ultimate vision was self-government like canada or australia — dominion status, not independence. methods: sending prayers & petitions, passing resolutions at annual sessions, using the press to express opinions, building a rich culture of debates. no mass action. no agitation on the streets. their approach was one of gradualism. ◆ their critics — and later the extremists — called this the "strategy of mendicancy," i.e., begging. the label captured the reality that their methods created little pressure on the british. defence of the moderates: to be fair to them, gokhale noted in 1913 that had moderates not followed the methods they followed, the british would not have allowed the inc to function. the culture of mass politics with direct confrontation with the colonial government had not yet developed. a movement that begins with petition & prayer is not necessarily weak — it is building the institutions & culture of modern politics for a country that had just begun with a modern national movement.

sections.chapterTitle: Moderates in INC: Ideology, Demands, Negatives
sections.title: Moderates' Demands
sections.norm: moderates' demands. on the question of governance & legislative reform: abolish the india council 15-member advisory body ilc 1931 inm on the question of economics: 1899–1901 volunteer army martial races trial by jury arms act 1878 1930 permanent settlement of 1793 ps1793 indentured labourers in assam tea plantations outcome two decades of petitions & prayers ww2 permanent settlement 1793. the moderates made several concrete demands. on the question of governance & legislative reform: 2.1) abolish the india council — the 15-member advisory body sitting in london around the secretary of state. the moderates' logic was simple: lobbying one secretary of state is easier than lobbying fifteen members of a council. 2.2) expand the imperial legislative council (ilc) and provincial legislative councils (plcs) — with at least 50% indirectly elected members. 2.3) greater powers to the ilc & plcs — meaningful legislative authority, not just advisory roles. 2.4) indianisation of the civil & military services — by holding the civil services examination simultaneously in india & britain, and raising the age limit to 23. this would make administration more responsive, less expensive, and less racist. the demand for indians at officer rank in the military was similarly rejected — the british simply could not imagine taking orders from indians. (it was only after the 1st round table conference of 1931 that indian officer appointments began in the military services (which led to the establishment of the indian military academy at dehradun in 1932), though even then the british were careful in selection. it was only during ww2 that indian officers were recruited in real numbers, in response to inm demands.) on the question of economics: 2.5) decrease & share military expenditure — the indian army was frequently used for british imperial adventures that had nothing to do with india, like the boxer rebellion (1899–1901) in china. this demand was partially met but no significant change occurred. 2.6) a volunteer army — recruitment open to all, not restricted by the "martial races" doctrine. (today india does have a volunteer army — anyone can apply. the british rejected this demand fearing disaffection, especially if marathas & bengalis joined in large numbers.) 2.7) trial by jury — the right to be judged by a jury of peers rather than by colonial officers. 2.8) repeal of the arms act 1878 — which had disarmed ordinary indians. the moderates framed this as a right to bear arms for self-defence, not as a call to violence. 2.9) decrease land revenue & end the salt tax. (salt tax — the same tax gandhi attacked in the salt march 1930. it had been a grievance for decades.) 2.10) extend the permanent settlement of 1793 (ps1793) outside bengal — so that land revenue could not be arbitrarily increased. this was partly a principled demand & partly, as we will see, a self-interested one. 2.11) end the exploitation of indentured labourers in assam tea plantations — workers who were bound to plantations under harsh contracts. outcome: no demands were met. the result of two decades of petitions & prayers was, in practice, zero.

sections.chapterTitle: Moderates in INC: Ideology, Demands, Negatives
sections.title: Weaknesses of the Moderates and the INC
sections.norm: weaknesses of the moderates and the inc. not a truly representative organization: inc low muslim participation: bombay's badruddin tyabji 1887 1892–1909 but this had negative consequences not full-time politicians: social background affected moderate politics: permanent settlement of 1793 ps1793 punjab land alienation bill of 1900 only indian capitalism could remove poverty and industrialize india lancashire were heavily lobbying for factory regulations what they specifically opposed: factories act 1881 ripon80-84 factories act 1891 lansdowne88-94 indian mines act 1901 curzon99-05 overall, the moderate politics was plagued by two structural problems first 90% hindu second the consequence: north-western provinces 1836 permanent settlement 1793 ripon lansdowne curzon. not a truly representative organization: this was the most serious structural weakness of the early inc. the organisation suffered from uneven representation & the total exclusion of non-elites. representation at the inc’s first session (bombay, 1885) was highly uneven: of its 72 delegates, 38 came from the bombay presidency, 21 from madras, only 3 from the extensive bengal–bihar–orissa–assam region, and the remaining 10 from punjab and the “north-western provinces and oudh” (nwp1836 & oudh’s administrations were placed under one head in 1877). [note: there was low participation from bengal in 1885 session as the 2nd indian national conference was held in calcutta by the indian association (1876) just before the inc session making it difficult for leaders such as surendranath banerjea (snb) to attend.] during its first two decades, the inc remained dominated by elites. they were western-educated-middle class professionals (lawyers, doctors, journalists, teachers etc) and elites including merchants, bankers, and landowners, belonging to upper castes, & concentrated mainly in the three presidencies—madras, bombay and bengal. madras, although educationally advanced by 1885, exercised less political influence because its educated elite was less politically organised than those of bengal and bombay. hence, the inc's claim of representing the whole nation was weak which hurt the success of inc programmes. low muslim participation: very few muslims participated in the early inc. bombay's badruddin tyabji — who became the first muslim president of the inc at the madras session of 1887 — was a notable exception. in the period 1892–1909, hindus made up 90% of members, with muslims at only about 6.5%. within the hindu membership, brahmins alone constituted roughly 40%, the remainder included non-brahmin hindus (many from upper castes), muslims, parsis and christians. to maintain unity, in 1886, the inc took the pragmatic but damaging decision to avoid all social questions — meaning issues of caste, social reform & religion — until 1907. inc was to focus only on political matters i.e. democratic reforms, governance, civil services, economic demands; communally sensitive social reform questions — caste, religion, personal law — were kept off the official agenda because they risked splitting the fragile hindu-muslim-parsi coalition before it had properly formed. the logic was that national political unity had to be built first. but this had negative consequences e.g. when cow-killing riots broke out in 1893, the inc stayed silent & did not condemn the violence. muslim participation dropped dramatically in the 1890s, and the inc made no concerted effort to reach out to the muslim community. not full-time politicians: moderate leaders were, for the most part, part-time politicians. most had lucrative legal practices & other professional commitments. the inc itself was organisationally weak — it functioned more like an annual conference lasting three days than a genuine political party. social background affected moderate politics: in the period 1892–1909, the inc membership consisted of approximately 20% landlords, 40% lawyers, and 15% traders — most from landed family background. this social background shaped their political positions in a way that prevented them from becoming popular among masses: 3.1) they did not take an anti-zamindar stand as they came from landed families. in fact, they wanted to extend the permanent settlement of 1793 outside bengal — a selfish demand, since ps1793 prevented the state from raising land revenue & was pro-big landlords. 3.2) they opposed the punjab land alienation bill of 1900, which was designed to prevent indebted peasants from losing their land to moneylenders. 3.3) they actively supported workers oppressed by british capitalists e.g. the workers of assam tea gardens agitating against the european plantation owners. however, they favored indian capitalists against the working-class as they believed that only indian capitalism could remove poverty and industrialize india. when it came to labour reforms that would hurt indian capitalists, the moderates opposed them consistently — and their reason was not simply class selfishness. it was the lancashire lobby argument. the british were not
