passing these labour laws out of sympathy for indian workers. british textile manufacturers in lancashire were heavily lobbying for factory regulations in india — so cost of production for indian manufacturers increases & reduce the competitiveness of indian textiles against british goods in global markets. the moderates argued that india's infant industries needed government support to grow, and that imposing heavy regulations prematurely would crush indigenous industrialisation before it had properly begun, keeping india permanently as a supplier of raw materials and an export market for british manufactured goods. with this context, here is what they specifically opposed: i) factories act 1881 (ripon80-84): applied to factories with 100 or more workers. banned employment of children under 7. restricted working hours for children aged 7–12 to 9 hours per day. mandated fencing of hazardous machinery. ii) factories act 1891 (lansdowne88-94): extended coverage to factories with 50 or more workers. raised the minimum working age from 7 to 9, and definition of child for labor purposes from 12 to 14 years of age. capped women's working hours at 11 hours per day with a 1.5-hour rest interval. iii) indian mines act 1901 (curzon99-05): the first major regulation of mining sector. set a minimum age for child labour in mines & improved working conditions for women & children underground. ◆ whether the moderates were right or wrong in opposing these acts is a complex question. the lancashire lobby motive was real — the british were not being philanthropists. but the consequence of moderate opposition was that indian workers, including children, continued to labour under harsh conditions for longer than desired. overall, the moderate politics was plagued by two structural problems that reinforced each other. first, the moderates did not represent masses. they were roughly 90% hindu, overwhelmingly drawn from the lawyer & landlord classes. second, they fundamentally distrusted the masses & refused to mobilise them, fearing that popular agitation would turn violent and become an uncontrolled mass movement. the consequence: a movement that neither represented the people nor threatened to unleash them. the colonial government could easily ignore petitions from a few hundred educated professionals with no mass base behind them.

sections.title: Nation Building
sections.norm: nation building. inc 1885 1886 1888 1889 ilc 1996 upsc 1997 2008 2013 2015 2018 2020. what was the first goal the inc declared? at the very first inc session in 1885 in bombay, the congress declared its goal as "building national unity." this was not an accident. india in 1885 was a land of regions, languages, castes, and religions — there was no pre-existing sense of a single indian political community. the moderates understood that building such a community was the first task, even before demanding rights from the british. to achieve this, they made a deliberate choice to focus only on issues common to all indians. in 1886, dadabhai naoroji laid down what became an informal inc rule — the congress would take up only political questions, not social or class questions, because social issues could divide indians against each other. (i.e. only issues where it was indians vs british — not hindu vs muslim, upper caste vs lower caste, men vs women, working class vs capitalist class, or ryots vs landlords. the congress was to be a platform against colonial rule, not a forum for internal indian disputes.) for hindu-muslim unity specifically, the inc took two concrete steps: - 1888 inc decision — no resolution would be passed by the inc if the majority of hindu or muslim members disagreed with it. - 1889 minority clause — the inc demanded that the british government reserve seats in the imperial legislative council (ilc) and the provincial legislative councils (plcs) for religious minorities in proportion to their share of the population. (both these decisions show that the moderates were trying to build a congress that worked for all indians. the 1889 minority clause is notable — it was the inc itself, not the muslim league, that first formally demanded minority representation in legislative councils.) another structural decision that built national unity was how inc sessions were organised. each session was held in a different part of the country, and the president was specifically not from the host region. the logic was straightforward: a bengali leader presiding in calcutta builds nothing new. but a marathi leader presiding in calcutta — speaking to bengali concerns — builds an all-india leadership & creates inter-regional bonds that would not exist otherwise. (imagine a bengali delegate/newspaper reader listening to/reading an article by a marathi president describe the problems of bengal peasants. the bengali now starts to see that marathi leader as his national leader too. and the marathi leader, by visiting bengal, becomes aware of bengal's issues. this is nation-building through simple structural design.) ⚠ alert (prelims 1996): upsc tested this. q) who among the following leaders did not believe in the drain theory of dadabhai naoroji? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) sir syed ahmed khan. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — b.g. tilak; (b) ✗ — r.c. dutt; (c) ✗ — m.g. ranade ⚠ alert (prelims 1997): upsc tested this. q) a graduate at 18, professor and associate editor of the sudharak at 20, secretary of the sarvajanik sabha and of the provincial conference at 25, secretary of the national congress at 29, leading... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) gopal krishna gokhale. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — pandit madan mohan malaviya; (b) ✗ — mahadev govind ranade; (d) ✗ — bal gangadhar tilak ⚠ alert (prelims 2008): upsc tested this. q) who among the following used the phrase 'un-british' to criticise the english colonial control of india? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) dadabhai naoroji. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — anandmohan bose; (b) ✗ — badruddin tyyabji; (d) ✗ — pherozeshah mehta ⚠ alert (prelims 2013): upsc tested this. q) consider the following statements the most effective contribution made by dadabhai naoroji to the cause of indian freedom movement was that he 1. exposed the economic exploitation of india by the... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) only 1. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — 2 and 3; (c) ✗ — 1 and 3; (d) ✗ — 1, 2 and 3 ⚠ alert (prelims 2015): upsc tested this. q) who of the following was/were economic critic/critics of colonialism in india? 1. dadabhai naoroji 2. g subramaniam iyer 3. rc dutt select the correct answer using the codes given below : to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — only 1; (b) ✗ — 1 and 2; (c) ✗ — 2 and 3 ⚠ alert (prelims 2018): upsc tested this. q) economic result of british rule in 19th century: to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) commercialization of agriculture. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — export of handicrafts; (b) ✗ — growth in indian factories; (d) ✗ — urban population increase ⚠ alert (prelims 2020): upsc tested this. q) which of the following statements correctly explains the impact of industrial revolution on india during the first half of the nineteenth century? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) indian handicrafts were ruined. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — machines were introduced in the indian textile industry in large numbers.; (c) ✗ — railway lines were laid in many parts of the country.; (d) ✗ — heavy duties were imposed on the imports of british manufactures.

sections.title: Building a Culture of Parliamentary Politics
sections.norm: building a culture of parliamentary politics. inc 1885. how did the inc sessions contribute beyond passing resolutions? the inc sessions were consciously modelled on parliamentary practice. there was a president who functioned like a speaker. members spoke, debated, and voted on resolutions. for india, this was new. (watch a lok sabha session today — the procedures, the order of speaking, the formal adoption of resolutions — all of this has roots in the culture built by inc sessions from 1885 onwards.) this is why it can be said that the modern political era in india, in a true sense, began with the inc.

sections.title: Supporting Indian Capitalists
sections.norm: supporting indian capitalists. 3.1 — the case for supporting indian capitalists not anti-poor — it was pro-industrialisation 1917 1929 1890 3.2 — drain theory drain theory economically exploiting india, not developing it white man's burden was false indian councils act of 1892 ica1892 1901 political control over the indian state to extract economic benefits it was exploitation 3.3 — impact of british industrialisation on india indian handicrafts sector was destroyed no industrialisation of india agriculture sector became overburdened 1859 1869 4,500 misuse of political power economic benefit of the colonial power 3.4 — components of the drain treaty of allahabad colony = source of raw materials & export market 1914–19 exchange rate manipulation benefitted british businesses 1833 goi did not get forex for its exports indian taxpayer money financed this trade eic salaries, pensions, and training costs of british officials & soldiers interest on foreign debt expenses of the secretary of state for india & the india council purchase of stores/goods for india by sos 1857 fdi the net effect — double drain through asymmetric trade. net exporter of rm council bills + home charges + guaranteed fdi interest double drain. asymmetric trade 3.5 — did british rule modernise india — the debate 2022 british argument railways linked india internally dalhousie48-56 1853 connected indian markets & sources of raw materials to ports did not connect indian markets to indian manufacturers technology transfer was very limited investment opportunities for british railway companies £ 100 £ 5 p.a. 99 years 1947 british-built canals permanent settlement 1793 permanent settlement of 1793 1943 1880 1897 1900 growth was regionally uneven neither the quantity nor the quality of development justified what india paid as the drain gdp 1999 upsc 2011 ww1 indian councils act 1892 dalhousie. 3.1 — the case for supporting indian capitalists why did the moderates support indian businessmen? this question often causes confusion. supporting capitalists sounds like it goes against the interests of workers & the poor. but the moderates' position was not anti-poor — it was pro-industrialisation. their argument was simple: india needs to industrialise like the west. and industrialisation in the 19th century ran on capitalism. every major industrialised country — britain, the us, germany, japan — had industrialised on the backs of its capitalist class. (the alternative model of communist-led industrialisation, as seen in soviet russia, was born only in 1917 & showed results only after 1929. in the 1880s & 1890s, that model did not yet exist. the moderates were working with the tools available to them.) there was a second reason too. indian capitalists of this period were not powerful monopolists — they were struggling. they were under severe competitive pressure from british imports flooding indian markets & from british businesses operating inside india with the government's backing. an indian capitalist in 1890 needed support, not criticism. 3.2 — drain theory what is the most important intellectual contribution of the moderates? without question, it is the drain theory — the systematic, evidence-based argument that british rule was economically exploiting india, not developing it, and that the entire claim of the white man's burden was false. the theory gained particular prominence after the bitter disappointment with the indian councils act of 1892 (ica1892), which failed to deliver any meaningful reform. its key architects were romesh chandra dutt( a former ics officer turned economic historian — authored the economic history of british india (vol. i, 1902) & india in the victorian age (vol. ii, 1904), which provided a detailed, data-driven account of how british land revenue policies, trade regulations, and fiscal management had impoverished india. his work gave the drain theory its historical depth & empirical backbone.), dadabhai naoroji, and mg ranade (often called the father of indian economics). (naoroji's book poverty & un-british rule in india (1901) was the most systematic presentation of the theory & remains a landmark text in the economic history of colonialism globally the core idea was straightforward: the british were using their political control over the indian state to extract economic benefits for britain. this was not charity or development — it was exploitation. in proving this with data & argument, the moderates built an economic critique of colonialism that was sharp, factual, and difficult to counter. (lenin & lala lajpat rai would later argue along similar lines — that colonialism is the product of british capitalism needing new markets & raw materials. the moderates arrived at this conclusion through an economic lens well before it became standard argument in global socialist circles.) 3.3 — impact of british industrialisation on india what exactly did british industrialisation do to india? british industrial capitalism converted india into two things: a source of raw materials & an export market for british factories. before british industrial dominance, india was a net exporter of finished goods — textiles, handicrafts, processed goods. post-industrialisation, india became a net exporter of raw materials, while finished goods flooded back in as imports. despite being an exporter of raw materials and an importer of finished goods, india ran a trade surplus — exports were worth more than imports. but be careful about whom the surplus was with. by the late nineteenth century india bought most of its imports from britain — machinery, and above all lancashire cloth — while selling most of its exports to china, japan, continental europe & america. so the surplus was earned from the rest of the world; with britain itself, india ran a deficit. think of it as trade/money surplus but wealth deficit: what india earned abroad was held in london and swallowed by the home charges, so it never came home. (think of an african country today that exports crude oil to the world and runs a trade surplus — yet the wealth that could have built its own industries for future generations is taken out by outside powers. trade surplus, wealth deficit. india’s relationship with britain followed this structure.) there was commercialisation of agriculture — indian agriculture was reoriented away from food crops & towards cash crops & raw materials meant for export to british factories. india’s peasants no longer grew what they ate; they grew what britain’s mills needed — cotton, indigo, jute, opium. the indian handicrafts sector was destroyed in this process. indian artisans lost both domestic & export markets. since there was no industrialisation of india — no indian factories came up to replace the handicrafts — these artisans had nowhere to go. they could not become factory workers because there were no indian factories. they were forced back onto agriculture. (an artisan uses skill & hands. a factory worker uses labour & machines. these are fundamentally different kinds of production — decentralised & rural vs centralised & urban. when the artisan is pushed off his trade but no factory exists to absorb him, he falls back to the land. the result is disguised unemployment in agriculture — too many people on too little land, each doing far less productive work than they could.) this is why the agriculture sector became overburdened — it was absorbing people it should never have had to absorb. (in a modern economy, the worker works in machine-based factories. agriculture employs a small fraction of the population. britain achieved this transition. india was denied it.) the revolution in transport made this drain worse, not better. steam-powered railways, steam-fitted ships, paved roads, modern ports, and the construction of the suez canal between 1859 & 1869 — which cut the sea distance between india & britain by 4,500 miles — all made it cheaper & faster to extract raw materials from india & ship finished goods back. what is the core argument of drain theory in one sentence? the misuse of political power over the state of the colony for the economic benefit of the colonial power. 3.4 — components of the drain how exactly did the money leave india? what were the specific mechanisms? the notes distinguish between two periods. pre-19th century (pre-1800s): - misuse of the dastaks (duty-free trade passes originally granted only for eic's own goods but misused by company servants for private trade) + the plassey plunder of 1757–65 + land revenue (lr) extraction from british india beginning 1765. (the lr extraction from bengal, orissa, and bihar formally began with the treaty of allahabad 1765.) - as a result, the structure of british trade with india reversed: earlier, gold flowed into india as payment for indian goods. after plassey & the acquisition of lr rights, gold flowed out of india. from 19th century (1813 onwards): the modern colonial relationship developed — colony = source of raw materials & export market. - absence of protective tariffs — no import duty was imposed on british goods entering india to protect indian manufacturers. this policy lasted until ww1 (1914–19), when protective tariffs were applied for the first time. the result: british goods flooded indian markets & indian manufacturers could not compete. - exchange rate manipulation — the rupee-to-pound exchange rate was managed in a way that benefitted british businesses. (think of how china has at times been accused of keeping its currency artificially undervalued to make chinese exports cheaper. the british did something similar in reverse — they manipulated the exchange rate to keep british exports competitive in india.) - tax-financed trade / council bills (post-1833) — this is the most complex mechanism & deserves careful attention. the secretary of state (sos) for india held india's foreign exchange (forex) in london. when a foreign importer wanted to buy indian goods, instead of paying in forex directly, he purchased council bills (cbs) — promissory notes issued by the india council in london. he paid for these cbs with his forex, which stayed in london. he then used the cbs in india to purchase indian goods, and the government of india (goi) accepted these cbs & gave indian rupees to the importer. (think of it like this: a foreign buyer gives his dollars not to india but to a london office. he gets a voucher. he uses the voucher in india to buy goods & gets rupees. india got rupees — its own currency — but never got the foreign exchange for its exports. the forex stayed in london. and where did india's rupees to pay the importer come from? from indian taxpayers.) so india did not get forex for its exports. instead, indian taxpayer money financed this trade. - eic earning forex by exporting indian goods — e.g. opium exported to china. this forex too was taken to london & did not return to india. - home charges — the word "home" here means britain, not india. these were charges that india was made to pay for goods & services supposedly provided to india by britain or the secretary of state. each item below carries the british justification of the day: - salaries, pensions, and training costs of british officials & soldiers (justification: they gave their careers to the service of india) - dividends to eic shareholders (justification: eic gave governance service to india by running the company state) - interest on loans taken by eic (justification: loans taken to meet expenses of the goi) - interest on foreign debt (justification: debt incurred for india's administration & development) - expenses of the secretary of state for india & the india council in london (earlier the board of control) - purchase of stores/goods for india by sos — stationery, steel, and other supplies - payments to the british war office — for weapons purchased for india's defence, and for use of the royal military during crises such as 1857 - interest on fdi — paid to british businesses who invested in india (justification: to attract fdi for india's development) (note: the use of the british indian army abroad — for imperial campaigns in afghanistan, africa, china — was not technically a "home charge" because in that case india was not receiving a service — it was giving one to the empire. the expenses of waging these wars outside india were charged directly to the indian budget as military expenditure, which was a separate — and equally egregious — drain on indian finances, but it falls outside the specific category of home charges.) the net effect — double drain through asymmetric trade. (i) net exporter of rm = india shipped out more raw material (cotton, jute, indigo, tea, opium) than it imported, on paper a ‘positive’ trade balance. but — the forex india earned were also drained via council bills + home charges + guaranteed fdi interest. so india shipped out wealth (rm) and shipped out the export earnings too. double drain. (ii) asymmetric trade — yes, india did not receive an equivalent value of finished goods back. british finished goods (cotton textiles, machine-made products) flooded india tariff-favoured, but their total value was less than the rm india shipped out. 3.5 — did british rule modernise india — the debate were there any genuine modernising benefits that justify the drain? this debate was structured by the moderates themselves. the british made certain arguments in their favour, and the moderates — and later historians — developed counter-arguments. one calibration before we begin: a 2022 estimate by utsa patnaik puts the total value of the drain at $45 trillion at 2022 prices. whatever modernisation happened, it happened as an unintended byproduct. no part of it was done for india. railways british argument: railways linked india internally & to the world economy through rail-to-port infrastructure. counter-arguments: - dalhousie48-56 introduced railways in 1853 primarily for faster movement of the british army — military control was the original purpose, not economic development. - railways connected indian markets & sources of raw materials to ports — and through ports to british manufacturers. they did not connect indian markets to indian manufacturers. - technology transfer was very limited, and even that was in low-technology areas like bridge-building & tunnelling. - the real goal was to create investment opportunities for british railway companies. - british capitalists received a guaranteed 5% annual interest on their invested capital, paid out in pound sterling in london. this payment started the moment they did the fdi into india. this meant investors earned 5% annually even during the years the railway was still under construction and not earning any revenue. once the railway began its operations and started earning revenue then in any year if the railway failed to make 5% profit, the goi made up the deficit and ensured the investors still received minimum 5% for that year. additionally, at any point they had the right to sell the railway line back to goi at price equivalent to the exact total fdi the company had made. hence overall if £ 100 was fdi, they received minimum £ 5 p.a. from the day of fdi and if decided to wrap up business in india before 99 years then will also get paid £ 100. hence fdi became fd (fixed deposit with simple interest paid p.a.), led to wasteful construction — profits were private while losses were of public. the same money could have been invested in irrigation for india’s food security. the byproduct, however, was real: by 1947, railways covered 78% of india. feeder roads built from indian factory hubs to railway lines allowed indian businesses to eventually use the network. railways also increased people-to-people contact across regions, which strengthened national unity & the inter-regional bonds that the indian national movement would depend upon. canals british argument: british-built canals became a role model for asia & helped develop irrigation infrastructure & food security. counter-arguments: - quantity: by 1947, only 25% of cultivated area was under public irrigation. - geography: canals were built only in non-permanent settlement 1793 areas — regions like punjab, western up, and coastal madras where land revenue could still be increased. bengal, bihar, and orissa, locked under the permanent settlement of 1793, saw little canal investment. - access: water from canals was not free. only rich farmers could afford it. - result: recurring famines through the 1860s & 1870s, and as late as the devastating bengal famine of 1943, are proof that there was no genuine food security. the british response to famines was itself telling — a series of famine commissions were appointed, including the strachey commission (1880), the lyall commission (1897), and the macdonnell commission (1900), but their recommendations were rarely implemented with any seriousness. the famines kept recurring because the structural problem — extractive land revenue, export-oriented agriculture, and inadequate irrigation — was never addressed. the british rejoinder — "drain was only 2%" british argument: the drain was only 2% of india's export value in the early 1900s. this small amount paid for real development — it attracted fdi into railways, roadways, and irrigation. counter-arguments: - quantity: gdp growth was not substantial. - quality: growth was regionally uneven, and investment in irrigation, health, and education remained low. - neither the quantity nor the quality of development justified what india paid as the drain. - dadabhai naoroji's argument cuts to the heart of it: even if 2% sounds small, this was surplus capital. if that surplus had been invested in india instead of drained to britain, it would have compounded over decades & generated significant gdp growth. it is not the absolute percentage that matters — it is what it could have become. (think of a savings account. 2% of your income seems small. but if you invest it instead of spending it, compounded over 50 years, it becomes substantial wealth. the drain robbed india of that compounding effect, year after year.) ◆ drain theory's central claim is structural: a colonial power using political control to redirect economic surplus. this made the economic critique inseparable from the political demand for swaraj — without self-rule, the drain could never be stopped. ⚠ alert (prelims 1997): upsc tested this. q) m.c. setalvad, b.n. rau and alladi krishnaswamy iyer were distinguished members of the (a) swarajist party (b) all india national liberal federation (c) communist party of india (d) indian civil service. correct answer: (b) all india national liberal federation. the ainlf was founded in 1918 after the surat split aftermath when moderates left inc under leaders like surendranath banerjea and tej bahadur sapru. all three named figures — m.c. setalvad (eminent jurist, later 1st attorney general of india), b.n. rau (constitutional adviser to the constituent assembly), and alladi krishnaswamy iyer (member of constituent assembly's drafting committee) — were associated with the federation in their early careers. memory hook: setalvad + rau + alladi = three eminent jurists → ainlf (1918 moderate splinter from inc). ⚠ alert (prelims 1999): upsc tested this. q) there was no independent development of industries in india during british rule because of the to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) absence of heavy industries. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — scarcity of foreign capital; (c) ✗ — scarcity of natural resources; (d) ✗ — preference of the rich to invest in land ⚠ alert (prelims 2008): upsc tested this. q) who among the following rejected the title of 'knighthood' and refused to accept a position in the council of the secretary of state for india? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) gk gokhale. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — motilal nehru; (b) ✗ — mg ranade; (d) ✗ — bg tilak ⚠ alert (prelims 2011): upsc tested this. q) with reference to the period of colonial rule in india, 'home charges' formed an important part of drain of wealth from india. which of the following funds constituted 'home charges'? 1. funds used to support the indian office in london. 2. funds used to pay salaries and pensions of british personnel engaged in india. 3. funds used for waging wars outside india by the british. to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) 1, 2 and 3. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — only 1; (b) ✗ — 1 and 2; (c) ✗ — 2 and 3

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: ICA 1892 — Significance
sections.norm: ica 1892 — significance. the indian councils act of 1892 ica 1892. the indian councils act of 1892 was simultaneously a result of the moderates' struggle & proof of its failure. the moderates had spent years petitioning, writing memorials, and presenting carefully reasoned arguments for constitutional reform. what they got in return was the ica 1892 — an act that gave just enough to show the british had listened, and little enough to show they had no intention of actually conceding power.

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: The "Indirect Election" That Wasn't Called an Election
sections.norm: the "indirect election" that wasn't called an election. ica 1892 ilc provincial legislative councils (plcs) nominated non-official members district boards, municipalities, universities. the most significant feature of ica 1892 was the introduction of indirectly nominated members in the ilc & the plcs — the first time something resembling representative membership appeared in these councils. but notice the careful choice of words: nominated, not elected. the word "election" was deliberately omitted from the text of the act. the legal mechanism was strictly defined as "nomination on the basis of recommendation." it was selection, not election. how did it work? the system worked on two distinct levels: 3.1) for the provincial legislative councils (plcs): governors nominated non-official members based on recommendations from district boards, municipalities, universities, trade associations, and zamindars. 3.2) for the imperial legislative council (ilc): the viceroy nominated non-officials based on recommendations from the non-official members of the plcs & the bengal chamber of commerce — not directly from local bodies. notable indians who served in the councils under this framework included gokhale & pherozeshah mehta — names that would dominate moderate politics for the next two decades. (in a proper 100% indirect election, the chain would be: people elect local body members → local body members elect mlas from among themselves → mlas elect mps from among themselves. and in a proper election the choice of voters is final. under ica 1892, neither condition held — the recommending bodies only sent names, and the final pick was the viceroy's or governor's. the "election" was really a shortlist.) 🚨 exam trap: if a question states "members of the ilc under ica 1892 were directly recommended by municipalities" — that is incorrect. municipalities fed into plcs; plcs fed into ilc. two separate tiers. direct recommendation to ilc was only from plcs & the bengal chamber of commerce.

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: Size of the Councils
sections.norm: size of the councils. ilc 1861 always comfortably outnumbered the non-official indians official majority. both the ilc & plcs were expanded in size. in the ilc, the total number of additional members was now set at 10 to 16 — and of these, at least half could be non-officials. (compare with 1861, when non-official members were only 3 to 6 of the 6–12 additional members.) but here is the point that the numbers hide: the viceroy's executive council plus the official additional members always comfortably outnumbered the non-official indians. the official majority was not just a political preference — it was mathematically guaranteed by the structure of the act. (think of it like a board meeting where the promoter group always holds majority votes regardless of how many independent directors are added. the independents may speak. they cannot win a vote.)

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: The Viceroy's Executive Council (VEC) — No Change
sections.norm: the viceroy's executive council (vec) — no change. vec did not change at all two distinct boxes cic ilc 1892 1861 1874. the vec under the indian councils act of 1892 did not change at all. whenever a question mentions the indian councils acts (1861, 1892, 1909), you must conceptually split the government into two distinct boxes in your mind: 5.1) box a: the executive council (vec): the inner cabinet (gg + cic + ordinary members). 5.2) box b: the legislative council (ilc): box a plus the "additional members" (who were a mix of officials & non-officials) the ordinary members (6) — these were the dedicated "ministers" who held specific administrative portfolios. they were called ordinary members. at this point in 1892, they were all nominated by the british crown. the six portfolios were: home, revenue/agriculture, law, military (an administrative counterpart to the c-i-c), finance (added in 1861), and public works (added in 1874).

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: What Members Could Do
sections.norm: what members could do. 6.1) questions ask questions to the executive 6 days' prior notice no discussion 6.2) resolutions could not bring any resolution 6.3) bills & legislation ilc 6.4) budget budget could be discussed for the first time neither vote on it nor amend it twr 1776. 6.1) questions for the first time, non-official members could ask questions to the executive — a genuine new right. but with strict conditions: 6 days' prior notice was required, there could be no discussion of the answers given, and no supplementary questions were allowed. you could ask. you could not follow up. 6.2) resolutions opposition members — i.e., the non-official, non-officer members, since the executive under the viceroy was made up entirely of officers — could not bring any resolution before the council, nor could they demand a vote on a government resolution. (a resolution here means a formally declared intent of policy — a motion that the council endorses a direction.) 6.3) bills & legislation the government could make laws without the ilc or plcs. the official majority meant that on every single bill, indian non-official members were simply outvoted. their presence was advisory, not decisive — the legislative function was recommendatory, not mandatory. (ordinance power: ica 1892 made no change. the ordinance power remained as it was under ica 1861 — a 6-month emergency instrument. the council was recommendatory because of the official majority & the viceroy's absolute veto, not because of any new bypass mechanism.) 6.4) budget the budget could be discussed for the first time — another genuine new right. but members could neither vote on it nor amend it. ◆ "taxation without representation" — twr — was the slogan that sparked the american revolution (1776). here, indians had a faint echo of representation: they could watch the budget & speak to it. they had zero power to change it. the british had learned from america what not to give; they had not learned why giving nothing was also eventually dangerous.

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: Federalism — One Small Step
sections.norm: federalism — one small step. one notable change in centre-province relations governor no longer needed the viceroy 1861 ica. ica 1892 made one notable change in centre-province relations: the governor no longer needed the viceroy's approval to nominate non-officers to the plc. until now, even though governors recommended names for their own provincial councils, the viceroy's sanction was required. ica 1892 ended this requirement. this was a small but genuine decentralisation — the first relaxation of the viceroy's iron grip over provincial council composition since 1861. all other aspects of the viceroy's control over provinces — rule-making powers, prior approval for certain bills, a single unified budget with no separate provincial budget, and the power to create new provinces & appoint lieutenant-governors — remained exactly as they were under ica 1861.

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: ICA 1892 Summary
sections.norm: ica 1892 summary. key names lord cross (sos) nomination on basis of recommendation ilc size additional members qs: allowed with 6 days notice no supplementary qs opposition could not bring resolutions did not need viceroy nominate non-officers in plc aitchison commission not a provision of ica 1892 lansdowne. key names: lord cross (sos), lansdowne88-94 (viceroy) election principle: nomination on basis of recommendation (word 'election' avoided) ilc size: vec + 10–16 additional members (up from 6–12 of 1861) official majority: yes vec: unchanged from 1874 qs: allowed with 6 days notice, no discussion, no supplementary qs budget: discussion allowed, no vote resolutions: opposition could not bring resolutions, no vote on govt resolution federalism: governor did not need viceroy's approval to nominate non-officers in plc civil services reform: aitchison commission: ccs→ics, ucs→pcs (not a provision of ica 1892 & done separately as admin measure)

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: A Separate Administrative Reform of the Same Era
sections.norm: a separate administrative reform of the same era. civil services changes 9.1) covenanted civil services (ccs) → renamed imperial civil services (ics) ucs pcs 9.3) statutory civil services (created 1878) → abolished ics indian councils act of 1892 ica lansdowne. 🚨 this is a classic exam trap — keep this clearly separated. during lansdowne88-94's tenure, on the recommendations of the aitchison commission (1886–88), the following civil services changes were made: 9.1) covenanted civil services (ccs) → renamed imperial civil services (ics) 9.2) uncovenanted civil services (ucs) → renamed provincial civil services (pcs) 9.3) statutory civil services (created 1878) → abolished (the ics-pcs split has a federal logic to it — centre & province as two levels, each with its own service cadre. this federal principle you will encounter repeatedly as constitutional reforms advance.) these facts are historically accurate & belong to this period. but they were administrative orders of the era, not provisions of the indian councils act of 1892. if a question asks which of the following were provisions of ica 1892and lists civil service changes — the answer is: not a provision of the act.

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: Scorecard — What the Moderates Won
sections.norm: scorecard — what the moderates won. indianisation of civil services & military proper indirect election only nomination on recommendation expansion of ilc & plcs dissatisfactory constitutionalism (preamble + basic structure) didn't even make it into the text of the act. indianisation of civil services & military: ✗ no non-official majority in councils: ✗ no elected majority: ✗ no proper indirect election: ✗ no — only nomination on recommendation expansion of ilc & plcs: ✓ yes — but dissatisfactory powerful legislatures: ✗ no constitutionalism (preamble + basic structure): ✗ no the word "election" didn't even make it into the text of the act. :(

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: What the Moderates Did Next
sections.norm: what the moderates did next. ica 1892 1906 drain theory systematically extracting india 1901 1867. disappointed by ica 1892, the moderates raised their ceiling of demand. they began asking for self-government on the lines of australia & canada — the dominion model, meaning full self-governance within the british empire without breaking from it. this officially became the goal of the indian national congress at the 1906 calcutta session, named swaraj — self-government within the empire, also called home rule. alongside this political shift, the moderates also developed & propagated the drain theory — the economic argument that british rule was systematically extracting india's wealth to britain, impoverishing the country. both the political demand for swaraj & the economic critique through drain theory became the twin pillars of moderate politics in the years that followed. (australia got self-government as a dominion in 1901. canada in 1867. both were majority white-settler colonies. the moderates' demand was quiet but pointed: if those colonies could govern themselves, why couldn't a civilisation far older & more complex than either of them?)

sections.chapterTitle: Indian Councils Act of 1892 (ICA 1892 or Lord Cross Act)
sections.title: Legacy — Catalyst for Extremism
sections.norm: legacy — catalyst for extremism. the act. ica 1892 matters not only for what it contained, but for what it proved. six demands — and one partially met. the moderates had played by every british rule, used every permissible channel, and mustered every rational argument. the act they received in return was hollow — expanded councils with no real power, a budget discussion with no vote, questions with no follow-up. this was the moment when the belief in british benevolence began to crack. if "prayers & petitions" could produce only this, then the method itself was bankrupt. the disillusionment seeded by ica 1892 was the soil in which extremism would take root in the decade that followed.

sections.chapterTitle: The Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement (1905–11)
sections.title: Drivers of Extremist Rise
sections.norm: drivers of extremist rise. extremist phase began lala lajpat rai bal gangadhar tilak sri aurobindo ghosh cambridge cse in 1890 horse-riding test baroda princely state vice-principal of baroda college bande mataram hasrat mohani 1921 ahmedabad session mahatma gandhi reason 1: the moderates had failed. inc 1885 reason 2: the extremists had a strategy the moderates did not — mass mobilisation through religion & culture. wemc 1893 1896 reason 3: curzon99-05 (1899–1905) made a mass movement possible by making mass anger unavoidable. viceroy curzon99-05 calcutta municipal corporation amendment act indian universities act indian official secrets amendment act 1998 upsc 2004 curzon. by 1905, the moderate phase of inm ended and extremist phase began under leadership of lala lajpat rai (punjab), bal gangadhar tilak (maharashtra), bipin chandra pal and sri aurobindo ghosh (bengal). for most extremist leaders, goal was swaraj within the british raj while for some like sri aurobindo and b.c. pal the goal was purna swaraj. sri aurobindo (studied in cambridge) qualified for the cse in 1890 but deliberately skipped the horse-riding test. instead, he joined the baroda princely state civil service, where he worked in administration and later served as the vice-principal of baroda college. he was the first to publicly demand absolute independence in 1907 through his writings in bande mataram. (*note:- 1st formal resolution for inc demand being upgraded to purna swaraj was by hasrat mohani (with swami kumaranand) at the 1921 ahmedabad session. it was rejected by the inc, primarily due to strong opposition from mahatma gandhi who argued that the demand was premature, irresponsible, and that the indian masses were not yet disciplined or prepared enough for complete independent state.) by 1905, the moderate phase of inm ended and extremist phase began under leadership of lala lajpat rai (punjab), bal gangadhar tilak (maharashtra), bipin chandra pal and sri aurobindo ghosh (bengal). for most extremist leaders, goal was swaraj within the british raj while for some like sri aurobindo and b.c. pal the goal was purna swaraj. rise of extremist leaders like lal-bal-pal-sri aurobindo was result of multiple factors. ◆ every phase of the inm was, in a sense, born from the failure of the phase before it. pre-1857 revolts failed → led to the 1857 revolt → whose failure → led to the modern inm → where failure of conservative earlier organisations → led to wemc-led regional organisations → their failure → led to the inc under moderates → moderates' failure → extremists → extremists' failure → revolutionaries → and so on, until gandhi. each failure raised the temperature of the next response. reason 1: the moderates had failed. the moderates had been at the helm of the inc since its founding in 1885. their method was petition, prayer, and press — respectful representations to the british. by the early 1900s, these methods had yielded almost nothing concrete. no self-governance. no economic relief. no political power. the extremists saw this not as a reason to be more patient, but as proof that gentler methods did not work against a colonial administration. the moderates' failure to move the needle created the political space — and the popular demand — for a harder line. reason 2: the extremists had a strategy the moderates did not — mass mobilisation through religion & culture. the moderates operated largely through newspapers, petitions, and annual inc sessions. their base was the western educated middle class (wemc). the extremists understood that to build real political pressure, you needed the religious masses — and to reach them, you needed to speak in cultural terms they already understood. this is why tilak organised the ganapati festival (1893) and the shivaji festival (1896) in maharashtra. these were not simply religious events. they were platforms for political mobilisation — turning cultural identity into nationalist consciousness. ◆ this was not a new idea in world history. across colonised & occupied nations, cultural nationalism has often been the first step toward political nationalism — particularly when direct political organisation is suppressed or underdeveloped. tilak was doing in the 1890s what many european nationalists had done in the 1820s & 1830s. reason 3: curzon99-05 (1899–1905) made a mass movement possible by making mass anger unavoidable. viceroy curzon99-05 (1899–1905) governed india with a level of arrogance & authoritarianism that managed to alienate even moderate opinion. his administration gave the extremists a ready target — and a ready audience. we will look at his specific measures in detail below, but the summary is simple: his policies concentrated power, tightened control, and communicated to educated indians that their opinions did not matter. that communicated message did more to strengthen the extremists than any pamphlet could. in particular, three reactionary laws passed under curzon — the calcutta municipal corporation amendment act (1899), the indian universities act (1904), and the indian official secrets amendment act (1904) — formed a chain of failures in british governance that directly birthed the extremist response. each law attacked a different pillar of indian public life — local self-governance, education, and the press — and together they proved to politically aware indians that the colonial administration would not reform itself voluntarily. this chain of provocations made extremism not just attractive but, for many, unavoidable. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following defines extremist ideology during the early phase of indian freedom movement? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) obtaining self government by aggressive means in place of petitions and constitutional ways. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — stimulating the production of indigenous articles by giving them preference over imported commodities; (c) ✗ — providing national education according the requirements of the country; (d) ✗ — organising coups against the british empire through military revolt ⚠ alert (prelims 2004): upsc tested this. q) consider the following viceroys of india during the british rule 1. lord curzon 2. lord chelmsford 3. lord hardinge 4. lord irwin which one of the following is the correct chronological order of... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) 1, 3, 2, 4. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — 2, 4, 1, 3; (c) ✗ — 1, 4, 2, 3; (d) ✗ — 2, 3, 1, 4

sections.chapterTitle: The Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement (1905–11)
sections.title: The Swadeshi Movement (Swadeshi05-11) — Context and Causes
sections.norm: the swadeshi movement (swadeshi05-11) — context and causes. curzon99-05 calcutta municipal corporation amendment act 1899 the indian universities act 1904 inc indian official secrets amendment act the act indian official secrets act 2015 upsc 2019 swadeshi curzon. the administration of curzon99-05 (1899–1905) before the swadeshi movement erupted, it was curzon99-05's own measures that set the stage. three laws in particular built the frustration that eventually exploded. the calcutta municipal corporation amendment act, 1899 reduced the number of elected members in municipalities. in one move, it rolled back whatever limited representative participation indians had managed to achieve in local governance. the indian universities act, 1904 brought universities under direct government control. curzon99-05's reasoning was explicit: he believed indian universities were becoming factories of sedition — that is, centres producing politically aware graduates who questioned british authority. his solution was to clamp down rather than to engage. ◆ the link between education & political consciousness was a consistent british anxiety throughout this period. educated indians were the ones writing the petitions, editing the newspapers, running the inc, and now leading the swadeshi movement. this is why education policy was always also colonial control policy. the indian official secrets amendment act, 1904 significantly reduced press freedom. it gave the government the power to censor & confiscate any publication that hurt the interests of the british empire. it made it a criminal offence to communicate any official secret, and defined 'official secret' broadly — as any information relating to affairs of the state or any matter specially notified by the government. the act remained in force until the indian official secrets act, 1923, which was, if anything, even more strict. ⚠ alert (prelims 2015): upsc tested this. q) which one of the following movements has contributed to a split in the indian national congress resulting in the emergence of 'moderates' and 'extremists'? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) swadeshi movement. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — quit india movement; (c) ✗ — non-cooperation movement; (d) ✗ — civil disobedience movement ⚠ alert (prelims 2019): upsc tested this. q) with reference to swadeshi movement, consider the following statements. 1. it contributed to the revival of the indigenous artisan crafts and industries. 2. the national council of education was... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) both 1 and 2. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — only 1; (b) ✗ — only 2; (d) ✗ — neither 1 nor 2 ⚠ alert (prelims 2023): upsc tested this. q) statement-i: 7th aug is national handloom day.statement-ii: swadeshi movement launched on same day in 1905. to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) both correct, ii explains i. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — both correct, ii doesn't explain i; (c) ✗ — i correct, ii incorrect; (d) ✗ — i incorrect, ii correct
