sections.title: Bengal Partition (Announced July 1905 / Effected 16 October 1905)
sections.norm: bengal partition (announced july 1905 / effected 16 october 1905). 1905 1765 1775 3.2) 1801: half of awadh subordinate alliance treaty "ceded provinces." "ceded and conquered provinces" bengal presidency- 1803, they got control of orrisa 1826 assam treaty of yandobo 1826 bengal presidency. 1836 "ceded and conquered provinces” nwp1836 1874 province 1874–1905 bengal presidency = bengal + orissa + bihar + bihar + orissa) 1911 bengal 310) 1936: official british rationale was administrative most populous province in india assam would grow in size own civil services cadre eba cheaper maritime outlet via chittagong port inm bengali bhadralok backbone of organised political activity appease elite muslims hindu cultural nationalism ml1906 2009 upsc 2010 north-western provinces 1836 muslim league 1906. what was the administrative history of bengal before the partition? to understand why the partition of bengal (1905) was so explosive, it helps to see how bengal's administrative boundaries had already been redrawn multiple times by the british — each time for their own administrative or political convenience. 3.1) 1765: the british obtained the diwani of bengal suba (bengal, orissa, bihar). in 1775, they annexed benaras & administered it as part of the bengal presidency. 3.2) 1801: half of awadh was formally ceded to the british in subordinate alliance treaty (treaty of lucknow 1801) and added to the bengal presidency as the "ceded provinces." then the scindhia’s territory conquered in 2nd anglo-maratha war (1803-05) was added to ceded provinces which was now called "ceded and conquered provinces" under bengal presidency. 3.3) bengal presidency- in 1803, they got control of orrisa by defeating bhonsle of nagpur in 2nd anglo-maratha war (while the british held the diwani of "orissa" since 1765, it practically only covered the midnapore region until bhonsle was defeated). 34) 1826: assam was annexed in treaty of yandobo 1826 after the 1st anglo-burma war (1824–26) and added to the bengal presidency. 35) 1836: "ceded and conquered provinces” (the half of awadh ceded to british in 1801 along with maratha territory mentioned above) was separated from the bengal presidency by creating the north west provinces (nwp1836). 36) 1874: assam was carved out & made a separate chief commissioner province (cc province = union territory equivalent — directly under central administration, not a full-fledged lieutenant-governor province). 37) 1874–1905: bengal presidency = bengal + orissa + bihar. assam existed separately as a cc province. 38) 1905: the partition created bengal (= wb + bihar + orissa) and the new province of east bengal & assam (eba = eb + assam). 39) 1911: the partition was annulled. bengal = wb + eb; assam and 'bihar & orissa' became separate. 310) 1936: bihar & orissa were also made full, separate provinces. what was the british justification for partitioning bengal? the official british rationale was administrative. undivided bengal was the most populous province in india & covered a massive area — too large, they argued, to be governed effectively by a single administration. beyond that, the british offered three specific benefits of the new arrangement: 3.10) assam would grow in size and, as part of a proper lieutenant-governor province, would finally get its own civil services cadre — improving administration there. 3.11) assam-bengal railways would come under the unified administration of the new eba province. 3.12) assam's tea gardens would gain a cheaper maritime outlet via chittagong port. what was the real reason? what did indians believe? indians — and not without reason — saw the partition as a divide & rule strategy, designed specifically to weaken the inm in bengal. their case was straightforward: if the real goal were better administration, the logical solution would have been to reorganise bengal on linguistic lines — not religious ones. instead, the partition created two provinces divided along the hindu-muslim demographic fault line. the indian argument was that this was not administrative logic. it was communal engineering. the mechanics of why this weakened the inm specifically need attention. the inm in bengal was led by the bengali bhadralok — upper-caste (uc) hindu educated professionals who were the backbone of organised political activity in the province. the partition ensured that bengalis became a minority in bengal (diluted by bihar & orissa) and hindus became a minority in the new eba. thus the inm's support base would shrink in both provinces simultaneously. it was a tidy design. the second objective was to appease elite muslims — to counter the rising tide of hindu cultural nationalism that had been building since the 1880s. ◆ the hindu cultural nationalism of the 1880s–1890s is worth tracking: bankim chandra chatterjee wrote anandamath (1882), which gave the concept of bharat mata & composed bande mataram. swami dayanand saraswati (died 1883) and swami vivekananda were building cultural nationalism ideologically. the ganapati festival (1893) and shivaji festival (1896) followed. notice how hindu nationalism in the late 1880s & 1890s was rising — and the british were watching this. partitioning bengal in 1905 by appeasing elite muslims was, in part, a response to this trend. eba (east bengal & assam) was therefore designed as a new muslim majority province (mmp). nawab salimullah of dacca & the elite muslim leadership welcomed the partition. the muslim league (ml1906), formed just a year later in 1906, actively supported it. ml1906 also worked with the ulamas — the muslim religious clerical class — who controlled muslim masses, further deepening communal lines & reducing the possibility of a joint hindu-muslim resistance to partition. ⚠ alert (prelims 2009): upsc tested this. q) in the context of the indian freedom struggle, 16th october, 1905 is well-known for which one of the following reasons? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) partition of bengal took effect. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — the formal proclamation of swadeshi movement was made in calcutta town hall; (c) ✗ — dadabhai naoroji declared that the goal of indian national congress was swaraj; (d) ✗ — lokmanya tilak started swadeshi movement in poona ⚠ alert (prelims 2010): upsc tested this. q) what was the immediate cause for the launch of the swadeshi movement? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) the partition of bengal done by lord curzon. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — a sentence of 18 months imprisonment imposed on lokmanya tilak; (c) ✗ — the arrest and deportation of lala lajpat rai and ajit singh; and passing of the punjab colonisation...; (d) ✗ — death sentence pronounced on the chapekar brothers

sections.chapterTitle: The Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement (1905–11)
sections.title: Events During the Swadeshi Movement
sections.norm: events during the swadeshi movement. built over two years spread well beyond bengal risley papers gazette of india july 1905 16 october 1905 1904 upsc 2020 1905 the boycott resolution snb movement's leaders lala lajpat rai (l.l. rai) ajit singh 1906 1882 1998 2002 1889 2008 2016 2018. how did the movement unfold, step by step? the movement did not begin on the day of partition. it built over two years, changed character, and eventually spread well beyond bengal. 1903 — risley papers: the preliminary partition proposals, contained in home secretary h. h. risley’s official letter of 3 december 1903, were published in the gazette of india on 12 december, bringing the scheme into the public domain and provoking widespread opposition. 1903–05 — moderate phase: press & constructive swadeshi. during this period, moderates like surendranath bannerjea (snb) and c.r. das ran a press campaign against partition through newspapers like bengalee, sanjibani, and hitabadi. simultaneously, mobilisation at the village level was attempted through constructive swadeshi — the most notable example being the shantiniketan ashram (1901) of rabindranath tagore. these methods failed to stop the partition, formally announced in july 1905 & effected on 16 october 1905. around this same period, an important intellectual contribution came from bengal. sakharam ganesh deuskar published desher katha (1904), a book that documented the economic exploitation of india under british rule. what made the book significant — and a upsc prelims 2020 point — was that deuskar used the word 'desh' to refer to the entire indian subcontinent, not just bengal. this was a conscious attempt to build a pan-indian economic consciousness against colonial drain, at a time when political organisation was still largely provincial. the book was widely read in bengal & contributed to the intellectual climate in which the swadeshi movement took shape. 7 august 1905 — the boycott resolution. in response to the partition announcement of july 1905, moderates including snb, k.k. mitra, anand mohan bose, and p.c. ray passed a resolution for boycott of british goods & institutions at calcutta town hall. this was significant — the moderates themselves had now crossed a line. the extremists take over the movement. the extremists saw the opportunity & widened both the goal & the method. to the demand for annulment of bengal partition, they added the goal of swaraj — self-rule. and to the method of boycott & swadeshi, they added passive resistance (pr) — a framework that included non-cooperation with british institutions, civil disobedience (cd), and the threat of violent agitation if the government responded with repression. they also took the movement out of bengal & spread it nationally. the movement's leaders were spread across the country: 4.1) bengal: c.r. das & b.c. pal 4.2) bombay: tilak 4.3) delhi: syed haidar raza 4.4) punjab: lala lajpat rai (l.l. rai) and ajit singh 4.5) madras: v.o. chidambaram pillai april 1906 — barisal conference. at the barisal conference, snb & aurobindo ghosh distributed badges of bande mataram. the police repressed the procession before it could even begin. ◆ bande mataram — composed by bankim chandra chatterjee in his novel anandamath (1882) — had by this point become the anthem of the movement. its association with bharat mata, and the visible use of hindu religious symbols, would later become a source of tension with muslim participation. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) assertion [a] partition of bengal in 1905 brought to an end the moderates role in the indian freedom movement. reason [r] the surat session of indian national congress separated the extremists from... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) a is false, but r is true. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — both a and r are true and r is the correct explanation of a; (b) ✗ — both a and r are true, but r is not the correct explanation of a; (c) ✗ — a is true, but r is false ⚠ alert (prelims 2002): upsc tested this. q) with reference to the period of extremist nationalist movement in india with its spirit of swadeshi, which one of the following statements is not correct? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) liakat hussain led the muslim peasants of barisal in their agitations. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — in 1889, the scheme of national education was formulated by satish chandra mukherjee; (c) ✗ — the bengal national college was founded in 1906 with aurobindo as the principal; (d) ✗ — tagore preached the cult of atmasakti, the main plank of which was social and economic regeneration. ⚠ alert (prelims 2008): upsc tested this. q) who among the following gave a systematic critique of the moderate politics of the indian national congress in a series of articles entitled 'new lamps for old'? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) aurobindo ghosh. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — rc dutt; (c) ✗ — syed ahmad khan; (d) ✗ — viraraghavachari ⚠ alert (prelims 2016): upsc tested this. q) the 'swadeshi' and 'boycott' were adopted as methods of struggle for the first time during the to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) agitation against the partition of bengal. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — home rule movement; (c) ✗ — non-cooperation movement; (d) ✗ — visit of the simon commission to india ⚠ alert (prelims 2018): upsc tested this. q) he wrote biographies of mazzini, garibaldi, shivaji and shrikrishna, stayed in america for sometime and was elected to the central assembly. he was to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) lala lajpat rai. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — aurobindo ghosh; (b) ✗ — bipin chandra pal; (d) ✗ — motilal nehru ⚠ alert (prelims 2020): upsc tested this. q) book “desher katha” by sakharam ganesh deuskar:1. warned against hypnotic conquest of mind.2. inspired swadeshi plays.3. ‘desh’ context of bengal. to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) 1 and 2 only. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — 2 and 3 only; (c) ✗ — 1 and 3 only; (d) ✗ — 1, 2 and 3

sections.chapterTitle: The Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement (1905–11)
sections.title: Methods of the Extremists During Swadeshi05-11
sections.norm: methods of the extremists during swadeshi05-11. wider & more confrontational toolkit i) non cooperation (nc), boycott, civil disobedience, and violent agitation ii) constructive work (cw) constructive work mass mobilisation iii) national education indian universities act 1904 ncert iv) swadeshi enterprises boycott real economic teeth swadeshi enterprises tisco 1907 5.2) bengal chemicals & pharmaceuticals (bcpl) by p.c. ray 5.3) bombay swadeshi stores (bss) by tilak & others 1906 pnb 1894 1878 picketing drew in women participants inc 1905 jatras raise awareness & build nationalist sentiment 1893 1896 c.r. das, liaqat hussain, and b.c. pal workers' strikes targeted the supply side swadeshi. the extremists deployed a wider & more confrontational toolkit than the moderates had ever used. their methods are worth examining one by one, because each had its own logic — and its own limitation. i) non cooperation (nc), boycott, civil disobedience, and violent agitation the extremists gave a call for non cooperation (nc) — boycott of british institutions & british goods — alongside the adoption of swadeshi (indian-made goods). to this they added civil disobedience (cd) — the deliberate violation of unjust laws. if the government responded with police repression, violent agitations were to follow. ii) constructive work (cw) constructive work continued alongside confrontation — for awareness-building & mass mobilisation. iii) national education because the british-controlled university system was now tightened further by the indian universities act 1904, the extremists set up parallel educational institutions. the bengal national college was set up with aurobindo as principal. the national council of education (think of it as an ncert equivalent — a national-level body for alternative educational content) and the bengal technical institute were also established. iv) swadeshi enterprises to give boycott real economic teeth, swadeshi enterprises were set up across sectors — soap, matches, chemicals, steel, banking, and shipping. notable examples include: 5.1) tata iron & steel company (tisco) — conceived by jamsetji tata; established by his son dorabji tata in 1907. 5.2) bengal chemicals & pharmaceuticals (bcpl) by p.c. ray 5.3) bombay swadeshi stores (bss) by tilak & others 5.4) swadeshi steam navigation company (1906) — founded by v.o. chidambaram pillai in tuticorin, to challenge british monopoly over coastal shipping. this was swadeshi applied to maritime trade — an indian-owned shipping line competing directly with the british india steam navigation company. chidambaram pillai's effort was among the most ambitious examples of economic nationalism during this period. 5.5) punjab national bank (pnb, 1894) — founded by dyal singh majithia & lala harkishen lal, with significant involvement of lala lajpat rai — along with the lakshmi insurance company (1906), was an attempt to channel indian capital into indian-owned financial institutions. this was a rare example of economic nationalism turning into actual institution-building. given his deep involvement with the arya samaj, l.l. rai heavily promoted the d.a.v. (dayanand anglo-vedic) movement, helping to establish schools & colleges that provided modern education rooted in indian culture. his lahore indian association (1878) led punjab canal colony agitations (1907). v) picketing picketing — physically preventing the sale of british goods at shops & liquor outlets — was a direct-action method that also drew in women participants, making it socially significant beyond its economic impact. vi) samitis / volunteer corps samitis were volunteer bodies set up for mass mobilisation & constructive work. they were also crucial for a specific organisational gap: the inc under the moderates had no ground-level structure. (the inc under moderates had no organisational presence at the ground level — this gap was filled by the samitis) a notable example is the swadesh bandhab samiti (1905) of ashwini kumar dutt in barisal, which conducted constructive work specifically among muslim ryots, contributing to muslim participation — and which organised the barisal conference 1906. vii) jatras (plays & theatre) jatras — traditional theatre performances — were used to raise awareness & build nationalist sentiment among audiences who would not read newspapers. viii) high use of religion for mobilisation religious processions like prabhat pheris (morning worship processions) were organised. the application of tilaks, religious pledges, and kali worship were used to build collective identity & mass participation. in maharashtra, tilak's ganpati festival (started 1893) and shivaji festival (started 1896) were the organisational anchors of this method. ix) workers' strikes c.r. das, liaqat hussain, and b.c. pal led workers' strikes in foreign-owned enterprises. the strategic logic went beyond reducing demand for british goods — it targeted the supply side too, by disrupting the production & distribution machinery that kept those goods moving.

sections.chapterTitle: The Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement (1905–11)
sections.title: Why the Swadeshi Movement Did Not Become a Proper Mass Movement
sections.norm: why the swadeshi movement did not become a proper mass movement. inc low number of swadeshi institutions remained thin relative to the scale of ambition ml1906 mass mobilisation failed boycott failed on its primary economic objective 1907 1908–14 1914 1920 1908 1911 1908–11 1998 upsc muslim league 1906. the extremists attempted the first real mass movement in the history of the inc. they did not fully succeed. the reasons are instructive — and again, they form a pattern that will reappear. 6.1) costly swadeshi goods. not enough swadeshi enterprises existed to meet demand at affordable prices. swadeshi goods were therefore more expensive. this meant low participation by the poor — muslim ryots, lower castes (lc), and blue-collar workers. 6.2) force & social boycott against lc & muslims. when these groups did not participate voluntarily, some student leaders and volunteers resorted to force & social boycott to compel them. this naturally deepened alienation rather than building solidarity. 6.3) low number of swadeshi institutions. the infrastructure of the movement — arbitration courts, educational institutions, enterprises — remained thin relative to the scale of ambition. 6.4) low muslim participation — multiple causes: i) jatras sometimes depicted muslims & the british as collaborators, leading to communal tension & further reducing muslim participation. ii) the muslim league (ml1906), dominated by elite muslims like nawab salimullah of dacca, supported the partition & partnered with ulamas who had control over muslim masses — actively working against the movement's reach. iii) the high use of hindu religious symbolism in the movement's methods — from bande mataram to kali worship — alienated muslims. ◆ notice the recurring problem: upper caste (uc) leadership → low lower caste (lc) participation. this same issue appeared in the criticism of social reformers, in the limitations of the moderates, and now here in the extremists' movement. it is a structural problem of indian social hierarchy intersecting with political organisation. the extremists, despite their more radical politics, did not escape it. 6.5) extremists focused more on capturing the inc than on the mass movement. internal factionalism — the effort to take over the inc organisation — distracted energy & resources from the ground-level mobilisation that a mass movement actually requires. the combined result: overall mass mobilisation failed. british goods imports were not significantly impacted. the boycott failed on its primary economic objective. and then, after the surat split of 1907 — which we will come to shortly — the movement was further wounded. the extremist leadership was repressed & scattered. tilak was deported to mandalay, burma (1908–14). aurobindo retired from active politics. b.c. pal retired temporarily. l.l. rai went abroad from 1914 to 1920, spending time in london & then the united states, where he set up the 'indian home rule league of america.' with the movement leaderless by 1908, the result was predictable. from 1908 to 1911, there was a rise of the revolutionaries — those who had concluded that even the extremists' methods of passive resistance & mass politics had failed. when constitutional & political methods exhaust themselves, more radical tendencies tend to fill the space. ◆ this, again, is the pattern: failure of one approach → more radical successor. the revolutionaries of 1908–11 did not emerge in a vacuum. they emerged because the extremists' mass politics had run out of steam. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) the indian muslims in general, were not attracted to the extremist movement because of the to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) extremists' policy of harping on hindu past. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — influence of the sir sayyid ahmed khan; (b) ✗ — anti - muslim attitude of extremist leaders; (c) ✗ — indifference shown to muslim aspirations

sections.chapterTitle: The Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement (1905–11)
sections.title: The Surat Split (1907)
sections.norm: the surat split (1907). inc 1906 inc session dadabhai naoroji as president four resolutions passed 7.1) swaraj (as the goal) 7.2) boycott (as method) 7.3) swadeshi (as method) 7.4) national education (as method) 1907 1906 allahabad convention (mehta congress) loyal to the raj 1920 1916 1999 upsc 2010 2016. how did the inc fracture — and why did it matter? the tension between moderates & extremists within the inc had been building since the swadeshi movement gave the extremists a platform. the bombay-based moderates opposed extremist methods on principle — they feared that confrontation would provoke british repression & damage the constitutional progress they believed in. the 1906 inc session was held in calcutta, with dadabhai naoroji as president — a figure respected by both factions. the extremists used this session effectively. they got four resolutions passed: 7.1) swaraj (as the goal) 7.2) boycott (as method) 7.3) swadeshi (as method) 7.4) national education (as method) the bengal partition was also separately condemned. tilak also set up an extremist/nationalist party within the incwith the explicit goal of converting the inc from within into an extremist organisation. for 1907, the session was originally planned for poona or nagpur — both extremist strongholds. the moderates shifted the venue to surat, where they had more control. ◆ morley's budget speech of 1906 — as secretary of state for india — had hinted at forthcoming council reforms. this gave the british an opening to deploy their divide & rule (dnr) tactic: the hint of reform motivated moderates to show the british that the inc was cooperative & in favour of truce, while extremists wanted nothing to do with such optics. at surat, the immediate flashpoint was a fight over the presidency of the session — between l.l. rai (extremist) and rash behari ghosh (moderate). l.l. rai eventually withdrew to prevent a split, but the extremists refused to accept any compromise unless the four calcutta resolutions were re-adopted. the session collapsed. shoes were hurled. chairs were broken. the extremists were expelled from the inc. !!!! in 1908, the allahabad convention (mehta congress) — a small meeting of senior inc leaders, as distinct from the annual december session which involves all inc members — declared: 'we are loyal to the raj.' (i.e. to the british)the 1908 inc annual session was held in madras with rash behari ghosh as president. the inc remained divided until 1920, when mahatma gandhi united the moderates & extremists. the extremists did re-enter the inc in 1916 — but re-entry is not the same as agreement on methods. the differences in approach persisted. it was only with gandhi's emergence, and his new method of mass politics, that the two wings found a common platform. ◆ the surat split was the inc's first organisational crisis. both factions wanted swaraj — they split over method: moderates believed in petition, extremists in confrontation. the 1907 split lasted 13 years until 1920, when gandhi reunified the congress. ⚠ alert (prelims 1999): upsc tested this. q) the congress policy of pray and petition ultimately came to an end under the guidance of to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) bal gangadhar tilak. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — aurobindo ghosh; (c) ✗ — lala lajpat rai; (d) ✗ — mahatma gandhi ⚠ alert (prelims 2010): upsc tested this. q) four resolutions were passed at the famous calcutta session of indian national congress in 1906. the question of either retention or of rejection of these four resolutions became the cause of a split... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) annulment of partition of bengal. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — boycott; (c) ✗ — national education; (d) ✗ — swadeshi ⚠ alert (prelims 2016): upsc tested this. q) what was the main reason for the split in the indian national congress at surat in 1907? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) extremists' lack of faith in the capacity of the moderates to negotiate with the british government. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — introduction of communalism into indian politics by lord minto; (c) ✗ — foundation of muslim league; (d) ✗ — aurobindo ghosh's inability to be elected as the president of the indian national congress

sections.chapterTitle: The Extremists and the Swadeshi Movement (1905–11)
sections.title: Impact of the Swadeshi Movement and the Curzonian Administration
sections.norm: impact of the swadeshi movement and the curzonian administration. swadeshi05-11 nationalism that never came down nationalist consciousness did not subside inm wemc from petitions to mass action mass action under extremist leadership negative consequences 1911 curzon99-05 ml1906 1947 muslim league 1906 swadeshi curzon. the swadeshi movement (swadeshi05-11) and the curzonian administration that triggered it reshaped the indian national movement in ways that outlasted the movement itself. the impact is best understood not as a single 'result' but as a set of lasting transformations. 8.1) a nationalism that never came down. the swadeshi period produced a level of nationalist consciousness — particularly in bengal & maharashtra — that did not subside even after the movement ended & its leaders were scattered. the emotional fire was lit, and it stayed lit. 8.2) the foundation of mass politics. for the first time in the inm, the attempt was made to involve not just the wemc but the working class (wc), the masses, and ordinary people. this attempt was incomplete — but it was the first attempt. the working class movement & revolutionary activities both grew from this foundation. 8.3) economic awareness spread. people became aware of the economic dimensions of british rule — drain of wealth, the role of british goods in impoverishing indian industry. boycott became a major tool of the future inm. (to convince poor masses to buy costlier swadeshi goods, extremists had to educate the common man in simple language about drain of wealth — this economic education was itself a lasting contribution) 8.4) nationalistic symbols became prominent. bande mataram became the anthem of the inm. rabindranath tagore's 'amar sonar bangla' (my golden bengal), written in protest against the partition, later became the national anthem of bangladesh. !!!! (recall that political symbols — grand marches, idea of fatherland, songs — had similarly played a major role as +ves of peasant revolts in earlier periods) 8.5) new methods developed for future inm use. the swadeshi period was the laboratory where the tools of later mass politics were tested: passive resistance in the form of non cooperation (nc) and civil disobedience (cd), constructive work (cw), use of theatre & plays (jatras), prabhat pheris (processions after morning worship). all of these were later highly used by mahatma gandhi — he inherited a tested toolkit, not a blank slate. 8.6) from petitions to mass action; from moderate to extremist leadership. the inm shifted away from the petition-and-pray model of the moderates toward mass action under extremist leadership — though the inc itself remained under moderate control until the 1920 nagpur session, when gandhi took over. (not 'extremist control of inc' in 1905 — only inm shifted; inc control passed to gandhi in 1920 nagpur session) however, the swadeshi period also set in motion some negative consequences: 8.7) 1911 — capital shifted to delhi, reducing bengal's dominance in the inm. curzon99-05 got his strategic outcome. (announced at delhi durbar, december 1911, during the coronation of king george v & queen mary as emperor & empress of india) 8.8) birth of ml1906 led to the formal & organised beginning of communal politics in india — a long shadow that stretched all the way to 1947. ⚠ alert (prelims 2014): upsc tested this. q) the partition of bengal made by lord curzon in 1905 lasted until to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) king george v abrogated curzon's act at the royal durbar in delhi, in 1911. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — the i world war when indian troops were needed by the british and the partition was ended; (c) ✗ — gandhiji launched his civil disobedience movement; (d) ✗ — the partition of india, in 1947 when east bengal became east pakistan

sections.chapterTitle: Revolutionary Activities and Repression of Extremists
sections.title: Rise of Revolutionaries
sections.norm: rise of revolutionaries. 1908 1857 individual heroic action assassinating hated british officials. with the swadeshi movement leaderless by 1908 — its prominent extremist leaders arrested, deported, or forced into exile — the question facing politically radicalised indians was simple: if mass politics has failed, what next? the revolutionaries who now came forward had two answers, and they pursued both simultaneously. the long-term goal was to repeat 1857 — to start a civil rebellion & cause disaffection within the army, eroding the british military foundation in india. the immediate method was individual heroic action — assassinating hated british officials to strike fear in british hearts, remove the fear of the british from among indians, and arouse nationalist sentiment. if caught, the courtroom itself became a platform: a public trial was an opportunity for propaganda, and a death sentence was an act of supreme sacrifice that could inspire others. ◆ the logic of individual heroic action — that a single dramatic act can inspire a mass — is not unique to indian history. russian revolutionary groups of the 1870s–80s (the narodniks & later the socialist revolutionary party) used similar 'propaganda by deed' tactics. the indian revolutionaries of this period were aware of these examples & consciously drew from them. veer savarkar's admiration for mazzini is itself evidence of this internationalist revolutionary consciousness.

sections.chapterTitle: Revolutionary Activities and Repression of Extremists
sections.title: Organisational Network of the Revolutionaries
sections.norm: organisational network of the revolutionaries. two types of organisations secret societies inside india centres abroad 2.1) the birth of organised militant nationalism in bengal (1902 onwards) 1902 1906 inc 2.2) the british intelligence response: cid (1903) indian police act of 1861 cid 1903 inm 2.3) inside india: the revolutionary organisations 1904 1899 1830 1870 veer savarkar went to london to study law abhinav bharat in london mazzini charitra 1906 two major revolutionary streams distinct operational philosophies jugantar vs dhaka anushilan samiti dramatic individual action now vs. slow mass organisation for later kept the british 2.4) centres abroad bases outside british jurisdiction veer savarkar abhinav bharat branch lala hardayal united states 1907 ajit singh 2.5) indian home rule society (ihrs), 1905 — revolutionary activity in britain 1905 ihrs secure self-rule in india propaganda in britain modern institution written constitution strong support among indian students close contact with revolutionaries in india india house in london student hostel 1995 upsc 1996 1999 2000. the logic of individual heroic action needed structure. the revolutionaries built two types of organisations: secret societies inside india & centres abroad that could operate with greater freedom, acquire weapons, and produce propaganda. these networks were linked & fed each other. 2.1) the birth of organised militant nationalism in bengal (1902 onwards) the roots of organised militant nationalism in bengal trace back to 1902, when pramathanath mitra (p. mitra)founded the anushilan samiti in calcutta. it began as a body for physical training & character building — but its inner purpose was to cultivate the spirit of armed resistance. by 1906, an impatient radical inner circle had formed within the samiti, driven by the conviction that immediate armed action could not wait. this faction coalesced around a fiercely anti-british newspaper named jugantar — meaning 'new era' — established by barindra kumar ghosh(younger brother of aurobindo ghosh), bhupendranath datta, and abinash bhattacharya. the network of revolutionaries that grew around this publication soon became known independently as the jugantar party. ◆ two brothers — aurobindo & barindra kumar ghosh — represent two different responses to the same colonial reality. aurobindo worked through writing, philosophy, and the inc; barindra went directly into revolutionary conspiracy. after the alipore case broke the jugantar leadership, aurobindo escaped to pondicherry & turned to spiritualism. barindra was transported to the cellular jail. 2.2) the british intelligence response: cid (1903) the british were not passive observers of this rising militant network. recognising the need for a specialised intelligence apparatus beyond the foundational indian police act of 1861, the colonial government formally established the criminal investigation department (cid) in 1903, following the recommendations of the fraser police commission of 1902. this was a professionalized network of spies & informers, embedded within indian society — designed specifically to track, infiltrate, and dismantle political dissent & secret societies. ◆ the cid (1903) was a structural response, not just a legal one — the british did not only pass sedition laws, they built intelligence machinery to identify threats early. this same cid remained central to colonial repression throughout the inm. 2.3) inside india: the revolutionary organisations abhinav bharat (1904) — the savarkar brothers, vinayak (veer savarkar) and ganesh, set up a secret society called mitra mela in 1899 in nasik. it was renamed abhinav bharat — or young india — in 1904 in pune. ◆ the inspiration for renaming was mazzini's 'young italy' — active in the revolts of 1830 in italy to overthrow austrian colonialism in northern italy & to unify the italian kingdoms. italian unification finally succeeded in 1870. mazzini's method was guerrilla warfare. savarkar saw a direct parallel between austrian colonialism over italy & british colonialism over india. when veer savarkar went to london to study law in 1906, he opened a branch of abhinav bharat in london & compiled mazzini charitra 1906 — a translation of mazzini's writings — there. savarkar also authored the indian war of independence 1857 (1909), a book that recast the 1857 revolt as a planned war of national liberation rather than a mere 'mutiny' — the british banned it even before publication, but copies circulated underground & became essential revolutionary reading. anushilan samiti of satish chandra basu operated from calcutta. simultaneously, a massive & distinct offshoot was growing in east bengal: in 1906, the dacca anushilan samiti was founded by pulin behari das, with the backing of p. mitra & bipin chandra pal. the jugantar faction — built around the newspaper of the same name (1906) — was a third major strand. after police repression of the barisal conference in april 1906, yugantar wrote defiantly: "30 crore indians should raise their 60 crore hands to end oppression." its message was unambiguous — force must be stopped by force. over time, these two major revolutionary streams developed completely distinct operational philosophies — and effectively broke apart: two revolutionary models — jugantar vs dhaka anushilan samiti axis jugantar dhaka anushilan samiti (under pulin behari das) structure loose, decentralized confederation of local revolutionary groups rigidly hierarchical, highly centralised, strictly disciplined method 'propaganda of the deed' — immediate, spectacular acts of violence & individual heroic action & martyrdom to awaken the masses long-term military preparation, deep infiltration of society, mass organisation for a future coordinated rebellion focus demonstrate that the british were not invincible through assassination of hated br officials less interested in isolated assassinations; built for slow mass action the contrast maps onto a debate that recurs in revolutionary politics globally: dramatic individual action now vs. slow mass organisation for later. neither fully succeeded — but together they kept the british intelligence machinery stretched & anxious. 2.4) centres abroad but the revolutionaries understood that operating freely required bases outside british jurisdiction. several key figures set up centres abroad: i) veer savarkar — london (abhinav bharat branch, from 1906) ii) lala hardayal — eventually reached the united states, where he became a key organiser iii) shyamji krishna varma — london iv) madame cama — paris. in august 1907, madame bhikaji cama unfurled the first version of the indian national flag at the international socialist congress in stuttgart, germany — a dramatic assertion of indian sovereignty on a global stage, years before any official tricolour was adopted. v) ajit singh — abroad after the swadeshi period also in 1906, an all bengal conference of revolutionary groups was held — a coordination meeting that led to the formation of the weekly newspaper yugantar/jugantar (1906). 2.5) indian home rule society (ihrs), 1905 — revolutionary activity in britain in 1905, shyamji krishna varma founded the indian home rule society (ihrs) in london, with support from bhikaji kama, dadabhai naoroji (dadabhai naoroji was not a revolutionary himself) and s.r. rana. its key features: i) goal: secure self-rule in india & do propaganda in britain. ii) method: all practicable means. iii) only indians could become members. iv) organised as a modern institution — it had a written constitution, modelled on british public institutions of the time. v) found strong support among indian students & other indians in britain. vi) maintained close contact with revolutionaries in india. vii) set up india house in london — a student hostel that actively promoted nationalist views among students. viii) ihrs & shyamji krishna varma's journal the indian sociologist (not socialist in ideology — the name is misleading) laid the foundation of militant indian nationalist movement in britain. after shyamji shifted to paris in 1907, the lead role at india house passed to abhinav bharat mandal / society — veer savarkar's secret nationalist society. ⚠ alert (prelims 1995): upsc tested this. q) the barrah dacoity was the first major venture of the revolutionary terrorists of the freedom movement in to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) east bengal. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — bombay - karnataka; (b) ✗ — punjab; (d) ✗ — the madras presidency ⚠ alert (prelims 1996): upsc tested this. q) match list i with list ii and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists: [list i] a. abhinav bharat society b. anushilan samiti c. ghadar party d. swaraj party [list ii] 1. sri... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) a-4 b-1 c-2 d-3. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — a-4 b-1 c-3 d-2; (b) ✗ — a-1 b-4 c-3 d-2; (c) ✗ — a-2 b-4 c-1 d-3 ⚠ alert (prelims 1999): upsc tested this. q) match list i with list ii and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists.list i (persons)a. shyamji krishna varmab. madam bhikaji camac. annie besantd. aurobindo ghoshlist... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) a-2 b-3 c-4 d-1. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — a-3 b-2 c-1 d-4; (c) ✗ — a-2 b-3 c-1 d-4; (d) ✗ — a-3 b-2 c-4 d-1 ⚠ alert (prelims 1999): upsc tested this. q) abhinava bharat a secret society of revolutionaries was organised by to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) v.d. savarkar. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — khudiram bose; (c) ✗ — prafulla chaki; (d) ✗ — bhagat singh ⚠ alert (prelims 2000): upsc tested this. q) the native state of tripura became involved in the freedom movement early in the 20th century because to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) the bengal revolutionaries took shelter in tripura. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — the kings of tripura were always anti-british; (c) ✗ — the tribes of the state were fiercely freedom loving; (d) ✗ — there were already some groups fighting again the kingship and its protector, the british ⚠ alert (prelims 2000): upsc tested this. q) match list i with
