sections.chapterTitle: Revolutionary Activities and Repression of Extremists
sections.title: Key Revolutionary Actions
sections.norm: key revolutionary actions. organisational network in place series of dramatic events 3.1) 1907 — attempt on the life of the lieutenant governor of bengal 1907 3.2) barrah dacoity, 1908 swadeshi dacoity in dhaka dacca anushilan samiti under pulin behari das 3.3) 1908 muzzafarpur conspiracy case failed attempt on the life of magistrate kingsford threw a bomb at his carriage 1908 muzzafarpur bombing alipore conspiracy case mass arrests aurobindo was defended by c.r. das b.c. pal refused to testify acquittal barindra kumar ghosh principal organiser of the jugantar faction ullaskar dutta pyq 1913–15 upsc b.c. pal was forced to retire 1910 3.5) tilak trial, 1908 kesari tilak condemned the violence defended both men condemn the act, explain the cause charge him with sedition deported to mandalay 1940 3.6) actions credited to abhinav bharat abhinav bharat network two major actions 1909 1899–1905. with the organisational network in place — secret societies inside india, centres abroad — the next phase was action. the revolutionary period produced a series of dramatic events, best understood in sequence: each event triggered a british response, which triggered the next escalation. 3.1) 1907 — attempt on the life of the lieutenant governor of bengal an attempt on the life of the lieutenant governor of bengal in 1907 — it failed. 3.2) barrah dacoity, 1908 a swadeshi dacoity in dhaka, east bengal, carried out by the dacca anushilan samiti under pulin behari das. the residence of the zamindar of barrah was looted — the funds were intended to finance revolutionary activities. ◆ the use of 'dacoity' — armed robbery — to fund revolutionary operations was deliberate. the revolutionaries needed money for weapons, printing, and travel. since they had no wealthy backers, they targeted zamindars & moneylenders who were seen as collaborators of the colonial order. 3.3) 1908 muzzafarpur conspiracy case this was a failed attempt on the life of magistrate kingsford — a particularly hated colonial official. prafulla chaki and khudiram bose threw a bomb at his carriage, but kingsford was not inside. two english women were killed instead. :( chaki shot himself in the mouth with his own revolver to avoid capture. khudiram bose was arrested, tried, and given the death sentence. ◆ khudiram bose was 18 years old when he was executed in 1908. his death made him an instant martyr across bengal. songs were written, his image printed on cloth & sold as mourning wear. the british had intended the execution to deter future revolutionaries — it had the opposite effect. !!!! 3.4) 1908 alipore conspiracy case (also: muraripukur / manicktolla conspiracy case) the muzzafarpur bombing alarmed the british into a broader crackdown. they wanted to go after the masterminds — not just the foot soldiers. this led to the alipore conspiracy case, which involved mass arrests including of aurobindo ghosh from his address on muraripukur road in manicktolla. aurobindo was defended by c.r. das. b.c. pal refused to testify — and without his testimony, aurobindo could not be convicted. on acquittal, aurobindo wrote further anti-british articles but, sensing imminent re-arrest, escaped to pondicherry — then under french control & therefore outside british jurisdiction. there he turned to spiritualism & withdrew permanently from politics. the case did far more damage to the jugantar network. barindra kumar ghosh — aurobindo's younger brother & the principal organiser of the jugantar faction — along with ullaskar dutta & several others were found guilty & sentenced to death. their sentences were later commuted to 'transportation for life' in the cellular jail (kala pani)in the andaman islands. the alipore case heavily decimated the early jugantar leadership — the very faction that had built the most active network of armed revolutionary cells in bengal. ⚠ ghadar pyq trap: barindra kumar ghosh was sentenced & transported to the cellular jail from 1908 onwards. this means he could not have been a participant in the ghadar movement (1913–15) — any upsc option linking him to ghadar is an elimination trap. once transported, he was cut off from all revolutionary activity on the mainland. b.c. pal was forced to retire temporarily from active politics as a result of the case. ◆ 'transportation for life' to the cellular jail was a fate the british considered worse than death — isolation, brutal prison conditions, and permanent removal from the mainland. savarkar too received this sentence in 1910. the andamans became the colonial state's preferred instrument for eliminating revolutionary leadership without creating more martyrs by hanging them publicly. 3.5) tilak trial, 1908 in his newspaper kesari, tilak condemned the violence of prafulla chaki & khudiram bose in the muzzafarpur case — but simultaneously defended both men on a deeper ground: that the british should understand that sustained oppression will produce violence. the article was titled 'arrival of bomb.' this nuanced position — condemn the act, explain the cause — was enough for the colonial government to charge him with sedition. tilak was sentenced to six years' imprisonment & deported to mandalay, burma. his legal defence was conducted by jinnah — an early & significant meeting of two men whose later relationship would define the partition of india. ◆ jinnah defending tilak in 1908. in 1908, jinnah was a young constitutional lawyer with nationalist sympathies — not yet the leader of the muslim league. he took tilak's case on principle. the two men disagreed fundamentally on methods but were, at this point, on the same side of the anti-colonial divide. the distance between this moment & 1940 — when jinnah would demand pakistan — is a measure of how much communal politics transformed in three decades. 3.6) actions credited to abhinav bharat the abhinav bharat network, operating across india & london, was responsible for two major actions: i) 1909, london — madan lal dhingra killed lt. col. william curzon-wyllie (not curzon the viceroy 1899–1905 — curzon-wyllie was a different person, who worked with the secretary of state for india). ii) 1909, nasik conspiracy case — district magistrate jackson was killed by anant laxman kanhere. savarkar had sent pistols to india from london, one of which was used by kanhere. as a consequence, in 1910, savarkar was sentenced to transportation for life — meaning imprisonment in the cellular jail in the andaman islands — in connection with the nasik conspiracy case (1909).

sections.chapterTitle: Revolutionary Activities and Repression of Extremists
sections.title: Result of the Revolutionary Phase
sections.norm: result of the revolutionary phase. repressed by the british impact was not nothing sense of pride & dignity to indians active agents capable of fighting back 1911 inm 1905 1912 eba1905 1874 4.3) delhi conspiracy case, 1912 viceroy hardinge10-16 1910–1916 rash behari bose escaped to japan indian independence league (iil) ina 1943 1905–12 curzon east bengal & assam 1905 hardinge. the revolutionary phase was repressed by the british. but its impact was not nothing. 4.1) the revolutionaries gave back a sense of pride & dignity to indians — the feeling that indians were not passive subjects but active agents capable of fighting back. many contemporaries felt that the morley-minto reforms of 1909were partly a result of british anxiety about the spread of revolutionary activities — a reform offered to buy peace. 4.2) in 1911, bengal partition was annulled & delhi was made the new capital — which ended bengal's dominance in the inm. the shift of capital to delhi was announced at the delhi durbar of december 1911, where king george v & queen mary were coronated as emperor & empress. the annulment of partition was the political concession. the capital shift was the strategic correction — reducing bengal's outsized influence over the national movement. ◆ curzon9905's legacy is contradictory: the partition he imposed was reversed in 1911, and the capital he governed from was shifted away from calcutta. in that narrow administrative sense, the swadeshi agitation succeeded — bengal was reunited. but the larger political design of 1905 — divide hindus & muslims, undercut bengal's dominance, shift capital — was substantially achieved. curzon was successful on the strategic questions. in 1912, the province of 'bihar & orissa' was separated from bengal presidency, and assam was made a full province from 'east bengal & assam' (eba1905). (assam had originally been made a chief commissioner province in 1874) these administrative changes were the post-1911 tidying up of bengal's territorial structure. 4.3) delhi conspiracy case, 1912 when the capital was shifted from calcutta to delhi in 1911, a grand procession was organised in delhi. rash behari bose planned & executed a failed assassination attempt against viceroy hardinge10-16 (1910–1916) in chandni chowk. hardinge was seated on an elephant during the procession. rash behari bose threw a bomb from a balcony — hardinge was wounded but survived. rash behari bose subsequently provided leadership to the ghadar movement (1913–15), escaped to japan in 1915. later, in 1942, he convened conferences in tokyo & bangkok to establish the indian independence league (iil). this league became the supreme political organization for indians living in southeast asia. it was under the political backing & guidance of rash behari bose’s iil that captain mohan singh was able to organize indian prisoners of war (captured by the japanese) into the first indian national army (ina). after arrest of captain mohan singh he took over leadership of ina & due to old age handed over its reign to netaji subhas chandra bose in 1943 who reorganized ina into azad hind fauj. ◆ the through-line from the delhi conspiracy case (1912) to the ina (1943) passes through rash behari bose. the revolutionary generation of 1905–12 did not vanish after repression — several resurfaced in later movements, often in more organised, internationally-connected forms.

sections.chapterTitle: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms
sections.title: Background: Census, Education, and Communal Consciousness
sections.norm: background: census, education, and communal consciousness. 1.1) census and communal consciousness census 1881 first full census of british india census had a deep dnr contribution consciousness of being a homogeneous religious group published reports on education, employment, and poverty religion-wise relative deprivation among muslims 1.4) why western education uptake was low among muslims low representation of muslims lower uptake of western education western education was expensive poor ryots ulamas resisted western education preserve persian rich muslim landlords had low utility hindus benefitted more accepted western education more readily 1.5) british — divide & rule 1871 1.6) the british deployed several specific dnr measures toward muslims: reservation in government jobs for muslims 1905 mmp. 1.1) census and communal consciousness as per census 1881 — the first full census of british india (first attempt was in 1872 but was not completed for all of british india; 1881 was the first full census, conducted every 10 years thereafter: 1881, 1891, 1901...) — muslim population was roughly 20% overall, with majority in punjab & roughly 50% in bengal. 1.2) the census had a deep dnr contribution: it created — and reinforced — a consciousness of being a homogeneous religious group among an otherwise heterogeneous muslim community. before mass enumeration, a poor muslim weaver in bengal & a rich muslim landlord in punjab had very different daily realities. the census told both that they were part of one community with one set of interests — and that hindus & muslims were two separate communities with separate, potentially competing interests. (shia-sunni differences, worker-peasant class differences — all came later; muslim identity was put first by the census logic) 1.3) this was compounded by the fact that the british government published reports on education, employment, and poverty religion-wise. this created a sense of relative deprivation among muslims — the data showed them behind hindus in government jobs, education, and the new middle-class professions. whether the cause was discrimination or other factors, the published comparison reinforced a feeling that hindus were gaining at muslims' expense. ◆ communalism is the organisation of society on the basis of religion & the ideology that every religious group has its own separate interests, which may be mutually exclusive. i.e., that the two communities cannot co-exist happily together, and that meeting one community's interests will necessarily hurt the other's. this is the logic that underpinned the demand for separate electorates & the demand for pakistan. 1.4) why western education uptake was low among muslims the low representation of muslims in new middle-class professions was partly a function of lower uptake of western education. the reasons were structural, not simply a matter of backwardness: i) western education was expensive, and most muslims in bengal were poor ryots who could not afford it. ii) the ulamas — the muslim clerical class — actively resisted western education. their concern was cultural & religious: western curriculum meant exposure to a way of life, family structures, and social values — through western literature — that contradicted islamic teaching & would erode their community control. (*think — literature has stories, values, attitudes, religious beliefs etc that shape way we think) iii) there was a desire to preserve persian — the language of muslim high culture & administration under the mughals — against the encroachment of english & hindi. iv) rich muslim landlords had low utility for middle-class government jobs & therefore low incentive to pursue western education. v) as a consequence, hindus benefitted more from the new middle-class professions created by british administration — because they accepted western education more readily & in greater numbers. 1.5) british — divide & rule w.w. hunter's book indian musalmans (1871) argued that the neglect of muslims — specifically their economic decline since the end of mughal rule — had contributed to the faraizi movement of the 1830s–70s in bengal, and therefore the british should appease muslims for greater political stability. this argument became a justification for the dnr approach of favouring muslim interests against hindu-dominated political formations. 1.6) the british deployed several specific dnr measures toward muslims: i) 1897: reservation in government jobs for muslims. ii) 1905: bengal partition — creating east bengal & assam as a muslim majority province (mmp), appeasing elite muslims & countering rising hindu nationalism.

sections.chapterTitle: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms
sections.title: Muslim WEMC Demands: From Association to Organisation
sections.norm: muslim wemc demands: from association to organisation. 2.1) muslim western-educated elite — path to separate political identity elite muslim political demands special political status 1855 1857 sir syed ahmed khan not a single nation but a summation of qaums 1875 1886 inc. 2.1) muslim western-educated elite — path to separate political identity the british dnr measures opened space for elite muslim political demands. the muslim upper & middle class — those who had accepted western education — began demanding special political status. this demand built gradually through the 19th century: i) mohammadan association (1855) was pro-british & opposed the 1857 revolts — it sought to secure benefits for muslims through loyalty to the british, not through joining the nationalist cause. ii) sir syed ahmed khan (1817–98) was the pivotal figure. he argued that india was not a single nation but a summation of qaums (qaum = community/nation, used in the sense of a distinct ethno-religious group), and that the hindu qaum & the muslim qaum were separate, with separate interests. (this was the early form of the two nation theory) he further argued that the muslim qaum — as the ruling community before the british — deserved special status, and that to claim it, muslims needed western education. hence he set up: ii.i) mohammadan anglo oriental college, 1875 (later aligarh muslim university) — to combine western education with islamic values, building a muslim middle class that could compete for government positions without abandoning core religious identity. ii.ii) mohammadan educational congress, 1886 — set up as a rival to the inc, because sir syed believed the inc was a hindu organisation. he actively discouraged muslim participation in the inc. ◆ sir syed ahmed khan was not a separatist in the full 1940s sense. he still believed in a unity of qaums. but his framing — that muslims are a separate qaum with separate interests — provided the intellectual architecture that later leaders used to build the full two nation theory.

sections.chapterTitle: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms
sections.title: Post-1883: Hindu Revivalism and Muslim Alienation
sections.norm: post-1883: hindu revivalism and muslim alienation. 3.1) hindu cultural nationalism deepens communal distance hindu cultural revivalism alienated muslims shudhhi movement & cow protection movement cow killing riots of 1893 1900 1877 swadeshi05-11 1905-11 swadeshi. 3.1) hindu cultural nationalism deepens communal distance the hindu cultural revivalism of the late 19th & early 20th centuries — shudhhi movement, cow protection movement, swadeshi period's use of hindu religious symbolism — alienated muslims from the congress-led national movement in successive waves. i) shudhhi movement & cow protection movement by arya samaj (1875) became more aggressive after swami dayanand saraswati died in 1883. the result was the cow killing riots of 1893. the inc did not condemn these riots — because its 1886 rule was to take up only political issues. this non-condemnation produced a sharp decline in muslim participation in the inc. ii) hindi-urdu controversy (1880s–1900) in 'north west provinces & awadh' (1877) — led by moderate madan mohan malviya — demanded official language status for hindi (spoken by majority) equivalent to urdu. success came in 1900. but the unintended byproduct was that hindi became associated with hindus & urdu with muslims. (*note — pakistan was linguistically dominated by punjabis & bengalis, but jinnah made urdu the official language for islamic image, not linguistic majority) iii) hindu symbolism during swadeshi05-11 (1905-11) — bande mataram, kali worship, prabhat pheris, ganpati & shivaji festivals — contributed further to muslim alienation from the movement, leading to low participation as already discussed.

sections.chapterTitle: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms
sections.title: The Simla Deputation (1906)
sections.norm: the simla deputation (1906). 4.1) simla deputation: what it demanded aga khan viceroy minto0510 shimla ilc separate electorates in future council reforms 1909 1947 minto. 4.1) simla deputation: what it demanded in 1906, elite muslims led by the aga khan met viceroy minto0510 (1905–1910) in shimla to secure muslim elite interests. their demands were: i) no annulment of bengal partition. ii) since muslims are a separate qaum with separate interests & a minority overall, give reservation proportional to population in the imperial legislative council (ilc), provincial legislative councils (plcs), and government jobs. iii) separate electorates in future council reforms. (separate electorates = only muslims to have the right to vote (r2v) in a seat reserved for a muslim candidate — this structurally promotes two nation theory, because it tells every muslim voter that their representative must be muslim & their interests are separate from hindu interests) ◆ the demand for separate electorates is the hinge of partition history. once you accept that muslims must elect muslim representatives from muslim-only constituencies, you have institutionally accepted the two nation theory. the morley-minto reforms of 1909 granted this demand — and that grant was the legislative seed of 1947.

sections.chapterTitle: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms
sections.title: Formation of All India Muslim League (ML1906)
sections.norm: formation of all india muslim league (ml1906). 1906 green book mohsin-ul-mulk & mohammed ali jauhar 1907–09 ml1906 inc 1920 1908 ameer ali indian councils act 1909 ica1909 2001 upsc muslim league 1906 morley-minto reforms 1909. the all india muslim league was set up by elite muslims in dacca, in december 1906, immediately following the simla deputation. its key features: 5.1) goal: to ensure the british did not go back on the promises made at the simla deputation (1906); to promote muslim interests; and to promote muslim loyalty to the british. 5.2) the constitution — called the green book — was written by mohsin-ul-mulk & mohammed ali jauhar, both of the aligarh movement. 5.3) 1907–09: provincial muslim leagues were set up. ml1906 had functional provincial structures reaching ground-level muslim communities for more than a decade before the inc's pccs became effective mass instruments — this gave communal politics an organisational head start on the ground. [note: provincial congress committees (pccs) had existed since the inc's 1908 constitution but were mapped to british administrative provinces & ran in english — keeping the congress elite. at the 1920 nagpur session, gandhi redrew pcc borders on linguistic lines, letting local congress work happen in the mother tongue & allowing the inc to penetrate the villages.] ⚠ prelims trap: if a statement says "pccs were established for the first time at the 1920 nagpur session" — false. pccs existed formally from the 1908 inc constitution. if it says "pccs were reorganised on linguistic lines at the 1920 nagpur session" — true. the distinction matters. 5.4) 1908: london branch of ml1906 set up under the presidency of ameer ali. this london branch influenced the indian councils act 1909 (ica1909) — which laid the foundation of partition politics by introducing separate electorates for muslims in the reformed councils. ⚠ alert (prelims 2001): upsc tested this. q) a london branch of the all india muslim league was published in 1908 under the presidency of to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) ameer ali. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — aga khan; (c) ✗ — liaquat ali khan; (d) ✗ — ma jinnah

sections.chapterTitle: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms
sections.title: The Long Thread: From ML1906 to 1947
sections.norm: the long thread: from ml1906 to 1947. ml1906 ica1909 muslim league 1906 morley-minto reforms 1909. ml1906 was set up in 1906 to preserve bengal partition & secure separate electorates. separate electorates were granted by ica1909 (morley-minto reforms). the inc's pccs only became effective mass instruments in 1920 — ml had functional provincial structures for 13 years before inc caught up. the formal, organised beginning of communal politics that ml1906 represented never reversed — it deepened decade by decade until 1947. this is why the birth of ml1906 is listed as one of the negative impacts of the swadeshi period: it was not simply a reaction to swadeshi, but the swadeshi period's hindu symbolism & the british dnr response together created the conditions for it.

sections.chapterTitle: Rise of Organised Muslim Politics and Morley-Minto Reforms
sections.title: Morley-Minto Reforms / Indian Councils Act, 1909 (ICA1909)
sections.norm: morley-minto reforms / indian councils act, 1909 (ica1909). minto05-10 indian councils act ica1909 partition of bengal in 1905 swadeshi movement sharper, angrier direction morley was a liberal giving indians more participation inc 1906 1907 4.1) nature of government introduced mla 4.2) the viceroy's executive council (vec) vec cic ica1892 4.3) the imperial legislative council (ilc) — composition ilc was expanded to 69 members 1874 ilc 60 additional members 27 were elected & 33 were nominated officer majority was maintained 4.4) provincial legislative councils (plcs) — composition plc 4.5) indians in the executive — a first indians were inducted into executive branches 4.6) the muslim separate electorate — communal appeasement 1889 only muslims could vote in muslim reserved seats right to vote in general (unreserved) seats reservation with joint electorates reservation with separate electorates income threshold was set lower for muslims mix of direct & indirect elections muslim reserved seats → 1st direct elections (but only for muslim seats) 4.7) powers of the legislature supplementary questions only the member who asked the original question initiate & pass resolutions recommendatory only 4.8) powers of the executive reject/disqualify any candidate politically dangerous 1892 1909 executive remained non-responsible to the legislature 5.1) the shortest-lived reform most short-lived of all the council reforms ica1861 goi act 1919 goi act 1935 5.2) the long shadow: foundation of partition 1947 5.3) benevolent despotism — again 1st time proper indirect elections direct elections (muslim seats only) vote on individual items, not whole budget supplementary qs allowed limited self-government benevolent despotism 10 years — shortest of all council reforms foundation of partition father of communal electorate indian councils act of 1909 indian councils act of 1861 indian councils act of 1892 india act of 1919 2002 upsc morley-minto reforms 1909 indian councils act 1892 indian councils act 1861 minto. 1. names behind the reform two men gave this reform its name. john morley was the secretary of state for india, sitting in london. lord minto (1905–1910), or minto05-10 as we will call him, was the viceroy & governor-general in india. together, their names became attached to what is formally called the indian councils act, 1909 (ica1909). 2. context: why this reform happened the context matters. india in 1905 was not quiet. the partition of bengal in 1905 had set off the swadeshi movement (1905–11), which pushed indian politics in a sharper, angrier direction. the period 1905–1908 saw the rise of extremist politics within the inc, and from 1908 onward, revolutionary activities became a real & growing force that worried the british. the british response to this political storm had two tracks — repression & reform — and they ran simultaneously. ica1909 was the reform track. but reform, in british hands, always came packaged with a political strategy. there was also a personal dimension. morley was a liberal in the british political tradition — meaning less authoritarian than many of his predecessors & open to giving indians more participation in governance. his own disposition, combined with political necessity, shaped the reform. 3. the divide & rule (dnr) strategy behind ica1909 the british wanted to split the indian political movement — specifically, to separate the moderates from the extremists within the inc. the strategy played out in two moves. 3.1) move 1 — split the inc. in 1906, morley gave a speech in the british parliament during the debate on india's budget & hinted strongly at upcoming council reforms. the message landed exactly as intended. moderate leaders began to worry that extremist agitation would harden british opinion & kill the chances of reform. this fault line widened until the surat split of 1907, where the extremists were expelled from the inc. with the extremists now outside the tent, the british moved to repress them directly. 3.2) move 2 — divide hindus & muslims. the vehicle for this was the introduction of separate electorates for muslims — a demand formally placed before minto05-10 by a delegation of muslim elites at the shimla deputation of 1906. (the shimla deputation of 1906: a group of muslim leaders met minto05-10 & asked not just for reserved seats, but for a system where only muslims could vote for muslim representatives. the british were happy to oblige — it suited their dnr strategy perfectly.) 4. provisions of ica1909 4.1) nature of government introduced i) morley stated explicitly — "there is no intent of responsible govt in india via ica1909." (fully responsible government means every minister must first be an elected member of the legislature — the executive is the child of parliament, and a child is always accountable to its mother. i.e., no minister had to be mp/mla first. ica1909 gave nothing of the sort.) ii) what ica1909 did introduce was representative government, also called limited self-government — it simply means people get to elect representatives to sit in a council & talk/advise i.e. meaning some partnership in domestic affairs, but not self-rule, not self government, not responsible government. ◆ this had been the goal of the inc until 1906. from the 1906 calcutta session onward, the inc's goal had shifted to swaraj. so even by the moderates' own older standard, this reform arrived too late. it was the second failure of the moderate approach. :( 4.2) the viceroy's executive council (vec) i) structure of vec remained: gg + commander-in-chief (cic) + 6 ordinary members — same as under ica1892. 4.3) the imperial legislative council (ilc) — composition i) the ilc was expanded to 69 members in total (9 + 60), structured as follows: a) 8 ex-officio members — drawn from the vec (gg + cic + 6 ordinary members, since 1874) b) 1 additional ex-officio member — the rotating governor or lieutenant-governor of the province where the ilc session was being held (so the 9th ex-officio slot changed with location of session) c) 60 additional members — of whom 27 were elected & 33 were nominated (28 officials + 5 non-officials) ii) result: at the centre, officer majority was maintained. officers = 9 ex-officio + 28 nominated officials = 37. non-officers = 27 elected + 5 nominated non-officials = 32. the british were not giving up control at the top. :( iii) the word 'election' was used officially for the first time in ica1909. proper indirect elections were introduced. the taxpayers & rent payers who met threshold criteria elected local bodies elected an electoral college from among themselves. this electoral college elected members of plcs who elected members of ilc. 4.4) provincial legislative councils (plcs) — composition i) for the first time, non-official majority was introduced — but only in the plcs, not in the ilc. however, most non-official members were nominated, not elected. (nominated non-officials are chosen by the government, not by the people. it is the difference between a government selecting a friendly face & the people actually electing their representative.) ii) bengal exception: bengal plc got an elected majority — the first province to have this. but 4 of those elected seats were reserved for european businesses. 4.5) indians in the executive — a first i) for the first time, indians were inducted into executive branches. ii) one indian inducted into the vec — satyendra prasanna sinha (s.p. sinha), appointed as law member. this was the first indian in the viceroy's executive council. (an indian, as minister — that was new.) iii) two indians had already been appointed to the secretary of state's india council in london in august 1907 — k.g. gupta & syed hussain bilgrami. this was a precursor action, not a provision of ica1909 itself, but it led to indian presence in the london administration for the first time. 4.6) the muslim separate electorate — communal appeasement i) for the first time, separate electorates for muslims were introduced — in the ilc, plcs, and local bodies. ii) in the ilc, 8 of the 27 elected seats were reserved for muslims — approximately 30% of elected seats. iii) muslim population in india was approximately 20%. the inc's own 1889 minority clause had asked for minority reservation proportional to population — i.e., 20% for muslims. the extra 10% beyond population share was pure appeasement politics. iv) due to separate electorates, only muslims could vote in muslim reserved seats. however, muslims also had the right to vote in general (unreserved) seats — they were not excluded from unreserved constituencies. this meant muslims effectively had a double advantage: they could influence both their own reserved seats & the unreserved seats. (compare with today's india: reservation exists for scheduled castes (scs) in parliament & state legislatures, but with joint electorates — meaning non-sc voters also vote in sc-reserved seats. what ica1909 gave muslims was institutionally far more separatist.) v) the conceptual difference is crucial: reservation with joint electorates = candidate of the people, for the people, by a community. reservation with separate electorates = candidate of a group, for a group, by a group. country = sum of constituencies — thus today it's our constituencies & tomorrow it's our pakistan. vi) right to vote (r2vote) was linked to income criteria. the income threshold was set lower for muslims than for other communities — making it easier for muslims to qualify. vii) the system was a mix of direct & indirect elections: unreserved seats → 1st proper indirect elections. muslim reserved seats → 1st direct elections (but only for muslim seats) (compare: ica1892 had used the word 'selection' — a fake indirect election where bodies nominated rather than elected.) 4.7) powers of the legislature i) members could now vote on individual items in the budget (bd) — but not on the budget as a whole. voting to reject the entire budget would have amounted to a no confidence motion, which the british were not about to allow. (compare: ica1892 had allowed discussion of the bd but no voting at all.) ii) members could now ask supplementary questions — but with a caveat: only the member who asked the original question could ask the supplementary. (compare: ica1892 had not allowed supplementary questions at all.) iii) members could initiate & pass resolutions — but the government was under no obligation to follow them. resolutions were recommendatory only. (compare: ica1892 had not allowed the opposition to move resolutions, and had not allowed voting on government resolutions.) 4.8) powers of the executive i) the government retained the power to reject/disqualify any candidate it considered politically dangerous (*nationalists). (in 1892, the british had the power of selection — choosing who could stand. by 1909, they had the power of rejection — removing those they didn't want. either way, nationalist leaders could be kept out of the councils.) ii) the executive remained non-responsible to the legislature. the viceroy's powers continued as before. this was not even remotely close to the position of a ceremonial president in a democracy. 5. impact of ica1909 was ica1909 a success? no — and by almost every measure, it failed. 5.1) the shortest-lived reform ica1909 is the most short-lived of all the council reforms. the lifespan tells its own story: ◆ ica1861 → 30 years | ica1892 → 17 years | ica1909 → 10 years | goi act 1919 → 16 years | goi act 1935 → 15 years | constitution of india 1950 it satisfied nobody. the moderates wanted real legislative power — what they got was still toothless. the inc's goal since 1906 was swaraj, and ica1909 was nowhere near it. the extremists had never cared for council reforms. and the muslims had been given separate electorates — which planted its own long-term disaster. 5.2) the long shadow: foundation of partition the most consequential impact of ica1909 was not what it gave — but what it planted. separate electorates for muslims, introduced here for the first time in the ilc, plcs, and local bodies, laid the direct foundation for the partition of india in 1947. when you tell a community that they must vote separately, you are telling them they are separate. over decades, this institutional separation hardened into political reality. (minto05-10 became known as the "father of communal electorate" — a title history has not handed down with pride.) 5.3) benevolent despotism — again since there was no responsible government, ica1909 produced what we can call benevolent despotism. "benevolent" because ica1909 was more democratic than ica1892 — more participation, more discussion rights, more elections. "despotism" because real power remained entirely with the british executive, answerable to nobody in india. ◆ we saw this same phrase when analysing ica1861 — despotism controlled from home was the core feature then. nearly five decades later, the core had not changed. the packaging had become slightly friendlier, but the structure of power was the same. 6. ica 1909 — summary card - key names: morley (sos, liberal), minto05-10 (viceroy) — morley-minto reforms - ilc size: 69 members (8 ex-officio + 1 rotating + 27 elected + 33 nominated) - official majority: yes in ilc (37 vs 32); 1st time non-official majority in plcs - elections: 1st time proper indirect elections (unreserved seats); direct elections (muslim seats only) - separate electorates: 8/27 muslim seats in ilc; only muslims vote in muslim seats; muslims could also vote in unreserved seats; lower income threshold for muslims - indians in executive: s.p. sinha (vec — under ica1909), k.g. gupta & bilgrami (india council of sos, london — appointed august 1907, precursor action) - budget: vote on individual items, not whole budget - questions: supplementary qs allowed (original questioner only) - resolutions: allowed but non-binding - nature of govt: limited self-government — benevolent despotism - lifespan: 10 years — shortest of all council reforms - legacy: foundation of partition; father of communal electorate (minto) ⚠ alert (prelims 1999): upsc tested this. q) the most short lived of all of britain's constitutional experiments in india was the to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) indian councils act of 1909. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — indian councils act of 1861; (b) ✗ — indian councils act of 1892; (d) ✗ — government of india act of 1919 ⚠ alert (prelims 2002): upsc tested this. q) with reference to the indian freedom struggle, which one of the following statements is not correct? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) the all-india muslim league which was formed in 1906 vehemently opposed the partition of bengal and separate electorates. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — hakim ajmal khan was one of the leaders to start a nationalist and militant ahrar movement; (b) ✗ — when the indian national congress was formed, sayyid ahmad khan opposed it; (d) ✗ — maulana barakatullah and maulana obeidullah sindhi were among those who formed a provisional government.

sections.title: The Ghadar Movement
sections.norm: the ghadar movement. ghadar movement punjabi nris & bengal revolutionaries secular republic of india 1857. 1.1) the ghadar movement was a revolutionary attempt by punjabi nris & bengal revolutionaries to overthrow british rule & establish a secular republic of india i.e. purna swaraj. 1.2) its method: first, a press campaign overseas; then, physically return to india to repeat a 1857-style revolt —i.e. causing disaffection in the army + a civil rebellion. (two-stage plan: stage one — build the fire abroad through narrative; stage two — light it inside india through arms & soldiers.)

sections.title: Drivers of the Ghadar Movement
sections.norm: drivers of the ghadar movement. inspiration from the swadeshi movement 1912 viceroy hardinge10-16 british policy of restricting indian migration 1908 treaty of paris 1907 hardinge. reason 1 — inspiration from the swadeshi movement 2.1) ghadar activists had been directly inspired by the swadeshi movement, particularly its revolutionary strand & especially the delhi conspiracy case 1912 where viceroy hardinge10-16 was targeted. reason 2 — british policy of restricting indian migration 2.2) indians had migrated to canada & the us for land & employment. many were ex-soldiers who had served the very british empire that was now shutting doors on them. british feared indians would be exposed to ideas of liberty, democracy & socialism. i) canada: restricted indian entry since 1908 — only those who made a direct journey from india allowed to enter canada. ii) usa: indians faced racism & were legally barred from buying land. (1783 treaty of paris between us & britain established perpetual friendship hence us respected the british interests) iii) the irony: same british government was sending indians as plantation labourers to fiji in the south pacific ocean. tarak nath das highlighted this in free hindustan (1907) from vancouver — britain sends indians to work on plantations but bars their entry into north america.

sections.title: Press Campaign Builds Narrative & Awareness
sections.norm: press campaign builds narrative & awareness. 1907 1909 1913 hardinge10-16 1910–16 1912 farmers, labourers, students, and ex-soldiers mostly punjabis 3.6) the word "ghadar" means revolt/mutiny — a deliberate invocation of 1857. 1998 upsc hardinge. 3.1) 1907 — tarak nath das, free hindustan, vancouver — exposed the plantation-versus-migration irony. 3.2) 1909— g.d. kumar, swadesh sevak (gurmukhi weekly), canada — directly asked indian troops to revolt. 3.3) 1913 — ghadar party set up by nris in us. sohan singh bhakna = 1st president. it’s headquarters in san francisco was called yugantar ashram (notice same terminology as of secret society of bengal) 3.4) 1913 — lala hardayal, professor of sanskrit & indian philosophy in san francisco, set up the weekly "the ghadr". had already praised the attack on hardinge10-16 (viceroy from 1910–16) in delhi conspiracy case 1912. 3.5) the party drew members from indian immigrants — farmers, labourers, students, and ex-soldiers — mostly punjabis. 3.6) the word "ghadar" means revolt/mutiny — a deliberate invocation of 1857. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) who was the leader of the ghadar party? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) lala hardayal. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — bhagat singh; (c) ✗ — bal gangadhar tilak; (d) ✗ — v.d. savarkar

sections.title: Lala Hardayal, Bakunin & the Anarchist Method
sections.norm: lala hardayal, bakunin & the anarchist method. 1912 1814–1876 4.3) the key anarchist concept for ghadar was "propaganda of the deed." viceroy hardinge10-16 smuggle arms, cause army disaffection, and trigger civil rebellion propaganda of the deed 4.4) the rank-and-file ghadarites were a different kind of person: punjabi immigrant labourers, peasants & ex-soldiers anti-colonial nationalism racial discrimination in north america egalitarian traditions of the sikh faith gave it a method european anarchist strategy 1917 1916 hardinge. 4.1) in 1912 — a year before the ghadar party was formally set up — hardayal established the bakunin institute in california, describing it as a "monastery of anarchism." 4.2) michael bakunin (1814–1876) was a russian thinker & founding figure of anarchism. his core argument: the state — all states, not just colonial ones — is an instrument of oppression. don't petition it, don't reform it — destroy it. and this destruction was not a reluctant last resort. for bakunin it was a creative act — demolish the old structure completely so a truly democratic system can be built (link stateless society of karl marx) 4.3) the key anarchist concept for ghadar was "propaganda of the deed." i) idea: specific political actions — including violence & armed mutiny — are more powerful than any speech or pamphlet in awakening the masses. words educate. acts ignite. the delhi conspiracy case 1912 — attempt to assassinate the viceroy hardinge10-16 publicly in the capital — was exactly this kind of act. ii) when ghadarites later planned to smuggle arms, cause army disaffection, and trigger civil rebellion simultaneously — that entire plan was propaganda of the deed in action. 4.4) the rank-and-file ghadarites were a different kind of person: i) mostly punjabi immigrant labourers, peasants & ex-soldiers. ii) driven by fierce anti-colonial nationalism, raw anger at racial discrimination in north america, and the egalitarian traditions of the sikh faith. 4.5) hardayal's unique role: he took this burning ground-level anger & gave it a method. he married european anarchist strategy to their immediate grievances. the result — a movement combining intellectual radicalism with mass fury. why it worried the british so much. (this combination — western-educated intellectual provides ideological framework, workers & ex-soldiers provide the muscle — recurs in the russian revolution 1917 and the irish easter rising 1916.)

sections.title: The Ghadr Newspaper — Propaganda of the Deed in Print
sections.norm: the ghadr newspaper — propaganda of the deed in print. 5.1) the ghadr newspaper was the most visible product of this method. every front page carried "angrezi raj ka kachcha chithha" — an exposé of british imperialism. it: summarised all inm demands & grievances indian war of independence 1909 1857 1906 urdu, punjabi, hindi, and sometimes english smuggled into india soldiers & peasants in punjab. 5.1) the ghadr newspaper was the most visible product of this method. every front page carried "angrezi raj ka kachcha chithha" — an exposé of british imperialism. it: i) summarised all inm demands & grievances so far. ii) published veer savarkar's indian war of independence 1909 in parts. iii) carried poems titled ghadr di goonj promoting patriotism & unity of all religions. (consciously echoed 1857 hindu-muslim unity.) iv) criticised the loyalist role of punjabis in 1857. (in 1857, punjabis had helped the british suppress the revolt. message= do penance, improve the past mistake) v) final call: "31 crore indians should rise against 1.2 lakh british & repeat 1857 revolt." (yugantar had given a similar call post-barisal conference repression 1906.) the masthead of the paper carried the date of the 1857 revolt — reinforcing its inspiration. 5.2) the newspaper was published in urdu, punjabi, hindi, and sometimes english. 5.3) it was smuggled into india & distributed among soldiers & peasants in punjab.

sections.title: The Komagata Maru Incident (1914)
sections.norm: the komagata maru incident (1914). turbocharged their anger unbroken direct journey from india 1914 6.4) the timeline: radicalised many punjabis humiliated both abroad & at home 2005 upsc. 6.1) before the ghadarites could act inside india, this incident turbocharged their anger. 6.2) canada rule: only indians making an unbroken direct journey from india could enter. 6.3) baba gurdit singh chartered a japanese ship called komagata maru from hong kong in 1914 to challenge canada's racist immigration laws. the ship carried 376 passengers — mostly punjabi sikhs — and sailed from hong kong to vancouver, canada. 6.4) the timeline: i) april 1914 — the ship departed hong kong. ii) may 1914 — the ship arrived in vancouver → shore committee set up to fight for passengers' rights → british refused. the canadian authorities refused to let the passengers disembark. a two-month standoff began. iii) july 1914 — the ship was forced out of canadian waters & began its journey back to india. iv) september 1914 — the ship arrived at budge budge near calcutta, where the british tried to forcibly transport the passengers to punjab by a special train. 6.5) the passengers resisted. in the budge budge riot (september 1914), police opened fire, killing around 20 passengers. 6.6) the incident radicalised many punjabis & fed directly into ghadar recruitment — it proved that indians were humiliated both abroad & at home. (the "direct journey" rule was a legal mechanism designed to keep indians out of canada — enforced by a country that simultaneously called indians- british subjects.) ⚠ alert (prelims 2005): upsc tested this. q) what was komagata maru? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) a navalship on voyage to canada. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — a political party based in taiwan; (b) ✗ — peasant communist leader of china; (d) ✗ — a chinese villager where mao tse tung began his long march

sections.title: Bagha Jatin — The Call for Sacrifice
sections.norm: bagha jatin — the call for sacrifice. jatindranath mukherjee bagha jatin (jatin the tiger) 1906 amra morbo, jagat jagbe we shall die to awaken the nation. 7.1) while hardayal provided the ideological framework from abroad, inside bengal it was revolutionary jatindranath mukherjee — universally known as bagha jatin (jatin the tiger) — who reorganised the shattered revolutionary network on the ground. 7.2) unified several disparate jugantar factions across bengal. (jugantar party 1906 was set up by b.k. ghosh, younger brother of aurobindo ghosh.) 7.3) his rallying cry: "amra morbo, jagat jagbe" — "we shall die to awaken the nation."

sections.title: WWI 1914–19: The Opportunity Arrives
sections.norm: ww1 1914–19: the opportunity arrives. 1914 komagata maru highly dangerous enemy operatives britain was stretched on multiple fronts ghadarites saw their opportunity ww1 . 8.1) ww1 began on july 28, 1914, when austria-hungary declared war on serbia. within a week, germany, russia, france, and britain had all formally entered the war. 8.2) because ww1 broke out in july/august while the komagata maru was sailing back across the pacific, the british authorities in india treated the returning passengers as highly dangerous enemy operatives when they landed in september under wartime conditions. 8.3) britain was stretched on multiple fronts. ghadarites saw their opportunity.

sections.title: Rodda & Co. Arms Heist (August 1914)
sections.norm: rodda & co. arms heist (august 1914). greatest daylight robbery r.b. rodda & co. british-owned gunsmith & arms dealer atmonnati samiti & mukti sangha planned the heist 9.4) insider: shrish chandra mitra, a trusted rodda employee. 1914 not a single shot was fired shrish mitra 202 wooden crates of arms 46,000 battle of balasore 1915. 9.1) the colonial statesman newspaper called it the "greatest daylight robbery" in the history of british india. 9.2) target: r.b. rodda & co. (calcutta) — a prestigious british-owned gunsmith & arms dealer which was primary supplier of firearms to british officials, military & wealthy elites. 9.3) revolutionary groups — atmonnati samiti & mukti sangha (affiliated with bagha jatin's jugantar network) — planned the heist. 9.4) insider: shrish chandra mitra, a trusted rodda employee. 9.5) august 1914: rodda received a major restricted german firearms shipment at calcutta customs house. shrish mitra was tasked with transporting it to the rodda warehouse. 9.6) not a single shot was fired. shrish mitra went to customs house with 7 bullock carts to collect 202 wooden crates of arms. revolutionary haridas datta disguised himself as an upcountry bullock cart driver — took control of the 7th cart. first 6 carts reached the rodda warehouse. shrish mitra quietly redirected the 7th cart into the narrow lanes of the malanga area — straight into a revolutionary safehouse. 9.7) the stolen arsenal from that single cart: 50 mauser c96 semi-automatic pistols — the famous "broomhandle" mauser & 46,000 rounds of 7.63mm ammunition. (why did the mauser matter? the mauser c96 came with a hollow wooden holster that attached to the grip, instantly converting the pistol into a short-barrelled carbine rifle — giving unprecedented rapid-fire capability & range. in the hands of five revolutionaries, it could pin down a police contingent.) 9.8) shrish mitra fled calcutta immediately — never captured. stolen mausers quickly distributed across the jugantar network. these exact pistols were used in almost every major political assassination & armed robbery in bengal over the next decade. and most famously — they were the weapons at battle of balasore (1915).

sections.title: Three Plots: Global Dimensions of the Ghadar Conspiracy
sections.norm: three plots: global dimensions of the ghadar conspiracy. san francisco (americas) to berlin (europe) to bengal to punjab (south asia) hindu-german conspiracy (the zimmermann plan) german foreign office three interconnected operational plots 10.1) plot 1 — rb bose’s planned punjab mutiny (feb 1915) plan: sepoy mutiny in punjab key leader: rash behari bose outcome: february 21, 1915 first lahore conspiracy trials 10.2) plot 2 — jugantar’s pacific arms plot (apr–jul 1915) 30,000 rifles & ammunition strategy: ss maverick jugantar cadres annie larsen and ss maverick 10.3) plot 3 — jugantar’s christmas day plot / bengal plot (dec 1915) uprising in calcutta on christmas day, 1915 bay of bengal or the sundarbans jatindranath mukherjee (bagha jatin) police act of 1861 international double agents indian cid 10.4) the martyr — bagha jatin 1915 battle of chasakhand battle of balasore bagha jatin & 4 other revolutionaries defensive military position chasakhand mauser c96 pistols five men pinned down a full police force bagha jatin died in hospital he kept his word ended the christmas day plot ww1 . the ghadar movement was a massive global conspiracy spanning across continents — san francisco (americas) to berlin (europe) to bengal to punjab (south asia). it was largely driven by the overarching hindu-german conspiracy (the zimmermann plan) — a ww1 strategy where the german foreign office sought to destabilize british india by funding & arming indian revolutionaries. this global strategy was executed through three interconnected operational plots: 10.1) plot 1 — rb bose’s planned punjab mutiny (feb 1915) plan: this was the primary ghadarite strategy. thousands of ghadarite nris returned to india from north america to trigger a massive sepoy mutiny in punjab & ignite civil rebellion. key leader: rash behari bose operated in lahore to establish contact with the sepoys. outcome: the mutiny was scheduled for february 21, 1915, but british intelligence deeply infiltrated the movement. the plot was crushed pre-emptively before it could begin, leading to the first lahore conspiracy trials. 10.2) plot 2 — jugantar’s pacific arms plot (apr–jul 1915) plan: germany financed a massive arms-smuggling operation to ship 30,000 rifles & ammunition from the united states to the eastern coast of india. strategy: the weapons were to be delivered via the ship ss maverick to jugantar cadres to trigger a coordinated, pan-indian military mutiny. outcome: the ships involved (including the annie larsen and ss maverick) were intercepted by us & british authorities, & the arsenal never reached the indian coast. 10.3) plot 3 — jugantar’s christmas day plot / bengal plot (dec 1915) plan: with the punjab mutiny crushed and the pacific arms intercepted, the focus shifted entirely to bengal. revolutionaries planned a massive uprising in calcutta on christmas day, 1915, expecting a separate delivery of german arms to land in the bay of bengal or the sundarbans. key leader: jatindranath mukherjee (bagha jatin) masterminded the indian side of the operation. outcome: british intelligence — strengthened significantly since the police act of 1861 — cracked the communication codes. using international double agents and the indian cid, the british intercepted the network and fatally crushed the final leg of the hindu-german conspiracy. 10.4) the martyr — bagha jatin 10.4.1) police forces tracked & cornered bagha jatin & a handful of followers near the banks of the burhabalanga river in balasore, odisha, in september 1915. iv) the five revolutionaries: bagha jatin, chittapriya ray chaudhuri, manoranjan sengupta, niren dasgupta & jyotish pal. v) rather than surrender, they fought. 10.4.2) "battle" of balasore / battle of chasakhand/ buribalam (september 1915) — (indian nationalist historiography calls it the "battle of balasore" or "battle of chasakhand" because of its immense symbolic weight. the reality of the scale:) i) numbers: bagha jatin & 4 other revolutionaries vs. [a heavily armed contingent of british colonial police + mobilised local villagers.] ii) duration: ~75 minutes. iii) tactic: instead of running, jatin & his men took up a defensive military position behind a termite mound & a raised embankment in a muddy paddy field at chasakhand. iv) why it felt like a battle: they were armed with the stolen rodda mauser c96 pistols — high-grade semi-automatic weapons whose effective range rivalled police rifles. five men pinned down a full police force in a trench-warfare-style standoff — until they literally ran out of ammunition. v) severely wounded in the crossfire, bagha jatin died in hospital the following day. "amra morbo, jagat jagbe." he kept his word. vi) this effectively ended the christmas day plot before the plan could materialise

sections.title: Failure & Aftermath of the Ghadar Movement
sections.norm: failure & aftermath of the ghadar movement. 11.1) why the movement failed british intelligence policing poor response from sepoys 1857 udasi sikh mahants 1914 1915 british pre-emptive strikes march 1915 (emergency): defence of india act rowlatt acts anarchical & revolutionary crimes act 1919 april–september first lahore conspiracy case 11.2) what the movement achieved lost a whole generation secular republic increased nationalism kartar singh sarabha first organised attempt to use the indian diaspora for armed revolution worked together without communal friction kisan sabhas communist movement akali movement global struggle san francisco to tokyo to berlin upsc hra hsra 1925 inm the battle ghadar movement timeline 2005 2014 2022 ww1 . 11.1) why the movement failed 11.1.1) strong british intelligence network & effective policing of the seas. 11.1.2) rb bose's efforts to mobilise sepoys in lahore failed — poor response from sepoys. (peel commission post-1857 had deliberately reduced political consciousness in the army. low western education among sepoys & hence ghadarite appeals found little traction.) 11.1.3) udasi sikh mahants — the socially influential priests of gurudwaras — were pro-british & actively asked religious masses to not support the ghadarites. (similar to ulamas aligning with british during swadeshi movement 0511. religious establishments tied to colonial order become instruments of counter-nationalism.) 11.1.4) late 1914 – early february 1915: the british pre-emptive strikes against ghadarites & regiments suspected of disloyalty. thus, the mutiny planned for february 21, 1915 was crushed before it could begin. 111.5) march 1915 (emergency): ghadarites suppressed under defence of india act, 1915 — a wartime emergency law. (link forward: rowlatt acts 1919 = anarchical & revolutionary crimes act 1919 sought to continue emergency powers even post ww1 ). under this act, revolutionaries could be detained without trial, special tribunals replaced ordinary courts & there was no right of appeal. 111.6) april–september 1915 (the mass trials — first lahore conspiracy case): following the failure of rash behari bose's planned february mutiny, the british launched the first lahore conspiracy case (1915) — a mass trial of captured ghadarites. many were sentenced to death, many to transportation for life, and hundreds were interned in their villages under the defence of india act, 1915. this trial effectively crushed the organisational backbone of the ghadar movement inside india. ⚠ upsc trap: do not confuse the first lahore conspiracy case (1915, ghadar) with the second lahore conspiracy case (1929–30, bhagat singh & hsra(1928)). 11.2) what the movement achieved 112.1) india lost a whole generation of secular, nationalistic indians who had given up comfortable lives abroad for a secular republic. 112.2) their sacrifice greatly increased nationalism & awareness of british colonialism among indian diaspora & indians. it inspired the next generation of revolutionaries. in november 1915, kartar singh sarabha was arrested & hanged — he was only 19 years old at the time. he became a martyr-hero of the revolutionary movement, and bhagat singh later said he kept sarabha's photograph in his pocket. (british failed to arrest rb bose who escaped to japan in may 1915.) 112.3) it was the first organised attempt to use the indian diaspora for armed revolution against the british. 112.4) it demonstrated that the spirit of 1857 had not died — indians overseas were willing to sacrifice everything to free their homeland. 112.5) sikh, hindu, and muslim revolutionaries worked together without communal friction. 112.6) those who survived became active in the later inm & peasant & working class movements— in the kisan sabhas, the communist movement, and the akali movement in punjab. 112.7) the ghadar movement is a reminder that the freedom struggle was not fought only on indian soil — it was a global struggle, waged from san francisco to tokyo to berlin. ⚠ upsc elimination tip: jogesh chandra chatterjee is sometimes confused with ghadar-era revolutionaries, but he belongs to the 1920s hra/hsra phase (kakori conspiracy case, 1925). do not associate him with the ghadar movement. ◆ the ghadar movement holds a special place in the inm. it was perhaps the first sustained revolutionary current explicitly & consciously secular in character — punjabis, largely sikh in origin, actively seeking hindu-muslim unity & rejecting religious identity as a basis for the nation. shaped by bakunin's conviction that oppressive structures must be demolished rather than reformed, and by the strategy of "propaganda of the deed," it imagined an india far more radical than the moderate nationalist mainstream. the battle of balasore was not just a military failure — it was the silencing of a particular — and very brave — vision of what india could be. ◆ key dates to remember: date event 1907 tarak nath das, free hindustan, vancouver 1909 g.d. kumar, swadesh sevak, canada 1912 hardayal sets up bakunin institute, oakland 1913 ghadar party founded in san francisco; the ghadr newspaper launched april 1914 komagata maru departs hong kong may 1914 komagata maru arrives in vancouver; standoff begins july 1914 komagata maru forced out of canada; ww1 begins august 1914 rodda & co. arms heist, calcutta (26 august) september 1914 budge budge riot; ghadarites start returning to india february 1915 planned mutiny on february 21 fails march 1915 defence of india act used to crush the movement april–september 1915 first lahore conspiracy case trials september 1915 battle of balasore / buribalam; bagha jatin martyred november 1915 kartar singh sarabha executed december 1915 christmas day plot collapses ghadar movement timeline ⚠ alert (prelims 2005): upsc tested this. q) where were the ghadar revolutionaries, who became active during the outbreak of the ww1 based? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (b) north america. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — central america; (c) ✗ — west america; (d) ✗ — south america ⚠ alert (prelims 2014): upsc tested this. q) the ghadr (ghadar) was a to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) a revolutionary association of indians with headquarters at san francisco. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — nationalist organisation operating from singapore; (c) ✗ — militant organisation with headquarters at berlin; (d) ✗ — communist movement for india's freedom with headquarters at tashkent ⚠ alert (prelims 2022): upsc tested this. q) who were actively associated with the ghadar party?1. barindra kumar ghosh 2. jogesh chandra chatterjee 3. rash behari bose to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) 3 only. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — 1 and 2; (b) ✗ — 2 only; (c) ✗ — 1 and 3

sections.title: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18)
sections.norm: home rule league movement (1916–18). hrl 1916–18 inc 2005 upsc. 1.1) the home rule league movement (hrl movement) of 1916–18 was not an inc initiative. it was launched independently by two leaders — bal gangadhar tilak & annie besant. its method was educative propaganda — spreading awareness about home rule & swaraj within the british empire. it was not a programme of non-cooperation or civil disobedience. ⚠ alert (prelims 2005): upsc tested this. q) who among the following was a proponent of fabianism as a movement? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) annie besant. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — ao hume; (c) ✗ — michael madhusudan dutt; (d) ✗ — r palme dutt

sections.chapterTitle: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) & Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.title: Context: Why the Movement Was Necessary
sections.norm: context: why the movement was necessary. 1914 inm indian councils act ica1909 inc 1906 morley-minto reforms 1909. 2.1) when tilak returned to india from mandalay (burma) in 1914, after six years of imprisonment, the inm was at a dull phase. 2.2) the extremists & revolutionaries had been firmly suppressed by the british. the moderates, on the other hand, had become irrelevant — not because they lacked sincerity, but because their approach had failed twice. in 1892 & again in 1909 with the indian councils act (ica1909), the moderates had worked within the system & obtained reforms, but those reforms had not delivered self-government, which was the goal inc had set for itself since the 1906 calcutta session. 2.3) (self-government, or swaraj, had been the declared goal of inc since 1906. the ica1909 gave an elected non-official majority only in provincial legislative councils, not in the imperial legislative council at the centre — and even that non-official majority was not an elected indian majority in the full sense. so from the movement's point of view, ica1909 was a disappointment.)

sections.chapterTitle: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) & Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.title: Tilak's Strategy
sections.norm: tilak's strategy. 3.1) to revive the inm, tilak wanted the extremists to re-enter inc — because organisation mattered for the success of any movement. he also understood that if extremists operated outside inc, the british could repress them more easily. so tilak took a deliberate & calculated position. he declared publicly that: swaraj means self-rule within the british empire overthrowing british rule is not his goal inm support the british war effort loyal to the crown inc. 3.1) to revive the inm, tilak wanted the extremists to re-enter inc — because organisation mattered for the success of any movement. he also understood that if extremists operated outside inc, the british could repress them more easily. so tilak took a deliberate & calculated position. he declared publicly that: i) swaraj means self-rule within the british empire — overthrowing british rule is not his goal. (the british were :) about this.) ii) violence has hurt inm's progress. (the british were :) again. moderates too were :).) iii) all indians should support the british war effort. (british :) ) iv) he is loyal to the crown. (british :). moderates reacted like: our sentence copied, our sentence copied.) 3.2) this was a tactical move. by saying these things, tilak made it difficult for the british to repress the extremists again, and simultaneously positioned extremists as compatible with inc's moderate framework.

sections.chapterTitle: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) & Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.title: Annie Besant's Role
sections.norm: annie besant's role. 1914 inc 1915 1916. 4.1) in 1914, annie besant — head of the theosophical society based in madras, an irish woman inspired by the home rule movement in ireland — joined inc. she too wanted self-rule for india. she campaigned within inc for the re-entry of extremists, wanting a stronger organisation. but her attempt failed in 1914 due to opposition from pherozshah mehta, the leader of bombay's moderates. 4.2) then, at the 1915 bombay session, inc finally decided to allow the re-entry of extremists, as p.m. mehta had died. (the actual re-entry happened at the 1916 lucknow session.) however, inc still did not agree to support the idea of home rule leagues — because moderates did not fully trust the extremists, worrying that educative propaganda might eventually slide into non-cooperation, civil disobedience, or violence.

sections.chapterTitle: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) & Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.title: Setting Up the Two Leagues
sections.norm: setting up the two leagues. 1916 5.2) september 1916 — besant set up the all india home rule league. 5.3) both leagues cooperated but chose not to merge into one — to prevent friction among their respective followers. they divided their areas of operation clearly: hrl all india hrl 200 branches hq at madras 2018 upsc 1920. 5.1) april 1916 — tilak set up the indian home rule league. (tilak is indian, hence indian home rule league.) 5.2) september 1916 — besant set up the all india home rule league. 5.3) both leagues cooperated but chose not to merge into one — to prevent friction among their respective followers. they divided their areas of operation clearly: i) tilak's indian hrl: bombay province/maharashtra (except bombay city), berar, karnataka, central provinces — 6 branches, hq at poona. ii) besant's all india hrl: rest of british india — 200 branches, hq at madras. ⚠ alert (prelims 2018): upsc tested this. q) in 1920, which of the following changed its name to swarajya sabha? to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (a) all india home rule league. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (b) ✗ — hindu mahasabha; (c) ✗ — south indian liberal federation; (d) ✗ — the servants of india society

sections.title: Demands & Spread of the Movement
sections.norm: demands & spread of the movement. 6.1) the goal was educative propaganda on home rule & swaraj. tilak's famous slogan — "swaraj is my birthright & i shall have it" — became the rallying cry. beyond swaraj, tilak also demanded: inc 1918 1893 demand for self-rule divergent national interests reduced the communal or religious colour lucknow pact of 1916 hrl 1884 india bill 1925 2013 upsc. 6.1) the goal was educative propaganda on home rule & swaraj. tilak's famous slogan — "swaraj is my birthright & i shall have it" — became the rallying cry. beyond swaraj, tilak also demanded: i) education in vernacular languages. ii) linguistic reorganisation of provinces of british india. (this was forward-thinking — linguistic unity would strengthen the organisation of mass movements, improve inc's functioning at the provincial level, and reduce provincial factionalism within inc.) iii) end to untouchability — tilak famously stated, "if god tolerates untouchability then i won't recognise him as god." (he delivered this specific quote slightly later at the 1918 all india depressed classes conference. however, his focus on caste unity went back much further — at the ganpati festival of 1893, tilak had made lord ganapati — worshipped by both upper castes & lower castes — the centrepiece.) 6.2) tilak argued that the demand for self-rule was not because the british are christians but because india & britain have divergent national interests. this framing reduced the communal or religious colouring of the demand. therefore tilak made less use of hindu nationalism. 6.3) in fact, it was the combined efforts of tilak, jinnah & annie besant that led to the lucknow pact of 1916 between inc & the muslim league — a significant moment of hindu-muslim political cooperation. (jinnah also joined besant's all india hrl & became the president of its bombay branch.) 6.4) apart from ground-level work promoting inc in villages, both leaders used the press aggressively. tilak published kesari (marathi) and maharatta (english). besant published new india & commonweal (meaning common/public welfare — from commonweal came the word commonwealth). she popularized the idea of a voluntary 'commonwealth of nations' (phrase coined by lord rosebery in 1884). besant later authored the commonwealth of india bill (1925), proposing dominion status for india — a direct extension of her lifelong campaign for self-governance within the empire. ⚠ alert (prelims 2013): upsc tested this. q) annie besant was 1. responsible for starting the home rule movement. 2. the founder of the theosophical society. 3. the president of the indian national congress. select the correct answer using the... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (c) 1 and 3. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — only 1; (b) ✗ — 2 and 3; (d) ✗ — all of these

sections.title: After Besant's Arrest (1917)
sections.norm: after besant's arrest (1917). 7.1) the arrest & internment of besant in 1917 became a turning point. far from weakening the movement, it energised it: even moderates joined the hrls united the factions 1900 1895 hrl 1905–06 1907–11. 7.1) the arrest & internment of besant in 1917 became a turning point. far from weakening the movement, it energised it: i) now even moderates joined the hrls — the british overreach had united the factions. ii) sir s. subramania iyer gave up his knighthood (knighted in 1900; appointed judge of the madras high court in 1895) — a powerful symbolic act of protest. he was the honorary president of besant's all india hrl. ◆ a note on administrative roles: iyer had previously served as recording secretary (1905–06) and then as vice-president (1907–11) of the theosophical society. a recording secretary is the custodian of official, legal records — writing minutes & maintaining archives. this is distinctly different from an organising secretary, who handles correspondence, campaigns & network-building. in besant's home rule league, that role of organising secretary was held by george arundale — the person doing the heavy lifting of building the league's network across india & acting as the right hand to besant.

sections.chapterTitle: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) & Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.title: The Two Subramania Iyers
sections.norm: the two subramania iyers. two different men who share a near-identical name 1855–1916 1878 swadesamitran in 1882 1884 inc 1885 1842–1924 hrl 1895 1900 acting chief justice of the madras high court 1916 1917 passive resistance besant sided with the moderates 1998 upsc ww1 . 8.1) students frequently confuse two different men who share a near-identical name & both have connections to madras & the early nationalist movement. 8.2) g. subramania iyer (the journalist, 1855–1916) — full name: ganapathy subramania iyer. he was the powerhouse of early nationalist journalism in south india. i) co-founded the english newspaper the hindu in 1878 — specifically to protest the appointment of an anglo-indian judge over a native indian candidate. ii) founded the tamil nationalist daily swadesamitran in 1882. iii) along with m. veeraraghavachariar & p. anandacharlu, founded the madras mahajan sabha in 1884. iv) at the very first session of inc in bombay in 1885, it was g. subramania iyer who moved the historically significant first resolution. 8.3) sir s. subramania iyer (the jurist, 1842–1924) — he was the legal heavyweight & the hrl figure we are discussing in this chapter. i) appointed judge of the madras high court in 1895; knighted in 1900 (k.c.i.e. — knight commander of the indian empire), giving him the title "sir." ii) later became acting chief justice of the madras high court. iii) co-founder & honorary president of the home rule league in madras (1916) alongside annie besant. iv) in 1917, he famously wrote an explosive letter to us president woodrow wilson & renounced his knighthood in protest of besant's arrest. simple way to keep them apart: g. subramania iyer = journalist + the hindu + 1885 first inc resolution. sir s. subramania iyer = judge + knighthood surrendered + home rule league. 8.4) mahatma gandhi began a signature campaign for besant's release. (gandhi was against using the opportunity of ww1 the way hrl leaders were. he had not joined the hrls & had instead travelled across india wanting youth to join the british india army to support britain in ww1 , believing the allies were on the side of justice as victims of aggression.) 8.5) result: besant was released & made inc president at the 1917 calcutta session. 8.6) however, the british deployed the montague statement of 1917 as a divide & rule tactic. (in layman's terms, montague's statement meant: british will give swaraj gradually.) 8.7) within the movement, extremists proposed a programme of passive resistance. moderates opposed it. besant sided with the moderates. ⚠ alert (prelims 1998): upsc tested this. q) what is the correct sequence of the following events?1. tilak's home rule league.2. komagata maru incident.3. mahatma gandhi's arrival in india.select the correct answer using the codes given... to answer right, the student should know — correct answer is (d) 2, 3, 1. wrong options (commonly picked by students who confuse the topic): (a) ✗ — 1, 2, 3; (b) ✗ — 3, 2, 1; (c) ✗ — 2, 1, 3
