sections.title: Understanding "Passive Resistance": Extremists, Besant, and Gandhi
sections.norm: understanding "passive resistance": extremists, besant, and gandhi. 9.1) the extremists' concept of "passive resistance" 1907 the doctrine 9.2) to aurobindo & the extremists, "passive resistance" was an umbrella term that explicitly included two interconnected concepts: first step (non-cooperation) boycotting british goods, government schools, courts escalation (civil disobedience) deliberately break those laws 9.3) the 1917 debate & besant's opposition 1917 inc 1920. 9.1) the extremists' concept of "passive resistance" when the extremists proposed "passive resistance" during the home rule league era — and earlier during the swadeshi movement — they were drawing directly from aurobindo ghosh. in april 1907, aurobindo published a famous series of seven articles in the daily newspaper bande mataram, collectively known as "the doctrine of passive resistance." 9.2) to aurobindo & the extremists, "passive resistance" was an umbrella term that explicitly included two interconnected concepts: i) the first step (non-cooperation): a comprehensive blueprint for boycotting british goods, government schools, courts, and administrative roles. ii) the escalation (civil disobedience): a clear directive that if the state passed oppressive, coercive laws to stop this peaceful boycott, it was the duty of the nationalist to deliberately break those laws & accept the punishment. 9.3) the 1917 debate & besant's opposition so in the context of the 1917 debate inside inc, when the extremists demanded a programme of "passive resistance," they were asking for exactly this — a comprehensive campaign of boycotts (nc) and potential law-breaking (cd). 9.4) annie besant backed away from this demand because she was fundamentally a constitutionalist. while she was willing to agitate, petition, and spread propaganda right to the edge of legality (which had in fact led to her own arrest), she possessed a deep-seated fear of anarchy. she strictly opposed the law-breaking aspect of the extremist plan, firmly believing that deliberately disobeying the law would inevitably lead to chaos & mob violence. this fundamental ideological divide is exactly why she later completely broke away from mg when he launched the non-cooperation movement in 1920.

sections.title: The Gandhian shift
sections.norm: the gandhian shift. . 10.1) it is important to note — for later chapters — that when mg took command of the national movement, he completely rejected the term "passive resistance." to gandhi, both non-cooperation & civil disobedience were highly active, fearless moral forces — satyagraha — never passive.

sections.chapterTitle: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) & Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.title: Overall Impact — Positives & Negatives
sections.norm: overall impact — positives & negatives. 1917–18 hrl inc 11.4) 60,000 members joined the hrls. inm prepared leadership for future gandhian struggle nehru joined besant's league 11.8) the hrl period permanently decreased the influence of moderates in inc. secular in its methods hindu-muslim unity. negatives: 11.1) by 1917–18, the british had successfully repressed the hrls. the hrls became defunct — educative propaganda could not convert itself into a mass movement. 11.2) hrls failed to develop a mass movement. in madras, for instance, lower castes did not support the all india hrl because its leadership was upper caste dominated. 11.3) extremists failed a second time to take over inc. moderates & extremists failed to unite on a common programme. positives: 11.4) 60,000 members joined the hrls. 11.5) the movement brought gujarat, sindh, united provinces, bihar & south india more actively into the inm — regions which had low participation until the hrl period. 11.6) it prepared leadership for future gandhian struggle. for example, nehru joined besant's league through this movement. 11.7) hrls created an organisational network that would be used in later phases of the inm. 11.8) the hrl period permanently decreased the influence of moderates in inc. 11.9) the movement was secular in its methods & helped hindu-muslim unity. (h-m unity)

sections.chapterTitle: Home Rule League Movement (1916–18) & Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.title: Lucknow Pact (1916)
sections.norm: lucknow pact (1916). the lucknow pact of 1916 ml1906 12.2) inc & ml1906 presented a common platform to the british: continue separate electorates ica1909 vec uaf motilal nehru report of 1928 lp1916 motilal nehru report inc india act 1919 the lucknow pact goi act 1919 muslim league 1906 morley-minto reforms 1909 lucknow pact 1916. 12.1) the lucknow pact of 1916 was an agreement between inc (founded 1885) and the muslim league (ml1906). it was the first time inc & ml1906 gave joint demands to the british for constitutional reforms. ml1906 also supported the hrls. (the context of rising tensions between ml1906 & the british needs to be understood in light of world history — see the section below on ml1906 vs the british.) 12.2) inc & ml1906 presented a common platform to the british: i) continue separate electorates in future council reforms. ii) expand councils & bring an elected majority. (ica1909 had brought only a non-official majority, and that too only in provincial legislative councils, not the imperial legislative council.) iii) at least 50% indians in the viceroy's executive council (vec — i.e. gg & ministers). iv) franchise as broad as possible & direct elections. (they did not yet demand universal adult franchise — the formal uaf demand would come with the motilal nehru report of 1928.) v) self-government at an early date — equal status with other self-governing dominions of the british empire. (on this basis, one can argue that dominion status was implicitly demanded by lp1916 — though at an early date, not immediately. in 1916 they were asking for something less than full self-rule e.g. only 50% indians in vec. the exact phrase "dominion status" was first used in the motilal nehru report of august 1928.) 12.3) the hindu-muslim electoral compromise: to forge a united front against the british, both sides made significant concessions. the muslim league agreed to give up its right to vote in general/unreserved constituencies. in exchange, the inc formally accepted the principle of separate electorates & agreed to a guaranteed, fixed quota of seats for muslims in the legislatures. the british later adopted the mechanics of this hindu-muslim compromise into the government of india act 1919, which officially created strictly segregated, "watertight" electoral rolls — meaning muslims would not vote in unreserved seats & would vote only in muslim-reserved seats. (this was the institutional hardening of communal division that lp1916 inadvertently set in motion.) how should we assess the lucknow pact? negative: 12.4) this was a major landmark in the two nation theory. by accepting separate electorates in future council reforms, inc formally conceded that hindus & muslims constituted separate political communities that needed separate electoral representation. this was a significant — and, in hindsight, a dangerous — concession. positive: 12.5) the lucknow pact led to inc-ml1906 unity, which mg later used effectively in the khilafat movement (1919–24) and the non-cooperation movement (1920–22). it created pressure on the british & contributed directly to the montague statement of 1917 & the goi act 1919. it also failed the british strategy of divide & rule.

sections.title: Why ML1906 Turned Against the British — World Context
sections.norm: why ml1906 turned against the british — world context. 1916 lucknow pact 1919 13.2) indian muslims had traditionally been more cautious than inc in opposing british rule. ml1906 was founded largely with british support & had initially maintained a loyal, deferential tone. however, a decade-long series of geopolitical shocks alienated them from the british empire. this "decade of alienation" unfolded in two distinct phases: 13.3) these early events shattered the illusion of british loyalty to muslim interests, pushing the league to join hands with inc in 1916: 1911 1905 ml1906 1912 1914 13.4) following the lucknow pact, subsequent british actions during & immediately after ww1 escalated this alienation into a full-blown mass movement: 1917 treaty of sevres harsh treaty breach of british promises arab regions of the ottoman empire were converted into colonies greece was given many turk-populated areas smyrna khalifa lost control over religious sites hagia sophia ww1 muslim league 1906. context 13.1) to fully understand the political shifts of this era — from the 1916 lucknow pact to the massive khilafat movement in 1919 — one needs to look at what was happening globally & how it was affecting indian muslim sentiment toward britain. 13.2) indian muslims had traditionally been more cautious than inc in opposing british rule. ml1906 was founded largely with british support & had initially maintained a loyal, deferential tone. however, a decade-long series of geopolitical shocks alienated them from the british empire. this "decade of alienation" unfolded in two distinct phases: phase 1: the triggers for the lucknow pact (1911–1914) 13.3) these early events shattered the illusion of british loyalty to muslim interests, pushing the league to join hands with inc in 1916: i) 1911 — annulment of bengal partition: the partition of bengal (1905), which ml1906 had supported as it created a muslim-majority east bengal, was abruptly reversed to appease extremist agitation. this was seen as a massive betrayal. ii) 1911 — italy took over libya from the ottoman empire, whose political head was the khalifa — also the religious head of the muslim world globally. britain did nothing to stop this. (notice the parallel: rome & the pope are the head of christianity in italy — so muslim sentiment about the khalifa was something western powers understood in principle but chose to ignore here.) iii) 1912 — 1st balkan war, in which montenegro, serbia, greece & bulgaria attacked & took over ottoman territories in the balkan peninsula. the ottoman empire was being dismembered piece by piece. iv) 1914 — outbreak of ww1 , where the ottoman empire fought as part of the central powers against britain & the allied powers, placing indian muslims in a deep moral crisis. phase 2: the triggers for the khilafat movement (1917–1920) 13.4) following the lucknow pact, subsequent british actions during & immediately after ww1 escalated this alienation into a full-blown mass movement: i) 1917 — balfour declaration: britain declared its intent to create a jewish homeland from palestine, which was part of the ottoman empire. (the ottoman empire was populated by turks & arabs. the arabs had supported britain in the war & had begun a civil war against the ottoman turks — britain's promise of a jewish homeland in palestine was therefore seen as a stab in the back by the arabs.) ii) 1920 — treaty of sevres: signed with the ottoman empire after ww1 (1914–19). it was a harsh treaty & was seen by indian muslims as a breach of british promises. during the war, the british had promised to maintain the dignity of the khalifa to secure the cooperation of indian muslims in the war effort (civilians not striking, joining the army, not resigning from army). the treaty of sevres violated this promise: ii.i) arab regions of the ottoman empire were converted into colonies of britain & france. (france — syria; britain — iraq, palestine, transjordan.) ii.ii) greece was given many turk-populated areas, including smyrna — which was actually in the turkish mainland — and eastern thrace. ii.iii) the khalifa lost control over religious sites like hagia sophia (as istanbul came under league of nations control).

sections.title: The Montagu Statement, 1917 — Why Did Britain Move at All?
sections.norm: the montagu statement, 1917 — why did britain move at all?. 1914-19 usa 1913-15 1916-18 lucknow pact of 1916 1.1) the montagu statement / august declaration, 1917 house of commons (british parliament) on 20 august 1917 gradual development of self-governing institutions progressive realisation of responsible government slow, controlled movement on british terms timeline was firmly kept in british hands goi 1919 ww1 1917 ww1 . ww1 (1914-19) created a strange problem for britain. the allies — britain, france, the usa — were fighting under the banner of democracy & self-determination. indians had fought & died in that war in large numbers. alongside this, political pressure within india had been building steadily — through the ghadar movement (1913-15), the home rule leagues (1916-18), and the coming together of the indian national congress & the muslim league through the lucknow pact of 1916. swaraj was no longer a fringe demand. it had moral weight. 1.1) the montagu statement / august declaration, 1917 issued by edwin montagu, secretary of state for india, in the house of commons (british parliament) on 20 august 1917, the statement declared: i) henceforth, british policy in india to be the "gradual development of self-governing institutions" with a view to the "progressive realisation of responsible government in india within the british empire." ii) the key words are 'gradual' and 'progressive.' britain was not promising self-governance — it was promising a slow, controlled movement toward it, on british terms. iii) the demand for swaraj was being acknowledged, but the timeline was firmly kept in british hands. iv) goi 1919 was thus conceived as the 1st step toward the progressive realisation of responsible government. ◆ world history link: the allied propaganda during ww1 (1914-19) was built on fighting for democracy & self-determination against absolute monarchies. this created a moral contradiction — fighting for freedom globally while denying it in colonies. the demand for swaraj was therefore no longer seditious in the post-1917 atmosphere; it had legitimacy even within the british imperial framework.

sections.title: The Montagu-Chelmsford Report, 1918
sections.norm: the montagu-chelmsford report, 1918. viceroy chelmsford16-21 chelmsford report india act the report 1947 chelmsford. before the act came the report. in 1917-18, secretary of state montagu personally visited india — an unusual step for someone in his position — and toured various provinces to assess conditions on the ground. the joint report that he co-authored with viceroy chelmsford16-21 became the foundational document for the act. it is known as the montagu-chelmsford report (1918), and it directly led to the government of india act, 1919 — which is why the act is also called the montagu-chelmsford reforms or simply the montford reforms. ◆ note: the report, the reforms, and the act — are they the same thing? students often use these three terms interchangeably. here is the precise distinction: montagu-chelmsford report (1918): the joint document authored by montagu & chelmsford after montagu's india visit. this was the recommendation, not yet the law. montagu-chelmsford reforms / montford reforms: the popular name for the entire package of changes — the report & the act together. used loosely to refer to the act itself. government of india act, 1919: the actual legislation passed by the british parliament. this is the law. the report was its blueprint. ◆ legacy link: the narendra mandal (see 3.2 below) would later become an important venue. when mountbatten made his famous speech in 1947 urging the princes to sign the instrument of accession, he addressed them in the very body created on the foundations of this act. ⚠ alert: examiner-tested anchor — the montagu-chelmsford report (1918) is the blueprint document; the government of india act, 1919 is the law. upsc has tested this triplet thrice — prelims 2003 (indian liberal federation, formed by moderates who left inc after condemning the report); prelims 2004 (report → act 1919 lineage); prelims 2015 (act 1919 defined centre-province jurisdiction). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Provisions of the Government of India Act, 1919
sections.norm: provisions of the government of india act, 1919. 3.1) bicameral legislature at the centre cla ica1909 pla adjournment motions allowed for the 1st time not goi act 1935 3.2) narendra mandal — chamber of princes narendra mandal chamber of princes advisory body chelmsford report goi act 1919 the act ww1 no legislative power purely advisory 3.3) elections & right to vote right to vote linked to strict income/property criteria lucknow pact of 1916 india act 3.4) separate electorates — expanded & made watertight goi 1919 lucknow pact separate electorates now extended to sikhs, anglo-indians, and christians watertight rolls depressed classes reservation of nominated seats — not elected seats 3.5) division of subjects between centre & provinces subjects were divided between centre & provinces for the first time coi1950 viceroy's executive council (vec) the goi act 1919 ica1861 vec the lucknow pact of 1916 3.7) powers of the viceroy — no responsible government at the centre responsible to the legislature ordinance power valid for 6 months power to restore cuts in grants 75% of budget items were non-votable real financial control stayed with the executive 3.8) simultaneous ics examination & public service commission ics 1922 1926 upsc since goi act 1919 lucknow pact 1916 rowlatt act 1919 ww1 morley-minto reforms 1909 constitution of india 1950 indian councils act 1861. 3.1) bicameral legislature at the centre i) bicameral legislature introduced at the centre for british india for the first time, consisting of the central legislative assembly (cla) — the lower house (~145 members) — and the council of states (cos) — the upper house (~60 members). ii) elected majority in cla, cos, and all provincial legislative assemblies (plas) — for the 1st time. (under ica1909, non-official majority existed only in plcs — not at centre.) iii) direct elections introduced for the first time in cla, cos, and plas. (note: cos also had direct elections with higher income criteria for the right to vote — an unusual feature for an upper house.) iv) cla life: 3 years. cos life: 5 years. v) in provinces: provincial legislative assemblies (plas) were unicameral, with elected majority (1st time) and direct elections (1st time). pla life: 3 years. (under ica1909, plcs had non-official majority but most non-officials were nominated, not elected.) vi) adjournment motions allowed for the 1st time. (*link end or mend councils resolution of pro-changers in the 1922 gaya session) ◆ note carefully: this bicameral structure was only for british india — not for the whole of india. it was only the goi act 1935 that extended the framework to include the princely states in an all-india federation. 3.2) narendra mandal — chamber of princes i) narendra mandal — a chamber of princes — created as an advisory body for the princely states. ii) it was a key recommendation of the montagu-chelmsford report (1918) and was formally constituted by royal proclamation in 1921 — not by the goi act 1919 itself. the act provided the framework; the proclamation brought it to life. iii) this was a reward to the princes for their support during ww1 — the british promised to consult the princes on policy matters affecting the princely states. iv) the narendra mandal carried no legislative power — it was purely advisory. 3.3) elections & right to vote i) right to vote linked to strict income/property criteria, as in ica1909. ii) women's franchise: the act did not directly grant women the right to vote. instead, it empowered provincial legislative assemblies to pass resolutions removing the sex disqualification. when women were admitted to vote, they had to meet the exact same strict property qualifications as men, meaning less than 1% of women actually qualified. iii) no universal adult franchise — the lucknow pact of 1916 had demanded franchise as broad as possible; this was not conceded. ⚠ exam alert — women's franchise: 1919 vs 1935 the 1919 act did not directly enfranchise women. it only allowed provincial legislatures to remove the sex disqualification. women who were admitted to vote had to meet the exact same strict property/income criteria as men — no lower threshold. the provision allowing voting based on a husband's property & lower income criteria for women came only with the government of india act, 1935. 3.4) separate electorates — expanded & made watertight i) separate electorates for muslims continued from ica1909, but with a critical change. ii) under ica1909, muslims could vote in muslim reserved seats & also in unreserved seats. under goi 1919, muslims could no longer vote in unreserved seats. in unreserved seats, only voters on the unreserved rolls could vote. the electorates became watertight. iii) this watertight segregation had its roots in the lucknow pact of 1916: to forge a united front against the british, the muslim league agreed to give up its right to vote in general/unreserved constituencies. in exchange, the inc accepted the principle of separate electorates & agreed to a guaranteed, fixed quota of seats for muslims. the british eagerly seized on the communal division logic embedded in this hindu-muslim compromise — it dovetailed perfectly with their divide-and-rule strategy. goi 1919 thus formally created the strictly segregated, watertight electoral rolls, and then extended the same communal separation further to communities the lucknow pact had never contemplated. iv) separate electorates now extended to sikhs, anglo-indians, and christians as well — all with watertight rolls. members of these communities could vote only in their respective reserved constituencies, not in unreserved seats. v) for depressed classes (lower castes): reservation of nominated seats — not elected seats — in all legislatures. (since the legislature now had an elected majority, the share through nominated seats was inherently small. ☹) 3.5) division of subjects between centre & provinces i) subjects were divided between centre & provinces for the first time. ii) however, this was not a federal distribution of subjects — there were no formal lists (no 7th schedule of coi1950). the centre could still take away any subject from a province or legislate upon it at will. iii) provincial budget separated from central budget for the first time. sources of revenue divided: land revenue (lr) — allocated to provinces; customs & income tax — retained by the centre. iv) allocation of seats in cla & cos to provinces was not by population but by perceived importance — e.g., punjab weighted for military importance, bombay weighted for commercial importance. 3.6) viceroy's executive council (vec) i) the goi act 1919 removed the old statutory maximum limit on the number of ordinary members of the vec. (under ica1861, the vec had 5 ordinary members; under the 1874 amendment, 6. goi 1919 lifted this cap.) ii) by convention (not statutory mandate), the vec after 1919 normally consisted of: viceroy + commander-in-chief + 6 ordinary members = 8 members total, of whom 3 of the 6 ordinary members were indians. this 3-indians convention was a political/administrative practice, not a hard legal requirement of the act. iii) the lucknow pact of 1916 had demanded that half the total vec be indians. 3 of 8 = demand unmet. :( 3.7) powers of the viceroy — no responsible government at the centre was the viceroy's executive council (vec) responsible to the legislature? no. there was no responsible government at the centre. the vec was not accountable to the legislature. ◆ constitutional note: 'responsibility' has a specific technical meaning here — a minister must be an elected member of parliament & is accountable through mechanisms like the no confidence motion. none of this existed for the central executive under goi 1919. morley had declared regarding ica1909: "there is no intent of responsible govt in india." the august declaration of 1917 promised 'progressive realisation' of responsible government — goi 1919 was only the 1st step, and the centre was not made responsible. the viceroy retained the following powers: i) veto power over all bills. ii) power to approve rejected bills — the viceroy could pass bills rejected by cla/cos. iii) ordinance power — the viceroy could make law by executive order, valid for 6 months. iv) power to restore cuts in grants — could override budget votes. v) 75% of budget items were non-votable — the legislature could discuss but real financial control stayed with the executive. ◆ this was the old colonial grievance — 'taxation without representation' — continuing even after 1919. indians were being taxed but had no real control over how that money was spent. 3.8) simultaneous ics examination & public service commission i) the goi act 1919 mandated that the ics examination be held simultaneously in india alongside england. the first examination in india was held in 1922. ii) section 96c of the act mandated the setting up of a public service commission for india. the commission was established in 1926 with ross barker as its first chairman. (this commission is the direct institutional ancestor of the modern upsc.) iii) the act also mandated a gradual increase to 33% indians in senior civil service positions. ◆ since goi act 1919 divided subjects between centre & provinces (dyarchy), the ics was split into all india services (ais) and central civil services — the structure of ais & central services that we see today in india is essentially this 1919 structure, continued & modified by the constitution. ⚠ alert: examiner-tested anchors on goi act 1919. prelims 1995 (sequence: partition of bengal 1905 → lucknow pact 1916 → rowlatt act 1919 → dyarchy via goi 1919); prelims 2012 (principal features of goi 1919); prelims 2017 (dyarchy = division of powers between centre & provinces / reserved & transferred at province); prelims 2022 (reserved subjects under dyarchy = justice + land revenue + police, not local self-govt). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Dyarchy at the Provincial Level — The Most Debated Feature
sections.norm: dyarchy at the provincial level — the most debated feature. dyarchy dual rule reserved & transferred 4.1) reserved subjects reserved subjects politically important law & order with the governor & his officials pla why irrigation was reserved — to protect british business interests. 1850s fdi 5% guaranteed fdi interest land revenue stayed reserved agriculture went to the transferred side reserving the spoils, transferring the tension. 4.2) transferred subjects transferred subjects less politically sensitive legislative power on transferred subjects was with the pla ministers who were responsible to the pla 4.3) why dyarchy was a problem in practice no control over finance or officials could not effectively govern became unpopular with the public exactly as the british designed hurt the legitimacy of indian ministers delaying the demand for full responsible government failure of constitutional machinery governor could take over overruled by the governor. what was dyarchy? the word 'dyarchy' means 'dual rule' (dy = two; archy = top authority). at the provincial level, all subjects were split into two categories — reserved & transferred — governed by different authorities. 4.1) reserved subjects i) reserved subjects were politically important — namely, law & order i.e. police, administration of justice, finance, land revenue, irrigation, and control over officials. ii) legislative & executive powers on reserved subjects were with the governor & his officials. iii) no accountability to the provincial legislative assembly (pla) on reserved subjects. ministers handling reserved subjects were not responsible to the pla. iv) why irrigation was reserved — to protect british business interests. from the 1850s onwards, canals across the indus basin, ganga, and krishna-godavari belts were built through fdi by british investors. keeping irrigation under the governor’s grip meant those returns could be shielded from indian-elected ministers — the same logic as the 5% guaranteed fdi interest on railways (link drain theory, ch 27). v) (*notice the asymmetry — land revenue stayed reserved while agriculture went to the transferred side. the british kept the lever that generated revenue; indian ministers inherited the lever that generated peasant complaints. reserving the spoils, transferring the tension.*) 4.2) transferred subjects i) transferred subjects were less politically sensitive — e.g., health, education, local government, agriculture. ii) legislative power on transferred subjects was with the pla. iii) administered by ministers who were responsible to the pla. 4.3) why dyarchy was a problem in practice i) indian ministers received the 'soft' subjects — health, education, agriculture — but had no control over finance or officials. ii) without money & without control over the bureaucracy, indian ministers could not effectively govern even the transferred subjects. iii) when they failed to deliver, they became unpopular with the public — exactly as the british designed. iv) the goal was to hurt the legitimacy of indian ministers & demonstrate that indians could not govern, thereby delaying the demand for full responsible government. v) in case of failure of constitutional machinery, the governor could take over executive & legislative powers over transferred subjects as well. vi) ministers from the pla could be overruled by the governor on any matter.

sections.title: Why Were INM Leaders Dissatisfied?
sections.norm: why were inm leaders dissatisfied?. dissatisfied with the goi act, 1919 not true federalism centre retained overriding power mockery of federalism governor, as agent of the centre lucknow pact 1916 no fully responsible government at provinces no responsible government at the centre 5.5) seats in cla & cos allocated by importance, not population. ica1909 morley-minto reforms 1909. the leaders of the indian national movement (inm) were dissatisfied with the goi act, 1919 on multiple counts: 5.1) unsatisfactory division of subjects between centre & provinces — not true federalism since the centre retained overriding power. (hence federalism ☹) 5.2) dyarchy also made a mockery of federalism at the provincial level — the governor, as agent of the centre, retained control over reserved subjects. (hence dyarchy also = federalism ☹) 5.3) no universal adult franchise — the right to vote remained income-linked, falling far short of the lucknow pact demand of 1916 for franchise as broad as possible. 5.4) no fully responsible government at provinces (only partially responsible for transferred subjects), and certainly no responsible government at the centre. 5.5) seats in cla & cos allocated by importance, not population. 5.6) goi 1919 did not bring effective self-government — an improvement over the limited self-government of ica1909, but far from swaraj (inc goal since 1906 calcutta session). (but > ltd sg of 1909)

sections.title: GOI Act 1919 — Summary Card
sections.norm: goi act 1919 — summary card. chelmsford16-21 cla separate electorates sikhs, anglo-indians, christians division of subjects not federal division vec cic viceroy powers 75% non-votable pla women's franchise plas could remove gender disqualification ics 1922 1926 mc report provincial details elected majority, direct elections, 3-year life dissatisfaction no responsible govt at centre chelmsford. key names: montagu (sos), chelmsford16-21 (viceroy) — montford reforms legislature: bicameral: cla (lower, ~145) + cos (upper, ~60) — 1st time at centre elected majority: 1st — in cla, cos, plas elections: 1st time: direct elections in cla, cos, plas + nominated seats reserved for depressed classes separate electorates: extended to sikhs, anglo-indians, christians; watertight rolls (muslims can no longer vote in unreserved seats) division of subjects: 1st time but not federal division — no lists like 7th schedule vec: gg + cic + upper limit removed on ordinary members (convention: 6, of which 3 indians) viceroy powers: veto, ordinance (6 months), approve rejected bills, restore cuts; 75% non-votable dyarchy: provinces: reserved (governor — law & order i.e. police, administration of justice, finance, land revenue, control over officials) + transferred (ministers → pla) women's franchise: not direct — plas could remove gender disqualification ics reform: simultaneous exam in india (first held 1922); public service commission mandated (section 96c, set up 1926, ross barker chairman) narendra mandal: advisory body for princely states; recommended by mc report; constituted by royal proclamation 1921 provincial details: plas — elected majority, direct elections, 3-year life dissatisfaction: no responsible govt at centre; only partially responsible at provinces; no true federalism; limited franchise — end of chapter —

sections.title: Who Was in South Africa — and Why Did It Matter?
sections.norm: who was in south africa — and why did it matter?. 1890. the union of south africa of the late 19th century was a stratified society. its population was broadly divided into four groups: the indigenous bantus (roughly 70%), european settlers (18%), mixed race (9%), and asians (3%) — the last group having been brought in as indentured labourers, a practice that accelerated after 1890 when white settlers recruited cheap labour from india & elsewhere. the indians in south africa fell into two distinct groups. the memon muslims were traders & merchants who had come voluntarily. then there were the indentured labourers — men & women brought under bond contracts, essentially tied labour, who arrived in significant numbers after 1890 to work on sugar plantations & in mines. their legal standing was precarious, their rights minimal, and their voice nearly non-existent. ◆ indentured labour was a step above slavery in name only. a labourer signed a contract — usually without fully understanding it — binding him to an employer for a fixed term under conditions he could not easily escape.

sections.title: How Did Gandhiji End Up Staying?
sections.norm: how did gandhiji end up staying?. 1893 plan changed almost immediately leaderless & without any educated advocate. mohandas karamchand gandhi arrived in south africa in 1893 as a young barrister — hired to handle a commercial legal case for a memon muslim merchant. shortly after landing, he experienced the incident that would change the course of his life: at pietermaritzburg railway station, gandhiji was ejected from a first-class compartment solely for being indian, despite holding a valid ticket. the humiliation of that night on the cold station platform became his political catalyst — the moment he resolved to fight racial discrimination rather than quietly endure it. he had planned to stay briefly & return to india. that plan changed almost immediately. the indian community, leaderless & without any educated advocate who understood both law & their grievances, persuaded him to stay on. he was, quite literally, the only person who could fight for them within the system. gandhiji agreed. what began as a short visit stretched into twenty-two years — years that would forge the methods & the man who would later transform india's independence movement.

sections.title: What Started the Struggle? The Two Trigger Laws
sections.norm: what started the struggle? the two trigger laws. two pieces of legislation first political response in south africa 3.1) franchise amendment bill, 1894 (natal) this bill 1894 twr 1776 3.2) immigration law amendment bill, 1895 (natal) indian indentured labourers a brutal choice poll tax. two pieces of legislation in the 1890s directly provoked gandhiji's first political response in south africa. 3.1) franchise amendment bill, 1894 (natal) this bill sought to disenfranchise indians — to strip them of the right to vote. some indians had earlier qualified for the vote based on a wealth criterion: if you owned property above a certain value, you could vote. the 1894 bill aimed to close that door entirely, purely on racial grounds. ◆ this is what later scholars called 'taxation without representation' (twr) in a different form — indians paid taxes, contributed to the economy, but were to be denied any say in who governed them. compare this with the american colonists' grievance against britain in 1776: they too objected to being taxed by a parliament in which they had no voice. 3.2) immigration law amendment bill, 1895 (natal) this law gave indian indentured labourers a brutal choice on completion of their work contract: leave south africa, or re-indenture for two more years. if they chose neither, they had to pay a poll tax of £3 per year — a significant sum for a labourer earning bare subsistence wages. ◆ think of it this way: you've served your time, you want to stay & build a life — and the government says either go back where you came from, sign another bond contract, or pay an annual penalty just for existing. this tax was not about revenue. it was about making indian settlement economically unsustainable.

sections.title: Phase 1 — The Constitutional Struggle (1896–1906)
sections.norm: phase 1 — the constitutional struggle (1896–1906). entirely within the law petitions, prayers, and public meetings natal indian congress inc. gandhiji's early response was entirely within the law. he organised petitions, prayers, and public meetings. he founded the natal indian congress — modelled on the indian national congress back home — to give the indian community a formal, organised political voice. he also launched a newspaper, indian opinion, as a platform to document & publicise indian grievances. the approach was moderate, respectful, and constitutional: appeal to the conscience of the rulers, expose injustice through argument, and trust that reason would prevail. ◆ this phase echoes almost exactly what the moderate leaders of the inc were doing in india at the same time — petitions, prayers, and press. gandhiji was, in spirit, a moderate in south africa before he became something far more in india.

sections.title: Phase 2 — The Extra-Constitutional Struggle (1906–1915)
sections.norm: phase 2 — the extra-constitutional struggle (1906–1915). 1906 5.1) what is a satyagrahi? not passive submission active, disciplined resistance truthful non-violent fearless ready to accept suffering 5.2) phoenix settlement (1904) 1904 phoenix settlement 1910 5.3) satyagraha against registration certificates (1906–1914) the asiatic law amendment act 1906 black act voluntarily registered first to register led by example bonfire of registration certificates courting arrest jail bharo 5.4) satyagraha against immigration laws the transvaal immigration restriction act 1907 1908 5.5) tolstoy farm, 1910 5.6) the visit of gokhale, 1912 inc 1912. by 1906, gandhiji had concluded that constitutional methods alone were not enough. the government was unmoved by petitions. something more direct was needed — but it had to remain non-violent. this was the crucible in which satyagraha was born. 5.1) what is a satyagrahi? gandhiji's satyagraha was not passive submission. it was active, disciplined resistance grounded in a very specific personal code. a true satyagrahi had to be: i) truthful — in word, action & intention. ii) non-violent — absolutely, even under provocation. iii) fearless — willing to face arrest, imprisonment, and physical suffering. iv) ready to accept suffering — not to inflict it. v) loving toward the wrongdoer — hate was to have no place. ◆ notice the standard. this was not 'protest when convenient.' it demanded a complete transformation of the individual. an undisciplined satyagrahi was a contradiction in terms. 5.2) phoenix settlement (1904) before the extra-constitutional phase formally began, gandhiji had already started experimenting with communal living. in 1904, inspired by john ruskin's unto this last, he established the phoenix settlement near durban. residents lived & worked together, practising self-reliance & simple living. the indian opinion newspaper was also printed here. phoenix was gandhiji's first communal living experiment — the philosophical precursor to tolstoy farm (1910) and, later, to his ashrams in india (link ch 36 — ruskin's influence on gandhian ideology). 5.3) satyagraha against registration certificates (1906–1914) the asiatic law amendment act 1906 — known bitterly as the 'black act' — was passed by the transvaal government. it required every indian to carry a registration certificate (rc) at all times. failure to produce it on demand could mean fine, imprisonment, and deportation. ◆ the rc was a physical identity card to be produced on demand to any authority, with deportation as the penalty for not carrying it — an instrument of racial surveillance. the government made an offer: if indians voluntarily registered, the law would be withdrawn. gandhiji, in a remarkable act of good faith, was the first to register. he led by example, expecting the government to keep its word. the government did not. the promise was broken. the response was swift. gandhiji organised a bonfire of registration certificates — a powerful public act of defiance — and then led indians in courting arrest (what we later called 'jail bharo'). the struggle was conducted through the passive resistance association. 5.4) satyagraha against immigration laws the transvaal immigration restriction act 1907 went further: it barred indians from moving freely between provinces — from cape province, natal, or orange free state into transvaal. indians were being physically caged within provincial boundaries. gandhiji's response: indians deliberately crossed provincial boundaries illegally, courted arrest, and refused bail. indians in transvaal engaged in hawking without a licence — a minor illegal act, deliberately committed to fill the jails. gandhiji himself was jailed in 1908. the prisons overflowed. the strategy was to make enforcement so costly that the government would be forced to negotiate. 5.5) tolstoy farm, 1910 extended struggle has a cost — on morale, on families, on livelihoods. gandhiji understood this. in 1910 he established tolstoy farm — a communal settlement near johannesburg — as a residential base for satyagrahis & their families during the passive phases of the struggle. it was named after the russian writer leo tolstoy, whose ideas on non-violent resistance had influenced gandhiji. ◆ tolstoy farm was part ashram, part training ground. residents were taught self-reliance — farming, crafts, basic trades. the idea was that if you are truly fearless & self-sufficient, the government has fewer levers to use against you. this is the philosophical seed of what later became gandhiji's ashram model in india. notice the progression: phoenix settlement (1904) → tolstoy farm (1910) → sabarmati/sevagram in india — each building on the last. 5.6) the visit of gokhale, 1912 gopal krishna gokhale — gandhiji's political mentor & one of the most respected moderate leaders of the inc — visited south africa in 1912. the south african government, impressed by his stature, promised gokhale that the discriminatory laws would be repealed. once again, the promise was broken after gokhale left. gokhale's strategic advice to gandhiji before leaving was precise: focus the movement on two specific & emotionally resonant demands — abolition of the poll tax (under the immigration law) and abolition of the registration certificate requirement (under the black act). these were the two issues most capable of mobilising mass participation. gokhale understood that a movement needs an issue people feel viscerally — and these two hit every indian household in south africa.

sections.title: The Poll Tax Campaign and the Final Countdown (1913)
sections.norm: the poll tax campaign and the final countdown (1913). 1913 events during the final struggle closest thing to a mass uprising hardinge. by 1913, the movement had reached a turning point. the poll tax campaign became the vehicle through which the struggle finally acquired a mass character. till now, it had largely been led by educated indians — lawyers, merchants, community leaders. the poll tax hit the indentured labourer directly. now the working class joined. then came an unexpected legal bombshell. in 1913, a south african supreme court judgement declared that only christian marriages were legally valid. marriages conducted under hindu, muslim, or other rites were not recognised by law. this meant that indian wives were legally not wives, and their children were potentially illegitimate. the community was outraged. overnight, the struggle was no longer just about taxes & documents — it was about family, dignity, and religious identity. events during the final struggle the sequence of events that followed was the closest thing to a mass uprising south africa's indian community had ever seen: year/event what happened step 1 illegal crossing into transvaal — indians defied the transvaal immigration restriction act openly. step 2 kasturba gandhi herself arrested. this galvanised the entire indian worker community. step 3 gandhiji organised a march of 2,000 workers into transvaal. arrested marchers rejoined after release, swelling numbers. step 4 all indian workers across the province went on strike. economic disruption became impossible to ignore. step 5 gokhale travelled across india, building indian public opinion & political pressure. step 6 viceroy hardinge10-16 publicly condemned the south african government’s treatment of indians — unprecedented diplomatic pressure from within the british empire itself. result the south african government came to the table. talks were held with gandhiji.

sections.title: Outcome — What Did Gandhiji Win?
sections.norm: outcome — what did gandhiji win?. conceding on all three key demands black act 1915. the negotiations concluded with the south african government conceding on all three key demands: i) poll tax abolished — the £3 annual penalty on ex-indentured labourers who chose to stay was removed. ii) registration certificates — the requirement under the black act was dropped. iii) indian marriages validated — marriages conducted under hindu, muslim & other rites were given legal recognition. these were not small victories. each one had direct, concrete impact on the lives of thousands of indian families. gandhiji returned to india in january 1915 — not as a defeated petitioner but as a leader who had won. ◆ the south african years did something that no amount of reading or debate could have done: they taught gandhiji that mass civil disobedience works. that ordinary people — not just educated elites — can be the soldiers of a non-violent movement. that the government's most powerful weapon (the law) can be neutralised when people voluntarily accept its punishment without fear. he would apply all of this in india. the laboratories of natal & transvaal produced the experiments that would be deployed at champaran, kheda, dandi & beyond.

sections.title: Quick Reference: Key Timeline
sections.norm: quick reference: key timeline. exam trap 1894 1885 nic inc not 1915 1917 2019 pyq hardinge. year event 1893 gandhiji arrives in south africa for a legal case; ejected from first-class at pietermaritzburg — his political catalyst. 1894 franchise amendment bill (natal) — indians to be disenfranchised. 1894 natal indian congress founded by gandhiji. 1895 immigration law amendment bill — poll tax or re-indenture. 1896–1906 constitutional phase: petitions, prayers, indian opinion newspaper. 1904 phoenix settlement established near durban, inspired by ruskin’s unto this last. 1906 black act (asiatic law amendment act, transvaal) — rc compulsory. 1906–1914 satyagraha against rcs via passive resistance association. 1907 transvaal immigration restriction act — inter-provincial movement barred. 1908 gandhiji jailed. prisons overflowing. 1910 tolstoy farm established for satyagrahis. 1912 gokhale visits; govt promises repeal; promise broken. 1913 sc invalidates non-christian marriages. poll tax campaign — movement goes mass. 1913 march of 2,000 workers. kasturba arrested. all-india strike. 1913 viceroy hardinge10-16 condemns south africa. talks begin. 1914 government agrees: poll tax abolished, rcs dropped, indian marriages validated. 1915 gandhiji returns to india. ⚠ exam trap the natal indian congress (1894) and the indian national congress (1885) are separate organisations founded in different countries for different contexts. do not confuse them. gandhiji founded the nic; he did not found the inc. ⚠ exam trap satyagraha was first developed & deployed in south africa — not in india. gandhiji brought it to india only after 1915. the champaran satyagraha (1917) was the first use of satyagraha on indian soil. ⚠ alert: examiner-tested anchor — mahatma gandhi was instrumental in the abolition of the system of indentured labour (prelims 2019). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Hind Swaraj (1909) — The Most Authentic Source
sections.norm: hind swaraj (1909) — the most authentic source. 1909. before we study gandhi's mass movements — non-cooperation, civil disobedience, quit india — it helps to first understand the man's mind. what did gandhi actually believe? what kind of india did he want? the most authentic source is hind swaraj, written in 1909 during a ten-day sea voyage, structured as a dialogue between a "reader" and an "editor." in it, gandhi takes positions that were unconventional — and remain so even today.

sections.title: What Kind of Nationalist Was Gandhi?
sections.norm: what kind of nationalist was gandhi?. cultural nationalist tradition that had been building 1875 ramakrishna mission 1897 took it further than any of his predecessors dressed like the masses ram rajya used religion to mobilise stronger social bond than class 1893 1896. gandhi was a cultural nationalist — and this places him in a tradition that had been building in india for several decades before he arrived. british racism had, ironically, provided a powerful stimulus to cultural nationalism. when the british looked down on indian civilisation as primitive & inferior, a generation of indians responded not by agreeing, but by asserting that indian civilisation was equally worthy of pride. swami dayanand saraswati & his arya samaj (1875), swami vivekananda & his ramakrishna mission (1897), and bankim chandra chattopadhyay all contributed to this cultural counter-assertion before gandhi arrived on the scene. (◆ cultural nationalism = the idea that a nation's identity is rooted in its civilisation, culture, and shared heritage — rather than in race, language, or territory alone. it is distinct from political nationalism, which is the demand for self-governance. the two often go together but are not the same thing.) gandhi stood in this tradition — but he took it further than any of his predecessors. he dressed like the masses, spoke the language of the masses, and invoked symbols the masses understood. when he spoke of ram rajya — the ideal kingdom of ram — he was not making a sectarian religious claim. he was reaching for a shared civilisational vocabulary that cut across class & caste in a way that constitutional arguments never could. when he used sita & draupadi as icons of suffering & resilience, he was drawing women — who had largely been spectators of the national movement — into its emotional ownership. he also used religion to mobilise — because in india, religion is a stronger social bond than class. (◆ this is something the moderates, with their constitutional petitions aimed at the western-educated middle class, never fully grasped. religion reached everyone.) but gandhi took the cultural nationalist argument all the way into a concrete economic & political programme — which is what made him unique among cultural nationalists. ◆ tilak used religion similarly — his ganesh chaturthi (1893) and shivaji festival (1896) mobilised masses through hindu pride. the key difference: tilak's religious mobilisation built combative nationalism; gandhi's aimed at universal inclusion across all communities. ◆ tagore shared gandhi's love of indian civilisation but feared that mass religious nationalism could slide into dangerous intolerance. gandhi's response: you cannot raise consciousness before you first mobilise the people.

sections.title: Was Gandhi Anti-Modern?
sections.norm: was gandhi anti-modern?. gandhi was not anti-modern criticised western modernity 1857 nation since ancient times civilisation, not race or language. a common misconception worth clearing at the outset. gandhi was not anti-modern. he criticised western modernity— the specific form that modernisation had taken in europe & america, built on industrial capitalism, the profit motive as sole purpose, and the coercive state. his critique was of the content of western modernity, not of reason, science, or human progress itself. his argument was pointed: modern western civilisations are godless — their only motive is profit, with no concern for morality. (◆ notice gandhi's persistent use of the language of morality. this connects directly to the pre-1857 & 1857 resistance movements, which were also framed in moral & religious terms — british rule as a polluter of the indian moral order. gandhi updated this civilisational resistance for a modern political context.) and in a striking moment of self-criticism, he argued that indians are themselves responsible for their own enslavement — because indian minds had adopted western capitalism, and doctors, lawyers, and railways had become instruments of an alien economic system looting india from within. ◆ swami dayanand saraswati made the same civilisational argument decades earlier — his call for swarajya was precisely this: indians enslaved themselves by abandoning their own heritage. gandhi extended dayanand's cultural argument into a full economic programme. india, he argued, is a nation since ancient times — and the basis of its oneness is civilisation, not race or language as in the western conception of nationhood. india's civilisational bond had held across millennia without railways or a centralised bureaucracy. the british had not created indian unity; they had disrupted it.

sections.title: Stateless Society and Enlightened Anarchism
sections.norm: stateless society and enlightened anarchism. stateless society same end-goal as marx swaraj every individual should be his own master self-rule of each individual critique of parliamentary democracy will of political parties, not the will of the people parliamentary democracy with a weak state transitional arrangement. gandhi believed in a stateless society — and here he arrives, from a completely different path, at the same end-goal as marx. (◆ both marx & gandhi envisioned the eventual withering away of the state. for marx it dissolves after the communist revolution; for gandhi, when individuals achieve perfect moral self-regulation. same destination, irreconcilably different journeys.) for gandhi, swaraj meant not merely national independence from britain, but that every individual should be his own master. the word swaraj — self-rule — he took entirely literally. in place of law made by a state, morality should guide individual behaviour. when there is perfect self-regulation, there is no need for even a representative democracy — let alone a coercive state. this is what gandhi called enlightened anarchism — true self-rule. gandhi wanted self-rule of each individual — not the home rule of the extremists, not the indirect democracy of the moderates, and not the class rule of marx. in place of the strong state-led democracy of the west, gandhi wanted village republics built on direct democracy & mutual cooperation. (◆ in the gram sabha, each villager is effectively an mp — this is direct democracy at its most literal. article 243 of the constitution, which establishes the gram sabha as the foundation of the panchayati raj system, is gandhi's most concrete institutional legacy in india's constitution.) his critique of parliamentary democracy was precise: multi-party democracy leads to the will of political parties, not the will of the people. the voter hands over power once every few years & is forgotten until the next election. (◆ this critique resonates strongly in india today — the debate about whether elected governments represent people or party high commands is alive in discussions around the anti-defection law, party whips overriding individual conscience, and the weakening of parliament as a deliberative institution.) ◆ tilak & nehru both wanted a strong central state to replace the british state. patel built one. bose wanted temporary authoritarian rule to eliminate poverty fast. gandhi was the only major leader who feared state power itself — not just british state power. ◆ ambedkar's sharpest disagreement with gandhi was precisely here: a strong state with constitutional law was the only protection the oppressed had. gandhi's village republic, in ambedkar's view, would simply be local caste dominance with a romantic name. gandhi was pragmatic enough to accept parliamentary democracy with a weak state as a transitional arrangement — but only until the higher morality required for a stateless society was achieved. it was a concession to present reality, not an endorsement of the model.

sections.title: The Economic Vision — Village Self-Sufficiency
sections.norm: the economic vision — village self-sufficiency. village-based, self-sufficient economy industrial revolution uproots rural masses 1958 1951. gandhi wanted india to return to a village-based, self-sufficient economy modelled on ancient india. the modern industrial revolution, in his view, uproots rural masses — tearing them from self-sufficient village life into urban factories where they are dependent, exploited, and cut off from their roots. ◆ on the industrial revolution, gandhi stood almost alone. marx, moderates, extremists, nehru, ambedkar — all were pro-ir. mao also turned anti-ir with his great leap forward (1958), but to protect communist power from the bourgeoisie industry creates. gandhi rejected it to protect the moral self-sufficiency of village life. same conclusion, entirely different reasoning. on land, gandhi opposed forceful redistribution — state coercion went against his core belief in morality over law. instead he favoured voluntary donation by landlords of their own moral accord. (◆ this directly inspired the bhoodan movement of vinoba bhave in telangana, 1951 — bhave walked village to village asking landlords to donate land to the landless. gandhi's morality-driven voluntary redistribution, brought to life.)

sections.title: Trusteeship and Arbitration — Reforming Capitalism Without Destroying
sections.norm: trusteeship and arbitration — reforming capitalism without destroying. did not demand the abolition or expropriation of capitalists trusteeship as a trustee 1920 1907. it gandhi did not demand the abolition or expropriation of capitalists. his concept of trusteeship was that a capitalist should hold his enterprise not merely for personal profit, but as a trustee — holding it on behalf of, and for the welfare of, his workers & the broader community. the ownership stays; the purpose of ownership changes. ◆ marx called capitalists parasites who must be expropriated by force. ambedkar wanted the state to control major industries. gandhi asked capitalists to reform themselves morally. the contrast says everything about the three approaches to inequality. for resolving disputes between workers & capitalists, gandhi preferred arbitration — transparent inquiry into both sides' accounts: the capitalist's balance sheet & the worker's cost of living — to find a just middle path, rather than strikes or lockouts that hardened conflict & caused economic disruption. (◆ gandhi applied the same arbitration principle to political disputes. in 1920, he united the moderates & extremists — split since surat (1907) — through the method of satyagraha: moderates accepted non-cooperation & civil disobedience; extremists gave up violence. each side gave up something; both gained a mass movement. that was arbitration in political form.)

sections.title: Universal Disarmament — Not Abstract Pacifism
sections.norm: universal disarmament — not abstract pacifism. the arms act of 1878 viceroy lytton76-80 lytton. gandhi favoured universal disarmament — but this was not naive idealism. it had a precise indian context. the arms act of 1878 under viceroy lytton76-80 had disarmed indian civilians while exempting anglo-indians & eurasians. the colonial state was arming itself while disarming the colonised. gandhi's demand for universal disarmament was a direct challenge to this asymmetry — disarmament is just only when it is universal, not when it is a colonial tool to keep one side defenceless.

sections.title: The Method of Satyagraha
sections.norm: the method of satyagraha. what was his method satyagraha truth-force extra-constitutional, non-violent mass struggle a third path non-cooperation civil disobedience constructive work non-violence militarily superior morally superior strategic logic truthful legitimacy of demands fearless non-violence is not cowardice non-violent widens participation ready to accept suffering loves the evil doer morally superior god is on the side of truth. so if gandhi rejected the moderates' petitions & the revolutionaries' violence, what was his method? satyagraha — literally "truth-force" or "soul-force." it was an extra-constitutional, non-violent mass struggle. not working within the system (moderates), not armed resistance (revolutionaries), but a third path: civil disobedience, non-cooperation, and peaceful mass non-compliance, combined with constructive work. satyagraha = non-cooperation + civil disobedience + constructive work + non-violence + spirituality/morality. the moral logic was this: the british were militarily superior — gandhi never denied it. but satyagrahis could be morally superior. there was also a precise strategic logic beyond the moral one: if a satyagrahi turns violent, it gives the british a justification for their own repression. the oppressor can say "they attacked first." non-violence removes that justification entirely. it also makes large-scale, long-duration movements possible — because anyone can participate, not just the physically strong or the armed. what qualities must a satyagrahi have? 8.1) truthful — truth increases the legitimacy of demands & gives personal courage; the satyagrahi has nothing to hide 8.2) fearless — non-violence is not cowardice; it demands far more courage than picking up a weapon 8.3) non-violent — this widens participation & reduces the risk of repression, enabling bigger & longer movements 8.4) ready to accept suffering; hate alien to his nature; loves the evil doer — (◆ the logic here is precise: if the satyagrahi responds to violence with calm dignity & love, the evil doer is forced to confront his own immorality. if the satyagrahi retaliates, the oppressor gets a moral escape route — "he attacked me first." non-violence removes that escape route.) 8.5) morally superior — this gave satyagrahis the inner courage & conviction that god is on the side of truth & morality ◆ bose's counter-argument: "give me blood, and i shall give you freedom." he believed a nation still in chains has no luxury of clean methods. gandhi's reply was implicit: a nation born of violence will remain violent. both arguments have never been fully settled. ◆ swami vivekananda's "strength is life, weakness is death" is often contrasted with gandhi's non-violence. but both agreed on fearlessness — vivekananda built the inner strength; gandhi channelled it into organised mass action.

sections.title: Two Principles That Defined Gandhi's Character
sections.norm: two principles that defined gandhi's character. do not benefit from the weakness of the evil doer rowlatt act 1919 1917 ww1 ww2 . first — do not benefit from the weakness of the evil doer. gandhi stood on the side of justice, not merely on the side of india. this is why he supported britain in both ww1 & ww2 , despite india still being under colonial rule. he would not exploit britain's moment of vulnerability for india's political advantage. a satyagrahi does not take what has not been earned through moral force. ◆ tilak took the opposite pragmatic position — he was willing to use ww1 as leverage to extract political concessions from a pressured britain. bose went further & allied with the axis powers to fight britain. gandhi refused both approaches on moral grounds. second — he hated breach of promise. rooted in his deepest commitment to truth. when the british broke a promise — as they did with the rowlatt act (1919), which came after montague's 1917 promise of greater self-governance — gandhi's response was not calculated political strategy. it was a moral response to a moral wrong. his entry into each campaign was typically triggered by this precise gap: between what was promised & what was delivered.

sections.title: The Strategic Method — Rising Tempo, Controlled Movement, and S-CW-S
sections.norm: the strategic method — rising tempo, controlled movement, and s-cw-s. distinctive rhythm & internal discipline set him apart from every leader rising tempo escalated gradually 1922 inc ramakrishna mission. gandhi's approach to mass movements had a distinctive rhythm & internal discipline that set him apart from every leader before him. rising tempo: he did not launch civil disobedience from day one. he began with lighter forms — signature campaigns, public meetings, hartals — and escalated gradually. each step gave the british a chance to respond; each refusal to respond gave the movement greater moral authority & popular momentum. the intensity rose like a tide, deliberately & steadily. controlled mass movement: gandhi insisted on strict adherence by the masses to the programme decided. spontaneous, uncoordinated agitation was dangerous — it led to violence, which he would then have to withdraw. (◆ this is why chauri chaura in february 1922 — where a mob burned a police station killing 22 policemen — led gandhi to withdraw the entire non-cooperation movement even as it was at its peak. to critics this looked like betrayal at the movement's most powerful moment. to gandhi, it was keeping a promise of non-violence. a satyagrahi who benefits from the mob's violence violates the same principle as one who benefits from the enemy's weakness.) struggle–constructive work–struggle (s-cw-s): the masses get tired — especially economically. sustained boycotts mean lost income; sustained hartals mean lost livelihoods. economic exhaustion leads to desperation, and desperation leads to violence. gandhi knew this. so the truce phase was never idle — it was filled with constructive work: atmashakti (inner strengthening), training in satyagraha, building inc's organisational network, identifying local leaders, raising political awareness at the grassroots. (◆ constructive work as nation-building had a lineage before gandhi: swami vivekananda's ramakrishna mission (1897) → arya samaj's dav schools → tagore's shantiniketan (1901) → tilak's constructive swadeshi → gandhi's tolstoy farm (1910, south africa) and sabarmati ashram (1917). each built on the one before. gandhi absorbed this entire tradition & made constructive work the structural middle phase of every movement.) the passive phase was preparation, not rest. s-t-s was really s-cw-s (political struggle — constructive work — political struggle).

sections.title: Why Was Satyagraha So Strategically Effective?
sections.norm: why was satyagraha so strategically effective?. 1907 allowed the common man & woman to participate opened the freedom struggle to peasants, women, workers prevent british repression propaganda disaster. 11.1) it united moderates & extremists. moderates were attracted to non-violence; extremists were attracted to mass struggle. satyagraha offered both — it was the bridge that healed the split of surat (1907). (◆ this is one of gandhi's most underrated achievements — he brought together two factions that had been bitterly divided for over a decade, simply by choosing a method that each could find something in.) 11.2) it allowed the common man & woman to participate. armed struggle requires weapons & military training. satyagraha requires only courage & conviction. this opened the freedom struggle to peasants, women, workers, and ordinary citizens who had previously been spectators. this is the democratic revolution within the freedom struggle — gandhi made it truly mass by making the method accessible to every indian regardless of age, gender, or class. 11.3) it had the potential to prevent british repression. when satyagrahis remained non-violent, violent british crackdowns became a propaganda disaster — in britain's parliament, in british public opinion, and increasingly in international opinion. the moral optics were devastating for the empire.

sections.title: The Inclusive Approach — Why Swaraj Was Deliberately Never Defined
sections.norm: the inclusive approach — why swaraj was deliberately never defined. plural nature of indian society never precisely defined deliberate political architecture swaraj meant different things to different sections simple attire invocation of ram rajya movement was personally theirs. gandhi was fully aware of the plural nature of indian society — its caste divisions, religious communities, linguistic diversity, and class differences. he made a strategic choice that is easy to miss: he never precisely defined the political goal of swaraj. this was not vagueness. it was deliberate political architecture. swaraj meant different things to different sections — to a peasant it meant end of high rents; to a worker, better wages; to a woman, dignity & agency; to a nationalist intellectual, self-governance. by leaving the definition open, gandhi maximised the support base of the movement across india's entire social plurality. his simple attire, his use of hindi, his invocation of ram rajya, and his use of icons like sita & draupadi allowed the masses — who would never attend a constitutional conference — to feel that this movement was personally theirs. ◆ jinnah's sharpest criticism of gandhi was this very ambiguity — he argued that "swaraj" was a hindu cultural concept dressed as a national one, and that muslim political interests could never be safe inside its undefined borders. gandhi's counter was that swaraj's deliberate openness was precisely what made it inclusive of all. ◆ tagore's worry was the mirror image: that undefined mass emotion — even well-intentioned — could become narrow & intolerant. gandhi's response remained the same: mobilise first, refine after. you cannot teach philosophy to an empty stomach.

sections.title: Key Intellectual Influences on Gandhi
sections.norm: key intellectual influences on gandhi. upsc 1862 phoenix settlement 1904 2011 1894 1910 1849 nishkama karma personal moral compass sermon on the mount teaching of non-violence. gandhi's ideology did not emerge in isolation — it was a synthesis shaped by several powerful texts & thinkers, both indian & western. understanding these influences is essential because upsc frequently tests them, and because they explain why gandhi's worldview combined spirituality, economics, and political resistance in a way no predecessor's did. 13.1) john ruskin — unto this last (1862): gandhi himself said this book "transformed my life." ruskin argued that the good of the individual lies in the good of all, that manual labour — the work of the farmer, the barber, the craftsman — has the same dignity as intellectual labour, and that a life of labour is truly worth living. gandhi read it on a train journey in south africa & was so moved that he immediately founded the phoenix settlement (1904) near durban — a cooperative community based on ruskin's principles of shared manual work & simple living. (⚠ prelims 2011 asked about the link between ruskin's unto this last & gandhi.) 13.2) leo tolstoy — the kingdom of god is within you (1894): tolstoy's central argument was that the state, the military, and the church all rest on organised violence — and that a morally self-regulated individual needs none of them. non-resistance to evil by force, and moral self-regulation as the only legitimate basis for society — these ideas struck gandhi with tremendous force. he corresponded directly with tolstoy & named the tolstoy farm (1910) near johannesburg after him — a satyagraha training commune that became the prototype for his later indian ashrams. 13.3) henry david thoreau — civil disobedience (1849): thoreau argued that when a law is unjust, the citizen has a moral duty to disobey it — that obedience to an unjust state is itself a moral failure. gandhi found in thoreau the western intellectual articulation of what he was already practising in south africa. the very term "civil disobedience" entered gandhi's political vocabulary through thoreau, and it became one of the two pillars of satyagraha alongside non-cooperation. 13.4) bhagavad gita — nishkama karma: the gita's doctrine of nishkama karma — action performed as duty without attachment to its result — was gandhi's personal moral compass throughout his life. it gave him the spiritual grounding to act decisively in politics while remaining inwardly detached from power, fame, or personal gain. he called the gita his "spiritual dictionary" and read from it every day. 13.5) sermon on the mount (new testament): christ's teaching of non-violence — turning the other cheek, loving one's enemy, overcoming evil with good — reinforced gandhi's conviction that non-violence was not passive weakness but the highest form of moral courage. the sermon on the mount & the gita together formed the twin spiritual pillars of ahimsa as gandhi understood it. (◆ notice how gandhi drew simultaneously from hindu, christian, and western secular traditions. this intellectual eclecticism was not accidental — it was central to his claim that satyagraha was a universal moral method, not a hindu religious one. it also made him credible to audiences across civilisational divides, from south africa to london to rural india.)

sections.title: Summary: The Core of Gandhian Ideology
sections.norm: summary: the core of gandhian ideology. civilisation civilisation — not race or language western civilisation is godless stateless society through enlightened anarchism village republics return to village self-sufficiency trusteeship over expropriation reject class concept & class war anti-untouchability phoenix settlement 2023 2016. 14.1) civilisation: india is a nation since ancient times; its civilisation — not race or language — is the source of its unity & values; western civilisation is godless, driven only by profit 14.2) state: ideal = stateless society through enlightened anarchism; interim = parliamentary democracy with a weak state + village republics as direct democracy 14.3) economy: reject industrial revolution & western capitalism; return to village self-sufficiency; trusteeship over expropriation; voluntary land redistribution through morality 14.4) society: reject class concept & class war; varnashram as non-hierarchical, non-hereditary guild-based cooperation; anti-untouchability as personal moral priority 14.5) method: satyagraha = nc + cd + cw + non-violence + morality; rising tempo; controlled disciplined mass movement; never exploit weakness of opponent; hate breach of promise 14.6) strategy: s-cw-s; ambiguous swaraj to maximise support across plural india; inclusive approach bringing all sections on to the streets 14.7) intellectual roots: ruskin (dignity of labour, phoenix settlement), tolstoy (non-resistance, tolstoy farm), thoreau (civil disobedience as moral duty), bhagavad gita (nishkama karma), sermon on the mount (love the enemy, turn the other cheek) (⚠ exam-linking cues: gandhi vs tagore — contrast nai talim (vocational) vs shantiniketan (creative); tagore warned against hyper-nationalism → tested in mains 2023. gandhi vs bose — contrast means vs ends; village republics vs heavy industrialisation → tested in mains 2016. for detailed point-by-point comparisons, see comparative tables in the companion chapter.)

sections.title: Table — Major Fasts of Mahatma Gandhi
sections.norm: table — major fasts of mahatma gandhi. upsc 1932 1933. (◆ gandhi's fasts were never random acts of self-denial — each was a precisely calibrated political or moral instrument. some targeted the british; others targeted indians themselves. understanding the specific trigger & objective of each fast is essential for upsc, which has asked about individual fasts in both prelims & mains.) fast year location trigger / reason outcome / significance 1. ahmedabad mill workers' fast 1918 ahmedabad mill workers' strike was weakening; workers losing resolve in their demand for a 35% wage hike workers held firm; mill owners agreed to arbitration; gandhi's first fast on indian soil — established fasting as a satyagraha tool 2. fast during non-cooperation movement withdrawal 1922 delhi chauri chaura violence (february 1922) — a mob burned a police station killing 22 policemen; gandhi withdrew ncm & fasted for five days as penance demonstrated that gandhi would sacrifice political momentum to preserve non-violence; controversial within congress 3. 21-day fast for hindu-muslim unity 1924 delhi (at the house of muhammad ali) widespread hindu-muslim communal riots across india, particularly after the kohat riots drew national attention to communal violence; temporarily shamed both communities into a fragile truce; reinforced gandhi's moral authority on communal harmony 4. epic fast (fast against communal award) 1932 yerwada jail, pune ramsay macdonald's communal award granted separate electorates to depressed classes — gandhi saw this as a permanent division of hindu society resulted in the poona pact (september 1932) — ambedkar agreed to joint electorates with reserved seats instead of separate electorates; number of reserved seats increased from 71 to 147 5. 21-day fast for self-purification 1933 yerwada jail, pune continuation of the anti-untouchability campaign; gandhi wanted to pressure caste hindus to open temples & wells to dalits government temporarily released him from jail fearing his death; accelerated the temple entry movement across india 6. fast in rajkot 1939 rajkot the thakore sahib of rajkot broke a promise to introduce political reforms; gandhi saw this as a breach of promise — his deepest moral trigger viceroy linlithgow intervened; the fast highlighted princely state misgovernance; however, the reforms were never fully implemented 7. 21-day fast during quit india detention 1943 aga khan palace, pune british accused gandhi of responsibility for quit india violence; gandhi denied this & fasted to assert his innocence & protest his detention without trial the viceroy refused to release him; gandhi nearly died; kasturba & mahadev desai both died during this detention period; international attention intensified on british treatment of indian leaders 8. fast for calcutta peace 1947 (september) calcutta (hydari mansion, beliaghata) horrific hindu-muslim rioting in calcutta following partition & the great calcutta killings of 1946;
