violence was spiralling out of control the "calcutta miracle" — rioting stopped within days; both hindu & muslim leaders came to gandhi & pledged peace; lord mountbatten called it a one-man boundary force 9. fast for delhi peace 1948 (january) birla house, new delhi communal violence in delhi against muslims following partition; hindu & sikh refugees from pakistan were attacking muslim residents; the government was failing to protect minorities delhi leaders signed a seven-point pledge guaranteeing muslim safety; mosques occupied by refugees were vacated; gandhi broke the fast — but was assassinated twelve days later on 30 january 1948 (⚠ exam trap: do not confuse the 1932 epic fast (against separate electorates for dalits) with the 1933 fast (for temple entry). the trigger, location, and objective were different — upsc has tested this distinction.)

sections.title: Table — Publications of Mahatma Gandhi
sections.norm: table — publications of mahatma gandhi. 1933 upsc. (◆ gandhi was not just a political leader — he was a prolific writer & editor. his newspapers & books were not commercial ventures; they were instruments of the freedom struggle, carrying his ideology directly to the reading public. several of these publications are directly exam-relevant.) publication type year started / published language key theme / focus 1. indian opinion newspaper 1903 english, gujarati, hindi, tamil founded in durban, south africa; voice of the indian community in south africa; covered issues of racial discrimination, passive resistance, and indian rights; ran until 1961 2. hind swaraj book 1909 gujarati (english translation 1910) the most authentic source of gandhi's ideology; written as a dialogue between "reader" and "editor" on a sea voyage; critiqued western civilisation, modern machinery, and parliamentary democracy; argued india is a nation since ancient times 3. young india weekly journal 1919 english succeeded the bombay chronicle as gandhi's primary english-language platform; carried his views on non-cooperation, khilafat, swaraj, swadeshi, and untouchability; ran until 1932 4. navajivan weekly journal 1919 gujarati gujarati counterpart of young india; reached the non-english-reading masses; carried the same political & social reform messaging in accessible language; ran until 1932 5. harijan weekly journal 1933 english launched after young india ceased; specifically focused on the anti-untouchability campaign & the uplift of depressed classes; the very name "harijan" (children of god) was gandhi's term for dalits; ran until 1948 6. harijan bandhu weekly journal 1933 gujarati gujarati edition of harijan; carried the anti-untouchability message to gujarat's reading public 7. harijan sevak weekly journal 1933 hindi hindi edition of harijan; extended the anti-untouchability campaign to the hindi-speaking heartland 8. the story of my experiments with truth autobiography 1927–1929 (serialised) gujarati (english translation 1940) gandhi's autobiography; covered his life from childhood through the south africa years to the early indian movements; personal — discussed his moral struggles, dietary experiments, celibacy vow (brahmacharya), and the evolution of satyagraha 9. satyagraha in south africa book 1928 gujarati (english translation 1950) detailed account of the south african indian resistance movement (1893–1914); documented the birth & development of satyagraha as a political method 10. constructive programme: its meaning & place booklet 1941 (revised 1945) english outlined the 18-point constructive programme — communal unity, removal of untouchability, prohibition, khadi, village industries, new education (nai talim), adult education, women's uplift, health & hygiene, provincial languages, national language (hindustani), economic equality, farmers, labour, adivasis, lepers, students 11. key to health book 1942 gujarati gandhi's views on diet, hygiene, nature cure, and physical self-sufficiency; reflected his belief that bodily discipline was inseparable from moral discipline 12. the collected works of mahatma gandhi compilation published 1958–1994 (posthumous) english 100 volumes covering all of gandhi's writings, speeches, and correspondence from 1884 to 1948; the definitive scholarly reference; published by the government of india (◆ notice the pattern: indian opinion in south africa → young india + navajivan during the 1920s movements → harijan series from 1933 onward when the anti-untouchability campaign became central. each publication phase maps directly to a phase of gandhi's political strategy. upsc has tested specific publications — particularly hind swaraj & young india — in both prelims & mains.)

sections.title: Table — Arrests and Imprisonments of Mahatma Gandhi
sections.norm: table — arrests and imprisonments of mahatma gandhi. upsc 1922 1942 ww2 . (◆ gandhi's imprisonments were not incidental to his career — they were central to the satyagraha method itself. a satyagrahi who accepts imprisonment without resistance demonstrates moral superiority over the state that jails him. each arrest also generated massive public sympathy & international attention, turning the courtroom & the prison into platforms for the freedom struggle. upsc has tested specific imprisonments — particularly the 1922 trial & the 1942 detention.) arrest year location of arrest trigger / reason trial / legal proceedings imprisonment details significance 1. first arrest in south africa 1906 johannesburg, transvaal defiance of the transvaal asiatic registration act (the "black act") requiring indians to carry registration certificates & submit to fingerprinting tried under the black act; pleaded guilty sentenced to 2 months simple imprisonment in johannesburg jail; released early after a compromise with general smuts gandhi's first experience of imprisonment as a political tool; established the principle of voluntarily courting arrest 2. second arrest in south africa 1908 johannesburg burned registration certificates at a mass meeting; re-arrested for refusing to carry the pass tried for failing to produce registration certificate sentenced to 2 months hard labour in volksrust jail demonstrated escalation within satyagraha — from defiance to public destruction of the hated documents 3. third arrest in south africa 1913 volksrust, natal border led the great march of indian miners from newcastle across the natal-transvaal border in defiance of immigration laws; protested the £3 tax on indentured labourers & the invalidation of non-christian marriages arrested multiple times during the march (arrested & released three times within days) sentenced to 9 months imprisonment with hard labour; released after negotiations led directly to the indian relief act (1914) — abolished the £3 tax, recognised indian marriages, and eased immigration restrictions; gandhi's final & greatest south african victory 4. first arrest in india (champaran) 1917 motihari, champaran, bihar arrived to investigate the grievances of indigo farmers under the tinkathia system; ordered by the district magistrate to leave champaran immediately; refused appeared before the magistrate at motihari; case withdrawn by the government under public pressure released immediately; the government appointed the champaran agrarian committee with gandhi as a member gandhi's first civil disobedience on indian soil; proved that the british would back down when confronted with non-violent moral force backed by mass support 5. arrest during rowlatt satyagraha 1919 palwal (on a train en route to delhi from bombay) called for a nationwide hartal against the rowlatt act; travelling to delhi to lead protests; government feared his presence would intensify agitation detained under orders of the punjab government; no formal trial taken off the train at palwal & sent back to bombay under police escort; not formally imprisoned triggered widespread protests & hartals across india; the news of gandhi's arrest directly contributed to the escalation that culminated in the jallianwala bagh massacre (13 april 1919) 6. the great trial 1922 ahmedabad (sabarmati ashram) charged for three seditious articles published in young india — "tampering with loyalty," "the puzzle & its solution," and "shaking the mane" tried before judge c.n. broomfield at the ahmedabad sessions court; gandhi pleaded guilty & delivered his famous courtroom speech asking the judge to impose the maximum penalty; judge broomfield called him "a man of high ideals & noble life" before sentencing him sentenced to 6 years imprisonment; held at yerwada central jail, pune; released early in february 1924 after an appendicitis operation the most celebrated trial of the indian freedom struggle; gandhi turned the courtroom into a stage for the moral indictment of british rule; his statement became a foundational document of the independence movement 7. arrest during salt satyagraha 1930 karadi, near dandi, gujarat (5 may 1930 — one month after completing the dandi march on 6 april) announced intention to raid the dharasana salt works; arrested at midnight under regulation xxv of 1827 (a colonial-era regulation requiring no trial) no trial — detained under an executive regulation that permitted imprisonment without judicial proceedings held at yerwada central jail, pune; released in january 1931 ahead of the gandhi-irwin pact negotiations arrest under a regulation with no trial exposed the arbitrary nature of colonial law; the dharasana salt works raid (led by sarojini naidu & abbas tyabji after gandhi's arrest) produced the iconic scenes of non-violent resisters being beaten — webb miller's press report shocked the world 8. arrest after breakdown of gandhi-irwin pact 1932 bombay (on return from the second round table conference in london) lord willingdon's government launched a massive crackdown on congress; gandhi was arrested within a week of landing in india for resuming civil disobedience no formal trial — detained under emergency ordinances held at yerwada central jail, pune; this was the imprisonment during which he undertook the epic fast (1932) against the communal award, leading to the poona pact; also the 1933 fast for self-purification; released in 1933 one of gandhi's longest & most politically productive imprisonments; the poona pact fundamentally reshaped the dalit political landscape 9. arrest during individual satyagraha 1940–1941 wardha / sevagram launched individual satyagraha against india's participation in ww2 without indian consent; selected individual satyagrahis (starting with vinoba bhave) to court arrest one by one no formal trial — detained under the defence of india rules (dir) detained briefly; released after a few weeks as the british did not want to escalate the situation during the war a deliberately restrained movement — gandhi kept the tempo low to maintain pressure without provoking a violent crackdown during wartime 10. arrest during quit india movement 1942 bombay (9 august 1942 — the morning after the "do or die" speech at the gowalia tank maidan) passed the quit india resolution at the aicc session on 8 august 1942; gave the famous "do or die" call; the entire congress leadership was arrested within hours in a pre-planned british operation no trial — detained under the defence of india rules (dir); the british government refused to try gandhi, fearing a repeat of the 1922 courtroom triumph held at the aga khan palace, pune, from august 1942 to may 1944 (nearly 21 months); kasturba gandhi died here on 22 february 1944; mahadev desai (gandhi's secretary) died here on 15 august 1942 gandhi's last & longest imprisonment; the leaderless movement exploded into the most widespread underground resistance of the entire freedom struggle; the british lost moral legitimacy permanently — within five years of this arrest, they left india (⚠ exam traps: i) the 1922 trial is the only major instance where gandhi was formally tried in a courtroom in india — most other detentions were under executive orders or emergency regulations with no trial. ii) do not confuse the 1930 arrest (salt satyagraha, no trial, regulation xxv of 1827) with the 1932 arrest (post-rtc, emergency ordinances) — both led to yerwada jail, but the triggers & legal bases were different. iii) the 1942 detention was at the aga khan palace, not yerwada — upsc has tested this distinction.)

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: The Three Pilot Projects (1917–1918)
sections.norm: the three pilot projects (1917–1918). arrived in india in january 1915 satyagraha ashram at kochrab sabarmati. gandhi (mg) arrived in india in january 1915. he did not rush into mass politics. he founded the satyagraha ashram at kochrab (1915), later relocated to sabarmati (1917), and travelled, listened, and understood the country for nearly two years before he acted. when he finally did, he chose three small, specific, carefully picked local struggles — one in bihar in 1917, two in gujarat in 1918 — and used each to test a different method. champaran tested passive resistance & civil disobedience. ahmedabad tested a mill strike, hunger strike, and arbitration. kheda tested non-cooperation through a no-revenue movement. together, these three form the laboratory in which gandhian mass politics was invented. ⚠ alert: pilot-projects pyq cluster. prelims 2005 (champaran-rajendra prasad pair); prelims 2007 (first indian satyagraha site = champaran); prelims 2008 (teacher-by-profession gandhian = j.b. kripalani); prelims 2011 (kheda satyagraha — plague-period revenue suspension issue); prelims 2018 (champaran significance — first civil disobedience on indian soil). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Champaran Satyagraha, 1917 — The First Civil Disobedience
sections.norm: champaran satyagraha, 1917 — the first civil disobedience. champaran satyagraha rajkumar shukla tinkathia system indigo plantation had shifted almost entirely to bihar german synthetic dyes 2.1) events champaran agricultural act 1918 ww1 . the champaran satyagraha - rajkumar shukla, a peasant leader from bihar, met mg at the lucknow session of the inc in 1916 & requested him to visit champaran. the grievance was the tinkathia system — ryots were forced to cultivate indigo on 3/20th of their land under contracts with british planters. (tinkathia literally refers to three kathas — a unit of land measurement. three kathas out of every twenty had to be under indigo cultivation as per contracts signed with planters.) after the indigo revolt (1859-60) in bengal, indigo plantation had shifted almost entirely to bihar by 1863. german synthetic dyes became popular after 1895 & began eating into the indigo market globally — but during ww1 , those dyes were unavailable. the planters now had a fresh incentive to extract maximum profits, and they pushed the tinkathia system harder than ever. 2.1) events mg arrived in champaran. british authorities ordered him to leave the district. he refused. this refusal — to comply with a direct official order — was the act of civil disobedience. he courted arrest. the government, uncertain how to handle the situation, made mg the head of an inquiry committee to investigate peasant grievances. he used this access to systematically document the exploitation. finally, he convinced the administration to abolish the tinkathia system. the british passed the champaran agricultural act, 1918 — though planter oppression did not fully stop even after it. ◆ the hallmark of champaran: civil disobedience. mg disobeyed a direct official order, accepted its legal consequence, and forced the system to follow method of arbitration. the outcome — an inquiry committee, then legislation resolving decades old grievance.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Ahmedabad Mill Strike, 1918 — The First Hunger Strike
sections.norm: ahmedabad mill strike, 1918 — the first hunger strike. new technique of arbitration 1st hunger strike 3.1) what was the grievance? ww1 arbitration board 27.5% wage increase 3.2) impact 1920 1928 2009 pyq ww1 . hallmark: new technique of arbitration + 1st hunger strike mg was invited to ahmedabad by anasuya sarabhai, a social worker. her brother ambalal sarabhai headed the ahmedabad mill owners' association. when mill workers went on strike, mg found himself in the middle of a dispute between the two sides — an awkward position, since he knew both parties personally. 3.1) what was the grievance? during ww1 , ahmedabad had been hit by plague deaths. to compensate workers for the risk of working through the epidemic, mill owners had been paying a plague bonus. once the worst of the plague was over, they discontinued it — even as ww1 inflation (compounded by the spanish flu epidemic) was crushing the purchasing power of workers. the demand of workers was a 50% wage increase. mill owners refused to even negotiate until all strikes ended first. mg stepped in & demanded a 35% wage increase. he began a fast unto death — directed as moral pressure at the mill owners. the fast also made it difficult for workers to abandon the strike (no one wants to be the reason their champion starves). an arbitration board was set up & settled on a 27.5% wage increase. 3.2) impact this strike laid the foundation of the working-class movement in ahmedabad, leading directly to the formation of the textile labour association in 1920. (make a wider connection: 1920 was a landmark year for organised labour in india. the all india trade union congress (aituc) was also formed in 1920 by lala lajpat rai — the first all-india organisation of the working class. and the communist party of india (cpi) was set up in 1920 in tashkent under m.n. roy, later reconstituted inside india in 1925. the working class was finding its political voice at exactly this moment.) ◆ two hallmarks: the first hunger strike by mg, and arbitration as method — finding an economic midpoint rather than a winner-takes-all outcome. this "midpath through arbitration" will reappear in bardoli 1928. ⚠ alert: prelims 2009 (ahmedabad textile labour association founder = mahatma gandhi himself, 1920). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Kheda Satyagraha, 1918 — The First Non-Cooperation Movement
sections.norm: kheda satyagraha, 1918 — the first non-cooperation movement. 1st non-cooperation / no revenue movement 4.1) what was the grievance? 1918 ww1 4.2) mg's action 4.3) impact 4.4) why is kheda called non-cooperation & not civil disobedience? war conference (delhi, 1918) ww1 . hallmark: 1st non-cooperation / no revenue movement 4.1) what was the grievance? under the ryotwari settlement system, farmers in kheda district of gujarat were entitled by law to a remission — a reduction — of land revenue (lr) if their crop yield fell below one-quarter of normal output. the 1918 harvest had failed. plague had compounded the misery. the government refused to grant the legally mandated remission — it needed money for ww1 , and the legal right of the ryots was inconvenient. 4.2) mg's action mg asked peasants to withhold payment of lr. the government eventually agreed not to confiscate the property of those who could not pay — effectively conceding the principle that only those who could pay would be required to do so. 4.3) impact sardar vallabhbhai patel became a follower of mg through this movement. kheda was patel's first experience of organised mass action. 4.4) why is kheda called non-cooperation & not civil disobedience? (an important conceptual exam distinction. when the goal is swaraj & we refuse to pay tax, it is civil disobedience — we are questioning the very right of the british to tax us. but in kheda, the goal was not swaraj. the ryots were not refusing to pay tax permanently. they were temporarily withholding payment because the law was on their side — crop failure legally entitled them to remission, and the government was violating its own law. the quarrel was not with the tax itself but with the government's refusal to apply its own legal provisions correctly. it is comparable to a businessman who accepts he must pay tax but disputes the assessed amount & approaches the courts — that is lawful resistance, not defiance of the state's fundamental authority. moreover, the law supported the ryots. hence, non-cooperation: withholding cooperation with an unjust action, without challenging colonial sovereignty as such.) between kheda & rowlatt came a telling episode. at the viceroy's war conference (delhi, 1918), mg actively supported the resolution to recruit indians for the ww1 — unlike many leaders who held back. his reasoning was that wartime help would be repaid with self-government; this is why the rowlatt act (next section) felt to him like a broken promise.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Rowlatt Satyagraha — April 1919
sections.norm: rowlatt satyagraha — april 1919. 5.1) what was the rowlatt act? inc 1919 ilc rowlatt act revolutionary crimes act home rule leagues lucknow pact of 1916 hindu-muslim cooperation goi act 1919 the act india act 1915 that act ww1 1917 1920 1925 5.2) why did mg react so strongly? 5.3) events 1st mass strike & the 1st all-india movement danger of mass politics without adequate organisation 1940 5.4) 13 april 1919 — jallianwala bagh jallianwala bagh in amritsar baisakhi general dyer ordered his troops to open fire 1,500 1913–15 5.5) results of rowlatt satyagraha 1st mass strike + 1st all-india movement beginning of mass politics high participation in urban areas low in rural areas revolutionary crime act 1919 chelmsford16-21 ww1 chelmsford. 5.1) what was the rowlatt act? the rowlatt satyagraha was called by mg alone — not by the inc. mg had not yet taken control of the inc; it was still not under his direction. in february 1919, the imperial legislative council (ilc) passed what became known as the rowlatt act — the anarchical & revolutionary crimes act. it was based on recommendations of a sedition committee chaired by justice s.a.t. rowlatt. two bills were produced by the committee & passed together as one act. note on the political context: the home rule leagues (tilak's and annie besant's, 1916-18) had built mass political mobilisation, and the lucknow pact of 1916 had brought hindu-muslim cooperation under inc. the imperial legislative council members at the time of the rowlatt bill — including jinnah, madan mohan malaviya, and mazharul haq — drew on the home rule political consciousness when they jointly resigned in 1919 to protest the bill. this is why upsc 2015 pyq on 'which leaders were associated with the home rule movement?' is also derivable from this section's context. (note carefully: this was passed by the ilc, not the central legislative assembly (cla). the cla came into existence only in december 1919 under the goi act 1919 — the montford reforms being finalised at this very time.) the act extended the emergency powers of the defence of india act 1915 into peacetime. that act had been enacted specifically for the duration of ww1 (1914–19) — the powers to detain without trial, suppress press freedom, try cases without juries. now the british wanted to keep those draconian powers permanently. critically, the act was passed despite unanimous opposition from every single indian member of the ilc. every indian member voted against it. it passed anyway. why? two reasons. first, the masses were restless — ww1 had brought inflation, food insecurity, and unemployment, and the spanish flu had killed an estimated 12 million indians. second, the british were alarmed by the october revolution of 1917 in russia. the communist party of india was set up in 1920 in tashkent under m.n. roy (and later reconstituted inside india in 1925). the fear of communist revolution spreading to colonial india was real to the british. 5.2) why did mg react so strongly? for mg this was a breach of promise. the montague statement of 1917 had spoken of india's gradual march towards self-government. the montford reforms — goi act 1919 — were being framed at the very same time. and yet, at this moment of apparent concession, the british wanted to retain their most coercive wartime powers in permanent peacetime law. mg gave a call for a nationwide non-violent strike — the first call for a nationwide action of this kind in indian history. 5.3) events it was the 1st mass strike & the 1st all-india movement — and it immediately revealed both the potential & the danger of mass politics without adequate organisation. mg's arrest, along with those of other leaders, left the movement without direction. (a truck moving at 200 km/hr with no driver — that is what mass energy without leadership becomes.) widespread violence followed, especially in punjab, where inc leaders dr. satya pal & dr. saifuddin kitchlew had already been arrested. under lieutenant governor o'dwyer, general dyer (colonel reginald dyer) applied martial law in punjab with o'dwyer's approval. public gatherings were banned. (future linkage: o'dwyer was assassinated by udham singh in london in 1940 — retribution for his role in the jallianwala bagh massacre.) 5.4) 13 april 1919 — jallianwala bagh people had gathered peacefully in the enclosed garden of jallianwala bagh in amritsar — to celebrate baisakhi & to protest the arrest of their leaders. without any warning, general dyer ordered his troops to open fire. the firing continued for 10 minutes. the garden's exits were narrow & blocked; people were trapped. official british records counted 379 dead. the inc's count was 1,500 dead. dyer later told the hunter committee — set up in october 1919, report in 1920 — that he had no remorse & would have used even more force if given the chance. the hunter committee found him guilty — but only of being overly zealous in the empire's service. no meaningful punishment followed. (to indians, this whitewashing was the second wound — the first being the massacre itself.) overwhelmed by the violence the movement had generated, mg withdrew it. he recognised that mass action without training & discipline was dangerous — a lesson he would carry forward. (the mahants of the golden temple actually honoured general dyer — because they were pro-british, as they had been during the ghadar movement of 1913–15.) 5.5) results of rowlatt satyagraha i) 1st mass strike + 1st all-india movement — the beginning of mass politics. ii) high participation in urban areas by the working class; low in rural areas. (organising a movement in an agrarian economy is structurally hard — the masses are in villages, but colonial government & nationalist leadership concentrate in cities. strong rural mobilisation needs strong local leadership, a solid organisation, and a felt local issue.) iii) mg drew two lessons: he needed control over the inc for a controlled mass movement, and indians needed training in non-violent satyagraha before the next round. ⚠ alert: rowlatt pyq cluster. prelims 1996 (anarchical & revolutionary crime act 1919 = rowlatt act); prelims 2004 (tagore returned knighthood — protest against jallianwala bagh); prelims 2008 (viceroy when rowlatt act passed = chelmsford16-21); prelims 2015 (rowlatt satyagraha facts — sedition committee report basis, imprisonment without trial). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Khilafat (1920–24) & Non-Cooperation Movement, NCM (1920–22)
sections.norm: khilafat (1920–24) & non-cooperation movement, ncm (1920–22). 6.1) reasons ww1 the rowlatt act the goi act 1919 1920 the harsh treaty the treaty 1906 inc lucknow pact of 1916 ncm 6.2) the khilafat committee & mg's decision 1919 control over muslim holy places arabs should not be under non-muslim rule once in a hundred years hindu-muslim unity launch the ncm 6.3) who opposed? annie besant & jinnah opposed extra-constitutional methods resigned from congress rowlatt act ww1 . 6.1) reasons grievances common to all: the backdrop was an india exhausted & angry. ww1 had brought inflation & food insecurity. unemployment was widespread. the spanish flu had killed approximately 12 million indians. the rowlatt act & jallianwala bagh had shattered whatever goodwill towards british governance remained. the goi act 1919 delivered no responsible government at the centre & only a watered-down dyarchy in provinces. the hunter committee report of 1920 did not hold dyer accountable in any real sense. the khilafat issue: the harsh treaty of sèvres (1920) imposed on the ottoman empire after ww1 was the specific trigger for india's muslim community. the ottoman khalifa (caliph) was regarded by many indian muslims as the spiritual head of the global islamic community. the treaty stripped the khalifa of suitable territory & control over muslim religious places, and placed arabs under non-muslim rule. indian muslims who had supported the british war effort felt this as a direct breach of promise. the issue triggered a political rise of the ulamas — islamic scholars — within muslim public life. seminaries like the deoband school & firangi mahal in lucknow (both in up) became politically active. within the muslim league (ml 1906), radical figures rose — muhammad ali jauhar, shaukat ali (the ali brothers), abul kalam azad, hakim ajmal khan, hasrat mohani — and became prominent. (jinnah had temporarily united ml & inc through the lucknow pact of 1916. but jinnah would oppose the ncm's methods & resign from congress.) 6.2) the khilafat committee & mg's decision in march 1919, the khilafat committee was set up by the ali brothers — md ali jauhar & shaukat ali. (this was not a muslim league initiative. many individual ml members, however, joined it.) their demands: revise the treaty of sèvres; restore the khalifa's dignity, suitable territory, and control over muslim holy places; arabs should not be under non-muslim rule. at the june 1920 allahabad conference of the khilafat committee, the khilafat movement was formally launched — with a call for boycott of titles, civil services, and the army, plus a no-tax campaign. they requested mg to lead. mg saw a "once in a hundred years" opportunity for hindu-muslim unity & convinced the inc to launch the ncm — including convincing leaders like c.r. das, who otherwise preferred fighting elections to oppose the british from within the councils (the 1919 adjournment motion approach). 6.3) who opposed? i) tilak: died august 1920, but while alive opposed supporting a religious goal, fearing it would breed communalism later. history proved him right. ii) b.c. pal: resigned from inc august 1920 — (1) opposed personality-centric inc; (2) opposed non-violence as an absolute principle; (3) disagreed with mg's definition of swaraj as "enlightened anarchy with a stateless society." iii) annie besant & jinnah: opposed extra-constitutional methods, resigned from congress. believed masses would not remain non-violent under british repression. iv) ml 1906: officially did not support ncm, though many individual members joined the all india khilafat committee. ⚠ alert: ncm pyq cluster. prelims 1996 (ncm = mass movement + hindu-muslim unity); prelims 2001 (independence as congress goal — hasrat mohani at ahmedabad 1921); prelims 2003 (mohammad ali & abul kalam azad — 1916 council resignation, a/r); prelims 2007 (rowlatt → jallianwala bagh popular-indignation chain); prelims 2012 (rowlatt act aim = imprisonment without trial + summary procedure); prelims 2025 (ncm — swaraj objective + non-violence). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Special Calcutta Session — September 1920
sections.norm: special calcutta session — september 1920. launched the ncm with three goals swaraj in one year 7.1) programme for the 1st year of nc — three streams: leave titles & honours boycott councils, courts, educational institutions boycott british goods 1905–11 1886 inc 2025 ncm pyq. president: lala lajpat rai inc formally launched the ncm with three goals: swaraj; redressal of punjab wrongs; redressal of khilafat wrongs. mg promised swaraj in one year. inc decided: non-cooperation for 1 year — and if swaraj not achieved, then launch cdm. (signature mg architecture: lighter action first, heavier next, with a clear timeline & escalating tempo.) 7.1) programme for the 1st year of nc — three streams: i) [boycott]: leave titles & honours + boycott councils, courts, educational institutions + boycott british goods. (why not boycott the executive? we are not ministers — we have already refused to sit in councils. the legislature is the entry point; once that is boycotted, the executive question does not arise.) ii) [swadeshi]: use panchayats as alternative dispute resolution + promote national education + use khadi. (in swadeshi 1905–11, the emphasis was on indian industrial goods broadly. here the focus shifts specifically to hand-spun khadi — a deeper, more rural form of economic self-reliance.) iii) [constructive work (cw)]: picketing of liquor shops + anti-untouchability campaign (a break from the 1886 inc rule of not raising social issues) + build hindu-muslim unity. ⚠ alert: prelims 2025 (ncm programme — boycott of law-courts + strict non-violence + retention of titles). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: INC Nagpur Session — December 1920
sections.norm: inc nagpur session — december 1920. 1920 1884 1882 fearless oratory uncompromising nature disagree even with gandhi inc ncm 8.1) organisational reforms [critical for upsc]: cwc aicc 1917 membership fee of 4 annas masses could join cdm. president: c. vijayaraghavachariar (common exam trap: the president of the nagpur session 1920 was c. vijayaraghavachariar — not c. rajagopalachari, who is sometimes confused with him given the similar first name chakravarti and also not m. vijayaraghavachariar who was a co-founder of the hindu newspaper (1878) and founding member of the madras mahajana sabha (1884) — one of the earliest political organisations in south india, which paved the way for the indian national congress.) ◆ who was c. vijayaraghavachariar? — the "lion of south india" c. vijayaraghavachariar earned the title "lion of south india" — and sometimes "hero of salem" — long before gandhi transformed the national movement. his defining moment came with the salem riot case of 1882. following communal riots in salem, british authorities falsely implicated him. he was sentenced to ten years of rigorous imprisonment & deported to the andaman islands. rather than accept his fate, he fought a relentless legal battle from within prison, proved his innocence, won an honourable acquittal, and — in an almost unheard-of act for an indian at the time — successfully sued the secretary of state for india for damages. winning a case against the british crown earned him a reputation for lion-like courage that stayed with him for life. he was known for fearless oratory & an uncompromising nature — willing to disagree even with gandhi when he felt a policy lacked sound legal or constitutional grounding. his peers respected him as a man who could not be intimidated by any authority. mg took over the inc at this session. (the ncm had been launched at calcutta in september; nagpur institutionalised mg's control of the organisation.) inc goal changed: swaraj by peaceful means — non-violent extra-constitutional mass struggle, replacing constitutional methods. 8.1) organisational reforms [critical for upsc]: i) cwc of 15 members — top executive body, so the movement continues even if senior leaders are arrested. (aicc was like an assembly — roughly 350 members; cwc = cabinet of 15 members — smaller, faster, always functional; full session had 1000s of members) ii) pccs on linguistic lines (link: tilak's 1917 demand for linguistic reorganisation of provinces). iii) membership fee of 4 annas — 1/16th of a rupee — so the masses could join & the organisation had funds. iv) hindi to be used as far as possible. v) members of princely states could join inc — though could not launch movements in inc's name. inc now truly all-india in reach. vi) therefore, mg shifted inc from class politics to mass politics — through method, language, structure, and constructive work as mass-contact tool. 8.2) 2nd phase cdm would include: no-tax campaign (= cd) + resignation from government services (= nc but far more powerful in impact — a civil servant quitting british service destabilises the entire administrative machinery. rising tempo made explicit.)

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Events of the NCM (1920–22)
sections.norm: events of the ncm (1920–22). rs. 1 crore 1920 9.2) gandhi–reading talks, 1921 viceroy reading talks failed 9.3) visit of prince of wales — november 1921 cdm 9.4) chauri chaura — february 1922, united provinces (agra & oudh, 1902) withdrew the mass movement stopped calling on the masses the bardoli resolution 1922 170 to death for chauri chaura madan mohan malaviya 19 were finally hanged. 9.1) tilak swaraj fund — mg raised rs. 1 crore, oversubscribed. named in honour of tilak who died august 1920. (mass movement needs money & organisation — mg understood both.) 9.2) gandhi–reading talks, 1921 viceroy reading (1921–26) sought talks with mg. (one year of nc was nearly over; british feared the coming cdm. reading had also read mg's step-tension-step (s-t-s) pattern.) talks failed — reading wanted mg to publicly criticise the ali brothers for speeches endorsing violence. mg refused to be used as an instrument of divide & rule. by holding firm, mg defeated the dnr strategy. 9.3) visit of prince of wales — november 1921 (britain = england + ireland + scotland + wales) — the prince represented the crown & colonial rule. his visit triggered nationwide strikes by workers — in cities, the working class responded with shutdowns & demonstrations. however, during the strikes, violence broke out against parsis, christians, and landlords who had supported the royal visit. mg grew alarmed. he decided: no all-india cdm; cdm to be confined to bardoli only via a limited no-tax campaign. (he feared the movement spiralling as rowlatt satyagraha had — mass energy without adequate non-violent discipline.) 9.4) chauri chaura — february 1922, united provinces (agra & oudh, 1902) at chauri chaura in up, police fired on a procession of satyagrahis, killing 3 of them. the crowd retaliated: 22 policemen were burned alive inside the police station. mg's response: i) withdrew the mass movement (ncm) — inc stopped calling on the masses to do non-cooperation. (but inc as a political institution would continue its own nc by boycotting the 1923 council elections. only the "m" — mass movement — was withdrawn; institutional nc continued.) ii) suspended the cdm planned for bardoli. the bardoli resolution (1922): training in non-violent satyagraha through constructive work (cw) must precede any future movement. (cw = apolitical activity — spinning khadi, building schools, fighting untouchability — used as preparatory training in non-violence.) the british sentenced 170 to death for chauri chaura. madan mohan malaviya fought their cases in court. after appeals, 19 were finally hanged — 22 satyagrahis paid for 22 policemen. ⚠ alert: ncm-events pyq cluster. prelims 1998 (ncm stopped 1922 — chauri chaura, a/r); prelims 1999 (gandhi's 1st all-india venture = rowlatt satyagraha); prelims 2000 (post-sa 1st successful satyagraha = champaran); prelims 2025 (chauri chaura accused — legal defence by madan mohan malaviya). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Results of the NCM
sections.norm: results of the ncm. 10.1) negatives: wemc low capitalist participation financial interest in the british trade system 1905–11 inc 1921 nov 1921 1922 1920–22 1922–24 ncm 1924 10.2) positives: nwfp 1901 1932 strong working class participation jm sen gupta prince of wales visit revolutionaries joined young bhagat singh strong peasant participation awadh kisan sabha inm hindu-muslim unity 1920 except malabar new regions participated for the first time 1920 cla goi act 1919 c.r. das left his lucrative legal practice anti-liquor campaign brought women into the movement subhas chandra bose, jawaharlal nehru, vallabhbhai patel cambridge 4th rank ncm 1920-22 akali movement control of gurudwaras from british-loyal mahants satyananda stokes (samuel evans stokes) — the american satyagrahi. aiks 1936 muslim league 1906. 10.1) negatives: i) low wemc participation in institution boycott — the western-educated middle class feared job loss; initially mg was more a rural leader. ii) low capitalist participation — importers had financial interest in the british trade system. (a businessman who profits from the existing system rarely leads its dismantling.) iii) khadi was expensive; masses were poor — same limitation as swadeshi 1905–11. not enough national education institutions either. iv) anti-untouchability remained mg's personal priority — not shared by inc leadership dominated by upper castes. v) movement turned violent — malabar (1921), visit of prince of wales (nov 1921), chauri chaura (1922). vi) communal violence increased — ulamas' role in mass mobilisation brought religiosity & communal tension. (even in swadeshi 1905–11, ml1906 had sought ulama support as they controlled the masses — this dynamic was not new) the moplah revolt 1921 in malabar began as a peasant revolt as inc had mobilised ryots on issue of khilafat with help of ulamas. but once inc leaders were arrested the movement became leaderless and turned communal with attacks on hindu janmies (landlords). post ncm (1920–22), there were communal riots in 1922–24. tilak had predicted this. thus, hindu-muslim unity was temporary. vii) revolutionaries bitterly disappointed by 1922 withdrawal — they had joined ncm enthusiastically, seeing in mg hope for decisive action. (recall alluri sitarama raju — his armed uprising in andhra forests was partly a response to disillusionment after ncm withdrawal.) viii) khilafat movement ended in 1924 — not by any indian decision, but because the people of turkey themselves abolished the khalifate & established a secular republic under mustafa kemal ataturk. a movement built on a foreign religious institution was always vulnerable to decisions made in ankara. 10.2) positives: i) rowlatt act repealed march 1922. ii) inc now popular in nwfp — muslim-majority province, created as chief commissioner's province from punjab in 1901, full province only in 1932. iii) strong working class participation — jm sen gupta led strikes in assam tea plantations & steamer services in bengal; wc also struck during prince of wales visit november 1921. (link the wc's journey: initiation at swadeshi 1905–11 → education at hrl 1916–18 → action at rowlatt 1919 → full mobilisation at ncm 1920–22.) iv) even revolutionaries joined — including a young bhagat singh. v) strong peasant participation. peasant movements of the period actively merged into ncm. the awadh kisan sabha, formally established in october 1920, is the clearest example — and it came with two very different kinds of leadership working together. baba ramchandra was the man who built the movement from the soil up. a fiji-returned indentured labourer, he had been organising peasants in awadh from around 1918–19 against exploitative taluqdars — illegal evictions, nazrana (forced gifts to landlords), and begar (unpaid forced labour). he held mass peasant meetings & built resistance from below. jawaharlal nehru entered in june 1920, visiting the villages of pratapgarh & seeing peasant conditions firsthand — an experience that radicalised him. he brought formal organisational structure & linked the movement to congress. ramchandra built the movement from the soil up; nehru gave it political shape & a congress connection. the eka movement (1921), led by madari pasi (extremist in method, not gandhian), and the akali movement (1920–25) for people's control over gurudwaras also merged into the ncm. (a two-way contract: inc raised ryot issues inside the national movement; ryots brought the swaraj agenda into their local struggles.) vi) tribal participation — tribals in andhra violated forest laws as cd. (link: alluri sitarama raju & the rampa rebellion.) vii) strong lower caste participation — untouchability became a mainstream political issue in inm for the first time. (future linkage: mg would later establish the all india anti-untouchability league in 1932 — covered in later chapters.) viii) great show of hindu-muslim unity 1920–22, except malabar. ix) new regions participated for the first time — rajasthan, gujarat, sindh, nwfp, up, south india. (in hrl 1916–18, these regions engaged in political education; in ncm, they participated in direct action — a deepening of geographic penetration.) x) economic boycott succeeded — british imports halved. (swadeshi 1905–11 could not sustain the boycott even in bengal; ncm achieved it at all-india scale.) xi) council boycott succeeded — only 5% voted in 1920 cla elections, under the goi act 1919 which introduced direct elections for the first time to give the new councils democratic legitimacy. a 5% turnout delivered exactly the opposite. xii) c.r. das left his lucrative legal practice — a powerful public signal. xiii) anti-liquor campaign succeeded & brought women into the movement in significant numbers. (women had participated in swadeshi too — this was a continuation & deepening.) xiv) strong regional leaders emerged — subhas chandra bose, jawaharlal nehru, vallabhbhai patel. (*note — s.c. bose studied in cambridge and qualified the exam in 1920 on his first attempt after only six months of preparation, securing 4th rank. he resigned in 1921 as decided not to serve colonial master & joined ncm 1920-22.) xv) akali movement 1920–25 supported ncm from 1921. the religious goal — taking over control of gurudwaras from british-loyal mahants — & merger into ncm brought religious punjabi masses into the inm. hindu-muslim-sikh unity existed. (similar: tilak's ganpati festivals 1893 & shivaji festivals 1896 — using religious & cultural mobilisation to build nationalist consciousness.) satyananda stokes (samuel evans stokes) — the american satyagrahi. an american who settled in himachal pradesh, stokes is celebrated for a dual legacy. on the practical side, he introduced the american red delicious apple to the himalayan region — transforming the rural economy of the shimla hills. on the political side, he is the only american ever arrested by the british under the sedition law for his active part in the non-cooperation movement (1921). he represents a rare instance of western individual participation in gandhian agitational politics — driven by his conversion to the indian cause as a personal moral cause. ◆ future linkage: the peasant participation that merged into ncm through kisan sabhas laid the organisational groundwork for what would become the all india kisan sabha (aiks) in 1936 — covered in later chapters.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: The Passive Phase (1922–27)
sections.norm: the passive phase (1922–27). 11.1) background & the debate that split the inc ncm was withdrawn in 1922 no cdm yet disagreed sharply inc 11.2) who were the swarajists? 1922 goi act 1919 strategic & hard to dismiss ncm political struggle & obstruction 1923 1919 11.3) who were the no-changers? no-changers continuing council boycott constructive work programme neglect of constructive work prevent another chauri chaura loss of revolutionary zeal political corruption cdm 11.4) what happened — and how was a surat-style split avoided? end or mend councils gaya session 1922 1907 mg opposed council entry he compromised das pact pyq 2009 2010 c.f. andrews (deenabandhu) — gandhian bridge to labour.. 11.1) background & the debate that split the inc the ncm was withdrawn in 1922. mg was in jail from 1922 to 1924. elections to the cla were scheduled for 1923. all inc leaders agreed on one thing: no cdm yet. but they disagreed sharply on what to do instead — and this disagreement produced the defining political debate of the passive phase. within the inc, two camps emerged: the swarajists (pro-changers) and the no-changers. 11.2) who were the swarajists? the swarajists — led by c.r. das & motilal nehru, with lala lajpat rai & madan mohan malviya also among them — proposed at the gaya session of 1922 a programme of "ending or mending the councils." their argument: the councils created by the goi act 1919 should either be fundamentally reformed or destroyed from within — and the way to do either was to enter them. their justification was strategic & hard to dismiss: i) they would use the councils for political propaganda, filling newspapers with nationalist demands & filling the political void left by the withdrawn ncm. ii) they would not use the councils to demand gradual reforms in the old moderate style — they would use them for political struggle & obstruction. iii) even without inc, the 1923 elections would happen. non-inc forces would enter the councils, weakening inc's political position. iv) if the public voted in good numbers without inc in the race, it would be a loss of face for inc. v) the british would claim the 1919 reforms were a success — a propaganda win they could not be allowed. 11.3) who were the no-changers? the no-changers were mg's supporters — vallabhbhai patel, rajendra prasad, c. rajagopalachari — those who still believed in continuing council boycott & the constructive work programme of the ncm. their argument against council entry: i) it would lead to neglect of constructive work — critical to prevent another chauri chaura by training people in non-violence before the next movement. ii) it would cause loss of revolutionary zeal — once politicians entered councils, the fire of mass politics would cool into parliamentary routine. iii) it would lead to political corruption — the temptations of office & legislative life would compromise the movement from within. their prescription: continue non-cooperation, continue boycott, continue constructive work, and wait for the relaunch of cdm. 11.4) what happened — and how was a surat-style split avoided? the swarajists' "end or mend councils" resolution failed at the gaya session 1922. in response, the swarajists resigned from their official posts within inc — not from inc membership itself. they formed the congress khilafat swaraj party (the swaraj party) and contested the 1923 elections. the word khilafat was added to get votes of muslim voters as the khilafat movement (1920–24) was still ongoing. (in 1907 at surat, the inc had split into moderates & extremists — a damaging rupture that took years to heal. here the disagreement was equally sharp. what prevented another surat?) mg opposed council entry — but he compromised. four things made the difference: i) all accepted mg's leadership — the inc had learnt from the surat split of 1907 that unity was more valuable than winning any internal argument. ii) mg's style of trust & respect — he extended genuine respect to the swarajists even while disagreeing with them, making it impossible to frame the conflict as personal hostility. iii) mg prevented british divide & rule — when the government repressed the bengal swarajists in the name of fighting terrorism, mg publicly supported them. the internal debate was a family argument, not a fracture. iv) by 1924 when mg was released from jail, council entry was already done. withdrawing at that point would have been pointless — and mg had the political maturity to recognise this. he graciously praised the swarajists for their good work in the councils & in the 1924 belgaum session (which was the only inc session ever presided over by mahatma gandhi) the gandhi-das pact (1924) recognised the swarajists as the parliamentary wing of inc. ⚠ alert: passive-phase pyq cluster. prelims 2009 (ahmedabad textile labour association founder = gandhi); prelims 2010 (champaran — rajendra prasad persuading gandhi, a/r). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq. c.f. andrews (deenabandhu) — gandhian bridge to labour. charles freer andrews was a close associate of mahatma gandhi during the south africa struggle. he moved to india in 1904 to teach at st. stephen's college, delhi, & became a vital intellectual & spiritual bridge between gandhi's political activism & rabindranath tagore's cultural vision at shantiniketan. gandhi gave him the title deenabandhu (friend of the poor) for his selfless service in the slums of delhi & during famines. andrews became a leader in the organised labour movement, serving as president of the all india trade union congress (aituc) in 1925 & again in 1927. beyond acting as a moral mediator between the inc & the british administration, he worked globally to expose the horrors of the indentured labour system — contributing materially to its eventual abolition.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Swarajists in the CLA — What They Actually Did
sections.norm: swarajists in the cla — what they actually did. swarajists were anything but decorative goi act 1919 1929 civil liberty via repeal of all repressive laws concessions for indian industry ncm 1919 12.1) negatives of the swarajists no street-level support no corresponding mass organisation 1925 1924 12.2) the responsivists — a fracture within 1926 bengal pact 12.3) swarajists' response: lahore congress resolution of 1929. inside the central legislative assembly, the swarajists were anything but decorative: i) motilal nehru demanded a new constitution in the very first session itself — pointing to the goi act 1919's own provision for constitutional review after ten years, meaning by 1929. (they were not waiting patiently — they were building the record & the demand from day one.) ii) they demanded civil liberty via repeal of all repressive laws. iii) they demanded concessions for indian industry. iv) used adjournment motion of goi act 1919 effectively. they did great work in the councils & filled the political void left by the withdrawn ncm. council chambers that might have become symbols of the success of the 1919 reforms became instead arenas of sustained nationalist confrontation. 12.1) negatives of the swarajists i) no street-level support alongside council work. the swarajists worked inside the councils & relied heavily on newspapers — but had no corresponding mass organisation working alongside them in the streets. the two tracks never reinforced each other the way they needed to. ii) c.r. das died in 1925. a severe blow. das had been the principal architect & most credible face of the swarajists. his death left a leadership vacuum the party never fully recovered from. iii) lost support of the muslim league — because the swarajists did not support the cause of muslim tenants in bengal, alienating the ml at a critical moment of communal tension. iv) communal riots of 1924 divided the councils on communal lines & cracked the swaraj party from within — producing the responsivists. 12.2) the responsivists — a fracture within after the 1924 riots, a faction called the responsivists emerged inside the swaraj party. they wanted to abandon the obstructionist strategy entirely, arguing for cooperating with the government rather than obstructing it. they also wanted british support for the protection of hindu interests in the aftermath of communal violence. leaders like lajpat rai & malviya were associated with this tendency — they accused motilal nehru of being too pro-muslim & formed their own hindu nationalist faction within the party. some went further — n.c. kelkar & jayakaractually joined the executive council in the central provinces, becoming what critics called "seat-hungry" — willing to hold posts wherever possible, entirely contrary to the spirit of the "end or mend" programme. the mid-1920s saw a massive surge in hindu-muslim riots across india. by the 1926 elections, any semblance of communal unity within the swaraj party had completely vanished. c.r. das's death in 1925 had already removed the one leader who could hold the coalition together, and the bengal pact collapsed with him. consequently, the swaraj party lost heavily in 1926, particularly because it lost almost all support from muslim voters & leaders. 12.3) swarajists' response: they reiterated their commitment to mass cdm when the time came. and institutionally, inc decided to withdraw from the councils in 1926. (all finally withdrew in 1930, after the lahore congress resolution of 1929 for purna swaraj.)

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: The Importance of Constructive Work During the Passive Phase
sections.norm: the importance of constructive work during the passive phase. constructive work programme during 1922 far more durable inc parallel grassroots institutions swadeshi education through national schools local panchayats. while the swarajist-no-changer debate occupied the political spotlight, the quieter work of the constructive work programme during 1922–27 was building something far more durable underneath: i) work for party cadre during a politically inactive phase — the cw programme kept the inc organisation alive, engaged, and purposeful even when there was no mass movement running. cadres were trained & retained, not left idle & drifting. ii) boosted unity within communities — upper-caste urban workers engaged in cw in rural areas became aware of the conditions of lower castes & rural communities. this bridged the rural-urban divide that had always limited mass mobilisation. iii) deepened inc's hold in rural areas — constructive work became a major recruitment tool for inc in villages where the party had previously had little organic presence. iv) built confidence of the masses in inc — ordinary people found in inc a body that came to their villages, worked alongside them, and addressed everyday grievances. this built a trust that no newspaper editorial or council speech could create. v) parallel grassroots institutions — swadeshi education through national schools freed the masses from colonial textbooks and teachers, while local panchayats acted as independent arbitration courts to bypass the british justice system. together, they nurtured nationalism entirely outside the reach of the colonial state.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Lala Lajpat Rai (1865–1928)
sections.norm: lala lajpat rai (1865–1928). 1905 1907 hindu nationalist & arya samajist 1905–08 rejecting british educational institutions d.a.v. (dayanand anglo-vedic) punjab colonisation bill nerve centre of sedition deported him to mandalay regulation iii of 1818 voluntary exile united states 1920 1928 1894 1929 ww1 . 14.1) one of the famous lal-bal-pal trio (lajpat rai, bal gangadhar tilak, bipin chandra pal) who led the extremist faction in congress. before 1905, congress relied on "prayers & petitions." lajpat rai & his peers argued that this approach had failed. they championed militant nationalist methods — absolute boycott of foreign goods, passive resistance, and pushing the ultimate goal toward swaraj (self-rule). this ideological shift between the extremists & moderates eventually led to the surat split of 1907. 14.2) ideologically a hindu nationalist & arya samajist. he was shaped by swami dayanand saraswati's reformist hinduism. for him, national regeneration & hindu cultural revival were two sides of the same coin. 14.3) his primary contribution during the swadeshi movement (1905–08) was transforming a regional grievance into a national struggle. while leaders like surendranath banerjee & bipin chandra pal focused on bengal, lajpat rai took charge of the northern front. he organised massive rallies, mobilised student groups, and delivered powerful speeches across punjab & the united provinces, urging people to adopt swadeshi goods & boycott british products. he expanded the movement's footprint far beyond bengal. 14.4) a core pillar of the swadeshi movement was rejecting british educational institutions. lajpat rai was perfectly positioned for this, given his deep involvement with the arya samaj. he heavily promoted the d.a.v. (dayanand anglo-vedic) movement, helping to establish schools & colleges that provided modern education rooted in indian culture — a direct alternative to government-run schools. this was national education as nationalist action. 14.5) he did not just talk about bengal — he linked the swadeshi spirit to local agrarian grievances. in 1907, he led the agitation against the oppressive punjab colonisation bill & the hike in water rates (the pagri sambhal jatta movement, alongside ajit singh). he used the momentum of the swadeshi movement to fuel this local agrarian revolt. his ability to unite urban nationalists with rural peasants terrified the british administration. 14.6) viewing him as the nerve centre of sedition in the north, the british arrested him in may 1907 & deported him to mandalay (burma) without trial under the draconian regulation iii of 1818. he was released later that year due to immense public pressure & lack of evidence. shortly after, he travelled to england in 1908 to lecture the british public & parliamentarians about the true conditions in india, countering the colonial government's narrative. he returned to india in 1909. 14.7) in 1914, he went to england again as part of a congress delegation. but ww1 broke out, and fearing arrest if he returned, he chose voluntary exile. he travelled briefly to japan & then moved to the united states, where he stayed until 1920. this period was the most critical phase of his career — he globalised the indian struggle for independence. he founded the indian home rule league of america (1917) in new york, established the indian information bureau to feed accurate news about india to the american press, and launched the monthly journal young india. he also wrote some of his most important books during this period — england's debt to indiaand the political future of india — both sharp critiques of british economic exploitation. in 1919, he managed to get the indian cause discussed in the us senate foreign relations committee — a massive diplomatic achievement for a stateless nationalist. 14.8) he returned to india in february 1920 with immense international stature. because of his towering reputation & his time away from the factional infighting of the 1910s, he was unanimously elected to preside over the special session of congress in calcutta (september 1920). it was at this very session that gandhi first introduced the non-cooperation resolution, which was then formally ratified a few months later at the nagpur session under c. vijayaraghavachariar. his book unhappy india (1928) was a sharp rebuttal to katherine mayo's mother india, which had painted indian society in a negative light. lajpat rai defended indian civilisation against what he saw as deliberate colonial misrepresentation. 14.9) was closely involved in the founding of punjab national bank (1894), established by dyal singh majithia & lala harkishen lal. he also founded the lakshmi insurance company to channel indian capital into indian-owned financial institutions. this was a rare example of economic nationalism turning into actual institution-building — not just speeches about swadeshi, but creating the financial infrastructure for it. 14.10) led the massive protest against the simon commission in lahore (october 1928). the commission had no indian members, and its arrival triggered nationwide protests. during the lahore demonstration, lajpat rai was severely beaten by police lathi-charges under superintendent scott's orders. he reportedly declared: "every blow on my body is a nail in the coffin of the british empire." he died on 17 november 1928 from injuries sustained in the lathi-charge. his death radicalised an entire generation. it directly inspired bhagat singh, rajguru, and sukhdevto assassinate j.p. saunders (a british police officer they mistook for scott) and set in motion the chain of events leading to the assembly bomb case (1929). his legacy sits at the intersection of economic nationalism, hindu revivalism, and militant constitutionalism — a bridge figure connecting moderate-era institution-building with the revolutionary turn of the late 1920s. he built banks & faced lathis. that combination made him unique. ⚠ alert: personalities pyq cluster. prelims 2004 (complete-independence proposal — hasrat mohani at ahmedabad 1921); prelims 1998 (madan mohan malaviya — bhu founder, a/r); prelims 2004 (chronological sequence — chauri chaura → minto-morley → dandi → montagu-chelmsford). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya (1861–1946)
sections.norm: pandit madan mohan malaviya (1861–1946). inc president 4 times moderate & gandhian eras 15.2) ideology — hindu nationalist hindi & devanagari script opposed separate electorates 15.3) methods 1919 ncm 1920–22 1922 1900 nwp 1877 15.5) communal unity but no appeasement: 1909 opposed nehru report 1928 bhu 1916 founded up kisan sabha constitutional methods 450 branches. 15.1) inc president 4 times: 1909, 1918, 1932, 1933; career spanned moderate & gandhian eras — rare leader active across both phases. 15.2) ideology — hindu nationalist i) championed hindi & devanagari script as national unifying symbols. ii) opposed separate electorates. iii) promoted swadeshi or nationalist education. iv) took up peasants' issues. v) opposed casteism. vi) active in early hindu mahasabha but stayed within inc; did not adopt hardline exclusivist communal position & worked for hindu-muslim unity. vii) called mahamana (great soul; not mahatma) for his integrity, moral stature & selfless service. viii) popularised satyameva jayate (truth alone triumphs) — part of a mantra from the mundaka upanishad linked to atharva veda; existed since millennia but malaviya turned it into a modern national clarion call during the freedom struggle. at the 1918 inc session (delhi), in his presidential address, he prominently quoted satyameva jayate to remind the indian public that their struggle against the british empire was fundamentally a moral one; urged the nation to adopt non-violence & truth. his continuous use of the phrase embedded it into the consciousness of the indian public. the phrase was unanimously adopted as the national motto of india on 26 january 1950 & is inscribed in devanagari script at the base of the lion capital of ashoka (india's national emblem). ix) posthumously awarded bharat ratna 2015. 15.3) methods i) not a mass leader in the gandhian mould but a builder of permanent structures: university, newspapers, legal defences, constitutional vision. ii) started as moderate — petitions, dialogue, working within british institutions. iii) founded & edited the leader (english) and abhyudaya (hindi) for spreading nationalist ideas via journalism. iv) post-jallianwala bagh 1919 — moved toward assertive nationalism but via aggressive use of councils, courts & public pressure, not full gandhian boycott (force constitutional change through system, not reject system itself). v) did not support ncm 1920–22 as rejected blanket boycott of councils, courts & schools — wanted to fight within these institutions, not abandon them; led legal defence of 170+ indians sentenced to death in chauri chaura case 1922 — most sentences reduced (only 19 hanged). 15.4) hindi–urdu controversy (1880s–1900) in nwp & awadh (province established 1877) — led by malaviya as moderate; demanded official language status for hindi (spoken by majority) equivalent to urdu. i) result? 1900 — hindi gained official language status equal to urdu. ii) unintended byproduct — hindi became associated with hindus & urdu became associated with muslims; deepened communal fault lines. (fun fact: pakistan linguistically dominated by punjabis & bengalis — but jinnah chose urdu as official language for islamic image, not linguistic majority. in contrast, india did not choose bande mataram as national anthem to not portray overt hindu image — nothing wrong in the truly nationalistic spirit of bande mataram.) 15.5) communal unity but no appeasement: i) opposed separate communal electorates of morley-minto reforms 1909. ii) did not support ncm 1920–22 as opposed khilafat linkage — saw it as tying national cause to pan-islamic demand (restoration of ottoman caliphate) with no real connection to indian self-rule. iii) opposed nehru report 1928 — proposed reserved seats for muslims in hindu-majority provinces but not for hindus in muslim-majority provinces; malaviya demanded reservation for hindus in punjab (roughly 30–35%) and bengal (roughly 45%) where hindus were clear minority; argument: minority protection must be reciprocal. 15.6) founded banaras hindu university (bhu 1916) — combined modern western education with hindu cultural identity; one of the largest residential universities in asia; his greatest institutional achievement & most visible legacy. 15.7) founded up kisan sabha (upks 1918) — addressed peasant issues via constitutional methods: petitions, legal help, pressure through councils; by 1919 it had 450 branches. once ncm 1920–22 began, upks split in 1920 when baba ramchandra & jawaharlal nehru co-founded the awadh kisan sabha (aks october 1920) as a breakaway faction — adopted direct mass action: no-rent campaigns, nai-dhobi bandhs, taluqdar boycotts; quickly grew to 300+ branches & aks also joined ncm 1920–22. aks turned violent in 1921: looting of bazaars, attacks on taluqdar houses — even inc leadership distanced itself. 15.8) pushed for abolition of untouchability & temple entry for dalits; worked with mg despite orthodox hindu background — showed reformist edge within his hindu nationalism.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: Chittaranjan Das (C.R. Das) (1870–1925)
sections.norm: chittaranjan das (c.r. das) (1870–1925). 1920 1908 democrat & a hindu-muslim unity advocate communal harmony 16.4) swaraj party & council entry gave up legal practice founded the swaraj party 1924 bengal pact pro-labour & pro-peasant political line progressive-left wing of congress responsive cooperation constitutional obstruction 1925 massive public mourning subhas chandra bose, his political disciple. 16.1) a leading barrister in bengal who earned the title deshbandhu (friend of the nation) for sacrificing a hugely successful legal career to join the non-cooperation movement in 1920. at the height of his practice, he was earning lakhs — and he gave it all up. 16.2) defended aurobindo ghosh in the alipore bomb case (1908) and secured his acquittal. this was one of the most celebrated legal victories of the nationalist movement. it made das a hero in bengal long before he entered active politics. 16.3) ideologically a democrat & a hindu-muslim unity advocate. he believed that indian self-governance must rest on communal harmony, not majoritarian dominance. this set him apart from hindu nationalist leaders like malaviya & lajpat rai. 16.4) swaraj party & council entry i) gave up legal practice during ncm (1920–22) and it served as a big inspiration. ii) after the suspension of non-cooperation (1922), he broke with gandhi's "no-council-entry" stance & founded the swaraj party (1923) along with motilal nehru. the idea was to contest elections & obstruct british legislative councils from within — wrecking unjust bills, demanding accountability, and proving that the colonial legislature could not function without indian cooperation. it won 42 out of 104 elected seats. iii) to get a working majority after the 1923 election, motilal nehru formed a parliamentary bloc called the "nationalist party" by forging an alliance with the "independents," a group led by m.a. jinnah (member of ml 1906 by affiliation but operated as leader of the independents bloc in the cla). together, motilal nehru & jinnah repeatedly outvoted the british government, rejecting the budget & forcing the viceroy to use his "certification" (veto) powers. 16.5) as leader of the swaraj party, he entered the bengal legislative council & became mayor of calcutta corporation (1924). he used municipal power to promote indian interests & push for employing indians in administration. this was constitutional nationalism in action — using the very institutions the british had created to advance indian interests. 16.6) bengal pact (1923) — authored after the 1923 elections as das needed support of muslim members (not ml 1906) for blocking british government's legislations — an agreement proposing proportional representation in bengal's local bodies & 60% reservation for muslims in new government jobs. this was despite muslims being in majority. hindu groups opposed it bitterly as usually there is no reservation for majority in democracy, but das saw it as the only way to build political unity. 16.7) advocated a pro-labour & pro-peasant political line. he was sympathetic to trade unions & tenant rights. this placed him on the progressive-left wing of congress, distinct from both gandhi's rural conservatism & the hindu right wing. 16.8) his strategy of "responsive cooperation" from within legislatures — wrecking unjust bills, demanding accountability, exposing colonial governance — became a template for constitutional obstruction within a colonial framework. it showed that you could fight the system from inside the system. 16.9) died in june 1925 at only 55, cutting short a career that many believed would have made him a dominant national leader rivalling gandhi. his early death left a vacuum in bengal politics that shaped the region's trajectory for decades. 16.10) his death triggered massive public mourning across india. subhas chandra bose, his political disciple, credited das with shaping his own nationalist vision. das remains one of the most respected but under-remembered leaders of the freedom movement — a man who combined legal brilliance, communal bridge-building, and institutional nationalism.

sections.chapterTitle: Champaran, Ahmedabad, Kheda, Rowlatt Satyagraha and Gandhian Era (1920+)
sections.title: C. Rajagopalachari (Rajaji) (1878–1972)
sections.norm: c. rajagopalachari (rajaji) (1878–1972). 1948–50 gandhian conservative free-market liberal opposed state-led heavy industrialisation 1930 1937–39 dmk 1944 1946–47 1959 1958 1954 sharp critic of dynastic politics conscience keeper of india inc 1927. 17.1) one of the foremost leaders of the freedom movement in south india. he served as the last governor-general of india (1948–50) — the only indian to ever hold that post. his appointment marked the symbolic end of british constitutional authority over india. 17.2) ideologically a gandhian conservative. he was committed to non-violence & swadeshi, but economically he was a free-market liberal who opposed state-led heavy industrialisation. this combination — socially conservative, economically liberal — made him unusual in indian politics. 17.3) led the famous salem-vedaranyam salt march (1930) in the madras presidency as a parallel to gandhi's dandi march. this made him the face of the civil disobedience movement in the south. 17.4) served as premier of the madras presidency (1937–39) under congress. his controversial introduction of compulsory hindi in schools triggered the anti-hindi agitation by dravidian parties. this was a political turning point in tamil nadu — it fuelled the rise of periyar's self-respect movement & eventually the dmk, reshaping south indian politics permanently. 17.5) proposed the "rajaji formula" (1944) — a plan to allow muslim-majority provinces to vote on separation after independence, attempting to break the congress-muslim league deadlock. congress rejected it as giving too much ground. the league found it insufficient. it failed, but it showed rajaji's willingness to think pragmatically about partition long before others. 17.6) served as home minister in the interim government (1946–47) and as governor of west bengal during the communal violence of partition. he was in the thick of the administrative crisis during india's most violent transition. 17.7) founded the swatantra party in 1959 — india's first major right-of-centre opposition party. he opposed nehru's socialist policies, the licence raj, and state control of industry. he called the permit-licence system a threat to individual freedom. the swatantra party was the first serious ideological challenge to congress's economic model from the right. 17.8) a brilliant tamil & english writer. his retellings of the mahabharata & ramayana in tamil are literary classics. he won the sahitya akademi award in 1958. he was that rare figure — a frontline politician who was also a genuine literary talent. 17.9) awarded the inaugural bharat ratna in 1954, alongside c.v. raman & s. radhakrishnan. 17.10) remained a sharp critic of dynastic politics & centralised planning until his death at 94. he earned the title "conscience keeper of india" — a man who spent his last decades warning that the congress system he had helped build was becoming exactly the kind of top-down power structure the freedom movement had fought against. ◆ the passive phase was called "passive" because there was no mass movement running against the british. but it was anything but passive in what it built — organisation, cadres, rural roots, mass trust, and nationalist consciousness. when the next round came, the inc would be a far stronger machine precisely because of these quiet years. the announcement of the simon commission in 1927 rekindled the indian national movement — ending the passive phase & opening the next chapter.

sections.title: How did Peasant Movements connect with INM?
sections.norm: how did peasant movements connect with inm?. heavily influenced by inm home rule league movement non-cooperation movement khilafat agitation inc. the peasant movements of the 1920s were heavily influenced by inm — specifically by the energy generated through the home rule league movement (1916–18), non-cooperation movement (1920–22), and the khilafat agitation. these movements created political awareness among the rural masses & gave them a vocabulary of protest. in turn, peasant movements merged with inm by bringing the countryside into the national struggle.
