(inc raised the issue of swaraj among peasants, and peasants raised the issue of land & rent within inm — a two-way street.) however, it is important to note that these peasant movements were not of inc & were independent of inc. the peasantry had its own grievances — illegal cesses, forced labour, eviction — and its own leaders. inc's relationship with these movements was sometimes supportive, sometimes distant, and sometimes uncomfortable, depending on how far the peasants were willing to go.

sections.title: Kisan Sabha Movement (1918) and Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920)
sections.norm: kisan sabha movement (1918) and awadh kisan sabha (1920). 2.1) what were the grievances? awadh oppression from big landlords illegal abwabs & nazrana bedakhli i.e. eviction forced labour i.e. hari & begar ww1 2.2) what role did the home rule leagues play? 1916–18 2.3) what were the organisations? up kisan sabha gauri shankar mishra, indra narayan dwivedi, and madan mohan malaviya 1920 2.4) what methods did the awadh kisan sabha follow? resisting eviction social boycott refusal to perform forced labour 2.5) what happened next? 1921 seditious meetings act (1911) awadh rent amendment act (1921) ww1 . 2.1) what were the grievances? the peasants in awadh faced strong oppression from big landlords (zamindars & taluqdars). their specific grievances included: i) illegal abwabs & nazrana — extra cesses imposed by landlords beyond the legal rent, with no authorisation. ii) bedakhli i.e. eviction — landlords could throw tenants off land at will, leaving them with no livelihood. iii) forced labour i.e. hari & begar — peasants were compelled to perform unpaid labour for the landlord. iv) ww1 -related inflation — prices had risen sharply during the war, but rents & cesses did not come down after it. (this is a recurring pattern — war-time inflation hurts those at the bottom the most because their incomes are fixed while prices rise.) 2.2) what role did the home rule leagues play? the home rule league movement (1916–18) played a significant role in creating political awareness among the masses. this awareness inspired the beginning of the kisan sabha movement itself — peasants who had heard the language of rights & self-rule now began to organise around their own demands. 2.3) what were the organisations? the up kisan sabha was set up in february 1918, co-founded by gauri shankar mishra, indra narayan dwivedi, and madan mohan malaviya. mishra and dwivedi were the operational organisers; malaviya served as the senior political patron lending his weight. (jawaharlal nehru was not associated with upks 1918 — he engaged with the kisan sabha movement only from june 1920 onwards, when he visited pratapgarh with baba ramchandra.) kisan sabha leaders attended inc sessions, establishing a connection between the peasant cause & the national movement. in 1920, baba ramchandra emerged as the leader of peasants in awadh, and nehru developed close contact with the movement. however, since malviya was a moderate, he did not support the non-cooperation movement. due to this, baba ramchandra (with nehru's support) set up the awadh kisan sabha in 1920 for extra-constitutional struggle — i.e. methods that went beyond petitions & prayers & moved towards active resistance. 2.4) what methods did the awadh kisan sabha follow? the methods included: resisting eviction, social boycott of those who did not join the movement, and refusal to perform forced labour. 2.5) what happened next? in 1921, the movement turned violent. the british suppressed it under the seditious meetings act (1911). additionally, the british brought the awadh rent amendment act (1921), which addressed some of the rent-related grievances & took the sting out of the agitation. the movement thus ended — partly through repression, partly through a legislative concession.

sections.title: Eka Movement (1921) — Awadh
sections.norm: eka movement (1921) — awadh. eka movement tyranny of thikedars madari pasi leader from the lower castes 1922 inm. the eka movement arose in awadh with the same grievances as the kisan sabha movement — oppression by landlords & the added tyranny of thikedars (rent collectors who squeezed peasants even harder than the zamindars themselves). the methods were also the same — resistance, boycott, refusal of forced labour. the key difference was the leadership. madari pasi, a leader from the lower castes, emerged at the head of this movement. (this is significant — it shows that the peasant struggle was not just an upper-caste affair but drew leaders from the most oppressed sections of rural society.) however, unlike the gandhian movements which insisted on non-violence as a non-negotiable principle, the eka movement did not adhere to non-violence. this made it easy for the british to repress the movement on grounds of law & order maintenance, and it was crushed by 1922. ◆ the eka movement is a good example of the tension within inm — gandhi's method required strict non-violence, but many peasant leaders, especially from lc backgrounds, saw non-violence as a restraint that favoured the oppressor. madari pasi was the extremist, not the gandhian, of the peasant world.

sections.title: Mapilla Revolt (1921) — Malabar
sections.norm: mapilla revolt (1921) — malabar. 4.1) what was the background? malabar mapillas or moplahs khilafat movement 4.2) what was the grievance? hindu jenmies heavy rents 4.3) what happened? inc 1921 ncm. 4.1) what was the background? in malabar (present-day kerala), the muslim tenants — called mapillas or moplahs — were part of the khilafat movement. (the mapillas had a long history of revolt — there had been earlier uprisings in the 1840s & 1870s as well, always driven by the same agrarian grievance.) 4.2) what was the grievance? the primary grievance was oppression by landlords. these landlords were predominantly hindu jenmies (hereditary landowners) who controlled vast tracts of land, and the mapilla tenants suffered under heavy rents & arbitrary eviction. 4.3) what happened? inc joined & supported the movement initially. however, when inc leaders were arrested, this led to a lack of leadership. without organised political guidance, the revolt turned violent & took a communal colour — the anger that had started against jenmies (landlords) as an economic class turned into hindu-muslim violence. the british declared martial law & suppressed the revolt. ◆ the mapilla revolt of 1921 is one of the saddest chapters of this period — a genuine agrarian grievance that got derailed into communal violence due to the absence of strong secular leadership. it also hurt hindu-muslim unity within ncm. :(

sections.title: Borsad Satyagraha (1922–24) — Gujarat (Post-NCM)
sections.norm: borsad satyagraha (1922–24) — gujarat (post-ncm). 5.1) what was the grievance? ncm 1922 5.2) what was the action? not pay the additional tax volunteer corps 5.3) what was the result? ordered an inquiry withdrawal of the additional tax. 5.1) what was the grievance? after ncm was withdrawn in 1922, gujarat saw a unique form of peasant mobilisation under vallabhbhai patel. in borsad, there was monetary collusion between dacoits & the police — i.e. the police were in league with the dacoits & were not protecting the people. on top of this, the government applied an additional tax on the villagers to fund the upkeep of an additional police force to deal with the dacoity problem. so the peasants faced a dual tyranny — dacoits looted them, the police who were supposed to protect them were in collusion with dacoits, and the government made the peasants pay for the extra police force that was not doing its job. 5.2) what was the action? patel asked villagers to not pay the additional tax, and to not resort to violence even if the government confiscated their movable property. volunteer corps were raised who alerted villagers when police came for confiscation — giving people time to prepare & remain non-violent. 5.3) what was the result? the governor of bombay, finally upset over the accusation of police-dacoit collusion, ordered an inquiry. this led to an immediate halt to confiscation & the withdrawal of the additional tax levied for the extra police force. ◆ borsad is a small but textbook gandhian satyagraha — specific grievance, non-violent resistance, moral pressure on the authorities, and a concrete outcome. patel's organisational skills were already becoming visible here.

sections.title: Bardoli Satyagraha (1928) — Surat, Gujarat
sections.norm: bardoli satyagraha (1928) — surat, gujarat. bardoli satyagraha of 1928 preparation ground for the civil disobedience movement 6.1) what was the background? ncm cdm 6.2) what was the grievance? hali system 30% increase 6.3) constructive work phase 1927 6.4) development of local leadership vallabhbhai patel took leadership 1928 6.5) what was the focus of the movement? not frame it as a revolt against the entire revenue system miscalculation in the 30% increase sardar women & ryots of bardoli 6.6) how did patel organise the masses? chhavnis women were included social boycott 6.7) how was pressure built on the government? pla 6.8) what was the result?. the bardoli satyagraha of 1928 was among the most significant peasant movements of the 1920s, and it served as a preparation ground for the civil disobedience movement (cdm) that would follow in 1930. (in fact, inc had originally planned cdm to begin from bardoli itself.) 6.1) what was the background? the people of bardoli in surat were already politically organised — this political consciousness had been built during ncm. the region had two main caste groups: kaliparaj (lower castes) and ujaliparaj (upper castes). there was a bonhomie between the two groups & efforts were underway to prepare for cdm. bhajan mandalis were used to raise political awareness among the rural population. 6.2) what was the grievance? the peasants faced two forms of oppression: hereditary forced labour & alcohol addiction leading to a debt trap — both tied to the hali system. on top of this, the government imposed a 30% increase in land revenue assessment — a hike that the peasants considered unjust & based on a miscalculation. 6.3) constructive work phase gandhi led a campaign through his newspapers young india & navjivan & visited bardoli in 1927. he worked towards uniting the low-caste kaliparaj with the ujaliparaj by opposing the hali system — this was essential because caste divisions would have weakened any collective resistance. gandhi renamed the kaliparaj as rani paraj i.e. people of the forests, giving them a dignified identity. 6.4) development of local leadership vallabhbhai patel took leadership of the movement in 1928. 6.5) what was the focus of the movement? the focus was kept limited to unjust aspects only — patel did not frame it as a revolt against the entire revenue system. he highlighted the miscalculation in the 30% increase & asked peasants to pay land revenue only at the old rates. he demanded the appointment of an independent tribunal to examine the assessment. it was here that patel received the title of "sardar" — from the women & ryots of bardoli. 6.6) how did patel organise the masses? patel showed great organisational skills. he used chhavnis as the basic unit for organising peasants. women were included in the movement. social boycott of non-supporters was practised. he also used the bardoli patrika — a local newspaper — for spreading awareness about the miscalculated assessment. 6.7) how was pressure built on the government? simultaneously, incremental pressure was applied: members of the provincial legislative assembly (pla) resigned — e.g. k.m. munshi. gandhi then reached bardoli in 1928, adding his weight to the agitation. (this is classic mg style — constructive work first, then localised agitation, then wider political pressure through resignations & personal presence, slowly rising the tempo.) 6.8) what was the result? finally, a truce was reached. an independent tribunal was appointed. the tribunal revised the land revenue increase down to 6.03% — a far cry from the original 30%. (mg style of arbitration to reveal economic truth — always seeking a middle path based on facts, not maximalist demands.)

sections.title: Akali Movement (1920–25) — Punjab
sections.norm: akali movement (1920–25) — punjab. 7.1) what was the background? akali movement control over gurudwaras udasi sikh mahants rs01-39 1801–1839 1849 1913 1919 7.2) what were the organisations formed? clear objectives & a well-organised institutional structure getting control of gurudwaras core demand gave control of the golden temple easily sgpc 1920 sad 7.3) what were the 3 important events? 1921 ncm keys affair keys of the toshikhana 1922 7.4) why did the british agree to akali demands? disaffection in the army sikhs formed a significant part of the british indian army 7.5) when did gandhi withdraw support? gandhi withdrew support restoration of the deposed raja of nabha turned violent 7.6) what was the final outcome? gurudwara reform act 1925 7.7) how did the akali movement strengthen inm? educated middle-class sikhs took over leadership unity was seen among rural & urban population hindu-muslim-sikh unity nationalist & anti-british sentiments princely states of punjab rooted in a religious issue encourage communalism split into three factions kirti kisan party akali dal. 7.1) what was the background? the akali movement was essentially a struggle for control over gurudwaras — sikh places of worship that had come under the control of udasi sikh mahants since the 18th century. its origins go back to the singh sabha movement of the 1880s, which had first raised the issue of sikh religious reform. why did mahants have control? because they had received rich lands from maharaja ranjit singh i.e. rs01-39 (1801–1839) — the ruler of the sikh empire. over time, the mahants became corrupt & lived lives of luxury. after the british annexation of punjab in 1849, the situation worsened. the british were in collusion with the mahants— as against the chadrites (the reform-minded devotees). for example, in 1913, the golden temple issued a hukumnama (an official religious decree) against chadrites — at the behest of the mahants. the mahants even honoured general dyer after the jallianwala bagh massacre of 1919. this triggered widespread outrage & protests by local sikh devotees, laying the foundation of the akali movement for wresting control of gurudwaras from the mahants. ◆ so it was jallianwala bagh that triggered the akali movement. when mahants honoured the very man who had ordered the massacre of sikhs at amritsar, ordinary sikh devotees decided they could no longer tolerate mahant control over their religious institutions. 7.2) what were the organisations formed? the akali movement (1920–25) had clear objectives & a well-organised institutional structure: i) getting control of gurudwaras — this was the core demand. ii) the british gave control of the golden temple easily — probably hoping this would pacify the akalis. (br policy of appeasing the moderates & suppressing the extremists among the akalis.) iii) the shiromani gurudwara prabandhak committee (sgpc) was formed in 1920 for organised management of the golden temple. iv) the shiromani akali dal (sad) was formed for further organised protests against mahants — for getting control of other gurudwaras beyond the golden temple. the british supported the mahants & tried to repress the movement. 7.3) what were the 3 important events? i) nankana tragedy (1921) — the mahant of nankana gurudwara used 500 mercenaries when sikhs tried to enter the gurudwara. hundreds of akalis were killed. however, eventually the akalis took control of nankana gurudwara. in 1921, the akalis passed a resolution adopting non-cooperation — and thus the akali movement became part of ncm. ii) keys affair — the akalis had got control over the golden temple, but not over the toshikhana (treasury) of the temple. this movement was specifically for getting the keys of the toshikhana. it was led by baba kharak singh, a moderate. the british soon gave the keys — following their policy of appeasing the moderates & suppressing the extremists among the akalis. iii) guru ka bagh incident (1922) — here, the gurudwara had been given to the akalis, but the mahant still controlled the lands around the gurudwara. the movement was to get control over these lands. there was high government suppression — ncm was already over, and the british wanted to restore their authority. however, the akalis continued to bear repression & finally won. 7.4) why did the british agree to akali demands? the british were anxious about disaffection in the army, since sikhs formed a significant part of the british indian army. (this is a key insight — the british did not concede on principle, they conceded because they could not afford sikh disaffection in their military ranks.) 7.5) when did gandhi withdraw support? gandhi withdrew support to the akali movement when the akalis protested for the restoration of the deposed raja of nabha (a princely state). the movement turned violent at this point, and gandhi's support was conditional on non-violence. 7.6) what was the final outcome? to prevent disaffection in the army, the british passed the gurudwara reform act, 1925. this was a success. the sgpc — an elected body of sikhs — got control over all gurudwaras. 7.7) how did the akali movement strengthen inm? positives: i) it led to the politicisation of punjab's peasantry. since it was a religious issue, peasants participated in large numbers, and later the movement merged into the non-cooperation movement (ncm). ii) it was only because of the akali movement that the educated middle-class sikhs took over leadership from the pro-british feudal class. iii) unity was seen among rural & urban population. iv) hindus & muslims actively participated in the akali movement — leading to hindu-muslim-sikh unity. v) it led to the growth of nationalist & anti-british sentiments in the princely states of punjab. negatives: i) since it was rooted in a religious issue, sikhs got religiously charged — and this would later encourage communalism. ii) post-movement, the akalis got split into three factions: the gandhians & leftists who formed the kirti kisan party; the communalists who continued as akali dal; and the loyalists to the british who formed the unionist party.

sections.title: A Note on Peasant Movements and INC
sections.norm: a note on peasant movements and inc. boosted by inm not of inc & were independent of inc their own grievances, their own leaders inm pyq 1996 1922 1997 2003 1928. the peasant movements of the 1920s were boosted by inm — by the home rule movement, by ncm, by khilafat. but they were not of inc & were independent of inc. the peasants had their own grievances, their own leaders, and often their own methods. inc's engagement with peasant issues was real but also strategic — the countryside gave inm its mass base, but inc leadership was not always comfortable with the direction peasant anger could take. ◆ this is an important distinction for the student: inm gave peasant movements political consciousness & language; peasant movements gave inm its mass character. the relationship was symbiotic, not hierarchical. ⚠ exam note: questions on peasant movements often test whether the student understands the distinction between inc-led movements & independent peasant agitations that were merely influenced by inm. always clarify that peasant movements of the 1920s ran parallel to, and were boosted by, ncm/khilafat — but were not controlled by inc. also note the trajectory: kisan sabha (1918) → awadh kisan sabha (1920) → eka (1921) → borsad (1922–24) → bardoli (1928) shows an evolution from disorganised unrest to disciplined gandhian satyagraha. ⚠ alert: peasant movements pyq cluster. prelims 1996 — sarabandi (no-tax) campaign 1922 leader = vallabhbhai patel. prelims 1997 — match-list: moplah revolt, pabna revolt, eka movement & bardoli paired with their leaders/regions. prelims 2003 — bardoli satyagraha 1928 leader = sardar vallabhbhai patel. prelims 2005 — up kisan sabha (feb 1918): not associated = jawaharlal nehru (he engaged the kisan sabha movement only from june 1920); founders associated with upks 1918 = gauri shankar mishra, indra narayan dwivedi & madan mohan malaviya (all three). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Why Did Revolutionary Activities Revive after 1922?
sections.norm: why did revolutionary activities revive after 1922?. india act 1915 revolutionaries disappointed parliamentary politics of the swarajists constructive work programme 1917 rr1917 ncm 1920–22 1907–15 1913–15 ww1 russian revolution 1917. during ww1 , the british had cracked down heavily on revolutionaries using the defence of india act 1915. many were jailed. after the war, an amnesty in 1920 led to their release from prison. these revolutionaries then enthusiastically joined gandhiji's non-cooperation movement (ncm). but ncm was abruptly withdrawn in february 1922 after the chauri chaura incident. this left the revolutionaries disappointed. they had no interest in the parliamentary politics of the swarajists(pro-changers), nor in the constructive work programme of the no-changers (gandhians). so they returned to what they knew — revolutionary activity. but this time, there was a difference. the russian revolution of 1917 (rr1917) had sent a wave of communist thought across the world. the revolutionaries of the 1920s were attracted not just to ending colonial oppression but also to ending class oppression (i.e. the exploitation of peasants by landed classes, and of workers by capitalist classes). they were also drawn to the method of armed struggle, having now concluded that non-violent methods had failed. they were attracted by socialism given the mass poverty under colonial rule & thus their ideological framework was evolving with passing years. definitely it was not just a passion for armed struggle (recall how they had left arms to join ncm 1920–22). ◆ unlike the earlier revolutionaries of 1907–15 who often drew on hindu religious imagery, the 1920s–30s revolutionaries were thoroughly secular in public though most were religious in personal life (just as an e.g. ram prasad bismil chanted the gayatri mantra before pulling the chain in the railway in the kakori robbery case) and thus religion continued to act as source of courage. their public secularism was a trait they shared with the ghadrites of 1913–15, reinforced by the influence of communist ideology which was inherently pro-secularism.

sections.title: Hindustan Republican Army / Association (HRA 1924)
sections.norm: hindustan republican army / association (hra 1924). hra 1924 1912 hra1924 hindustan republican army 1924 hindustan republican association 1924. who set up hra & what was its goal? hra was set up in 1924 by ram prasad bismil, ashfaqullah khan, jogesh chatterjee, chandrashekhar azad, and sachin sanyal. (sachin sanyal was associated with the delhi conspiracy case of 1912 & had written bandi jeevan, a guide to revolutionary activities.) the goal of hra1924 was clear — armed revolution to establish a "united states of india" with universal adult franchise.

sections.title: The 1925 Kakori Robbery Case
sections.norm: the 1925 kakori robbery case. hra1924 1925 hindustan republican army 1924 hindustan republican association 1924. hra1924 needed money to buy arms. in 1925, they looted cash from a train in the kakori robbery case. but many members were arrested. ram prasad bismil & ashfaqullah khan were hanged. chandrashekhar azad, however, was not caught. with its key leaders either executed or on the run, hra1924 went inactive.

sections.title: Hindustan Socialist Republican Army / Association (HSRA 1928)
sections.norm: hindustan socialist republican army / association (hsra 1928). hra1924 hsra1928 1930 hindustan socialist republican army 1928 hindustan socialist republican association 1928 hindustan republican army 1924 hindustan republican association 1924. how was hsra1928 different from hra1924? azad & bhagat singh revived hra1924 as hsra1928 — note the addition of the word "socialist" in the name, reflecting the leftward ideological shift of the revolutionaries. hsra1928 brought together all the revolutionaries of north india. key members included sukhdev, rajguru, and bhagwati charan vohra. vohra was killed on 28 may 1930 while testing a bomb near the river ravi, lahore — a significant loss to the movement.

sections.title: Lahore Conspiracy Case 1928–31
sections.norm: lahore conspiracy case 1928–31. 1928 dsp 1931. reason lala lajpat rai — the sher-e-punjab — had been brutally assaulted during anti-simon commission protests in november 1928. he died from injuries sustained in the lathi-charge. bhagat singh decided to avenge his death. events the target was james scott, sp (superintendent of police), who had personally ordered & led the assault on lala lajpat rai. but in a case of mistaken identity, john saunders, dsp (deputy superintendent of police), was killed instead. consequence bhagat singh, sukhdev, and rajguru were hanged after trial on 23 march 1931. chandrashekhar azad was killed in an encounter at alfred park (now chandrashekhar azad park), allahabad, on 27 february 1931 — he shot himself rather than surrender to the british.

sections.title: 1929 Bomb in CLA by Bhagat Singh & B.K. Dutt
sections.norm: 1929 bomb in cla by bhagat singh & b.k. dutt. cla public safety bill trade disputes bill bhagat singh deliberately courted arrest court trial as a platform for propaganda. why was the bomb thrown? the central legislative assembly (cla) was discussing the public safety bill & the trade disputes bill. both bills were aimed at curbing the working class (wc) movement & communists, as the british feared the rising influence of communist ideas in india. what actually happened? bhagat singh & b.k. dutt threw a harmless bomb inside the cla, along with leaflets carrying the now-famous phrase — "to make the deaf hear." the intention was not to kill anyone but to draw attention. bhagat singh deliberately courted arrest. he then used the court trial as a platform for propaganda — to inspire nationalism among the masses. (the courtroom became his stage, and his speeches during the trial did more for the nationalist cause than the bomb ever could.)

sections.title: Revolutionaries in Bengal
sections.norm: revolutionaries in bengal. supported the swarajist leader c.r. das repress bengal's swarajists c.r. das died in 1925 factionalism weakened the bengal congress s.c. bose yugantar j.m. sen gupta anushilan samiti gopinath saha arrest of s.c. bose. what was the connection between revolutionaries & swarajists in bengal? the revolutionaries in bengal had supported the swarajist leader c.r. das. this association led the british to repress bengal's swarajists as well. when c.r. das died in 1925, factionalism weakened the bengal congress. two rival groups emerged: s.c. bose — who had the support of the revolutionary group yugantar j.m. sen gupta — who had the support of the revolutionary group anushilan samiti the repression intensified further after a failed attempt on the life of the police commissioner by gopinath saha. this led to the arrest of s.c. bose & a fresh wave of repression in bengal.

sections.title: Chittagong Armory Raid 1930–33
sections.norm: chittagong armory raid 1930–33. cdm 1930–34 ira 1857 1931 1932 1854 1912 muslim villagers gave food & shelter 1933 1934 ncm pyq 1997 2001. context while gandhiji was leading the civil disobedience movement (cdm 1930–34), revolutionaries in east bengal began their own armed struggle under surya sen, a school teacher. events surya sen set up the indian republican army (ira) — and notably, he mobilised even women into it. they raided the chittagong armory & began an armed struggle. they declared a provisional revolutionary government & cut off chittagong from the rest of bengal by destroying communication systems & railway lines. when the british attacked, they moved to hills & villages for guerrilla warfare. this was the first time since 1857 that there was group action in armed struggle — and significantly, many muslims & women fought & died as part of ira. pritilata waddedar (age 21) consumed potassium cyanide to avoid capture by the british & became a martyr. kalpana dutt received life imprisonment. school girls shanti ghosh (age 15) and suniti chaudhary (age 14) shot dead the district magistrate of comilla, c.g.b. stevens, on 14 december 1931. bina das (age 21) fired five shots at governor stanley jackson during a convocation ceremony at calcutta university in february 1932 — he survived (post of lieutenant-governor of bengal was created in 1854 & elevated back to governor in 1912). muslim villagers gave food & shelter to the revolutionaries (showing the deep secular & communal solidarity of the movement). in 1933, jawaharlal nehru was arrested on sedition charges & sentenced to two years in prison for condemning imperialism & praising the heroism of the revolutionaries. consequence by 1933, the chittagong revolutionaries were crushed. in 1934, surya sen was captured & hanged. the revolutionary movement post-ncm came to an end, though it had greatly inspired nationalism across india. ⚠ alert: revolutionaries pyq cluster. prelims 1997 (match-list: chittagong armoury raid + kakori conspiracy + lahore conspiracy + ghadar party + their leaders); prelims 2001 (chittagong armoury raid organiser = surya sen). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Overall Assessment of Revolutionaries of 1920s–30s
sections.norm: overall assessment of revolutionaries of 1920s–30s. qualitatively different breed ira ncm 1920–22 more politically aware & ideologically strong writing theoretical works. how were these revolutionaries different from the earlier ones (1907–15)? the post-1922 revolutionaries were a qualitatively different breed from their predecessors. the key differences were: 9.1) no use of religious symbolism — unlike the earlier revolutionaries (e.g. anushilan samiti & jugantar of the swadeshi era) who often used hindu religious rituals like oath-taking ceremonies, the 1920s–30s revolutionaries dropped all such practices in their organisations. this facilitated muslim participation — surya sen's ira in chittagong, for instance, had muslim cadre members like sattar, mir ahmad, fakir ahmad mian, and tunu mian. 9.2) developed political ideology — they were attracted by socialism given the mass poverty under colonial rule & thus their ideological framework was evolving with passing years. definitely it was not just a passion for armed struggle (recall how they had left arms to join ncm 1920–22). 9.3) more politically aware & ideologically strong — they were well-read & articulate, capable of writing theoretical works & conducting propaganda. the revolutionaries of this era were not just fighters — they were thinkers.

sections.title: Ideology of Bhagat Singh and HSRA1928
sections.norm: ideology of bhagat singh and hsra1928. philosophy of bomb bhagwati charan vohra & azad independence — social, economic, and political bhagat singh was a marxist end of capitalism & class domination freedom from exploitation peasants & workers 10.4) they supported the class rights of workers & peasants. socialism in state policy nationalisation of large-scale industries they were secular communalism is as big an enemy as colonialism hindustan socialist republican army 1928 hindustan socialist republican association 1928. bhagat singh & hsra1928 had a well-developed ideological position, captured in the "philosophy of bomb" written by bhagwati charan vohra & azad. this document was significant — it elaborated the ideology of revolutionaries & defined them as what they were: not criminals, not misguided youth, but revolutionaries with a clear vision. the key elements were: 10.1) they defined revolution as "independence — social, economic, and political." it was not just about removing the british. 10.2) bhagat singh was a marxist. he defined socialism as the end of capitalism & class domination. 10.3) they argued that real independence will come only when there is freedom from exploitation. thus peasants & workers need to be freed from the oppression of landlords & capitalists. 10.4) they supported the class rights of workers & peasants. 10.5) they favoured socialism in state policy — for example, they wanted nationalisation of large-scale industries. 10.6) they were secular. bhagat singh argued that communalism is as big an enemy as colonialism.

sections.title: Bhagat Singh in Jail
sections.norm: bhagat singh in jail. inc inm 1923 1926 1930 hunger strike in jail jatin das died on the 64th day. while in jail, bhagat singh set up a library — he believed more in the power of the pen than in violence. he stated that he had acted like a terrorist but he was not a terrorist. he did not appeal to youth to follow the path of revolutionary activities. instead, he urged them to join inc & the inm. for this purpose, he had worked actively in the lahore student union (set up in 1923 by lala lajpat rai) and had set up the punjab naujawan bharat sabha 1926 to educate youth on mass politics. he wrote the essay "why i am an atheist" in jail in 1930 — a powerful articulation of his rationalist worldview, rejecting religious dogma & affirming his commitment to reason & revolutionary ideals. he also started a hunger strike in jail against inhuman living conditions of prisoners. his fellow prisoner jatin das died on the 64th day of the hunger strike due to forced feeding. :(

sections.title: Indian Statutory Commission / Simon Commission (1927)
sections.norm: indian statutory commission / simon commission (1927). marked the end of inc's passive phase goi act 1919 reviewing constitutional reforms after 10 years appointed 2 years ahead of schedule. seven member simon commission sir john simon not a single indian was included indians were not given any say in their own future constitution birkenhead, challenged indians to draft a constitution. the appointment of the indian statutory commission in 1927 marked the end of inc's passive phase that had lasted since the bardoli resolution of 1922. the goi act 1919 had a built-in provision for reviewing constitutional reforms after 10 years — this was the link to the gradual swaraj promise made in the montague statement of 1917. however, the commission was appointed 2 years ahead of schedule. the conservative government in britain did not want to leave this politically sensitive matter to the next government. additionally, there was pressure from pro changers within inc, rising revolutionary activity throughout the 1920s, and growing fear of communism spreading in india during the 1920s. the seven member simon commission was headed by sir john simon & consisted of members of the british parliament — one of whom was clement attlee, who later became prime minister of britain (1945–51) and oversaw indian independence. not a single indian was included among its 7 members. inc opposed the commission precisely on this ground — that the principle of self-government promised in the montague statement of 1917 was being violated, as indians were not given any say in their own future constitution. (icas & goi acts were legal instruments serving british administrative purposes — they were not a constitution of indians, and being excluded from even this review was an insult.) in the british parliament, the secretary of state for india, birkenhead, challenged indians — not inc specifically — to draft a constitution themselves. he believed that indian leaders could not overcome their internal differences & act unitedly. (birkenhead was essentially taunting indians, and as we will see, he was partially proved right — not because indians lacked ability, but because british-era communal divisions made consensus difficult.)

sections.title: What did INC do? — The 1927 INC Madras Session
sections.norm: what did inc do? — the 1927 inc madras session. inc rejected the simon commissio set up an all party conference(apc) for drafting the principles of a constitution. massive anti-simon protests lala lajpat rai was subjected to a brutal lathi charge by sp james scott. at its madras session in 1927, inc rejected the simon commission & decided to set up an all party conference(apc) for drafting the principles of a constitution. (think of this as drafting the basic structure of a constitution — the actual legal language of a full constitution would take years.) when the simon commission visited india for the second time in october 1928, it triggered massive anti-simon protests across the country. during these protests in lahore, lala lajpat rai was subjected to a brutal lathi charge by sp james scott, and the injuries from this assault led to his death in november 1928. (this led to the assassination of john saunders — a british police officer mistaken for scott — by bhagat singh, which was investigated as the lahore conspiracy case of 1928.)

sections.title: Four Delhi Proposals (December 1927) by ML1906
sections.norm: four delhi proposals (december 1927) by ml1906. the demands were: one-third reservation 3 new muslim majority provinces reservation in the mmps of punjab & bengal willing to accept joint electorates. first & last time ml1906 agreed to joint electorates muslim league 1906. even as inc was setting up the apc, the muslim league (ml1906) put forward its own proposals — the four delhi proposals of december 1927 — addressed to motilal nehru. inc initially accepted these proposals, but they were later rejected by the apc. the demands were: 3.1) one-third reservation for muslims in the central legislature. (muslims were about 20% of the population — so asking for 33% was classic over-bargaining, like how one bargains in a shop.) 3.2) creation of 3 new muslim majority provinces (mmps) — by separating sindh from the bombay presidency, and granting full province status to baluchistan & nwfp. (the reason was simple: more provinces meant more mlas, more mps, and more ministers from ml1906 — i.e. more political power.) 3.3) reservation in the mmps of punjab & bengal in proportion to the muslim share of population. 3.4) if the above 3 conditions were met, ml1906 was willing to accept joint electorates. (this was the first & last time ml1906 agreed to joint electorates — but it came loaded with conditions.)

sections.title: Nehru Report (August 1928)
sections.norm: nehru report (august 1928). 1928 apc nehru report 4.1) what did it demand? dominion status a union of india 4.2) other key provisions: linguistic reorganization of provinces 1916–18 supreme court independent judiciary. bicameral legislature governor-general to function on the aid & advice of the executive council universal adult franchise (dpsps). fundamental rights 4.3) what about the communal question? no separate electorates nwfp baluchistan separation of sindh from the bombay no reservation for muslims in mmps reservation for muslims in muslim minority provinces & at the centre reservation for non-muslim minorities reservation to last only for 10 years no state religion pyq 1998 2013 2010 1995 inc 2011 nehru report 1928 2017 1927 lucknow pact 1916 muslim league 1906. in 1928, the apc was formally set up in delhi, headed by m.a. ansari. in may 1928, a committee under the apc was constituted under motilal nehru to draft the principles of a constitution. the result was the nehru report of august 1928 — the first indian attempt at a constitutional blueprint. 4.1) what did it demand? the nehru report asked for dominion status — the maximum level of self-government possible without leaving the british empire. under dominion status, sovereignty would remain with the british crown. britain would retain the power to change the constitution & would be overall responsible for defence & foreign policy. but in the domestic sphere, indians would have self-government. (compare this with the princely states, where paramountcy since 1858 effectively meant dominion status minus democracy — the indian prince had self-governance in domestic affairs but the british crown controlled everything else.) for the first time, the report demanded a union of india — bringing together british india & the princely states — with federal relations between the two. (think of this as 565 versions of article 370 & without democracy — non-interference by the centre, which would be dominated by british india's politicians, in the affairs of princely states.) for british india itself, the report proposed a unitary structure — a strong centre with residuary powers lying with the centre in relation to provinces. 4.2) other key provisions: i) linguistic reorganization of provinces of british india. (this was originally tilak's demand, taken up during the home rule league movement of 1916–18, and again demanded by inc in 1917. it would eventually materialise through the states reorganization act of 1956.) ii) a supreme court & an independent judiciary. iii) a bicameral legislature at the centre — with a 7-year term for the upper house & a 5-year term for the lower house. iv) the governor-general to function on the aid & advice of the executive council. v) universal adult franchise — demanded clearly for the first time. vi) directive principles for state's policy (dpsps). vii) 19 fundamental rights — key rights included universal adult franchise, women's equality, trade union rights, and dissociation of state from religion, along with rights focusing on liberty, education, workers, lower castes, and minorities. 4.3) what about the communal question? the communal provisions of the nehru report were where the real political friction lay: i) no separate electorates. (this was a direct reversal of lp1916 & a blow to ml1906.) ii) nwfp & baluchistan to be made full provinces. (ml1906 wanted this — accepted.) iii) separation of sindh from the bombay presidency — but only after dominion status was achieved & only if sindh was financially viable. (ml1906 wanted unconditional separation — so this was a conditional concession, not a full acceptance.) iv) no reservation for muslims in mmps. (ml1906 unhappy.) v) reservation for muslims in muslim minority provinces & at the centre — but in proportion to their percentage in population, not the 1/3rd that ml1906 demanded. (ml1906 unhappy.) vi) reservation for non-muslim minorities in sindh & nwfp. vii) reservation to last only for 10 years & to be reviewed after that. (like the coi 1950 provision on reservation.) viii) no state religion, but protection of culture of minorities. ⚠ alert: simon-to-delhi-manifesto pyq cluster. prelims 1998 + 2013 (simon commission boycott reason = no indian member); prelims 2010 (simon commission's key recommendation = abolition of dyarchy at provincial level); prelims 1995 (independence for india league founders = nehru & bose, opposed to dominion-status wing of inc); prelims 2011 (nehru report 1928 recommendations — dominion status, joint electorates, fundamental rights); prelims 2017 (butler committee 1927 object = improve relations between government of india & princely states). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Three Calcutta Amendments (December 1928) by ML1906
sections.norm: three calcutta amendments (december 1928) by ml1906. these were: central legislative assembly (cla) mmps of punjab & bengal until universal adult franchise residuary powers rejected by the apc muslim league 1906. in december 1928, the apc met in calcutta where jinnah proposed three calcutta amendments to the nehru report. these were: 5.1) one-third reservation for muslims in the central legislative assembly (cla). 5.2) reservation in the mmps of punjab & bengal in proportion to muslim population, until universal adult franchise was implemented. (this was a new addition — the logic being that under income-based voting criteria, muslims, who were generally poorer, may not form a majority in the voter list even in muslim majority provinces.) 5.3) residuary powers to be given to provinces, not to the centre. (a minority or regional party always desires federalism because it knows it will not be in power at the centre.) all three amendments were rejected by the apc.

sections.title: INC Calcutta Session (December 1928)
sections.norm: inc calcutta session (december 1928). inc formally approved the nehru report resolution to adopt purna swaraj if dominion status was not granted within one year civil disobedience movement (cdm) constructive work (cw) resolution prepare the masses for non-violent satyagraha. at the calcutta session in december 1928, inc formally approved the nehru report. s.c. bose moved a resolution to adopt purna swaraj (complete independence) as inc's goal instead of dominion status, but it failed. as a compromise between the old guard & the younger leaders, inc decided: if dominion status was not granted within one year, inc's goal would become purna swaraj & it would launch a civil disobedience movement (cdm) for it. inc also passed a constructive work (cw) resolution, since gandhiji wanted to prepare the masses for non-violent satyagraha before launching any mass movement. the focus areas were: boycott of foreign cloth & promotion of khadi & self-reliance (not for political swaraj but for the income of the poor — thus not non-cooperation), anti-liquor campaign, anti-untouchability campaign, awareness on women empowerment, training in non-violent satyagraha, and organizational strengthening of inc.

sections.title: Jinnah's 14 Points Demand (March 1929)
sections.norm: jinnah's 14 points demand (march 1929). "14 points demand" blueprint for all future political actions of ml1906 the 14 demands were: separate electorates. veto power central legislature. reservation in cabinet all elected bodies government services. reservation in mmps. new mmps federal constitution. residuary powers provincial autonomy. constitutional amendment territorial reorganization culture muslim league 1906. after failure of the four delhi proposals (december 1927) and the three calcutta amendments (december 1928) now jinnah/ml1906 brought "14 points demand" in march 1929. (birkenhead won the challenge that indian leaders could not agree on a constitution.) this document was a summary of every communal demand ever made by any muslim organisation. it became the blueprint for all future political actions of ml1906. (it contained every divisive demand — except the demand for pakistan, which came later.) the 14 demands were: 7.1) separate electorates. 7.2) veto power on bills if 3/4th of minority members opposed it. (this borrowed from the 1888 inc rule.) 7.3) one-third muslims in central legislature. 7.4) minimum one-third reservation in cabinet at the centre & in provinces. 7.5) reservation in all elected bodies, even where muslims were in a majority. 7.6) reservation in government services. 7.7) reservation in mmps. 7.8) creation of new mmps — sindh, baluchistan, and nwfp. 7.9) a federal constitution. 7.10) residuary powers to provinces. 7.11) provincial autonomy. 7.12) no constitutional amendment without consent of provinces. 7.13) no territorial reorganization that would negatively affect muslim majority status in any province. 7.14) protection of the culture of muslims.

sections.title: Butler Committee (1927), Report (1929)
sections.norm: butler committee (1927), report (1929). butler committee relationship between the british crown & the princely states british paramountcy over princely states was re-affirmed not be transferred into a union of india without their own consent all india state people's congress (aispc) aispc — not the princes — should be treated as the representative body. the butler committee was appointed in 1927 to examine & clarify the relationship between the british crown & the princely states. its report, published in 1929, had two key findings. first, british paramountcy over princely states was re-affirmed. second, and more importantly, paramountcy should remain intact to preserve the princely states — they should not be transferred into a union of india without their own consent. (this is why the goi act 1935 used the mechanism of an instrument of accession (ioa) for princely states to join the proposed federation — which remained operative as our coi until 26 january 1950.) ◆ the all india state people's congress (aispc), set up in 1927, was an inc-like organisation working within the 565 princely states. it submitted to the butler committee that the aispc — not the princes — should be treated as the representative body of the princely states. this was a challenge to the feudal authority of the princes from their own people.

sections.title: Diwali Declaration / Irwin Statement (31 October 1929)
sections.norm: diwali declaration / irwin statement (31 october 1929). diwali declaration intent of the british to give dominion status at a future date round table conference (rtc) in london no decision — only an intent the british offered nothing concrete delhi manifesto in november 1929 irwin. viceroy irwin26-31 issued a statement on 31 october 1929 — the diwali declaration — which read: "dominion status is implicit in the montague statement of 1917 & it is the intent of the british to give dominion status at a future date, and for this purpose britain will hold a round table conference (rtc) in london." notice the carefully chosen words. there was no decision — only an intent. there was no timeline — only a vague future date. and the mechanism was a round table conference in london — not a constituent assembly in india. in short, the british offered nothing concrete. thus, inc responded with the delhi manifesto in november 1929.

sections.title: Delhi Manifesto (November 1929)
sections.norm: delhi manifesto (november 1929). specific conditions on inc's participation constituent assembly (ca) 10.2) a majority of the indian delegates in the rtc should be from inc. amnesty "bomb in cla" meerut conspiracy case of 1929. a meeting of national leaders of inc passed the delhi manifesto, which placed specific conditions on inc's participation in the proposed round table conference: 10.1) the rtc should act as a constituent assembly (ca) — that is, it should draft a constitution implementing dominion status, not merely discuss reforms. 10.2) a majority of the indian delegates in the rtc should be from inc. 10.3) amnesty in the case of the "bomb in cla" incident of 1929. (this referred to bhagat singh's action of throwing a bomb in the central legislative assembly — not to the lahore conspiracy case of 1928 which was about the saunders assassination.) also, amnesty in the meerut conspiracy case of 1929, where many communists were arrested due to ongoing rail strikes & attempts at establishing an indian branch of the comintern — and as a result, the working class movement was repressed.

sections.title: The INC Lahore Session, December 1929
sections.norm: the inc lahore session, december 1929. irwin26-31 rejected the delhi manifesto manifesto had asked for three things: inc lahore session of december 1929 jawaharlal nehru as president. inc took five major decisions: purna swaraj 26 january 1930 independence day inc rejected the rtc withdraw from legislatures empowered to launch the civil disobedience movement cdm pyq 1995 2006 1929 2009 2012 2014 irwin. viceroy irwin26-31 (1926–1931) had rejected the delhi manifesto in november 1929. the manifesto had asked for three things: that the round table conference function as a constituent assembly drafting a constitution with dominion status; that a majority of indian representatives in the rtc come from inc; and that amnesty be granted in the bomb in cla case (1929) and the meerut conspiracy case (1929). irwin26-31 refused all of it. the response came at the inc lahore session of december 1929, with jawaharlal nehru as president. inc took five major decisions: 1.1) the goal of inc was now purna swaraj — not dominion status, but complete independence. 1.2) 26 january 1930 was to be celebrated as independence day by taking an independence pledge. the date was chosen because it was the last sunday of january 1930 — a holiday — ensuring maximum public participation & publicity. (this is why 26 january was later chosen as republic day in 1950 — the date already carried symbolic weight from 1930. constitution day is 26 november because on that day in 1949 the constitution was adopted, i.e. finalised. it came into effect — became applicable as law — on 26 january 1950.) 1.3) inc rejected the rtc (three sessions of rtc were held — in 1930, 1931, and 1932) and therefore did not participate in the 1st session of rtc of 1930. 1.4) inc decided to withdraw from legislatures immediately — this meant the end of the pro-changer strategy of working the cla, cos, and plas from within. 1.5) the aicc (set up by the nagpur session of 1920) was empowered to launch the civil disobedience movement (cdm) at an appropriate time. ⚠ alert: lahore-session + cdm-launch pyq cluster. prelims 1995 (cdm started from = dandi/sabarmati ashram); prelims 2006 (lahore session 1929 president = jawaharlal nehru); prelims 2009 (dandi march began the cdm); prelims 2012 (lahore session 1929 importance — purna swaraj resolution); prelims 2014 (1929 session importance — purna swaraj declared as goal). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Why Was CDM Not Launched Immediately?
sections.norm: why was cdm not launched immediately?. several forces actively opposed an immediate cdm: inc muslim leaders an inc-ml1906 unity pact before cdm capitalist class great depression (gd1929) ml1906 hindu raj sikh parties, hindu mahasabha, and the justice party of madras raise inc's popularity cpi1925 labelled bose, nehru, and inc as agents of the bourgeoisie mg therefore gave his 11-point demands muslim league 1906 lucknow pact 1916 great depression 1929 communist party of india 1925. the 1928 calcutta session had resolved that if dominion status was not granted within one year, inc would launch cdm for purna swaraj. that year was now up. there was high pressure on mg to act. but mg — true to his style of inclusiveness — wanted broad consensus before moving. several forces actively opposed an immediate cdm: 2.1) inc muslim leaders wanted an inc-ml1906 unity pact before cdm — similar to the lucknow pact (lp1916) that had preceded the non-cooperation movement (ncm 1920–22). their logic was practical: without such a pact, they would face opposition from muslim masses when mobilising them. 2.2) the capitalist class was unsure about the economic impact of a cdm at that moment because the great depression (gd1929) had begun in october 1929 with the us stock market crash. (the us economy was interlinked with the world economy via import-export & fdi, and by 1914 the us was the world's top economy — hence a depression in the us meant a depression globally.) 2.3) ml1906 labelled cdm a ploy by inc to establish hindu raj. 2.4) sikh parties, hindu mahasabha, and the justice party of madras — a party representing lower castes that had not supported ncm 1920–22 — all opposed cdm because it would raise inc's popularity among the people. (these were not straightforwardly pro-british parties — except the justice party, they had participated in the all parties conference & either demanded purna swaraj or dominion status — but they did not want inc to emerge as the sole mass leader.) 2.5) cpi1925 opposed cdm on directions from the comintern (also called the third international — the body of all communist parties of the world, headed by the communist party of the ussr). cpi1925 labelled bose, nehru, and inc as agents of the bourgeoisie & called inc a party of the capitalist class. instead of launching cdm directly, mg therefore gave his 11-point demands in january 1930.

sections.title: MG's 11-Point Demands, January 1930
sections.norm: mg's 11-point demands, january 1930. what was the logic behind these demands? the 11 demands defined what swaraj would actually mean for the masses the demands fell into three categories: four middle-class / bourgeoisie issues: depreciation of the rupee 1s 6d protective tariffs for cotton indian tariff board postal reservation bill two peasants' issues: 50% decrease in land revenue (lr) zero lr during famine release confiscated property five general issues: decrease military expenditure arms act 1878 total prohibition release political prisoners abolish the salt tax 1851 1852 charter act of 1853 the salt act 1882 irwin26-31 rejected all 11 demands cdm was now inevitable cdm rtc pyq 1996 1930-32 2003 irwin. what was the logic behind these demands? the 11 demands defined what swaraj would actually mean for the masses — what benefits would reach ordinary people under self-government. mg's argument was this: if the british were willing to deliver these benefits to the masses on their own, inc was ready to sacrifice its own party interest in political power. (notice mg's style of arbitration — offering the british a chance to deliver the substance of swaraj without a confrontation.) the demands fell into three categories: four middle-class / bourgeoisie issues: 3.1) lower the exchange rate for the rupee to 1 rs = 1s 4d (1 shilling & 4 pence) — i.e. depreciation of the rupee, which would boost indian exports & discourage import of british goods by making them costlier. (in line with make in india i.e. domestic production.) *note-in 1926, the hilton-young commission fixed the rupee high at 1s 6d. this kept remittances to britain flowing easily because fewer rupees were needed to pay fixed debts in pounds. easily paying foreign debts made india look financially stable to lenders. the high rupee helped britain by making british goods cheaper in india, while hurting indian capitalists, workers, and farmers by making indian goods expensive abroad. indian businesses pressed for a lower 1s 4d rate since 1926 to reverse this, as seen in chapter 47. 3.2) protective tariffs for cotton — import duty on imported cotton cloth. 3.3) full status & powers to the indian tariff board, so indian businessmen would have a say in deciding import/export duties. 3.4) pass the postal reservation bill to reserve 50% seats in the postal department for indians, i.e. jobs for the western educated middle class (wemc). two peasants' issues: 3.5) 50% decrease in land revenue (lr) and zero lr during famine. 3.6) release confiscated property of those who participated in the bardoli satyagraha (1928). five general issues: 3.7) decrease military expenditure & salary of civil servants. 3.8) amend the arms act 1878 to give indians the right to bear arms for self-defence. 3.9) total prohibition on intoxicants. 3.10) release political prisoners not guilty of violence. 3.11) abolish the salt tax (which formed 8.2% of government revenue) and the government salt monopoly. ◆ the demand to abolish salt tax was not new. the british indians' association (1851), madras native association (1852), and bombay association (1852) had sent similar demands to the british parliament before the charter act of 1853. the salt act 1882 had applied tax on salt & reaffirmed the government's monopoly over it. irwin26-31 rejected all 11 demands. cdm was now inevitable. ⚠ alert: cdm-plan + rtc pyq cluster. prelims 1996 (indian-british meetings 1930-32 in london = round table conferences); prelims 2003 (indian freedom struggle — chronological / sequence facts). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM), 1930–34
sections.norm: civil disobedience movement (cdm), 1930–34. reasons rejection of mg's 11-point demands economic grievances great depression (gd1929) great depression 1929 irwin. reasons 4.1) rejection of mg's 11-point demands by irwin26-31. 4.2) economic grievances generated by the great depression (gd1929): i) cash crop prices crashed in international markets — cotton & jute, both export crops, were badly hit. this devastated the ryots. (recall — the end of the us civil war 1861–65 had similarly caused a fall in raw cotton prices, contributing to the bombay deccan riots of 1875.)ii) prices of wheat & rice also fell in domestic markets, further destroying farm income — but land revenue (lr) stayed the same. moneylenders stopped lending & demanded repayment of old loans. peasants had to sell land just to raise money for the next sowing season. iii) the working class (wc) suffered low wages & lay-offs due to gd1929. iv) thus, both ryots in rural areas & wc in urban areas were restless.

sections.title: Structure of CDM
sections.norm: structure of cdm. cdm moved through two phases gandhi-irwin pact of 1931 1st phase: 1930–31 truce: gandhi-irwin pact, 5 march 1931 2nd rtc 2nd phase: 1932–34. cdm moved through two phases, separated by a truce in the form of the gandhi-irwin pact of 1931: 5.1) 1st phase: 1930–31 5.2) truce: gandhi-irwin pact, 5 march 1931, followed by the 2nd rtc (september–december 1931, london), where inc participated. 5.3) 2nd phase: 1932–34

sections.title: CDM Plan of MG
sections.norm: cdm plan of mg. illegal manufacture of salt consumed by everyone non-cooperation (nc) boycott of british institutions no-revenue campaign ryotwari & mahalwari areas non-payment of chowkidari tax zamindari areas indians versus the british violation of forest laws muslim league 1906 communist party of india 1925. (notice mg's style of rising tempo — gradual escalation.) 1st stage: 6.1) marches by leaders in coastal areas for illegal manufacture of salt — i.e. civil disobedience against the salt law. salt was chosen as the issue because: i) it was consumed by everyone. ii) the salt issue would highlight british oppression of indians even in regard to basic necessities. iii) it would unite all, especially the poor. iv) salt was neither a hindu issue (so ml1906 could not object on communal grounds) nor a bourgeoisie issue (so cpi1925 could not label it a capitalist cause). v) there was less chance of immediate repression, as abolishing salt tax would not significantly hurt government revenues. 6.2) non-cooperation (nc): i) boycott of british institutions — lawyers & civil servants to resign; boycott of courts. ii) boycott of british goods & use of swadeshi goods, e.g. khadi. 2nd stage: 6.3) no-revenue campaign in ryotwari & mahalwari areas, where the masses paid lr directly to the government. 6.4) non-payment of chowkidari tax in zamindari areas — a tax to pay for salaries of chowkidars or village watchmen under the indian police act 1861. mg deliberately chose this issue because he wanted the confrontation framed as indians versus the british. a no-rent campaign in zamindari areas would have hurt unity among indians — indian ryot versus indian landlord. high rents were the real grievance of tenant ryots, but they were deliberately not made the demand. 6.5) violation of forest laws in central provinces.

sections.title: Implementation: 1st Stage (March 1930 – May 1930)
sections.norm: implementation: 1st stage (march 1930 – may 1930). dandi march began in march 1930 sabarmati ashram break the salt law salt satyagraha was not limited to dandi regional leaders launched their own campaigns madras: rajaji's vedaranniyam march c. rajagopalachari tiruchirappalli to vedaranniyam 98 volunteers criminal offence to provide food, water, or shelter rukmini lakshmipathi malabar: kelappan's salt march k. kelappan calicut to poyannur maulana abdul hamid khan bhashani sylhet to noakhali inchudi in balasore gopabandhu chaudhuri & harekrushna mahatab ankola sanikatta salt works shiroda salt works vile parle kamaladevi chattopadhyay sibirams konda venkatappaiah non-cooperation also began 1920 cwc aicc cdm inc 1905–11 pyq 2015 2025. the dandi march began in march 1930 — mg marched from the sabarmati ashram (set up in 1917) to the dandi coast to break the salt law. huge crowds joined, including women. what made cdm truly an all-india movement was that the salt satyagraha was not limited to dandi. regional leaders launched their own campaigns across the country, making cdm far more geographically spread than any previous movement. madras: rajaji's vedaranniyam march c. rajagopalachari marched from tiruchirappalli to vedaranniyam with a handpicked group of 98 volunteers — selected from over a thousand applicants & trained to endure police brutality without retaliating. the march was strategically launched on 13 april 1930 — a date chosen because it was both the tamil new year (puthandu) and the day commemorating the jallianwala bagh massacre: two powerful emotional triggers in one day. they reached the coast on 28 april & broke the salt law on 30 april. the district collector of tanjore, j.a. thorne, issued orders making it a criminal offence to provide food, water, or shelter to the marchers. the local population responded by tying food packets to tree branches & leaving provisions at secret spots along the route — so the marchers were fed without anyone being directly caught. :) the march had its own anthem, composed by namakkal kavignar ramalingam pillai — "kathi indri ratham indri yuddham ondru varugudhu"(a war is coming without swords, without blood). rajaji was arrested on 30 april. rukmini lakshmipathi became the first woman in india to pay a penalty for violation of the salt laws. malabar: kelappan's salt march in a coordinated move, k. kelappan — known as "the kerala gandhi" — launched his malabar salt march from calicut to poyannur on the exact same day, 13 april 1930. (he is also known for leading the guruvayur temple entry satyagraha of 1931–32.) assam: maulana abdul hamid khan bhashani marched from sylhet to noakhali in bengal. odisha: inchudi in balasore district became so prominent it was called the "second dandi" — led by gopabandhu chaudhuri & harekrushna mahatab, and notable for massive women's participation under leaders like rama devi & malati choudhury. karnataka: ankola in uttara kannada earned the title "bardoli of karnataka" for its intense no-tax & salt campaigns, with raids on the sanikatta salt works. key leaders: m.p. nadkarni, r.r. diwakar, karnad sadashiv rao. maharashtra & bombay: the shiroda salt works in ratnagiri saw massive raids. in bombay city, vile parle served as movement headquarters, organised by jamnalal bajaj. kamaladevi chattopadhyay sold contraband salt outside the bombay stock exchange & the bombay high court. :) andhra: leaders set up military-style training camps called sibirams in krishna, godavari, and guntur districts to train satyagrahis before marching to the coast. konda venkatappaiah directed operations from a sibiram in vijayawada; pattabhi sitaramayya played a major organising role. non-cooperation also began alongside the salt campaigns — boycott of british goods & institutions. ◆ notice how mg's organisational groundwork since 1920 — pccs on linguistic lines, cwc, aicc, local congress committees — was now paying off. cdm was not a movement that depended on mg personally reaching every village. the inc machinery ensured regional leaders could run disciplined, coordinated campaigns independently. this was the key difference between cdm & the swadeshi movement of 1905–11, which had remained largely confined to bengal. ⚠ alert: 1st-stage cdm pyq cluster. prelims 2015 (tanjore coast salt march = c. rajagopalachari, vedaranyam); prelims 2025 ("sedition has become my religion" — gandhiji's famous cdm-era statement). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: NWFP: The Khudai Khidmatgars and the Qissa Khwani Bazaar Massacre
sections.norm: nwfp: the khudai khidmatgars and the qissa khwani bazaar massacre. north-west frontier province (nwfp) one of the most remarkable chapters of cdm khan abdul ghaffar khan frontier gandhi khudai khidmatgars red shirts 23 april 1930 qissa khwani bazaar royal garhwal rifles chandra singh garhwali flatly refused 2002 nwfp pyq. the movement in the north-west frontier province (nwfp) was one of the most remarkable chapters of cdm. khan abdul ghaffar khan — known as the frontier gandhi, badshah khan, and fakhr-e-afghan (pride of afghans) — was an educator & social reformer who had opened schools across nwfp & published an influential pashto-language political journal called pakhtun (started 1928). in 1929, he founded a volunteer brigade called the khudai khidmatgars (servants of god), popularly known as the red shirts or surkh posh — their uniforms were dyed with cheap brick-dust, since white khadi got dirty too quickly in the rugged terrain. ◆ what made the khudai khidmatgars extraordinary was the ideological fusion ghaffar khan achieved. he integrated the traditional pashtun code of honour (pukhtunwali) with gandhian non-violence — framing non-violence not as weakness but as the ultimate test of bravery for a true muslim & a true pashtun. volunteers took a solemn oath to forgive their oppressors, live a pure life, and serve humanity without reward. for the british, a disciplined, non-violent army of tens of thousands of pashtuns — a people historically feared for their martial spirit — was a strategic nightmare. on 23 april 1930, the british arrested ghaffar khan in peshawar. massive unarmed crowds gathered at the qissa khwani bazaar (the storytellers' market) to protest. the british sent armoured cars into the crowd, ran over several people, and opened machine-gun fire. hundreds of peaceful protesters were killed — yet the crowd initially refused to disperse & kept coming forward to face the bullets. eventually the pashtuns erupted & responded with violence. during the massacre, the british ordered the royal garhwal rifles — predominantly hindu garhwali soldiers — to open fire on the unarmed muslim crowds. the soldiers, led by chandra singh garhwali, flatly refused. they stated they would not shoot unarmed citizens. they were court-martialled & given severe prison sentences for mutiny. (their defiance became the ultimate symbol of hindu-muslim unity during cdm — and proof that mg's idea of non-violent resistance had penetrated even the british indian army. !!!!) ⚠ alert: prelims 2002 (khudai khidmatgars = red shirts, nwfp, abdul ghaffar khan). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Implementation: 2nd Stage (May 1930 – March 1931)
sections.norm: implementation: 2nd stage (may 1930 – march 1931). dharasana satyagraha, may 1930 (gujarat) mg gave the british prior warning mg's arrest in may 1930 abbas tyabji sarojini naidu beaten mercilessly webb miller turned international opinion against british rule cunningham circular. dharasana satyagraha, may 1930 (gujarat) mg gave the british prior warning about a planned peaceful raid on the dharasana salt works (south of dandi). (notice the fearlessness of the satyagrahi — crimes are hidden, but politics is public.) this led to mg's arrest in may 1930, and the 2nd stage of cdm now began. leadership of the dharasana raid first passed to abbas tyabji, a 76-year-old retired judge, who marched with mg's wife kasturbai at his side — both were arrested before reaching dharasana. then sarojini naidu, mg's son manilal, and imam saheb (a follower of mg since the south african struggle) took charge of the raid on 21 may 1930. around 2,500 volunteers marched towards the salt works where about 400 police awaited them with steel-tipped lathis. the satyagrahis were beaten mercilessly — not one raised an arm to fend off the blows. over 300 were injured. the american journalist webb miller of united press witnessed the entire raid. his report — published in over a thousand newspapers worldwide — turned international opinion against british rule. (the british tried to censor miller's dispatch, but the truth got out. mg later said miller "helped make" indian independence through his eyewitness account. :) ) in assam, protests erupted against the cunningham circular in 1930–31, which forced parents to give an assurance of good behaviour of their children — essentially, a mechanism to prevent youth from joining cdm.

sections.title: Impact of CDM's 1st Phase (March 1930 – March 1931)
sections.norm: impact of cdm's 1st phase (march 1930 – march 1931). high participation more radicalism than he had in ncm cd happened at an all-india level capitalist class 50% decrease in import of foreign cloth women's participation no major working class participation cpi1925 boycotted low muslim participation no inc-ml1906 pact middle-class youth inspired by revolutionaries capitalist participation decreased peasant participation decreased property confiscation no-rent campaigns mg cautious government repression illegal (1930) communist party of india 1925 muslim league 1906 lucknow pact 1916 great depression 1929. positives: 10.1) high participation in both urban & rural areas. 10.2) mg showed more radicalism than he had in ncm (1920–22) — he did not withdraw the movement despite initial violence. 10.3) not just nc but also cd happened at an all-india level. this was important progress in the inm — people were willing to bear repression & go to jail, since cd involves breaking the law while nc does not. 10.4) for the first time, massive participation of the capitalist class — especially traders who stopped importing british cloth, leading to a 50% decrease in import of foreign cloth. (unlike the swadeshi movement, and like ncm 1920–22.) the great depression had also contributed to the decline in imports as overall demand crashed, but the active role of traders was significant. 10.5) for the first time, large-scale women's participation — in both urban & rural areas. people were shocked to see huge gatherings of women on the streets. mg's image as mahatma & his focus on women's empowerment through years of constructive work had steadily reduced the opposition of indian men to women entering mainstream politics. negatives: 10.6) no major working class participation except in sholapur & nagpur, because cpi1925 boycotted cdm; workers were not attracted to non-violent methods; and mg was himself cautious about wc participation due to the communist influence on workers & the fear of violence that came with it. 10.7) low muslim participation due to lack of hindu-muslim unity — there was no inc-ml1906 pact this time, unlike lp1916 before ncm. 10.8) middle-class youth were not attracted to non-violent satyagraha, as they were inspired by revolutionaries like bhagat singh. 10.9) capitalist participation decreased as financial losses mounted. 10.10) peasant participation decreased gradually due to property confiscation on non-payment of tax. 10.11) tenant ryots began no-rent campaigns on their own — gd1929 had crashed crop prices, making them desperate. this made mg cautious: no-rent campaigns could have hurt unity among indians (indian ryot versus indian landlord), so they were not formally adopted as part of cdm. 10.12) government repression drove down participation, especially after september 1930 — and the movement had begun only in march 1930. 10.13) for the first time, the government declared the congress & its allied bodies illegal (1930) — outlawing the congress working committee & provincial committees. (this first ban came during the salt campaign; it returned in january 1932.)

sections.title: Why Was CDM's 1st Phase Suspended?
sections.norm: why was cdm's 1st phase suspended?. mg's decision to suspend cdm rising violence chittagong armory raid (1930–33) surya sen qissa khwani bazaar massacre workers in sholapur parallel government suspended under the gandhi-irwin pact of 1931. the main reason for mg's decision to suspend cdm was the rising violence: 11.1) the chittagong armory raid (1930–33) by the indian republican army of surya sen in east bengal. 11.2) violence following the arrest of khan abdul ghaffar khan in peshawar — the qissa khwani bazaar massacreand its violent aftermath, described above. 11.3) huge violence by workers in sholapur after mg's arrest in may 1930 — burning of liquor & foreign cloth shops, burning of the railway station, and a massive strike by textile workers. they even established a parallel government, forcing the british to impose martial law. cdm was therefore suspended under the gandhi-irwin pact of 1931. (recall mg's sts — struggle-truce-struggle — strategy. this was a truce because masses had got tired & violence had escalated.)

sections.title: Gandhi-Irwin Pact 1931 (Delhi Pact, 5 March 1931)
sections.norm: gandhi-irwin pact 1931 (delhi pact, 5 march 1931). reasons rising violence 1st rtc of 1930 had been a failure features cdm was suspended participate in the 2nd rtc salt for personal use picketing of liquor shops withdrawal of emergency ordinances release of political prisoners return of confiscated lands the british rejected commutation bhagat singh 23 march 1931 irwin pact pyq 2020 rtc 2005 1931 2010. reasons for mg, it was the rising violence during cdm's 1st phase. for the british, the 1st rtc of 1930 had been a failure due to non-participation of inc, and the massive participation in cdm had proved that any constitutional settlement without inc would carry no popular legitimacy. features 12.1) cdm was suspended. 12.2) inc to participate in the 2nd rtc (1931). 12.3) right to make salt for personal use. 12.4) right to picketing of liquor shops. 12.5) withdrawal of emergency ordinances. 12.6) release of political prisoners not charged with violence. 12.7) cancellation of fines & return of confiscated lands of peasants. 12.8) however, the british rejected commutation of the death sentence of bhagat singh, who was martyred on 23 march 1931. ⚠ alert: gandhi-irwin pact + karachi pyq cluster. prelims 2020 (gandhi-irwin pact terms — rtc invitation, prisoner release except violence-convicted, salt-tax relief in coastal areas); prelims 2005 (karachi 1931 fundamental rights resolution drafted by jawaharlal nehru); prelims 2010 (karachi 1931 session president = sardar vallabhbhai patel). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Karachi Special Session of INC, March 1931
sections.norm: karachi special session of inc, march 1931. significant for four reasons approved the gandhi-irwin26-31 pact fundamental rights (frs) national economic programme defined swaraj for the masses economic freedom black flags to mg tribute was paid to the martyrs irwin. the karachi session was significant for four reasons. 13.1) inc approved the gandhi-irwin26-31 pact. 13.2) inc passed resolutions on fundamental rights (frs) and a national economic programme influenced by socialist principles. the purpose was to communicate to the people what inc would stand for at the 2nd rtc. 13.3) inc defined swaraj for the masses — political freedom must include economic freedom. the underlying question was: inc will get power, but what will the people get? the answer: economic freedom from oppression of the poor by the rich, to be delivered through policy by a future self-government. 13.4) s.c. bose's supporters showed black flags to mg — "mg go back." youth at the karachi session were angry that mg had not secured commutation of bhagat singh's death sentence during the irwin pact negotiations — the failure to save bhagat singh, who had been executed barely days before, was a raw wound. despite this anger, bose & others ensured that a formal tribute was paid to the martyrs — bhagat singh & others.

sections.title: 2nd Round Table Conference, September–December 1931
