sections.norm: 2nd round table conference, september–december 1931. 2nd rtc failed deadlock over separate electorates b.r. ambedkar mg accordingly announced the resumption of cdm inc was banned yeravda prison the british, for their part, declared: nwfp full province sindh separated from bombay communal award if indians failed to reach consensus rtc pyq 1997 2005 not inc. the 2nd rtc failed due to a deadlock over separate electorates. all minorities — muslims, anglo-indians, europeans in india, indian christians, and the depressed classes — demanded separate electorates. the depressed classes were represented by b.r. ambedkar. mg & inc opposed separate electorates. (recall that the nehru report of august 1928 had proposed joint electorates.) the british also rejected the demand for purna swaraj. mg accordingly announced the resumption of cdm — what would become its 2nd phase (1932–34). in january 1932, inc was banned & mg was imprisoned in yeravda prison. the british, for their part, declared: 14.1) nwfp would be made a full province (done in 1932). 14.2) sindh would be separated from bombay & given full province status (done in 1936). 14.3) a communal award — i.e. separate electorates — would be imposed by the government if indians failed to reach consensus on joint electorates. ⚠ alert: 2nd rtc + 1st rtc pyq cluster. prelims 1997 (match-list: rtc delegates + roles); prelims 2005 (1st rtc: all major political organisations of india did not participate — inc boycotted). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: 3rd Round Table Conference, November–December 1932
sections.norm: 3rd round table conference, november–december 1932. without inc participation white paper (1933) government of india act 1935. the 3rd rtc was held without inc participation — inc had been banned in january 1932. it produced a white paper (1933), which was examined by a joint parliamentary committee (jpc). the jpc's report formed the basis of the government of india act 1935 (covered in detail in the next chapter).

sections.title: Communal Award / MacDonald Award, August 1932
sections.norm: communal award / macdonald award, august 1932. communal award was announced by british pm ramsay macdonald could not reach consensus on joint electorates extended separate electorates to the depressed classes inc neither accepted nor rejected the award poona pact pyq 2013 1932 2002 2025 1997 not. the communal award was announced by british pm ramsay macdonald because indians could not reach consensus on joint electorates. it extended separate electorates to the depressed classes as well. (other minorities had already had separate electorates since the goi act 1919.) inc neither accepted nor rejected the award — because separate electorates had been demanded by the depressed classes themselves & had not been imposed on them by the british alone. ⚠ alert: communal award + poona pact pyq cluster. prelims 2013 (gandhi's 1932 fast unto death — against communal award's separate electorate for depressed classes); prelims 2002 (match-list: persons + events of colonial period); prelims 2025 (gandhiji included upliftment of harijans after poona pact); prelims 1997 (poona pact = between mahatma gandhi & dr b.r. ambedkar, not british government). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Poona Pact, September 1932
sections.norm: poona pact, september 1932. separate electorates for the depressed classes would permanently divide hindus against the method of separate electorates mg undertook a 21-day fast unto death ambedkar madan mohan malviya rejected the communal award 71 to 147 seats 18% reservation in the cla separate electorates were removed joint electorates with reserved seats the poona pact. mg feared that separate electorates for the depressed classes would permanently divide hindus & make untouchability a permanent feature of indian political life. he was not against greater reservation — he was against the method of separate electorates. his issue was with how the representation would be elected, not with how much representation there should be. mg undertook a 21-day fast unto death against the communal award. the pact was signed after his release from the fast. ambedkar signed on behalf of the lower castes (lc). madan mohan malviya signed on behalf of the upper castes (uc). the pact: 17.1) rejected the communal award of august 1932 (insofar as it applied separate electorates to the depressed classes). 17.2) increased reservation for the depressed classes — from 71 to 147 seats in plas, plus 18% reservation in the cla. the outcome: separate electorates were removed, but as compensation, the number of reserved seats was more than doubled. the depressed classes would contest in joint electorates with reserved seats — a model that forms the basis of sc/st reservation in indian elections to this day. ⚠ exam note: the poona pact rejected the communal award's method (separate electorates) but increased the reservation offered under it (from 71 to 147 seats). students often confuse "rejection" of the communal award with "reduction" in reservation — the opposite is true.

sections.title: CDM 2nd Phase, September 1932–1934
sections.norm: cdm 2nd phase, september 1932–1934. inc banned yeravda prison mg released on health grounds primary focus: anti-untouchability campaign shifted decisively to an anti-untouchability campaign penance eradication of untouchability internal reforms among harijans harijan sevak sangh (1932) harijan magazine (1933) 1920 ncm. timeline: 18.1) january 1932 — inc banned; mg imprisoned in yeravda prison (due to decision to resume cdm). 18.2) september 1932 — mg released on health grounds after his 21-day fast against separate electorates. primary focus: anti-untouchability campaign mg's primary focus in the 2nd phase shifted decisively to an anti-untouchability campaign: 18.3) mg asked hindus to do penance & appealed for the complete eradication of untouchability. 18.4) he worked on internal reforms among harijans in the domains of education, health, and hygiene — and appealed to harijans to remove untouchability from within their own communities as well. 18.5) to lead the campaign in an organised form, mg set up: i) harijan sevak sangh (1932) / all india anti-untouchability league (1932) ii) harijan sevak fund (1932) iii) to raise awareness: the harijan magazine (1933), a 20,000 km march across india, and two fasts. ◆ mg was an organisation man. recall the tilak swaraj fund of 1920 for ncm — whenever mg launched a campaign, there was an organisational structure, a dedicated fund, and a media arm to sustain it.

sections.title: Results of CDM's 2nd Phase
sections.norm: results of cdm's 2nd phase. low response demoralisation lc were becoming more radical formally ended in 1934 inc benefitted 1937 provincial elections nellie sengupta third woman 1997 cdm pyq. 19.1) low response — there was demoralisation after the suspension of the 1st phase. 19.2) neither upper castes nor lower castes showed much enthusiasm for the harijan campaign. the lc were becoming more radical & wanted political & economic rights; mg mainly addressed social dignity. 19.3) government repression did the rest. cdm was formally ended in 1934. 19.4) yet inc benefitted — it performed very well in the 1937 provincial elections held under the goi act 1935. the political capital accumulated during years of mass mobilisation — even from a cdm that ended in apparent failure — was cashed in at the ballot box. nellie sengupta — third woman inc president (1933 calcutta session). during the peak of british repression in 1933, nellie sengupta (born edith ellen gray in cambridge, england, married to j.m. sengupta) took the mantle of the inc presidency at the calcutta session. following the arrest of the designated president, madan mohan malaviya, she defied a government ban to chair the session — demonstrating that the commitment to india's cause was not bound by ethnicity. she holds the distinction of being the third woman (after annie besant in 1917 & sarojini naidu in 1925) — & the second foreign-born woman — to preside over the congress, symbolising the universal moral appeal of the movement. ⚠ alert: prelims 1997 (match-list: events of cdm 2nd phase + their leaders/dates). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Government of India Act, 1935 & Congress Ministries
sections.title: Why Was the GOI Act 1935 Passed?
sections.norm: why was the goi act 1935 passed?. did not emerge from any genuine british desire linlithgow36-43 two kinds of pressure pressure from below revolutionaries the masses the great depression of 1929 1.4) legal basis was built through the stages discussed below. 2018 goi act 1935 pyq hindustan republican army 1924 hindustan republican association 1924 hindustan socialist republican army 1928 hindustan socialist republican association 1928 great depression 1929 government of india act 1935 linlithgow. 1.1) the goi act 1935 did not emerge from any genuine british desire to give indians self-government. linlithgow36-43 (viceroy from 1936 to 1943, who actually implemented the act in 1937) was candid about this. he stated plainly that the goi act 1935 was "the best way to maintain control over india." that is the honest summary of a 321-section act. 1.2) the circumstances linlithgow36-43 referred to were two kinds of pressure — pressure from below & pressure from legal consultations above. 1.3) pressure from below came from every direction. revolutionaries had kept the british nervous through the hra1924, hsra1928, and the chittagong armory raid of 1930–33. the masses had made their presence felt through anti-simon agitations in 1928 & the civil disobedience movement of 1930–34. the great depression of 1929 had caused mass economic suffering & deepened anger against british rule. (notice how every section of indian society — youth, peasants, workers, capitalists — and even world history in the form of gd1929 fed into the pressure that produced goi1935) 1.4) legal basis was built through the stages discussed below. ⚠ alert: prelims 2018 (goi act 1935 — provincial autonomy + federal structure proposed). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Government of India Act, 1935 & Congress Ministries
sections.title: Legal Basis
sections.norm: legal basis. 2.1) simon commission report (june 1930) no indian member it recommended: provincial autonomy no change at the centre expansion of franchise retention of separate electorates re-affirmed province status for nwfp full province status be given to sindh separation of burma from india. 2.2) the three round table conferences (rtcs) 1st rtc (1930) the princes demanded a federation inc boycotted. 2nd rtc (1931) — inc participated. indian demands were rejected the nehru report remained a wish — unfulfilled 3rd rtc (1932) practically irrelevant 2.3) thus, goi act 1935 was against the principle of self-government no indian in the 7-member simon commission inc boycotted the 1st & 3rd rtcs the 2nd rtc was a failure stayed unfulfilled goi 1935 pyq 2000 2004 2005 india act 1935 1950 2009 rtc. 2.1) simon commission report (june 1930) the seven-member simon commission had no indian member !!!! it recommended: i) provincial autonomy — abolition of the dyarchy system introduced under goi 1919 & replacement with full responsible government in the provinces, though with some emergency powers retained by the governor. ii) no change at the centre — meaning the centre remained under british despotism. iii) expansion of franchise — widening the electorate, though still far short of universal adult franchise. iv) retention of separate electorates — the communal electorate system was to continue. v) re-affirmed province status for nwfp with a weak legislature, and recommended that full province status be given to sindh only after a finance boundary commission's recommendations. (nwfp was carved from punjab as a chief commissioner or cc province in 1901 & raised to a governor's province in 1932 with a limited legislative council & dyarchy-type arrangements — but without full responsible government) vi) separation of burma from india. (the 1st burma war of 1824–26 & 2nd burma war of 1852–53 had led to its annexation; it was finally separated from india in 1937) 2.2) the three round table conferences (rtcs) i) 1st rtc (1930) — representatives of the princely states & non-inc parties participated. the princes demanded a federation, i.e. a union combining british india & the princely states. inc boycotted. ii) 2nd rtc (1931) — inc participated. indian demands of a federation with responsible government at the centre & purna swaraj were rejected. the nehru report of august 1928, which had been the wish of the all party conference, remained a wish — unfulfilled by the goi act 1935. iii) 3rd rtc (1932) — inc boycotted. participation was so low the conference was practically irrelevant. 2.3) thus, goi act 1935 was against the principle of self-government i) no indian in the 7-member simon commission (1927). ii) inc boycotted the 1st & 3rd rtcs; the 2nd rtc was a failure. iii) the nehru report of august 1928 — merely a wish of the all party conference — stayed unfulfilled. ⚠ alert: goi 1935 legal-basis pyq cluster. prelims 2000 (simon commission features → goi 1935 lineage); prelims 2004 (joint-parliamentary-committee head = lord linlithgow); prelims 2005 (government of india act 1935 — basis for constitution of india 1950); prelims 2009 (rtc outcomes → communal award → goi 1935). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Government of India Act, 1935 & Congress Ministries
sections.title: Territorial and Administrative Reorganisation
sections.norm: territorial and administrative reorganisation. full province status to orissa (1936) and bihar (1936) sindh was separated from bombay nwfp as a full province only a limited legislative council full responsible government in nwfp 1937 burma was separated from india in 1937. government of india act 1935. 3.1) goi1935 gave full province status to orissa (1936) and bihar (1936), separating the two from the combined "bihar & orissa" province created in 1912. sindh was separated from bombay & given full province status (1936). 3.2) the status of nwfp as a full province (created 1932 when it was raised from a chief commissioner's province to a governor's province) was reaffirmed. however, in 1932 nwfp received only a limited legislative council of about 40 members with dyarchy-type arrangements — the governor retained very strong reserve & veto powers, and the executive was not responsible to the council. full responsible government in nwfp came only with the implementation of goi 1935 from 1937, when dyarchy was abolished, a proper legislative assembly was constituted, and a premier with a council of ministers responsible to the pla was introduced. 3.3) burma was separated from india in 1937. (united provinces as a name was formalised in 1937)

sections.chapterTitle: Government of India Act, 1935 & Congress Ministries
sections.title: Features at the Centre — The Part That Never Happened
sections.norm: features at the centre — the part that never happened. everything at the centre remained on paper goi act 1919 continued to govern the centre 4.1) a federation of british india & the princely states union of british india & the princely states at least 50% of princes to sign the instrument of accession that threshold was never met. transfer only defence, foreign affairs, and communications why the princes refused to sign: paramountcy was not abolished two bosses financial autonomy compel princes to contribute to the defence budget low representation at the centre feared democracy inc could launch movements inside those states 4.2) a bicameral legislature at the centre federal assembly (fa) council of states (cos) nominees of the princes — not elected eliminated the chances of an inc majority cos were to be direct fa were to be indirect limit inc strength cos was to be permanent fa was to have a 5-year life 4.3) right to vote — expanded but restricted only 10% of the population actually qualified deny voting rights women's franchise — derived, not independent voting rights under goi1935 were tied to patriarchal structures largely derived from her husband's status income or property kept lower than the threshold required for men a widow could vote sixth schedule literacy alone was sufficient for a woman higher educational threshold 4.4) representation — continuation & expansion of communal politics separate electorates for all minorities continued scheduled castes reservation in elected seats reservation for women & labour/workers 4.5) first federal distribution of subjects for the first time proper federal distribution of subjects federal, concurrent, and provincial goi1919 goi1935 1935 1861 motilal nehru report 1928 4.6) budget & financial controls at the centre 80% of the budget at the centre was still non-votable the viceroy retained 4.7) dyarchy at the centre dyarchy now proposed at the centre itself reserved & transferred reserved subjects (strictly 4) absolute legislative & executive control of the viceroy not responsible to the legislature transferred subjects included finance & home partially responsible government at the centre ⚠ exam trap — the home & finance confusion 4.8) fiscal autonomy to goi from secretary of state financial control over british india was transferred to the viceroy in india nehru 4.9) federal court establishment of a federal court first court with jurisdiction over disputes set up in 1937 4.10) reserve bank of india not a provision of goi1935 itself rbi act 1934 operational on 1 april 1935 goi pyq 1996 1937 2001 rbi 2019 2024 government of india act 1935 government of india act 1919 constitution of india 1950 government of india act 1858. everything at the centre under goi1935 remained on paper. the central federal provisions never became operational & goi act 1919 continued to govern the centre. this is important to hold onto. 4.1) a federation of british india & the princely states india was to become a union of british india & the princely states with federal relations between the two. (this mirrored the structure proposed in the nehru report of august 1928) this required at least 50% of princes to sign the instrument of accession (ioa) as defined in section 6 of goi1935. that threshold was never met. (the butler committee of 1927 had promised the british would not change the status of the princely states without the consent of the princes — the princes used that promise as cover to stay out) after signing the ioa, a princely state would transfer only defence, foreign affairs, and communications to the union government. (this is structurally identical to how jammu & kashmir signed only an ioa in 1947 & not a full merger agreement — art. 370 is that legacy) why the princes refused to sign: i) paramountcy was not abolished by goi1935. the princes therefore faced the prospect of two bosses — the union government of india & the british crown — and wanted neither. ii) financial autonomy was at stake. once inside the union, the goi could compel princes to contribute to the defence budget. (e.g. goi can force princely states to fund the army once the ioa is signed) iii) smaller princely states felt they would get low representation at the centre in the proposed legislatures. iv) they feared democracy. once the princely states joined the union, inc could launch movements inside those states too. (as one country, not separate territories, the rules of political activity would change entirely) 4.2) a bicameral legislature at the centre the proposed central legislature consisted of a federal assembly (fa) and a council of states (cos). (under goi1919, the corresponding bodies were the central legislative assembly or cla & the council of states or cos — both only for british india, not the princely states) i) one-third of fa members were to be nominees of the princes — not elected. this practically eliminated the chances of an inc majority in the fa, which was the more powerful lower house. ii) elections to the cos were to be direct (!!!) for better representation of different regions & communities. but elections to the fa were to be indirect — specifically to limit inc strength in the more powerful house. (regional parties do better than all-india parties when elections are indirect, so inc would win fewer fa seats) iii) the life of the cos was to be permanent, with one-third of its members retiring every third year. (compare: coi1950 has one-third retiring every 2 years) the fa was to have a 5-year life. (compare: the cla under goi1919 had a 3-year life) 4.3) right to vote — expanded but restricted the right to vote was extended to more indians, but income & education criteria still meant only 10% of the population actually qualified. the intent was clear: deny voting rights to inc's support base — the poor peasants & workers (ryots & working class) women's franchise — derived, not independent women's voting rights under goi1935 were tied to patriarchal structures. a woman's right to vote was not independent — it was largely derived from her husband's status. i) a woman could vote on the basis of her husband's income or property, though the financial threshold required for this derived right was kept lower than the threshold required for men to qualify directly. ii) if the husband was deceased, a widow could vote on the basis of property or income left by the dead husband. iii) voting qualifications were defined in the sixth schedule & varied from province to province. in many provinces, literacy alone was sufficient for a woman to qualify, whereas men without property often had to meet a higher educational threshold such as middle school or matriculation. 4.4) representation — continuation & expansion of communal politics i) separate electorates for all minorities continued as under goi1919. ii) scheduled castes now got reservation in elected seats in the fa, cos, and plas. (under goi1919, reservation for depressed classes was only in nominated seats — this was a step forward) iii) reservation for women & labour/workers was also provided. 4.5) first federal distribution of subjects goi1935 introduced, for the first time, a proper federal distribution of subjects into three lists: federal, concurrent, and provincial. (this is the ancestor of the 7th schedule of coi1950) ◆ under goi1919, the centre had outsourced some subjects to provinces but constitutional ownership remained with the centre. under goi1935, provinces received constitutional ownership of their subjects. this is why 1935 marks the peak of federalism in the british era — the journey began in 1861 & peaked here. for the princely states that signed the ioa, only three subjects — defence, communications, foreign affairs — were to go to the centre, structurally like art. 370. recall also that the motilal nehru report of august 1928 had a similar federal distribution structure. 4.6) budget & financial controls at the centre 80% of the budget at the centre was still non-votable. the viceroy retained residual powers, veto powers, ordinance powers, the power to restore cuts in grants, and the power to certify rejected bills. (the viceroy under goi1935 was not a powerless ceremonial president) 4.7) dyarchy at the centre ironically, the dyarchy that had been applied in provinces under goi1919 was now proposed at the centre itself. federal subjects were divided into two legal categories: reserved & transferred. reserved subjects (strictly 4) — defence, external affairs, ecclesiastical affairs (church), and tribal areas — were to remain under the absolute legislative & executive control of the viceroy, administered with the help of up to 3 counselors who were not responsible to the legislature. (link: 5th schedule of coi1950 for tribal areas) transferred subjects — all other subjects on the federal list, which inherently included finance & home — were to be administered by the viceroy on the aid & advice of a council of ministers responsible to the fa & cos. this made only a partially responsible government at the centre. ⚠ exam trap — the home & finance confusion — finance & home were legally transferred subjects, not reserved subjects. however, section 12 of the act gave the viceroy overarching "special responsibilities" that allowed him to intervene: (i) to protect the "financial stability & credit of the federal government" — which gave him effective power to override the finance minister. (ii) to prevent any "grave menace to the peace or tranquillity of india" — which gave him effective power to override the home minister. the reserved subjects were strictly only four: defence, external affairs, ecclesiastical affairs, and tribal areas. if a prelims statement says "finance was a reserved subject under goi1935" — it is strictly incorrect. finance was a transferred subject, just one the viceroy could shadow through special responsibilities. 4.8) fiscal autonomy to goi from secretary of state financial control over british india was transferred from the secretary of state for india (sosforindia) in london to the viceroy in india. (since goi1858, the sosforindia had been the top authority on indian finances — that is precisely why morley made his famous budget speech in 1906) nehru called this "the only major change" in the entire goi1935. 4.9) federal court the goi act 1935 provided for the establishment of a federal court — the first court with jurisdiction over disputes between provinces & between provinces & the centre. the federal court was actually set up in 1937. (this was the institutional ancestor of the supreme court of india under coi1950) 4.10) reserve bank of india though not a provision of goi1935 itself, the reserve bank of india was established under the rbi act 1934 & became operational on 1 april 1935 — timed to coincide with the broader constitutional & financial restructuring of british india in the mid-1930s. (the rbi was set up as the central banking authority to manage currency & credit, a prerequisite for the kind of fiscal federalism goi1935 envisaged) ⚠ alert: goi 1935 centre + federation pyq cluster. prelims 1996 (princely states accession needed for federation — never achieved, so federation never came into effect); prelims 1996 (federal court 1937 — predecessor of supreme court of india); prelims 2001 (rbi 1935 — established under goi 1935 framework as central monetary authority); prelims 2019 (goi 1935 — federal structure proposed, dyarchy at centre, provincial autonomy); prelims 2024 (goi 1935 provisions verbatim). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Features at the Provinces — The Part That Did Work (from 1937)
sections.norm: features at the provinces — the part that did work (from 1937). the provincial provisions came into force in 1937 real structural difference 5.1) provincial autonomy all subjects in provinces became transferred subjects aid & advice of the council of ministers 5.2) fully responsible government in provinces dyarchy ended. premier (chief minister) for the first time, genuine responsible government upper house 5.3) the governor was still too powerful 40% of the provincial budget was non-votable the governor retained a formidable set of powers override the elected government summon the pla veto power ordinance power. administration of tribal areas protect minority rights, british business interests, and privileges of civil servants take over the government & run it indefinitely 5.4) goi act 1935 — summary card government of india act 1935 government of india act 1919 constitution of india 1950 linlithgow. the provincial provisions came into force in 1937. this is where goi1935 made a real structural difference. 5.1) provincial autonomy the federal distribution of subjects & the end of dyarchy meant all subjects in provinces became transferred subjects — under plas & popular ministers. the governor was now expected to act on the aid & advice of the council of ministers. (governor = agent of the centre, which is why the 1919 dyarchy was not only anti-democratic but also anti-federal. federalism in india began in 1861 & peaked in 1935) 5.2) fully responsible government in provinces dyarchy ended. a council of ministers headed by a premier (chief minister) was made responsible to the pla. this was, for the first time, genuine responsible government at the provincial level. direct elections & separate electorates continued as under goi1919. some provinces were given an upper house. (an upper house gives voice to one administrative level below the legislature — it is a representation mechanism) 5.3) the governor was still too powerful however — and this is the crucial qualification — 40% of the provincial budget was non-votable, and the governor retained a formidable set of powers that could at any moment override the elected government. (an indian mla would be sad about the 40% non-votable budget; an indian minister perhaps less so — but from a democratic standpoint, this was anti-democratic, not merely pro-british) i) discretionary powers to summon the pla. ii) veto power over bills. iii) ordinance power. iv) administration of tribal areas. (link: 5th schedule of coi1950) v) special powers to protect minority rights, british business interests, and privileges of civil servants. vi) power to take over the government & run it indefinitely. (link: art. 356 of coi1950) 5.4) goi act 1935 — summary card feature detail key quote linlithgow36-43: "best way to maintain control" federal structure federation of british india + princely states (50% ioa needed — never met) centre legislature fa (indirect, 1/3 prince nominees) + cos (direct, permanent) federal subjects federal, concurrent, provincial lists (ancestor of 7th schedule) dyarchy at centre 4 reserved (defence, ea, ecclesiastical, tribal) + transferred (all others incl. finance/home) provincial autonomy end of dyarchy; all subjects transferred; premier responsible to pla governor powers veto; ordinance; take over govt (→ art. 356) viceroy powers 80% non-votable; veto; ordinance; certify rejected bills voters 10% qualified; women's derived right from husband's income/property + lower criteria scs elected reserved seats with joint electorates (first time — up from nominated) fiscal autonomy transferred from sos to viceroy (nehru: "only major change") federal court established under goi 1935, set up 1937 rbi established under rbi act 1934, operational 1 april 1935 territorial orissa (1936), bihar (1936), sindh separated (1936), burma separated (1937), nwfp (1937 — province with fully responsible govt)

sections.title: The Evolution of Voting Rights and Communal Representation
sections.norm: the evolution of voting rights and communal representation. most complex & frequently misunderstood here is a clear breakdown 6.1) the core definitions a separate electorate voter pool is strictly segregated a reserved seat seat is guaranteed for a specific group 6.2) phase 1: the 1909 act (the birth of separate electorates & the "double vote") separate electorates for muslims voter rolls were not mutually exclusive 6.3) phase 2: the 1919 act (watertight compartments) hindu-muslim compromise of the 1916 lucknow pact in exchange for a guaranteed quota of seats legally watertight electoral rolls cross-voting was strictly banned. 6.4) phase 3: the 1935 act (expansion and "internal carve-outs") took the watertight compartments of 1919 expanded them to new groups combinations of reservation & separate electorates women step 1 step 2 the result: remained untouched labour true separate electorates the differential franchise lowered the bar for women simple literacy was enough men without property faced a much higher hurdle 6.5) summary takeaway from overlapping voting rights to a rigidly divided society highly calculated math without upsetting the delicate & fiercely negotiated communal ratios goi 1935 pyq 2002 2005 1937 2021. (1909–1935) this is one of the most complex & frequently misunderstood areas of modern indian constitutional history. textbooks often use shorthand that blurs the lines between "reserved seats" and "separate electorates." here is a clear breakdown of how the franchise & communal representation evolved from 1909 to 1935. 6.1) the core definitions before tracking the historical timeline, it is essential to separate two concepts. a separate electorate means the voter pool is strictly segregated by identity — only voters of a specific community can vote for candidates of that community (e.g., only muslims voting for a muslim candidate). a reserved seat means a seat is guaranteed for a specific group, but who gets to vote for it can vary — the candidate pool is restricted, but the voter pool might not be. 6.2) phase 1: the 1909 act (the birth of separate electorates & the "double vote") i) the policy: the indian councils act of 1909 formally introduced separate electorates for muslims. ii) the reality (the double vote): at this stage, voter rolls were not mutually exclusive. qualified muslim voters were given a "double vote." they could vote in their newly created separate muslim constituencies & they were still legally allowed to vote in the standard "general" constituencies. 6.3) phase 2: the 1919 act (watertight compartments) i) the policy: the government of india act 1919 adopted the hindu-muslim compromise of the 1916 lucknow pact. muslims surrendered the "double vote" in exchange for a guaranteed quota of seats & the acceptance of separate electorates. ii) the reality (strict segregation): the 1919 act created legally watertight electoral rolls. you were either on a special minority roll (like the muslim roll) or the "general" roll (everyone else, which meant predominantly hindus). iii) the rule of exclusion: cross-voting was strictly banned. a muslim voter had absolutely no right to vote for a general seat, and a general voter had no right to vote for a muslim seat. 6.4) phase 3: the 1935 act (expansion and "internal carve-outs") the goi act 1935 took the watertight compartments of 1919 & expanded them to new groups using complex combinations of reservation & separate electorates. i) women (communal segregation via "internal carve-outs"): the act provided reserved seats for women, but did so without altering or hurting the overall share of seats assigned to any specific religious community. to achieve this, the british used an "internal carve-out" method. step 1 (the quota): the british first fixed the absolute total number of seats each community would receive to maintain the "communal balance" (e.g., deciding the muslim community gets exactly 30% of seats in a province). step 2 (the carve-out): once locked in, they looked inside that quota. if the muslim quota was 30 total seats, they might designate that 2 must be strictly reserved for muslim women. this left 28 standard muslim seats & 2 reserved muslim women's seats. the exact same rule applied to the general (hindu) quota. the result: the total number of representatives for a community remained untouched. the only "losers" were the men within those specific communities, who had slightly fewer seats they could legally contest. crucial clarification on voting: these seats were not a gender-exclusive electorate. both men & women voted for these seats. however, the watertight communal rule still applied: only muslim men & women could vote for the muslim women's seat, and only general men & women could vote for the general women's seat. ii) labour (special constituencies): labour received true separate electorates. seats were allocated to specific registered trade unions or factory groups. only qualified workers within those groups could vote for the labour representatives. iii) the differential franchise (voting qualifications): to artificially increase the number of female voters without granting universal adult suffrage, the 1935 act lowered the bar for women. in many provinces, simple literacy was enough to earn a woman the right to vote. meanwhile, men without property faced a much higher hurdle; they typically needed a formal educational qualification like middle school or matriculation to get on the voter roll. 6.5) summary takeaway from 1909 to 1935, the british indian electoral system moved from overlapping voting rights to a rigidly divided society where religion or social class dictated exactly which box a citizen was legally locked into. "general" did not mean "open to everyone" — it simply meant "those left over after all the separate electorates were carved out." ultimately, this highly calculated math was the british way of granting special representation to new groups without upsetting the delicate & fiercely negotiated communal ratios between hindus, muslims, and sikhs. ⚠ alert: goi 1935 voting rights + communal representation pyq cluster. prelims 2002 (communal award + goi 1935 separate electorates for depressed classes); prelims 2005 (1937 elections — congress majorities in 8 of 11 provinces); prelims 2021 (1935 act expanded electorate from ~3% to ~14% of population). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

autonomy at provinces congress ministries — 28-month rule (1937–39) [photo: map of india showing provinces where inc formed government in 1937] 1. why did inc decide to form governments? 1.1) goi1935 came into effect in 1937. inc made the strategic decision to contest the provincial elections & form governments — for two reasons: i) the same logic that had driven the pro-changers to enter the central legislative assembly (cla) in 1923: prevent non-inc parties from becoming powerful by occupying the space themselves. ii) to promote constructive work — and unlike in 1923, inc would now be in the executive as well, not just the legislature. 2. election results 2.1) inc won majority in 6 provinces (madras, bombay, up, cp, bihar, orissa) but formed ministries in 8 out of 11 provinces. in bengal, assam, and nwfp, inc emerged as the largest party without a majority; it set up coalition governments in assam & nwfp. (nwfp had been carved from punjab as a cc province in 1901 & raised to a governor's province in 1932 with a limited legislative council; full responsible government came only in 1937 under goi1935) 2.2) in punjab, the unionist party under sikandar hayat khan won the majority. ml1906 managed only 2 out of 175 seats in punjab. in sindh, the sind united party won. 3. impact of the congress ministries 3.1) morale & organisational strength congress ministries boosted the morale of party cadre, peasants, and workers. peasant & working class movements strengthened because inc was now in government — it was no longer just an agitational party but a governing one. 3.2) governance experience inc gained crucial administrative & governance experience during this 28-month period — experience that proved invaluable after 1947. 3.3) inm strengthened in the princely states the rise of inc to power in provinces inspired people in the princely states. if inc could extract swaraj from the british, the states' people reasoned, perhaps they too could win democratic rights from their indian princes. new praja mandals or state people's congresses (spcs) were set up in more princely states, and membership of existing spcs increased. ◆ after goi1919, the narendra mandal or chamber of princes had been set up in 1921 as an advisory body of the princely states to the british — that was the british response to the princely states question from above. the congress ministries of 1937–39 energised the popular response from below.

sections.chapterTitle: WW II (1939–45) & the Indian National Movement
sections.title: Setting the Stage: Three Players, Four Questions
sections.norm: setting the stage: three players, four questions. here is a quick map of those four questions @top — transfer of executive power at centre: actual responsible government @swaraj — what kind of freedom? purna swaraj dominion status @coi — constitution of india: draft their own constitution constituent assembly @unity — one india or many? united india pakistan study tool pyq 2008 linlithgow36-43 2009 1939 2012 ww2 muslim league 1906 linlithgow. before we dive into the events, it helps to understand what the years 1939 to 1947 were actually about at their core. essentially, three players — the british, the inc, and the muslim league (ml1906) — were constantly negotiating, pressuring, and manoeuvring around four central questions. every event in this period, every offer & every rejection, is a move in this four-dimensional game. here is a quick map of those four questions — and we will tag every major development against them as we go: @top — transfer of executive power at centre: this means viceroy to be a powerless constitutional head, and real executive power to be with an indian prime minister & an indian council of ministers. not just "more indians in the viceroy's council" — actual responsible government, where ministers are accountable to an elected legislature, not to london. @swaraj — what kind of freedom? will indians get purna swaraj — full, complete independence — or merely dominion status, which keeps india tethered within the british empire? @coi — constitution of india: will indians have the right to draft their own constitution? through a constituent assembly composed entirely of elected indians? or will the british retain a hand in shaping it? @unity — one india or many? will there be a united india? will british create pakistan? will the princely states be merged into india or left to float as separate entities? throughout the following pages, you will see (@top), (@swaraj), (@coi), and (@unity) as tags — they are a study tool to help you organise your thinking for theme-based upsc mains answers. (note for students: these tags are a pedagogic device. in the examination hall, do not write them — the examiner does not need them & they may confuse your answer. the text reads perfectly well without them. use the tags only to think & revise.) ⚠ alert: stage-setting pyq cluster (sec. 1). prelims 2008 (linlithgow36-43 era — ww2 indian context); prelims 2009 (congress working committee's 1939 stance — conditional support to war); prelims 2012 (forward bloc — formed by subhas chandra bose 1939 after expulsion from congress). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: 1939: Where Did the INC Stand @WW II?
sections.norm: 1939: where did the inc stand @ ww2 ?. britain declared india a belligerent linlithgow36-43 did not bother to consult indian leaders colonial arrogance there were at least three distinct views: mahatma gandhi support britain unconditionally netaji subhas chandra bose immediate civil disobedience movement roman script for hindi tripuri session (1939) pattabhi sitaramayya formed the forward bloc (1939) capture the inc from within three-way fracture of the left communists (cpi) socialists (csp/jp narayan) mn roy's followers pant resolution abstained only faction that stayed with bose no base left inside the congress nehru no cooperation in the war no mass movement during the war privately favoured an allied victory victorious powers had taken over the colonies colony of japan not going to simply hand over cooperation for free the inc put forward demands immediately establish responsible government at the centre promise a constituent assembly after the war declare its war aims linlithgow36-43 rejected all three only an advisory committee inc 1939 pyq 1999 2010 ww1 linlithgow. when britain declared war on germany in september 1939, it simultaneously declared india — a country it ruled without consent — a belligerent. the viceroy linlithgow36-43 (1936–43) did not bother to consult indian leaders. this single act of colonial arrogance set the tone for the next six years. inside the inc, there was no single position. there were at least three distinct views: 2.1) mahatma gandhi's position was that justice was on the allied side — nazi germany & fascist italy were aggressors, and morally, india should support britain unconditionally. to take advantage of britain's difficulty would be wrong. 2.2) netaji subhas chandra bose took the opposite view. britain's weakness was india's opportunity, and the moment called for an immediate civil disobedience movement. (cdm = civil disobedience movement) bose had first been elected congress president at the haripura session (1938). in that presidential address he also urged adopting the roman script for hindi, to make a common national language easier to learn. bose had already been on a collision course with the gandhi-led congress leadership. at the tripuri session (1939), bose had defeated gandhi's preferred candidate pattabhi sitaramayya in the presidential election — prompting gandhi to declare, "pattabhi's defeat is my defeat." unable to function as president without the support of the cwc, bose resigned from the inc & formed the forward bloc (1939) — a left-wing faction inside the inc (like the congress-khilafat swaraj party (1923) or the congress socialist party (1934)). aim was to consolidate the left wing within the congress so as to capture the inc from within. the deeper reason for bose's resignation was a three-way fracture of the left. the left had united to elect bose — communists (cpi), socialists (csp/jp narayan), and mn roy's followers all voted for him. but when the crisis hit at tripuri, the coalition collapsed. the gandhian right wing passed the pant resolution — demanding bose form his cwc strictly per gandhi's wishes. the congress socialist party (csp) led by jayaprakash narayan and mn roy's supporters abstained on the pant resolution, choosing congress unity over bose — fearing a permanent split would destroy the anti-imperialist movement. the communists (cpi) were the only faction that stayed with bose and voted against the resolution. with the right wing hostile and the left fragmented, bose had no base left inside the congress. (the forward bloc would later become the political base from which bose launched his international campaign & eventually the ina — covered in ch 45.) 2.3) nehru's position was more calibrated: no cooperation in the war unless india received actual independence — purna swaraj — but also, no mass movement during the war itself. the majority of inc leaders, however, privately favoured an allied victory — and for a cold, strategic reason. after ww1 (1914–19), the victorious powers had taken over the colonies of the defeated powers. (e.g., german colonies in africa went to britain & france; ottoman territories became british & french mandates.) if the axis powers won, all progress made by the inm could be lost. india could become a colony of japan. and the axis powers were themselves dictatorships (when they did not give democracy to their own people, why would they give it to the people of their colonies?). still, britain had dragged india into war without consent — and the inc was not going to simply hand over cooperation for free. so the inc put forward demands. if britain wanted indian support in the war effort (i.e., inc asking indians to join the army, prevent strikes by workers, stop revenue campaigns & protests), it had to: i) (@top) immediately establish responsible government at the centre — indian ministers, indian accountability. ii) (@coi) promise a constituent assembly after the war to frame india's own constitution. iii) (@swaraj) declare its war aims regarding india's future — i.e., tell indians whether they were fighting for their own freedom or for someone else's empire. (notice how the inc's position was a middle path — neither gandhi's unconditional support, nor bose's immediate confrontation, nor nehru's hard "purna swaraj first." it was a negotiating position.) linlithgow36-43 rejected all three & offered instead only an advisory committee of indian politicians from british india & representatives of the princely states — so indians could "advise" the british on the war. (so indians feel they are being consulted, without actually being given power — classic.) ⚠ alert: inc 1939 stance pyq cluster (sec. 2). prelims 1999 (congress demand for declaration of war aims by britain); prelims 2010 (congress ministries resignation october 1939 — linlithgow declaration without consulting them). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: WW II (1939–45) & the Indian National Movement
sections.title: 1939 Wardha Meet of the Congress Working Committee
sections.norm: 1939 wardha meet of the congress working committee. swift & decisive wardha meet the inc refused to support the british war effort congress ministries in the provinces were directed to resign the impact was significant on all three fronts linlithgow36-43 panicked & promised dominion status march 1940 ml1906 lahore resolution creation of pakistan muslim league 1906 linlithgow. the inc's response was swift & decisive. at the wardha meet of the congress working committee (cwc): 3.1) the inc refused to support the british war effort. 3.2) congress ministries in the provinces were directed to resign. the impact was significant on all three fronts of the four-question game: 3.3) (@swaraj) linlithgow36-43 panicked & promised dominion status after the war. 3.4) (@unity) march 1940 — ml1906 saw its opportunity in the inc's confrontation with the british & passed the lahore resolution, demanding the creation of pakistan. (note: the word "pakistan" was not coined at this resolution. choudhary rahmat ali made it earlier, in his 1933 pamphlet "now or never" — from punjab, afghania (nwfp), kashmir, sindh and the "-tan" of balochistan. the 1940 lahore resolution itself never used the word "pakistan"; the press and public attached the name to it later.)

sections.chapterTitle: WW II (1939–45) & the Indian National Movement
sections.title: August Offer (AO1940) by Linlithgow36-43
sections.norm: august offer (ao1940) by linlithgow36-43. shook the british the august offer it promised: advisory war council executive council (vec) expanded to include more indians a constituent assembly mainly indians the first time the british formally promised dominion status after the war. effectively giving ml1906 veto power ww2 august offer 1940 muslim league 1906 linlithgow irwin. the resignation of congress ministries shook the british. the august offer was linlithgow36-43's attempt to bring the inc back to the table. it promised: 4.1) an advisory war council would be set up. 4.2) (@top) the viceroy's executive council (vec) would be expanded to include more indians. (after goi act 1919, it became a convention that 3 of 8 members of the vec were indians — nominated as per the wish of the viceroy. the vec structure was: viceroy + commander-in-chief (c-i-c) + 6 ordinary members, of which 3 were indian.) 4.3) (@coi) a constituent assembly would be set up after the war, where mainly indians would frame the constitution. (note the word "mainly" — some british members could still be part of it.) this was, however, the first time the british formally promised that constitution-making would be "primarily the responsibility of indians themselves" — a significant rhetorical & constitutional advance over all previous offers. 4.4) (@swaraj) dominion status after the war. (montagu's 1917 statement said swaraj gradually. irwin26-31 in 1929 said dominion status gradually. now linlithgow36-43 in 1940 says dominion status after the war — for the first time with a clear timeline. thank you, hitler, or rather, thank you, ww2 — !!!! ) 4.5) (@unity) linlithgow36-43 stated that "no future constitution without the consent of minorities" — effectively giving ml1906 veto power over the framing of india's constitution. (imagine a constituent assembly in session. article 1 is proposed: "there shall be a union of india." ml1906 votes no. the article fails. a hung assembly. and if british don't then create pakistan, ml keeps using its veto & india remains ungoverned.)

sections.chapterTitle: WW II (1939–45) & the Indian National Movement
sections.title: Impact of AO1940 — Why Both Sides Rejected It
sections.norm: impact of ao1940 — why both sides rejected it. inc rejected it at the wardha meet (1940) dominion status instead of purna swaraj backdoor partition mechanism ml1906 also rejected it opposite reason no explicit mention of two separate constituent assemblies neither power nor pakistan august offer 1940 muslim league 1906. 5.1) the inc rejected it at the wardha meet (1940). (@swaraj) accepting the august offer meant accepting dominion status instead of purna swaraj, which had been the inc's stated goal since 1929. it also implicitly meant accepting partition, because the veto clause was a backdoor partition mechanism. inc's goal was purna swaraj, not dominion status. 5.2) ml1906 also rejected it — but for the opposite reason. (@unity) the offer made no explicit mention of two separate constituent assemblies or of pakistan. ml1906's deeper anxiety was this: if the british transfer executive power at the centre, a hindu-majority government could simply ignore ml's veto in the constituent assembly & use force to prevent the creation of pakistan. and what if the british didn't follow through on creating pakistan even after ml used its veto? ml would be left with neither power nor pakistan. (imagine in the constituent assembly — article 1 is proposed: "there shall be a union of india." ml1906 votes no, the article fails — and then? if british continue to rule india because of a hung ca, ml's pakistan is still not created.)

sections.chapterTitle: WW II (1939–45) & the Indian National Movement
sections.title: Individual Satyagraha (Oct 1940)
sections.norm: individual satyagraha (oct 1940). mg came under pressure from within the inc he resisted individual satyagraha public anti-war speech narrow demand for freedom of speech the first three satyagrahis vinobha bhave, nehru, and brahma dutt in that order delhi chalo movement & the jail bharo movement organisational tempo feed into the larger quit india movement 2009 1940 pyq august offer 1940. with ao1940 having failed in august, mg came under pressure from within the inc to launch a civil disobedience movement. he resisted — and instead launched a carefully limited, symbolic protest: individual satyagraha. the form of protest was deliberate & precise. the satyagrahi was to make a public anti-war speech & assert the right to freedom of speech. the goal was not purna swaraj — it was the specific, narrow demand for freedom of speech. (this was individual civil disobedience as against the defence of india act, 1939, which was essentially an emergency law restricting civil liberties during wartime.) the first three satyagrahis were vinobha bhave, nehru, and brahma dutt — arrested in that order under the defence of india act, 1939. the movement then generated its own energy. satyagrahis launched the delhi chalo movement & the jail bharo movement — make your anti-war speech, demand your freedom of speech, get arrested, and if not arrested, keep marching to delhi until you are. individual satyagraha built the organisational tempo & popular mood that would feed into the larger quit india movement of 1942–45. ⚠ alert: prelims 2009 (individual satyagraha october 1940 — gandhi launched it with vinoba bhave first, then nehru — selective & symbolic). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: WW II (1939–45) & the Indian National Movement
sections.title: VEC Expanded in 1941
sections.norm: vec expanded in 1941. rose from 3 out of 8 members 8 out of 12 members defence, home, and finance indian ministers were in a majority. in 1941, as war pressures mounted, the british expanded the viceroy's executive council. the number of indians in the vec rose from 3 out of 8 members (as under goi act 1919) to 8 out of 12 members. however, (@top) the defence, home, and finance portfolios were not to be held by indian ministers. for the first time, indian ministers were in a majority at the centre — but the portfolios that mattered most remained outside their reach.

sections.title: Cripps Mission (1942)
sections.norm: cripps mission (1942). 8.1) background germany attacked the ussr japan attacked the united states at pearl harbour fear of japanese invasion of india december 1941 the inc offered to support the british war effort if: purna swaraj after the war immediate transfer of power at the centre japan occupied rangoon intense pressure from the united states & the ussr britain sent the cripps mission in march 1942 nehru & maulana azad 8.2) provisions / offer dominion status after the war indian control over foreign policy a constituent assembly after the war composed solely of indians elected members nominees of the princely states most explosive provision not join the union frame its own constitution the step-by-step logic of this provision was: step 1 step 2 step 3 step 4 576 countries possible defence would continue under the viceroy no dilution talks actually broke down cripps offer — 4-point summary: @top — failed: @swaraj — failed: @coi — partially advanced: @unity — gravely threatened: 8.3) result mg called the cripps offer a post-dated cheque nothing was immediate purna swaraj after the war, not dominion status elected members — not nominees of the princes no right to secede ml1906 opposed two constituent assemblies inc did concede ground autonomy for muslim majority provinces cripps mission pyq 2003 2009 2016 inc 2022 1942 august offer 1940 muslim league 1906. 8.1) background the strategic situation of the war shifted dramatically in the second half of 1941. in june 1941, germany attacked the ussr. in december 1941, japan attacked the united states at pearl harbour in hawaii. the axis powers now appeared unstoppable, and the fear of japanese invasion of india became very real. in december 1941, the inc made a significant move — overriding the individual objections of both nehru & mg — and offered to support the british war effort if: i) (@top) purna swaraj after the war; and ii) (@swaraj) immediate transfer of power at the centre (i.e., viceroy becomes a powerless president + indian prime minister + indian ministers). then in march 1942, japan occupied rangoon (burma). the fall of burma meant india's eastern border was now directly exposed. britain, under intense pressure from the united states & the ussr — both now allied partners — needed to demonstrate that india was a willing partner in the war, not an unwilling colony. under this pressure, britain sent the cripps mission in march 1942, led by sir stafford cripps, a minister in the war cabinet of prime minister winston churchill. other members were senior british officials. inc's official negotiators with cripps were nehru & maulana azad (the serving inc president). 8.2) provisions / offer (#uncle chips — think of a crispy chip that snaps & breaks into smaller & smaller pieces. similarly, the cripps plan, if accepted, could in theory crumble india into 565 + 11 parts — 565 princely states & 11 provinces, all potentially becoming separate entities with dominion status within the british empire. crispy chip. cripps plan. remember it.) i) (@swaraj) dominion status after the war, plus indian control over foreign policy. (dominion status had already been offered in ao1940 — so this was something more, since it now added foreign affairs/diplomacy to the package. but it was still dominion status, not purna swaraj.) ii) (@coi) a constituent assembly after the war, composed solely of indians (unlike ao1940, where it was "mainly" indians — so some british members possible. cripps upgraded this to solely indian). the constituent assembly would consist of: a) elected members from the provincial legislative assemblies (plas) after fresh elections under the goi act 1935; and b) nominees of the princely states. (think of the composition like the rajya sabha model — indirectly elected representatives plus nominated members.) iii) (@unity) this was the most explosive provision. once the constitution was framed by the constituent assembly, if any province of british india or any princely state did not agree with the constitution so framed, it had the option to: a) not join the union, and b) frame its own constitution or set up its own union within the british empire. the step-by-step logic of this provision was: step 1 — constituent assembly frames a constitution for india. step 2 — members of the constituent assembly representing a province or a princely state pass a resolution that they disagree with the constitution framed. step 3 — that province or princely state is then allowed to secede from the union. step 4 — it can then frame its own constitution or set up its own union within the british empire. hence, technically: 565 princely states + 11 provinces = 576 countries possible. !!!! iv) (@top) if power was to be transferred during the war itself (i.e., before the war ended), defence would continue under the viceroy & there would be no dilution of the viceroy's powers over ministers. (i.e., the viceroy would not become a powerless constitutional president acting purely on the aid & advice of popular ministers — he would retain real power over defence.) it was on this last point that the talks actually broke down. the british adopted a "take it or leave it" approach on the viceroy's war powers. cripps offer — 4-point summary: @top — failed: viceroy retained defence; no real transfer of executive power.@swaraj — failed: only dominion status offered, not purna swaraj. @coi — partially advanced: constituent assembly would be solely indian for the first time — but princely state representatives would be unelected nominees of the princes, not elected members. @unity — gravely threatened: right to secede could fragment india into 576 separate entities. 8.3) result mg called the cripps offer a post-dated cheque — most things were to take effect after the war, and nothing was immediate. :) i) (@swaraj) inc wanted purna swaraj after the war, not dominion status. ii) (@coi) inc wanted princely states to be represented in the constituent assembly by elected members — not nominees of the princes. (the 1938 haripura session of inc, with netaji bose as president, had declared that purna swaraj is the goal for the whole of india including the princely states, and that the princely states are an integral part of india — meaning no special status, no nominees, elected representatives only.) iii) (@unity) inc wanted no right to secede given to any province or princely state. ml1906 opposed the offer because it wanted two constituent assemblies — one for what would become pakistan & one for the rest of india. (@unity) however, during the cripps negotiations, the inc did concede ground on one point — it agreed to autonomy for muslim majority provinces within the future constitution of india. (this meant that in relation to those provinces, the centre could be weak as compared to non-muslim majority provinces. in a sense, this was article 370 — not just for kashmir, but as a principle applicable to all muslim majority provinces.) (importantly, this inc concession was made during negotiations, not in the formal cripps offer itself.) ⚠ alert: cripps mission pyq cluster (sec. 8). prelims 2003 (cripps mission rejected — dominion status only, no immediate indianisation, princely state accession voluntary); prelims 2009 (cripps offer = post-war constituent assembly + dominion status); prelims 2016 (cripps mission rejected by inc + ml for different reasons); prelims 2022 (cripps proposals 1942 — main features & rejection grounds). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: What Was the Quit India Movement?
sections.norm: what was the quit india movement?. first mass movement to include the princely states truly all-india in character yusuf meherally two major political forces, however, stayed out. communist party of india (cpi1925) soviet union was fighting on the british side muslim league(ml1906) calculating its own gains qim pyq 2005 aicc 1942 2009 2011 2013 ww2 communist party of india 1925 muslim league 1906. the quit india movement (qim(1942-45)) holds a special place in the indian national movement. it was the first mass movement to include the princely states, making it truly all-india in character. this was no small thing — for the first time, the people of those states stood alongside british india in demanding freedom. the phrase "quit india" itself was coined by yusuf meherally — the same man who had earlier coined the term "simon go back." two major political forces, however, stayed out. the communist party of india (cpi1925) did not join because the soviet union was fighting on the british side in ww2 & the cpi1925 followed that line. the muslim league(ml1906) also did not participate — it was against the inc & was calculating its own gains from the british, hoping to extract concessions in exchange for cooperation. ⚠ alert: qim origin pyq cluster (sec. 1). prelims 2005 (cripps failure → aicc bombay 8 august 1942 quit india resolution); prelims 2009 (bombay 8 august 1942 resolution — "do or die" call); prelims 2011 (quit india slogan coiner = yusuf meherally); prelims 2013 (qim features — leaderless decentralised mass movement, parallel governments, underground radio). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Reasons for Launching the QIM(1942-45)
sections.norm: reasons for launching the qim(1942-45). why did the inc choose this moment? three pressures came together in 1942 failure of the cripps mission removed the last hope of a negotiated settlement popular anger war-related inflation britain had abandoned the people of its colonies in burma & malaya indians feared the same fate high-spirited, nationalist people would resist a japanese invasion. why did the inc choose this moment? three pressures came together in 1942 to make action unavoidable. first, the failure of the cripps mission in 1942 removed the last hope of a negotiated settlement. the mission had offered vague post-war promises but nothing on real transfer of power during the war. it proved, clearly, that britain wanted to continue ruling india on its own terms regardless of indian opinion. second, popular anger was building fast. war-related inflation was squeezing ordinary people hard, and there was no relief in sight. the cost of living was rising while british policy ignored it entirely. third, and perhaps most urgently, britain had abandoned the people of its colonies in burma & malaya when japan invaded. indians watched this & feared the same fate awaited them. the inc did not want indians to face a japanese invasion in a state of low morale & passive helplessness. mg's idea was that a high-spirited, nationalist people would resist a japanese invasion far better than a demoralised, colonially-exhausted one.
