impending raids businessmen donated generously sumati morarjee the boost from mg's fast (1943): aga khan palace, pune he refused 21-day fast two personal losses mahadev desai kasturba gandhi the impact of the fast was significant: mass upsurge of demonstrations & strikes indian members executive council resigned international media the fast brought unity 3.5) the parallel governments emergence of parallel governments replaced british rule locally ballia, eastern up (august 1942) — the first chittu pandey overthrew the district collector historically significant as the first jatiya sarkar, midnapore, bengal (december 1942 – september 1944) more sustained administration extensive constructive work the jatiya sarkar: arbitration courts grants to schools distributed rice cyclone relief vidyut vahini patri sarkar, satara, maharashtra (mid-1943 – 1945) — the most successful most successful & long-running nana patil lion of satara yb chavan harsh punishment what the patri sarkar did: people's courts & village libraries prohibition on alcohol gandhi marriages mid-1943 to 1945 qim pyq 1998 1942 1999 2000 2009 2011 ina rin cabinet mission 2021 communist party of india 1925 muslim league 1906. the movement unfolded in five overlapping phases: 3.1) the inc quit india resolution 3.2) the mass struggle phase — six weeks 3.3) british repression 3.4) underground activity 3.5) the mushrooming of parallel governments 3.1) the inc quit india resolution after the cripps mission collapsed, mg drafted a resolution demanding quit india & committing the inc to non-cooperation against japan if india were invaded. in july 1942, the congress working committee (cwc) accepted the idea at wardha. on 8th august 1942, the inc held a special session in bombay, followed by a massive public meeting at gowalia tank (azad maidan). the qim(1942-45) resolution was passed at the session with the demand for immediate purna swaraj. at the public meeting the same evening, mg gave his historic speech — including his famous call "do or die" (karo ya maro) — laying out the plan of action for the public. however, the same night — 9th august 1942 — the entire top inc leadership was arrested. the detailed resolution could not be made public. this had an important consequence: the public only knew what mg had said in his speech the evening before. everything not mentioned in that speech became, effectively, the private strategy of the movement. what mg told the public in his speech: i) government servants: do not resign. stay in your posts but declare your loyalty to the inc & to the people of india. ii) soldiers: support britain against the fascists — that was the allied war effort — but do not fire on your own countrymen. iii) students: leave your studies & join the qim(1942-45). iv) princes: accept the sovereignty of your own people & stop supporting the british. v) people of the princely states: declare that you are part of india. support your prince only if he is anti-british. what the public was not told — the plan kept private: i) peasants: do not pay land revenue. ii) tenants: pay only a fair rent — and pay it only if your zamindar is anti-british. (this was the first time inc explicitly raised a no-rent campaign as part of its programme.) iii) inc's position:land belongs to its actual tiller. ◆ that last line — land belongs to the actual tiller — was a significant ideological step. inc was stating for the first time that its vision of a free india included ryotwari for all, not zamindari. quiet, but important. 3.2) the mass struggle phase — six weeks from 9th august 1942 the mass struggle phase was not non-violent. with the entire leadership under arrest, people acted on their own understanding of what the movement meant, and that understanding was raw & angry. the primary target was the symbols of british authority. crowds removed railway tracks, blew up bridges, cut telephone & telegraph wires, attacked railway stations, police stations, courts, and post offices. the tricolour flag was hoisted on trains & public buildings. who participated? i) common people showed unparalleled heroism & faced the harshest repression yet seen in the entire inm. ii) leadership passed to provincial & local inc leaders, since the top leadership was behind bars. iii) villagers joined the urban protesters as news of the arrests spread. iv) peasants were the soul of the qim(1942-45) — especially in eastern up, bihar, midnapore (bengal), and satara (maharashtra). both rich & poor peasants actively participated, their anger was directed entirely at the british with no violence against zamindars or moneylenders. v) zamindars — big zamindars stayed neutral & did not help the british either. smaller zamindars actively participated, especially in up & bihar. vi) workers — the cpi1925 did not participate, yet many worker strikes broke out independently. the ahmedabad mills saw a strike that lasted 3.5 months. hundreds of individual communists participated despite the cpi1925's official stand. vii) women — school & college girls played a vital role. aruna asaf ali & sucheta kriplani were active organisers during the underground phase. usha mehta ran the congress radio to coordinate underground activities. viii) students left their studies, led processions, distributed illegal patrikas (leaflets), and acted as couriers for the emerging underground networks. ix) muslims — overall participation was not high since the ml1906 had opposed the qim(1942-45). however, even ml1906 supporters gave shelter to underground activists & did not act as informers for the british. there was a total absence of communal violence throughout the movement. (jinnah u were wrong :) x) most active region: eastern up & bihar — regions where the inc had done the highest level of constructive work in recent years, which translated directly into organised mass participation. 3.3) british repression british repression was immediate & severe — the harshest response to any movement in the history of the inm. the british were already prepared. they had legal tools in place: the revolutionary movement ordinance & the defence of india rules (which gave powers of preventive detention). the entire top inc leadership was arrested on 9th august itself. the press was gagged. machine guns were deployed on aircraft. collective fines were imposed on villages. whole villages were burnt. by the end of 1942, 60,000 people had been arrested. the mass struggle phase was crushed in six weeks. :( but by going underground, the movement refused to die. mirabehn (madeleine slade) — gandhi's english disciple. the daughter of a british admiral, madeleine slade famously renounced her life in england to live in gandhi's sabarmati ashram from 1925 — gandhi renamed her mirabehn. she became one of his closest confidants. during the quit india movement (1942), she was a key campaigner & was imprisoned alongside gandhi & other congress leaders. her contribution went beyond politics into the localised gandhian ideal — after independence, she focused on rural development, animal husbandry, & environmental sustainability in the himalayan foothills around rishikesh & later in the kumaon region. she eventually returned to europe in 1959. 3.4) the underground phase when the mass phase was suppressed, the movement shifted underground. the leadership of this phase came primarily from the congress socialist party, and it included some of the most remarkable personalities of the freedom struggle. the underground network was led by: achyut patwardhan, ram manohar lohia, biju patnaik, aruna asaf ali, sucheta kriplani, chhotu bhai puranik, ramnath goenka (founder of indian express), and jayaprakash narayan (jp). (a mnemonic for remembering the underground leaders: jp goenka asa ram se bacho — jp, goenka, aruna asaf ali, sucheta, achyut, ram manohar lohia, biju. a strange sentence, but it works.) what this network did: i) supplied bombs & arms to activists. ii) pilots & train drivers delivered these supplies — meaning the underground had penetrated even critical british infrastructure. iii) students acted as couriers; villagers refused to give information to the police. iv) government officials & police officers leaked details of impending raids — a remarkable sign of how far british authority had eroded even within its own apparatus. v) businessmen donated generously. sumati morarjee— who would later become one of india's leading women industrialists — gave achyut patwardhan a different car every single day so he could not be tracked. the boost from mg's fast (1943): a major boost to the underground phase came from mg himself. he was being held at aga khan palace, pune. the british wanted him to condemn the violence of the movement. he refused — and instead began a 21-day fast as a protest against british violence. (mg, detained, fasting — the british had imprisoned the man but could not imprison the moral argument.) during his detention, mg suffered two personal losses. earlier, his personal secretary mahadev desai died on 15 august 1942 in aga khan palace — a loss mg described as losing his right hand. then, his wife kasturba gandhidied on 22 february 1944 in the same palace. both deaths deepened public demands for mg's release. the impact of the fast was significant: i) it triggered a mass upsurge of demonstrations & strikes across the country. ii) indian members of the viceroy's executive council resigned — they did not want to be held responsible for mg's death. iii) international media focused attention on british repression in india. iv) even those who had opposed the qim(1942-45) now demanded mg's release — the fast brought unity that the movement itself had struggled to generate. 3.5) the parallel governments the most dramatic consequence of the collapse of british authority in certain areas was the emergence of parallel governments — people's administrations that replaced british rule locally & actually functioned. ballia, eastern up (august 1942) — the first led by chittu pandey, the people of ballia overthrew the district collector & freed inc leaders from jail. the parallel government held briefly until british forces returned, at which point it dissolved. short-lived, but historically significant as the first. british failed to arrest pandey. he later became a member of parliament. jatiya sarkar, midnapore, bengal (december 1942 – september 1944) this was a more sustained administration. the inc had already done extensive constructive work in midnapore, which gave the parallel government its organisational foundation. the jatiya sarkar: i) set up arbitration courts. ii) gave grants to schools. iii) distributed rice to the poor. iv) provided cyclone relief. v) established an armed wing called vidyut vahini. ◆ the vidyut vahini was not just symbolic — it was the enforcement arm of a functioning parallel state, a direct challenge to british sovereignty in the region. patri sarkar, satara, maharashtra (mid-1943 – 1945) — the most successful the patri sarkar of satara was the most successful & long-running of the parallel governments. it was set up by nana patil (who had earlier been engaged in robin hood-style robberies against colonial targets) and received guidance from achyut patwardhan, who earned the title lion of satara for his role. yb chavan was its most important leader until his arrest at the end of 1942. (an amusing detail: nana achyut chavan once attended a gandhi marriage organised by the patri sarkar & brought a book on patri justice as a gift — because gifting alcohol was prohibited under the patri sarkar's own rules. the joke writes itself.) the name patri referred to the harsh punishment given to those who opposed the parallel government — government officials & informers who collaborated with the british. what the patri sarkar did: i) set up people's courts & village libraries. ii) enforced prohibition on alcohol. iii) organised gandhi marriages where dalits were invited & given proper respect — a direct challenge to caste hierarchy embedded in the work of a parallel government. iv) functioned continuously from mid-1943 to 1945. ⚠ alert: qim significance + personalities pyq cluster (sec. 6). prelims 1998 (bombay 8 august 1942 — wavell's offer / cripps failure background); prelims 1999 (quit india movement leaders — aruna asaf ali, ram manohar lohia, jayaprakash narayan, achyut patwardhan); prelims 2000 (parallel government at ballia = chittu pandey; tamluk-midnapore = tamralipta sarkar; satara = y.b. chavan + nana patil); prelims 2009 (aruna asaf ali hoisted national flag at gowalia tank maidan); prelims 2011 (qim results — ina + rin mutiny + inc-ml deadlock resolved through cabinet mission & partition); prelims 2021 (underground/leaderless aspects of qim = chapter's "spontaneous" sec. 4 debate). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Was the QIM(1942-45) Spontaneous?
sections.norm: was the qim(1942-45) spontaneous?. yes — and no. appeared spontaneous leaderless at the top not unorganised from below nagpur session of 1920 individual satyagraha of 1940–41 rootless, no.. yes — and no. it appeared spontaneous because the arrests of 9th august meant the public did not know the full plan of action. the movement was, in that sense, leaderless at the top. however, it was not unorganised from below. since the nagpur session of 1920, mg had systematically strengthened inc at the grassroots level. the individual satyagraha of 1940–41 had kept the tempo of the movement alive. decades of constructive work had trained ordinary people to act. when the formal leadership disappeared, this deeper preparation carried the movement forward. leaderless at the top, yes. rootless, no.

sections.title: How Did the QIM(1942-45) End?
sections.norm: how did the qim(1942-45) end?. mg was released from detention in may 1944 constructive work all inc leaders were released in june 1945 simla conference formally marked the end ww2 . mg was released from detention in may 1944 on health grounds. he turned to constructive work. with the end of ww2 , all inc leaders were released in june 1945 to participate in the simla conference (june 1945). this formally marked the end of the quit india movement. (germany surrendered in may 1945. japan surrendered in september 1945. britain's position in india was never the same again.)

sections.title: Results and Significance of the QIM(1942-45)
sections.norm: results and significance of the qim(1942-45). psychological paradigm shift made the end of colonial rule inevitable india proved ungovernable by force. the loyalty of the british administrative machinery broke. rusting from within parallel governments showed indians could self-govern. international attention shifted decisively. the movement unified forces that had been fragmented. no longer a matter of whether, but when cdm 1930–34 qim 1942-45 1947 1942. the qim(1942-45) did not achieve immediate independence, but it produced a psychological paradigm shift — both within india & in the british mind — that made the end of colonial rule inevitable. i) india proved ungovernable by force. the sheer scale of the movement — parallel governments functioning for months, underground networks the british could not dismantle, ordinary people choosing arrest over submission — demonstrated that no amount of repression could hold india indefinitely. the british administrative machinery, stretched thin by war & now facing a population that had decisively turned against it, could no longer sustain the fiction of stable governance. ii) the loyalty of the british administrative machinery broke. government officials leaking raid plans, police officers turning a blind eye, indian members of the viceroy's executive council resigning — these were not minor cracks. the steel frame that had held british india together for nearly a century was rusting from within. iii) parallel governments showed indians could self-govern. the jatiya sarkar, the patri sarkar, and even the brief experiment in ballia proved that ordinary indians — peasants, local leaders, students — could set up courts, distribute relief, enforce law, and administer territories. this was not abstract theory. it was demonstrated fact. the british argument that india was "not ready" for self-rule lost whatever credibility it still had. iv) international attention shifted decisively. mg's fast, the scale of arrests (60,000 by end of 1942), the use of aircraft-mounted machine guns against civilians — all of this received global coverage. the united states, now an ally of britain but increasingly uncomfortable with colonialism, began applying quiet pressure. britain's moral authority to hold india was publicly questioned as never before. v) the movement unified forces that had been fragmented. even those who had initially opposed the qim(1942-45) — including some who had criticised mg for launching it — rallied behind the demand for his release & for an end to repression. the movement created a post-1942 consensus: independence was no longer a matter of whether, but when. ◆ if the cdm (1930–34) had made the world notice india's demand, the qim(1942-45) made the world accept that the demand could not be denied. the british did not leave india in 1947 because they suddenly became generous. they left because, after 1942, they knew they could not stay.

sections.title: Bengal Famine (1943)
sections.norm: bengal famine (1943). 1.1) was there actually a food shortage? not caused by a failure of crops man-made famine 5 million indians died four factors food supplies diverted to europe food imports from burma logistics & supply chains poorly war-driven speculation 1.2) impact deep & lasting distrust churchill denied both compared to hitler most british politicians were sympathetic to indian independence 1.3) famine inquiry commission (1945) and amartya sen's analysis famine inquiry commission (1945) sir john woodhead blamed natural factors amartya sen lost their entitlement to food failure of access, not of supply cpi-led tebhaga movement (1946–47) from half to one-third 2008 1943 pyq linlithgow. 1.1) was there actually a food shortage? no. that is the most important thing to understand about the bengal famine of 1943 — it was not caused by a failure of crops. it was a man-made famine, and roughly 5 million indians died in it. four factors combined to produce it. food supplies from india, including bengal, were being diverted to europe to feed british soldiers & european civilians — the needs of the army & europeans were given priority over indian lives :(. when japan occupied burma in march 1942, food imports from burma, which bengal had been receiving, stopped entirely. the government managed logistics & supply chains poorly, making the distribution of whatever food existed chaotic. and war-driven speculation pushed market prices to levels ordinary people simply could not afford. 1.2) impact the famine produced a deep & lasting distrust of british rule among indians, and not without reason. european lives had been visibly prioritised above indian ones, and the government did little by way of relief. viceroy linlithgow36-43 (1936–1943) did request food for india & proposed a ban on food exports from bengal — but prime minister churchill denied both, and instead reportedly asked whether gandhi was still alive or had died in his ongoing fast unto death (1943). in britain, churchill was compared to hitler for this. public opinion in britain shifted noticeably — by 1943, most british politicians were sympathetic to indian independence, and the famine accelerated that shift. 1.3) famine inquiry commission (1945) and amartya sen's analysis the famine inquiry commission (1945), headed by sir john woodhead, investigated the causes of the bengal famine. the commission largely blamed natural factors & supply disruption, but its analysis remained incomplete & was criticised for not holding the colonial administration adequately accountable. decades later, nobel laureate amartya sen offered a far more penetrating explanation through his "entitlement failure" theory. sen demonstrated that the famine occurred not because there was insufficient food in bengal, but because large sections of the population lost their entitlement to food — their wages collapsed, prices skyrocketed due to speculation, and government procurement policies drained food from rural markets. it was a failure of access, not of supply. (this insight — that famines are caused by entitlement collapse rather than absolute shortage — became one of the most influential ideas in development economics.) the devastation of bengal's peasantry during 1943 deepened the agrarian crisis that fuelled the cpi-led tebhaga movement (1946–47), demanding the landlord's share be reduced from half to one-third. (future linkage → ch 47 for tebhaga & peasant mobilisation under cpi.) ⚠ alert: prelims 2008 (bengal famine 1943 — administrative causes + amartya sen entitlements framework). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Indian National Army / Azad Hind Fauj (1942–1945)
sections.norm: indian national army / azad hind fauj (1942–1945). 2.1) how did the ina come into existence? dramatic collapse of british power malaya, singapore, and burma stunning defeats captain mohan singh conceived the idea of the ina first division in september 1942 40,000 pows captain mohan singh was arrested demanded a primary role & genuine autonomy ina 1942 1943 pritam singh, swami satyananda puri indian independence league (iil) bangkok quit india movement began rash behari bose took over the leadership of the ina 2.2) netaji subhas chandra bose & the ina most remarkable individual journeys broken with the gandhian leadership founded the forward bloc consolidate the left & radical elements more militant approach tripuri session consecutive second term haripura session (1938) had to leave the inc british arrested him overthrow british rule directly forced the british to release him house arrest in calcutta escaped in disguise as an afghan arrived in germany in march 1941 azad hind radio hitler to be a racist german submarine to a japanese one took over leadership of the iil & of the ina rapid expansion of the ina funded by indian money rani jhansi regiment gandhi regiment & a nehru regiment crucial assurance from japanese general tojo for indian independence, not a japanese empire 21st october 1943 provisional government of free india democratically elected one 2.3) the andaman & nicobar islands rama krishna ina liberated the andaman & nicobar islands renamed the islands the british recaptured the islands in 1945 2.4) the kohima & imphal campaign (1944) — and the end attacked the india–burma border kohima & imphal it failed. discriminated against by the japanese qadam qadam badhaye ja jai hind & delhi chalo japan surrendered alleged plane crash at taihoku airport surrounded by controversy pyq 2000 2017. 2.1) how did the ina come into existence? the ina's birth is tied directly to the dramatic collapse of british power in south-east asia. in january, february, and march 1942, japan took over malaya, singapore, and burma respectively from the british. these were stunning defeats — the british had held these territories for decades, and they fell in a matter of weeks. following the fall of singapore in february 1942, captain mohan singh conceived the idea of the ina by organising indian pows, leading to the formal establishment of its first division in september 1942. he approached the japanese army & convinced them to hand over indian prisoners of war (pows) — 40,000 pows in singapore joined. however, in december 1942, captain mohan singh was arrested by the japanese — he had demanded a primary role & genuine autonomy for the ina in any attack on british india, which created friction with the japanese command. ⚠ prelims trap: mohan singh conceived & first organised the ina in 1942. bose took over its leadership in 1943. claiming the ina "came into existence" in 1943 is factually incorrect — the ina existed from september 1942 under mohan singh; what happened in 1943 was a change of leadership, first to rash behari bose & then to netaji. in june 1942, motivated by japanese victories, indian independence-minded non-resident indians (nris) — mainly pritam singh, swami satyananda puri, and others — set up the indian independence league (iil) in bangkok, thailand. (iil = political organisation; ina = its military arm — two wings, one purpose.) meanwhile in august 1942, the quit india movement began in india. in early 1943, an aged rash behari bose — who had escaped to japan after the ghadar movement (1913–15) — took over the leadership of the ina & reorganised it. 2.2) netaji subhas chandra bose & the ina the story of netaji bose is one of the most remarkable individual journeys in the entire indian national movement. bose had already broken with the gandhian leadership before the tripuri session. in may 1939, he founded the forward bloc within congress — an attempt to consolidate the left & radical elements who opposed the gandhian old guard's dominance. the forward bloc advocated a more militant approach to achieving independence & sought to rally socialists, communists, and other anti-imperialist groups into a unified front. (the forward bloc was founded while bose was still technically within the congress fold — it preceded his formal resignation. however, after bose's departure from india, the forward bloc's organisational strength declined significantly.) at the tripuri session of inc in december 1939, bose was elected president for a consecutive second term, following his election at the haripura session (1938). but his differences with gandhian leadership were irreconcilable, and he had to leave the inc. in july 1940, the british arrested him, viewing him as a political threat to their stability in india. he favoured starting a movement to overthrow british rule directly. then, in january 1941, his failing health from a hunger strike forced the british to release him, placing him under house arrest in calcutta. what followed was the stuff of legend. he escaped in disguise as an afghan, made his way to afghanistan, then crossed into the ussr, and from there travelled in disguise as "orlando mazzotta" all the way to italy. he arrived in germany in march 1941. in 1942, from germany, he set up azad hind radio, from which he broadcast messages to india to boost the morale of those in the quit india movement (1942–45). in february 1943, he left germany — he had found hitler to be a racist who considered the british a ruling race & indians as not. (bose needed allies, not patrons who looked down on india. hitler was the wrong ally.) in the indian ocean, he transferred from a german submarine to a japanese one, and arrived in singapore in july 1943. there, in a ceremony, he took over leadership of the iil & of the ina from an aged r.b. bose. netaji now began a rapid expansion of the ina. he raised huge funds from nris, deliberately wanting the ina to be funded by indian money & not be dependent on japan. he raised the rani jhansi regiment, an all-women nri regiment. (notice the symbolism — revolutionaries always held the 1857 revolt as a reference point, and the rani of jhansi was its most iconic symbol.) the ina also had a gandhi regiment & a nehru regiment. he extracted a crucial assurance from japanese general tojo: "japan does not want to annex india post victory." this was not a trivial assurance — it was netaji's way of ensuring the ina's fight was for indian independence, not a japanese empire. on 21st october 1943, netaji established the provisional government of free india, with ina headquarters in rangoon (burma) and singapore. he called it "provisional" deliberately — he believed a permanent government could only be a democratically elected one. 2.3) the andaman & nicobar islands an indian independence league branch had been set up in the andaman & nicobar islands by rama krishna in april 1942. in 1943, the ina liberated the andaman & nicobar islands. netaji bose visited the islands on 29–31 december 1943, hoisted the indian flag at gymkhana ground (now netaji stadium), and renamed the islands — the andamans as "shaheed dweep" and the nicobars as "swaraj dweep." the british recaptured the islands in 1945. 2.4) the kohima & imphal campaign (1944) — and the end in 1944, the ina & japan attacked the india–burma border. the campaign targeted kohima & imphal. it failed. worse, during the imphal campaign, indian ina soldiers were discriminated against by the japanese in the allocation of weapons & supplies — a reminder that being an ally of japan did not mean being treated as an equal. the ina marching song was qadam qadam badhaye ja. netaji gave india the slogans jai hind & delhi chalo. on 15th august 1945, japan surrendered. on 18th august 1945, an alleged plane crash at taihoku airport in taipei (taiwan) reportedly killed netaji bose — a death that has remained surrounded by controversy ever since !!!! ⚠ alert: ina pyq cluster. prelims 2000 (ina founder — captain mohan singh in singapore 1942, later led by subhas chandra bose from 1943); prelims 2017 (ina first division/brigades + azad hind government 1943 + rani of jhansi regiment for women). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: INA Trials and INA Agitations (November 1945 – 1946)
sections.norm: ina trials and ina agitations (november 1945 – 1946). 3.1) why did the trials backfire so badly on the british? put ina men red fort shah nawaz khan prem sehgal, and gurbaksh singh dhillon miscalculated completely mass upsurge across india so much sympathy among indians maximum unity seen throughout the inm started by the people themselves arose spontaneously part of its election campaign bullabhai desai ina relief committee government officials openly supported a movement even bollywood 2021 ina 1945 pyq. 3.1) why did the trials backfire so badly on the british? in november 1945, the british put ina men — now pows — on trial. the most famous trial was held at the red fort: shah nawaz khan (a close aide of netaji), prem sehgal, and gurbaksh singh dhillon were the accused. the british had miscalculated completely. the trials produced a mass upsurge across india cutting across all sections of society, supported by every political party. the british themselves admitted it: they stated that no issue in the entire history of the indian national movement had generated so much sympathy among indians. the ina agitations represented the maximum unity seen throughout the inm. these agitations were started by the people themselves — no political party gave the call. they arose spontaneously. the inc made the ina agitations part of its election campaign, demanding the release of ina men. it fought cases for the accused under bullabhai desai, lawyer & inc leader in the central legislative assembly. it set up an ina relief committee that raised funds, gave money to ina men on their release, and worked for their rehabilitation. for the first time in indian history, government officials openly supported a movement — contributing money for ina men. common people, gurudwaras, and even bollywood contributed funds. ⚠ alert: prelims 2021 (ina trials red fort nov 1945 — defence panel led by bhulabhai desai, tej bahadur sapru, jawaharlal nehru, asaf ali; three defendants — prem sehgal (hindu), shah nawaz khan (muslim), gurbaksh singh dhillon (sikh) — sentenced but released after public agitation). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: The Naval Ratings Mutiny (February 1946)
sections.norm: the naval ratings mutiny (february 1946). february 1946 talwar their grievances were three: fear of unemployment poor service conditions & racial discrimination inspiration from the ina the ratings revolted tricolour flags workers across bombay went on a massive strike aruna asaf ali advised the ratings airforce men in karachi began sympathy strikes withdrawal of support by the inc & the muslim league sardar patel & jinnah most ina men & naval ratings were not recruited into the armed forces 4.1) why the naval & riaf mutinies mattered beyond the event itself royal indian air force (riaf) strikes coordinated, politicised acts of defiance the british had irrevocably lost control of the indian armed forces 1946 2005 ina 20,000 inc pyq communist party of india 1925. the mutiny began in february 1946, during the ina agitations, when naval ratings on his majesty's indian ship (hmis) talwar went on strike. their grievances were three: i) fear of unemployment — losing their jobs once the war ended. ii) poor service conditions & racial discrimination in salaries. (relate 1857 — the racial differential in pay & treatment had been a constant grievance in the indian armed forces since the sepoy era.) iii) inspiration from the ina — they had supported ina agitations & contributed money for ina men, and felt a direct identification with the cause. what happened next showed how far things had moved since the disciplined satyagrahas of earlier decades. the ratings revolted & raised tricolour flags on their ships, alongside flags of the ina, the inc, and the muslim league. they wrote "quit india" on ships — including on hmis talwar. they drove through bombay in trucks carrying pictures of netaji bose. the communist party of india (cpi1925) gave them support, and workers across bombay went on a massive strike, bringing the city to a standstill. aruna asaf ali advised the ratings & provided leadership despite opposition from gandhi & the inc, who felt it was a truce period & time for negotiations. airforce men in karachi began sympathy strikes. the mutiny ended — british repression played a role, but so did the withdrawal of support by the inc & the muslim league. sardar patel & jinnah personally held meetings to calm the ratings down. after independence, most ina men & naval ratings were not recruited into the armed forces, on grounds of breach of discipline. :( 4.1) why the naval & riaf mutinies mattered beyond the event itself the naval ratings mutiny, combined with the royal indian air force (riaf) strikes in several stations, shattered the "martial races" myth that the british had carefully cultivated since 1857 — the notion that certain indian communities were inherently loyal to the crown & could always be relied upon to enforce imperial authority against other indians. when indian sailors & airmen turned against british command — not as isolated incidents but as coordinated, politicised acts of defiance — it proved that the british had irrevocably lost control of the indian armed forces. (the entire edifice of british india rested on using indian soldiers against indians. once that instrument cracked — visibly, publicly, and with political consciousness — the game was over.) ◆ the naval ratings mutiny of 1946 is significant not just as an event but as a signal. the indian armed forces — the last reliable instrument of british control — were showing cracks. the british had always maintained their india by their ability to use indian soldiers against indians. that ability was now visibly in doubt. it is widely seen as one of the key factors that convinced the british that the transfer of power could not be postponed. ⚠ alert: prelims 2005 (royal indian navy mutiny february 1946 — bombay-led, ina-trial-inspired, spread to 78 ships + 20 shore establishments + 20,000 sailors; tricolour, crescent & hammer-sickle hoisted side-by-side; suppressed by 23 february with inc + ml cooperation). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.norm: proposals. the formula had three main planks: ml1906 should support the goal of purna swaraj coalition government at the centre plebiscite confederation — a weak common centre liaqat pact pyq 1998 1944 2003 inc 2010 liaqat pact 1945 2015 muslim league 1906. the formula had three main planks: 1.1) (@ swaraj) ml1906 should support the goal of purna swaraj. 1.2) (@ transfer of power) inc & ml1906 should be ready to form a coalition government at the centre. 1.3) (@ unity) after the war, a plebiscite would be held in muslim-majority regions on the question of partition. if the vote was in favour, the result would be a confederation — a weak common centre with strong provinces. sections.title: Result: Talks Collapse
sections.norm: result: talks collapse. talks failed jinnah's demands were very different separate electorates only muslims would vote fully separate, independent pakistan before the british left jinnah did not trust the inc failed completely how far inc was willing to bend. gandhi & jinnah met to discuss the formula, but the talks failed. jinnah's demands were very different from what rajagopalachari had proposed: 2.1) voting on the question of partition should be based on separate electorates — meaning only muslims would vote. 2.2) the outcome should not be a weak common centre but a fully separate, independent pakistan. (i.e. not two nations, one state — but two nations, two states.) 2.3) all of this should be implemented before the british left, since jinnah did not trust the inc to honour any agreement once in power. the formula failed completely. but it had shown jinnah exactly how far inc was willing to bend — and he had found the answer useful.

sections.title: Desai-Liaqat Pact, 1945
sections.norm: desai-liaqat pact, 1945. bullabhai desai & liaqat ali khan build inc-ml unity proposed two things all ministers would be indians 50% would be from inc & 50% from ml1906 20% of seats would be reserved for minorities jinnah refused to acknowledge any knowledge of it raising jinnah's floor muslim league 1906 lucknow pact 1916. the desai-liaqat pact was negotiated & finalised by bullabhai desai & liaqat ali khan — the leaders of inc & ml1906 respectively in the central legislative assembly (cla). the goal was the same as the rajaji formula: build inc-ml unity & present joint demands to the british (like lp1916) to ensure a smoother transfer of power. the pact proposed two things for the british to accept at the time of transfer of power. first, in the viceroy's executive council (vec), all ministers would be indians — except the governor general & the commander-in-chief. of these indian ministers, 50% would be from inc & 50% from ml1906. second, in the central legislature, 20% of seats would be reserved for minorities — especially dalits & sikhs — and the remaining seats split equally between inc & ml1906. these seats would initially be filled by nomination, with elections — direct or indirect — to follow later. gandhi was aware of the pact. it failed because jinnah refused to acknowledge any knowledge of it. (he was testing how far inc could bend. now he had a minimum base. any future negotiation would need to offer ml1906 something even more to get agreement.) each concession was not building goodwill — it was raising jinnah's floor.

sections.title: Wavell Plan, 1945
sections.norm: wavell plan, 1945. shimla conference in june 1945 release of inc leaders formally ended the qim british domestic politics visible progress based closely on the desai-liaqat pact (1945) 4.1) proposals wavell4347 proposed: all ministers would be indians 50% of indian ministers would be hindus & 50% would be muslims the governor general / viceroy aid & advice retain veto power foreign affairs would be offered to indians joint list of names 4.2) why it failed collapsed on a single point muslim ministers in the vec should come only from ml1906 inc was not a hindu organisation implicit veto boosted the prestige of ml1906 december 1945 elections wavell plan pyq 1996 1945 1998 cic 2000 why wavell plan 2007 ina wavell muslim league 1906. (wavell4347, 1943–47) the wavell plan was discussed at the shimla conference in june 1945, held after the release of inc leaders who had been imprisoned during the quit india movement (1942–45). the release of the leaders also formally ended the qim. the timing was driven by british domestic politics. winston churchill wanted some visible progress on the india problem before elections in britain. the wavell plan was therefore based closely on the desai-liaqat pact (1945) — because inc & ml1906 had already agreed on it in principle, making rapid acceptance by both parties more likely. also, any changes to the vec could be made swiftly at the behest of the governor general. 4.1) proposals wavell4347 proposed: i) in the vec, all ministers would be indians except the governor general & the commander-in-chief (c-i-c). 50% of indian ministers would be hindus & 50% would be muslims. ii) the governor general / viceroy would rule on the aid & advice of ministers but retain veto power. iii) the portfolio of foreign affairs would be offered to indians. (recall: in the cripps mission 1942, foreign policy had already been offered to indians — so this was consistent with that.) iv) wavell demanded that a joint list of names for ministership be submitted by the political parties. if a joint list was not possible, each party would submit a separate list. 4.2) why it failed the plan collapsed on a single point. ml1906 insisted that muslim ministers in the vec should come only from ml1906 — not from inc, which had its own muslim leaders. ml1906 rejected the plan when wavell4347 refused to guarantee this. inc, on its part, refused ml1906's demand, arguing that inc was not a hindu organisation & that muslim leaders of inc also had the right to be ministers. wavell4347 announced the failure, saying ml1906 could not be convinced. in effect, this amounted to an implicit veto being given to ml1906 on the question of transfer of power. the announcement boosted the prestige of ml1906 enormously — and ml1906 did very well in the december 1945 elections in seats reserved for muslims. ⚠ alert: wavell plan pyq cluster (sec. 4). prelims 1996×2 (simla conference 1945 + wavell plan provisions); prelims 1998×2 (wavell plan composition — parity hindus/muslims in executive council, all indian members except viceroy + cic); prelims 2000 (why wavell plan failed — jinnah's demand for ml monopoly on muslim seats); prelims 2007 (ina trials context for wavell plan acceptance). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Cabinet Mission Plan (CMP1946)
sections.norm: cabinet mission plan (cmp1946). 5.1) background clement atlee had become british pm japan surrendered ina trials then began december 1945 elections inc got majority everywhere except bengal, punjab, and sindh inc formed a coalition government with the akalis & the unionist party ml1906 got majority in bengal & sindh cabinet mission arrived lord pethick-lawrence sir stafford cripps a.v. alexander naval mutiny broke out shaken them badly no longer had confidence in the loyalty of the indian military wrecked the british economy only proposal where the british offered a united india & purna swaraj anti-partition statement direct reversal 5.2) proposals peaceful transfer of executive power constituent assembly (ca) the structure it proposed was: weak common centre defence, communications, and foreign affairs confederation of india no two constituent assemblies no veto to ml1906 inc-ml consensus three sections section a section b section c group constitution union constitution nominees of the princely states & elected members from the plas populated by august 1946 only after 10 years come out of its group full independence immediate transfer of executive power interim government advisory committee major communal question majority of both hindu & muslim members 5.3) debates on cmp1946 the plan immediately ran into disagreement on interpretation: ml1906 wanted the right to question the union constitution immediately inc argued that grouping was not compulsory ml1906 argued grouping was compulsory partition is implicit within the plan central fault-line direct action day elected representatives from the princely states nwfp & assam would not join ml1906 therefore rejected cmp1946 16th august 1946 communal riots in calcutta 5,000 people died ml1906 did join the interim government out of fear finance ministry could not function 5.4) constituent assembly in favour of two constituent assemblies demanded dissolution 9 december 1946 dr. sachchidananda sinha provisional president dr. rajendra prasad permanent president cabinet mission pyq 1996 1999 2000 2002 2003 2004 2013 2024 cabinet mission 1946 nwfp 1946 ww1 ww2 cabinet mission plan 1946 muslim league 1906. 5.1) background by 1946, a great deal had changed. in july 1945, clement atlee had become british pm after churchill lost the elections. japan surrendered on 15 august 1945. the ina trials then began — with the trial at the red fort of prem sehgal, shah nawaz khan, and gurbaksh singh dhillon drawing massive public attention & generating remarkable communal unity during the ina agitations of 1945–46. then came the december 1945 elections to the provincial legislative assemblies (plas): i) inc got majority everywhere except bengal, punjab, and sindh. ii) in punjab, inc formed a coalition government with the akalis & the unionist party. iii) ml1906 did very well in seats reserved for muslims & got majority in bengal & sindh. (**inc got majority in nwfp & assam. in nwfp, the poor muslim masses supported khan abdul gaffar khan — the frontier gandhi — and his khudai khidmatgars or red shirts, as inc had their support since the khilafat movement of 1920–24. the elite khans, however, were pro-ml1906. in assam, only 31% of the population was muslim, and they were concentrated mainly in the sylhet district where muslims were in majority.*) in february 1946, the cabinet mission arrived in india. the mission consisted of three members: lord pethick-lawrence (secretary of state for india), sir stafford cripps (president of the board of trade), and a.v. alexander(first lord of the admiralty). on the same day, the naval mutiny broke out in bombay. the timing was not a coincidence — it was a signal. why did the british now offer a united india? the sequence of events had shaken them badly: qim (1942–45), then ina agitations (1945–46), then the naval mutiny (1946). the british realised that if the cabinet mission failed, the next movement would overthrow them violently — because they no longer had confidence in the loyalty of the indian military. add to this the fact that in three decades, three events had wrecked the british economy: ww1 (1914–19), the great depression (1929), and ww2 (1939–45). britain was exhausted. cmp1946 was the only proposal where the british offered a united india & purna swaraj. (@ cold war — the cold war had begun in 1945 & britain wanted a strong, friendly india for influence in south asia post-decolonisation. a partition would be a diplomatic failure — britain could not keep india united.) in march 1946, atlee made his anti-partition statement: "a minority won't be allowed veto over majority." this was a direct reversal of the august offer (1940), the cripps mission (1942), and the wavell plan (1945) — all three of which had, in effect, given ml1906 exactly that veto. 5.2) proposals the goal of cmp1946 was a peaceful transfer of executive power at the centre & the setting up of a constituent assembly (ca) for framing the constitution of an independent india. cmp1946 provided a "one state, two nation" solution to the question of partition. (this is what syed ahmed khan had hinted at decades earlier — and what the rajaji formula had also gestured toward.) the structure it proposed was: i) a weak common centre handling only three union subjects: defence, communications, and foreign affairs. all other subjects & residual powers would be with the provinces — effectively a confederation of india. (link: rajaji formula 1944.) ii) no two constituent assemblies — and no veto to ml1906. but the british also would not accept a constitution not based on inc-ml consensus. (i.e. decisions during constitution-framing would be taken by majority vote, but overall agreement of ml1906 on the constitution framed would be needed.) iii) provinces would be divided into three sections: a) section a = hindu-majority provinces b) section b = muslim-majority provinces of the west (nwfp, punjab, sindh) c) section c = muslim-majority provinces of the east, i.e. bengal. (assam was not a muslim-majority province — only 31% muslims — but sylhet district of assam had a muslim majority, and so assam was placed in section c.) iv) each section would frame its own group constitution for all subjects except defence, communications, and foreign affairs. (this is effectively art. 370 for all 11 provinces, grouped into three sections — meeting jinnah's 14-point demands of march 1929 in spirit.) v) the union constitution — covering only the three union subjects — would be framed by a constituent assembly consisting of nominees of the princely states & elected members from the plas. (the december 1945 direct elections to plas had already taken place — same approach as cripps mission 1942.) (the constituent assembly = group a + group b + group c + nominees of princely states. the maximum number of constitutions possible was: constitutions for each of the princely states + 3 group constitutions + 1 union constitution. the minimum was 3 group constitutions + 1 union constitution = 4.) vi) the constituent assembly was to be populated by august 1946. vii) future changes to constitutions only after 10 years. (i.e. a united india guaranteed for at least a decade.) viii) after general elections, a province could come out of its group. (this meant a group's constitution would not be permanently binding on a province that chose to leave.) ix) full independence once the constitution was drafted. x) (@ transfer of power) immediate transfer of executive power to an interim government at the centre. (this was done in september 1946, with j.l. nehru as prime minister.) xi) an advisory committee to be formed on the rights of citizens, tribals, and minorities. xii) any decision on a major communal question in the central legislature would require a majority of both hindu & muslim members along with an overall majority. 5.3) debates on cmp1946 the plan immediately ran into disagreement on interpretation: i) ml1906 wanted the right to question the union constitution immediately — rather than after 10 years — since the union constitution would establish a united india. ii) inc argued that grouping was not compulsory, i.e. groups may be created but a province should not be compelled to join a prescribed group. (inc was in power in nwfp & assam & did not want them to follow the constitution of group b & group c respectively.) ml1906 argued — and the british agreed — that grouping was compulsory for all muslim-majority provinces to join group b & group c. ml1906's logic was that if grouping is compulsory, partition is implicit within the plan: cmp1946 was a one-state, two-nation solution. if the british agreed with this interpretation, ml1906 would accept cmp1946; if not, it would reject it. (explicit partition = two separate states. implicit partition = one state, two nations, i.e. a pakistan within india in the form of group b & group c.) this was the central fault-line of the cmp debate: inc thought grouping voluntary; ml1906 thought compulsory. the british clarification that grouping was compulsory gave jinnah the trigger — he called direct action day. iii) inc wanted elected representatives from the princely states in the constituent assembly — as it had demanded during the cripps mission 1942 also. iv) inc decided in july 1946 that nwfp & assam would not join group b & group c respectively. nehru further stated in july 1946 that the only binding decision of the cabinet mission was the formation of a constituent assembly. ml1906 therefore rejected cmp1946, refused to join the interim government & the constituent assembly, and gave the call for direct action — to be observed on 16th august 1946 — for the creation of pakistan. the direct action day led to communal riots in calcutta in which 5,000 people died in a single week. :( v) later, ml1906 did join the interim government — not out of agreement, but out of fear. ml1906 did not want inc holding executive power at the centre without them. ml1906 got the finance ministry & used it to ensure the government could not function. 5.4) constituent assembly on 6th december 1946, the british took a stand in favour of two constituent assemblies — stating that if ml1906-ruled provinces did not join the constituent assembly, the constitution framed by it would not apply to those provinces. in february 1947, ml1906 demanded dissolution of the constituent assembly on the grounds that it was not truly representative. the constituent assembly convened on 9 december 1946 with dr. sachchidananda sinha as its provisional president. two days later, on 11 december 1946, dr. rajendra prasad was elected as the permanent president of the constituent assembly. (pyq prelims 2024) ⚠ alert: cabinet mission pyq cluster (sec. 5). prelims 1996×2 + 1999 + 2000 + 2002×3 + 2003 + 2004 + 2013 + 2024 — 11 pyqs on cabinet mission 1946. anchors: pethick-lawrence + cripps + alexander composition; three-tier federation; three groups (a: hindu provinces; b: nw muslim — punjab + nwfp + sind + balochistan; c: ne muslim — bengal + assam); constituent assembly elected by provincial legislatures; rejection of full pakistan demand; direct action day 16 aug 1946 by ml. full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Atlee Statement (February 1947)
sections.norm: atlee statement (february 1947). pro-balkanisation statement 30th june 1948 with or without a constitution deliberate threat of anarchy the princely states not to be under any future government of india power would be transferred to the interim government mountbatten (mtb) would replace wavell4347. victory for ml1906 widespread communal violence coalition government in punjab was overthrown muslim league 1906 wavell. the atlee statement of february 1947 was, in effect, a pro-balkanisation statement — very much like the cripps mission (1942) before it. (recall: cripps 1942 had given provinces the option to not join the union.) atlee stated that by 30th june 1948, the british would leave india — with or without a constitution. this was a deliberate threat of anarchy, designed to force inc & ml1906 into a compromise. but the details of the statement were far more damaging: 6.1) the princely states (all 565 of them) were not to be under any future government of india. (i.e. effectively 565 independent countries — since paramountcy over the princely states would lapse & would not be transferred to the successor government.) power would be transferred to the interim government at the centre under nehru & to the provincial governments of provinces that had not joined the constituent assembly. (i.e. provinces which had not joined the constituent assembly would receive power directly & could, in effect, become independent.) 6.2) mountbatten (mtb) would replace wavell4347. this was a victory for ml1906. widespread communal violence followed, and the coalition government of inc, akalis, and the unionist party in punjab was overthrown by direct action led by muslims under ml1906.

sections.title: Plan Balkan / Ismay Plan / Dickie Bird Plan (April 1947)
sections.norm: plan balkan / ismay plan / dickie bird plan (april 1947). voluntary union independence to each province & each princely state option of partition transferring power to 11 individual provinces separately nehru opposed it immediately. (by mountbatten — "dickie" was mountbatten's nickname; ismay was a member of his committee) this plan proposed a voluntary union — on the model of the united states. it would give independence to each province & each princely state, give punjab & bengal the option of partition, and give every province & princely state the choice of joining or not joining the constituent assembly for a united india. in effect, it proposed transferring power to 11 individual provinces separately — a prospect nehru violently opposed as "balkanization" of india. nehru opposed it immediately. it was not discussed further.

sections.title: 3rd June Plan / Mountbatten Plan (1947)
sections.norm: 3rd june plan / mountbatten plan (1947). 8.1) context deadline of october 1947 dead horses two countries friendly to britain partition was avoidable passive role dominion status to both india & pakistan trade & business benefits 8.2) since inc agreed to partition & dominion status, all other inc demands were accepted: pakistan to be as small as possible the princely states would not be given independence a strong centre for india exit in 72 days 15th august 1947 8.3) the mechanics of partition simple majority of either hindu or muslim members which areas would join pakistan: plebiscite in sindh referendum in nwfp sylhet district voting by political leaders in baluchistan referendum was therefore chosen split into two constituent assemblies power would be transferred to two centres both accepted the mountbatten plan favour of partition in punjab & bengal voted to join pakistan 8.4) boundary commission two boundary commissions sir cyril radcliffe never been to india unilateral decision pyq 1998 1947 1948 1999 dickie bird plan cabinet mission plan 1946 muslim league 1906. 8.1) context mountbatten (mtb) had been given a deadline of october 1947 to explore options for unity & partition. within two months, he concluded that the cabinet mission plan (cmp1946) and the idea of a united india were dead horses — entirely due to jinnah. british national interest now pointed in a different direction: it was better to have two countries friendly to britain than to risk an unfriendly pakistan created by direct action or civil war. as atlee later stated, "britain wanted a united india, tried but failed." (the 1st choice was india as a colony; the 2nd choice was a friendly united india; the 3rd choice — now the only realistic one — was a friendly india & a friendly pakistan.) there is also a harder point to make here: partition was avoidable if the british had acted against communal violence rather than playing the passive role of a mediator between inc & ml1906. they chose the passive role — because it served british national interest. (in british national interest) the 3rd june plan gave dominion status to both india & pakistan — keeping both in the british commonwealth, even if temporarily. the commonwealth was the network of british colonies that had a special economic relationship with britain, and commonwealth membership translated into trade & business benefits for british firms. dominion status was therefore a political victory for the british government among the british people. 8.2) since inc agreed to partition & dominion status, all other inc demands were accepted: i) pakistan to be as small as possible, with an informal promise that the princely states (all 565 of them) would not be given independence. ii) a strong centre for india (unitary structure — like the nehru report 1928 & unlike the rajaji formula 1944). iii) the british would exit in 72 days from 3rd june, i.e. on 15th august 1947 — one year ahead of the deadline set in the atlee statement. 8.3) the mechanics of partition in punjab & bengal, a simple majority of either hindu or muslim members of the plas in favour of partition would lead to partition. (decision of partition was thus by the two big muslim-majority provinces.) since partition was now decided, the remaining question was which areas would join pakistan: i) plebiscite in sindh ii) referendum in nwfp & in the sylhet district of assam iii) voting by political leaders in baluchistan inc had won the december 1945 elections in nwfp & assam. a referendum was therefore chosen for these regions to get a clear, direct answer from the people. (a plebiscite only seeks a non-binding opinion; a referendum is binding.) if the votes came out in favour of partition, the constituent assembly set up by the cabinet mission would be split into two constituent assemblies for two dominions, and power would be transferred to two centres by 15th august 1947 — the "appointed day." (this is why india became an "indestructible union of destructible states" — because power was transferred only to the union at the centre, and the provinces did not separately decide to form a union as in the usa.) inc & ml1906 both accepted the mountbatten plan. votes came out in favour of partition in punjab & bengal. nwfp, sindh, baluchistan, and sylhet voted to join pakistan. (frontier gandhi — khan abdul gaffar khan — boycotted the referendum & passed the bannu resolution in june 1947, demanding an independent pakhtonistan for the pashtuns. thus nwfp's vote went in favour of pakistan — as the followers of frontier gandhi did not vote. pakistan banned the khudai khidmatgars in 1948. "pakhto" means the pakhtun code of life. some pashtuns wanted to join afghanistan. today nwfp is called khyber pakhtunwa.) 8.4) boundary commission two boundary commissions were set up to demarcate borders in the west (punjab) and the east (bengal). both were headed by sir cyril radcliffe, a british jurist who had never been to india. each commission had four judges — two nominated by inc & two by ml1906 — who were completely deadlocked on partisan lines. the boundary lines were therefore radcliffe's unilateral decision. (the radcliffe line was announced on 17 august 1947 — two days after independence — ensuring maximum chaos during the transfer of power.) ⚠ alert: atlee statement + plan balkan pyq cluster (sec. 6-7). prelims 1998 (atlee statement feb 1947 — june 1948 deadline for british departure); prelims 1999 (plan balkan / dickie bird plan — multiple successor states proposal, rejected by nehru). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: Integration of Princely States
sections.norm: integration of princely states. 565 officially recognised princely states 40% of the landmass 23% of its population ended british paramountcy sardar vallabhbhai patel v.p. menon 552 were geographically contiguous 549 states signed the instrument of accession three states initially held out: jammu & kashmir invasion junagadh public plebiscite hyderabad military operation 552 states joined the indian union 13 princely states acceded to the dominion of pakistan butler committee report 1927 1950 indian independence act 1947. before august 1947, there were 565 officially recognised princely states in the indian subcontinent, covering approximately 40% of the landmass & containing about 23% of its population. the indian independence act (july 1947) ended british paramountcy over all 565 states, legally freeing each to choose independence. the question of their future was therefore one of the gravest challenges facing the new indian state. sardar vallabhbhai patel, as head of the states department, along with v.p. menon as its secretary, undertook the integration. of the 565 states, 552 were geographically contiguous to the dominion of india. through intense diplomatic efforts — a combination of persuasion, pressure, and appeals to patriotism — 549 states signed the instrument of accession by or shortly after 15 august 1947. three states initially held out: i) jammu & kashmir — acceded to india in october 1947 following an invasion by pakistani-backed tribal militias. ii) junagadh — integrated in february 1948 following a public plebiscite where the overwhelming majority voted to join india, after its nawab had initially attempted to accede to pakistan. iii) hyderabad — integrated in september 1948 following a military operation known as "operation polo." ultimately, all 552 states contiguous to india joined the indian union. the remaining 13 princely states — geographically contiguous to pakistan's borders — acceded to the dominion of pakistan. these included bahawalpur (punjab region), khairpur (sindh region), the khanate of kalat, makran, las bela, and kharan (balochistan region), and swat, chitral, hunza, nagar, amb, phulra, and dir (north-west frontier/gilgit region). (552 to india + 13 to pakistan = 565 total.) ◆ a note on numbers: the claim that "sardar patel integrated 562 princely states into india" is one of the most widely repeated factual errors on the internet. some earlier british colonial records — such as the butler committee report (1927) — cited 562, but 565 is the final accepted count at the time of british withdrawal. the authoritative source for the correct breakdown is the white paper on indian states (1950), published by the ministry of states under sardar patel & v.p. menon, read together with the records of the indian independence act (july 1947). per these documents: 565 total → 552 to india (549 by accession + 3 subsequently integrated) → 13 to pakistan.

sections.title: Indian Independence Act (July 1947)
sections.norm: indian independence act (july 1947). gave legal status to the mountbatten plan its key provisions were: two independent dominions 15th august 1947 governor general appointed by the king jinnah would be its gg pass constitutions that ended dominion status end of jurisdiction of the british parliament end of paramountcy abolition of the title abolition of the office of the secretary of state for india government of india act 1935 would apply boundary commission dominion of britain 26th january 1950. the indian independence act (july 1947) gave legal status to the mountbatten plan. its key provisions were: 10.1) partition of british india into two independent dominions — independent of each other — on the appointed day of 15th august 1947. 10.2) each dominion would be headed by a governor general appointed by the king. the same governor general would serve both dominions until their respective constituent assemblies passed a law for a separate governor general. pakistan decided that jinnah would be its gg. 10.3) the constituent assemblies of the two dominions could pass constitutions that ended dominion status. (ca of india did so on 26th january 1950.) 10.4) end of jurisdiction of the british parliament over british india on the appointed day + end of paramountcy over the 565 princely states on the appointed day. paramountcy was not to be transferred to any government in the two dominions. (i.e. legally, each of the 565 princely states had the right to independence.) 10.5) abolition of the title "emperor of india" and abolition of the office of the secretary of state for india. (the office of the secretary of state for india had been created in 1858.) 10.6) until the passage of a new constitution, the government of india act 1935 would apply. 10.7) territories of india & pakistan to be determined "before or after" the appointed day by a boundary commission appointed by the governor general. india was a dominion of britain from 15th august 1947 until 26th january 1950 — when our constitution came into effect.

sections.title: Why Partition?
sections.norm: why partition?. bipin chandra inc failed on two counts won 90% of muslim seats given up on a united india a compulsion, not a choice the major factors were: 11.1) british divide & rule (dnr) sustained, structural effort indian musalmans (1871) separate, neglected political category census 1881 homogeneous religious identity reservation in government jobs for muslims (1897) bengal partition (1905) simla deputation (1906) formation of ml1906. separate electorates for muslims ml1906 was given veto on constitutional progress 11.2) role of western-educated middle-class muslims (wemc muslims) syed ahmed khan gave the two-nation theory delhi proposals (december 1927) calcutta amendments (december 1928) 14-point demands (march 1929) opposed cdm (1930–34) and qim (1942–45) 11.3) hindu revivalism (1880s–1900s) shuddhi movement & the cow protection movement became aggressive cow-killing riots (1893). hindu-urdu controversy identification of hindi with hindus & urdu with muslims inc did not condemn the 1893 riots 1886 rule muslim participation in inc declined hindu religious symbolism 11.4) role of inc compounded the problem inc accepted provincial autonomy for muslim-majority provinces inc agreed to a plebiscite partially conceding the right to self-determination inc opposed only compulsory grouping inc first explicitly mentioned partition in march 1947 there were also two false beliefs that proved costly: partition would be temporary hearts do not make borders appeasement of ml1906 every concession by inc increased the prestige of ml1906 each one raised could not start a movement against partition communalism had by then spread too far gandhi was alone culmination of a long process 2000 independence act 1947 pyq muslim league 1906 cabinet mission plan 1946 minto. this is the question that every student of this period must sit with. the acceptance of partition in the 3rd june plan was not a sudden decision — it was the culmination of a long process. as per historian bipin chandra, inc failed on two counts: it failed to bring muslims into the inm as a mass constituency, and it failed to curb muslim communal forces — especially from 1937 onwards. the proof is stark: ml1906 won 90% of muslim seats in the 1945 elections to plas. by june 1947, inc had given up on a united india — defeated by a combination of communal violence, the failure of the interim government, and ml1906's refusal to join the constituent assembly (august 1946). even the bengal government of ml1906 promoted communal riots. therefore, the 3rd june plan was a compulsion, not a choice. (@ essay on partition) the major factors were: 11.1) british divide & rule (dnr) a sustained, structural effort across decades: i) hunter's indian musalmans (1871) argued that british neglect of muslims had contributed to the faraisi movement (1830–70s) — an argument that planted the idea that muslims were a separate, neglected political category requiring special attention. ii) census 1881 contributed to a sense of homogeneous religious identity among hindus & muslims — communities that were in reality internally very heterogeneous. by publishing religion-based statistics & reports, government brought religious identity into the domain of public policy & governance. iii) reservation in government jobs for muslims (1897). iv) bengal partition (1905) — creating a muslim-majority province & rewarding elite muslims. v) positive response of minto05-10 to the simla deputation (1906). vi) formation of ml1906. vii) separate electorates for muslims under ica 1909. viii) in august offer (1940) and wavell plan (1945), ml1906 was given veto on constitutional progress. 11.2) role of western-educated middle-class muslims (wemc muslims) muslim organisations led by syed ahmed khan gave the two-nation theory, labelled inc as a hindu organisation, demanded reservation & special status for the muslim quam, and supported the british in return. the four delhi proposals (december 1927), three calcutta amendments (december 1928) all failed, and jinnah then issued the 14-point demands (march 1929) — which became the blueprint for all future politics of ml1906. ml1906 also opposed cdm (1930–34) and qim (1942–45), reducing muslim participation in the inm. 11.3) hindu revivalism (1880s–1900s) i) the shuddhi movement & the cow protection movement of the arya samaj became aggressive after the death of swami dayanand saraswati in 1883. ii) cow-killing riots (1893). iii) the hindu-urdu controversy (1880s–1900) in the north-west provinces & awadh (set up in 1877). its impact was the identification of hindi with hindus & urdu with muslims — a cultural fault-line that deepened communal identity. inc did not condemn the 1893 riots — because of its 1886 rule that inc would not take up social issues. muslim participation in inc declined thereafter, and inc did not do much to reclaim muslim leadership. the swadeshi movement (1905–11) also hurt muslim participation through its heavy use of hindu religious symbolism, depiction of muslims & british as partners in jatras, and social boycott that hurt poorer communities disproportionately. ml1906 & the ulamas actively discouraged muslim participation. 11.4) role of inc inc's own actions compounded the problem across decades: i) in cripps mission (1942), inc accepted provincial autonomy for muslim-majority provinces. (like art. 370) ii) in mg-jinnah talks on the rajaji formula (1944), inc agreed to a plebiscite for "partition without independence" (like art. 370 for mmps) — partially conceding the right to self-determination of muslim-majority provinces. iii) in cmp1946, inc opposed only compulsory grouping — not the idea of grouping itself. (cmp1946 was, in essence, a two-nation, one-state solution — which is what syed ahmed khan had originally hinted at.) iv) inc first explicitly mentioned partition in march 1947 — stating that punjab & bengal would have to be partitioned if the country was divided. this was months before the 3rd june plan. there were also two false beliefs that proved costly: v) that partition would be temporary. gandhi told inc — "don't accept partition in your hearts." but hearts do not make borders. vi) that appeasement of ml1906 would reduce the fear-of-majority complex. instead, every concession by inc increased the prestige of ml1906 & brought it closer to its goal. the lucknow pact (1916), the rajaji formula (1944), the desai-liaqat pact (1945) — each one raised ml1906's floor for the next negotiation. gandhi could not start a movement against partition because communalism had by then spread too far. he stated that hindus & sikhs also desired partition — which made muslims hate him. and it made hindus & sikhs abandon him. by mid-1947, gandhi was alone. mountbatten later called him a "one-man boundary force" against communal violence. the acceptance of partition through the 3rd june plan was, therefore, the culmination of a long process — not a single act of failure. :( ⚠ alert: prelims 2000 (independence act 1947 + princely state integration — patel + v.p. menon's standstill + instrument of accession framework). full stem & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: The Working Class Movement
sections.norm: the working class movement. 1.1) who was the modern indian worker? did not exist in any meaningful number growth of modern industries immediate economic grievances social fact long before it existed as a political force sasipada bannerjee working men's club narayan lokhande bombay mills & mill hands association madras labour union (1918) b.p. wadia 1.2) why did the moderates pay
