real wages russian revolution of 1917 several developments defined this period: home rule league movement ahmedabad mill strike (1918) textile labour association (tla, 1920) gandhian arbitration rowlatt satyagraha (1919) strikes spread across multiple sectors jm sen gupta prince of wales the working class moved steadily margins of the inm into its mainstream 1.5) aituc (1920): the first all-india organisation of workers all india trade union congress (aituc) in 1920 lala lajpat rai first all-india organisation of workers international labour organisation (ilo) lajpat rai first indian leader to explicitly connect imperialism with capitalism stronger & longer strikes hind mazdoor sabha (hms) 1.6) inc gaya session (1922): a change of position cr das made the argument independent class-based movements bring their demands within the nationalist programme formally welcomed the aituc (1920) trusteeship & arbitration 1.7) the communist party of india (cpi) and the growth of the left within inc established in tashkent m.n. roy, abani mukherji kanpur conference held in december 1925 s.v. ghate, m. singaravelu chettiar satyabhakta s.a. dange, muzaffar ahmad, and p.c. joshi 1924 kanpur bolshevik conspiracy case s.a. dange (shripad amrit dange) bombay textile strikes (1928) girni kamgar union (gku) gandhi vs. lenin (1921) the socialist muzaffar ahmad commanded the east workers & peasants party (wpp) meerut conspiracy case (1929–1933) courtroom as a massive propaganda platform p.c. joshi (puran chand joshi) general secretary of the cpi1925 from 1935 to 1947 infiltrated the congress socialist party indian people's theatre association (ipta) prog communist party of india 1925. 1.1) who was the modern indian worker? the modern indian worker did not exist in any meaningful number before the second half of the 19th century. it was the growth of modern industries — railways, telegraphs, textile mills — that brought this new social class into being. (contrast this with europe, where the industrial revolution had already produced a large organised working class by the early 19th century. in india, industrial capitalism arrived later, and under colonial conditions.) at first, workers organised only around immediate economic grievances — a wage dispute here, a local walkout there. strikes happened, but they were scattered, short-lived, and unconnected to any wider politics. the working class existed as a social fact long before it existed as a political force. the earliest signs of organised effort came in 1870, when sasipada bannerjee, a brahmo samajist reformer, set up a working men's club & launched a monthly journal called bharat shramjeevi. a decade later, in 1880, narayan lokhande started the anglo-marathi weekly deen bandhu, and by 1890 had set up the bombay mills & mill hands association — a philanthropic body focused on workers' welfare rather than a trade union in the modern sense. the first modern organised trade union in india was the madras labour union (1918), founded by b.p. wadia. these were small but meaningful beginnings. the emergence of the working class as an all-india organised force would come only through its growing connection with the indian national movement (inm). 1.2) why did the moderates pay so little attention to workers? the inc (1885) moderates, who dominated the congress in its early decades, paid very little attention to working class questions. there was a considered logic to this position. the moderates took the view that inc should focus only on political questions common to all indians — not on social divisions or class grievances. dadabhai naoroji formalised this at the 1886 inc session, establishing that the congress would not take up issues that could set indians against one another. the reasoning was practical: if inc took a strongly pro-peasant stand, it risked antagonising zamindars who were also part of the nationalist coalition. picking sides in economic disputes between indians would fracture a movement that was still in the process of building unity across castes, classes, and communities. (in a movement that needed hindu-muslim unity & cross-class participation, premature class conflict was a strategic liability, not a moral failing.) there was also a view about economic development. indian industry was at a nascent stage, facing stiff competition from british imports & british-owned businesses operating in india, with no support from the colonial government for indian manufacturers. the moderates believed that industrial capitalism was the path to modernising india, and so were reluctant to weaken indian manufacturers. on that basis, they opposed the factory acts of 1881 & 1891 — laws that reduced working hours — because the reduced hours raised costs for indian mill owners who were already under pressure. the one consistent exception to this position was significant. the moderates did support workers in foreign-owned enterprises, because there the employer was british & the grievance fitted naturally within an anti-colonial frame. in 1881-82, they strongly backed workers in the assam tea gardens, which were british-owned. in 1899, when the signallers' strike broke out in the great indian peninsular (gip) railways — the first organised industrial strike in india — the inc supported it for the same reason. the pattern was consistent: where the employer was indian, the inc stood aside; where the employer was british, the inc engaged. this was a coherent position for its time, though one that would become harder to sustain as the working class grew in size & the inm required broader mass participation. 1.3) how did workers first enter the inm? by the end of the 19th century, the growth in the number of industrial workers made the moderate position increasingly difficult to hold. inc extremists — lal, bal, pal, and aurobindo ghosh — began arguing that inc must take up the issues of all workers if the inm was to become a genuine mass movement. the swadeshi movement (1905-11) was the turning point. important strikes in foreign enterprises were led by cr das, bc pal, and liaquat hussain. the first attempt at forming an all-india union of workers was made during the swadeshi years — it did not succeed, but the attempt reflected a new political awareness. for the first time, workers were drawn into the inm & exposed to wider national questions beyond their immediate workplace concerns. (before swadeshi, a mill worker's political horizon was largely his mill. swadeshi expanded that horizon to the nation.) the tilak trial (1908) demonstrated what mass sentiment around a national cause could look like. when tilak was tried on sedition charges for writing in kesari in support of prafulla chaki & khudiram bose in connection with the muzaffarpur conspiracy case (1908), one of the largest working class demonstrations in india to that point took place in his support. the russian revolution of 1905, and the visible role workers had played in it, also made an impression on the extremist leadership. they saw organised labour as a potential source of strength for the inm. this was also the beginning — cautious & tentative — of socialist thinking making its way into inc circles. when the inm receded after the swadeshi movement, the working class movement receded with it. the two were now clearly linked. 1.4) the revival: workers during & after ww1 the working class movement revived sharply during & after the ww1 (1914-18), driven by both economic hardship & political awakening. wartime inflation eroded the real wages of industrial workers. workers who were already at the lower end of the economic scale found that rising prices made their position worse. the russian revolution of 1917 demonstrated, to those who were watching, that organised workers could be a decisive political force. (the lessons of 1917 were drawn differently by different people — some saw a model for revolution, others saw a model for mass organisation. in india, both readings coexisted.) several developments defined this period: 1.4.i) workers participated actively in the home rule league movement (hrl, 1916-18). 1.4.ii) the ahmedabad mill strike (1918), led by mahatma gandhi, produced the textile labour association (tla, 1920) in ahmedabad — an early working model of gandhian arbitration between labour & capital. 1.4.iii) workers were among the main participants in the rowlatt satyagraha (1919). 1.4.iv) during the non-cooperation movement (ncm, 1920-22), strikes spread across multiple sectors. jm sen gupta led strikes in railways, steamer services, and tea plantations in assam. workers also struck during the visit of the prince of wales in november 1921. through this period, the working class moved steadily from the margins of the inm into its mainstream. 1.5) aituc (1920): the first all-india organisation of workers the most important institutional development of this period was the formation of the all india trade union congress (aituc) in 1920, under the leadership of lala lajpat rai. it was the first all-india organisation of workers in indian history, and it represented india at the international labour organisation (ilo) of the league of nations from the outset. lajpat rai also made a wider intellectual contribution. he was the first indian leader to explicitly connect imperialism with capitalism — to argue that colonial rule & capitalist exploitation were not independent problems but parts of a single structure. (a colonial power, in this analysis, holds a territory to serve as a reliable source of cheap raw materials & a captive market for goods produced by its own industries. the economic interests of the colonial power & its business class are therefore aligned.) this framing gave the working class a role not just in trade unionism but in the anti-colonial movement itself. the 1920s saw stronger & longer strikes, and the working class now had an organisation to coordinate them. (note: after independence, rival central trade-union federations emerged. the hind mazdoor sabha (hms) was founded at howrah on 29 december 1948 by socialists & forward bloc unionists — ashok mehta, t.s. ramanujam & g.g. mehta.) 1.6) inc gaya session (1922): a change of position at the gaya session of 1922, cr das made the argument that finally moved the inc's position. he contended that if the congress continued to ignore the grievances of workers & peasants, these groups would launch independent class-based movements — workers against capitalists, peasants against landlords — which would fragment the national coalition. the only way to hold the movement together was to bring their demands within the nationalist programme. the inc accepted this reasoning. it formally welcomed the aituc (1920) and, after 1922, began supporting workers' and peasants' issues as part of the national struggle. gandhi, characteristically, offered a middle path alongside this shift — the concept of trusteeship & arbitration, under which those with capital would hold it in trust for the benefit of society, and disputes between labour & capital would be resolved through negotiation rather than confrontation. (gandhi's approach was not anti-capitalist; it was an attempt to make capitalism compatible with a broadly equitable social order.) 1.7) the communist party of india (cpi) and the growth of the left within inc the october revolution of 1917 in russia did not only inspire workers. it prompted the formation of communist parties across the world. the cpi was first established in tashkent (in uzbekistan in ussr) in 1920 by m.n. roy, abani mukherji, and others & then set up within india in the kanpur conference held in december 1925 to unite scattered communist groups across india into a single legal party. the key leaders were s.v. ghate, m. singaravelu chettiar(from madras; presided over the kanpur session; was the first to celebrate may day in india in 1923). satyabhaktaconvened the kanpur conference, but he wanted a purely "nationalist" communist party completely independent of the comintern. he was outvoted by ghate & singaravelu & resigned shortly after. s.a. dange, muzaffar ahmad, and p.c. joshi were the three tallest leaders of cpi (1925–1947). s.a. dange, muzaffar ahmad, and shaukat usmaniwere imprisoned in the 1924 kanpur bolshevik conspiracy case. s.a. dange (shripad amrit dange) led the communist trade union movement & was the face of cpi1925 in bombay (the industrial heart of india). the bombay textile strikes (1928) were his defining moment — dange led a massive, six-month-long strike & built the girni kamgar union (gku) into one of the most formidable & militant trade unions in indian history. he authored gandhi vs. lenin (1921) and founded the socialist, the first communist journal in india, which laid the intellectual groundwork for the movement. muzaffar ahmad commanded the east (bengal). if dange commanded the west, muzaffar ahmad commanded the east. he was instrumental in building the peasants-workers alliance in the form of the workers & peasants party (wpp) in bengal, which acted as a legal front for communist activities when the cpi was banned, effectively mobilising agrarian workers alongside urban labour. in the meerut conspiracy case (1929–1933), muzaffar ahmad was the prime accused, where he used the courtroom as a massive propaganda platform to broadcast communist ideology & demanded complete independence. p.c. joshi (puran chand joshi) was the most important organisational leader. he served as the general secretary of the cpi1925 from 1935 to 1947. he infiltrated the congress socialist party (csp, 1934: set up within inc) to gain mass cadres, and transformed the cpi1925 from a fringe group of revolutionaries into a massive, disciplined, pan-india political machine. recognising that politics needed art, joshi spearheaded the creation of the indian people's theatre association (ipta) and the progressive writers' association (pwa). through these fronts, he recruited india's top intellectuals, poets, actors, and writers (like kaifi azmi, mulk raj anand, and balraj sahni) to take the anti-imperialist & communist message to the rural masses through plays & songs. through the 1920s, a left wing began to take shape inside the inc, represented by leaders like jawaharlal nehru & subhas chandra bose. at the provincial level, workers & peasants parties (wpps) were set up within the inc structure from early 1927, under the communist leader sa dange. by 1928, an all-india wpp had been formed, and communist influence within the congress was a visible & growing factor. working class participation in the anti-simon commission agitations (october 1928) was also substantial. 1.8) the trade union act, 1926 the trade union act of 1926 was a landmark in indian labour history. it gave legal recognition to trade unions for the first time, protected union funds from arbitrary seizure, and granted immunity to union members & office-bearers for legitimate strike action. by providing a statutory framework, the act transformed trade unionism from an informal, legally vulnerable activity into a recognised institution with enforceable rights. (the irony was not lost on contemporaries: the colonial government that sought to suppress organised labour through the meerut case (1929) and the trade disputes bill (1929) also felt compelled to give it legal standing — partly under ilo pressure, partly to channel labour agitation into regulated forms rather than let it run wild.) 1.9) british approach to rise of left in india the british responded to the growth of communist & labour activity with a series of measures — reformative, regulatory (trade union act, 1926) and coercive. the public safety bill (1929) gave the government powers of deportation. the trade disputes bill (1929) imposed significant restrictions on labour action, limiting the ability of workers to organise & strike effectively. both bills were directed at curtailing what the british administration saw as a threat to public order & industrial stability. (◆ this was also the context for the bomb thrown in the central legislative assembly (cla) on 8 april 1929 by bhagat singh & bk dutt. the assembly was that day discussing these very bills. the action was designed to be heard, not to kill — bhagat singh later stated it was meant to force attention on legislation that was being passed over the heads of the people.) the meerut conspiracy case (1929) went further. a large number of communists — including foreign nationals — were arrested under section 121a of the indian penal code (1860), charged with conspiracy to deprive the king of sovereignty over british india. the immediate triggers were ongoing railway strikes & attempts to establish a branch of the communist international (comintern) in india. the meerut trial dragged on for years & significantly weakened the communist & workers' movement organisationally. also in 1929, the whitley commission — formally the royal commission on labour (1929), chaired by jh whitley — was appointed to investigate labour conditions across british india, with six indian members including gd birla & nm joshi. it submitted its report in 1931. the commission found poverty to be the root cause of india's industrial problems & was critical of british employers' role in perpetuating them. it recommended legal recognition of trade unions & their right to collective bargaining, standardised wages in cotton & jute industries, the creation of works committees at factory level, appointment of conciliation officers for dispute resolution, and systematic collection of labour statistics. its recommendations on tripartite consultative bodies — bringing together government, employers, and workers — laid the intellectual foundation for the indian labour conference established after independence. implementation under colonial rule was limited, but the whitley commission's report became the blueprint for india's post-independence labour legislation, including the factories act (1948) and minimum wages act (1948). 1.10) the cpi's break with the inc while british pressure was doing its damage from outside, a strategic error by the cpi1925 weakened the workers' movement from within. the 6th world congress of the comintern (1928) directed communist parties worldwide to oppose all non-communist political forces. following this directive, the cpi1925 declared the inc a party of the bourgeoisie & described nehru & bose as representatives of propertied class interests. in taking this position, the cpi1925 severed itself from the largest mass movement in india, and in doing so made it far easier for the british to suppress it. the cpi1925 went on to oppose the civil disobedience movement (cdm, 1930-34), characterise the goal of swaraj as illusory, and present the gandhi-irwin pact (1931) as evidence that the inc had compromised the national cause. by 1934, the wpps inside the inc had also been wound up by the communists themselves. the inc, meanwhile, declared during the cdm that workers were the "hands & feet" of the movement. workers did participate — but the cpi1925's stance meant that participation fell well short of what it could have been. there were nonetheless moments of real intensity: after gandhi's arrest in may 1930, textile workers in sholapur launched strikes serious enough that the british imposed martial law. gip railway workers, in a notable act of satyagraha, lay down on the tracks to stop trains. in 1934, a group of young left-leaning leaders within the inc — jayaprakash narayan, minoo masani, and acharya narendra dev — formed the congress socialist party (csp, 1934). they were critical of gandhi & the inc leadership over the withdrawal of the cdm, but they equally rejected the cpi1925's decision to work against the congress. their response was to remain inside the inc & work to shift it from within. 1.11) the comintern reverses course: 1935 onwards the 7th world congress of the comintern (1935) brought a significant shift in direction. with the rise of hitler & the threat of fascism in europe, the comintern directed communist parties to unite with all anti-fascist forcesregardless of ideology. under pc joshi's leadership, the cpi1925 moved back into alignment with the inc & worked to influence it from within. from 1936 to 1942, communists built substantial peasant movements in kerala, andhra, bengal, and punjab, recovering much of the credibility they had lost in the early 1930s. in 1936, the all india kisan sabha (aiks, 1936)was established in bihar under swami sahajanand saraswati. under the kisan manifesto, it demanded that ownership of agricultural land be given to those who actually cultivated it. the period of inc provincial ministries from 1937 to 1939 gave the working class movement a further lift, with aituc (1920) actively supporting the inc in elections. then came another reversal. in june 1941, germany attacked the soviet union. the cpi1925 declared the ww2 a "people's war" and swung to supporting the british war effort — which meant formally opposing the quit india movement (qim, 1942). this damaged the cpi1925's standing with the broader nationalist public considerably. even so, many individual communists & workers participated in the inm on their own initiative, regardless of the official party line. 1.12) workers in the final phase of the inm the december 1945 provincial elections confirmed a political landscape now dominated by the inc & the muslim league (ml, 1906). smaller parties, including those associated with the left, fared poorly. in the final stretch of the freedom struggle, the workers' movement contributed in several ways. but before noting that contribution, it is worth pausing on a striking inconsistency. the cpi1925 had, during the war years, denounced subhas chandra bose & the ina in the harshest possible terms — at one point comparing netaji to "tojo's dog," a reference to the japanese prime minister under whose military umbrella the ina operated. (the cpi1925's position was that any alliance with the axis powers, even in pursuit of indian independence, was a betrayal of the anti-fascist cause. that was, at least, an ideological position. what was harder to defend was the tone — comparing one of india's most admired freedom fighters to a collaborator.) then, the moment the war ended & the ina trials (1945-46) became a flashpoint of nationalist anger, the cpi1925 was among those participating in the agitations in support of the very ina soldiers it had previously condemned. the same netaji whose name the cpi1925 had dragged through the mud was now, conveniently, a symbol worth rallying around. :) the december 1945 elections had made the cpi1925's political irrelevance clear. participation in the ina agitations was, in that context, as much about recovering lost standing as it was about principle. that said, workers did participate — and their participation mattered. when ratings of the royal indian navy mutinied in bombay in february 1946 (royal indian navy mutiny, 1946), the cpi1925 called on bombay's workers to strike in solidarity — a moment where the labour movement & a section of the armed forces acted in public alignment. finally, when travancore, junagarh, and hyderabad declined to sign the instrument of accession to india, communists & workers were among those leading popular agitations within these princely states demanding democratic rights & integration with india. their participation contributed to the political pressure that brought about the accession of these princely states. whatever the cpi1925's record of strategic inconsistency through the preceding two decades, the workers who participated in these final struggles — many of them acting on conviction rather than party direction — played a real part in the making of independent india. ⚠ alert: working class + capitalists pyq cluster (sec. 1-2). 17 pyqs from 1995-2019. anchors: aituc 1920 (founder = n.m. joshi; first president = lala lajpat rai); bombay textile workers strike 1908 (tilak's sedition trial); trade union act 1926; royal commission on labour 1929; industrial disputes act 1947; ficci 1927 (purshotamdas thakurdas + gd birla); bombay plan 1944 (tata, birla, dalmia — capitalist statement of post-independence economic policy); capitalist support to inm through indirect funding while capitalists like walchand hirachand and others opposed gandhi's anti-modernist khadi line. full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.title: The Role of Indian Capitalists in the INM
sections.norm: the role of indian capitalists in the inm. 2.1) who were indian capitalists & what were their grievances? grew under conditions that were deliberately unfavourable structured to serve british commercial interests high duties in britain both economic & political their core economic complaints were these: favoured british manufacturers heavy taxation income tax introduced in 1868 restrictions on production preference to british firms no developmental support british textiles entered india virtually duty-free countervailing excise duty fiscal autonomy convention meaningful protective tariffs pushed by the lancashire textile lobby raised indian production costs opposed the acts ficci organised voice of indian business refused to negotiate with the british government approval or participation of the inc 2.2) why were capitalists ambivalent about the inm? never fully comfortable disrupted the smooth functioning of industry & trade did not necessarily want revolution their own workers made capitalists anxious 2.3) varying positions through the inm: a phase-by-phase view swadeshi movement (1905-11) most enthusiastically aligned bengal chemical industries swadeshi steam navigation company tisco — tata iron & steel company punjab national bank (pnb) against worker demands ambalal sarabhai method of arbitration prevent class conflict from escalating funding the movement jamnalal bajaj & gd birla land for the sabarmati ashram contributed to inc funds civil disobedience movement (cdm, 1930-34) currency league traders actively stopped importing british cloth fell by roughly 50% opposed the escalation do not let the movement threaten capitalism itself 2nd round table conference (1931) ficci boycotted ficci supported congress quit india movement (qim, 1942) businessmen donated generously sumati morarjee acts of personal courage 2.4) the bombay plan (1944) bombay plan (1944) a plan of economic development for india eight leading indian industrialists jrd tata, gd birla, purushottamdas thakurdas first ever national economic plan mixed economy with heavy state investment per capita income within 15 years endorsed by ficci (1927) first five year plan the bombay plan 2.5) ina trials & the final phase (1945-46) ina defence committee gd birla bhulabhai desai diaspora merchant communities 2.6) the relationship triangle: capitalists, workers, and peasants relationship with three other groups with the inc & the moderate leadership, the relationship was comfortable natural allies with the extremists & the gandhian phase complex but workable with workers & the left consistently tense uncomfortable when the same movement began fighting them with peasants more distant not their cause 2.7) assessment indian capitalists remained ambivalent ambivalence is not the same as absence real — it was simply conditional bombay plan ww1 . 2.1) who were indian capitalists & what were their grievances? the indian capitalist class — industrialists, traders, mill owners, merchants — did not emerge from thin air. they grew in the second half of the 19th century alongside modern industry, and they grew under conditions that were deliberately unfavourable to them. the colonial economy was structured to serve british commercial interests. indian manufacturers faced heavy competition from british imports that entered india at low tariffs while indian goods faced high duties in britain. (this is the classic colonial trade trap: your market is open to them, their market is closed to you.) indian businessmen had no support from the colonial government in building industries, no protection against british competition, and no representation in the bodies that made economic policy. their grievances were therefore both economic & political — and that is what made them, eventually, a part of the inm. their core economic complaints were these: 2.1.i) british trade & tariff policy systematically favoured british manufacturers over indian ones. 2.1.ii) heavy taxation — including income tax introduced in 1868 despite famines — drained indian wealth. 2.1.iii) restrictions on production of certain goods, including low-grade steel, protected british industrial interests. 2.1.iv) the colonial government consistently gave preference to british firms in contracts & procurement. 2.1.v) indian industry received no developmental support or institutional credit infrastructure from the state. the tariff structure told the story most clearly. for most of the 19th century, british textiles entered india virtually duty-free, while indian goods faced prohibitive duties in britain. when a modest import duty on cotton goods was introduced in 1894, the lancashire lobby forced the imposition of a matching countervailing excise duty on indian mill-produced cloth — so that even domestic production received no advantage. (an excise duty on your own country's production, designed to cancel out an import duty on the competitor's goods — that is how far the colonial government was willing to go to protect british industry.) the fiscal autonomy convention after ww1 gave india some tariff-setting power, and the post-cdm period finally brought meaningful protective tariffs — indian capitalists had, through sustained nationalist pressure, secured a concrete economic gain from the inm. even ostensibly pro-worker legislation served british commercial interests. the factory acts of 1881 & 1891 were pushed by the lancashire textile lobby in britain — stricter labour regulations in india raised indian production costs, reducing the competitiveness of indian textiles in global markets. indian capitalists & moderate leaders recognised this & opposed the acts, arguing that india's infant industries needed room to grow before being subjected to the same compliance burden as established british manufacturers. (the british were not regulating indian factories out of sympathy for indian workers — they were regulating them out of fear of indian competition.) ficci (federation of indian chambers of commerce & industry, 1927), set up in 1927, became the organised voice of indian business in making these grievances heard. ficci refused to negotiate with the british government on constitutional or economic issues without the approval or participation of the inc. (think of that for a moment — india's big business lobby had effectively made the inc its political representative. that tells you everything about the relationship between indian capital & the nationalist movement.) 2.2) why were capitalists ambivalent about the inm? despite sharing grievances with the nationalist movement, indian capitalists were never fully comfortable inside it. their ambivalence had clear reasons. mass movements — hartals, strikes, boycotts, processions — disrupted the smooth functioning of industry & trade. a hartal shut down a market. a strike idled a mill. a boycott of british goods was good for indian industry in theory, but the disorder & uncertainty of a mass agitation was bad for business in practice. capitalists wanted protection from british competition; they did not necessarily want revolution. (the difference between wanting a fairer set of rules & wanting to overturn the table entirely — that was the distance between the average indian businessman & the average congress street agitator.) moreover, as the inm became more mass-based & workers & peasants entered it in larger numbers, capitalists faced a new problem: their own workers. the same movement that was fighting british imperialism was also raising questions about labour rights, wages, and working conditions. the rise of aituc (1920), the trade unions act (1926), and the growing communist influence within the labour movement made capitalists anxious. supporting the inm too enthusiastically risked strengthening the very forces that challenged their authority over their own workforce. (this is the dilemma of every propertied class in a revolutionary era: the movement that liberates them from one oppressor might turn around & challenge their own position next.) 2.3) varying positions through the inm: a phase-by-phase view swadeshi movement (1905-11) the swadeshi movement was the moment indian capitalists were most enthusiastically aligned with the inm — because the inm's demand at this stage happened to be exactly what they wanted: buy indian goods, boycott british goods. the swadeshi spirit produced a burst of indian enterprise. pc ray's bengal chemical industries thrived. chidambaram pillai's swadeshi steam navigation company challenged the british shipping monopoly on indian coastal routes. tisco — tata iron & steel company — was set up by jamsetji tata. tilak set up bombay swadeshi stores. lala lajpat rai founded the indian national bank, later the punjab national bank (pnb). (the swadeshi movement was the inm's most capitalist-friendly phase — business & nationalism pointed in the same direction, at least for a while.) :) against worker demands as workers organised & their demands grew, capitalists showed the other side of their ambivalence. the ahmedabad mill strike (1918) is the clearest example. workers demanded better wages & conditions. mill owners, including ambalal sarabhai, resisted. gandhi mediated — and while he sided with the workers on the principle of a living wage, his method of arbitration was specifically designed to prevent class conflict from escalating. the textile labour association (tla, 1920) set up in ahmedabad was explicitly gandhian — non-confrontational, focused on negotiation. for capitalists, gandhi's model of labour relations was the most comfortable version available: workers got some rights, but class war was avoided. (gandhi's trusteeship idea — that owners hold wealth in trust for society — was something indian capitalists could accept. outright nationalisation or workers' control was not.) funding the movement the relationship between indian capitalists & the inm was not only ideological — it was also financial. capitalists like jamnalal bajaj & gd birla were personally close to gandhi & funded his work consistently. bajaj provided land for the sabarmati ashram. birla funded gandhi's activities & hosted him regularly. vaidilal mehta & other businessmen contributed to inc funds across different periods of the movement. (funding gandhi was not purely selfless — a free india under inc leadership was likely to be far better for indian industry than continued british rule. political & business interests aligned, even if imperfectly.) civil disobedience movement (cdm, 1930-34) currency was one grievance that pulled business & the congress together. the high 1s 6d rupee fixed in 1926 (hilton-young commission) suited british exporters but squeezed indian producers. so indian businessmen pressed for a lower 1s 4d rate & set up a currency league in bombay (1926), with the blessings of gandhi & patel. when gandhi made 1s 4d one of his eleven demands (1930 — see ch 41), the businessmen's demand had become the congress's own — the base for the capitalists' active part in cdm. capitalist participation reached a new level during the cdm. for the first time, traders actively stopped importing british cloth — and the results were visible: british cloth imports fell by roughly 50%. this was not purely nationalist sentiment; it was also good business sense, since indian textile mills stood to gain from reduced british competition. capitalists contributed financially to the movement & were part of the inc coalition pressing for constitutional change. however, they consistently opposed the escalation of mass civil disobedience beyond a point. ficci (1927) refused to negotiate with the british on economic issues without congress participation — but it also opposed the forms of mass agitation that threatened property & public order. the line ficci drew was: support the inc politically, but do not let the movement threaten capitalism itself. 2nd round table conference (1931) at the 1st round table conference (1930), ficci boycotted proceedings in solidarity with the inc. at the 2nd round table conference (1931), when gandhi attended, ficci supported congress. this was a concrete political act — india's organised business community publicly standing with the nationalist negotiating team at a constitutional forum. quit india movement (qim, 1942) even during the qim, when the inc had adopted its most confrontational posture, individual businessmen acted with nationalist sentiment. during the second, underground phase of the movement, businessmen donated generously to keep the movement alive. sumati morarjee, a businesswoman, gave achyut patwardhan a different car each day so he could evade detection by the british. these were acts of personal courage, not institutional policy. 2.4) the bombay plan (1944) the most significant intellectual contribution of indian capitalists to the idea of independent india was the bombay plan (1944) — formally titled a plan of economic development for india. it was drafted by eight leading indian industrialists & technocrats: jrd tata, gd birla, purushottamdas thakurdas, ardeshir dalal, kasturbhai lalbhai, ad shroff, lala shri ram, and john mathai. published in january 1944 at the height of the bengal famine (1943) and the qim repression, it was the first ever national economic plan for india. the bombay plan proposed a mixed economy with heavy state investment in basic industries, infrastructure, transportation, power generation, and social welfare — education, housing, healthcare. it called for doubling india's per capita income within 15 years through three five-year plans. (the bombay plan was, in effect, india's leading capitalists telling the future government: we want a planned economy, because we know indian private capital alone cannot build the infrastructure & heavy industry this country needs. the same men who ran cotton mills & steel plants were asking for state intervention in the economy. that is how weak indian capital was relative to the scale of the task.) the plan was widely read, translated into several languages, reprinted multiple times, and endorsed by ficci (1927) at its annual meeting in 1944. its influence on independent india's first five year plan is direct & acknowledged by most historians. ◆ the bombay plan drew criticism from all sides. the left said it did not go far enough & was designed to protect private property. the right said it was socialist & dangerous. the british were stung — the viceroy's office reportedly discussed producing a "rival pamphlet" in response. that it upset everyone roughly equally is perhaps the clearest sign that it was a genuinely centrist document. 2.5) ina trials & the final phase (1945-46) during the ina agitations (1945-46), capitalists & businessmen contributed funds, provided material support, and openly backed the ina men's defence. the ina defence committee raised funds for the trials, with gd birla among the major contributors, while bhulabhai desai led the legal defence at the red fort. even before the trials, indian businessmen in southeast asia — the diaspora merchant communities in malaya, singapore, and burma — had been a major source of funding for the ina & the indian independence league (iil) during the war itself. this was significant — it was one of the first times business leaders openly supported a political movement against the colonial government in a manner that could not be framed as merely self-interested economic lobbying. 2.6) the relationship triangle: capitalists, workers, and peasants the position of indian capitalists within the inm was defined by their relationship with three other groupssimultaneously. with the inc & the moderate leadership, the relationship was comfortable. the moderates believed capitalism would modernise india, opposed factory acts that reduced working hours, and kept the inc away from class conflict. capitalists were natural allies of the moderate position. with the extremists & the gandhian phase, the relationship was more complex but workable. gandhi's model — swadeshi, trusteeship, arbitration — gave capitalists a framework that preserved their position while asking them to behave responsibly toward workers & society. they could live with that. with workers & the left, the relationship was consistently tense. capitalists supported the inm as long as it was fighting the british. they were uncomfortable when the same movement began fighting them. this tension was never fully resolved — and it explains why ficci consistently opposed mass civil disobedience even while politically supporting the inc. with peasants, the relationship was more distant. most large indian capitalists were urban & industrial. the agrarian question — zamindari abolition, debt relief, land redistribution — was not their cause. they watched the peasant movements of the 1930s with the same anxiety they watched the labour movement: too much social disruption was bad for stability, and stability was what business required. 2.7) assessment the topper answer quoted in the question captures the essential truth well: indian capitalists remained ambivalent in their support for the inm throughout. but ambivalence is not the same as absence. they contributed financially, they boycotted british goods at critical moments, they stood with the inc at constitutional conferences, they produced the bombay plan (1944) as a vision for an independent indian economy, and individual capitalists took personal risks during the qim. their contribution to the inm was real — it was simply conditional. they supported the movement against british imperialism. they resisted the movement when it pointed its energy at indian property & indian capital. the two positions coexisted, without contradiction, in the same set of men throughout the entire period. (◆ in post-independence india, this ambivalence found its resolution — partly. indian capitalism survived independence & thrived under the mixed economy framework the bombay plan had itself proposed. the state took over heavy industry; private capital took consumer industry. it was, in its own way, the deal indian capitalists had been seeking all along: freedom from british competition, protection from socialist expropriation, and a state large enough to build the infrastructure they could not.)

sections.chapterTitle: Many Voices of the Nation: Workers, Capitalists, Dalits, Women, Peasants
sections.title: The Voice of Dalits
sections.norm: the voice of dalits. 3.1) how did dalit movements operate? not a single organised force denied an entire section of humanity symbolic direct action gopal baba walangkar 3.2) vaikom satyagraha (1924-25) vaikom satyagraha (1924-25) first major organised temple-entry movement ezhava community narayan guru & k. kesava menon public roads near the vaikom temple all-india movement periyar — ev ramaswamy naicker 1925 compromise 3.3) the self-respect movement (1925) periyar founded the self-respect movement rejected caste hierarchy self-respect marriages 3.4) guruvayur satyagraha (1931-33) guruvayur satyagraha (1931-33) k. kellapan fast unto death ak gopalan royal proclamation opening all temples 3.5) dr br ambedkar: a different path dr br ambedkar more confrontational, more political, and more radical mahad satyagraha, 1927 right to draw water from a public tank led the dalits physically to the tank publicly burnt the manusmriti most powerful symbolic acts boycott temples altogether no solution within hinduism education & political power reservation in education, government jobs, and political representation 3.6) why were dalits alienated from the inc? not accidental deep structural roots dominated by upper castes hardened caste lines 1886 policy systematically excluded gandhi upheld the varnashrama system until the 1940s moral & religious did not empower them politically or economically nehru refused to recognise caste as a political problem 3.7) gandhi vs ambedkar on varna: the fundamental divide (pyq: mains 2015) not merely political — it was philosophical reform from within varna system was fundamentally sound corruption of varna into caste moral persuasion annihilation logical consequence oppressive by design destroy the authority of the shastras exit hinduism altogether 3.8) the organisations & the political battle all india depressed classes association (aidca, 1926) mc rajah all india depressed classes congress (aidcc, 1930) anti-inc in orientation appeared before the simon commission demanded separate electorates for dalits ambedkar participated decisive confrontation dalits were hindus never be able to elect genuine dalit representatives the communal award (august 1932) ramsay macdonald sided with ambedkar fast unto death from jail the poona pact (september 1932) joint electorates instead of separate ones number of reserved seats was actually increased harijan campaign other inc leaders were largely indifferent inc won only half of the reserved dalit seats 3.9) ambedkar's political organisations independent labour party (ilp, 1936) merge the politics of class & caste won most reserved seats in bombay labour minister all india scheduled castes federation (aiscf, 1942) dalits are distinct from hindus struggled to hold its ground formed late marginalised 3.10) the final chapter: co-option, the constitution, and the break co-opted ambedkar chairman of its constitution drafting committee untouchability was made illegal under article 17 law minister hindu code bill inc r. 3.1) how did dalit movements operate? dalit movements in colonial india were not a single organised force. they were a collection of local struggles, regional assertions, and gradually a national political voice — all driven by one central fact: that the indian caste system had, for centuries, denied an entire section of humanity the most basic dignities of life. the methods these movements used reflected both their defiance & their constraints. one form of resistance was symbolic — dalits wearing the sacred thread, participating in community pujas, performing rituals that upper-caste hindus had claimed as exclusively their own. (think of what this meant: not just a religious act, but a direct statement that we are equal human beings & will act like it.) another was direct action — forcing entry into temples from which they were barred. both forms were visible, confrontational, and deliberate. one of the earliest dalit pioneers was gopal baba walangkar, a mahar ex-soldier. in 1888 he started vital-vidhvansak ('destroyer of ceremonial pollution') — the first monthly journal aimed at the untouchable community, well before ambedkar's generation. 3.2) vaikom satyagraha (1924-25) the vaikom satyagraha (1924-25) in travancore was the first major organised temple-entry movement of the modern period. it was led by the ezhava community, with narayan guru & k. kesava menon at the forefront. the immediate demand was the right to use public roads near the vaikom temple — roads that were officially prohibited to lower castes. what started as a local struggle became an all-india movement. people came from across the country to join or support the satyagrahis. among them was periyar — ev ramaswamy naicker — who would go on to become the most radical voice of dravidian anti-caste politics. the inc formally supported the satyagraha. savarnas — upper castes — boycotted avarnas & pro-satyagraha congressmen in response. gandhi visited in 1925 & met the queen of travancore, which eventually led to a compromise: some roads near the temple were opened to avarnas, others remained reserved for savarnas, and some temple gates remained closed to lower castes. (a compromise, yes — but a partial one. the fundamental principle of equality was acknowledged, but not yet enforced fully. half a win is still a win when you started with nothing. :)) 3.3) the self-respect movement (1925) in 1925, periyar founded the self-respect movement in the madras presidency — a direct assault on brahminical social dominance. the movement rejected caste hierarchy, denounced brahminical rituals, and promoted self-respect marriages — weddings conducted without brahmin priests, without sanskrit mantras, as a practical demonstration that social life did not require upper-caste intermediaries. the self-respect movement was not merely about religious reform; it was an assertion that lower-caste communities could define their own dignity, their own ceremonies, and their own social rules. (pyq: prelims 2019. the self-respect movement is a recurring exam favourite — remember the link between periyar's participation in the vaikom satyagraha & his founding of this movement in the very same year.) 3.4) guruvayur satyagraha (1931-33) the guruvayur satyagraha (1931-33) took the temple-entry demand further. guruvayur is in malabar — in what is today thrissur district of kerala — and the guruvayur temple was one of the most important krishna temples in south india. k. kellapan led a march to the temple for temple entry & went on a fast unto death. he broke his fast only on gandhi's personal appeal. ak gopalan — later a major communist leader — walked across malabar on foot as part of the agitation. the pressure continued until 1936, when the king of travancore issued a royal proclamation opening all temples in travancore to all hindus regardless of caste. (1936 — the same year the inc held its faizpur session & aiks (1936) was founded. one india, many struggles, all running simultaneously.) 3.5) dr br ambedkar: a different path the figure who most fundamentally challenged both the caste system & the inc's approach to it was dr br ambedkar. his path was distinct from the temple-entry movements — more confrontational, more political, and more radical in its conclusions. in 1927, ambedkar organised a massive satyagraha of 15,000 dalits in mahad, maharashtra (mahad satyagraha, 1927), asserting the right to draw water from a public tank. the colonial administration had technically granted this right, but the upper-caste community had refused to accept it. ambedkar led the dalits physically to the tank & drew water — a simple act that was, in practice, a revolution. (you have water. everyone needs water. and yet, for centuries, an entire community had been denied the right to touch public water. let that land for a moment. :( ) in december 1927, at the same mahad conference, ambedkar publicly burnt the manusmriti — the ancient hindu legal text that had codified caste hierarchy & the subjugation of dalits & women. it was one of the most powerful symbolic acts of the entire colonial period. by 1934, however, ambedkar had reached a sharper conclusion. when temple-entry satyagrahis were agitating at the kalaram temple in nasik, ambedkar asked them to stop — and instead boycott temples altogether. his reasoning was blunt: there is no solution within hinduism. seeking entry into the very system that had created the injustice was not the path forward. the solution lay in education & political power. and the compensation for centuries of oppression was non-negotiable — reservation in education, government jobs, and political representation. (ambedkar & gandhi agreed on the goal of dalit dignity. they disagreed completely on how to get there. gandhi wanted hinduism reformed from within. ambedkar did not believe hinduism could reform itself. this was not a small difference — it was a fundamental one.) 3.6) why were dalits alienated from the inc? the alienation of dalits from the inc was not accidental. it had deep structural roots. the bengal renaissance of the 19th century — the great flowering of indian social thought — was dominated by upper castes. its concerns were largely upper-caste concerns. the hindu revivalism of the 1870s & 1880s hardened caste lines rather than softened them. and the inc's own 1886 policy of not taking up social questions — designed to prevent class & caste conflicts from fracturing the national coalition — meant that dalit grievances were systematically excluded from the national agenda for decades. by 1920, it was too late to easily undo this damage. gandhi, despite his genuine personal commitment to dalit dignity, upheld the varnashrama system until the 1940s. his approach was moral & religious: ask hindus to do penance, glorify the work of sweepers, make untouchability socially unacceptable. this dignified dalits in a certain way. but it did not empower them politically or economically. (ambedkar's critique was precise: gandhi's approach treated dalits as objects of upper-caste compassion rather than as agents of their own liberation.) nehru, for his part, refused to recognise caste as a political problem — seeing it as a social question that would dissolve with modernisation & economic development. (both gandhi & nehru, in their different ways, sidestepped the direct political confrontation with caste that ambedkar demanded. one offered religion. the other offered economics. neither offered power.) 3.7) gandhi vs ambedkar on varna: the fundamental divide (pyq: mains 2015) the disagreement between gandhi & ambedkar was not merely political — it was philosophical, and it went to the root of how each understood caste, hinduism, and the path to dalit emancipation. gandhi's position was reform from within. he held that the varna system was fundamentally sound — a division of labour sanctioned by hindu tradition that, in its ideal form, assigned dignity to all occupations without hierarchy. what had gone wrong, in gandhi's view, was the corruption of varna into caste — the addition of untouchability, pollution norms, and hereditary exclusion that had no sanction in the original scriptures. his remedy was moral persuasion: upper-caste hindus must do penance, open their temples & wells, treat dalits as equals — not because the law forced them to, but because their own religion demanded it. gandhi believed hinduism could reform itself, and that the initiative must come from within the hindu fold. ambedkar's position was annihilation. he argued that caste was not a corruption of varna but its logical consequence — that the hierarchical ordering of communities, the prohibition on inter-dining & inter-marriage, and the sanctioning of untouchability were all built into the structure of the hindu shastras themselves. there was no "pure varna" to return to; the system was oppressive by design. his remedy was therefore radically different: destroy the authority of the shastras, enact statutory safeguards — reservation, legal prohibition of untouchability, constitutional rights — and, if hinduism could not accommodate equality, exit hinduism altogether. moral persuasion, ambedkar held, was useless against a system sustained not by individual cruelty but by scriptural authority & institutional power. (the distance between these two positions was not bridgeable. gandhi said: change the heart. ambedkar said: change the law, because the heart will not change on its own. one trusted religion. the other trusted the state. independent india, through the constitution, largely adopted ambedkar's institutional approach — article 17, reservation, the scheduled castes order — while continuing to invoke gandhi's moral language. the tension between the two remains alive.) 3.8) the organisations & the political battle in 1926, the all india depressed classes association (aidca, 1926) was formed under mc rajah of madras. in 1930, ambedkar formed the all india depressed classes congress (aidcc, 1930) — explicitly anti-inc in orientation & designed to negotiate with the british directly as a distinct political voice. in 1928, ambedkar appeared before the simon commission (1927-29) and demanded separate electorates for dalits — the same mechanism that had been granted to muslims in the indian councils act (1909) and that the inc had accepted for muslims in the lucknow pact (1916). (ambedkar was not asking for anything that had not already been given to others. but when a dalit asked, the inc's response was very different.) at the 1st round table conference (1930) — which the inc boycotted — ambedkar participated & again demanded separate electorates. at the 2nd round table conference (1931), the decisive confrontation came: gandhi versus ambedkar on the question of separate electorates for dalits. gandhi argued that dalits were hindus & should not be separated from the hindu electorate — that it would permanently divide hindu society. ambedkar argued that without separate electorates, dalits would always be dependent on upper-caste hindu voters & would never be able to elect genuine dalit representatives. the communal award (august 1932), issued by british prime minister ramsay macdonald, sided with ambedkar — granting dalits reserved seats through separate electorates. gandhi responded with a fast unto death from jail. (gandhi's fast was not against dalit rights per se — he explicitly supported reservation. his objection was to separate electorates, which he believed would permanently divide hindus. but the political effect of the fast was to put enormous moral pressure on ambedkar to surrender the separate electorate demand. ambedkar described signing the poona pact as one of the worst days of his life.) the poona pact (september 1932) resolved the crisis: dalits retained reserved seats, but with joint electorates instead of separate ones. the number of reserved seats was actually increased under the poona pact compared to the communal award — but the crucial instrument of electoral independence was gone. this reservation structure was formalised in the government of india act (1935). post poona pact, gandhi launched his harijan campaign — touring the country, opening wells & temples to dalits, raising funds for dalit welfare. it was sincere. but other inc leaders were largely indifferent. nehru refused to recognise caste as a political problem. the result was visible in hard numbers: in the 1937 provincial elections, the inc won only half of the reserved dalit seats. the inc governments (1937-39) did not meaningfully work for dalit interests in the provinces they governed. 3.9) ambedkar's political organisations in 1936, ambedkar formed the independent labour party (ilp, 1936), designed to bring together poor workers & untouchables — an attempt to merge the politics of class & caste into a single movement. (this was a significant analytical insight: the poorest industrial workers & the most oppressed caste group were, in many cases, the same people. merging their struggles made both logical & political sense.) the ilp won most reserved seats in bombay in the 1937 elections. in 1942, ambedkar became labour minister in the viceroy's executive council — working within the colonial administration. in the same year, just a few days before the quit india movement (qim, 1942), he formed the all india scheduled castes federation (aiscf, 1942), with the explicit motto that dalits are distinct from hindus. but after the qim, the aiscf struggled to hold its ground. many dalits were personally followers of gandhi & were swept up in the tide of mass nationalism. the aiscf was formed late & had a weak organisational structure. communists actively eroded its support base among poorer dalits. in the 1946 elections, like every minor political party, the aiscf was marginalised by the dominant contest between the inc & the muslim league (ml, 1906), with the qim legacy, ina trials, and the pakistan demand consuming all political oxygen. 3.10) the final chapter: co-option, the constitution, and the break after the 1946 elections, the inc co-opted ambedkar — in the most consequential possible way. he was made a member of the constituent assembly & then chairman of its constitution drafting committee. the man the inc had opposed at the round table conferences was now tasked with writing the constitution of independent india. untouchability was made illegal under article 17. ambedkar became law minister in nehru's cabinet. but the fundamental disagreement remained. when ambedkar introduced the hindu code bill — a sweeping reform of hindu personal law covering inheritance, marriage, divorce, and property rights for women — the inc refused to support it. (the party that had spoken for decades about social equality could not pass a law reforming hindu personal law when it actually held power. the upper-caste majority within the inc was not ready for it.) ambedkar resigned from the cabinet in 1951. five years later, in october 1956, just one & a half months before his death, he converted to buddhism along with 3.8 lakh followers — his final statement that there was no solution within hinduism, and no political home within the inc. ⚠ alert: dalit voices pyq cluster (sec. 3). prelims 2013 (ambedkar's mahad satyagraha 1927 — public water access at chavdar tank); prelims 2021 (periyar ev ramasamy — self-respect movement, tamil nadu); prelims 2025 (ambedkar's constitutional contributions + round table conference depressed classes representation). full stems & options in companion appendix pyq.

sections.chapterTitle: Many Voices of the Nation: Workers, Capitalists, Dalits, Women, Peasants
sections.title: The Voice of Women
sections.norm: the voice of women. 4.1) why did the 19th-century reform movement not produce women leaders? talked about women did not talk with women subject of reform, not its participants hindu revivalism had pushed back purdah spread 4.2) women's education: who wanted it & why not altruistic raise pro-western children educated companion barometer of civilisation all male agendas on terms defined by men bethune school (1849) drinkwater bethune hunter commission (1882) social stereotyping two women challenged the framework itself. tarabai shinde comparison between women & men (1882) pativrata pandita ramabai refused the new model married a sudra man converted to christianity 4.3) the economic dimension not only cultural — it was also economic paid lower wages craft & cottage industries withdrawal of women from labour 4.4) women & the inm: participation without power the inc until 1917 did not take up social questions symbolic roles sarala debi chaudhrani physical culture movement support roles invisible & uncredited annie besant sarojini naidu right to vote for women president of the inc — the first woman 4.5) gandhi & women: a transformation changed the terms more than any other single factor no longer required physical strength courage, discipline, and willingness to suffer negated the centrality used religion to mobilise women sita, draupadi spin the charkha & picket liquor shops greater strength of soul the results were visible across movements: specific call to women joined boycotts & swadeshi activities basanti devi bi amman lifting purdah thousands of women joined chittagong revolutionary group under surya sen never involved women in decision-making 4.6) women's organisations independent of the inc bharat stree mandal (1910) aiwc, 1927 margaret cousins nationalist first, feminist second 4.7) legislative progress right to vote reserved seats in legislatures universal adult franchise the sarda act (1929) child marriage restraint act 14 for girls 4.8) the 1940s: the final phase great participation by women lifting of the ban on the cpi1925 mahila atmaraksha samiti (1942) famine relief work the tebhaga movement (1946) two-thirds of their produce dalit & tribal women 1,500 women joined the rani jhansi regiment imphal campaign (1944) 4.9) the honest assessment fought more for nationalism than for their own rights low priority still unfinished ncm cdm ww1 communist party of india 1925. 4.1) why did the 19th-century reform movement not produce women leaders? the bengal renaissance & the social reform movements of the 19th century talked a great deal about women. they passed laws against sati, for widow remarriage, for women's education. but they talked about women — they did not talk with women, or for women as agents of their own lives. women were the subject of reform, not its participants. by the end of the 19th century, hindu revivalism had pushed back against even these limited reforms. conservatism reasserted itself on women's questions. purdah spread — not only among muslims but increasingly among hindu upper-caste families too, as a marker of respectability & caste status. (sanskritisation — the process by which lower castes adopted upper-caste customs to improve their social standing — actually hurt the freedom of lower-caste women. purity of women became a symbol of caste honour. widow remarriage, which lower-caste communities had practised, was given up. women's freedom contracted as caste aspiration rose.) 4.2) women's education: who wanted it & why the british interest in women's education was not altruistic. they wanted english-educated women who would raise pro-western children — and by keeping women in the domestic sphere, they hoped to prevent women from joining the inm. the indian bhadralok — the educated middle class — wanted an educated companion, a wife who could participate in refined social life. social reformers wanted to counter the british civilisational critique that indian society was backward, since the status of women was used as a barometer of civilisation. these were all male agendas. women's education grew, but on terms defined by men. the bethune school (1849), established by drinkwater bethune — the law member of the governor-general's council, with special interest from dalhousie — was a landmark in women's formal education. the hunter commission (1882) provided liberal grants & scholarships for women's education. but social stereotyping remained a massive barrier. two women challenged the framework itself. tarabai shinde published comparison between women & men (1882) — a fierce argument that men enjoyed all rights while women were reduced to the stereotype of the pativrata, the devoted wife who exists only in service to her husband. pandita ramabai went further still. a brahmin woman, she refused the new model being offered — the educated but obedient wife. she stayed unmarried for years, then married a sudra man, was widowed, went to england to study medicine, converted to christianity, went to the united states & raised funds for a widow's home in bombay. she was criticised not just by traditionalists but by the very reformers who claimed to support women. (a woman who converted, crossed caste lines in marriage, and asked foreigners for money to help indian widows — she was too much even for the progressives. :) ) 4.3) the economic dimension women's confinement was not only cultural — it was also economic, and industrial change made it worse. as men migrated to factories in cities, women were left behind in villages, tied to agricultural labour but with no formal economic participation or recognition. in the factories themselves, women were paid lower wages because of the gender stereotype that their primary skills were domestic. when mechanisation arrived, it displaced women's traditional craft & cottage industries more than men's, since mills were dominated by male labour. economic prosperity — when it came to peasant families — often manifested as the withdrawal of women from labour, since confinement to the home was a sign of status. (so economic development, in this context, actually reduced women's participation in public life. a family got richer & the first thing it did was put the women behind closed doors. :( ) 4.4) women & the inm: participation without power the inc until 1917 did not take up social questions at all — and women's questions were social questions. when women appeared in early nationalist movements, they were cast in symbolic roles: keepers of the household, guardians of swadeshi, boycotters of foreign goods. during the swadeshi movement (1905-11), the focus on "mother india" kept women's participation in stereotyped domestic activities. there was one notable exception: sarala debi chaudhrani, who was involved in the physical culture movement for bengal's youth — training young men in martial exercises, a decidedly unfeminine activity by the standards of the time. in the revolutionary activities too, women's roles were support roles — giving shelter, acting as couriers, passing messages. brave & dangerous work, but invisible & uncredited. post ww1 , two women emerged as significant national figures: annie besant, already central to the home rule league movement (hrl, 1916-18), and sarojini naidu. in 1917, sarojini naidu led a delegation to the secretary of state demanding the right to vote for women. the goi act (1919) did give women the right to vote — though subject to property qualifications. she then demanded equal eligibility criteria for voting rights within the inc in 1918. in 1925, she was elected president of the inc — the first woman to hold that position. 4.5) gandhi & women: a transformation gandhi's arrival changed the terms of women's participation in the inm — more than any other single factor. his focus on non-violence & moral authority was crucial. the inm under gandhi no longer required physical strength — it required courage, discipline, and willingness to suffer. these were qualities that could not be denied to women on the grounds of physical weakness. gandhi shifted the symbolic frame: from "motherhood" — passive, domestic, protective — to "sisterhood" — active, equal participants in a shared struggle. in doing so, he negated the centrality of women's sexuality to their public role, which had been the main mechanism of their exclusion. he used religion to mobilise women — invoking sita, draupadi, and other models of courage & independent virtue, figures that indian men could not object to without contradicting their own values. he told women they had a duty to look after the home — but also to spin the charkha & picket liquor shops. men & women were equal, he said, but had different roles. women were physically weaker but had greater strength of soul. (this was a carefully constructed argument. by not challenging gender roles directly, gandhi disarmed the opposition of indian men — and got millions of women into the street. strategically brilliant. philosophically limited.) the results were visible across movements: 4.5.i) rowlatt satyagraha (1919): gandhi gave a specific call to women to participate for the first time. 4.5.ii) ncm (1920-22): women joined boycotts & swadeshi activities. they agitated against the visit of the prince of wales in november 1921. basanti devi, wife of cr das, courted arrest in december 1921. muslim women joined the khilafat movement — the most remarkable moment being bi amman, mother of the ali brothers (shaukat ali & mohammad ali), who addressed public crowds for the first time in her life, lifting purdah, addressing the crowds as her children. 4.5.iii) cdm (1930-34): thousands of women joined. everyone was shocked by the scale. the chittagong revolutionary group under surya sen also included women participants. but a sharp contradiction persisted throughout. the inc never involved women in decision-making. it never took up women's issues as political demands. sarala debi chaudhrani captured this precisely: "the inc wants women only to be lawbreakers, not lawmakers." 4.6) women's organisations women's organisations began emerging in the 1900s, independent of the inc. sarala debi chaudhrani established the bharat stree mandal (1910), opening branches across india to promote women's education. the most significant organisation was the all india women's conference (aiwc, 1927), founded under margaret cousins, an irish feminist. unlike the inc, the aiwc took up women's issues directly: promoting women's education, lobbying for political rights, marriage reforms, and rights for women workers. its methods were moderate — lobbying & petitions rather than mass agitation. it placed the inm before women's issues. women's organisations in this period were nationalist first, feminist second. 4.7) legislative progress from 1921 to 1930, several provincial legislatures used powers given by the goi act (1919) to grant women the right to vote — though subject to property qualifications. the goi act (1935) extended the right to vote to more women & gave them reserved seats in legislatures. women leaders were not satisfied with reservation — they wanted universal adult franchise, which would make reservation unnecessary. that came only with the constitution of 1950. the sarda act (1929) — formally the child marriage restraint act — set minimum ages of marriage at 14 for girlsand 18 for males. in the 1930s, bills on property rights, inheritance, divorce, dowry, and prostitution were passed in central & provincial legislatures. 4.8) the 1940s: the final phase the quit india movement (qim, 1942) saw great participation by women, especially in rural areas. the lifting of the ban on the cpi1925 in 1942 also aided women's political participation, since many women had been cpi1925 members since the 1920s & 1930s. in bengal in 1942, leftist women leaders organised the mahila atmaraksha samiti (1942)and did famine relief work during the devastating bengal famine (1943). the tebhaga movement (1946) in bengal — sharecroppers demanding two-thirds of their produce — saw high participation by dalit & tribal women, who fought the british & sacrificed lives in what became a violent resistance. (the women who participated in tebhaga were not doing so for abstract nationalism. they were fighting for the rice that fed their children. their courage was economic & visceral — the most honest kind.) in the ina, 1,500 women joined the rani jhansi regiment & fought in the imphal campaign (1944). women also participated in the muslim league's pakistan campaign in the 1940s. 4.9) the honest assessment overall, women fought more for nationalism than for their own rights. the movements that brought millions of women into the street did so largely by asking them to serve a national cause — not by addressing the specific conditions of their lives. the inc took women's participation gratefully & gave women's issues a low priority in return. independence came in 1947. the constitution of 1950 gave women full political equality. but the social & economic transformation that tarabai shinde & pandita ramabai had demanded in the 1880s is still unfinished. (◆ there is a thread that runs from the bengal renaissance through the swadeshi movement through gandhi's ncm through the cdm through independence & into the present: every time indian society faced a crisis, women were called upon to sacrifice. every time the crisis passed, their own demands were deferred. the women of the rani jhansi regiment fought in burma. the women of the tebhaga movement died in bengal. the women who picketed liquor shops were arrested & jailed. they fought for a nation. whether the nation fought for them with equal commitment is a different question — one that independent india is still answering.)

sections.chapterTitle: Many Voices of the Nation: Workers, Capitalists, Dalits, Women, Peasants
sections.title: Peasant Movements (1930s–1940s)
