the aiks 800,000 by 1939 had outgrown the inc 5.6) the 1940s: war, quit india, and the peasant upsurge cpi took increasing organisational control mass organisation of the communist party left the aiks requisitioning of grain forced procurement bengal famine of 1943 peasantry was its backbone soul of the quit india movement parallel governments nationalist outburst class struggle politically radicalised, economically desperate, and organisationally experienced wave of post-war peasant uprisings 5.7) post-war peasant movements (1945–1951) 5.7.1) the worli uprising (maharashtra, 1945–1947) worlis veth begar godavari parulekar refused to perform forced labour yield by 1947 5.7.2) the bakasht land re-occupations (bihar, 1946–1947) second, more intense phase in 1946-47 restoration of their hereditary tenancy rights direct action bihar bakasht disputes settlement act in 1947 5.7.3) the punnapra-vayalar uprising (kerala, 1946) princely state of travancore sir c.p. ramaswami iyer declare travancore an independent state october 1946 1,000 peasants & workers we. 5.1) why did peasants become more radical in the 1930s? peasant movements in the 1920s were mostly local — one district, one landlord, one specific grievance. even the most organised of them, like the bardoli satyagraha of 1928, stayed within the gandhian framework of negotiation & arbitration. the 1930s were different. peasant movements became larger, more ideologically aware, and more nationally networked. three things drove this change. first, the great depression hit indian agriculture hard. between 1929 & 1933, agricultural prices fell by roughly half. a farmer who sold grain at rs 10 a year earlier was now getting rs 5. but the rent he owed the zamindar did not fall. the land revenue he owed the colonial government did not fall. the debt he owed the moneylender did not fall. income fell by half; obligations stayed the same. the result was mass debt, and for many families, loss of land altogether. (think of it this way: global commodity prices collapsed because of events in new york & london — events that a farmer in up or bihar had no role in, no knowledge of, and no protection against. yet he paid the full price.) second, the civil disobedience movement (cdm) of 1930-34 had pulled the peasantry into active politics. no-tax campaigns, no-rent campaigns, refusal to pay land revenue — these were not just economic acts but political ones. peasants who had participated in the cdm were politically awake by the time it was withdrawn in 1934. the withdrawal was the inc's decision, made for reasons of strategy. but for the rural masses, it felt like the movement had been pulled away just as it was finding its feet. they were now politically conscious but organisationally homeless. that gap was waiting to be filled. third, the left moved in. the congress socialist party (csp), formed in 1934, and the communist party of india (cpi) both invested heavily in rural organisation during this decade. they gave the peasant movement an ideological framework — not just "reduce my rent" but "the zamindari system itself must go" — and the organisational skills to build at scale. 5.2) the all india kisan sabha (aiks), 1936 the institutional result of all this was the all india kisan sabha (aiks), founded in lucknow on 11 april 1936, timed to coincide with the inc session that year. swami sahajanand saraswati of bihar became its first president, and ng ranga its first general secretary. the kisan manifesto of august 1936 stated the demands clearly: abolish the zamindari system, tax agricultural wealth on a graduated scale, cancel the hereditary debts of peasants, and grant occupancy rights to tenants. (occupancy rights means the legal right to stay on & till a piece of land — without it, a tenant could be evicted at the zamindar's will at any time.) these demands went well beyond what the inc was ready to adopt as official policy. the aiks developed strong regional centres. in bihar, the movement was the most militant, and its central fight was over bakasht lands. (bakasht lands were tenant plots that zamindars had seized during the depression years when tenants fell into debt & could not pay rent. the zamindar took back the land, and the tenant who had tilled it for years — sometimes for generations — was left with nothing. :() (see sections 4 & 7 for the two phases of this struggle)sahajanand saraswati led the bihar provincial kisan sabha (bpks), which he had originally founded in 1929, and it became the most organised & aggressive arm of the peasant movement in bihar. in andhra, ng ranga led agitation against the zamindari system & proposals to hike revenue assessments. bengal deserves a separate note. the peasant cause there was channelled largely through a different vehicle — the krishak praja party (kpp), founded by ak fazlul huq in 1936. (the kpp was not part of the aiks structure — it was an independent political party specific to bengal, particularly east bengal, representing the interests of muslim peasants against largely hindu zamindars & moneylenders.) the kpp demanded abolition of zamindari, debt relief, and an end to the permanent settlement. it performed well in the 1937 elections, winning 36 seats in the bengal assembly, though it later formed a coalition with the muslim league rather than with the inc. 5.3) the inc & the peasant movement: alliance that got complicated the relationship between the aiks & the inc in the 1930s started as a genuine working alliance — and the intellectual groundwork for it had been laid earlier. at the karachi session of march 1931, presided over by sardar patel & with the resolution drafted by nehru, the inc for the first time defined what swaraj would actually mean for the masses. the resolution declared that political freedom must include real economic freedom — and it backed this with concrete demands: substantial reduction of land revenue & rent, relief for uneconomic holdings, cancellation of agricultural debt, a living wage for workers, and state ownership of key industries. (this was the first time the inc told the peasant & the worker specifically what independence would do for them — not just that the british would leave, but what would change in their lives. the colonial government was alarmed enough by its near-socialist content to spread rumours that communist money had secretly reached karachi. :))these commitments gave the inc real credibility with the rural masses going into the 1930s. building on this, the faizpur session of 1936 was the first ever inc session held in a village — a deliberate symbolic act signalling the party's orientation toward the peasantry. the aiks & inc held a joint meeting there, and kisan demands substantially shaped the inc's manifesto for the 1937 provincial elections. the result was a strong inc performance, winning clear majorities in most provinces. (the inc did not win everywhere — it fell short of majorities in bengal, punjab, assam, sindh, and the nwfp. but in the provinces it did win, it won convincingly.) then the inc formed governments — and everything got more complicated. 5.4) congress ministries (1937-39): from agitation to administration the 28-month period of inc provincial rule from 1937 to 1939 was the inc's first real experience of governing. and governing is not the same as protesting. protest has one job: apply pressure. governing has many jobs at once — and they pull in different directions. the inc was a coalition of many classes. its voters included peasants & workers, but also lawyers & professionals, indian merchants & industrialists, and in many regions zamindars who were themselves part of the nationalist movement. all of them had voted inc. all of them now expected something in return. in bihar & up, the congress ministries passed agrarian legislation that tried to find a middle ground. they did not immediately abolish zamindari. (abolishing zamindari overnight would mean extinguishing millions of legal property rights at once, without a replacement system in place & ready to function. the risk of agrarian chaos was real — and a government that creates chaos cannot govern.) instead, they passed incremental laws: some relief for tenants in arrears, some protection against arbitrary eviction, some reduction in rent burdens. the bakasht agitation in bihar brought this tension to its sharpest point. under the bihar provincial kisan sabha, peasants launched satyagrahas to reclaim lands seized by zamindars — physically entering disputed fields & harvesting crops. the congress ministry under sri krishna sinha worked out a negotiated settlement between tenants & zamindars — a compromise that returned a portion of the seized land to tenants while giving zamindars legal stability over their remaining claims. the outcome was weighted: the tenant got partial restoration of what had been taken from him by force; the zamindar got legal protection of what he still held. when the kisan sabha continued with agitations that were turning volatile, the congress ministry did what every government must eventually do: it used the police to control the situation. by august 1939, a combination of concessions, legislation, and the arrest of around 600 activists had brought the agitation under control. rahul sankrityayan — scholar, communist, and one of the most prominent peasant leaders in bihar — was among those arrested during the congress ministry period for organising a satyagraha. (sankrityayan's more famous imprisonment — two years in hazaribagh jail — came in 1940, after the congress ministries had already resigned in october 1939. that later arrest was under british authority, not the congress government.) the left called the congress ministry's handling of bakasht a betrayal. the more balanced reading is that the inc was facing the basic problem of all democratic governance: you are elected by groups with conflicting interests, and you cannot fully satisfy one without shortchanging another. (this is not a colonial-era dilemma — it is the permanent condition of any government in a society with economic inequality. it did not disappear after 1947.) 5.5) the split: inc steps back, cpi steps in at the haripura session of 1938, presided over by subhas chandra bose, the inc passed a formal resolution on kisan sabhas. it reaffirmed the right of peasants to organise — but stated clearly that the congress could not associate itself with any activities incompatible with its basic principles, and would not permit congressmen who were kisan sabha members to create an atmosphere hostile to congress policy. provincial congress committees were directed to take suitable action wherever necessary. (the resolution was rushed through with very little discussion. supporters of the kisan sabha who had come prepared for a real debate left disappointed. the inc had drawn its line — quietly, but firmly.) peasant activists now had a choice to make: stay within the constitutional, moderate framework of the inc, or pursue the militant, class-based path of the aiks. many chose the aiks — and the cpi, which had been working inside both the csp & the aiks, moved steadily into the organisational space the inc had vacated. despite the haripura resolution, the aiks continued to expand rapidly, reaching a membership of over 800,000 by 1939. by the close of the 1930s, the peasant movement had outgrown the inc's tent — what happened next would be shaped not by congress resolutions but by a world war. 5.6) the 1940s: war, quit india, and the peasant upsurge the organisational drift that began in the late 1930s accelerated sharply once war broke out. as congress provincial leaders stepped back from radical agrarian politics, the cpi took increasing organisational control of the aiks. by the early 1940s, the aiks had changed from a broad peasant front allied with the inc into, in practical terms, a mass organisation of the communist party. sahajanand saraswati himself, and ng ranga, eventually left the aiks as they found it impossible to address peasants while following the cpi's pro-british "people's war" line after 1941. meanwhile, the ww2 made things dramatically worse for rural india. wartime requisitioning of grain, forced procurement at below-market prices, rampant inflation, and severe food shortages pushed the peasantry to the edge. the bengal famine of 1943 was the most catastrophic expression of this crisis, but distress was not limited to bengal — across provinces, the rural poor bore the heaviest burden of a war they had no part in choosing. (link ch45 — bengal famine) into this pressure cooker came the quit india movement of 1942. with the entire inc leadership arrested within hours of the august 8 resolution, the movement was carried forward by the masses themselves — and the peasantry was its backbone. historians widely argue that peasants were the soul of the quit india movement: they cut telegraph lines, disrupted rail communications, attacked police stations, and in several districts established parallel governments (the satara prati sarkar, the ballia & midnapore uprisings being the most famous). for the rural poor, qim was simultaneously a nationalist outburst — a vent for anti-british fury built up over years of exploitation — and a class struggle, since the colonial revenue machinery, the zamindar's rent collector, and the moneylender's account book were all part of the same oppressive system. the two impulses fused: attacking british authority & attacking feudal extraction felt like the same act. (link ch44 — quit india movement) the war years thus produced a peasantry that was politically radicalised, economically desperate, and organisationally experienced. when the war ended in 1945, this energy did not dissipate — it exploded into a wave of post-war peasant uprisings across the country. these movements were often organised locally by kisan sabha cadres or left organisers, but at their core they represented the organic, desperate demand of the rural poor to shatter british-backed feudalism & enter a free india with dignity. 5.7) post-war peasant movements (1945–1951) 5.7.1) the worli uprising (maharashtra, 1945–1947) the worlis were a impoverished tribal community in the thane district of bombay presidency. under british administration, local landlords, moneylenders, and forest contractors treated them virtually as bonded labour. the central grievance was veth begar — forced, unpaid labour extracted by landlords, accompanied by physical abuse & starvation wages. in 1945, finding a voice through organisers like godavari parulekar, the tribal peasants launched a massive, unified strike — they simply refused to perform forced labour. despite brutal crackdowns by british police, the worlis' unprecedented solidarity forced the landlords to yield by 1947, successfully restoring their human dignity. 5.7.2) the bakasht land re-occupations (bihar, 1946–1947) the bakasht struggle in bihar, which had its roots in the 1930s agitation (sec. 5.4), entered a second, more intense phase in 1946-47. as the threat of famine loomed & wartime distress deepened, starving evicted peasants demanded the immediate restoration of their hereditary tenancy rights. led again by swami sahajanand saraswati, peasants bypassed petitions & resorted to direct action — physically marching onto the bakasht lands to plant their own crops, facing the lathi-wielding private armies of zamindars & british police. their massive agitation eventually forced the provincial government to pass the bihar bakasht disputes settlement act in 1947. 5.7.3) the punnapra-vayalar uprising (kerala, 1946) this uprising occurred in the princely state of travancore, where the autocratic dewan, sir c.p. ramaswami iyer, had hatched a plan to declare travancore an independent state allied directly with the british crown — refusing to join the indian union. the local populace was already suffering from severe wartime food hoarding & brutal feudal exploitation of coir-factory workers, fishermen, and agricultural labourers. finding organisational leadership through local communist party (cpi) and congress socialist party (csp) cadres, the impoverished workers & peasants mobilised. in october 1946, they armed themselves with little more than sharpened bamboo sticks to fight both their economic oppressors & the dewan's separatist agenda — a crucial instance where the left's radical agrarian agitation directly served the vital national interest of preventing india's balkanisation. they established self-rule camps in the villages of punnapra & vayalar. the dewan sent the state military, equipped with british machine guns, to crush the rebellion — an estimated 1,000 peasants & workers were killed over a few days. however, this immense sacrifice shattered the dewan's authority. he was eventually forced to flee, permanently ending his separatist ambitions & ensuring travancore's integration into the indian republic. 5.7.4) the tebhaga movement (bengal, 1946–1947) the tebhaga movement was a pre-independence peasant struggle that confronted the bengal provincial government while india was still under british rule. "tebhaga" means three parts — peasants demanded the landlord's share be reduced from half (1/2) to one-third (1/3), with the tenant keeping two-thirds. (prelims 2013) the intellectual basis for this demand had been laid by the floud commission (1940) — formally the bengal land revenue commission — which recommended the abolition of the permanent settlement & a restructuring of the landlord-tenant revenue share. however, the bengal government never implemented the floud commission's recommendations — which is precisely why the peasants had to fight for them six years later through the tebhaga agitation. 5.7.5) the telangana armed struggle (1946–1951) the telangana armed struggle was born out of the genuine, horrific exploitation of the rural poor by the nizam of hyderabad's feudal landlords (deshmukhs) through forced labour (vetti) and violent evictions. while the peasants' initial armed resistance against the nizam's brutal razakar militia heroically aided india's national integration, the cpi leadership hijacked the movement's direction. following hyderabad's liberation by the indian army in 1948 (operation polo), the cpi directed the peasants to refuse disarmament & turn their weapons against the newly independent democratic indian republic, transforming a just anti-feudal rebellion into a misguided ideological war that the indian state suppressed by 1951. both tebhaga & telangana operated entirely outside the gandhian framework. 5.8) two ways of looking at this: the historiography of the peasant upsurge historians have disagreed on how to interpret this massive two-decade trajectory of peasant mobilisation — and for a upsc student, understanding both perspectives is essential for mains answers. bipan chandra's view (the nationalist perspective) is that the peasant movement was fundamentally an integral part of the broader anti-colonial struggle. in his reading, the inc provided the initial political awakening, and its left wing successfully pushed the party toward real agrarian reform. even during the massive upsurges of the 1940s — most notably the quit india movement — the peasants' primary target was the colonial state. chandra argues that even the radical, left-led post-war movements (like tebhaga or punnapra-vayalar) struck at the feudal pillars of the british empire, thereby aiding national liberation. the tensions with congress ministries in the 1930s, and the cpi's later anti-national deviation in telangana, are viewed as secondary to this overarching anti-imperialist reality. sekhar bandyopadhyay's perspective (the subaltern/critical perspective) focuses on class conflict & the autonomous consciousness of the peasantry. he argues that "freedom" meant vastly different things to different social groups. when congress ministries accommodated zamindar interests in 1937-39, it revealed the strict class limits of the inc's bourgeois leadership. in this reading, the explosion of the post-war movements (worli, tebhaga, telangana) confirms his central thesis: frustrated by the inc's protection of propertied interests, the rural masses broke free of the congress umbrella. they built their own independent, radical path to fight a parallel class war entirely outside the gandhian framework. the synthesis: both views catch something true. the inc was genuinely anti-colonial, and it brought the peasantry into national politics. it was also a multi-class coalition that could not govern without managing the interests of the propertied classes. the peasantry's journey — from participating peacefully in gandhi's civil disobedience in 1930, to forming the aiks in 1936, to waging armed communist rebellions in 1946 — perfectly illustrates this unresolved tension. the national movement succeeded in throwing out the british, but it left the class struggle in the countryside to be fought out in the early years of the independent republic.
